Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (commentary) on Surat al-Baqarah: It is a Madani surah, revealed over various periods.

It is also said that it was the first surah revealed in Madinah, except for the verse ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], for it is the last verse revealed from the heavens. It was revealed on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) during the Farewell Pilgrimage at Mina. The verses on riba (usury) are also among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed. End of quote.

Abu al-Duraysh in his Fada'il (Virtues), Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas in al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh (Abrogating and Abrogated), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (Proofs of Prophethood) narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Surat al-Baqarah was revealed in Madinah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Abu Dawud in al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: The first surah to be revealed in Madinah was Surat al-Baqarah.

Hadiths have been related on its virtue, among them what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Qur'an will be brought, and those who acted upon it in the world, with Surat al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran going before them." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave three parables for them, and I have not forgotten them since. He said: "It is as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or two dark canopies, or two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companion."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Darimi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, leaving it is a regret, and the idle (al-batalah) cannot master it." Then he was silent for a while and said: "Learn Surat al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two luminous ones. They will shade their companion on the Day of Resurrection, as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds in ranks."

Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is good (hasan) according to the condition of Muslim.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ahmad, Humayd ibn Zanjawayh, Muslim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani and Abu Dharr al-Harawi also narrated something similar, with a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Bazzar in his Sunan also narrated something similar, with a sound chain, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make your houses graves. Indeed, Satan flees from the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated something similar from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil and Ibn 'Asakir in his History narrated something similar from Abu al-Darda', traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated something similar, with a weak chain, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain is weak.

Al-Darimi, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated it from his hadith with similar wording.

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah. Whoever recites it in his house by day, Satan will not enter his house for three days, and whoever recites it in his house by night, Satan will not enter his house for three nights."

Ahmad, Muhammad ibn Nasr, and al-Tabarani narrated with a sound chain from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Baqarah is the summit and the peak of the Qur'an. With each of its verses, eighty angels were sent down, and the verse ﴿Allah – there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer﴾ was extracted from beneath the Throne and joined to it."

Al-Baghawi in Mu'jam al-Sahabah and Ibn 'Asakir in his History narrated from Rabi'ah al-Jarasi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Which part of the Qur'an is best?" He said: "The surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned." It was said: "Which part of al-Baqarah is best?" He said: "The Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi) and the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, which were sent down from beneath the Throne."

Abu 'Ubayd, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his Sahih as a suspended report (ta'liq), Muslim, and al-Nasa'i narrated from Usayd ibn Hudayr, who said: "While he was reciting Surat al-Baqarah at night, and his horse was tethered beside him, the horse began to move about. He fell silent, and it became calm. Then he recited again, and the horse moved about. He fell silent, and it became calm. Then he recited again, and the horse moved about, and he fell silent, and it became calm. He then turned to his son Yahya, who was near it, and feared it might harm him. When he took him, he raised his head toward the sky and saw something like a canopy with lamps in it, which rose up into the sky until he could no longer see it. When morning came, he told the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do you know what that was?' He said: 'No, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Those were angels who drew near to your voice. Had you continued reciting, people would have seen them in the morning, and they would not have been hidden from them.'" This hadith has several wordings.

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a detachment and asked each man among them what he had of the Qur'an" (meaning what he had memorized). "He came to a man, the youngest of them in age, and said: 'What do you have, so-and-so?' He said: 'I have such-and-such and Surat al-Baqarah.' He said: 'Do you have Surat al-Baqarah?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Go, for you are their commander.'"

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed me, though I was the youngest of the delegation from Thaqif who had come to him, because I had memorized Surat al-Baqarah."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated with a sound chain from al-Salsal ibn al-Dayhamis that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Surat al-Baqarah in your houses, and do not make them graves." He said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Baqarah on a night (p-22) will be crowned with a crown in Paradise."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad, from Jarir ibn Hazim, from his paternal uncle Jarir ibn Yazid, that the elders of the people of Madinah related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that it was said to him: "Have you not seen Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas? His house has not ceased to shine with lamps the previous night." He said: "Perhaps he recited Surat al-Baqarah." Thabit was asked and said: "I recited Surat al-Baqarah."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a good chain, except that it contains vagueness (ibhām), and it is also mursal (its transmission breaks off).

The imams of hadith have related many hadiths and numerous reports from the Companions on its virtues. Among its virtues are those specific to the Verse of the Throne, those specific to the final verses of this surah, some of which has already been mentioned, and those concerning its virtue and the virtue of Al 'Imran, some of which has also already been mentioned. Among them are also those concerning the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal). Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I have been given the seven in place of the Torah, I have been given the hundreds (al-mi'in) in place of the Gospel, I have been given the oft-repeated (al-mathani) in place of the Psalms, and I have been favored with the detailed surahs (al-mufassal)." In its chain is Sa'id ibn Bashir, who is weak, and it was also narrated by another chain from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal.

He also narrated from 'A'ishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever takes up the seven is good." Ahmad narrated it from her in his Musnad with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever takes up the first seven from the Qur'an is good.'"

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr: 87]. He said: They are the seven long surahs: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and Yunus. Mujahid, Makhul, 'Atiyyah ibn Qays, Abu Muhammad al-Qari Shaddad ibn 'Abd Allah, and Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Dhimari also said this.

There has come what indicates the disliking of one saying: "Surat al-Baqarah," or "Surat Al 'Imran," or "Surat al-Nisa'," and likewise "the Qur'an in its entirety."

Ibn al-Durays and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated with a weak chain from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not say: 'Surat al-Baqarah,' nor 'Surat Al 'Imran,' nor 'Surat al-Nisa',' and likewise 'the Qur'an in its entirety.' Rather, say: 'the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned,' and 'the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned,' and likewise 'the Qur'an in its entirety.'" Ibn Kathir said: This is a gharib hadith whose attribution to the Prophet is not sound. Its chain includes Yahya ibn Maymun al-Khawwas, who is weak in narration and cannot be used as evidence.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated with a sound chain from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Do not say 'Surat al-Baqarah,' but say 'the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned.'"

Something contrary to this has also been related from a group of Companions.

It is established in the two Sahihs from Ibn Mas'ud that he threw the pebble at Jamrah from the bottom of the valley, placing the House on his left and Mina on his right, and then said: "This is the place of the one upon whom Surat al-Baqarah was revealed."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: "I prayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night in Ramadan. He began with al-Baqarah, and I said: 'He will pray it in one rak'ah.' Then he began al-Nisa' and recited it, then he began Al 'Imran and recited it slowly..." The hadith continues.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "I used to stand in prayer at night with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would recite al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, and al-Nisa'."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi in al-Shama'il, al-Nasa'i, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "I stood in prayer with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night. He stood and recited Surat al-Baqarah, and he did not pass any verse of mercy without stopping at it..." The hadith continues.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: The commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the letters that occur at the beginnings of the surahs. Al-Sha'bi, Sufyan al-Thawri, and a group of hadith scholars said: They are the secret of Allah in the Qur'an. For Allah has a secret in each of His books. They are part of the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters, the knowledge of which Allah has reserved for Himself. We do not wish to speak about them, but we believe in them, and they are recited as they came.

This view is also reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

He said: Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi mentioned, from 'Umar, 'Uthman, and Ibn Mas'ud, that they said: The disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) are among the hidden matters that are not to be explained.

Abu Hatim said: We do not find the letters in the Qur'an except at the beginnings of the surahs, and we do not know what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended by them.

He said: A large group of scholars said: Rather, we wish to speak about them, seek the benefits beneath them, and the meanings that may be derived from them.

They differed on this in many opinions. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and also from 'Ali that the disjointed letters in the Qur'an are the Greatest Name of Allah, except that we do not know how it is composed from them.

Qutrub, al-Farra', and others said: They are an indication of the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-hijA'), by which Allah informed the Arabs, when He challenged them with the Qur'an, that it is composed of letters from which their speech is built, so that their inability to produce its like would be a more compelling proof against them, since it did not depart from their language.

Qutrub said: They used to flee when they heard the Qur'an. When ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ and ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ were revealed, they found this utterance strange. When they listened attentively to him (ﷺ), he addressed them with the Qur'an composed of these letters, so that it would fix itself in their hearing and their ears, and establish the proof against them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

Some people said: It has been narrated that when the polytheists turned away from the Qur'an in Makkah, Allah revealed ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during its recitation, that you may prevail."﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. They found this strange, so they opened their ears and listened to the Qur'an after that, and thus the proof was established against them.

A group said: They are letters that indicate names, from which some letters were taken and the rest omitted. This is like the saying of Ibn Abbas and others: the alif is from Allah (Allah), the lam from Jibril (Jibril), and the mim from Muhammad (Muhammad).

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) followed this view and said: I hold that each letter among them conveys a meaning.

The Arabs have indeed spoken with the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah), as in the saying of the poet:
"I said to her, 'Stop (qifi)!' and she said, 'Qaf!'"
That is, "I stopped."

In a hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim with half a word." Shaqiq said: This means that he says to someone who says "uqtul" (kill): "uq." Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The sword suffices as shā," meaning shāfiyan (curing); in another version it is shāhidan (as a witness).

Zayd ibn Aslam said: They are names of the surahs.

Al-Kalbi said: They are oaths which Allah swore by, for their nobility and excellence, and they are among His names.

Among the most subtle things that the theologians (al-mutakallimun) brought forth regarding the meanings of these letters is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Kashshaf. He said: "Know that when you consider the names that Allah, Mighty is His authority, has placed at the openings of the surahs, you will find that they are exactly half of the names of the letters of the alphabet, fourteen in number: they are alif, lam, mim, sad, ra, kaf, ha, ya, ayn, ta, sin, ha, qaf and nun, across twenty-nine surahs, corresponding to the number of the letters of the alphabet. Then, when you look at these fourteen, you will find that they include half of each class of letters.

The explanation of this is that among the whispered letters (al-mahmusah), half are: sad, kaf, ha, sin and ha. Among the voiced letters (al-majhurah), half are: alif, lam, mim, ra, ayn, ta, qaf, ya and nun. Among the plosive letters (al-shadidah), half are: alif, kaf, ta and nun. Among the fricative letters (al-rikhwah), half are: lam, mim, ra, sad, ha, ayn, sin, ha, ya and nun. Among the emphatic letters (al-mutbaqah), half are: sad and ta. Among the open letters (al-munfatihah), half are: alif, lam, mim, ra, kaf, ha, ayn, sin, ha, qaf, ya and nun. Among the raised letters (al-musta'liyah), half are: qaf, sad and ta. Among the lowered letters (al-munkhafidah), half are: alif, lam, mim, ra, kaf, ha, ta, ayn, sin, ha and nun. Among the echoing letters (huruf al-qalqalah), half are: qaf and ta.

Then, when you survey the words and their compositions, you will find that the letters Allah omitted from mention in these classes are stored within the ones mentioned. Glory be to Him, in whose wisdom every thing is finely wrought. You know that the majority of a thing, and most of it, takes the place of its whole, and this matches the subtleties of the revelation and its brevity. It is as if Allah, Mighty is His name, enumerated for the Arabs the letters from which their speech is composed, as an indication of what I have mentioned: rebuking them and establishing the proof against them. What indicates that He deliberately mentioned the most frequently occurring of the letters of the alphabet in the compositions of words is that alif and lam, since their occurrence is so abundant, came in most of these openings doubled. These are the openings of the surahs al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Rum, al-'Ankabut, Luqman, al-Sajdah, al-A'raf, al-Ra'd, Yunus, Ibrahim, Hud, Yusuf and al-Hijr." End of quote.

I say: This precision brings no benefit that is worth considering. Its clarification is that if its purpose is to establish the proof and rebuke, as he said, then this is easily achieved by saying to them: "This Qur'an is made of the letters you speak with; it is not made of letters different from them." This would be a rebuke and a proof that every listener among them understands, without riddles, obscurity, or the scattering of these letters across the openings of twenty-nine surahs. Moreover, this kind of lengthy matter, which the listener cannot complete except by hearing all these openings, is also something that none of the listeners could understand or comprehend anything of, let alone that it would be a rebuke to them or an establishment of proof against them, whatever it may be. For that is a matter beyond understanding, dependent upon it, and the listener did not understand it. Nor did the scholars report that any individual of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) to whom the Qur'an was addressed reached an understanding of even some of this, let alone all of it.

Then, that these letters comprise half of all the letters from which the language of the Arabs is formed, and that half includes half of those types of letters that are characterised by those attributes, is a matter that brings no benefit to any person of the Jahiliyyah or of Islam, to one who affirms or denies, to one who accepts or opposes. It is not valid that this should be one of the purposes of the Lord, glory be to Him, who sent down His Book for guidance to its laws and for the guidance it provides.

Suppose this is a wondrous craft and a strange subtlety; still, this is not something characterised by eloquence (fasahah) or rhetorical excellence (balaghah), so as to indicate that it is an eloquent or rhetorically excellent speech. This is because these letters found at the openings are not of the type of the speech of the Arabs, so as to be described by these two qualities. At most, they are of the type of the letters of their speech, and this has no bearing on what has been mentioned.

Furthermore, even if we suppose that they are words formed by supposing something before or after them, they still could not be described as such, because they are an obscure concealment, not understood by the listener unless someone comes who intends to explain them with the same effort as one who explains riddles and enigmas. That is not eloquence or rhetorical excellence in either source or outcome; rather, it is the opposite of both and the reverse of their form.

Knowing this, be aware that whoever speaks about explaining the meanings of these letters while being certain that this is what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended, has committed the gravest error, has plunged deeply into understanding, and has made the most outrageous claim. For if his interpretation of them, by what he has explained them, is referred to the language of the Arabs and its sciences, then it is pure falsehood. The Arabs never spoke anything of that kind, and if a listener among them heard it, it would be considered by him as babbling (al-ratanah). This does not contradict the fact that they sometimes restrict themselves to some letters or a letter of the word they want to pronounce; but they only do that after something has preceded it which indicates it and conveys its meaning, such that it is not confused for the listener, as in the example mentioned earlier.

Of this type is what occurs among them in tarkhim (apocope, the shortening of words). But where are these openings at the beginnings of the surahs in relation to this? When it has been established for you that what they have claimed cannot be drawn from the language of the Arabs and its sciences, then only one of two matters remains:

The first is interpretation by mere opinion (tafsir bi-mahd al-ra'y), which has been prohibited and for which a warning has been issued. The people of knowledge are the most worthy of avoiding it, keeping away from it, and steering clear of its path. They are too fearful of Allah, glory be to Him, to make the Book of Allah, glory be to Him, a plaything for them, toying with it and placing the follies of their speculations and the nonsense of their thoughts upon it.

The second is interpretation based on tawqif (authoritative transmission) from the Lawgiver. This is the clear path and the straight way, indeed the main road, besides which there is only rejection, and the thriving path, besides which there is nothing. Whoever finds something of this kind is not obliged to speak boldly and say whatever his knowledge reaches. Whoever has not reached anything of this kind should say: "I do not know," or "Allah knows best what He intends." The prohibition against seeking to understand the mutashabih (ambiguous verses) and attempting to grasp their knowledge has been established, even though they are Arabic words and intelligible constructions. Allah has made the pursuit of this the practice of those in whose hearts there is deviation. So how about what we are dealing with here? It should be said of it that it is "the ambiguity of the ambiguous," even on the supposition that there is a way to understanding it and a place for the Arabic language in it. How much more so when it lies outside of that under every assumption.

Consider how the Jews understood upon hearing ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾. When they did not find it in the pattern of the Arabic language, they understood that these letters were a symbol for a number they conventionally assigned to them. This is as Ibn Ishaq and al-Bukhari in his History, and Ibn Jarir with a weak chain, reported from Ibn Abbas, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with some men from the Jews while he was reciting the opening of surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book; there is no doubt in it.﴾ So he came to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab with some men of the Jews and said: "By Allah, you know I heard Muhammad reciting in what was revealed to him: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book.﴾" Huyayy said: "Did you hear it yourself?" He said: "Yes." So Huyayy set out with those men to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, did you not mention that you recite in what was revealed to you: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book﴾?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Did Jibril bring you this from Allah?" He said: "Yes."

They said: "Allah sent prophets before you, and we do not know that anyone among them was told the duration of his kingdom or the lifespan of his nation except you." Huyayy ibn Akhtab then turned to those who were with him and said: "Alif is one, lam is thirty, and mim is forty; these add up to seventy-one years. Will you enter the religion of a prophet whose kingdom and the lifespan of whose nation is only seventy-one years?" Then he turned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, is there anything more with this?" He said: "Yes." He asked: "What is it?" He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾. He said: "This is heavier and longer: alif is one, lam is thirty, mim is forty, and sad is ninety. These add up to one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything more with this, O Muhammad?" He said: "Yes." He asked: "What is it?" He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾. He said: "This is heavier and longer: alif is one, lam is thirty, and ra is two hundred. This is two hundred and thirty-one years. Is there anything more with this?" He said: "Yes, ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾." He said: "Then this is heavier and longer: alif is one, lam is thirty, mim is forty, and ra is two hundred. These add up to two hundred and seventy-one years." Then he said: "Your matter has been confused for us, O Muhammad, to the point that we do not know whether you have been given little or much." Then they got up. Abu Yasir said to his brother Huyayy and those rabbis with him: "What do you know? Perhaps all of this has been gathered for Muhammad: seventy-one, and one hundred and sixty-one, and two hundred and thirty-one, and two hundred and seventy-one, which makes seven hundred and thirty-four years." They said: "His matter has become confused for us." So they claimed that these verses were revealed about them: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definitive, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

So look at how far their understanding went regarding this matter, which pertained to them specifically, concerning the number of the letters, even though it is not from the language of the Arabs at all. Consider what place is more deserving of clarification from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than this one. These accursed people made what they understood upon hearing ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book﴾ from that number an obstacle to responding to him and entering his law. If there had been a meaning that could be understood and an indication that could be grasped, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have repelled their assumption from the outset, so that the doubts they brought to those with him would not have had any effect.

If you ask: Has anything from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) been established regarding these openings that is suitable to be relied upon? I say: I do not know of any statement by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about any of their meanings. Rather, the most that has been established from him is merely the number of their letters. Al-Bukhari in his History, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and al-Hakim, who also graded it sound, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of Allah, for him there is a good deed, and a good deed is multiplied by ten. I do not say that Alif Lam Mim is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lam is a letter, and mim is a letter." This hadith has several chains (turuq) from Ibn Mas'ud.

and Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bazzar narrated with a weak chain, from Awf ibn Malik and al-Ashja'i, something similar to it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

If you ask: has anything of this been related from the Companions with a continuous chain back to the one who said it, or is there nothing beyond what preceded from al-Qurtubi's report from Ibn Abbas and Ali? I say: Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi, in Kitab al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Alif-lam-mim is a letter, derived from the letters of the name of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ and ﴿Nun﴾, that he said: "It is a disjointed name."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Asma' related from Ibn Abbas also, regarding His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad﴾, ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾, ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾, ﴿Ta-Ha﴾, ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾, ﴿Ta-Sin﴾, ﴿Ya-Sin﴾, ﴿Sad﴾, ﴿Ha-Mim﴾, ﴿Qaf﴾ and ﴿Nun﴾, that he said: "It is an oath which Allah swore, and it is one of the names of Allah."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying "﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾" that he said: "It is the Greatest Name of Allah."

Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His saying "﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾" that he said: "The Alif is the key to His name Allah, the Lam is the key to His name Latif (the Subtle), and the Mim is the key to His name Majid (the Glorious)."

Similar interpretations have been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un), among them Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan.

If you ask: may one follow any of the Companions who spoke on the interpretation of some of these openings with a statement whose chain is sound back to him? I say: No, for the reasons we have given, unless it is known that he said that on knowledge he took from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If you ask: this is a matter in which there is no room for ijtihad (independent reasoning) and no place for the Arabic language, so why should it not have the ruling of the attributed-to-the-Prophet (marfu') report? I say: Giving this the status of a marfu' report, even though some people of usul (legal theory) and others have said so, is not something that the hearts of the fair-minded are at ease with, especially when it concerns this station, which is the interpretation of the speech of Allah, glorified is He, for this is entering into the gravest danger with nothing sound as proof except the mere claim that it is very unlikely for a Companion to say, by his own opinion alone, something in which there is no room for ijtihad. Yet this mere improbability does not justify falling into the danger of a severe warning.

Moreover, it is possible that some Companions went to interpret some of the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), as you find often in their reported interpretations, and that they regarded these openings as part of the mutashabih. Then there is another obstacle: what is related from the Companions on this is conflicting and contradictory. If we act on what one of them said to the exclusion of the other, it would be arbitrary with no basis; and if we act on all of them, it would be acting on what is contradictory, which is not permitted.

Then there is another obstacle beyond this one: if any of what they said had been taken from the Prophet (ﷺ), they would have agreed upon it and would not have differed, like the rest of what is taken from him. Since they differed on this, we know that it was not taken from the Prophet (ﷺ). Furthermore, if they had had anything from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this, they would not have abandoned relating it from him and attributing it to him, especially given their disagreement and the confusion of their statements on such speech, in which the Arabic language has no room and no place.

What I hold for myself, and for everyone who loves safety and follows the pious predecessors of this Community, is that one should not speak anything about these, while acknowledging that in their revelation there is a wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which our minds cannot reach and our understandings cannot grasp. When you reach safety in your own sphere, do not go beyond it. Later, at the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book, in it are verses that are definite—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], there will be a lengthy discussion, and the verification of its acceptance by sound minds and sound intellects.

The demonstrative in His words "that" refers to the Book mentioned after it.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿That Book﴾ means "this Book." Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jurayj also said the same, and al-Bukhari related it from Abu ʿUbaydah.

The Arabs sometimes use the demonstrative for something distant and absent in place of the demonstrative for something near and present, as Khufaf said:

"I say to him while the spear bends his side: Consider Khufaf, that I am that one (dhalika)."

That is, "I am this one." From this usage is His saying: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [al-Sajdah: 6]; ﴿And that is Our argument, which We gave to Abraham﴾ [al-Anʿam: 83]; ﴿Those are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 252]; ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10].

It has also been said that the demonstrative refers to something absent, and there is disagreement about which absent thing is meant. It was said that it is the Book that was written over the creatures concerning their happiness and misery, their term of life and their provision.

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ means there is no one who can alter it. It was also said that "that Book" is the Book which Allah wrote over Himself in eternity, that His mercy precedes His wrath, as in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah finished creating the creation, He wrote in a Book, which is placed with Him, concerning Himself: 'Indeed My mercy overcomes My anger.'"

In another narration: "precedes."

It was also said that the demonstrative refers to what had been revealed in Makkah. It was said to refer to what is in the Torah and the Gospel. It was said that it refers to His earlier words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this view. Disagreement on this point reached ten opinions, as related by al-Qurtubi, and the most preferred of them is what we have presented first.

The demonstrative is the subject (mubtadaʾ), ﴿the Book﴾ is its attribute (ṣifah), and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾. Whoever permits beginning with ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ makes ﴿that﴾ a second subject, and its predicate is ﴿the Book﴾, or it is its attribute, and the predicate is ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾; the whole clause is then the predicate of the first subject.

It is also permissible for the subject to be implied, with its predicate being ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ and what follows it.

Al-rayb is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is the unease and agitation of the soul. It was said that al-rayb is doubt.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: I know of no disagreement on this.

Al-rayb may also be used in the sense of accusation and need, as al-Qurtubi related.

The meaning of this general negation is that the Book is not a place for doubt, because its indication is so clear that it stands in the place of proof, requiring that doubt about it should not be entertained in any way.

The pause on ﴿in it﴾ is the well-known one. It has been related from Nafiʿ and ʿAsim that they paused at ﴿there is no doubt﴾.

In al-Kashshaf it says: The one who pauses must intend a predicate, and a parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They said: No harm﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ: 50], and the saying of the Arabs: "No harm (lā baʾs)," and such expressions are many in the speech of the people of the Hijaz. The implied meaning is: "There is no doubt in it, it is guidance."

Guidance (al-hudā) is a verbal noun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the indication that leads to the desired goal, as evidenced by the fact that error is set against it, and that is the end of his words.

Its position is nominative as a subject, and its predicate is the prepositional phrase mentioned before it, as previously explained.

Al-Qurtubi said: Guidance is of two kinds: the guidance of indication (hudā dalālah), which the Messengers and their followers are able to provide. Allah said: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Raʿd: 7], and He said: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. So He attributed to them the guidance whose meaning is indication, calling and admonition. And He, glorified is He, alone holds the guidance whose meaning is support and enabling success, so He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. Thus guidance in this sense comes to mean the creation of faith in the heart, and from this is His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾, and His saying: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾. End of quotation.

Al-Muttaqin are those in whom taqwa is established.

Ibn Faris said: Its original meaning in the language is the scarcity of speech.

In al-Kashshaf it says: The muttaqi in the language is an active participle from their saying: "He protected him (waqāhu), so he became protected (ittaqā)." Al-wiqāyah is protection. From this comes the expression "a protective horse (faras wāqin)." And this animal protects from its hoof-covering when it is hurt by a stone from the roughness of the ground or the thinness of the hoof, so it protects its hoof from anything small that would hurt it.

In the sharīʿah (sacred law), it means one who protects himself from engaging in what would make him deserve punishment, whether by doing or by abandoning. End of quotation.

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Masʿud that "the Book" is the Qur'an, and "there is no doubt in it" means there is no uncertainty in it.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, that he said: there is no uncertainty in it.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Darda', who said: al-rayb is doubt.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah something similar, and Ibn Jarir related it from Mujahid likewise.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Masʿud, regarding His saying ﴿a guidance for the muttaqin﴾, that he said: a light for the muttaqin, and they are the believers.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿a guidance for the muttaqin﴾, that they are those who fear Allah's punishment by abandoning what they know of the guidance, and who hope for His mercy by affirming what has come from Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muʿadh ibn Jabal that he was asked: Who are the muttaqun? He said: A people who guarded against shirk and the worship of idols, and devoted worship purely to Allah.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related from Abu Hurayrah that a man asked him: What is taqwa? He said: Have you ever found a path with thorns? He said: Yes. He said: What did you do? He said: When I saw the thorns, I turned away from them, or I passed beyond them, or I fell short of them. He said: That is taqwa.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd related from Abu al-Darda', who said: The completeness of taqwa is that a servant fears Allah to the point that he guards himself even from the weight of an atom, by leaving some of what he sees as permissible, out of fear that it may become a barrier between him and the forbidden.

Something similar to what Abu al-Darda' said has been related from a group of the Successors (tabiʿun).

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab related from ʿAtiyyah al-Saʿdi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A servant does not reach the level of being among the muttaqin until he abandons what is not harmful to him, out of caution about what may be harmful." Therefore, acting on what this hadith conveys is obligatory, and this would be a legal (sharʿī) meaning of the muttaqi, more specific than the meaning we presented earlier from the author of al-Kashshaf, who claimed that it is the legal meaning.

(p-26) It is a descriptive qualification of *al-muttaqin* (the God-conscious), clarifying their nature. *Al-iman* (faith) linguistically means *al-tasdiq* (affirmation and acceptance), and in the sacred law (*al-shar'*) it is what will be explained later.

*Al-ghayb* (the unseen), in the speech of the Arabs, is everything that is absent from you.

Al-Qurtubi said: The exegetes differed over the interpretation of *al-ghayb* here. One group said: *al-ghayb* in this verse is God, the Exalted, and Ibn al-Arabi regarded this view as weak.

Others said: it is the divine decree and destiny (*al-qada' wa al-qadar*).

Others said: it is the Qur'an and what it contains of unseen matters.

Others said: *al-ghayb* is everything the Messenger reported that reason cannot reach, such as the signs of the Hour, the punishment of the grave, the gathering, the resurrection, the bridge (*al-sirat*), the scale (*al-mizan*), Paradise and Hell.

Ibn Atiyya said: These statements do not contradict one another; rather, *al-ghayb* applies to all of them. He said: This is the sacred-law meaning of *iman* (faith) referred to in the hadith of Jibril (Gabriel), when he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Inform me about *iman*." He (ﷺ) said: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in the divine decree, its good and its evil." He said: "You have spoken truly." End of quotation.

This hadith is authentically established in the *Sahih* with the wording: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and in the decree, its good and its evil."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym, all in *Ma'rifat al-Sahaba* (Knowledge of the Companions), transmitted from Tuwaylah bint Aslam, who said: "I prayed the noon or the afternoon prayer in the mosque of Bani Harithah. We faced the mosque of Iliya (Jerusalem) and prayed two prostrations. Then a man came to us and informed us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had turned to face the House (the Ka'bah). So the men moved to the women's place and the women to the men's place. We then prayed the remaining two prostrations facing the Sacred House. When this reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: 'Those are a people who believed in the unseen.'"

Al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said: 'Tell me, who are the people with the best faith (*iman*)?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, the angels.' He said: 'They are so, and it is their due. Why would they not be, when God has given them the station He gave them?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, the prophets, whom God honored with His message and prophethood.' He said: 'They are so, and it is their due. Why would they not be, when God has given them the station He gave them?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, the martyrs who were slain with the prophets.' He said: 'They are so, and why would they not be, when God has honored them with martyrdom?' They said: 'Then who, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'People who will be in the loins of men, who will come after me, who believe in me though they have not seen me, and who affirm me though they have not seen me. They will find the leaf (scroll) hanging and act upon what is in it. These are the best of the people of faith in faith.'"

In its chain is Muhammad ibn Abi Humayd, and there is weakness in him.

Al-Hasan ibn Arafa in his well-known *Hizb* and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* transmitted from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, and mentioned something similar to the first hadith. In its chain is al-Mughira ibn Qays al-Basri, who is *munkar al-hadith* (a narrator whose reports are rejected).

Al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Isma'ili transmitted from Abu Hurayra, also traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Bazzar from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Shaybah in his *Musnad* transmitted from Awf ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Would that I had met my brothers." They said: "O Messenger of God, are we not your brothers?" He said: "Yes, but they are a people who will come after you, who believe in me as you believe, affirm me as you affirm, and support me as you support. Would that I had met my brothers." Ibn Asakir transmitted something similar in *al-Arba'in al-Suba'iyya* from the hadith of Anas, and in its chain is Abu Hudba, who is a liar. In it he added: "Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen and establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3], the verse."

Ahmad, al-Darimi, al-Baroudi and Ibn Qani' together in *Mu'jam al-Sahaba*, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim transmitted from Abu Jumu'a al-Ansari, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, is there any people greater in reward than us? We believed in you and followed you.' He said: 'What prevents you from that, when the Messenger of God is among you, bringing you revelation from heaven? Rather, there will be a people who come after you, to whom the Book of God will be given between two covers, and they will believe in me and act upon what is in it. Those are greater in reward than you.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Hakim transmitted from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Juhani, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), two riders appeared. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Two men from Kinda or Madhhij.' They came until they reached him. They were two men from Madhhij. One of them drew near to pledge allegiance to him. When he took his hand, he said: 'O Messenger of God, what do you say of one who came to you, believed in you, followed you, and affirmed you? What is his reward?' He said: 'Blessed is he.' He then wiped his forearm and departed. Then the other came, took his hand to pledge allegiance, and said: 'O Messenger of God, what do you say of one who believed in you, affirmed you, followed you, and did not see you?' He said: 'Blessed is he, then blessed is he.' Then he wiped his forearm and departed."

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim transmitted from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Blessed is the one who saw me and believed in me, and blessed is the one who believed in me without seeing me, seven times."

Ahmad and Ibn Hibban transmitted from Abu Sa'id that a man said: "O Messenger of God, blessed is the one who saw you and believed in you?" He said: "Blessed is the one who saw me and believed in me, and blessed, then blessed, then blessed is the one who believed in me without seeing me." Al-Tayalisi and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted something similar from Ibn Umar.

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani transmitted from the hadith of Anas something similar to the hadith of Abu Umama al-Bahili mentioned above.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad ibn Mani' in his *Musnad*, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Dubari and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "By the One besides whom there is no god, no one has believed with a faith better than faith in the unseen." Then he recited: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ up to His words: ﴿the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:1-5].

There are views among the Successors (*al-tabi'un*), but the preponderant view is what has preceded: that the sacred-law *iman* applies to everything mentioned here.

Ibn Jarir said: The better view is that you are described as those who believe in the unseen in statement, belief and action.

He said: The fear of God enters into the meaning of *iman*, which is the affirmation of speech by action.

*Iman* is a comprehensive term for acknowledging God, His books and His messengers, and confirming that acknowledgment by deed.

Ibn Kathir said: The sacred-law *iman* that is required is not complete except as belief, speech and action. This is the view of most of the imams.

Indeed, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Ubayd and others have related as a consensus (*ijma'*) that *iman* is speech and action, and that it increases and decreases.

Many verses have been revealed concerning this.

End of quotation.

* *

﴿And who establish the prayer﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) upon ﴿they believe﴾. *Al-iqama* (establishment) originally means continuance and steadfastness (*al-dawam wa al-thabat*) (p-27).

It is said: "The thing stood" (*qama al-shay'*), meaning it lasted and remained. It is not from standing on the foot; rather, it is from your saying "the truth stood," meaning it became manifest and firm. The poet said:

"And war stood with us upon its shank."

Another said:

"When it is said: 'Stand up,' you do not stir until the horses establish the market of spear-thrusting."

*Iqamat al-salat* (establishing the prayer) means performing it with its pillars, its sunan (recommended practices) and its forms, at its appointed times.

*Al-salat* originally means, linguistically, supplication, from *sallaa yusalli* when he supplicated. Al-Jawhari and others mentioned this.

Some said it is derived from *al-sala*, which is a vein in the middle of the back that splits at the hip. From this the rider in horse racing took his name, because he comes in the race with his head beside the sala of the leading horse. So *al-salat* was derived from it, because it is second to *iman*, and the one who prays among the horses is likened to it.

Or because the bowing person bends his two *salawayn* (sides of the back), and the *sala* is the place where the tail joins the horse, and the two are *salawan*. The one who prays is the follower of the leader, because his head is beside his *salw*.

Al-Qurtubi mentioned this in his *Tafsir*.

The second meaning was mentioned in *al-Kashshaf*. This is the linguistic meaning.

As for the sacred-law meaning, it is this prayer that consists of pillars and invocations.

The people of knowledge have differed over whether it has retained its linguistic meaning or was established by the sacred law as a fresh technical term from the outset.

It has been said: the first. The sacred law only added supplements, which are the conditions and obligations established in it.

Others said: the second.

*Al-rizq* (provision), according to the majority, is whatever is fit to be benefited from, whether lawful or unlawful, contrary to the Mu'tazila. They said: the unlawful is not provision. The discussion of this question has a place other than this.

*Al-infaq* (spending) is taking money out of the hand. In bringing *min* (from) here as partitive (*tab'idiyya*), there is a subtle point: guidance toward avoiding extravagance (*al-israf*).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Ishaq transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿they establish the prayer﴾ that he said: "The five prayers." ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾: "The zakat of their wealth."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatada that the establishment of the prayer is guarding its times, its ablution, its bowing and its prostration. ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾: "They spent in God's obligations which He imposed upon them in His obedience and His path."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ that he said: "It is a man's expenditure upon his family."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "Expenditures were acts of devotion by which they drew near to God, the Mighty and Majestic, according to their means and effort, until the obligatory charities were revealed in Surat Bara'a. They are the *al-nasikhat al-mubayyinat* (abrogating and clarifying ones)."

Ibn Jarir chose that the verse is general, covering zakat and expenditures. This is the truth, without distinction between spending on relatives and others, and between obligatory and voluntary charity. The non-specification of any type among the kinds to which the name *infaq* applies gives the most complete indication of generality.

* *

﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the successful﴾ (p-28)

This is a new statement (*kalam mustanaf*) in an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if it were said: "What is the state of these people who combine God-consciousness, belief in the unseen, performance of the obligations, and belief in what was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to those prophets before him, peace be upon them?" So it was said: ﴿They are upon guidance﴾. It is also possible that this is a predicate about those who believe in the unseen, etc., in which case it is connected to what precedes it.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The meaning of the elevation in His words "upon guidance" is a metaphor for their firm establishment in guidance, their steadfastness upon it and their clinging to it. Their state is likened to that of one who rises above a thing and mounts it. Similar is: "He is upon the truth" and "He is upon falsehood." They have clarified this in His words: "He made error a mount, rode ignorance, and settled upon the wandering of desire." End of quotation.

The verifiers have extended discussion on this beyond what the present place can contain. The disagreement over this became famous between the verifier al-Sa'd and the verifier al-Sharif.

Those after them differed over preferring the stronger of the two views. I have compiled a treatise on this titled [*Al-Tawd al-Muneef fi Tarjih ma qalahu al-Sa'd ala ma qalahu al-Sharif*]. Whoever wishes for the matter to become clear and to gather the aspects of the discussion completely should refer to it.

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning of ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ is: upon light from their Lord, proof, rectitude and right direction, by God's guidance of them and His granting them success. ﴿And the successful﴾, that is, those who succeed, who are mindful of what they sought from God through their deeds, their faith in God, His books and His messengers.

This is the meaning of his statement.

Al-Falah (success) originally means, in the language, splitting and cutting. Abu 'Ubayd said this. It is also said that the one whose lip is split is "aflah" (having a cleft lip), and from this the farmer was called "fallah" (ploughman), because he splits the earth with tilling. So the one who attains success has cut through difficulties until he has reached what he sought.

Al-Qurtubi said: It may also be used for victory and survival, and this too is its original meaning in the language. So the meaning of ﴿Those are the successful ones﴾ is: those who triumph with Paradise and those who remain in it.

In al-Kashshaf, he said: "The muflih (successful one) is the one who attains the desired goal, as if the doors of victory have been opened for him and have not been locked against him." End of quote.

Falah has also been used for the pre-dawn meal (suhur). From this is the hadith recorded by Abu Dawud: "Until we nearly missed al-falah with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." I said: "And what is al-falah?" He said: "The suhur."

So the sense of the hadith is that by suhur the fast continues, and for this reason it was called falah.

The repetition of the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) indicates that each of guidance and success is independent in distinguishing them from others, such that if either one alone were present, it would suffice as a distinction on its own.

The purpose of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) is to indicate that the subject is exclusively attributed to the predicate and to no other.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik and Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions, that ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ are the believers among the Arabs who believe in what was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and what was revealed before him, and the believers among the People of the Book. Then He gathered the two groups and said: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful ones﴾. We have already mentioned this, and what is more preponderant than it, as is transmitted from Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we recite from the Qur'an and we hope, and we recite and nearly despair,' or as he said. He said: 'Shall I not inform you about the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ up to his words ﴿the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–5] — these are the people of Paradise. They said: 'We hope that we are among these.' Then he said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is alike for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6] up to his words ﴿a great punishment﴾ — these are the people of the Fire. They said: 'Are we not them, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Indeed.'"

Hadiths have been related concerning the excellence of these noble verses. Among them is what 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad recorded in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, and al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a Bedouin came and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, my brother has an ailment.' He said: 'What is his ailment?' He said: 'He has a jinn-possession (lamam).' He said: 'Bring him to me.' So he placed him before him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited over him the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah), four verses from the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, these two verses ﴿Your God is One God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], the Verse of the Throne, three verses from the end of Surat al-Baqarah, a verse from Al 'Imran ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], a verse from al-A'raf ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], the end of Surat al-Mu'minun ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 116]—(note: 114), a verse from Surat al-Jinn ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾ [al-Jinn: 3], ten verses from the beginning of al-Saffat, three verses from the end of al-Hashr, and Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad and the two protective surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn). Then the man stood up as if he had never complained at all."

Ibn al-Sunni in 'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Layla narrated a similar report through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Ya'la, from a man, from Ubayy, like it.

al-Darimi and Ibn al-Durays recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Whoever recites four verses from the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, the Verse of the Throne, two verses after the Verse of the Throne, and three from the end of Surat al-Baqarah, no devil will approach him or his family that day, nor anything he dislikes regarding his family or his wealth, and it is not recited over a madman except that he recovers."

al-Darimi, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani recorded from him: "Whoever recites ten verses from Surat al-Baqarah in a night, no devil will enter that house that night until morning: four from its beginning, the Verse of the Throne, two after it, and three at its end, beginning with ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Darimi and al-Bayhaqi recorded from al-Mughirah ibn Subay', who was among the companions of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, something similar.

al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, do not hold him back; hasten him to his grave, and let there be recited at his head the opening of Surat al-Baqarah, and at his feet the closing of Surat al-Baqarah." Other than this has also been related concerning that.

It has been said: they are the believers among the People of the Book, for they combined belief in what Allah sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) and what He sent down to those before him, and the verse was revealed concerning them.

Ibn Jarir (Ibn Jarir al-Tabari) favoured this view. al-Suddi transmitted it in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Companions. Ibn Jarir cited as evidence the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to you and what has been sent down to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], and the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it. And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were Muslims before it." Those will be given their reward twice﴾ [al-Qasas: 52-54], and so on to the end of the verse.

The first verse was revealed concerning the believers among the Arabs.

It has also been said: both verses together refer to believers in general.

On this view, this sentence is joined to the first sentence as a further description of the muttaqun (the God-conscious), one description after another. It may also be in the nominative (marfu') by way of resumption (al-istinaf, a new sentence beginning without grammatical dependence on what precedes). It may also be governed by the muttaqun, so that the sense is: "a guidance for the God-conscious and for those who believe in what has been sent down to you."

What is meant by "what was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ)" is the Qur'an, and what was sent down before him is the earlier scriptures.

Al-iqan (certainty) is the certainty of knowledge that doubt and suspicion have no place in it. So said al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf. The meaning is that they are certain of the Resurrection, the rising again, and the rest of the matters of the Hereafter, without doubt.

Al-akhirah is the feminine form of al-akhar (the other), which is the opposite of al-awwal (the first), and it is an attribute of the abode, as in the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the Abode of the Hereafter. We make it for those who do not desire haughtiness on earth or corruption﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. The placing of the adverbial phrase (bi-al-akhirah) before the verb, together with the construction of the verb upon the pronoun mentioned, indicates restriction (al-hasr): that everything other than this matter, which is the foundation and head of faith, is not deserving of being held with certainty and firmly affirmed.

He expressed it in the past tense (anzala) although at that time only some of it had been revealed, not all of it, by way of giving precedence to what exists over what does not yet exist (al-taghlib), or to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as if it were already in the position of what has descended before its descent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾, that the meaning is: they affirm you in what you have brought from Allah, and what the messengers before you brought, they do not make distinction between them, nor do they deny what came to them from their Lord. ﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾: certainty in the Resurrection, the Judgement, Paradise and Hell, the reckoning and the balance. That is, they are not like those who claim that they believe in what was before you and disbelieve in what has come from your Lord.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted similar to this from Qatadah.

The truth is that this verse concerns believers in the same way as the one before it. The mere mention of belief in what was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ) and what was sent down to those before him does not necessitate making that a description specific to the believers among the People of the Book. Nothing has come to require opposition to this, nor does the Qur'anic composition require it.

Praise has been established for those among the believers who combined these two matters in more than one verse.

Among them is the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book that He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book that He sent down before﴾ [al-Nisa: 136]. Likewise His words: ﴿And say: "We believe in what has been sent down to us and what has been sent down to you"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46]; and His words: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. All of them believe in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]; and He said: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 152].

"Sawā'" (equal) is a noun meaning "equality," described by it as nouns are described by verbal nouns (maṣādir). The hamza and "am" are both used to express equality, not in their original interrogative sense. It is valid to begin with the verb and to predicate "sawā'" of it, turning away from the wording toward the meaning, as if he said: "Warning them and not warning them are equal," like the saying of people: "Hearing about al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him," meaning: your hearing of him.

The root meaning of kufr (disbelief) in the language is covering and concealment. The poet said:

*In a night whose clouds concealed the stars*

meaning, covered them. From this the disbeliever is named "kāfir," because by his disbelief he covers what must be upon him of faith.

Al-indhār (warning) is conveying and informing.

Al-Qurṭubī said: The scholars differed in interpreting this verse. It was said: it is general in wording but specific in meaning, referring to those upon whom the word of punishment has preceded, and whom God knew in advance would die upon their disbelief.

God, exalted is He, wanted to inform people that among them are those whose condition is this, without specifying anyone.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Kalbī said: It was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, and their like.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: It was revealed concerning those among the leaders of the confederates (al-Aḥzāb) who were killed on the day of Badr. The first view is more correct, for whoever specifies a particular individual has only given an example of one whose death upon disbelief was unveiled as unseen. End of quotation.

His saying "lā yu'minūn" (they do not believe) is the predicate of a deleted subject: that is, "they do not believe." It is a resumed (mustaʾnafah) sentence, because it is the answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What will these, whose condition is equal regarding warning and non-warning, do?" It was answered: "They do not believe." Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf (the Kashshaf): it is a sentence emphasizing the first sentence, or it is the predicate of "inna," and the sentence before it is a parenthetical interjection. End of quotation.

What we have mentioned is preferable, because the intent is to inform that their warning is not taken into account, and that it accomplishes nothing, but is as if it were nonexistent. This sentence is the one that came as the predicate of "inna," and what follows it, the non-belief, is a consequence of it, not the intended point.

Al-Qurṭubī said the same as the statement of al-Zamakhsharī.

Ibn Kaysān said: the predicate of "inna" is "sawā'," and what follows it stands in the position of a relative clause (ṣilah).

Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad said: "sawā'" is raised by the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is "a-anzartahum am lam tundhirhum" (whether you warned them or did not warn them), and the sentence is the predicate of "inna." The khatm (sealing) is the verbal noun of "khatamtu al-shay'" (I sealed the thing), and its meaning is covering over the thing and making it secure so that nothing enters it, and from it come the sealing of a book, a door, and what resembles that, so that what is in it cannot be reached and nothing else can be placed in it.

Al-ghishāwah (covering) is the cover, and from it comes ghāshiyat al-sarj (the saddle cover). What is meant by the sealing and the covering here are the two figurative ones, not the physical ones. That is: since their hearts were not receptive to what reached them, and their hearing was not conveying to the intellect in an understandable way the clear signs that struck it, and their sight was not guided to looking at His creatures and the wonders of His made things, they were treated as things sealed with a physical seal, and secured with a real securing, and covered with a perceptible covering, metaphorically or by way of analogy. The attribution of the sealing to God has been used as an argument by the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) against the Muʿtazilah, and they have tried to repel this argument with the same thing mentioned by the author of al-Kashshāf. The discussion of such matters is established in its proper places.

It has been disputed concerning His saying, exalted is He: "wa-ʿalā samʿihim" (and upon their hearing), whether it falls under the ruling of the sealing, so that it is conjoined to the hearts, or under the ruling of the covering. It was said: the pause upon His saying "wa-ʿalā samʿihim" is complete, and what follows is an independent statement, so the sealing is upon the hearts and the hearing, and the covering is upon the sight, as a group of scholars said. It has also been read "ghishāwatan" with a fatḥah.

Ibn Jarīr said: it is possible that he put it in the accusative by supposing a verb, its estimate being "and He placed upon their sight a covering," and it is possible that its accusative is by way of following the grammatical place of "wa-ʿalā samʿihim," like His saying, exalted is He: "wa-ḥūrun ʿīn" (and dark-eyed maidens) [al-Wāqiʿah: 22], and like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them chaff and cool water*

He made "samʿ" (hearing) singular while the hearts and sights are plural, because it is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many.

Al-ʿadhāb (punishment) is that which causes pain, and it is derived from restraint and prevention. It is said in the language: aʿdhabahu ʿan kadhā, meaning he restrained him and prevented him from such a thing, and from it comes ʿudhūbat al-māʾ (the sweetness of water), because it is held back in the vessel until it becomes clear.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His saying: "sawā'un ʿalayhim a-anzartahum" (it is equal for them whether you warned them), that he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, was eager that all people would believe and follow him in guidance, so God informed him that none believes except one for whom God has already decreed happiness in the first Remembrance (al-dhikr al-awwal), and none goes astray except one for whom God has already decreed wretchedness in the first Remembrance.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning the interpretation of the verse: that they had disbelieved in what they possessed of your mention, and denied the covenant that was taken from them, so how would they listen to you for warning and admonition, when they have disbelieved in what they have of your knowledge?

"God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sights is a covering" [al-Baqarah: 7].

[Ibrāhīm: 28]. He said: They are those who were killed on the day of Badr, and none of the leaders entered Islam except two men: Abū Sufyān and al-Ḥakam ibn al-ʿĀṣ.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddī concerning His saying: "a-anzartahum am lam tundhirhum": he said: Did you admonish them or did you not admonish them?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from Qatādah concerning this verse, he said: They obeyed Satan, so he overcame them, and God sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sights a covering, so they do not see guidance, nor do they hear, nor do they understand, nor do they reason.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The sealing is upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and the covering is upon their sights.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing," so they do not understand and do not hear, and He placed upon their sights, meaning their eyes, a covering, so they do not see.

Al-Suddī narrated that from a group of the Companions.

But if he increases (in sin), it increases until it closes over his heart, and that is the rān (rust) of which God said: 'Nay, but what they have earned has rusted over their hearts' [al-Muṭaffifīn: 14]."

Al-Tirmidhī transmitted it through this route and graded it authentic (ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Nasāʾī also transmitted it.
