Ibn Jarīr said: it is possible that he put it in the accusative by supposing a verb, its estimate being "and He placed upon their sight a covering," and it is possible that its accusative is by way of following the grammatical place of "wa-ʿalā samʿihim," like His saying, exalted is He: "wa-ḥūrun ʿīn" (and dark-eyed maidens) [al-Wāqiʿah: 22], and like the saying of the poet:

*I fed them chaff and cool water*

He made "samʿ" (hearing) singular while the hearts and sights are plural, because it is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many.

Al-ʿadhāb (punishment) is that which causes pain, and it is derived from restraint and prevention. It is said in the language: aʿdhabahu ʿan kadhā, meaning he restrained him and prevented him from such a thing, and from it comes ʿudhūbat al-māʾ (the sweetness of water), because it is held back in the vessel until it becomes clear.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His saying: "sawā'un ʿalayhim a-anzartahum" (it is equal for them whether you warned them), that he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, was eager that all people would believe and follow him in guidance, so God informed him that none believes except one for whom God has already decreed happiness in the first Remembrance (al-dhikr al-awwal), and none goes astray except one for whom God has already decreed wretchedness in the first Remembrance.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning the interpretation of the verse: that they had disbelieved in what they possessed of your mention, and denied the covenant that was taken from them, so how would they listen to you for warning and admonition, when they have disbelieved in what they have of your knowledge?

"God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sights is a covering" [al-Baqarah: 7].

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Abū al-ʿĀliyah concerning His saying: "Inna alladhīna kafarū" (Indeed, those who disbelieve), that he said: These two verses were revealed concerning the leaders of the confederates, who are those whom God mentioned in this verse: "Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of God for disbelief?" [Ibrāhīm: 28]. He said: They are those who were killed on the day of Badr, and none of the leaders entered Islam except two men: Abū Sufyān and al-Ḥakam ibn al-ʿĀṣ.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddī concerning His saying: "a-anzartahum am lam tundhirhum": he said: Did you admonish them or did you not admonish them?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from Qatādah concerning this verse, he said: They obeyed Satan, so he overcame them, and God sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sights a covering, so they do not see guidance, nor do they hear, nor do they understand, nor do they reason.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The sealing is upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and the covering is upon their sights.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing," so they do not understand and do not hear, and He placed upon their sights, meaning their eyes, a covering, so they do not see.

Al-Suddī narrated that from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The sealing is upon the heart and the hearing, and the covering is upon the sight. God, exalted is He, said: "If God wills, He will seal upon your heart" [al-Shūrā: 24], and He said: "And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart, and placed upon his sight a covering" [al-Jāthiyah: 23].

Ibn Jarīr said concerning the meaning of the sealing: The truth in my view regarding this is what is authentically established in a parallel report from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. Then he mentioned a connected chain (isnād) going back to Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Indeed, when the believer commits a sin, a black spot appears on his heart. If he repents, abandons it, and seeks to make amends, his heart is polished. But if he increases (in sin), it increases until it closes over his heart, and that is the rān (rust) of which God said: 'Nay, but what they have earned has rusted over their hearts' [al-Muṭaffifīn: 14]."

Al-Tirmidhī transmitted it through this route and graded it authentic (ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Nasāʾī also transmitted it.

Then Ibn Jarīr said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, informed that when sins follow one another upon the hearts, they close them, and when they close them, the sealing from God, exalted is He, and the stamping (ṭabʿ) then come upon them, so there is no path to them and no escape from disbelief through them. That is the sealing which God mentioned in His saying: "God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing." It is similar to the stamping and sealing upon what the eyes perceive of vessels and containers, which cannot be reached in what they contain except by removing that from them and then untying it. So faith does not reach the hearts of those whom God described as having sealed upon their hearts, except after breaking open His seal and untying its binding from them.

The commentary opens by noting that at the beginning of this surah God mentioned the sincere believers, then after them the sincere disbelievers, and then thirdly the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). The hypocrites are those who did not belong to either of the two groups but formed a third group, because they agreed outwardly with the first group and inwardly with the second. Despite this, they are the people of the lowest level of the Fire.

The word *nas* (people) originally had its hamza dropped for ease of pronunciation. It derives from *al-naws*, meaning movement. One says *nasa yanusu*, meaning "he moved." It is one of the collective nouns (asma' al-jumu'), the plural of *insan* and *insanah* but not formed from their root. The *lam* attached to it is the *lam* of the genus. The *min* in *min al-nas* is partitive, meaning "some of the people." The *min* is also descriptive: "and among the people there are those who say."

"The Last Day" refers to the time that does not end but is everlasting forever.

*Khida'* (deception) in its basic linguistic sense means corruption. Tha'lab related this from Ibn al-A'rabi, and he recited:

"White of complexion, delicate in its taste, sweet of saliva, when the saliva deceives."

It is also said that its root meaning is concealment. From this comes *makhda'* (a private inner room) of the house, where a thing is kept safe. Ibn Faris and others related this.

The meaning of their deceiving God is that they acted toward Him the way deceivers act, although the All-Knowing, to whom nothing is hidden, cannot be deceived.

The form *fa'ala* indicates mutual participation in the basic action. So their statement ﴿they seek to deceive God and those who believe﴾ indicates that God and those who believe are deceiving them as well.

The meaning of God's deceiving them is that when He applied to them the rulings of Islam, although they had no real part in it, it was as if He deceived them just as they deceived Him by displaying Islam and concealing disbelief. This is a case of *mushakalah* (matching one action with another), since it answers what they did with a similar act.

The meaning of the believers deceiving them is that they applied to them the rulings of Islam that God had commanded outwardly, even though they knew the corruption of their inner states. In the same way, the hypocrites deceived them by displaying Islam and concealing disbelief.

The meaning of God's words ﴿and they deceive none but themselves﴾ is to indicate that when they deceived one who cannot be deceived, they were in fact deceiving themselves, because deception happens only with one who does not know the inner states.

As for one who knows the inner states, whoever enters into deception with Him is only deceiving himself, and he does not perceive it. From this is the saying of one who said: "Whoever you deceive and he is deceived on your behalf, he has deceived you."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *yukhadi'una* in both places. Hamzah, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read *yakhda'una* in the second place.

The meaning of their deceiving themselves is that they feed themselves false wishes, and these in turn deceive them.

The lexicographers said: *sha'artu bi-al-shay'* means "I perceived the thing, I became aware of it."

Al-Zamakhshari in the *Kashshaf* said: *al-shu'ur* is knowledge of a thing by sensation, from *al-shi'ar* (undergarment). *Mashya'ir al-insan* are his senses.

The meaning is that the harm of this act reaches them as something perceptible, yet because of their prolonged heedlessness they are like one who has no sensation.

The word *anfus* here means their very selves, not the other meanings that fall under the name *nafs*, such as spirit, blood, or heart.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were the hypocrites from the Aws and the Khazraj and those who held their position.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The intended meaning of this verse is the hypocrites."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Sirin that he said: "Nothing was more frightening to them than this verse: ﴿And among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God and the Last Day,' but they are not believers.﴾"

Ibn Sa'd related from Hudhayfah that he was asked: "What is hypocrisy (nifaq)?" He said: "That one speaks with Islam and does not act by it."

Ahmad ibn Mani' related in his *Musnad*, with a weak chain, from a man among the Companions that a sayer among the Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, what is salvation tomorrow?" He said: "Do not deceive God." He said: "And how do we deceive God?" He said: "That you act by what God has commanded you, desiring by it other than Him. So beware of showing off (riya'), for it is associating partners with God. The one who shows off will be called on the Day of Resurrection before the heads of all creatures by four names: O disbeliever, O sinner, O loser, O traitor. Your deed has gone astray and your reward is void, so there is no share for you today with God. So seek your reward from the one for whom you were acting, O deceiver." And he recited verses from the Qur'an: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and the verse, and ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive God﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], and the verse."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Wahb that he said: "I asked Ibn Zayd about His words ﴿they seek to deceive God and those who believe﴾." He said: "These are the hypocrites who deceive God and His Messenger, and those who believe, in that they believe in what the hypocrites displayed."

Concerning His words ﴿but they deceive none but themselves and they do not perceive﴾, he said: "They harmed themselves by what they concealed of disbelief and hypocrisy."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His words "they seek to deceive God." He said: "They display 'there is no god but God,' desiring by it to preserve their blood and their property, while in their souls is other than that."

al-Maradh: every condition that takes a person out of the state of soundness, whether a sickness, an expenditure, or a shortcoming in some matter. So said Ibn Faris. It has also been said that it means pain; on this reading it is used metaphorically for the corruption in their beliefs, either doubt and hypocrisy, or denial and rejection. The placement of the predicate first (fi qulubihim) indicates that the sickness is specific to those hearts, with emphasis on how firmly this disease is attached to those hearts, because of the intensity of envy and extreme enmity they held.

By His saying, ﴿so Allah increased them in sickness﴾, what is meant is the report that they are in this state, together with the blessings that continually renew for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the favours of Allah, both worldly and religious, that repeatedly come to him.

It is also possible that this is an invocation against them: an increase in doubt, a succession of regret, and extreme hypocrisy.

Alim means mu'lim, i.e., painful. The ma in His saying, ﴿because of what they used to lie﴾, is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: because of their denial. This is their saying: ﴿We believe in Allah and the Last Day, but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. The readers are unanimous on the fatha of the ra' in His saying "maradun" (marad), except what al-Asma'i narrated from Abu 'Amr, that he recited it with a sukun on the ra'. Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read "yakdhibun" with lightening (takhfif), and the rest read it with doubling (tashdid).

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying, ﴿in their hearts is a sickness﴾, that he said: doubt. ﴿So Allah increased them in sickness﴾, he said: an increase in doubt.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding His saying, ﴿in their hearts is a sickness﴾, that he said: hypocrisy. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, he said: a painful chastisement. ﴿Because of what they used to lie﴾, he said: they would alter and distort.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud the same as what Ibn 'Abbas said first.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: everything in the Qur'an described as alim is mu'lim (painful).

He also related the same from Abu al-'Aliyah.

Ibn Jarir related the same from al-Dahhak as well.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah: ﴿in their hearts is a sickness﴾, meaning doubt and suspicion regarding the matter of Allah. ﴿So Allah increased them in sickness﴾, meaning increased suspicion and doubt. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment because of what they used to lie﴾, he said: Beware of lying, for it is the gateway to hypocrisy.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd who said: This is a sickness in the religion, not a sickness in the bodies, and they are the hypocrites.

Al-Maradh: the doubt that entered into Islam.

It is narrated from 'Ikrimah and Tawus that al-Maradh is showing off (riya').

"Idhā" is in the accusative position as an adverb of time (ẓarf), and the governing element (al-ʿāmil fīhi) is the verb "qālū" mentioned after it.

It carries the sense of a conditional (sharṭ).

Corruption (al-fasād) is the opposite of righteousness (al-ṣalāḥ), and its reality is deviation from uprightness toward its opposite.

The thing corrupted (fasada al-shayʾu) corrupts, with corruption (fasādan) and decay (fusūdan); so it is corrupt (fāsid) and fasīd.

What is meant in the verse, ﴿Do not cause corruption on the earth﴾, is through hypocrisy, allying with the disbelievers, and separating people from faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. For when you do that, what is on the earth is corrupted through the destruction of bodies, the ruin of dwellings, and the nullification of means, as is witnessed when trials (fitan) and disputes erupt.

"Innamā" is among the particles of restriction (adawāt al-qaṣr), as is explained in the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿānī).

Righteousness (al-ṣalāḥ) is the opposite of corruption.

When God forbade them from the corruption that was their habit, they answered with this grand claim, and they transferred themselves from being characterized by what they truly were, namely corruption, to being characterized by its opposite, namely righteousness. They did not stop at this pure lie and sheer falsehood, but made the attribute of righteousness exclusive to themselves, pure for them alone. So God refuted them with the most eloquent refutation, owing to what the particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbīh) conveys of the certainty of what follows it, and owing to the emphasis in ("inna"), and what is in the definiteness of the predicate together with the insertion of the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), which is an emphatic restriction, by combining two of the matters that convey it. And He returned them to the attribute of corruption, which they truly possess, with a emphatic and intensified refutation, exceeding what their false claim contained of mere restriction derived from "innamā".

As for the negation of awareness (shuʿūr) from them, it is possible that, since they used to show righteousness while knowing that they were in pure corruption, they thought that this would pass with the Prophet (ﷺ) and that the invalidity of what they concealed would be hidden from him, and they did not realize that he knew it, and that news of it would reach him from heaven. So the negation of awareness from them is in this respect, not on the ground that they are unaware that they are in corruption.

It is also possible that their corruption was, in their own view, righteousness, because the love of disbelief and enmity toward Islam had become settled in their minds.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "Corruption here is disbelief and acting in disobedience."

Ibn Jarir said: It is possible that Salman meant by this that those who come with this attribute are greater in corruption than those who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ); not that he meant that none with this attribute had passed. End.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 13:

When it is said to the hypocrites: "Believe as the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) believed, among the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar)," they answer with the most foolish reply and the furthest from truth and rightness. Thus they attributed foolishness to the believers, in mockery and belittlement, and by this they brought upon themselves Allah's recording of foolishness against them in the most eloquent expression and the most emphatic statement.

He restricted foolishness, which is the thinness of wisdom, the corruption of insight and the feebleness of intellect, to them, while they do not know that they are so, whether literally or figuratively, treating their persistence in foolishness as if it were the absence of knowledge that they are upon it and characterized by it. And since Allah mentioned foolishness here, the negation of knowledge about them is fitting, because no one acts foolishly except an ignorant person.

The kaf (ك) in كَما is in the accusative position, because it is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar): i.e., "a belief like the belief of the people."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people believe"﴾ (p. 32), i.e., "Affirm as the Companions of Muhammad affirmed that he is a Prophet and Messenger, and that what was revealed to him is true." ﴿They said, "Shall we believe as the foolish believe?"﴾ They mean the Companions of Muhammad. Surely they are the foolish. He says: "The ignorant." But they do not know: he says: "They do not understand."

It is narrated from Ibn Asakir in his History, with a weak chain, that he said: "Believe as the people believe: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying: ﴿as the foolish believed﴾, he said: "They mean the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

And he related the same from al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the Jews: i.e., when it is said to them, meaning the Jews, "Believe as the people believe," namely Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, they said: "Shall we believe as the foolish believe?"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 14–15:

The original form of *laqu* (لَقُوا) is *laqyu* (لَقْيُوا). The damma was moved onto the qaf, and the ya' was dropped because two unvowelled letters came together (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*, the meeting of two sukun-marked letters).

The meaning of *laqītuhu* and *lāqaytuhu* is: I encountered him, meeting him face to face (*istaqbaltuhu qarīban*).

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani and Abu Hanifa read *lāqū* (لاقُوا). Its original form is *lāqayū* (لاقَيُوا). The ya' became vowelled and the letter before it took a fatha, so it changed into an alif. Then the alif was dropped because two unvowelled letters came together.

*Khalawtu bi-fulān wa-ilayhi* means: I was alone with him, or I withdrew privately with him (*idhā infaradtu bihi*).

The verb is construed with *ilā* although it normally takes *bi*. One says *khalawtu bihi*, not *khalawtu ilayhi*. The construction with *ilā* is used because the verb includes the sense of *dhahabū* (they went) and *insarafū* (they departed).

*Al-shayāṭīn* is the broken plural (*jam' taksīr*) of *shayṭān*.

Sibawayh's statements about the *nūn* of *shayṭān* differ. In one place of his book he treats it as original (radical), and in another as an added (augmentative) letter. According to the first view, the word derives from *shaṭana*, meaning he went far from the truth. According to the second, it derives from *shaṭṭa*, meaning he went far or was ruined; from *shāṭa*, meaning he was destroyed; or from *ashāṭa*, meaning he perished. The poet said: "The champion may perish on our spears," that is, he perishes.

Another poet said:

"A fair-skinned man of rank, our spears destroyed him
in a battlefield among the horsemen, a dead man."

That is, they destroyed him.

Sibawayh also reports that the Arabs say *tashayṭana fulān*, meaning: Fulan acted like the devils, that is, he behaved like a devil.

If the word were from *shāṭa*, they would have said *tashayyaṭa*. From this comes the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Whatever rebellious devil (*shāṭin*) disobeys him, he (Allah) subdues him,
and casts him into prison and chains."

The words *innā ma'akum* (إنّا مَعَكم, "we are with you") mean: we are your companions in your religion, and we agree with you in it.

*Al-huzu'* means mockery and play.

The reciter (*rājiz*) said:

"Umm Taysala has mocked me,
she said: I see him as destitute, he has no wealth."

In *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) it is said: The root meaning of this word is lightness from mockery, and *huzu'* is quick killing. *Hazi'a yahza'u* means he died on the spot.

From some Arabs: "I walked and grew weary, so I thought I would die (*la-ahza'anna*) on my spot." And his she-camel *tahza'u bihi* means she hastens and moves lightly.

It is also said that the root meaning is revenge. The poet said:

"They have mocked them (*istahzaw minhum*) with two thousand armoured men,
their chiefs lying dead in the open plain."

So their saying *innā ma'akum* indicates that they remain firm in disbelief. Their saying *innamā nahnu mustahzi'ūn* (إنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِءُونَ, "we are only mockers") rejects Islam and asserts that they are above the truth. It is as if it were a reply to an implied question arising from their saying *innā ma'akum*: "If you are with us, then what is your situation when you meet the believers and agree with them?" They answered: "We are only mocking them in that agreement, and our inner selves did not agree with them or incline toward them."

Allah rejected this with His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, that is, He sends humiliation and degradation upon them, takes vengeance on them, and makes light of them, as retribution on their behalf for His believing servants. Glorified is He, in making what came from Him to be called mockery, even though it is a punishment and a requital, by way of *musha-kalah* (rhetorical correspondence of wording). The Arabs, when they placed one word opposite another as its response and recompense, mentioned it with the same wording, even if its meaning differed.

This occurs much in the Qur'an, such as: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Recompense is not itself an evil deed, and retaliation is not transgression, because it is a right.

Also: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]; ﴿Indeed they are scheming a scheme﴾ and ﴿And I am scheming a scheme﴾ [al-Tariq: 15–16]; ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9]; ﴿They deceive Allah, and He is the one who deceives them﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]; ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

This is also much in the Sunnah, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah does not tire until you tire."

He said "Allah mocks them" because it indicates renewal from time to time, and it is more severe on them, more painful to their hearts, and more agonizing to them than continuous, fixed mockery expressed by the nominal sentence. This is because what is felt is that a punishment occurring at one time and then another, and renewed from time to time, is harsher on the one who receives it than a constant, unbroken punishment, since the latter becomes familiar and the soul accommodates to it.

*Al-madd* means increase.

Yunus ibn Habib said: It is said *madda* in evil and *amadda* in good. From this is: ﴿And We have increased you with wealth and children﴾ [al-Isra': 6], and ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat﴾ [al-Tur: 22].

Al-Akhfash said: *madadtu lahu* means when I left him alone, and *amdadtu* means when I gave him.

Al-Farra' and al-Lihyani said: *madadtu* is used when its increase is of the same kind, as one says *madda al-nahr* (the river rose). From this is: ﴿And the sea, after it, seven seas extend it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. *Amdadtu* is used when its increase comes from something else. From this is: ﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125].

*Al-tughyān* means exceeding the limit and extremism in disbelief. From this is: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond bounds﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11], that is, it exceeded the measure which the keepers had set. His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24] means he went to excess in his claim when he said: "I am your Lord, the Most High" [al-Nazi'at: 24].

*Al-'amah* and *al-'ami* mean one who is bewildered and wavering. One whose camels are lost in confusion (*al-'ummah*) is one who does not know where they went. *Al-'amah* in the heart is like blindness in the eye.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: *al-'amah* is like *al-'amā*, except that *al-'amā* is in sight and opinion, whereas *al-'amah* is specifically in opinion.

The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, prolongs their term for them and gives them respite, as He said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Ibn Jarir said: As for ﴿in their transgression they wander blindly﴾, it means in their error and disbelief which has overwhelmed them, they wander bewildered and astray, finding no way out of it, because Allah has sealed their hearts and set a seal upon them, and blinded their sight from guidance and covered it. So they see no right course and find no path.

Al-Wahidi (p-33) and al-Tha'labi transmitted with a weak chain (*sanad wāh*), because in it is Muhammad ibn Marwan, who is abandoned (*matrūk*), from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: This verse was revealed about 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. He mentioned an incident that happened between them and Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: Some men of the Jews, when they met the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) or some of them, said: "We are upon your religion." And "when they went privately to their devils," who were their brethren, they said: "We are with you in the same as what you are upon; we are only mocking the companions of Muhammad." ﴿Allah mocks them﴾: he said: He ridicules them in order to take vengeance on them. ﴿And He prolongs them in their transgression﴾: he said: in their disbelief. ﴿They wander blindly﴾: he said: they hesitate.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-l-Sifat* transmitted from him something similar and longer.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him something similar to the first report.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying ﴿And when they go privately to their devils﴾: he said: their chiefs in disbelief.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Malik, who said: *wa-idhā khalaw* means they went away.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada something similar to what Ibn Mas'ud said.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying "and He prolongs them": he said: He gives them respite. ﴿In their transgression they wander blindly﴾: he said: in their disbelief they persist.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas something similar to what Ibn Mas'ud said in the explanation of *ya'mahūn* (they wander blindly).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid: *yamuddu-hum* means yazīduhum (He increases them). ﴿In their transgression they wander blindly﴾: he said: they play and hesitate in error.

Ahmad in *al-Musnad* transmitted from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We seek refuge in Allah from the devils of mankind and jinn." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, do mankind have devils?" He said: "Yes."

Yahya ibn Ya'mar read it with a kasra on the waw, according to the original rule for the meeting of two quiescent letters.

Abu al-Sammak al-'Adawi read it with a fatha, for the lightness of the fatha.

Al-Kisa'i permitted hamzating the waw.

Here shira' (buying) is used figuratively to mean exchange (istibdal), i.e., they exchanged misguidance for guidance, like His saying: ﴿فَاسْتَحَبُّوا الْعَمَى عَلَى الْهُدَى﴾ [Fussilat: 17], "they preferred blindness over guidance." As for shira' meaning exchange in its literal sense, as its original meaning is, that is not the case, because the hypocrites were not believers so that they could sell their faith. The Arabs use this for anyone who exchanges one thing for another.

Abu Dhu'ayb said:
"Even if you claim that I was ignorant among you,
I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance."

The original meaning of dalal (misguidance) is confusion, deviation from the right course, and loss of guidance. It is also used for forgetfulness, as in His saying, [quoting the speaker]: ﴿فَعَلْتُهَا إِذًا وَأَنَا مِنَ الضَّالِّينَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 20], "I did it then, and I was of those who are astray," and for destruction, as in His saying: ﴿أَإِذَا ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], "Shall we, when we are lost in the earth?" The original meaning of ribh (profit) is surplus.

Tijara (trade) is the occupation of the merchant. He attributed the profit to it, following the Arab custom in saying: "your sale profited (rabiha bay'uka) and your deal lost (wa-khasirat safqatuka)." This is metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), which is the ascription of a verb to something connected with the doer, as is established in the science of ma'ani (rhetoric).

The meaning intended is: they profited and they lost.

Guidance (al-ihtida') has already been discussed: i.e., they were not guided in their purchase of misguidance. It was also said: this refers to God's prior knowledge.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "They bought misguidance with guidance," i.e., disbelief in exchange for faith. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "They took misguidance and left guidance."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah that he said: "They preferred misguidance over guidance. By God, you have seen them leave guidance for misguidance, the community for division, security for fear, and the Sunnah for innovation."

**Their likeness** (*mathaluhum*) is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence). Its predicate (*khabar*, the comment on the subject) is either the **kaf** in His words **"like"** (*ka-*), since it is a noun here, meaning "the likeness of a likeness," as in al-A'sha's verse:

*"Will you refrain, while he will not restrain the perverse? Like a spear-thrust in which the oil and the wick go (in)."*

And Imru' al-Qays's verse:

*"And we set off with a son of water, who is led through the middle; the eye aims at him at times, and at times it climbs."*

He meant "the likeness of the spear-thrust" and "like the son of water." It is also possible that the predicate is omitted, meaning: "their likeness is radiant, like the likeness of…" In that case the **kaf** is a particle (*harf*).

**Mathal** means likeness or resemblance, and **mithlan** means two things that resemble each other. The relative pronoun **alladhi** ("the one who") is used in place of **alladhina** ("those who"): i.e., "like the likeness of those who kindled." This usage is found in Arabic speech, as in the poet's verse:

*"Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Falaj, they are the people, all the people, O Umm Khalid."*

From this usage is also His words: **"and you plunged in as those (alladhi) plunged in"** (Surah al-Tawbah 9:69), and **"And the one (alladhi) who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the God-fearing"** (Surah al-Zumar 39:33).

**Wuqud al-nar** (the blaze of the fire) is its radiance and the rising of its flame. **Istawqada** here means the same as **awqada** (kindled), just as **istajaba** means the same as **ajaba** (answered). The **sin** and **ta'** are then additions. This is what al-Akhfash said.

From this is the poet's verse:

*"And a caller called out, 'O you who answer the calls of the people!' But no one answered him at that moment."*

That is, he did not answer him.

**Al-idaa'ah** is the intense shining of light, and its verb may be intransitive (*lazim*) or transitive (*muta'addi*).

**Ma hawlahu**: it was said that **ma** is an extra particle (*za'idah*). It was also said that it is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) in the accusative position, functioning as the object of **adaat** (it lit up), with **hawlahu** in the accusative as a locative (*zarf*). **Dhahaba** is from *dhahab*, which means the departure of a thing, i.e., its removal.

**Wa tarakahum** means He left them, i.e., kept them, **fi zulumat** (in darkness), the plural of **zulmah**.

Al-A'mash read **zulumat** with a sukun on the lam, according to the original form. Ashhab al-Uqayli read it with a fatha on the lam, and that means the absence of light.

**Summun** and what follows it is the predicate of an omitted subject: i.e., **hum** (they are). Ibn Mas'ud read **summan bukman 'umyan** in the accusative, as a form of dispraise (*dhamm*). It may also be accusative governed by **tarakahum** (He left them).

**Al-sammam** is blockage. One says a **qanah** (spear shaft) is **samma'** (solid) if it is not hollow. One says **sammamtu al-qarurah** (I sealed the bottle) when I sealed it. A man is **asamm** (deaf) when the openings of his ears are blocked.

**Al-abkam** is one who neither speaks nor understands. If he understands but does not speak, he is **al-akhras** (mute). It was also said that **al-akhras** and **al-abkam** are the same.

**Al-'ama** is the loss of sight.

What is meant by His words **"so they do not return"** is that they do not return to the truth.

The response (*jawab*) of **lamma** (when) in His words **"when it lit up"** is said to be **"God took away their light"**. It was also said that it is omitted, its estimated form being: "it went out, so they remained bewildered." According to the second view, His words **"God took away their light"** are a new independent sentence (*kalam mustaanaf*), or an apposition (*badal*) to the omitted element.

God struck this likeness for the hypocrites, to make clear that what they show of faith, together with what they conceal of hypocrisy, does not establish for them the rulings of Islam, like the likeness of one who kindled a fire that lit up, then went out. He returns to darkness, and that brief light does not benefit him. The remaining of the kindler in darkness, unable to see, is like the remaining of the hypocrite in his bewilderment and vacillation.

This fire is described as light though it is a fire of falsehood, because falsehood is like this: the tips of its flame blaze for a moment, then die down.

From this is the saying: "Falsehood has a momentary surge, then it vanishes."

It is established among the scholars of eloquence (*balaghah*) that the striking of parables has a great role in bringing out hidden meanings and lifting the veils from concealed subtleties. For this reason He used them abundantly in His Mighty Book, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to use them abundantly in his addresses and admonitions.

Ibn Jarir said: Those to whom this parable is struck here never believed at any time, and he cited His words: **"And among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God and the Last Day,' but they are not believers"** (Surah al-Baqarah 2:8).

Ibn Kathir said: The correct view is that this is information about them in their state of hypocrisy and disbelief. This does not deny that they had attained faith before that, then it was taken from them and a seal was set upon their hearts, as His words indicate: **"That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so a seal was set upon their hearts, and so they do not understand"** (Surah al-Munafiqun 63:3).

Ibn Jarir said: It is valid to strike a parable of a group with one individual, as He said: **"You see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one who is overcome by death"** (Surah al-Ahzab 33:19), meaning like the rolling of the eyes of one overcome by death. And He, exalted is He, said: **"The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like a donkey carrying books"** (Surah al-Jumu'ah 62:5). Ah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: **"Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire,"** he said: This is a parable God struck for the hypocrites, who used to take pride in Islam, so the Muslims married them, inherited from them, and shared the spoils with them. When they died, God stripped them of honor, as He stripped the owner of the fire of its light. **"And He left them in darkness, not seeing"** means: in punishment. **"Deaf, dumb, blind"**: they do not hear guidance, do not see it, and do not understand it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, concerning His words: **"Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire,"** they said: Some people entered Islam at the arrival of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Medina, then they became hypocrites. Their likeness was that of a man who was in darkness, then kindled a fire, which lit up what was around him of filth and harm, so he saw and recognized what to guard against. While he was in that state, his fire went out, and he remained not knowing what to guard against of harm.

So too the hypocrite was in the darkness of polytheism, then he became Muslim, and recognized the lawful from the unlawful, and good from evil. While he was in that state, he disbelieved, and became one who does not know the lawful from the unlawful, nor good from evil. So they are **deaf, dumb**, meaning mute, **"so they do not return"** to Islam.

And His words **"God took away their light"**: as for the light, it is their faith which they profess with their tongues; and as for the darkness, it is their misguidance.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of this from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

They both also transmitted something similar from Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas something similar to what has preceded.

*"Will you refrain, while he will not restrain the perverse? Like a spear-thrust in which the oil and the wick go (in)."*

And Imru' al-Qays's verse:

*"And we set off with a son of water, who is led through the middle; the eye aims at him at times, and at times it climbs."*

He meant "the likeness of the spear-thrust" and "like the son of water." It is also possible that the predicate is omitted, meaning: "their likeness is radiant, like the likeness of…" In that case the **kaf** is a particle (*harf*).

**Mathal** means likeness or resemblance, and **mithlan** means two things that resemble each other. The relative pronoun **alladhi** ("the one who") is used in place of **alladhina** ("those who"): i.e., "like the likeness of those who kindled." This usage is found in Arabic speech, as in the poet's verse:

*"Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Falaj, they are the people, all the people, O Umm Khalid."*

From this usage is also His words: **"and you plunged in as those (alladhi) plunged in"** (Surah al-Tawbah 9:69), and **"And the one (alladhi) who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the God-fearing"** (Surah al-Zumar 39:33).

From this is the poet's verse:

*"And a caller called out, 'O you who answer the calls of the people!' But no one answered him at that moment."*

That is, he did not answer him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 19–20:

He conjoined this simile to the first simile with the particle *aw* (or), which expresses doubt, for the purpose of giving a choice between the two similes: that is, "Liken them to this or to that." Although *aw* originally denotes doubt, its use has been extended until it signifies mere equivalence without any doubt. It has also been said that it carries the meaning of *wa* (and). This was stated by al-Farra' (a grammarian of Kufa) and others, and he recited:

*And Layla has claimed that I am wicked; for myself is its piety, or upon it is its wickedness.*

Another poet said:

*He attained the caliphate, or it was decreed for him, just as his Lord came to Moses at an appointed time.*

The word *al-sayyib* refers to rain. Its derivation is from *sāba yasūbu*, meaning "it descended."

Alqama said:

*So do not put me on equal terms with Mughammar; may the water-skins of death give you to drink wherever it pours down.*

Its original form is *sayyūb*. The *yā'* and the *wāw* came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun (vowel-less letter), so the *wāw* was changed to a *yā'* and the two were assimilated, as they did in *mayyit* and *sayyid*.

*Al-samā'* (the sky) originally means everything that is above you and shelters you. From this, the roof of a house is called *samā'*.

*Al-samā'* also means rain, and it was so named because it descends from it. The mention of its descending from the sky, although it can only come from it, serves to indicate that its descent is not restricted to one side of the sky rather than another. The use of *al-samā'* to mean rain is very common in Arabic speech. Among its instances is the verse of Hassan:

*Abodes of the Banu al-Hasḥas, desolate, effaced by the dark storms and the rain.*

Another poet said:

*When the rain descends upon the land of a people...*

*Al-zulumāt* (the darknesses) has already been explained. He used the plural to indicate that the darkness of the clouds was added to the darkness of the night.

*Al-ra'd* (thunder) is the name for the voice of the angel who drives the clouds.

Al-Tirmidhi has transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about thunder, what it is. He said: "It is an angel among the angels, who has in his hand whips of fire with which he drives the clouds wherever Allah wills." They said: "What is this sound that we hear?" He said: "It is his driving of the clouds; when he drives them, they proceed until they reach the place they were commanded to reach." They said: "You have spoken the truth." The hadith is given in full, and there is some discussion regarding its chain of narration.

Al-Qurtubi said: Most scholars hold this interpretation. It has also been said that thunder is the turbulence of the bodies of the clouds when rain descends from them. This view was adopted by a group of exegetes who followed the philosophers and ignorant theologians. Other views have also been stated.

*Al-barq* (lightning) is an iron whip in the hand of the angel who drives the clouds. This was the view of many of the Companions and of the majority of the scholars of the Shari'ah, on the basis of the hadith cited above.

Some exegetes, following the philosophers, said: Lightning is what is struck out from the collision of the bodies of accumulated clouds, formed from rising vapours, which contain a fiery element that flares up upon collision.

His statement, ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾, is a resumed sentence (*jumla mustanafa*, a sentence beginning a new thought) with no grammatical position, as if someone had asked: "What is their state at that thunder?" It is therefore said: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾.

The use of *al-usbu'* (finger) to refer to part of it is a well-known figurative usage (*majāz*), the relationship being that of part and whole, since what is placed in the ear is only the tip of the finger.

*Al-sawā'iq* (or *al-sawāqi'*, thunderbolts) are pieces of fire that break off from the whip of the angel who drives the clouds when he becomes angry and strikes them with great force. This is supported by the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that we mentioned in part above, and many scholars of the Shari'ah held this view.

Some said: They are fire that comes out of the angel's mouth.

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said: It is a severe crash of the sound of thunder, sometimes accompanied by a piece of fire that burns whatever it reaches.

Abu Zayd said: *al-sā'iqa* is fire that falls from the sky during violent thunder.

Some exegetes, following the philosophers and those who share their view, said: It is a subtle fire that is struck out from the clouds when their bodies collide.

Further explanation and elaboration of thunder, lightning and thunderbolts, which is of additional benefit, will come, God willing, in surah al-Ra'd.

*Hadhar al-mawt* (for fear of death) is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*, an object indicating the reason for the action).

Al-Farra' said: It is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*, an accusative clarifying the sense of what precedes).

*Al-mawt* (death) is the opposite of life.

*Al-ihāṭa* (encompassing) means seizing from all directions, so that nothing of the one encompassed escapes in any way.

His statement, ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾, is a resumed sentence, as if it were said: "What is their state with that lightning?" *Yakādu* means "it nearly" or "it approaches."

*Al-khaṭf* (snatching) means seizing swiftly, and from this the bird is called *khaṭṭāf* because of its speed.

Mujahid recited *yakhtiṭu* with a kasra on the *ṭā'*, but the fatha is more eloquent.

His statement, ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾, is a new utterance, as if it were said: "How do you act during the moments of the flashing of the lightning and its stillness?" It is a depiction of the severity of the matter for the hypocrites, through its severity upon the people of the rain.

﴿And had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ by increasing the thunder and lightning. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾. This is among the things within His power, glorified be He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: *Aw ka-sayyib* refers to rain, and it is a simile struck in the Qur'an. ﴿Therein are darknesses﴾ means trial. ﴿Thunder and lightning﴾ means warning. ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ means: the firm Qur'an nearly reveals the faults of the hypocrites. ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ means: whenever the hypocrites gain honour from Islam, they feel at ease; but if some calamity befalls Islam, they stand up to return to disbelief, as in His statement: ﴿And among mankind is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Hajj: 11], and the verse continues.

Ibn Jarir transmitted, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and a number of Companions, who said: Two hypocrites from the people of Madinah fled from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the polytheists. This rain, in which Allah mentioned thunder, severe thunderbolts and lightning, struck them. Whenever the thunderbolts struck them, they would put their fingers in their ears out of fear that the thunderbolts would enter their ears and kill them. When the lightning flashed, they walked by its light, and when it did not flash, they could not see, so they stood still in their places and did not walk. They then said: "Would that morning would come, so that we might go to Muhammad and place our hands in his hand." Morning came, and they went to him, embraced Islam, placed their hands in his hand, and their Islam became sound. Allah struck the case of these two hypocrites who went out as a simile for the hypocrites who were in Madinah. Whenever the hypocrites attended the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ), they would put their fingers in their ears out of fear of his speech, lest something be revealed concerning them or they be mentioned in a way that would get them killed, just as those two hypocrites who went out used to put their fingers in their ears. ﴿And whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾: that is, when their wealth and children increased and they obtained spoils and conquest, they walked in it and said: "The religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) is then true," and they stood firm upon it, just as those two hypocrites used to walk when the lightning lit up for them. When it grew dark for them, they stood still. Whenever their wealth and children were destroyed and affliction befell them, they said: "This is because of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)," and they apostatised into disbelief, just as those two hypocrites stood still when the lightning went dark for them.

Ibn Jarir transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Aw ka-sayyib*" refers to rain. It is a simile for the hypocrite in its light: he speaks with what he has of the Book of Allah, showing off before people. When he is alone, he acts contrary to it. Thus he is in darkness so long as he remains in that state.

As for *al-zulumāt* (the darknesses), they are the misguidances.

As for *al-barq* (the lightning), it is faith, and they are the People of the Book.

And as for ﴿when it grows dark for them﴾, it refers to a man who grasps the edge of the truth but cannot go beyond it.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, something similar to what has preceded.

Its interpretation in a similar manner has also been reported from a group of the Followers (*tābi'īn*).

Know that the hypocrites are of several types. Among them are those who show Islam and conceal disbelief. Among them are those of whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as established in the two Sahihs (*al-Ṣaḥīḥayn*, the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere: "Whoever has three qualities is a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has a characteristic of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; and when he is entrusted, he betrays." It is also reported with the wording "four," adding: "and when he disputes, he is treacherous." It is also reported with the wording: "and when he makes a covenant, he breaks it treacherously."

Ibn Jarir and those who followed him among the exegetes mentioned that these two similes concern one single category of hypocrites.

Abu Zayd said: *al-sā'iqa* is fire that falls from the sky during violent thunder.

Some exegetes, following the philosophers and those who share their view, said: It is a subtle fire that is struck out from the clouds when their bodies collide.

Further explanation and elaboration of thunder, lightning and thunderbolts, which is of additional benefit, will come, God willing, in surah al-Ra'd.

*Hadhar al-mawt* (for fear of death) is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*, an object indicating the reason for the action).

Al-Farra' said: It is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*, an accusative clarifying the sense of what precedes).

*Al-mawt* (death) is the opposite of life.

*Al-ihāṭa* (encompassing) means seizing from all directions, so that nothing of the one encompassed escapes in any way.

His statement, ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾, is a resumed sentence, as if it were said: "What is their state with that lightning?" *Yakādu* means "it nearly" or "it approaches."

*Al-khaṭf* (snatching) means seizing swiftly, and from this the bird is called *khaṭṭāf* because of its speed.

Mujahid recited *yakhtiṭu* with a kasra on the *ṭā'*, but the fatha is more eloquent.

His statement, ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾, is a new utterance, as if it were said: "How do you act during the moments of the flashing of the lightning and its stillness?" It is a depiction of the severity of the matter for the hypocrites, through its severity upon the people of the rain.

﴿And had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ by increasing the thunder and lightning. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾. This is among the things within His power, glorified be He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: *Aw ka-sayyib* refers to rain, and it is a simile struck in the Qur'an. ﴿Therein are darknesses﴾ means trial. ﴿Thunder and lightning﴾ means warning. ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ means: the firm Qur'an nearly reveals the faults of the hypocrites. ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ means: whenever the hypocrites gain honour from Islam, they feel at ease; but if some calamity befalls Islam, they stand up to return to disbelief, as in His statement: ﴿And among mankind is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Hajj: 11], and the verse continues.

Ibn Jarir transmitted, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and a number of Companions, who said: Two hypocrites from the people of Madinah fled from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the polytheists. This rain, in which Allah mentioned thunder, severe thunderbolts and lightning, struck them. Whenever the thunderbolts struck them, they would put their fingers in their ears out of fear that the thunderbolts would enter their ears and kill them. When the lightning flashed, they walked by its light, and when it did not flash, they could not see, so they stood still in their places and did not walk. They then said: "Would that morning would come, so that we might go to Muhammad and place our hands in his hand." Morning came, and they went to him, embraced Islam, placed their hands in his hand, and their Islam became sound. Allah struck the case of these two hypocrites who went out as a simile for the hypocrites who were in Madinah. Whenever the hypocrites attended the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ), they would put their fingers in their ears out of fear of his speech, lest something be revealed concerning them or they be mentioned in a way that would get them killed, just as those two hypocrites who went out used to put their fingers in their ears. ﴿And whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾: that is, when their wealth and children increased and they obtained spoils and conquest, they walked in it and said: "The religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) is then true," and they stood firm upon it, just as those two hypocrites used to walk when the lightning lit up for them. When it grew dark for them, they stood still. Whenever their wealth and children were destroyed and affliction befell them, they said: "This is because of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)," and they apostatised into disbelief, just as those two hypocrites stood still when the lightning went dark for them.

Ibn Jarir transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*Aw ka-sayyib*" refers to rain. It is a simile for the hypocrite in its light: he speaks with what he has of the Book of Allah, showing off before people. When he is alone, he acts contrary to it. Thus he is in darkness so long as he remains in that state.

As for *al-zulumāt* (the darknesses), they are the misguidances.

As for *al-barq* (the lightning), it is faith, and they are the People of the Book.

And as for ﴿when it grows dark for them﴾, it refers to a man who grasps the edge of the truth but cannot go beyond it.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, something similar to what has preceded.

Its interpretation in a similar manner has also been reported from a group of the Followers (*tābi'īn*).

Know that the hypocrites are of several types. Among them are those who show Islam and conceal disbelief. Among them are those of whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as established in the two Sahihs (*al-Ṣaḥīḥayn*, the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere: "Whoever has three qualities is a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has a characteristic of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; and when he is entrusted, he betrays." It is also reported with the wording "four," adding: "and when he disputes, he is treacherous." It is also reported with the wording: "and when he makes a covenant, he breaks it treacherously."

Ibn Jarir and those who followed him among the exegetes mentioned that these two similes concern one single category of hypocrites.

When He, glorified is He, had finished mentioning the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites, He turned to them directly in address, by way of *iltifāt* (a shift of address, from the third person to the second), for the subtle point already noted in al-Fātiḥa.

*Yā* is a particle of calling.

The one called upon is *ayyu* (أيُّ), which is a singular noun built on a *ḍamma* (the vowel *u*). *Hā* is a particle of alerting, inserted between the one called and his attribute.

Sībawayh said: "It is as if you repeated *yā* twice, and the noun stands between them, as they say: *hā huwa dhā* (ها هو ذا, "here he is")."

The discussion of the meaning of *al-nās* (the people) and *al-ʿibāda* (worship) has already been given.

He singled out the blessing of creation and bestowed it upon them as a favour, because all the blessings follow from it (p-36), and it is its root, such that nothing of them exists without it. Moreover, the disbelievers acknowledge that God is the Creator: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. So He bestowed upon them a favour which they acknowledge and do not deny.

Regarding the original meaning of *al-khalq* (creation), there are two views. The first is *al-taqdīr* (measuring, determining). It is said: "I *khalaqtu al-adīm lil-siqāʾ*" (I cut the hide for the waterskin), meaning: when I measured it before cutting.

Zuhayr said:

> "You cut what you measure, while some of the people measure and then do not cut."

The second is *al-inshāʾ* (bringing into being), *al-ikhtirāʿ* (originating) and *al-ibdāʿ* (innovating).

Now *laʿalla* originally signifies hope, desire, expectation and apprehension, and that is impossible for God, glorified is He. But since the address from Him to mankind is in the manner of human speech, it stands in the position of His saying to them: "Do that, hoping and desiring from you." This view was held by a group of the imams of the Arabic language, among them Sībawayh.

It is also said that the Arabs used *laʿalla* free of doubt, with the meaning of *lām kay* (in order that). The meaning here is "so that you may be God-fearing." Whatever occurs in this position is similar, and among it is the poet's saying:

> "You said to us: 'Cease the wars, so that we may cease,' and you pledged to us every pledge.
> But when we ceased the war, your covenants were like a mirage shining in the open plain."

That is, "Cease from war so that we may cease." Had *laʿalla* signified doubt, they would not have given every pledge. This view was held by a group including Quṭrub.

It is also said that it means "exposing oneself to something", as if He said: "Exposing yourselves to God-fearing."

*Jaʿala* here means *ṣayyara* (to make, to render), because it takes two objects. Among that is the poet's saying:

> "I began to see two as four, and four as two, when old age had weakened me."

*Firāshan* means a bed-spread upon which they settle.

When He had mentioned the blessing of their creation, He followed it with the blessing of the earth as a bed for them, since the earth is their dwelling and the place of their settling, and among the greatest of what their need calls for. Then He followed that with the blessing of making the sky like a dome raised over them, and a roof for the house in which they dwell, as He said: ﴿And We made the sky a protected roof﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 32].

The root of *al-binā'* (building) is placing one brick upon another.

Then He bestowed upon them the favour of sending down water from the sky. The original form of *māʾ* (water) is *mawah*; the *wāw* was changed to *alif* because it was vowelled and the letter before it was open, so it became *māh*. Then two light letters came together, so the *hāʾ* was changed to a *hamza*.

*Al-thamarāt* is the plural of *thamara* (fruit).

The meaning is: We brought forth for you varieties of fruits and kinds of plants, so that this should be a provision for you for a time.

*Al-andād* is the plural of *nidd*, which means a like and an equal.

His saying: ﴿while you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), and the address is to the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

If it is asked: how does He describe them with knowledge when He has described them with the opposite, where He said: ﴿but they do not know﴾ [al-Baqara: 13], ﴿but they are not aware﴾ [al-Baqara: 12], ﴿and they were not guided﴾ [al-Baqara: 16], ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqara: 18]?

It is said: what is meant is that their ignorance and their lack of awareness do not extend to this, that is, to their knowing that He alone is the Bestower of favour and not any other of the equals. They knew this and did not deny it, as God related of them in more than one verse.

It may also be said that what is meant is: ﴿while you know﴾ His oneness by potential and possibility, if you reflected and considered.

In this is evidence for the obligation of employing proofs and abandoning *taqlīd* (blind imitation).

Ibn Furak said: what is meant is: "and you make for God equals after your knowledge, which is the negation of ignorance, that God is one." End of quotation.

The object of *taʿlamūn* is omitted, to indicate that what they have of knowledge is not restricted to one single kind of the kinds that necessitate monotheism.

Al-Bazzār, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Dalāʾil* related from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "Whatever begins with *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* (O you who believe) was revealed at Medina, and whatever begins with *yā ayyuhā al-nās* (O people) was revealed at Mecca."

Something similar was related from Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ*, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it.

Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related something like it as the saying of ʿAlqama.

Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk the like of it.

Abū ʿUbayd likewise related it from Maymūn ibn Mihrān.

Ibn Abī Shayba and Ibn Mardawayh also related something similar from ʿUrwa and ʿIkrima.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿O people﴾: "It is for both groups together, the disbelievers and the believers."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Abū Mālik, regarding His saying ﴿so that you may﴾: "That is, *kay* (in order that)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba, who said: "*Laʿalla* from God is a binding obligation."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn Masʿūd and some of the Companions, regarding His saying: ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 22], that is, you walk upon it, and it is the cradle and the abode; ﴿and the sky a building﴾ [al-Baqara: 22], he said: "like the shape of a dome, and it is the roof of the earth."

Abū l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAẓama* related from al-Ḥasan that he was asked: "Does the rain come from the sky or from the clouds?" He said: "From the sky."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from Kaʿb, who said: "The cloud is the sieve of the rain. Were it not for the cloud, when the water descends from the sky, it would ruin what falls upon it of the earth and the seed."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from Khālid ibn Maʿdān, who said: "The rain is water that comes out from beneath the Throne, and descends from sky to sky until it gathers in the lowest sky, and gathers in a place called *al-Abzam*. Then the black clouds come and enter it and drink it like a sponge drinks, and God drives them wherever He wills."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from ʿIkrima, who said: "The water descends from the seventh sky, and a drop of it falls according to measure, like a camel."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from Khālid ibn Yazīd, who said: "Part of the rain is from the sky, and part of it is what the cloud draws up from the sea, and thunder and lightning make it sweet."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā in *Kitāb al-Maṭar* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When the drop comes from the sky, the shells open for it, and it becomes pearl."

al-Shāfiʿī in *al-Umm*, Ibn Abī l-Dunyā in *Kitāb al-Maṭar*, and Abū l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAẓama* related from al-Muṭṭalib ibn Ḥanṭab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no hour of night or day but the sky rains in it, which God turns wherever He wills."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā and Abū l-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "No rain descends from the sky except that with it is the seed. Indeed, if you spread a leather mat, you would see it."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā and Abū l-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Rain is a mixture from Paradise. When the mixture is abundant, the blessing is great even if the rain is little; and when the mixture is little, the blessing is little even if the rain is abundant."

Abū l-Shaykh related from al-(p-37)Ḥasan, who said: "No year rains more than another year, but God turns it wherever He wills, and with the rain there descend so many angels who write where the rain falls, and who is provided by it, and who comes out from it with every drop."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿So do not set up for God equals﴾, that is: do not associate with Him any other of the equals which neither harm nor benefit, while you know that there is no lord for you who provides for you except Him.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *andādan* (equals), that he said: "Likenesses."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn Masʿūd, regarding *andādan*, that he said: "Equals from among men, whom they obey in disobedience to God."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from Qatāda, regarding *andādan*, that he said: "Partners."

Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Māja and Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Ḥilya* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'What God wills and you will.' He said: 'You have made me an equal to God! Rather, what God alone wills.'"

Ibn Saʿd related from Quteyla bint Ṣayfī, who said: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) from among the rabbis came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muḥammad, you are an excellent people, were it not that you associate partners.' He said: 'How so?' He said: 'One of you says: No, by the Kaʿba.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever swears, let him swear by the Lord of the Kaʿba.'

He said: 'O Muḥammad, you are an excellent people, were it not that you make equals for God.' He said: 'How is that?' He said: 'One of you says: What God wills and you will.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'So whoever among you says: What God wills, let him say: Then you will.'"

Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Māja and al-Bayhaqī related from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not say: What God wills and so-and-so wills; say: What God wills, then so-and-so wills."

Aḥmad, Ibn Māja, al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ṭufayl ibn Sakhbara that "he saw in what the sleeper sees, as if he passed by a company of Jews, and said: 'You are an excellent people, were it not that you claim that ʿUzayr is the son of God.' They said: 'And you are an excellent people, were it not that you say: What God wills and Muḥammad wills.'

Then he passed by a company of Christians, and said: 'You are an excellent people, were it not that you say: the Messiah is the son of God.' They said: 'And you are an excellent people, were it not that you say: What God wills and Muḥammad wills.'

When he rose in the morning, he informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: 'Ṭufayl saw a vision, and you say a word which shame would have prevented me from mentioning to you, so do not say it. Rather say: What God alone wills, with no partner for Him.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The equals are *shirk* (association), more hidden than the crawling of an ant on black rock in the darkness of night. It is that you say: 'By God and your life, O so-and-so, and my life'; and you say: 'Were it not for this dog of his, the thieves would have come to us'; and 'Were it not for the cat in the house, the thieves would have come'; and a man's saying: 'What God wills and you will'; and a man's saying: 'Were it not for God and so-and-so.' All of this is *shirk*."

al-Bukhārī and Muslim related from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you make for God an equal, when He created you.'" The hadith.
