Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from ʿIkrima, who said: "The water descends from the seventh sky, and a drop of it falls according to measure, like a camel."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū l-Shaykh related from Khālid ibn Yazīd, who said: "Part of the rain is from the sky, and part of it is what the cloud draws up from the sea, and thunder and lightning make it sweet."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā in *Kitāb al-Maṭar* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When the drop comes from the sky, the shells open for it, and it becomes pearl."

al-Shāfiʿī in *al-Umm*, Ibn Abī l-Dunyā in *Kitāb al-Maṭar*, and Abū l-Shaykh in *al-ʿAẓama* related from al-Muṭṭalib ibn Ḥanṭab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no hour of night or day but the sky rains in it, which God turns wherever He wills."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā and Abū l-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "No rain descends from the sky except that with it is the seed. Indeed, if you spread a leather mat, you would see it."

Ibn Abī l-Dunyā and Abū l-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Rain is a mixture from Paradise. When the mixture is abundant, the blessing is great even if the rain is little; and when the mixture is little, the blessing is little even if the rain is abundant."

Abū l-Shaykh related from al-(p-37)Ḥasan, who said: "No year rains more than another year, but God turns it wherever He wills, and with the rain there descend so many angels who write where the rain falls, and who is provided by it, and who comes out from it with every drop."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿So do not set up for God equals﴾, that is: do not associate with Him any other of the equals which neither harm nor benefit, while you know that there is no lord for you who provides for you except Him.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding *andādan* (equals), that he said: "Likenesses."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn Masʿūd, regarding *andādan*, that he said: "Equals from among men, whom they obey in disobedience to God."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from Qatāda, regarding *andādan*, that he said: "Partners."

Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Māja and Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Ḥilya* related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'What God wills and you will.' He said: 'You have made me an equal to God! Rather, what God alone wills.'"

Ibn Saʿd related from Quteyla bint Ṣayfī, who said: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) from among the rabbis came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muḥammad, you are an excellent people, were it not that you associate partners.' He said: 'How so?' He said: 'One of you says: No, by the Kaʿba.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever swears, let him swear by the Lord of the Kaʿba.'

He said: 'O Muḥammad, you are an excellent people, were it not that you make equals for God.' He said: 'How is that?' He said: 'One of you says: What God wills and you will.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'So whoever among you says: What God wills, let him say: Then you will.'"

Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Māja and al-Bayhaqī related from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not say: What God wills and so-and-so wills; say: What God wills, then so-and-so wills."

Aḥmad, Ibn Māja, al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ṭufayl ibn Sakhbara that "he saw in what the sleeper sees, as if he passed by a company of Jews, and said: 'You are an excellent people, were it not that you claim that ʿUzayr is the son of God.' They said: 'And you are an excellent people, were it not that you say: What God wills and Muḥammad wills.'

Then he passed by a company of Christians, and said: 'You are an excellent people, were it not that you say: the Messiah is the son of God.' They said: 'And you are an excellent people, were it not that you say: What God wills and Muḥammad wills.'

When he rose in the morning, he informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: 'Ṭufayl saw a vision, and you say a word which shame would have prevented me from mentioning to you, so do not say it. Rather say: What God alone wills, with no partner for Him.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The equals are *shirk* (association), more hidden than the crawling of an ant on black rock in the darkness of night. It is that you say: 'By God and your life, O so-and-so, and my life'; and you say: 'Were it not for this dog of his, the thieves would have come to us'; and 'Were it not for the cat in the house, the thieves would have come'; and a man's saying: 'What God wills and you will'; and a man's saying: 'Were it not for God and so-and-so.' All of this is *shirk*."

al-Bukhārī and Muslim related from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you make for God an equal, when He created you.'" The hadith.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 23–24:**

*fī rayb*: that is, doubt, regarding *mimmā nazzalnā ʿalā ʿabdinā*: that which We sent down upon Our servant, meaning the Qur'an, which He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The word *ʿabd* (servant) is derived from *taʿabbud*, which means humbling oneself.

*Tanzīl* (sending down) means gradual revelation, sending down in stages.

As for His saying *fa-ʾtū*: the *fa* is the response (*jawāb*) of the conditional clause, and the imperative here carries the meaning of *taʿjīz* (rendering one incapable, i.e., a challenge to prove inability).

When He had argued against them with what establishes Divine Oneness and refutes polytheism, He followed it with what is the proof for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what removes the doubt about the Qur'an being a miracle, so He challenged them to produce a single *sūrah* like its *sūrahs*.

*Sūrah* is a portion of the Qur'an that is named by a specific name. It was called that because it contains its words, as a city wall (*sūr*) encloses the city.

The *min* in His saying *min mithlihi* is extra (*zāʾidah*), in accordance with His saying *fa-ʾtū bi-sūratin mithlihi*.

The pronoun in *mithlihi* refers to the Qur'an according to the majority of the scholars.

It was said that it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, since the meaning would be: "Produce a *sūrah* from a book like it, for it confirms what is in it."

It was also said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning would be "from a human like Muhammad," that is, one who neither writes nor reads.

*Shuhadāʾ* is the plural of *shahīd*, meaning one present, or one who bears witness, or one who helps. What is meant here is the deities.

The meaning of *dūn* is the nearest place to a thing, and its usage was extended until it came to be used for passing beyond a thing to another thing, and of this is what is in this verse. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 28]. It has other meanings, among them falling short of the goal and lowliness; it is said: "This thing is *dūn*," that is, lowly. From this is the saying: "When a man aspires to high station, he seeks glory, but he who is lowly is content with what is lowly." It also means nearness; it is said: "This is *dūn* that," that is, nearer to it. It can also be an incitement, as you say: *dūnaka Zaydan*, that is, take him from the nearest place.

*Min dūni Allāh* is connected to *udʿū* (call upon). That is: call upon those who can bear witness for you apart from God, if you are truthful in what you say, that you are able to match it. This is a challenge to them and a clarification of their inability.

*Al-ṣidq* is the opposite of falsehood, and it is the correspondence of a statement to reality, or to belief, or to both, according to the known disagreement in the science of rhetoric (*ʿilm al-maʿānī*).

*Fa-in lam tafʿalū*: that is, in the past; *wa-lan tafʿalū*: that is, you will not be able to do it in the future. When your inability to match it becomes clear to you, then *fa-ttaqū al-nār* (guard yourselves against the Fire) by believing in God, His books, and His messengers, performing His obligations, and avoiding what He has forbidden. He expressed the act of producing with the verb *tafʿalū* (do), because producing is one of the acts, for the sake of brevity. The clause *lan tafʿalū* has no place in the grammatical structure, because it is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyyah*). *Lan* is for emphatic negation of what it precedes. This is among the unseen matters that the Qur'an announced before they occurred, for no one among the disbelievers has produced such a challenge in the days of Prophethood, nor after it, up to now.

*Al-waqūd* with a *fatḥah* means firewood, and with a *ḍammah* means the blazing, that is, the verbal noun; it has also come with the *fatḥah*.

By "the stones" is meant the idols they used to worship, because they associated themselves with them in this world, so they were made fuel for the Fire along with them.

This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 98], that is, firewood for Hell.

It was said that what is meant by them is brimstone stones. In this there is a terror beyond measure, since this Fire is kindled with people and stones, so it is kindled with the very things it is intended to burn.

By His saying *ʾuʿiddat* (it has been prepared) is meant: it was made ready as a provision for their punishment and was prepared for that.

God, glory be to Him, has repeated this challenge to the disbelievers in several places in the Qur'an. Among them is this one; and among them is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Qaṣaṣ: ﴿Say: Then bring a book from God that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 49]. (p-38) He said in Surat al-Isrāʾ: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to help one another﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 88]. He said in Surat Hūd: ﴿Or do they say, "He has forged it"? Say: Then bring ten *sūrahs* like it, forged, and call upon whomever you can besides God, if you are truthful﴾ [Hūd: 13]. He said in Surat Yūnus: ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been forged apart from God, but it is a confirmation of what lies before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has forged it"? Say: Then bring a *sūrah* like it, and call upon whomever you can besides God, if you are truthful﴾ [Yūnus: 37, 38].

Scholars have disagreed about whether the aspect of the miraculousness of the Qur'an is that it stands at the lofty rank of eloquence beyond the capacity of humans, or whether the inability to match it is due to a *ṣarfah* (a Divine diversion) from God, exalted is He, which turned them away from opposing it. The correct view is the first, and the discussion of this is fully set out in its proper places.

Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Dalāʾil* related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given what a human being believed in because of its like. What I was given is revelation which God revealed to me, so I hope that I will have the most followers among them on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Ḥasan regarding His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, he said: "This is the saying of God to those among the disbelievers who doubted what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, he said: "In doubt" ﴿about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a *sūrah* like it﴾; he said: "Like the Qur'an, in truth and sincerity, without any falsehood or lie in it."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Mujāhid: ﴿Then produce a *sūrah* like it﴾, he said: "Like the Qur'an." ﴿And call upon your witnesses﴾, he said: "People who will testify for you, when you produce it, that it is like it."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: *shuhadāʾakum* (your witnesses), he said: "Your helpers in what you are upon." ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ — "then He has made the truth clear to you."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr related from Qatādah: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾, he said: "He means: you will not be able to do that, and you will never be able to bear it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from Mujāhid that he used to read every occurrence in the Qur'an of *wuqūduhā* with a *ḍammah* on the first *wāw* (*wuqūdu-hā*), except the one in Surat al-Burūj, ﴿the Fire of the fuel﴾ [al-Burūj: 5], which he read with a *fatḥah* on the *wāw*.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Kabīr*, and al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, related from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "The stones that God mentioned in the Qur'an in His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24] are stones of brimstone that God created near Himself however He wished."

Ibn Jarīr related the like of this from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Jarīr also related the like of this from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* related from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾, and said: 'It was kindled for a thousand years until it became red, and a thousand years until it became white, and a thousand years until it became black. So it is black and dark, its flame is never extinguished.'"

Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī related from Abū Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of this.

Aḥmad, Mālik, al-Bukhārī, and Muslim related from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The fire of the children of Adam which you kindle is one part of seventy parts of the Fire of Hell." They said: "O Messenger of God, would it not be sufficient?" He said: "It has been made superior to it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."

al-Tirmidhī related, and graded as ḥasan, from Abū Saʿīd, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Mājah and al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, related from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Mālik in *al-Muwaṭṭaʾ* and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "Do you see it red like your fire that you kindle? Indeed it is far blacker than pitch."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, he said: "That is, for whoever is like you in disbelief."

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, he said: "That is, for whoever is like you in disbelief."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 25:

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the recompense of the disbelievers, He followed it with the recompense of the believers, so as to combine encouragement (al-targhib) and warning (al-tarhib), and promise and threat, as is His way in His Mighty Book. This serves to spur His believing servants on to His acts of obedience and to deter His disbelieving servants from His acts of disobedience.

Al-tabshir (giving good news) is informing someone of a matter whose effect appears on the bashara, which is the outer skin, from joy and happiness (al-bishr wa-al-surur).

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that if a legally responsible person says, "Whoever among my slaves gives me good news, he is free," and then one of his slaves, or more than one, gives him good news, the first of them becomes free and not the second. They differed, however, if he says, "Whoever among my slaves informs me of such-and-such, he is free." The followers of al-Shafi'i said that it applies to all of them, because each one of them is an informant. Our scholars said: No, because the legally responsible person intended only a report that would be good news, and that is specific to the first one. End of quote.

The truth is that if he intended the content of the report, they are all freed; and if he intended the report qualified by being good news, only the first is freed. Thus the disagreement is verbal.

As for the one commanded to give the good news, it was said to be the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was said to be everyone, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "Give good tidings to those who walk in the darkness to the mosques." Although these sentences are introduced by an imperative form (insha'), this does not undermine their being conjoined to what precedes them, because the intention is to conjoin the sentence describing the reward of the obedient to the sentence describing the punishment of the disobedient, without regard to the different kinds of speech (declarative and imperative) that the two descriptions contain.

It was also said that His saying "and give good news" is conjoined to His saying "so beware of the Fire" [al-Baqarah: 24], but this is not a sound view.

Al-salihat (the righteous deeds) are the upright deeds.

What is meant here are the deeds required of them and obligatory upon them. In this there is a refutation of those who say that faith alone suffices; rather, Paradise is attained through faith and righteous deeds.

Al-jannat (the gardens) are orchards. They were named jannat because they conceal what is in them (tujinnu ma fihi), i.e., they cover it with their trees. It is a name for the whole abode of reward, which includes many gardens.

Al-anhar is the plural of nahr, which is a wide watercourse larger than a rivulet (jadwal) and smaller than the sea. What is meant is the water that flows in them. The flowing is ascribed to them figuratively, while the one that actually flows is the water, as in His saying, exalted is He: "and ask the town" [Yusuf: 82], meaning its people, and as the poet said:

"I was told that after you the fire was kindled,
and after you, O Kulayb, the assembly fell to abuse."

The pronoun in His saying "from beneath them" refers to the gardens, because they contain the trees: i.e., from beneath their trees.

His saying "Whenever they are provided with a provision from it" is another description of the gardens, or it is a new independent sentence, as if a questioner asked, "What are its fruits like?"

Min thamarah (of fruit) in the sense of "min ayyi thamarah" (of whatever fruit): i.e., a kind of the varieties of fruit.

What is meant by His saying: "This is what we were provided with before" is that it resembles it and is its counterpart, not that it is the same, because the essence of the present thing cannot be the essence of the absent thing, given their difference. Rather, the color resembles the color, even though the size, taste, smell, and substance differ.

The pronoun in bihi (with it) refers to the provision. It was also said that what is meant is that they are brought what they are provided with in Paradise in a similar form, so that what comes to them at the beginning of the day resembles what comes to them at its end; they then say, "This is what we were provided with before." But when they eat it, they find a taste for it different from the taste of the first.

Mutashabihan (resembling one another) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

What is meant by the purification of the spouses is that they are not afflicted by what afflicts women of impurity from the filth of menstruation and postnatal bleeding, and all other uncleanliness whose attachment to the women of this world is not impossible.

Al-khulud (eternity) is lasting permanence that does not end. It may be used figuratively for what is long, but what is meant here is the first sense.

Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in his work on the description of Paradise, al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anyone who strives for Paradise? For Paradise has no equal. By the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is a shining light, a swaying fragrant plant, a lofty palace, a flowing river, a ripe fruit, a beautiful and lovely wife, many garments, and a dwelling forever in a safe abode, and fresh fruit..." and the hadith continues.

The hadiths describing Paradise are very numerous and firmly established in the two Sahihs and elsewhere.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The rivers of Paradise flow from beneath mountains of musk."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Hibban, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, who authenticated it, transmitted a similar report from Ibn Mas'ud as a statement of his own (mawquf).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Malik regarding His saying "beneath which rivers flow": he said, "It means the dwellings, beneath which their rivers flow."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and some Companions regarding His saying "Whenever they are provided with a provision from it, from fruit": he said, "They are brought fruit in Paradise and they look at it and say, 'This is what we were provided with before in this world,' and 'they are brought it resembling one another,' in color and appearance, though it does not resemble in taste."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted a similar report from Ali ibn Zayd and Qatadah.

Musaddad in his Musnad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in Paradise except the names."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ikrimah, who said: "Their saying 'before' (min qabl) means: this is like what was yesterday."

Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "Resembling one another in color, differing in taste."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan regarding His saying "resembling one another": he said, "All of it is excellent; some of it resembles the others, with no inferior part in it. Do you not see that you discard some of the fruits of this world?"

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted a similar report from Qatadah.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying "and for them therein are purified spouses," that he said: "From menstruation, defecation, spittle, and phlegm."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "From filth and harm."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "They do not menstruate, nor do they excrete wind, nor do they spit phlegm."

A similar report has been transmitted from a group of the Successors (tabi'un). It is firmly established from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the attributes of the people of Paradise, in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, through a number of Companions, that the people of Paradise do not spit, do not blow their noses, and do not defecate.

It is also firmly established from the Prophet (ﷺ), in many hadiths in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, concerning the attributes of the women of the people of Paradise, more than the space here can contain; so let one look into the collections of Islam and others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying "and they therein are abiding" (khalidun), i.e., abiding forever. It informs them that the reward, whether for good or for evil, remains upon its people forever, with no cessation.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying "and they therein are abiding": he meant "they do not die."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. Then a caller stands among them, saying: 'O people of the Fire, there is no death! O people of Paradise, there is no death! Each one abides eternally in what he is in.'"

Al-Bukhari transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Mu'adh.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym transmitted from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If it were said to the people of the Fire, 'You will remain in the Fire for a number equal to every pebble in the world,' they would rejoice at it. And if it were said to the people of Paradise, 'You will remain for a number equal to every pebble,' they would grieve. But Allah has granted them eternity (al-abad)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 2):

Allah revealed this verse in response to the disbelievers, when they denied the parables (amthal, sing. mathal) that He had coined, such as His saying: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. They said: "Allah is too exalted and too high to coin parables."

Al-Razi said: When He, exalted is He, demonstrated by proof that the Qur'an is inimitable (mu'jiz), He then raised here an objection (shubhah) that the disbelievers had raised to disparage it, and He answered it. The statement of the objection is that the Qur'an mentions the bee (nahl), the spider (ankabut) and the ant (naml), and these things are not fitting to mention in the speech of eloquent people. So the inclusion of these in the Qur'an impugns its eloquence (fasahah), let alone its being inimitable. Allah answered it by saying that the smallness of these things does not impugn eloquence when mentioning them includes a profound wisdom (hikmah balighah). End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that presenting this objection in this way, and reducing the denial to mere eloquence, has no basis (mustanad) and no proof. Someone before him, the author of al-Kashshaf, touched on something of this. The apparent meaning is what we mentioned first, because this verse comes right after the two parables mentioned before it. Their denial of coining parables with lowly things does not necessarily mean that this was because it impugns eloquence and inimitability.

Al-haya' (shame/modesty) is a change and a breaking that afflicts a person out of fear of being blamed or censured. So says al-Kashshaf, and al-Razi followed it in Mafatih al-Ghayb.

Al-Qurtubi said: The origin of al-istihya' is recoiling from a thing and refraining from it out of fear of falling into what is ugly. This is impossible for Allah. End of quotation.

They differed in interpreting the mention of haya' in this verse. It was said: it occurs because it appears in the speech quoted from the disbelievers. It was said: it is by way of mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence, using a word for something because it accompanies a similar word), as was mentioned earlier. It was said: it is taken as a figurative expression (tamthil).

Al-Kashshaf said: Like His leaving off disappointing a servant, and that He does not send back his hands empty of His gift, out of His generosity, by the example of one who refrains from turning away a needy person he is able to help, out of shame before him. End of quotation.

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, read ﴿yastahi﴾ with a single yā', and this is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr ibn Wa'il. The vowel of the first yā' was moved to the ḥā', so it became sakin; then the ḍammah on the second was felt heavy, so it became sakin; and one of the two was deleted because two sakins met.

Ḍarb al-mathal (coining a parable) means devising it and composing it.

The mā in His saying ﴿mā baʿūḍatan﴾ is ibhāmiyyah, that is, it causes what it is attached to to become vague, until it becomes more general than it was and more widespread among its instances. It is in a place of nasb (accusative) as a badal (substitution/apposition) of the word mathalan, and baʿūḍatan is its ṣifah (attribute/qualifier) because of its vagueness. This was said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Tha'lab. It was said: it is redundant (za'idah), and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ is a badal of mathal.

The nasb of baʿūḍatan in these two views is clear. It was said: it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and the estimate is: "an yaḍriba mathalan mā bayna baʿūḍatin," so the word bayna was deleted. This is narrated from al-Kisa'i. It was said: if yaḍrib means yaj'al (makes), then baʿūḍatan is the second object.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj read ﴿baʿūḍatun﴾ with ḍammah (raf'), and this is the dialect of Tamim.

Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: The reason for that is that mā is a noun in the position of alladhi (which), and baʿūḍatun is raised by an implied mubtada' (subject). It is also possible that mā is interrogative, as if He said, exalted is He: ﴿mā baʿūḍatan fa-mā fawqahā﴾ — "what is a mosquito, and what is above it?" — so that the parable is not coined with it, but rather it is compared to something much less than that. Baʿūḍah is on the pattern fa'ūlah from baʿaḍa, meaning "to cut," as is said: baʿaḍa and baḍa'a have the same meaning. Al-Ba'ūḍ is al-baqq (gnats/bugs), its singular is baʿūḍah, and it was named so for its smallness. So said al-Jawhari and others.

His saying ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾: al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾ — and Allah knows best — means "what is below it" (mā dūnahā), that is, that it is above it in smallness, like its wing.

Al-Kisa'i said: This is like your saying in speech, "Do you see him as short?" and the speaker replies, "Or above that," meaning, "shorter than what you see." End of quotation.

It is possible that it means "what is beyond it in size," and a group has said this.

His saying ﴿fa-ammā alladhīna āmanū﴾: amma is a particle that carries the meaning of a condition (sharṭ). Sibawayh estimated it as "mahmā yakun min shay'in fa-kadhā" (whatever may be the case, then such-and-such). Al-Kashshaf mentioned that its benefit in speech is that it gives it extra emphasis (tawkīd), and he took Sibawayh's estimate as evidence of this.

The pronoun in ﴿annahu﴾ refers back to the parable (mathal).

Al-ḥaqq (the truth) is the established reality, the opposite of falsehood. Al-ḥaqq is the singular of ḥuqūq (rights), and what is meant here is the first sense.

The grammarians differed concerning ﴿mādhā﴾. It was said: it is like a single noun meaning "what thing did Allah intend," so it is in the place of nasb by irada (to intend). Ibn Kaysan said: This is the better view. It was said: mā is a complete noun in the place of raf' by being a mubtada' (subject), and dhā means alladhī (which), and it is the khabar (predicate) of the subject together with its ṣilah (relative clause). Its answer (jawāb) would be mansūb according to the first view and marfū' according to the second.

Irada (intention/will) is the opposite of karahah (dislike). The Muslims have agreed that it is permissible to apply this word to Allah, glorified is He.

Mathalan: Tha'lab said: it is mansūb as a qaṭ' (accusative of separation), and the estimate is "arāda mathalan" (He intended a parable). Ibn Kaysan said: it is mansūb as a tamyīz (specification) that occupies the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial state), and this is stronger than the first view.

His saying ﴿yuḍillu bihi kathīran wa-yahdī bihi kathīran﴾ is like an explanation of the two previous clauses introduced by amma, so it is a khabar (statement) from Allah, glorified is He.

It was said: it is a quotation of the speech of the disbelievers, as if they said: "What is Allah's purpose in this parable by which He divides people into misguidance and guidance?" But this is not correct, because the disbelievers do not acknowledge that there is any guidance in the Qur'an, nor do they confess against themselves to any misguidance.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement that His saying ﴿wa-mā yuḍillu bihi illā al-fāsiqīn﴾ is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He. End of quotation.

Al-Razi refined the discussion in his tafsir, Mafatih al-Ghayb, in this place with a precious refinement, and he perfected it and lengthened it and clarified its branches and roots. So let one refer to it, for it is very beneficial.

As for the author of al-Kashshaf, he relied here on his staff, on which he leans in his tafsir: he made the attribution of misguidance to Allah, glorified is He, as being through causation, so it is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi) to something connected to the real agent.

Al-Qurtubi related from the people of truth among the exegetes that the meaning of ﴿yuḍillu﴾ is "yakhdhulu" (forsakes/abandons).

Al-fisq (ungodliness/transgression) is going out from something. It is said: "fasaqat al-rutabah" when the date emerged from its skin, and "al-fa'rah min juḥrihā" (the mouse from its hole). Al-Farra' mentioned this meaning.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari, in his book al-Zahir, cited as evidence for the meaning of fisq the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj:

They go down into Najd and into the low ground, deep-going,
swerving from their course, veering aside.

Ibn al-A'rabi claimed that he had never heard fasiq at all in the speech or poetry of the Jahiliyyah, and this is refuted, for a group of linguistic authorities, such as Ibn Faris, al-Jawhari and Ibn al-Anbari and others, have related it from the Arabs and that it is part of their speech.

It is established in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Five fawāsiq..." (the hadith).

In al-Kashshaf: Al-fisq is going out of the straight course. Then he mentioned the second half of Ru'bah's verse mentioned above. Then he said: The fāsiq in the Shari'ah is the one who goes out of the command of Allah by committing a major sin. End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said: Fisq in the customary usage of the Shari'ah is going out of obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It may apply to one who goes out by disbelief and to one who goes out by disobedience. End of quotation.

This is the most suitable to the linguistic meaning, and there is no justification for restricting it to some of those who go out rather than others.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: The people of the qiblah (Muslims) differed over whether the fāsiq is a believer or a disbeliever. According to our companions (the Ash'arites), he is a believer. According to the Khawarij, he is a disbeliever. According to the Mu'tazilah, he is neither a believer nor a disbeliever. The opponent argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the fāsiqūn﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and His saying: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it pleasing in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, wickedness and disobedience﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. This question is lengthy and is discussed in the science of kalam (theology). End of quotation.

His saying ﴿alladhīna yanquḍūna﴾ is in a place of nasb as a ṣifah (descriptive attribute) of al-fāsiqīn.

Al-naqḍ is the undoing of what has been firmly made, whether a building, a rope or a covenant. Al-nuqāḍah is what has been unraveled of a hair rope.

Al-'ahd (covenant): It was said: it is the covenant that Allah took from the children of Adam when He brought them out from his back. It was said: it is the charge of Allah to His creatures and His command to them of what He commanded them concerning His obedience, and His prohibition to them of what He forbade them concerning His disobedience, in His books upon the tongues of His messengers. Their breaking of that is abandoning acting upon it. It was said: rather, it is the establishing of proofs for His oneness through the heavens and the earth and the rest of His creatures, and breaking it is abandoning reflection upon it. It was said: it is what He entrusted to those given the Book, that they would make it clear to the people.

Al-mīthāq (pact): a covenant made firm by oath. It is on the pattern mif'āl, from al-withāqah, which is firmness in tying and binding. The plural is al-mawāthīq and al-mayāthīq. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

A sanctuary that none may violate for all time except by our leave,
and we do not ask the peoples for the covenant of pledges.

Using naqḍ for annulling a covenant is by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

Qaṭ' (cutting) is well known, and its verbal noun regarding kinship is qaṭī'ah (severance). One says "qaṭa'tu al-ḥabl qaṭ'an" (I cut the rope) and "qaṭa'tu al-nahr qaṭ'an" (I crossed the river).

The mā in His saying ﴿mā amara Allāh bihi﴾ is in the place of nasb by yaqṭa'ūna (they sever), and an-yūṣala (that it be joined) is in the place of nasb by amara (He commanded). It is possible that it is a badal (substitution) of mā, or of the hā' in bihi.

They differed over what is the thing Allah commanded to be joined. It was said: the kinship ties (al-arḥām). It was said: He commanded that speech be joined to action. It was said: He commanded that belief be joined to all His laws and limits which He commanded in His revealed books and upon the tongues of His messengers, to preserve them. So it is general, and the majority hold this view, and it is the truth.

What is meant by corruption (fasad) on the earth is the acts and sayings that oppose what Allah commanded, such as worshipping other than Him, harming His servants, and altering what He commanded to be preserved. In summary, everything that opposes righteousness (ṣalāḥ), whether by the Shari'ah or by reason, is corruption.

Al-khusrān is loss (nuqṣān), and the khāsir (loser) is one who has diminished himself of success and triumph. These people, when they exchanged breaking for fulfillment and severing for joining, their deeds became corruption, because they diminished their own selves of success and profit.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions that he said: When Allah struck these two parables for the hypocrites, His saying: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] and His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], the hypocrites said: "Allah is higher and more exalted than to coin these parables." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example...﴾ (the verse).

Al-Wahidi related in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Allah mentioned the gods of the polytheists, and said: ﴿And if the flies should snatch away from them a thing, they could not recover it from them﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and He mentioned the plot of the gods and made it like the spider's web. So they said: "Do you see that when Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in what He revealed of the Qur'an to Muhammad, what did He mean by this?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed...﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah something similar to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: When ﴿O people, a parable has been struck﴾ was revealed, the polytheists said: "This is not one of the parables that are to be struck?" So Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. He said: The believer believes in it, and they know that it is the truth from their Lord, and Allah guides them by it. And the fāsiqūn recognize it, but they disbelieve in it.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions concerning His saying: ﴿He misguides thereby many﴾, meaning the hypocrites; ﴿and He guides thereby many﴾, meaning the believers; ﴿and He misguides thereby none except the fāsiqīn﴾. He said: They are the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 26–27 (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, ﴿They break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾, he said: It is what He covenanted with them in the Qur'an, so they acknowledged it, then they disbelieved and broke it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, ﴿And He does not cause to go astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾, that he said: "The disbelievers recognize it, and then they disbelieve in it."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "The Harurites (al-Harooriyyah) are those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification," and he used to name them "the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, who said: "We do not know of any sin for which Allah has threatened [a punishment] as He threatened for breaking this covenant. Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and His pledge from the fruit of his heart, let him fulfil it to Allah." It has been firmly established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in hadiths that are sound in the Sahih and other collections, through a group of the Companions, the prohibition of breaking the covenant and the severe warning against it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His saying, ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, that he said: "The ties of kinship and relationship."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying, ﴿And they cause corruption in the earth﴾, that he said: "They act within it with disobedience."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Muqatil regarding His saying, ﴿It is those who are the losers﴾, that he said: "They are the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every term that Allah attributes to people other than the people of Islam, such as 'losers' (khasir), 'extravagant' (musrif), 'wrongdoers' (zalim), 'criminals' (mujrim) and 'defiantly disobedient' (fasiq), He means by it disbelief; and whatever He attributes to the people of Islam, He means by it reproach."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 26–27 (part 1 of 2):

Allah revealed this verse in response to the disbelievers, when they denied the parables (amthal, sing. mathal) that He had coined, such as His saying: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. They said: "Allah is too exalted and too high to coin parables."

Al-Razi said: When He, exalted is He, demonstrated by proof that the Qur'an is inimitable (mu'jiz), He then raised here an objection (shubhah) that the disbelievers had raised to disparage it, and He answered it. The statement of the objection is that the Qur'an mentions the bee (nahl), the spider (ankabut) and the ant (naml), and these things are not fitting to mention in the speech of eloquent people. So the inclusion of these in the Qur'an impugns its eloquence (fasahah), let alone its being inimitable. Allah answered it by saying that the smallness of these things does not impugn eloquence when mentioning them includes a profound wisdom (hikmah balighah). End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that presenting this objection in this way, and reducing the denial to mere eloquence, has no basis (mustanad) and no proof. Someone before him, the author of al-Kashshaf, touched on something of this. The apparent meaning is what we mentioned first, because this verse comes right after the two parables mentioned before it. Their denial of coining parables with lowly things does not necessarily mean that this was because it impugns eloquence and inimitability.

Al-haya' (shame/modesty) is a change and a breaking that afflicts a person out of fear of being blamed or censured. So says al-Kashshaf, and al-Razi followed it in Mafatih al-Ghayb.

Al-Qurtubi said: The origin of al-istihya' is recoiling from a thing and refraining from it out of fear of falling into what is ugly. This is impossible for Allah. End of quotation.

They differed in interpreting the mention of haya' in this verse. It was said: it occurs because it appears in the speech quoted from the disbelievers. It was said: it is by way of mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence, using a word for something because it accompanies a similar word), as was mentioned earlier. It was said: it is taken as a figurative expression (tamthil).

Al-Kashshaf said: Like His leaving off disappointing a servant, and that He does not send back his hands empty of His gift, out of His generosity, by the example of one who refrains from turning away a needy person he is able to help, out of shame before him. End of quotation.

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, read ﴿yastahi﴾ with a single yā', and this is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr ibn Wa'il. The vowel of the first yā' was moved to the ḥā', so it became sakin; then the ḍammah on the second was felt heavy, so it became sakin; and one of the two was deleted because two sakins met.

Ḍarb al-mathal (coining a parable) means devising it and composing it.

The mā in His saying ﴿mā baʿūḍatan﴾ is ibhāmiyyah, that is, it causes what it is attached to to become vague, until it becomes more general than it was and more widespread among its instances. It is in a place of nasb (accusative) as a badal (substitution/apposition) of the word mathalan, and baʿūḍatan is its ṣifah (attribute/qualifier) because of its vagueness. This was said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Tha'lab. It was said: it is redundant (za'idah), and ﴿baʿūḍatan﴾ is a badal of mathal.

The nasb of baʿūḍatan in these two views is clear. It was said: it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and the estimate is: "an yaḍriba mathalan mā bayna baʿūḍatin," so the word bayna was deleted. This is narrated from al-Kisa'i. It was said: if yaḍrib means yaj'al (makes), then baʿūḍatan is the second object.

Al-Ḍaḥḥak, Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj read ﴿baʿūḍatun﴾ with ḍammah (raf'), and this is the dialect of Tamim.

Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: The reason for that is that mā is a noun in the position of alladhi (which), and baʿūḍatun is raised by an implied mubtada' (subject). It is also possible that mā is interrogative, as if He said, exalted is He: ﴿mā baʿūḍatan fa-mā fawqahā﴾ — "what is a mosquito, and what is above it?" — so that the parable is not coined with it, but rather it is compared to something much less than that. Baʿūḍah is on the pattern fa'ūlah from baʿaḍa, meaning "to cut," as is said: baʿaḍa and baḍa'a have the same meaning. Al-Ba'ūḍ is al-baqq (gnats/bugs), its singular is baʿūḍah, and it was named so for its smallness. So said al-Jawhari and others.

His saying ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾: al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾ — and Allah knows best — means "what is below it" (mā dūnahā), that is, that it is above it in smallness, like its wing.

Al-Kisa'i said: This is like your saying in speech, "Do you see him as short?" and the speaker replies, "Or above that," meaning, "shorter than what you see." End of quotation.

It is possible that it means "what is beyond it in size," and a group has said this.

His saying ﴿fa-ammā alladhīna āmanū﴾: amma is a particle that carries the meaning of a condition (sharṭ). Sibawayh estimated it as "mahmā yakun min shay'in fa-kadhā" (whatever may be the case, then such-and-such). Al-Kashshaf mentioned that its benefit in speech is that it gives it extra emphasis (tawkīd), and he took Sibawayh's estimate as evidence of this.

The pronoun in ﴿annahu﴾ refers back to the parable (mathal).

Al-ḥaqq (the truth) is the established reality, the opposite of falsehood. Al-ḥaqq is the singular of ḥuqūq (rights), and what is meant here is the first sense.

The grammarians differed concerning ﴿mādhā﴾. It was said: it is like a single noun meaning "what thing did Allah intend," so it is in the place of nasb by irada (to intend). Ibn Kaysan said: This is the better view. It was said: mā is a complete noun in the place of raf' by being a mubtada' (subject), and dhā means alladhī (which), and it is the khabar (predicate) of the subject together with its ṣilah (relative clause). Its answer (jawāb) would be mansūb according to the first view and marfū' according to the second.

Irada (intention/will) is the opposite of karahah (dislike). The Muslims have agreed that it is permissible to apply this word to Allah, glorified is He.

Mathalan: Tha'lab said: it is mansūb as a qaṭ' (accusative of separation), and the estimate is "arāda mathalan" (He intended a parable). Ibn Kaysan said: it is mansūb as a tamyīz (specification) that occupies the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial state), and this is stronger than the first view.

His saying ﴿yuḍillu bihi kathīran wa-yahdī bihi kathīran﴾ is like an explanation of the two previous clauses introduced by amma, so it is a khabar (statement) from Allah, glorified is He.

It was said: it is a quotation of the speech of the disbelievers, as if they said: "What is Allah's purpose in this parable by which He divides people into misguidance and guidance?" But this is not correct, because the disbelievers do not acknowledge that there is any guidance in the Qur'an, nor do they confess against themselves to any misguidance.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement that His saying ﴿wa-mā yuḍillu bihi illā al-fāsiqīn﴾ is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He. End of quotation.

Al-Razi refined the discussion in his tafsir, Mafatih al-Ghayb, in this place with a precious refinement, and he perfected it and lengthened it and clarified its branches and roots. So let one refer to it, for it is very beneficial.

As for the author of al-Kashshaf, he relied here on his staff, on which he leans in his tafsir: he made the attribution of misguidance to Allah, glorified is He, as being through causation, so it is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi) to something connected to the real agent.

Al-Qurtubi related from the people of truth among the exegetes that the meaning of ﴿yuḍillu﴾ is "yakhdhulu" (forsakes/abandons).

Al-fisq (ungodliness/transgression) is going out from something. It is said: "fasaqat al-rutabah" when the date emerged from its skin, and "al-fa'rah min juḥrihā" (the mouse from its hole). Al-Farra' mentioned this meaning.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari, in his book al-Zahir, cited as evidence for the meaning of fisq the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj:

They go down into Najd and into the low ground, deep-going,
swerving from their course, veering aside.

Ibn al-A'rabi claimed that he had never heard fasiq at all in the speech or poetry of the Jahiliyyah, and this is refuted, for a group of linguistic authorities, such as Ibn Faris, al-Jawhari and Ibn al-Anbari and others, have related it from the Arabs and that it is part of their speech.

It is established in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Five fawāsiq..." (the hadith).

In al-Kashshaf: Al-fisq is going out of the straight course. Then he mentioned the second half of Ru'bah's verse mentioned above. Then he said: The fāsiq in the Shari'ah is the one who goes out of the command of Allah by committing a major sin. End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said: Fisq in the customary usage of the Shari'ah is going out of obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It may apply to one who goes out by disbelief and to one who goes out by disobedience. End of quotation.

This is the most suitable to the linguistic meaning, and there is no justification for restricting it to some of those who go out rather than others.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: The people of the qiblah (Muslims) differed over whether the fāsiq is a believer or a disbeliever. According to our companions (the Ash'arites), he is a believer. According to the Khawarij, he is a disbeliever. According to the Mu'tazilah, he is neither a believer nor a disbeliever. The opponent argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the fāsiqūn﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and His saying: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it pleasing in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, wickedness and disobedience﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. This question is lengthy and is discussed in the science of kalam (theology). End of quotation.

His saying ﴿alladhīna yanquḍūna﴾ is in a place of nasb as a ṣifah (descriptive attribute) of al-fāsiqīn.

Al-naqḍ is the undoing of what has been firmly made, whether a building, a rope or a covenant. Al-nuqāḍah is what has been unraveled of a hair rope.

Al-'ahd (covenant): It was said: it is the covenant that Allah took from the children of Adam when He brought them out from his back. It was said: it is the charge of Allah to His creatures and His command to them of what He commanded them concerning His obedience, and His prohibition to them of what He forbade them concerning His disobedience, in His books upon the tongues of His messengers. Their breaking of that is abandoning acting upon it. It was said: rather, it is the establishing of proofs for His oneness through the heavens and the earth and the rest of His creatures, and breaking it is abandoning reflection upon it. It was said: it is what He entrusted to those given the Book, that they would make it clear to the people.

Al-mīthāq (pact): a covenant made firm by oath. It is on the pattern mif'āl, from al-withāqah, which is firmness in tying and binding. The plural is al-mawāthīq and al-mayāthīq. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

A sanctuary that none may violate for all time except by our leave,
and we do not ask the peoples for the covenant of pledges.

Using naqḍ for annulling a covenant is by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

Qaṭ' (cutting) is well known, and its verbal noun regarding kinship is qaṭī'ah (severance). One says "qaṭa'tu al-ḥabl qaṭ'an" (I cut the rope) and "qaṭa'tu al-nahr qaṭ'an" (I crossed the river).

The mā in His saying ﴿mā amara Allāh bihi﴾ is in the place of nasb by yaqṭa'ūna (they sever), and an-yūṣala (that it be joined) is in the place of nasb by amara (He commanded). It is possible that it is a badal (substitution) of mā, or of the hā' in bihi.

They differed over what is the thing Allah commanded to be joined. It was said: the kinship ties (al-arḥām). It was said: He commanded that speech be joined to action. It was said: He commanded that belief be joined to all His laws and limits which He commanded in His revealed books and upon the tongues of His messengers, to preserve them. So it is general, and the majority hold this view, and it is the truth.

What is meant by corruption (fasad) on the earth is the acts and sayings that oppose what Allah commanded, such as worshipping other than Him, harming His servants, and altering what He commanded to be preserved. In summary, everything that opposes righteousness (ṣalāḥ), whether by the Shari'ah or by reason, is corruption.

Al-khusrān is loss (nuqṣān), and the khāsir (loser) is one who has diminished himself of success and triumph. These people, when they exchanged breaking for fulfillment and severing for joining, their deeds became corruption, because they diminished their own selves of success and profit.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions that he said: When Allah struck these two parables for the hypocrites, His saying: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] and His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], the hypocrites said: "Allah is higher and more exalted than to coin these parables." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example...﴾ (the verse).

Al-Wahidi related in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Allah mentioned the gods of the polytheists, and said: ﴿And if the flies should snatch away from them a thing, they could not recover it from them﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and He mentioned the plot of the gods and made it like the spider's web. So they said: "Do you see that when Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in what He revealed of the Qur'an to Muhammad, what did He mean by this?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed...﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah something similar to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: When ﴿O people, a parable has been struck﴾ was revealed, the polytheists said: "This is not one of the parables that are to be struck?" So Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. He said: The believer believes in it, and they know that it is the truth from their Lord, and Allah guides them by it. And the fāsiqūn recognize it, but they disbelieve in it.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions concerning His saying: ﴿He misguides thereby many﴾, meaning the hypocrites; ﴿and He guides thereby many﴾, meaning the believers; ﴿and He misguides thereby none except the fāsiqīn﴾. He said: They are the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 26–27 (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, ﴿They break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾, he said: It is what He covenanted with them in the Qur'an, so they acknowledged it, then they disbelieved and broke it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, ﴿And He does not cause to go astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾, that he said: "The disbelievers recognize it, and then they disbelieve in it."

Al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "The Harurites (al-Harooriyyah) are those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification," and he used to name them "the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, who said: "We do not know of any sin for which Allah has threatened [a punishment] as He threatened for breaking this covenant. Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and His pledge from the fruit of his heart, let him fulfil it to Allah." It has been firmly established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in hadiths that are sound in the Sahih and other collections, through a group of the Companions, the prohibition of breaking the covenant and the severe warning against it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His saying, ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, that he said: "The ties of kinship and relationship."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying, ﴿And they cause corruption in the earth﴾, that he said: "They act within it with disobedience."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Muqatil regarding His saying, ﴿It is those who are the losers﴾, that he said: "They are the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every term that Allah attributes to people other than the people of Islam, such as 'losers' (khasir), 'extravagant' (musrif), 'wrongdoers' (zalim), 'criminals' (mujrim) and 'defiantly disobedient' (fasiq), He means by it disbelief; and whatever He attributes to the people of Islam, He means by it reproach."

How (كَيْفَ) is built on fatḥ (the vowel "a") because it is light, and it is in the accusative position governed by *takfurūn* ("you disbelieve"). It is used to ask about a state (ḥāl), and this interrogation is for rebuking them and expressing wonder at their condition. It contains the interrogative hamza. The *wāw* in *wa-kuntum* ("and you were") is the *wāw* of the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with *qad* implied (muqaddarah), as al-Zajjāj and al-Farrā' said. This past verb can be a circumstantial clause because the circumstance is not only the statement *kuntum amwātan* ("you were dead"), but it and what follows it up to *turja'ūn* ("you will be returned"), as Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) firmly held. It is as if He said: "How do you disbelieve, while this is your story?" That is, "while you know this account and its beginning and its end."

*Al-amwāt* is the plural of *mayyit* (dead). The exegetes (mufassirūn) differed about the order of these two deaths and two lives. It was said: the meaning is "you were dead before you were created," that is, non-existent, because the name of death may be applied to the non-existent, since both share the absence of perception. *Fa-aḥyākum* then means He created you, *thumma yumītukum* means He causes you to die when your terms (ājāl) end, and *thumma yuḥyīkum* means He brings you to life on the Day of Resurrection.

A group of the Companions and those after them held this view.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This view is the one intended by the verse, and it is the one from which the disbelievers have no escape. When the souls of the disbelievers acknowledge that they were non-existent, then living in this world, then dead in it, they are bound to affirm the life of the Hereafter.

Another (scholar) said: The life that is in the grave, on this interpretation, is in the ruling of the life of this world.

It was also said: the meaning is "you were dead in the loins of Adam," then He brought you out from his loins like particles (al-dharr), then He causes you to die the death of this world, then He resurrects you.

It was also said: "you were dead," that is, drops (nuṭaf) in the loins of men, then He gave you life, the life of this world, then He causes you to die after this life, then He brings you to life in the graves. (*Thumma yumītukum*) means in the grave, (*thumma yuḥyīkum*) means the life after which there is no death.

Al-Qurṭubī said: On this interpretation there are three deaths and three lives. Their being dead in the loins of Adam, their being brought out of his loins, and their being made witnesses against themselves are other than their being drops in the loins of men. On this view there are four deaths and four lives.

It has also been said: Allah brought them into existence before the creation of Adam like animals and caused them to die, so on this view there are five deaths and five lives, and a sixth death for the disobedient of the Ummah of Muḥammad (ﷺ), as has been reported in the hadith: "But there are people whom the Fire has afflicted because of their sins, so Allah caused them to die a death, until when they had become charcoal, He permitted intercession, and they were brought... " until he said: "they sprout like the seed growing in the debris of the flood." It is in the Ṣaḥīḥ (authentic collection) from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd.

His words *thumma ilayhi turja'ūn* ("then to Him you will be returned") mean: to Allah, glorified is He, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Mujāhid, Salām and Yaʿqūb read the letter of present-tense prefix (ḥarf al-muḍāraʿah) with fatḥ (*yurja'ūn* as *yarja'ūn*?), while the majority (al-jamāʿah) read it with ḍammah.

Al-Kashshāf said: He conjoined the first with *fa-* and what follows it with *thumma* ("then"), because the first life followed death without delay, whereas death came after the life with a delay. The second life is similarly delayed after death, if by it is meant resurrection, with a clear delay. If by it is meant the life of the grave, then knowledge of its delay is acquired from it. The return to the reckoning is also delayed after the resurrection. End of quote.

It is not hidden from you that if he meant by his statement that the first life followed death immediately that it occurred to one who is characterized by death, then the other death occurred to one characterized by life. If he meant that the first life occurred at the very first moment of his being characterized by death, unlike the second, this is not granted, for it occurred at the last moments of his death, just as the second occurred at the last moments of his life. So reflect on this.

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn Masʿūd and a number of the Companions regarding His words, "And you were dead" (the verse), that he said: "You were not anything, then He created you, *thumma yumītukum thumma yuḥyīkum* (then He causes you to die, then He brings you to life)" on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah something similar as well.

Ibn Jarīr reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ that he said: "He causes you to die, then brings you to life in the grave, then causes you to die."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah regarding His words, "And you were dead," that he said: "When you were not anything. Then He caused them to die, then brought them to life on the Day of Resurrection, then they return to Him after life."

Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "He created them from the loins of Adam, took the covenant from them, then caused them to die, then created them in the wombs, then caused them to die, then brought them to life on the Day of Resurrection." The correct view is the first.

Ibn Kaysan said: "He created for you" means "for your sake." This indicates that the basic principle regarding created things is permissibility, until there is evidence that transfers a thing from this basic principle. There is no difference between animals and other things that can be benefited from without harm. The emphasis in His words "all of it" (jamì'an) is also stronger evidence for this.

This verse has been cited as evidence for the prohibition of eating clay (ṭīn), because He, exalted is He, created for us what is in the earth, not the very earth itself.

Al-Razi said in his commentary: One may say that within the totality of the earth there is that which is described as being "in the earth," so it encompasses both descriptions. Without doubt, minerals fall within this, and likewise the veins of the earth and what is similar to them. And the singling out of a thing by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. End of quote.

The author of al-Kashshaf has mentioned something clearer than this, saying: If you ask, is there any soundness to the view of those who claim that the meaning is "He created for you the earth and what is in it"? I say: If by "the earth" one means the lower directions, not the dusty ground, just as "the heaven" is mentioned and the upper directions are meant, that is permissible, for the dusty ground and what is in it lie in the lower directions. End of quote.

As for soil (turāb), its prohibition has been reported in the Sunnah, and it is also harmful, so it is not among what is benefited from by eating. However, it is benefited from in other uses. The intended benefit is not a particular benefit such as the benefit of eating; rather, it is anything that truly counts as being benefited from in some way. And "jamì'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

Al-istiwā' ( istiwā', "to settle/rise") in the language means balance and uprightness, as stated in al-Kashshaf. It is also used to mean elevation and height over something. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you and those with you are settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28], and He said: ﴿That you may sit firmly upon its back﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13]. This meaning is the one appropriate to this verse.

It has been said that this verse is among the (p-43) difficult verses (al-mushkilāt).

Many of the imams went to affirming it and leaving off probing its interpretation, while others disagreed with them.

The pronoun in His words "fasawwāhunna" is ambiguous and is explained by what follows it, like the saying: "Zayd, a man." It has been said that it refers to the heaven, since it has the sense of a genus. The meaning is that He made their creation balanced, so there is no crookedness in it.

The words "thumma istawā" have been cited as evidence that the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the heaven.

The same applies to the verse in Ḥā Mīm al-Sajdah.

He said in al-Nazi'at: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He built it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]. He described its creation, then said: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30]. So it appears on this reading that the heaven was created before the earth. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Praise be to Allah who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. It has been said that the creation of the substance of the earth precedes the heaven, while its spreading out comes later.

A group of the people of knowledge have mentioned something similar to this, and this is a good and sound view to which one must turn. But the creation of what is in the earth cannot occur except after the spreading out, and the verse mentioned here indicates that He created what is in the earth before creating the heaven. This requires that the difficulty remain and that it not be resolved by such a reconciliation.

His words "seven heavens" explicitly state that the heavens are seven. As for the earth, no mention of its number has come except His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and of the earth, the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]. It has been said: that is, in number; and it has been said: that is, in their thickness and what lies between them.

Al-Dawudi said: The earth is seven, but some of it has not been split from some of it.

The correct view is that it is seven, like the heavens.

It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes a span of land unjustly, Allah will collar him with it from the seven earths." This is authentic from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah and Saʿid ibn Zayd.

The meaning of His words "sawwāhunna" is: He made their surfaces level by smoothing them. It has also been said: He made them equal.

Al-Razi said in his commentary: If it is said: does the explicit mention indicate seven heavens only, i.e., no more? We say: The truth is that the singling out of a number by mention does not indicate the negation of what is more, and Allah knows best. End of quote.

In this there is an allusion to what the philosophers have mentioned concerning more than seven.

We say: No report has come to us from Allah or from His Messenger other than seven, so we restrict ourselves to that and do not act on anything beyond it unless it comes through a legal channel, and nothing of that has come. Allah, glorified is He, affirmed for Himself that He is knowing of everything, because He must know all that is proven to be His creation.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾. He said: He subjected to you all that is on the earth as an honour from Allah and a blessing for the son of Adam, a provision and a benefit for a term.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah reported from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾. He said: He subjected to you all that is on the earth, ﴿then He istawā toward the heaven﴾. He said: He created the earth before the heaven, and when He created the earth, smoke rose from it, and that is His saying: ﴿then He istawā toward the heaven, and made them seven heavens﴾, meaning: He created seven heavens, some above others, and seven earths, some above others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud and some of the Companions concerning His words: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾, the verse. They said: Allah's Throne was upon the water, and He had created nothing before the water. When He wanted to create creation, He brought forth smoke from the water, and it rose above the water and towered over it, so He named it "sky" (samaʾ). Then the water was spread out and He made it one earth, then He split it into seven earths in two days, Sunday and Monday. He created the earth upon a fish, and that is the one He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1]. The fish is in the water, the water is upon the back of a rock, the rock is upon the back of an angel, the angel is upon a stone, and the stone is in the wind, and that is the stone of which Luqman spoke, which is neither in the heaven nor in the earth. Then the fish moved and stirred, so the earth quaked, and He set the mountains upon it and it became steady. That is His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15]. He created the mountains in it and the sustenance of its people, subjecting them and what befits them, in two days, Tuesday and Wednesday. That is His saying: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?﴾ up to His saying ﴿and blessed in it﴾ [Fussilat: 9]. He said: He made its trees grow. ﴿And measured in it its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10]: He said: the sustenance of its people. ﴿In four days, equal for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10]: He said: whoever asks, so the matter is thus. ﴿Then He istawā toward the heaven when it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. That smoke was from the breath of the water when it breathed; He made it one heaven, then split it and made it seven heavens in two days, Thursday and Friday. The day of Friday was named so because He gathered in it the creation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. He said: He created in each heaven its creation of angels and what is in it, of seas, mountains of hail, and what is not known. Then He adorned the lowest heaven with the stars, making them an adornment and a protection from the devils. When He had finished creating what He willed, He istawā upon the Throne.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿Then He istawā toward the heaven﴾, meaning: His command ascended to the heaven. ﴿And made them complete﴾, meaning: He created seven heavens. He said: He sent fire upon the water, and it evaporated the sea, and it rose into the air, and He made the heavens from it.

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) took my hand and said: "Allah created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created the light on Wednesday, scattered the creatures in it on Thursday, and created Adam on Friday after the afternoon prayer."

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) by various routes, with the people of the Sunan and others, from a group of Companions, hadiths describing the heavens: that the thickness of each heaven is a five-hundred-year journey, and the distance between each heaven and the next is five hundred years; that they are seven heavens; and that the earth is seven earths. Likewise, reports describing the heaven have come from a group of Companions.

al-Suyuti mentioned some of that in al-Durr al-Manthur in the interpretation of this verse, but we have left its mention here because it is not specifically connected to this verse, rather it is connected to what is more general than it. (p-44)

"إذ" is one of the adverbs of time, used for a fixed point in time. It is used for the future, and "إذا" (idha) is used for the past. Each of them may sometimes be used in the place of the other.

Al-Mubarrad said: "Idh is used for the past when it is with a future verb, and for the future when it is with a past verb."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Here it is redundant (za'ida)."

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Nahhas reported this and said: "It is an adverb of time, not one of those that are used redundantly. Here it is in the accusative position, with the implied verb 'udhkur' (remember) or 'qalu' (they said)." It was also said that it is connected to "khalaqa lakum" (He created for you), but this is not apparent.

"Al-mala'ika" (the angels) is the plural of "malak," on the pattern "fa'al." This was said by Ibn Kaysan. It was also said that it is the plural of "mal'ak," on the pattern "maf'al," as Abu 'Ubayda said, from "la'aka," meaning "he sent." "Al-ula'ka" means "the message."

Labid said:

"And a youth whom his mother sent with a message, so we gave what he asked."

Adi ibn Zayd said:

"Convey to al-Nu'man from me a message, that my detention and waiting have lasted long."

It is said "alikni," meaning "send me."

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "There is no etymology (ishtiqaq) for 'malak' among the Arabs." The "ha'" in "al-malaika" is for emphasis on the feminine form of the plural. Similar to it is "al-sula'dima," and "al-sula'dim" means strong horses, the singular of which is "sil'dam." It was also said that the "ha'" is for intensification, like "'allama" and "nassaba," and "ja'il" here is in the sense of "man ja'ala," which takes two objects.

Al-Mutarrizi mentioned that it means "khaliq" (creator), and this requires that it take one object.

"Al-ard" (the earth) here is this grey (ghabra') earth, and this is not restricted to one place rather than another. It was also said that it is Makkah.

"Al-khalifa" here means one who succeeds those who were before him among the angels. It is possible that it means "one who is succeeded" (al-makhlūf), i.e., another will succeed him. It was said that it is Adam. It was also said that it is everyone who has a succession on the earth. What strengthens the first view is that it is "khalifa" and not "khala'if" (plural). Adam is mentioned, so there is no need to mention what follows him.

It was said: Allah addressed the angels with this address not for consultation, but to draw out what is within them. It was also said: He addressed them with this so that this question would come from them, and they would be answered with that answer. It was also said: for the sake of teaching His servants the legitimacy of consultation with them.

As for their saying: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ its apparent meaning is that they disapproved of the succession of the children of Adam on the earth, because they are a likely cause of corruption on the earth. They said this statement before they had any knowledge of the children of Adam, indeed before the existence of Adam, let alone his descendants, due to knowledge they had from Allah, the Glorified, in some way, because they do not know the unseen. A group of the exegetes said this.

Some exegetes said: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "I am placing on the earth a successor who will do such and such." So they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ And His saying "yufsidu" (will cause corruption) stands in the place of the second object.

"Al-fasad" (corruption) is the opposite of "al-salah" (righteousness). "Safk al-dam" means pouring blood. This was said by Ibn Faris and al-Jawhari, who said: "The word 'safk' is used only with blood." The singular of "al-dima'" (bloods) is "dam," and its original form is "damiya," from which the final letter was dropped. The clause ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal).

"Al-tasbih" (glorification) in the language of the Arabs means declaring Allah free of imperfection and keeping Him far from evil, in a manner of exalting Him.

Al-A'sha said:

"I say, when his boasting came to me: Glory be to the one who surpasses 'Alqama in boasting."
