"Bihamdika" (with Your praise) is in the place of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "while praising You." The meaning of "hamd" has already been explained.

"Al-taqdis" means purification, i.e., "and we purify You from what does not befit You, of what the atheists attribute to You and the deniers fabricate."

Al-Kashshaf mentioned that the meaning of "tasbih" and "taqdis" is one, which is keeping Allah far from evil, and that both come from "sabaha fi al-ard wa al-ma'" (he swam in the land and the water) and "qaddasa fi al-ard" (he went into the land and went far).

The Qamus and other lexicons contain what guides to what we have mentioned. Establishing a new meaning (ta'sis) is better than emphasis (ta'kid), especially in the speech of Allah, the Glorified.

Since their question was about an attribute that necessitates affirming some knowledge for themselves,

Allah, the Glorified, answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know.﴾ In this general statement there is what suffices instead of detail, because whoever knows what the one addressing him does not know is worthy that his actions be accepted from him, and whoever does not know must acknowledge to the one who knows that his actions proceed according to what knowledge requires and what the prevailing benefit and the far-reaching wisdom demand.

The object of His saying "ta'lamun" (you know) is not mentioned, so as to convey generality. The listener at that point goes in every direction, acknowledges incapacity, and admits deficiency.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Allah brought Adam out of the Garden before He created him, then recited: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor.﴾" al-Hakim also reported it, and authenticated it, from him as well, similar to it, with an addition.

And before he was created by two thousand years, there were in it the jinn, the sons of al-Jann. They caused corruption on the earth and shed blood. When they caused corruption on the earth, Allah sent against them armies of angels, who struck them until they drove them to the islands of the seas. So when Allah said: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor,﴾ they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ as those jinn had done. Then Allah said: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know.﴾ Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAmr something similar to it.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas a longer version of it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Ibn Masʿud and a number of the Companions that he said: "When Allah finished creating what He wished, He established Himself on the Throne, and He appointed Iblis over the dominion of the lowest heaven. He was from a group of angels called the jinn, and they were named jinn because they were the guardians of the Garden. Iblis, with his dominion, was a guardian. Pride entered his heart, and he said: 'Allah gave me this only because of a merit in me.' Allah became aware of that from him, and He said to the angels: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor.﴾ They said: 'Our Lord, what will that successor be?' He said: 'He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth, envy one another, and kill one another.' They said: 'Our Lord, ﴿will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾' ﴿He said: Indeed, I know what you do not know.﴾" ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada concerning the verse, who said: "The angels knew, and Allah knew, that there is nothing more hateful to Allah than shedding blood and corruption on the earth."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Beware of personal opinion (ra'y), for Allah rejected the opinion of the angels. That is because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor.﴾ The angels said: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know.﴾"

Ibn Jarir (p-45), Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Abu Sabit that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth was spread out from Makkah, and the angels used to circumambulate the House." So it was the first to be circumambulated, and it is the earth about which Allah said: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor.﴾ Ibn Kathir said: "This is a mursal (a hadith whose chain omits a Companion) with weakness in its chain, and it contains an interpolation (mudraj), namely that the intended meaning of 'the earth' is Makkah. The apparent meaning is that 'the earth' is more general than that, ending quote."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada who said: "The glorification and sanctification mentioned in the verse is the prayer (salah)."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported in the Book of Repentance from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The first to respond with 'labbayka' were the angels. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, I am placing in the earth a successor. They said: Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾' He said: They were turned away, so He turned away from them. They circumambulated the Throne for six years, saying: 'Labbayka, labbayka,' apologizing to You; 'labbayka, labbayka,' we seek Your forgiveness and repent to You."

And it is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Dharr that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most beloved speech to Allah is what He chose for His angels: 'Glory be to my Lord and His is the praise.'"

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Masʿud and a number of the Companions concerning His saying: ﴿and we sanctify You﴾ that he said: "We pray to You."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "Taqdis means purification." ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿and we sanctify You﴾ that he said: "We exalt You and magnify You."

Both of them reported from Abu Salih who said: "We exalt You and glorify You."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ that he said: "He knew from Iblis disobedience, and He created him for it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada concerning its explanation, who said: "It was in Allah's knowledge that from the successor would come prophets, messengers, righteous people, and inhabitants of the Garden."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When Allah sent Adam down to the earth, the angels said: 'O Lord, ﴿will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾' (the verse). They said: 'Our Lord, we are more obedient to You than the children of Adam.' Allah said to His angels: 'Bring two angels from among the angels, so that they may descend to the earth and We will see how they act.' They said: 'Our Lord, Harut and Marut.' He said: 'Descend to the earth.' Then Venus (al-Zuhra) appeared to them in the form of a woman of the most beautiful of mankind," and he mentioned the story.

It has been established in the authentic books of hadith, from the routes of a group of the Companions, reports concerning the description of His creation of Adam, the Glorified, and they are available, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 31–34:**

"Ādam" (آدَمُ): its original form is * Open ask* (أأْدَمُ) with two hamzas, but they softened the second one. When it is vocalized, it changes into a *waw*, as they said in the plural *awādim* (أوادِمٌ). This is what al-Akhfash said.

Scholars differed about its derivation. It was said that it comes from *adīm al-arḍ* (أدِيمُ الأرْضِ), meaning the surface of the earth. It was also said that it comes from *al-udma* (الأُدْمَةُ), meaning brownish complexion.

In *al-Kashshaf*, [al-Zamakhshari] said: "Ādam is only a non-Arabic (ʿajamī) name. The closest explanation of it is that it follows the pattern *fāʿal* (فاعَلَ), like Āzar, ʿĀzar, ʿĀbar, Shālakh, Fālagh and similar names." The word *al-asmāʾ* (الأسماءَ) means expressions, and the intended meaning is the names of the named things (*asmāʾ al-musammayāt*). Most scholars held this view, and it is the real meaning of *al-ism* (the name).

The emphasis in His words ﴿كُلَّها﴾ ("all of them") indicates that He taught him all the names, and that nothing of them was excluded, whatever it might be.

Ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] said that they are the names of the angels and the names of the descendants of Ādam. Then he preferred this view, though it is not the preferred one.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the names of the descendants (*al-dhurriyya*).

al-Rabīʿ ibn Khaytham said: they are the names of the angels.

The scholars differed over whether the named things (*al-musammayāt*) or the names (*al-asmāʾ*) were presented to the angels. The apparent view is the first, because presenting the names themselves is not clear.

*ʿArḍ al-shayʾ* (عَرْضُ الشَّيْءِ) means displaying it, and from this comes *ʿarḍ al-shayʾ lil-bayʿ* (offering a thing for sale).

The pronoun for those presented (*al-maʿrūḍīn*) is given in the masculine plural (*hum*) only to give precedence to rational beings (*al-ʿuqalāʾ*) over others.

Ibn Masʿūd read *ʿaraḍahunna* (عَرَضَهُنَّ), and Ubayy read *ʿaraḍahā* (عَرَضَها). The pronoun referring to the presented "named things" (*al-musammayāt*) appears even though they were not previously mentioned, because something that indicates them had already been mentioned, namely their names.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "What appears to be the case is that God taught Ādam the names, and presented to him, along with that, the species as individuals. Then He presented those to the angels and asked them about the names of the things named, which Ādam had learned. So Ādam said to them: 'This is its name, and this is its name.'"

al-Mawardi said: "The more correct view is that the presentation was directed to the named things (*al-musammayn*)."

Then, regarding the time of the presentation, there are two opinions. The first is that He presented them after He created them. The second is that He formed them in the hearts of the angels and then presented them.

As for His saying to the angels, ﴿Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾, this was a statement from Him, exalted is He, meant to rebuke them, though He knew that they would be unable to do that.

The intended meaning of ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is that the children of Ādam will cause corruption on earth, so inform Me. This is what al-Mubarrad said.

Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn Jarir said: some exegetes said that the meaning of ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is "since you are," and they said: this is an error.

The meaning of *anbi'ūnī* (أنْبِئُونِي) is "inform me."

When He said that to them, they acknowledged their inability and inadequacy, and said: ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾. *Subḥānaka* (سُبْحانَ) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh. al-Kisa'i said it is in the accusative as a *munādā muḍāf* (a vocative construction with an annexed noun), but this is very weak.

*Al-ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing) is in the form that expresses intensity and indicates the abundance of known things.

*Al-Ḥakīm* (the All-Wise) is an intensive form affirming wisdom for Him.

Then God, exalted is He, commanded Ādam to inform them of their names after He had presented them to the angels. They were unable to do so and acknowledged their inadequacy.

For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did I not tell you﴾ and so on [the verse].

He had said earlier: ﴿I know what you do not know﴾. Then He said here: ﴿I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, moving gradually from the general to what is explained somewhat in detail and expanded somewhat.

In the restriction of the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth to Him, there is a rejection of what many of the servants pretend, namely to have insight into some of the knowledge of the unseen, like astrologers, soothsayers, people of geomancy (*ahl al-ramal*), magic and charlatanry.

The meaning of ﴿what you reveal and what you conceal﴾ is what you show and what you hide, as the meaning of this is understood by the Arabs. Whoever explains it as something specific is not accepted in that unless there is evidence.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and al-Ḥakim [who authenticated it] narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Ādam was named so because he was created from the surface of the earth (*adīm al-arḍ*)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿And He taught Ādam the names, all of them﴾ that he said: "He taught him the names of the dish, the pot, and everything."

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from him.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from him, in explanation of the verse, that he said: "He presented to him the names of his offspring, person by person, and the animals, and it was said: 'This is the camel, this is the donkey, this is the horse.'"

al-Ḥakim in his *Tarikh*, Ibn ʿAsakir and al-Daylami narrated from ʿAṭiyya ibn Bishr, as a *marfūʿ* report (traced to the Prophet), regarding His words ﴿And He taught Ādam the names, all of them﴾, that he said: "God taught Ādam, among those names, a thousand crafts from the crafts, and said to him: 'Tell your children and your descendants: if you cannot be patient about the world, then seek it through these crafts, but do not seek it through the religion, for the religion is for Me alone, sincerely. Woe to whoever seeks the world through the religion, woe to him.'"

al-Daylami narrated from Abu Rafiʿ, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My community was displayed to me in water and clay, and I was taught all the names, just as Ādam was taught all the names." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd, in explanation of the verse, that he said: "[He taught him] the names of all his descendants." ﴿Then He presented them﴾: "He took them out of his back."

He narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, who said: "[They were] the names of the angels."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse, that he said: "These are the names by which people know one another." ﴿Then He presented them﴾ means: He presented the names of all the things that He had taught Ādam, of all kinds of creation.

﴿He said: Inform Me﴾ means: tell Me ﴿of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾, if you know that I have not placed a successor (*khalīfa*) on the earth. ﴿They said: Glory be to You﴾, declaring God free from anyone other than Him knowing the unseen. "We repent to You." ﴿We have no knowledge﴾: they disavowed knowledge of the unseen from themselves, ﴿except what You have taught us﴾, as You taught Ādam.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "He presented the owners of the names (*aṣḥāb al-asmāʾ*) to the angels."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾ that he said: "The All-Knowing is the one whose knowledge is perfect, and the All-Wise is the one whose judgment is perfect."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Masʿud and a group of the Companions regarding His words ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that the children of Ādam cause corruption on earth and shed blood. ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾: he said, "it is their statement ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?﴾" ﴿and what you were concealing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30–33]: meaning what Iblis concealed within himself of arrogance.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "﴿What you reveal﴾ is what you show, ﴿and what you were concealing﴾ means: I know the secret as I know the open."

The word *al-asmāʾ* (الأسماءَ) means expressions, and the intended meaning is the names of the named things (*asmāʾ al-musammayāt*). Most scholars held this view, and it is the real meaning of *al-ism* (the name).

The emphasis in His words ﴿كُلَّها﴾ ("all of them") indicates that He taught him all the names, and that nothing of them was excluded, whatever it might be.

The pronoun for those presented (*al-maʿrūḍīn*) is given in the masculine plural (*hum*) only to give precedence to rational beings (*al-ʿuqalāʾ*) over others.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 35–39 (part 1 of 2)**

*uskun* (﴿اسْكُنْ﴾): i.e., take the Garden as a dwelling (*maskan*), which is the place of residence. As for what some of the commentators (*mufassirun*) have said, that in His words ﴿uskun﴾ there is a hint that they would be made to leave, because dwelling (*sukna*) does not amount to ownership, and that this is derived from the statement of a group of scholars that whoever houses a man in a dwelling belonging to him does not thereby come to own it, and that he may evict him from it, then this is a customary (*'urfi*) meaning. What is obligatory is to adopt the linguistic Arabic meaning when no technical legal usage (*haqiqah shar'iyyah*) has been established for the word.

*wa-anta* (﴿وَأَنْتَ﴾): is an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the concealed pronoun in the verb, so that coordination (*'atf*) with it is valid, as is established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*): that coordination with a concealed nominative pronoun is not permissible except after emphasizing it with a detached pronoun.

Coordination may rarely come without emphasis, as in the words of the poet:

*"I said, when she approached, and the bright-faced ones, swaying like the cows of the plain, went through the sand in a winding path."*

And His words: *wa-zawjuka* (﴿وَزَوْجُكَ﴾), i.e., Hawwa'. This is the eloquent dialect, *zawj* without the *ha'* (of feminine marking). It has also come with the *ha'* rarely, as in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was with one of his wives when a man passed by him, so he called him and said: "O so-and-so, this is my wife, so-and-so," and the hadith continues. From this is also the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed the one who seeks to corrupt my wife is like a runner toward the lions of the thicket, trying to lure her."*

*raghadan* (﴿رَغَدًا﴾): with a *fatha* on the letter *ghayn*. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a *sukun*. *Al-raghad* is pleasant living in which there is no hardship. It is in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (*masdar*).

*haythu* (﴿حَيْثُ﴾): is indeclinable (*mabniyyah*) on *damm*, and it has many dialectal forms mentioned in the books of Arabic grammar.

*al-qurb* (﴿الْقُرْبَ﴾): is nearness (*al-dunuww*).

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): *qaruba al-shay'* (with a *damma*), *yaqrubu qurban*, meaning it drew near; *qaribtuhu* (with a *kasra*), *aqrabuhu quraban*, meaning I drew near to it; and *qarabtu aqrubu qarabatan*, like *katabtu aktubu kitabatan*, when you travel toward water with a night's distance between you and it. The noun is *al-qurb*. Al-Asma'i said: I said to a Bedouin: "What is *al-qurb*?" He said: "Traveling by night in order to arrive at the morning."

The prohibition of approaching (*al-qurb*) involves blocking the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*) and cutting off the way (*qat' al-wasilah*). That is why it was phrased as a substitute for eating. It is not hidden that the prohibition of approaching does not necessarily entail the prohibition of eating, because a person may eat from the fruit of the tree while being far from it, if it is brought to him. So it is better to say that the prohibition of eating is derived from the context (*al-maqam*).

*al-shajar* (﴿الشَّجَرَةَ﴾): is that which has a trunk from the plants of the earth. Its singular is *shajarah*. It has been read with a *kasra* on the *shin* and with a *ya'* in place of the *jim*.

Ibn Muhaysin read *hadhi* (﴿هَذِي﴾) with a *ya'* in place of the *ha'*, and this is the original form.

The scholars differed in identifying this tree. It was said to be the vine (*karm*), and it was said to be the ear of grain (*sunbulah*), and it was said to be the fig (*tin*), and it was said to be wheat (*hintah*). What was transmitted from the Companions and those after them regarding its identification will come.

His words *fa-takuna* (﴿فَتَكُونَا﴾) are coordinated with *taqraba* in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), or they are in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition, and this is the more apparent view.

*al-zulm* (﴿الظُّلْمُ﴾): its origin is placing a thing in other than its proper place. *Al-ardh al-mazlumah* is land that has never been dug and then was dug. A *zalim* man is one who is severe in wrongdoing.

What is meant here by ﴿فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ ("then you would be among the wrongdoers") is wronging themselves through disobedience. The discourse of the scholars on the infallibility of the prophets (*'ismah*) and the differences of their schools in this matter is recorded in its proper places. Al-Razi lengthily discussed this in his commentary at this point, so let the reader refer to it, for it is beneficial.

*fa-azallahuma* (﴿فَأَزَلَّهُمَا﴾): from *al-zallah*, which is sin (*al-khati'ah*), i.e., he caused them to slip and brought them into it. Hamzah read *fa-aza'lahuma* (with an *alif*, from *al-izalah*, which is *al-tahtiyyah* in the sense of: he removed them). The rest read it without the *alif*.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is from *al-zawal*, i.e., he turned them away from the obedience they were upon to disobedience.

Al-Qurtubi said: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning, except that the reading of the majority is more precise in meaning. It is said: *azlaltuhu fa-zalla*. *Wa-'anha* (﴿عَنْهَا﴾) is connected with His words *azallahuma*, with the verb being understood as containing the meaning of *asdara* (to cause to issue): i.e., Satan caused their slip to issue from it, that is, because of it, meaning the tree.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Garden. According to this, the verb is understood as containing the meaning of *ab'adahuma* (to drive far away): i.e., he drove them far from the Garden.

His words *fa-akhrajahuma* (﴿فَأَخْرَجَهُمَا﴾): are an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the content of the first clause, i.e., he caused them to slip, if its meaning is that they left their place. If its meaning is not so, then it is an establishing (*ta'sis*) of a new meaning, because expulsion (*ikhraj*) involves something beyond mere turning away, distancing and the like. Turning away from the tree and distancing from it may occur while they remain in the Garden, unlike expelling them from what they were in of bliss and honor, or from the Garden. He attributed this to Satan because he was the one who undertook to seduce Adam until he ate from the tree.

The scholars differed concerning the manner in which Satan carried out their slipping. It was said that it occurred through direct speech from him to them, and this is the view of the majority, who argued for it with His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَقَاسَمَهُمَا إِنِّي لَكُمَا لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("And he swore to them: Indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers") [al-A'raf: 21]. The *muqasamah* (swearing) apparently means direct speech. It was said that nothing proceeded from him except mere whispering (*waswasah*), and it was said other than that, as will come in what is related from the early generations (*salaf*).

His words *ihbitu* (﴿اهْبِطُوا﴾): are addressed to Adam and Hawwa'. They were addressed with what is addressed with the plural, because two is the least of the plural according to some of the leading Arabic grammarians. [p. 48] It was also said that it is addressed to them and to their offspring, because since they were the origin of this human species, they were treated as its representative. This is indicated by His words: ﴿بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("some of you are enemies to others"), for this clause, which occurs as a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) clarifying the state established for those commanded to descend, conveys that meaning.

*al-'aduww* (﴿الْعَدُوُّ﴾) is the opposite of friend. It is from *'adā* when he wronged. It is said: a wolf that is *'adawan*, i.e., it attacks people. *Al-'udwan* is blatant wrongdoing. It was also said it is derived from transgressing (*al-mujawazah*); one says *'adahu* when he passed beyond him. The two meanings are close, for whoever wrongs has transgressed.

He reported about *ba'dukum* (﴿بَعْضُكُمْ﴾) with His words *'aduww* (enemy) even though it is singular, because the word *ba'd* (some), although its meaning admits of multiplicity, is singular in form. So regard was given to the wording, and he reported about it with the singular. Sometimes regard is given to the meaning, and it is reported about with the plural.

It may be answered that *'aduww*, although singular, may be used in the position of the plural, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَهُمْ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("and they are an enemy to you") [al-Kahf: 50], and His words: ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ هُمُ الْعَدُوُّ﴾ ("they think every cry is against them; they are the enemy") [al-Munafiqun: 4]. Ibn Faris said: *al-'aduww* is a comprehensive noun for the singular, the dual and the plural.

*al-mustaqarr* (﴿الْمُسْتَقَرُّ﴾): is the place of settling. From it is His words: ﴿أَصْحَابُ الْجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا﴾ ("the companions of the Garden that day are better in their resting place") [al-Furqan: 24]. It may also mean the act of settling, and from it is His words: ﴿إِلَى رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ﴾ ("to your Lord that day is the settling") [al-Qiyamah: 12]. So the verse admits of both meanings. Similar to it is His words: ﴿جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ قَرَارًا﴾ ("He made for you the earth as a resting place") [Ghafir: 64].

*al-mata'* (﴿مَتَاعٌ﴾): is that which is enjoyed of food, drink, clothing and the like.

The commentators differed concerning His words *ila hin* (﴿إِلَى حِينٍ﴾): it was said, until death; and it was said, until the establishment of the Hour.

The basic meaning of *al-hin* linguistically is a long period of time. From it is His words: ﴿هَلْ أَتَى عَلَى الْإِنْسَانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ ("Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?") [al-Insan: 1]. *Al-hin* is also an hour, and from it is His words: ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ حِينَ تَرَى الْعَذَابَ﴾ ("or says when he sees the punishment") [al-Zumar: 58]. It is also a portion of time, and from it is His words: ﴿فَذَرْهُمْ فِي غَمْرَتِهِمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ﴾ ("so leave them in their confusion until a time") [al-Mu'minun: 54], i.e., until their lifespans end. It is also applied to a year, and it was said to six months, and from it is His words: ﴿تُؤْتِي أُكُلَهَا كُلَّ حِينٍ﴾ ("it gives its produce every season") [Ibrahim: 25]. It is also applied to evening and morning, and from it is His words: ﴿حِينَ تُمْسُونَ وَحِينَ تُصْبِحُونَ﴾ ("when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning") [al-Rum: 17]. Al-Farra' said: *al-hin* is of two kinds: one kind whose limit cannot be specified, and then he mentioned the other *hin*. Its variation according to the variation of contexts is as we have mentioned.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: an unknown *hin* has no ruling attached to it, and a known *hin* is a year.

The meaning of Adam's receiving (*talaqqi*) the words (*kalimat*) is his taking them, his acceptance of what is in them, and his acting upon them. It was said: his understanding of them and his perceptiveness of what they contained.

The basic meaning of *al-talaqqi* is receiving/meeting (*al-istiqbal*): i.e., he received the words revealed to him. Whoever read *Adama* with the accusative made its meaning: the words received him (*istaqbalathu*).

It was said that the meaning of *talaqqa* is *talaqqana* (to be taught), and there is no basis for this in Arabic.

The early generations differed concerning specifying these words, and that will come.

*al-tawbah* (﴿التَّوْبَةُ﴾) is return. One says *taba al-'abd* when he returned to the obedience of his Master. A *tawwab* servant is one who returns often. So the meaning of *taba 'alayhi* is: he turned to him with mercy, and so accepted his repentance, or granted him success in repenting.

He limited the mention of repentance to Adam, not Hawwa', despite their sharing the sin, because the discourse from the beginning of the narrative was with him, so it continued in that way, and the mention of repentance upon him sufficed for not mentioning it upon her, since she is a follower of him. Likewise, the attribution of the sin to him sufficed for not attributing it to her, as in His words: ﴿وَعَصَى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوَى﴾ ("Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray") [Ta-Ha: 121].

As for His words ﴿قُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا﴾ after His words ﴿قُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا﴾ (earlier), He repeated it for emphasis and for stressing.

It was also said: since a ruling different from the first ruling became attached to it, He repeated it, and there is no conflict among the implications. So the repetition may be for both matters together.

The answer to the conditional in His words ﴿فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدًى﴾ ("if guidance comes to you from Me") is the second condition together with its answer, as said by Sibawayh. Al-Kisa'i said: the answer to both the first and second conditions is His words ﴿فَلَا خَوْفٌ﴾ ("no fear").

They differed concerning the meaning of the mentioned guidance (*huda*). It was said: it is the Book of Allah. It was said: it is the granting of success (*tawfiq*) to guidance.

*al-khawf* (﴿الْخَوْفُ﴾): is dread (*al-du'r*), and it occurs only regarding the future.

Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Ammar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *fa-la khawfa* (﴿فَلا خَوْفَ﴾) with a *fatha* on the *fa'*.

*al-huzn* (﴿الْحُزْنُ﴾) is the opposite of joy (*al-surur*).

Al-Yazidi said: *hazanahu* is the dialect of Quraysh, and *ahzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim. Both have been read.

Their companionship with the Fire (*sahbat ahl al-nar*) means being attached and constantly accompanying.

The explanation of *al-khulud* (eternal abiding) has been mentioned before.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded, on the authority of Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me, was Adam a prophet?" He said: "Yes, he was a prophet, a messenger, whom Allah addressed directly. He said to him: ﴿O Adam, dwell you and your wife in the Garden﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani recorded, on the authority of Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who was the first of the prophets?" He said: "Adam." I said: "Was he a prophet?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Then who?" He said: "Nuh, and between them were ten fathers."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, recorded something similar from the hadith of Abu Dharr, marfu'ly, and added: "How many were the messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi recorded, on the authority of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, was Adam a prophet?" He said: "Yes." He said: "How far was between him and Nuh?" He said: "Ten centuries." He said: "How far between Nuh and Ibrahim?" He said: "Ten centuries." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, how many are the prophets?" He said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, how many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude."

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh recorded something similar from the hadith of Abu Umamah, and stated explicitly that the questioner was Abu Dharr.

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim (who declared it sound) recorded, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Adam did not dwell in the Garden except between the time of the afternoon prayer (*'asr*) and the setting of the sun."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him, who said: "The sun did not set on that day until he was brought down from the Garden."

al-Firyabi, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded, on the authority of al-Hasan, who said: "Adam remained in the Garden for an hour of a day, and that hour was one hundred and thirty years of the days of this world."

The estimate of his stay in the Garden has also been transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr in the same manner as what came before from Ibn 'Abbas, as Ahmad recorded in al-Zuhd.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 35–39 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, that they said: When Adam dwelt in the Garden, he walked in it alone, a lonely creature with no spouse to find comfort in. He slept a sleep, and when he awoke, there was a woman sitting at his head, whom Allah had created from his rib.

al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Be good to women, for woman was created from a rib, and the most crooked part of the rib is its top. If you try to straighten it, you will break it, and if you leave it, it will remain crooked. So be good to women."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Hawwa' (Eve) was named so only because she is the mother of every living being.

Ibn Adi and Ibn Asakir narrated, from al-Nakha'i, who said: When Allah created Adam and created his spouse for him, He sent an angel to him and commanded him to have intercourse with her, and he did. When he finished, Hawwa' said to him: "O Adam, this is good; give us more of it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: al-Raghad means "pleasant and wholesome."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from Ibn Abbas, who said: al-Raghad means "abundance of livelihood."

Both of them also narrated from him, concerning His words ﴿And eat from it abundantly wherever you wish﴾, that he said: "There is no reckoning upon you."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Asakir narrated, through several chains, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The tree which Allah forbade Adam was the ear of grain (sunbulah). In another wording: it was wheat (al-burr).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: It was the grapevine (al-karm).

Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him that he said: It was the almond (al-lawz).

Ibn Jarir narrated from one of the Companions that he said: It was the fig (al-tinah).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated the same from Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: It was wheat (al-burr).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he said: It was the date palm (al-nakhlah).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt that he said: It was the citron (al-utrujj).

Ahmad, in Kitab al-Zuhd (the Book of Asceticism), narrated from Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i that he said: It resembles wheat and is called al-da'ah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿fa-azallahuma﴾ (so He caused them to slip), that he said: "fa-aghwahuma" (so He led them astray).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Asim ibn Bahdalah that he said: "fa-azallahuma" means "fa-nahhahuma" (so He removed them).

Abu Dawud, in al-Masahif (the Codices), narrated from al-A'mash that he said: Our recitation in al-Baqarah in place of ﴿fa-azallahuma﴾ is ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (so he whispered).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: Iblis wanted to enter the Garden to reach them both, but the guardians (al-khazanah) prevented him. So he came to the serpent (al-hayyah), which was a creature with four legs, like a camel, and it was the most beautiful of animals. He spoke to it, asking it to let him into its mouth so that it could bring him in to Adam. It let him into its mouth, and the serpent passed by the guardians and entered, and they did not know what Allah intended by the matter. He spoke to Adam from its mouth, but Adam paid no heed to his words. So Iblis came out to him and said: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?" [Ta-Ha 20:120], and he swore to them both by Allah: ﴿Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:21]. Adam refused to eat from it, but Hawwa' went ahead and ate. Then she said: "O Adam, eat, for I have eaten and it has not harmed me." When they both ate, ﴿their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf 7:22].

Ibn Abbas narrated the story of the serpent and Iblis's entry along with it through Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir.

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam was a tall man, like a towering palm tree, sixty cubits in height, with abundant hair on his head. When he committed the sin, his private parts became apparent to him..." and the hadith continues.

Ibn Mani', Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah said to Adam: "What led you to eat from the tree which I forbade you?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' made it attractive to me." He said: "Then I have punished her by making her bear children only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I have caused her to bleed twice every month."

al-Bukhari and al-Hakim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Were it not for the Children of Israel, meat would not spoil, and were it not for Hawwa', no woman would ever betray her husband."

Many hadiths have been authentically narrated from a group of Companions in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, concerning the debate between Adam and Musa, in which Adam won the argument by saying: "Do you blame me for a matter which Allah had decreed for me before I was created?"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾, that he said: "Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent." ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, he said: "The graves." ﴿And provision for a time﴾, he said: "Life."

Similar things were narrated from Mujahid, Abu Salih and Qatadah. Abu al-Shaykh narrated the first and second of these, and Abd ibn Humayd narrated the third.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, that he said: "The graves." ﴿And provision for a time﴾, he said: "Until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: Adam was sent down at al-Safa and Hawwa' at al-Marwah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The first place to which Allah sent Adam down was the land of India." In another wording: "At Dajna, the land of India."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he was sent down to a land between Makkah and al-Ta'if.

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "The finest scent of the earth is that of India. Adam descended there, and its trees took on the scent of the Garden."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Adam was sent down to India and Hawwa' to Jeddah. He went searching for her until he came to Jam', and Hawwa' drew near to him, which is why it was called al-Muzdalifah, and they gathered at Jam'.

al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to India and became lonely. Jibril descended and called the adhan, and when Adam heard the mention of Muhammad, he said: 'Who is this Muhammad?' He said: 'This is the last of your offspring among the prophets.'"

It has been narrated from a group of Companions that Adam was sent down to the land of India, including Jabir, narrated by Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Asakir, and Ibn Umar, narrated by al-Tabarani.

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ali, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the world, He did not create gold or silver in it. When He sent Adam and Hawwa' down, He sent gold and silver down with them, and He caused them to flow in springs in the earth, as a benefit for their offspring after them. He made that the bridal gift (sadaq) for Hawwa'. So no one should marry except with a bridal gift."

Ibn Asakir narrated, through a weak chain, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam and Hawwa' were sent down both naked, with leaves of the Garden upon them. Adam sat weeping and said to her: 'O Hawwa', the heat has harmed me.' So Jibril brought cotton to her and commanded her to spin, and taught her, and commanded Adam to weave, and taught him."

al-Daylami, in Musnad al-Firdaws, narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The first to weave was Adam, peace be upon him."

Stories have been narrated from a group of Companions and Successors and those after them about the manner of Adam's descent from the Garden, what was sent down with him, and what he did upon reaching the earth, but there is no need for us to expand on all of that.

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾: "He said: 'My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did You not settle me in Your Garden?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, You will return me to the Garden?' He said: 'Yes.'"

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Asakir narrated, through a weak chain, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When Allah sent Adam down to the earth, he stood opposite the Ka'bah and prayed two rak'ahs." The hadith continues.

A similar report has been narrated through a chain that is acceptable (la ba'sa bihi), by al-Azraqi in Tarikh Makkah, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in al-Da'awat and Ibn Asakir, from the hadith of Buraydah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, that he said: "They are His words: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾" [al-A'raf 7:23].

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same through the chain of Ibn Jarir from him.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, the same.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid the same.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak the same.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he was asked: "What are the words which Adam received from his Lord?" He said: "The knowledge of the matter of the Hajj, and those are the words."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abd Allah ibn Zayd, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, that he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You, my Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy upon me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You, my Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so turn to me in forgiveness, for You are the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful."

al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman and Ibn Asakir narrated a similar report from Anas.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated a similar report here, and in al-Zuhd, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Asakir narrated a similar report through the chain of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas.

al-Daylami, in Musnad al-Firdaws, narrated a similar report, through a weak chain, from Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His words ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me﴾, that he said: "The guidance is the prophets, the messengers and the clarification."

Ibn al-Anbari, in al-Masahif, narrated from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿fa-man tabi'a hudaya﴾ (whoever follows My guidance), with the letter ya' (y) doubled (tashdid) and vowelled with a fatha."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His words ﴿Then no fear will be upon them﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, meaning they will not grieve over death.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 35–39 (part 1 of 2)**

*uskun* (﴿اسْكُنْ﴾): i.e., take the Garden as a dwelling (*maskan*), which is the place of residence. As for what some of the commentators (*mufassirun*) have said, that in His words ﴿uskun﴾ there is a hint that they would be made to leave, because dwelling (*sukna*) does not amount to ownership, and that this is derived from the statement of a group of scholars that whoever houses a man in a dwelling belonging to him does not thereby come to own it, and that he may evict him from it, then this is a customary (*'urfi*) meaning. What is obligatory is to adopt the linguistic Arabic meaning when no technical legal usage (*haqiqah shar'iyyah*) has been established for the word.

*wa-anta* (﴿وَأَنْتَ﴾): is an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the concealed pronoun in the verb, so that coordination (*'atf*) with it is valid, as is established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*): that coordination with a concealed nominative pronoun is not permissible except after emphasizing it with a detached pronoun.

Coordination may rarely come without emphasis, as in the words of the poet:

*"I said, when she approached, and the bright-faced ones, swaying like the cows of the plain, went through the sand in a winding path."*

And His words: *wa-zawjuka* (﴿وَزَوْجُكَ﴾), i.e., Hawwa'. This is the eloquent dialect, *zawj* without the *ha'* (of feminine marking). It has also come with the *ha'* rarely, as in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was with one of his wives when a man passed by him, so he called him and said: "O so-and-so, this is my wife, so-and-so," and the hadith continues. From this is also the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed the one who seeks to corrupt my wife is like a runner toward the lions of the thicket, trying to lure her."*

*raghadan* (﴿رَغَدًا﴾): with a *fatha* on the letter *ghayn*. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a *sukun*. *Al-raghad* is pleasant living in which there is no hardship. It is in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (*masdar*).

*haythu* (﴿حَيْثُ﴾): is indeclinable (*mabniyyah*) on *damm*, and it has many dialectal forms mentioned in the books of Arabic grammar.

*al-qurb* (﴿الْقُرْبَ﴾): is nearness (*al-dunuww*).

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): *qaruba al-shay'* (with a *damma*), *yaqrubu qurban*, meaning it drew near; *qaribtuhu* (with a *kasra*), *aqrabuhu quraban*, meaning I drew near to it; and *qarabtu aqrubu qarabatan*, like *katabtu aktubu kitabatan*, when you travel toward water with a night's distance between you and it. The noun is *al-qurb*. Al-Asma'i said: I said to a Bedouin: "What is *al-qurb*?" He said: "Traveling by night in order to arrive at the morning."

The prohibition of approaching (*al-qurb*) involves blocking the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*) and cutting off the way (*qat' al-wasilah*). That is why it was phrased as a substitute for eating. It is not hidden that the prohibition of approaching does not necessarily entail the prohibition of eating, because a person may eat from the fruit of the tree while being far from it, if it is brought to him. So it is better to say that the prohibition of eating is derived from the context (*al-maqam*).

*al-shajar* (﴿الشَّجَرَةَ﴾): is that which has a trunk from the plants of the earth. Its singular is *shajarah*. It has been read with a *kasra* on the *shin* and with a *ya'* in place of the *jim*.

Ibn Muhaysin read *hadhi* (﴿هَذِي﴾) with a *ya'* in place of the *ha'*, and this is the original form.

The scholars differed in identifying this tree. It was said to be the vine (*karm*), and it was said to be the ear of grain (*sunbulah*), and it was said to be the fig (*tin*), and it was said to be wheat (*hintah*). What was transmitted from the Companions and those after them regarding its identification will come.

His words *fa-takuna* (﴿فَتَكُونَا﴾) are coordinated with *taqraba* in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), or they are in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition, and this is the more apparent view.

*al-zulm* (﴿الظُّلْمُ﴾): its origin is placing a thing in other than its proper place. *Al-ardh al-mazlumah* is land that has never been dug and then was dug. A *zalim* man is one who is severe in wrongdoing.

What is meant here by ﴿فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ ("then you would be among the wrongdoers") is wronging themselves through disobedience. The discourse of the scholars on the infallibility of the prophets (*'ismah*) and the differences of their schools in this matter is recorded in its proper places. Al-Razi lengthily discussed this in his commentary at this point, so let the reader refer to it, for it is beneficial.

*fa-azallahuma* (﴿فَأَزَلَّهُمَا﴾): from *al-zallah*, which is sin (*al-khati'ah*), i.e., he caused them to slip and brought them into it. Hamzah read *fa-aza'lahuma* (with an *alif*, from *al-izalah*, which is *al-tahtiyyah* in the sense of: he removed them). The rest read it without the *alif*.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is from *al-zawal*, i.e., he turned them away from the obedience they were upon to disobedience.

Al-Qurtubi said: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning, except that the reading of the majority is more precise in meaning. It is said: *azlaltuhu fa-zalla*. *Wa-'anha* (﴿عَنْهَا﴾) is connected with His words *azallahuma*, with the verb being understood as containing the meaning of *asdara* (to cause to issue): i.e., Satan caused their slip to issue from it, that is, because of it, meaning the tree.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Garden. According to this, the verb is understood as containing the meaning of *ab'adahuma* (to drive far away): i.e., he drove them far from the Garden.

His words *fa-akhrajahuma* (﴿فَأَخْرَجَهُمَا﴾): are an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the content of the first clause, i.e., he caused them to slip, if its meaning is that they left their place. If its meaning is not so, then it is an establishing (*ta'sis*) of a new meaning, because expulsion (*ikhraj*) involves something beyond mere turning away, distancing and the like. Turning away from the tree and distancing from it may occur while they remain in the Garden, unlike expelling them from what they were in of bliss and honor, or from the Garden. He attributed this to Satan because he was the one who undertook to seduce Adam until he ate from the tree.

The scholars differed concerning the manner in which Satan carried out their slipping. It was said that it occurred through direct speech from him to them, and this is the view of the majority, who argued for it with His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَقَاسَمَهُمَا إِنِّي لَكُمَا لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("And he swore to them: Indeed I am to you among the sincere advisers") [al-A'raf: 21]. The *muqasamah* (swearing) apparently means direct speech. It was said that nothing proceeded from him except mere whispering (*waswasah*), and it was said other than that, as will come in what is related from the early generations (*salaf*).

His words *ihbitu* (﴿اهْبِطُوا﴾): are addressed to Adam and Hawwa'. They were addressed with what is addressed with the plural, because two is the least of the plural according to some of the leading Arabic grammarians. [p. 48] It was also said that it is addressed to them and to their offspring, because since they were the origin of this human species, they were treated as its representative. This is indicated by His words: ﴿بَعْضُكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("some of you are enemies to others"), for this clause, which occurs as a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) clarifying the state established for those commanded to descend, conveys that meaning.

*al-'aduww* (﴿الْعَدُوُّ﴾) is the opposite of friend. It is from *'adā* when he wronged. It is said: a wolf that is *'adawan*, i.e., it attacks people. *Al-'udwan* is blatant wrongdoing. It was also said it is derived from transgressing (*al-mujawazah*); one says *'adahu* when he passed beyond him. The two meanings are close, for whoever wrongs has transgressed.

He reported about *ba'dukum* (﴿بَعْضُكُمْ﴾) with His words *'aduww* (enemy) even though it is singular, because the word *ba'd* (some), although its meaning admits of multiplicity, is singular in form. So regard was given to the wording, and he reported about it with the singular. Sometimes regard is given to the meaning, and it is reported about with the plural.

It may be answered that *'aduww*, although singular, may be used in the position of the plural, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَهُمْ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("and they are an enemy to you") [al-Kahf: 50], and His words: ﴿يَحْسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيْحَةٍ عَلَيْهِمْ هُمُ الْعَدُوُّ﴾ ("they think every cry is against them; they are the enemy") [al-Munafiqun: 4]. Ibn Faris said: *al-'aduww* is a comprehensive noun for the singular, the dual and the plural.

*al-mustaqarr* (﴿الْمُسْتَقَرُّ﴾): is the place of settling. From it is His words: ﴿أَصْحَابُ الْجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا﴾ ("the companions of the Garden that day are better in their resting place") [al-Furqan: 24]. It may also mean the act of settling, and from it is His words: ﴿إِلَى رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ﴾ ("to your Lord that day is the settling") [al-Qiyamah: 12]. So the verse admits of both meanings. Similar to it is His words: ﴿جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ قَرَارًا﴾ ("He made for you the earth as a resting place") [Ghafir: 64].

*al-mata'* (﴿مَتَاعٌ﴾): is that which is enjoyed of food, drink, clothing and the like.

The commentators differed concerning His words *ila hin* (﴿إِلَى حِينٍ﴾): it was said, until death; and it was said, until the establishment of the Hour.

The basic meaning of *al-hin* linguistically is a long period of time. From it is His words: ﴿هَلْ أَتَى عَلَى الْإِنْسَانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ ("Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?") [al-Insan: 1]. *Al-hin* is also an hour, and from it is His words: ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ حِينَ تَرَى الْعَذَابَ﴾ ("or says when he sees the punishment") [al-Zumar: 58]. It is also a portion of time, and from it is His words: ﴿فَذَرْهُمْ فِي غَمْرَتِهِمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ﴾ ("so leave them in their confusion until a time") [al-Mu'minun: 54], i.e., until their lifespans end. It is also applied to a year, and it was said to six months, and from it is His words: ﴿تُؤْتِي أُكُلَهَا كُلَّ حِينٍ﴾ ("it gives its produce every season") [Ibrahim: 25]. It is also applied to evening and morning, and from it is His words: ﴿حِينَ تُمْسُونَ وَحِينَ تُصْبِحُونَ﴾ ("when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning") [al-Rum: 17]. Al-Farra' said: *al-hin* is of two kinds: one kind whose limit cannot be specified, and then he mentioned the other *hin*. Its variation according to the variation of contexts is as we have mentioned.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: an unknown *hin* has no ruling attached to it, and a known *hin* is a year.

The meaning of Adam's receiving (*talaqqi*) the words (*kalimat*) is his taking them, his acceptance of what is in them, and his acting upon them. It was said: his understanding of them and his perceptiveness of what they contained.

The basic meaning of *al-talaqqi* is receiving/meeting (*al-istiqbal*): i.e., he received the words revealed to him. Whoever read *Adama* with the accusative made its meaning: the words received him (*istaqbalathu*).

It was said that the meaning of *talaqqa* is *talaqqana* (to be taught), and there is no basis for this in Arabic.

The early generations differed concerning specifying these words, and that will come.

*al-tawbah* (﴿التَّوْبَةُ﴾) is return. One says *taba al-'abd* when he returned to the obedience of his Master. A *tawwab* servant is one who returns often. So the meaning of *taba 'alayhi* is: he turned to him with mercy, and so accepted his repentance, or granted him success in repenting.

He limited the mention of repentance to Adam, not Hawwa', despite their sharing the sin, because the discourse from the beginning of the narrative was with him, so it continued in that way, and the mention of repentance upon him sufficed for not mentioning it upon her, since she is a follower of him. Likewise, the attribution of the sin to him sufficed for not attributing it to her, as in His words: ﴿وَعَصَى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوَى﴾ ("Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray") [Ta-Ha: 121].

As for His words ﴿قُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا﴾ after His words ﴿قُلْنَا اهْبِطُوا﴾ (earlier), He repeated it for emphasis and for stressing.

It was also said: since a ruling different from the first ruling became attached to it, He repeated it, and there is no conflict among the implications. So the repetition may be for both matters together.

The answer to the conditional in His words ﴿فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدًى﴾ ("if guidance comes to you from Me") is the second condition together with its answer, as said by Sibawayh. Al-Kisa'i said: the answer to both the first and second conditions is His words ﴿فَلَا خَوْفٌ﴾ ("no fear").

They differed concerning the meaning of the mentioned guidance (*huda*). It was said: it is the Book of Allah. It was said: it is the granting of success (*tawfiq*) to guidance.

*al-khawf* (﴿الْخَوْفُ﴾): is dread (*al-du'r*), and it occurs only regarding the future.

Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Ammar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *fa-la khawfa* (﴿فَلا خَوْفَ﴾) with a *fatha* on the *fa'*.

*al-huzn* (﴿الْحُزْنُ﴾) is the opposite of joy (*al-surur*).

Al-Yazidi said: *hazanahu* is the dialect of Quraysh, and *ahzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim. Both have been read.

Their companionship with the Fire (*sahbat ahl al-nar*) means being attached and constantly accompanying.

The explanation of *al-khulud* (eternal abiding) has been mentioned before.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh recorded, on the authority of Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me, was Adam a prophet?" He said: "Yes, he was a prophet, a messenger, whom Allah addressed directly. He said to him: ﴿O Adam, dwell you and your wife in the Garden﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani recorded, on the authority of Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who was the first of the prophets?" He said: "Adam." I said: "Was he a prophet?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Then who?" He said: "Nuh, and between them were ten fathers."

Ahmad and al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, recorded something similar from the hadith of Abu Dharr, marfu'ly, and added: "How many were the messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sound) and al-Bayhaqi recorded, on the authority of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, was Adam a prophet?" He said: "Yes." He said: "How far was between him and Nuh?" He said: "Ten centuries." He said: "How far between Nuh and Ibrahim?" He said: "Ten centuries." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, how many are the prophets?" He said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, how many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude."

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh recorded something similar from the hadith of Abu Umamah, and stated explicitly that the questioner was Abu Dharr.

'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim (who declared it sound) recorded, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Adam did not dwell in the Garden except between the time of the afternoon prayer (*'asr*) and the setting of the sun."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi recorded from him, who said: "The sun did not set on that day until he was brought down from the Garden."

al-Firyabi, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded, on the authority of al-Hasan, who said: "Adam remained in the Garden for an hour of a day, and that hour was one hundred and thirty years of the days of this world."

The estimate of his stay in the Garden has also been transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr in the same manner as what came before from Ibn 'Abbas, as Ahmad recorded in al-Zuhd.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 35–39 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, that they said: When Adam dwelt in the Garden, he walked in it alone, a lonely creature with no spouse to find comfort in. He slept a sleep, and when he awoke, there was a woman sitting at his head, whom Allah had created from his rib.

al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Be good to women, for woman was created from a rib, and the most crooked part of the rib is its top. If you try to straighten it, you will break it, and if you leave it, it will remain crooked. So be good to women."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Hawwa' (Eve) was named so only because she is the mother of every living being.

Ibn Adi and Ibn Asakir narrated, from al-Nakha'i, who said: When Allah created Adam and created his spouse for him, He sent an angel to him and commanded him to have intercourse with her, and he did. When he finished, Hawwa' said to him: "O Adam, this is good; give us more of it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Asakir narrated, from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: al-Raghad means "pleasant and wholesome."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from Ibn Abbas, who said: al-Raghad means "abundance of livelihood."

Both of them also narrated from him, concerning His words ﴿And eat from it abundantly wherever you wish﴾, that he said: "There is no reckoning upon you."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Asakir narrated, through several chains, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The tree which Allah forbade Adam was the ear of grain (sunbulah). In another wording: it was wheat (al-burr).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: It was the grapevine (al-karm).

Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him that he said: It was the almond (al-lawz).

Ibn Jarir narrated from one of the Companions that he said: It was the fig (al-tinah).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated the same from Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: It was wheat (al-burr).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he said: It was the date palm (al-nakhlah).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt that he said: It was the citron (al-utrujj).

Ahmad, in Kitab al-Zuhd (the Book of Asceticism), narrated from Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i that he said: It resembles wheat and is called al-da'ah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿fa-azallahuma﴾ (so He caused them to slip), that he said: "fa-aghwahuma" (so He led them astray).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Asim ibn Bahdalah that he said: "fa-azallahuma" means "fa-nahhahuma" (so He removed them).

Abu Dawud, in al-Masahif (the Codices), narrated from al-A'mash that he said: Our recitation in al-Baqarah in place of ﴿fa-azallahuma﴾ is ﴿fa-waswasa﴾ (so he whispered).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: Iblis wanted to enter the Garden to reach them both, but the guardians (al-khazanah) prevented him. So he came to the serpent (al-hayyah), which was a creature with four legs, like a camel, and it was the most beautiful of animals. He spoke to it, asking it to let him into its mouth so that it could bring him in to Adam. It let him into its mouth, and the serpent passed by the guardians and entered, and they did not know what Allah intended by the matter. He spoke to Adam from its mouth, but Adam paid no heed to his words. So Iblis came out to him and said: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?" [Ta-Ha 20:120], and he swore to them both by Allah: ﴿Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:21]. Adam refused to eat from it, but Hawwa' went ahead and ate. Then she said: "O Adam, eat, for I have eaten and it has not harmed me." When they both ate, ﴿their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf 7:22].

Ibn Abbas narrated the story of the serpent and Iblis's entry along with it through Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir.

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam was a tall man, like a towering palm tree, sixty cubits in height, with abundant hair on his head. When he committed the sin, his private parts became apparent to him..." and the hadith continues.

Ibn Mani', Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah said to Adam: "What led you to eat from the tree which I forbade you?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' made it attractive to me." He said: "Then I have punished her by making her bear children only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I have caused her to bleed twice every month."

al-Bukhari and al-Hakim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Were it not for the Children of Israel, meat would not spoil, and were it not for Hawwa', no woman would ever betray her husband."

Many hadiths have been authentically narrated from a group of Companions in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, concerning the debate between Adam and Musa, in which Adam won the argument by saying: "Do you blame me for a matter which Allah had decreed for me before I was created?"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾, that he said: "Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent." ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, he said: "The graves." ﴿And provision for a time﴾, he said: "Life."

Similar things were narrated from Mujahid, Abu Salih and Qatadah. Abu al-Shaykh narrated the first and second of these, and Abd ibn Humayd narrated the third.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, that he said: "The graves." ﴿And provision for a time﴾, he said: "Until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: Adam was sent down at al-Safa and Hawwa' at al-Marwah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The first place to which Allah sent Adam down was the land of India." In another wording: "At Dajna, the land of India."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he was sent down to a land between Makkah and al-Ta'if.

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him that he said: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "The finest scent of the earth is that of India. Adam descended there, and its trees took on the scent of the Garden."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Adam was sent down to India and Hawwa' to Jeddah. He went searching for her until he came to Jam', and Hawwa' drew near to him, which is why it was called al-Muzdalifah, and they gathered at Jam'.

al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to India and became lonely. Jibril descended and called the adhan, and when Adam heard the mention of Muhammad, he said: 'Who is this Muhammad?' He said: 'This is the last of your offspring among the prophets.'"

It has been narrated from a group of Companions that Adam was sent down to the land of India, including Jabir, narrated by Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Asakir, and Ibn Umar, narrated by al-Tabarani.

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ali, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the world, He did not create gold or silver in it. When He sent Adam and Hawwa' down, He sent gold and silver down with them, and He caused them to flow in springs in the earth, as a benefit for their offspring after them. He made that the bridal gift (sadaq) for Hawwa'. So no one should marry except with a bridal gift."

Ibn Asakir narrated, through a weak chain, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam and Hawwa' were sent down both naked, with leaves of the Garden upon them. Adam sat weeping and said to her: 'O Hawwa', the heat has harmed me.' So Jibril brought cotton to her and commanded her to spin, and taught her, and commanded Adam to weave, and taught him."

al-Daylami, in Musnad al-Firdaws, narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The first to weave was Adam, peace be upon him."

Stories have been narrated from a group of Companions and Successors and those after them about the manner of Adam's descent from the Garden, what was sent down with him, and what he did upon reaching the earth, but there is no need for us to expand on all of that.

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾: "He said: 'My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, did You not settle me in Your Garden?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'My Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, You will return me to the Garden?' He said: 'Yes.'"

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Asakir narrated, through a weak chain, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When Allah sent Adam down to the earth, he stood opposite the Ka'bah and prayed two rak'ahs." The hadith continues.

A similar report has been narrated through a chain that is acceptable (la ba'sa bihi), by al-Azraqi in Tarikh Makkah, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in al-Da'awat and Ibn Asakir, from the hadith of Buraydah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, that he said: "They are His words: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾" [al-A'raf 7:23].

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same through the chain of Ibn Jarir from him.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, the same.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid the same.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak the same.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he was asked: "What are the words which Adam received from his Lord?" He said: "The knowledge of the matter of the Hajj, and those are the words."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abd Allah ibn Zayd, concerning His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, that he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You, my Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy upon me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise be to You, my Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so turn to me in forgiveness, for You are the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful."

al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman and Ibn Asakir narrated a similar report from Anas.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated a similar report here, and in al-Zuhd, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Asakir narrated a similar report through the chain of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas.

al-Daylami, in Musnad al-Firdaws, narrated a similar report, through a weak chain, from Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His words ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me﴾, that he said: "The guidance is the prophets, the messengers and the clarification."

Ibn al-Anbari, in al-Masahif, narrated from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿fa-man tabi'a hudaya﴾ (whoever follows My guidance), with the letter ya' (y) doubled (tashdid) and vowelled with a fatha."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His words ﴿Then no fear will be upon them﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, meaning they will not grieve over death.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 35–39 (part 1 of 2)**

*uskun* (﴿اسْكُنْ﴾): i.e., take the Garden as a dwelling (*maskan*), which is the place of residence. As for what some of the commentators (*mufassirun*) have said, that in His words ﴿uskun﴾ there is a hint that they would be made to leave, because dwelling (*sukna*) does not amount to ownership, and that this is derived from the statement of a group of scholars that whoever houses a man in a dwelling belonging to him does not thereby come to own it, and that he may evict him from it, then this is a customary (*'urfi*) meaning. What is obligatory is to adopt the linguistic Arabic meaning when no technical legal usage (*haqiqah shar'iyyah*) has been established for the word.

*wa-anta* (﴿وَأَنْتَ﴾): is an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the concealed pronoun in the verb, so that coordination (*'atf*) with it is valid, as is established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*): that coordination with a concealed nominative pronoun is not permissible except after emphasizing it with a detached pronoun.

Coordination may rarely come without emphasis, as in the words of the poet:

*"I said, when she approached, and the bright-faced ones, swaying like the cows of the plain, went through the sand in a winding path."*

And His words: *wa-zawjuka* (﴿وَزَوْجُكَ﴾), i.e., Hawwa'. This is the eloquent dialect, *zawj* without the *ha'* (of feminine marking). It has also come with the *ha'* rarely, as in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was with one of his wives when a man passed by him, so he called him and said: "O so-and-so, this is my wife, so-and-so," and the hadith continues. From this is also the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed the one who seeks to corrupt my wife is like a runner toward the lions of the thicket, trying to lure her."*

*raghadan* (﴿رَغَدًا﴾): with a *fatha* on the letter *ghayn*. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read it with a *sukun*. *Al-raghad* is pleasant living in which there is no hardship. It is in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (*masdar*).

*haythu* (﴿حَيْثُ﴾): is indeclinable (*mabniyyah*) on *damm*, and it has many dialectal forms mentioned in the books of Arabic grammar.

*al-qurb* (﴿الْقُرْبَ﴾): is nearness (*al-dunuww*).

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): *qaruba al-shay'* (with a *damma*), *yaqrubu qurban*, meaning it drew near; *qaribtuhu* (with a *kasra*), *aqrabuhu quraban*, meaning I drew near to it; and *qarabtu aqrubu qarabatan*, like *katabtu aktubu kitabatan*, when you travel toward water with a night's distance between you and it. The noun is *al-qurb*. Al-Asma'i said: I said to a Bedouin: "What is *al-qurb*?" He said: "Traveling by night in order to arrive at the morning."

The prohibition of approaching (*al-qurb*) involves blocking the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*) and cutting off the way (*qat' al-wasilah*). That is why it was phrased as a substitute for eating. It is not hidden that the prohibition of approaching does not necessarily entail the prohibition of eating, because a person may eat from the fruit of the tree while being far from it, if it is brought to him. So it is better to say that the prohibition of eating is derived from the context (*al-maqam*).

*al-shajar* (﴿الشَّجَرَةَ﴾): is that which has a trunk from the plants of the earth. Its singular is *shajarah*. It has been read with a *kasra* on the *shin* and with a *ya'* in place of the *jim*.

Ibn Muhaysin read *hadhi* (﴿هَذِي﴾) with a *ya'* in place of the *ha'*, and this is the original form.

The scholars differed in identifying this tree. It was said to be the vine (*karm*), and it was said to be the ear of grain (*sunbulah*), and it was said to be the fig (*tin*), and it was said to be wheat (*hintah*). What was transmitted from the Companions and those after them regarding its identification will come.

His words *fa-takuna* (﴿فَتَكُونَا﴾) are coordinated with *taqraba* in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), or they are in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition, and this is the more apparent view.

*al-zulm* (﴿الظُّلْمُ﴾): its origin is placing a thing in other than its proper place. *Al-ardh al-mazlumah* is land that has never been dug and then was dug. A *zalim* man is one who is severe in wrongdoing.

What is meant here by ﴿فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ ("then you would be among the wrongdoers") is wronging themselves through disobedience. The discourse of the scholars on the infallibility of the prophets (*'ismah*) and the differences of their schools in this matter is recorded in its proper places. Al-Razi lengthily discussed this in his commentary at this point, so let the reader refer to it, for it is beneficial.

*fa-azallahuma* (﴿فَأَزَلَّهُمَا﴾): from *al-zallah*, which is sin (*al-khati'ah*), i.e., he caused them to slip and brought them into it. Hamzah read *fa-aza'lahuma* (with an *alif*, from *al-izalah*, which is *al-tahtiyyah* in the sense of: he removed them). The rest read it without the *alif*.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is from *al-zawal*, i.e., he turned them away from the obedience they were upon to disobedience.

Al-Qurtubi said: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning, except that the reading of the majority is more precise in meaning. It is said: *azlaltuhu fa-zalla*. *Wa-'anha* (﴿عَنْهَا﴾) is connected with His words *azallahuma*, with the verb being understood as containing the meaning of *asdara* (to cause to issue): i.e., Satan caused their slip to issue from it, that is, because of it, meaning the tree.

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Garden. According to this, the verb is understood as containing the meaning of *ab'adahuma* (to drive far away): i.e., he drove them far from the Garden.
