Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His words ﴿And if guidance comes to you from Me﴾, that he said: "The guidance is the prophets, the messengers and the clarification."

Ibn al-Anbari, in al-Masahif, narrated from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿fa-man tabi'a hudaya﴾ (whoever follows My guidance), with the letter ya' (y) doubled (tashdid) and vowelled with a fatha."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His words ﴿Then no fear will be upon them﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, meaning they will not grieve over death.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 1 of 2):

.
Know that many exegetes (mufassirun) came up with artificial knowledge, plunged into a sea they were not obliged to swim, and spent their time on a discipline that brings them no benefit. Rather, they exposed themselves to speaking on the basis of mere personal opinion, which is forbidden in matters concerning the Book of God, the Glorified. This is because they wished to mention the connection (munasaba) between the Qur'anic verses arranged in this order found in the copies of the Qur'an, so they brought forth affectations and far-fetched interpretations from which fairness disowns itself and which the speech of eloquent people, let alone the speech of the Lord, the Glorified, is free from. To the point that they devoted this to separate works of authorship and made it the most important aim of their composition, as al-Biqa'i did in his tafsir and those before him, as he mentioned in his introduction. This is among the most astonishing things heard by one who knows that this Qur'an continued to be revealed in pieces, according to the events that required its revelation, from the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until God, Mighty and Majestic, took him to Himself. Every sane person, let alone a scholar, does not doubt that these events requiring the revelation of the Qur'an are different in themselves, and may even be contradictory: such as the prohibition of a matter that was lawful, the permitting of a matter that was unlawful, and the affirming of a matter for a person or persons that contradicts what had been affirmed for them before it. Sometimes the speech is with the Muslims, sometimes with the disbelievers, sometimes with those who have passed, sometimes with those present; sometimes about worship, sometimes about dealings; at times in encouragement, at times in warning; at moments in glad tidings, at moments in admonition; at one time about worldly affairs, at another about the affairs of the Hereafter; once about obligations that are to come, and once about past stories.

If the occasions of revelation are thus varied, and so divergent that agreement is not easily achieved with them, then the Qur'an revealed concerning them is, in its own nature, different just as they are different. So how can a sane person seek a connection between the lizard (dabb) and the fish (nun), the water and the fire, the sailor and the driver of camels? Is this anything but opening the doors of doubt and widening the circle of suspicion for one in whose heart there is a disease, or whose disease is merely ignorance and deficiency? For when he finds the people of knowledge speaking about the connection between all the verses of the Qur'an and devoting separate works to it, it becomes firmly established in his mind that this is a necessary matter, and that the Qur'an cannot be eloquent and miraculous unless the aspect requiring connection appears and the matter necessitating linkage is made clear. Then, if he finds disagreement between the verses, and he returns to what the speakers on this subject have said and finds it to be pure artifice and clear far-fetchedness, there arises in his heart what had been in safety and soundness. This is on the assumption that the revelation of the Qur'an was arranged in this order that exists in the copy (mushaf). So how much more so, when everyone with even minimal knowledge of the Book, and the slightest share of acquaintance with it, knows with certainty that it was not like that? And whoever doubts this, even if it is not something the people of knowledge doubt, should return to the words of the people of knowledge who are acquainted with the occasions of revelation and familiar with the events of prophethood. For his chest will be relieved and doubt will leave him by looking at one surah of the medium-length surahs, let alone the long ones, because he will inevitably find it containing verses that were revealed concerning different events and at different times, with no correspondence between their occasions and what was revealed concerning them in the order (of the mushaf). Everyone, the deficient and the complete, knows that God, the Glorified, described this Qur'an as being in Arabic, and revealed it in the language of the Arabs, following their paths of speech and proceeding in their modes of address.

We know that their orator would stand in one station and produce various arts and different methods, let alone two stations, let alone many stations, let alone everything he said as long as he lived. Likewise their poet.

Let us be content with this warning about this corruption in whose arenas many of the researchers have stumbled. So if an artificial objector says: "How does this connect with what precedes it?" We say: "No, not how:"
"Leave aside the plunder that was cried out in its chambers, and bring a tale: what is the tale of the riding camels?"

His saying: "O Children of Israel." The exegetes agree that Israel is Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, and its meaning is "servant of God", because "isr" in their language means "servant" and "il" means "God." Al-dhikr is the opposite of listening silently (al-inssat). Some of the lexicographers made it a shared term between remembrance of the heart and of the tongue.

Al-Kisa'i said: What is by the heart has a dammah on the dhal, and what is by the tongue has a kasrah on the dhal.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning in the verse is: "Remember the thanks for My blessing," so he omitted "thanks" by being content with mention of "blessing," which is a generic noun. Among its components is that He made prophets from among them, sent down the Books upon them, the manna and the quails, brought forth water for them from the rock, saved them from the people of Pharaoh, and other things.

The covenant has already had its explanation discussed.

The scholars differed concerning what the covenant mentioned in this verse is. It was said: it is the one mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. It was said: it is what is in His saying: ﴿And God had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12]. It was said: it is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

Al-Zajjaj said: It is what was taken from them in the Torah regarding following Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: it is the performance of the obligations. There is no barrier to carrying it on all of that.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿Fulfill My covenant﴾ means: "fulfill what I have guaranteed you of reward."

Al-rahab and al-rahbah: fear. The command to it includes the meaning of threat. The fronting of the verb's object indicates restriction, as has already passed in ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. When the fronting is by way of pronominalization and explanation, like: "Zayd, I struck him," as in ﴿And of Me alone, be fearful﴾, it is more emphatic in indicating restriction. The ya' was dropped from His saying: ﴿fa-rhabun﴾ because it is the end of a verse (ra's aya). And muşaddiqan is a state (hal) referring to "ma" in His saying: "ma anzaltu" (what I have sent down), or to its implied pronoun after the verb, meaning "anzaltuhu" (I sent it down).

His saying: ﴿the first to disbelieve in it﴾ came in the singular, and it did not say "disbelievers" so as to agree with what precedes it, because it is an adjective for an omitted noun that is singular in form but plural in meaning, like firq (group) or fawj (company).

Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: It is taken as referring to the meaning of the verb, because the meaning is "the first who disbelieved."

It was also said that it refers back to the Qur'an, indicated by His saying: "bima anzaltu" (in what I have sent down). And it was said it refers back to the Torah, indicated by His saying: "limā ma'akum" (for what is with you).

"You see the companion who speaks the truth, you think him rightly guided, but far from it; look at what has confused him."
"Believe his speech, beware his enmity, and confuse him with matters like what he confused."

Al-'Ajjaj said:
"When I mixed the truth with accusation, they blamed me and took Zayd in my place."

And from it is the saying of 'Antara:

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 2 of 2)**

*(Poetry)*
> "And a battalion I put on over another battalion,
> until, when they became confused, I shook off my hand from them."

It has also been said that *al-talbis* (لبس, "confusing" or "mixing") is derived from *al-taghtiyah* (التغطية, "covering"). The meaning is: do not cover the truth with falsehood. From this is the verse of al-Ja'di:

> "When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends over him, and she is a garment."

And the verse of al-Akhtal:

> "I have worn this matter, its very core, until gray hair covered my head and blazed."

The first meaning is preferable.

*Al-batil* (الباطل, "falsehood") in the speech of the Arabs means that which is passing away. From this is the line of Labid:

> "Certainly everything other than God is passing away."

*Batala al-shay'* (بطل الشيء) means a thing becomes void, with *butul* and *butlan*. Another person makes it void (*abtalahu*). It is said: *dhahaba damuhu batalan*, meaning his blood was lost without retribution (*hadran*). *Al-batil* can also mean Satan. A brave man is called *batal* because he nullifies (*yubtilu*) the courage of his companion. The meaning here is the opposite of the truth (*al-haqq*).

The *ba'* (باء) in God's words *bi-al-batil* may be a connecting particle (*silah*), or it may denote instrumentality (*al-isti'anah*). Al-Zamakhshari (author of *al-Kashshaf*) mentioned its meaning in *al-Kashshaf*, and al-Razi, in his tafsir, preferred the second.

His words *wa-taktumu* (وتكتموا, "and conceal") may be included under the prohibition, or it may be in the subjunctive governed by an implied *an* (أن). On the first reading, each of the mixing (*al-labs*) and the concealing (*al-katm*) is forbidden. On the second reading, what is forbidden is the combining of the two matters. From this it appears preferable that it falls under the prohibition, and that each of them is not permissible on its own.

The intended meaning is the prohibition of concealing the proofs of God which He obligated them to convey and which He took a covenant from them to explain. Whoever interprets *al-labs* or *al-katm* as a particular thing with a specific meaning has not been correct, if he means that this alone is what is intended and nothing else. It is not wrong if he means that it is one of the things it covers.

His words *wa-antum ta'lamun* (وأنتم تعلمون, "while you know") form a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). In it is the indication that their disbelief was disbelief of obstinacy (*kufr 'inad*), not disbelief of ignorance (*kufr jahl*). That is more severe as a sin and more deserving of punishment. This restriction does not imply that mixing and concealing are permissible in ignorance, because the ignorant person is obligated not to proceed with anything until he knows its ruling, especially in matters of religion. Speaking about them, and presuming to issue or narrate rulings in their domains, is only permitted by God to one who is a leader in knowledge and unique in understanding. What business do the ignorant have in entering what is not their concern, or sitting in places that are not their seats?

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding God's words: "O Children of Israel," he said to the rabbis of the Jews: ﴿Remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾, that is, My trial among you and among your forefathers when He rescued them from Pharaoh and his people. ﴿And fulfill My covenant﴾, which I took upon your necks for the Prophet (ﷺ) when he comes to you: ﴿I will fulfill your covenant﴾, that is, I will fulfill for you what I promised you, by affirming him and following him, by removing from you the burden and the shackles that were upon you. ﴿And fear Me﴾, lest I send down upon you what I sent down upon those who were before you, your forefathers, of retributions. ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, while you have in it knowledge that others do not have. ﴿And do not conceal the truth while you know﴾, that is, do not conceal what you have of knowledge of My Messenger and of what has come to you through him, while you find it with you in what you know from the books that are in your hands.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding God's words: "Fulfill My covenant," that he said: "I will be pleased with you and admit you into Paradise."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding God's words: ﴿I will fulfill your covenant﴾, that he said: it is the covenant which He took from them in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿God had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12], and the rest of the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Hasan, who said: "Fulfill for Me what I have made obligatory upon you, and I will fulfill for you what I promised you."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh reported something similar from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding God's words: ﴿And fear Me﴾, he said: "Dread Me."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Juraij reported from Mujahid regarding God's words: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾, he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿Confirming what is with you﴾, he said: "The Torah and the Gospel."

Ibn Juraij reported from Ibn Jarir regarding God's words: ﴿The first to disbelieve in it﴾, he said: "in the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding the verse, he said: He says: O assembly of the People of the Book, believe in what I have sent down upon Muhammad, confirming what is with you, because they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, that is, the first to disbelieve in Muhammad. ﴿And do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾: he says, do not take a wage for it. He said: and it is written with them in the first Book: "O son of Adam, teach freely as you were taught freely."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, he said: "Do not take a wage for what you teach. The reward of scholars, wise men, and forbearing people is only with God."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding God's words: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾, he said: "Do not mix the truth with lies." ﴿And conceal the truth﴾, he said: "Do not conceal the truth while you have known that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah regarding God's words: "And do not mix..." (the verse), he said: "Do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, and conceal the truth." He said: "They concealed Muhammad while they knew that he is the Messenger of God; they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel."

Ibn Jarir reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The truth is the Torah, and the falsehood is what they wrote with their own hands."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 1 of 2):

Know that many exegetes (mufassirun) came up with artificial knowledge, plunged into a sea they were not obliged to swim, and spent their time on a discipline that brings them no benefit. Rather, they exposed themselves to speaking on the basis of mere personal opinion, which is forbidden in matters concerning the Book of God, the Glorified. This is because they wished to mention the connection (munasaba) between the Qur'anic verses arranged in this order found in the copies of the Qur'an, so they brought forth affectations and far-fetched interpretations from which fairness disowns itself and which the speech of eloquent people, let alone the speech of the Lord, the Glorified, is free from. To the point that they devoted this to separate works of authorship and made it the most important aim of their composition, as al-Biqa'i did in his tafsir and those before him, as he mentioned in his introduction. This is among the most astonishing things heard by one who knows that this Qur'an continued to be revealed in pieces, according to the events that required its revelation, from the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until God, Mighty and Majestic, took him to Himself. Every sane person, let alone a scholar, does not doubt that these events requiring the revelation of the Qur'an are different in themselves, and may even be contradictory: such as the prohibition of a matter that was lawful, the permitting of a matter that was unlawful, and the affirming of a matter for a person or persons that contradicts what had been affirmed for them before it. Sometimes the speech is with the Muslims, sometimes with the disbelievers, sometimes with those who have passed, sometimes with those present; sometimes about worship, sometimes about dealings; at times in encouragement, at times in warning; at moments in glad tidings, at moments in admonition; at one time about worldly affairs, at another about the affairs of the Hereafter; once about obligations that are to come, and once about past stories.

If the occasions of revelation are thus varied, and so divergent that agreement is not easily achieved with them, then the Qur'an revealed concerning them is, in its own nature, different just as they are different. So how can a sane person seek a connection between the lizard (dabb) and the fish (nun), the water and the fire, the sailor and the driver of camels? Is this anything but opening the doors of doubt and widening the circle of suspicion for one in whose heart there is a disease, or whose disease is merely ignorance and deficiency? For when he finds the people of knowledge speaking about the connection between all the verses of the Qur'an and devoting separate works to it, it becomes firmly established in his mind that this is a necessary matter, and that the Qur'an cannot be eloquent and miraculous unless the aspect requiring connection appears and the matter necessitating linkage is made clear. Then, if he finds disagreement between the verses, and he returns to what the speakers on this subject have said and finds it to be pure artifice and clear far-fetchedness, there arises in his heart what had been in safety and soundness. This is on the assumption that the revelation of the Qur'an was arranged in this order that exists in the copy (mushaf). So how much more so, when everyone with even minimal knowledge of the Book, and the slightest share of acquaintance with it, knows with certainty that it was not like that? And whoever doubts this, even if it is not something the people of knowledge doubt, should return to the words of the people of knowledge who are acquainted with the occasions of revelation and familiar with the events of prophethood. For his chest will be relieved and doubt will leave him by looking at one surah of the medium-length surahs, let alone the long ones, because he will inevitably find it containing verses that were revealed concerning different events and at different times, with no correspondence between their occasions and what was revealed concerning them in the order (of the mushaf). Rather, it suffices the negligent to know that the first thing revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], and after it ﴿O you wrapped up﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1]; and let him look at where these verses and surahs are placed in the order of the mushaf. If the matter is like this, then what is the meaning of seeking a connection between verses of which we know for certain that what God revealed earlier has been placed later in the order of the mushaf, and what God revealed later has been placed earlier? This is an activity that does not go back to the order of the revelation of the Qur'an, but rather to the order that resulted during its collection by those among the Companions who undertook that task. How little benefit such a thing has, how meagre its fruit, and how worthless its usefulness! Rather, to one who understands what he says and what is said to him, it is a squandering of time and an expenditure of hours on a matter that brings no benefit to its doer nor to those people who look into it. You know that if a man of knowledge took it upon himself to find a connection between what a certain eloquent person said in his sermons, letters and compositions, or between what a certain poet said in his poems, which are sometimes praise, sometimes satire, sometimes amatory prologue and sometimes elegy, and other varied types, then this one who undertook it went and gathered that collection and found a connection between its sections and parts. Then he made another artifice and found a connection between the sermon he delivered concerning jihad, the sermon concerning the pilgrimage, the sermon he delivered at a marriage, and the like; and he connected the composition said at a condolence and the composition said at a celebration, and what resembles them. Such a person would be considered to have lost his mind, toying with his time and playing with his life, which is his capital. If this is his station when it comes to human speech, and it is the riding of folly in the speech of people, then how would it be in the speech of God, the Glorified, whose eloquence has rendered the eloquent of the Arabs incapable, and whose rhetoric has struck dumb the orators of 'Adnan and Qahtan?

Everyone, the deficient and the complete, knows that God, the Glorified, described this Qur'an as being in Arabic, and revealed it in the language of the Arabs, following their paths of speech and proceeding in their modes of address.

We know that their orator would stand in one station and produce various arts and different methods, let alone two stations, let alone many stations, let alone everything he said as long as he lived. Likewise their poet.

Let us be content with this warning about this corruption in whose arenas many of the researchers have stumbled. We have only mentioned this discussion here because the speech has moved here with the Children of Israel, after it had previously been with the father of mankind, Adam (peace be upon him). So if an artificial objector says: "How does this connect with what precedes it?" We say: "No, not how:"
"Leave aside the plunder that was cried out in its chambers, and bring a tale: what is the tale of the riding camels?"

His saying: "O Children of Israel." The exegetes agree that Israel is Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, and its meaning is "servant of God", because "isr" in their language means "servant" and "il" means "God." It was said that he had two names; and it was said that Israel is a title for him. It is a non-Arabic proper noun that is not declined (ghayr munsarif), and it has seven dialects: Isra'il on the pattern of Ibrahim; Isra'il with a hamza and a short vowel, transmitted by Ibn Shanbudh from Warsh; Isra'il with a long vowel after the ya' without hamza, which is the reading of al-A'mash and Isa ibn Umar; al-Hasan read it without hamza or long vowel; Isra'il with a kasra on the hamza; Isra'al with a fatha on the hamza; and the Tamim say Isra'in.

Al-dhikr is the opposite of listening silently (al-inssat). Some of the lexicographers made it a shared term between remembrance of the heart and of the tongue.

Al-Kisa'i said: What is by the heart has a dammah on the dhal, and what is by the tongue has a kasrah on the dhal.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning in the verse is: "Remember the thanks for My blessing," so he omitted "thanks" by being content with mention of "blessing," which is a generic noun. Among its components is that He made prophets from among them, sent down the Books upon them, the manna and the quails, brought forth water for them from the rock, saved them from the people of Pharaoh, and other things.

The covenant has already had its explanation discussed.

The scholars differed concerning what the covenant mentioned in this verse is. It was also said that it refers back to the Qur'an, indicated by His saying: "bima anzaltu" (in what I have sent down). And it was said it refers back to the Torah, indicated by His saying: "limā ma'akum" (for what is with you).

His saying: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a little price﴾: that is, "My commands and My prohibitions." ﴿A little price﴾: meagre livelihood and leadership without any worth.

He made what they accepted in exchange a "price," and attributed the buying to it, even though the price is what is bought with, because the buying here is used figuratively for exchange. That is: "Do not exchange My signs for a little price." Such usage occurs frequently in their speech.

We have already presented the discussion of it in the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. From the use of the name "price" for gaining some worldly commodity is the saying of the poet:
"If you sought the world, or you gained it, you did not gain, by abandoning the pilgrimage, anything of value."

This is because they wished to mention the connection (munasaba) between the Qur'anic verses arranged in this order found in the copies of the Qur'an, so they brought forth affectations and far-fetched interpretations from which fairness disowns itself and which the speech of eloquent people, let alone the speech of the Lord, the Glorified, is free from. To the point that they devoted this to separate works of authorship and made it the most important aim of their composition, as al-Biqa'i did in his tafsir and those before him, as he mentioned in his introduction. This is among the most astonishing things heard by one who knows that this Qur'an continued to be revealed in pieces, according to the events that required its revelation, from the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until God, Mighty and Majestic, took him to Himself. Every sane person, let alone a scholar, does not doubt that these events requiring the revelation of the Qur'an are different in themselves, and may even be contradictory: such as the prohibition of a matter that was lawful, the permitting of a matter that was unlawful, and the affirming of a matter for a person or persons that contradicts what had been affirmed for them before it. Sometimes the speech is with the Muslims, sometimes with the disbelievers, sometimes with those who have passed, sometimes with those present; sometimes about worship, sometimes about dealings; at times in encouragement, at times in warning; at moments in glad tidings, at moments in admonition; at one time about worldly affairs, at another about the affairs of the Hereafter; once about obligations that are to come, and once about past stories.

If the occasions of revelation are thus varied, and so divergent that agreement is not easily achieved with them, then the Qur'an revealed concerning them is, in its own nature, different just as they are different. So how can a sane person seek a connection between the lizard (dabb) and the fish (nun), the water and the fire, the sailor and the driver of camels? Is this anything but opening the doors of doubt and widening the circle of suspicion for one in whose heart there is a disease, or whose disease is merely ignorance and deficiency? For when he finds the people of knowledge speaking about the connection between all the verses of the Qur'an and devoting separate works to it, it becomes firmly established in his mind that this is a necessary matter, and that the Qur'an cannot be eloquent and miraculous unless the aspect requiring connection appears and the matter necessitating linkage is made clear. Then, if he finds disagreement between the verses, and he returns to what the speakers on this subject have said and finds it to be pure artifice and clear far-fetchedness, there arises in his heart what had been in safety and soundness. This is on the assumption that the revelation of the Qur'an was arranged in this order that exists in the copy (mushaf). So how much more so, when everyone with even minimal knowledge of the Book, and the slightest share of acquaintance with it, knows with certainty that it was not like that? And whoever doubts this, even if it is not something the people of knowledge doubt, should return to the words of the people of knowledge who are acquainted with the occasions of revelation and familiar with the events of prophethood. For his chest will be relieved and doubt will leave him by looking at one surah of the medium-length surahs, let alone the long ones, because he will inevitably find it containing verses that were revealed concerning different events and at different times, with no correspondence between their occasions and what was revealed concerning them in the order (of the mushaf). Rather, it suffices the negligent to know that the first thing revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], and after it ﴿O you wrapped up﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1]; and let him look at where these verses and surahs are placed in the order of the mushaf. If the matter is like this, then what is the meaning of seeking a connection between verses of which we know for certain that what God revealed earlier has been placed later in the order of the mushaf, and what God revealed later has been placed earlier? This is an activity that does not go back to the order of the revelation of the Qur'an, but rather to the order that resulted during its collection by those among the Companions who undertook that task. How little benefit such a thing has, how meagre its fruit, and how worthless its usefulness! Rather, to one who understands what he says and what is said to him, it is a squandering of time and an expenditure of hours on a matter that brings no benefit to its doer nor to those people who look into it. You know that if a man of knowledge took it upon himself to find a connection between what a certain eloquent person said in his sermons, letters and compositions, or between what a certain poet said in his poems, which are sometimes praise, sometimes satire, sometimes amatory prologue and sometimes elegy, and other varied types, then this one who undertook it went and gathered that collection and found a connection between its sections and parts. Then he made another artifice and found a connection between the sermon he delivered concerning jihad, the sermon concerning the pilgrimage, the sermon he delivered at a marriage, and the like; and he connected the composition said at a condolence and the composition said at a celebration, and what resembles them. Such a person would be considered to have lost his mind, toying with his time and playing with his life, which is his capital. If this is his station when it comes to human speech, and it is the riding of folly in the speech of people, then how would it be in the speech of God, the Glorified, whose eloquence has rendered the eloquent of the Arabs incapable, and whose rhetoric has struck dumb the orators of 'Adnan and Qahtan?

Everyone, the deficient and the complete, knows that God, the Glorified, described this Qur'an as being in Arabic, and revealed it in the language of the Arabs, following their paths of speech and proceeding in their modes of address.

We know that their orator would stand in one station and produce various arts and different methods, let alone two stations, let alone many stations, let alone everything he said as long as he lived. Likewise their poet.

Let us be content with this warning about this corruption in whose arenas many of the researchers have stumbled. We have only mentioned this discussion here because the speech has moved here with the Children of Israel, after it had previously been with the father of mankind, Adam (peace be upon him). So if an artificial objector says: "How does this connect with what precedes it?" We say: "No, not how:"
"Leave aside the plunder that was cried out in its chambers, and bring a tale: what is the tale of the riding camels?"

His saying: "O Children of Israel." The exegetes agree that Israel is Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them all, and its meaning is "servant of God", because "isr" in their language means "servant" and "il" means "God." It was said that he had two names; and it was said that Israel is a title for him. It is a non-Arabic proper noun that is not declined (ghayr munsarif), and it has seven dialects: Isra'il on the pattern of Ibrahim; Isra'il with a hamza and a short vowel, transmitted by Ibn Shanbudh from Warsh; Isra'il with a long vowel after the ya' without hamza, which is the reading of al-A'mash and Isa ibn Umar; al-Hasan read it without hamza or long vowel; Isra'il with a kasra on the hamza; Isra'al with a fatha on the hamza; and the Tamim say Isra'in.

Al-dhikr is the opposite of listening silently (al-inssat). Some of the lexicographers made it a shared term between remembrance of the heart and of the tongue.

Al-Kisa'i said: What is by the heart has a dammah on the dhal, and what is by the tongue has a kasrah on the dhal.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning in the verse is: "Remember the thanks for My blessing," so he omitted "thanks" by being content with mention of "blessing," which is a generic noun. Among its components is that He made prophets from among them, sent down the Books upon them, the manna and the quails, brought forth water for them from the rock, saved them from the people of Pharaoh, and other things.

The covenant has already had its explanation discussed.

The scholars differed concerning what the covenant mentioned in this verse is. It was said: it is the one mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. It was said: it is what is in His saying: ﴿And God had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12]. It was said: it is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

Al-Zajjaj said: It is what was taken from them in the Torah regarding following Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: it is the performance of the obligations. There is no barrier to carrying it on all of that.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿Fulfill My covenant﴾ means: "fulfill what I have guaranteed you of reward."

Al-rahab and al-rahbah: fear. The command to it includes the meaning of threat. The fronting of the verb's object indicates restriction, as has already passed in ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. When the fronting is by way of pronominalization and explanation, like: "Zayd, I struck him," as in ﴿And of Me alone, be fearful﴾, it is more emphatic in indicating restriction. For this reason the author of al-Kashshaf said: "It is more emphatic in indicating restriction than ﴿You alone we worship﴾."

The ya' was dropped from His saying: ﴿fa-rhabun﴾ because it is the end of a verse (ra's aya). And muşaddiqan is a state (hal) referring to "ma" in His saying: "ma anzaltu" (what I have sent down), or to its implied pronoun after the verb, meaning "anzaltuhu" (I sent it down).

His saying: ﴿the first to disbelieve in it﴾ came in the singular, and it did not say "disbelievers" so as to agree with what precedes it, because it is an adjective for an omitted noun that is singular in form but plural in meaning, like firq (group) or fawj (company).

Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: It is taken as referring to the meaning of the verb, because the meaning is "the first who disbelieved."

It may also be of the type of their saying: "He is the most elegant of the youths and the most handsome," as Sibawayh related. Then this singular stands in place of the plural. He said "first" even though the disbelievers of Quraysh preceded them in disbelief in it, because what is meant is "the first disbeliever in it from among the People of the Book," since they are the ones who know what is owed to the prophets and what necessarily follows from believing in them. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ): that is, "Do not be the first to disbelieve in this Prophet, while you have found him written with you in the Torah and the Gospel, given glad tidings of him in the Books sent down to you."

Al-Razi, in his tafsir at this point, recounted what he had come across of the glad tidings of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the former Books. It was also said that it refers back to the Qur'an, indicated by His saying: "bima anzaltu" (in what I have sent down). And it was said it refers back to the Torah, indicated by His saying: "limā ma'akum" (for what is with you).

His saying: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a little price﴾: that is, "My commands and My prohibitions." ﴿A little price﴾: meagre livelihood and leadership without any worth.

He made what they accepted in exchange a "price," and attributed the buying to it, even though the price is what is bought with, because the buying here is used figuratively for exchange. That is: "Do not exchange My signs for a little price." Such usage occurs frequently in their speech.

We have already presented the discussion of it in the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. From the use of the name "price" for gaining some worldly commodity is the saying of the poet:
"If you sought the world, or you gained it, you did not gain, by abandoning the pilgrimage, anything of value."

Although this verse is addressed to the Children of Israel and is a prohibition for them, it encompasses this community as well, by the implication of the address or by its indication. So whoever among the Muslims takes a bribe to nullify a truth God commanded, or to affirm a falsehood God forbade, or refrains from teaching what God has taught and conceals the clarification upon which God took his covenant, has indeed bought with God's signs a little price.

His saying: ﴿And fear Me, so be mindful of Me﴾: the discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And of Me alone, be fearful﴾, which has passed shortly before.

Al-labs: mixing. It is said: "labastu 'alayhi al-amra, ulbisuhu," when I mix its truth with its falsehood and its clear with its obscure. God, Exalted, said: ﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Al-Khansa' said:
"You see the companion who speaks the truth, you think him rightly guided, but far from it; look at what has confused him."
"Believe his speech, beware his enmity, and confuse him with matters like what he confused."

Al-'Ajjaj said:
"When I mixed the truth with accusation, they blamed me and took Zayd in my place."

And from it is the saying of 'Antara:

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 2 of 2)**

*(Poetry)*
> "And a battalion I put on over another battalion,
> until, when they became confused, I shook off my hand from them."

It has also been said that *al-talbis* (لبس, "confusing" or "mixing") is derived from *al-taghtiyah* (التغطية, "covering"). The meaning is: do not cover the truth with falsehood. From this is the verse of al-Ja'di:

> "When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends over him, and she is a garment."

And the verse of al-Akhtal:

> "I have worn this matter, its very core, until gray hair covered my head and blazed."

The first meaning is preferable.

*Al-batil* (الباطل, "falsehood") in the speech of the Arabs means that which is passing away. From this is the line of Labid:

> "Certainly everything other than God is passing away."

*Batala al-shay'* (بطل الشيء) means a thing becomes void, with *butul* and *butlan*. Another person makes it void (*abtalahu*). It is said: *dhahaba damuhu batalan*, meaning his blood was lost without retribution (*hadran*). *Al-batil* can also mean Satan. A brave man is called *batal* because he nullifies (*yubtilu*) the courage of his companion. The meaning here is the opposite of the truth (*al-haqq*).

The *ba'* (باء) in God's words *bi-al-batil* may be a connecting particle (*silah*), or it may denote instrumentality (*al-isti'anah*). Al-Zamakhshari (author of *al-Kashshaf*) mentioned its meaning in *al-Kashshaf*, and al-Razi, in his tafsir, preferred the second.

His words *wa-taktumu* (وتكتموا, "and conceal") may be included under the prohibition, or it may be in the subjunctive governed by an implied *an* (أن). On the first reading, each of the mixing (*al-labs*) and the concealing (*al-katm*) is forbidden. On the second reading, what is forbidden is the combining of the two matters. From this it appears preferable that it falls under the prohibition, and that each of them is not permissible on its own.

The intended meaning is the prohibition of concealing the proofs of God which He obligated them to convey and which He took a covenant from them to explain. Whoever interprets *al-labs* or *al-katm* as a particular thing with a specific meaning has not been correct, if he means that this alone is what is intended and nothing else. It is not wrong if he means that it is one of the things it covers.

His words *wa-antum ta'lamun* (وأنتم تعلمون, "while you know") form a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*). In it is the indication that their disbelief was disbelief of obstinacy (*kufr 'inad*), not disbelief of ignorance (*kufr jahl*). That is more severe as a sin and more deserving of punishment. This restriction does not imply that mixing and concealing are permissible in ignorance, because the ignorant person is obligated not to proceed with anything until he knows its ruling, especially in matters of religion. Speaking about them, and presuming to issue or narrate rulings in their domains, is only permitted by God to one who is a leader in knowledge and unique in understanding. What business do the ignorant have in entering what is not their concern, or sitting in places that are not their seats?

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding God's words: "O Children of Israel," he said to the rabbis of the Jews: ﴿Remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾, that is, My trial among you and among your forefathers when He rescued them from Pharaoh and his people. ﴿And fulfill My covenant﴾, which I took upon your necks for the Prophet (ﷺ) when he comes to you: ﴿I will fulfill your covenant﴾, that is, I will fulfill for you what I promised you, by affirming him and following him, by removing from you the burden and the shackles that were upon you. ﴿And fear Me﴾, lest I send down upon you what I sent down upon those who were before you, your forefathers, of retributions. ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, while you have in it knowledge that others do not have. ﴿And do not conceal the truth while you know﴾, that is, do not conceal what you have of knowledge of My Messenger and of what has come to you through him, while you find it with you in what you know from the books that are in your hands.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding God's words: "Fulfill My covenant," that he said: "I will be pleased with you and admit you into Paradise."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid regarding God's words: ﴿I will fulfill your covenant﴾, that he said: it is the covenant which He took from them in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿God had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12], and the rest of the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Hasan, who said: "Fulfill for Me what I have made obligatory upon you, and I will fulfill for you what I promised you."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh reported something similar from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding God's words: ﴿And fear Me﴾, he said: "Dread Me."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Juraij reported from Mujahid regarding God's words: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾, he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿Confirming what is with you﴾, he said: "The Torah and the Gospel."

Ibn Juraij reported from Ibn Jarir regarding God's words: ﴿The first to disbelieve in it﴾, he said: "in the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding the verse, he said: He says: O assembly of the People of the Book, believe in what I have sent down upon Muhammad, confirming what is with you, because they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, that is, the first to disbelieve in Muhammad. ﴿And do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾: he says, do not take a wage for it. He said: and it is written with them in the first Book: "O son of Adam, teach freely as you were taught freely."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, he said: "Do not take a wage for what you teach. The reward of scholars, wise men, and forbearing people is only with God."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding God's words: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾, he said: "Do not mix the truth with lies." ﴿And conceal the truth﴾, he said: "Do not conceal the truth while you have known that Muhammad is the Messenger of God."

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah regarding God's words: "And do not mix..." (the verse), he said: "Do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, and conceal the truth." He said: "They concealed Muhammad while they knew that he is the Messenger of God; they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel."

Ibn Jarir reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The truth is the Torah, and the falsehood is what they wrote with their own hands."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the meaning and derivation of establishing the prayer (iqamat al-salah) has already preceded. Here, what is meant is the well-known prayer (al-salah al-ma'hudah), which is the prayer of the Muslims, with the definite article being for specification (al-'ahd). It is also permissible for it to be for the category (al-jins). Likewise is zakah (obligatory almsgiving).

And al-iytha' (giving) means al-i'ta' (bestowing). It is said: "ataytuhu," meaning "a'taytuhu" (I gave him).

Zakah is derived from al-zakah, which is growth. "Zaka al-shay'" means when a thing grows and increases. A "rajul zaki" means a man abundant in goodness. The removal of a portion of wealth is called zakah, meaning increase, even though it is a reduction from it, because it multiplies its blessing by this, or multiplies the reward of its owner. It is also said that zakah is derived from purification (al-tathir), as one says "zaka fulan," meaning he became pure.

Apparently, salah, zakah, hajj, sawm (fasting) and similar terms have been transferred by the Shari'ah (the revealed law) to specific legal meanings, which are the ones intended wherever they are mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah.

The scholars have discussed this at length, in a manner that the context does not allow to be expanded upon.

The scholars have differed regarding what is meant by zakah here. It is said that it means the obligatory zakah, because it is linked with the prayer. It is said that it means the zakat al-fitr (charity of fast-breaking). The apparent meaning is that what is intended is more general than that.

Ruku' (bowing) linguistically means bending, and every one who bends is "rakI'" (bowing). Labid said:

"I relate the reports of past generations, I walk, as if I, whenever I stand, am bowing."

It is said that bending includes both ruku' and sujud (prostration). Ruku' is also used metaphorically for a decline in rank. A poet said:

"Do not belittle the poor, lest you [one day] bow [in humiliation], while time has raised him."

The reason the ruku' is specifically mentioned here is that the Jews have no ruku' in their prayer. It is also said that it is because it was burdensome upon the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period). It is also said that by ruku' is meant all the pillars (arkan) of the prayer.

The Shari'ah definition of ruku' is that a man bends, stretches his back and neck, spreads the fingers of his hands, grips his knees, and then settles calmly in ruku', remembering Allah with the prescribed dhikr.

His saying ﴿with those who bow﴾ contains guidance to attend congregational prayer (jama'ah) and to go out to the mosques.

Regarding this, there are authentic hadiths, established in the Two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, that are well known.

Some scholars have made attendance at the congregation obligatory, with disagreement among them over whether it is an individual obligation (ayn) or a communal obligation (kifayah). The majority (al-jumhur) held that it is a strongly emphasized sunnah, encouraged but not obligatory, and this is the truth, due to the authentic hadiths narrated from a group of the Companions, that congregational prayer surpasses the prayer of an individual by twenty-five degrees, or twenty-seven degrees.

It is established in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The one who prays with the imam is better than the one who prays alone and then sleeps."

The discussion is long in its ramifications and abundant in its reports.

The hamzah in His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾ is for interrogation together with rebuke of the addressees. The intent is not to rebuke them for the very act of enjoining righteousness, for that is a good deed which is recommended. Rather, the rebuke is because of leaving off the performance of righteousness, which is understood from His saying ﴿and forget yourselves﴾, together with purifying themselves by praising their own souls and standing in the position of callers of creation to the truth, giving the people the illusion and deceiving them, as Abu al-'Atahiyah said:

"You described piety until it seemed as if you were pious, while the scent of sins rises from your garments."

Al-birr (righteousness) means obedience and righteous deeds. Al-birr also means abundance of good and kindness; al-birr means truthfulness; al-birr means the young of the fox; al-birr means driving sheep. From its application to obedience is the saying of a poet:

"O Lord, may those who are beneath You, who obey You [in the sense of "birruka"] and disobey You [in the sense of "yafjuruna"]..." Meaning: they obey You and disobey You.

Al-nisyan (forgetting), with a kasrah on the nun, here means abandonment, i.e., ﴿and you abandon yourselves﴾. Originally it means the opposite of remembrance and retention, that is, the disappearance of the image that was preserved from the perceiver and the retainer.

Al-nafs (self, soul) means the spirit (al-ruh). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], meaning the spirits.

Abu Khirash said:

"Salim escaped, and the soul (of the one who was after him) was in his jaws."

Al-nafs also means blood. From this is the saying: "his nafs flowed," meaning his blood flowed. A poet said:

"Our souls flow along the edge of swords, and they flow only upon the tips [of spears]."

Al-nafs also means the body. From this is:

"I was informed that the Banu Suhaym entered their tents with the tha'mur (the blood, or essence) of the self of al-Mundhir."

Al-ta'mur means the body.

His saying ﴿while you recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hal) containing the greatest reproach, the most severe rebuke, and the most eloquent condemnation.

That is: how do you abandon righteousness, which you command the people to, while you are among the people of knowledge, who know the ugliness of this act and the severity of the threat against it, as you see it in the Book that you recite and the verses that you read from the Torah?

Al-tilawah (recitation) means reading, and that is what is intended here. Its original meaning is following. One says "talawtuhu," meaning when I followed him. The reciter is called "tali," and the recitation is called "tilawah," because he follows some speech with other speech in the order in which it is arranged.

His saying ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is an interrogation of denial against them and a reproach to them. It is stronger than the first. The strongest rebuke Allah made in this place is against one who commands good and does not do it, from among the scholars who do not act upon their knowledge. So He first denounced their commanding the people to righteousness while forgetting themselves in that matter, the matter which they stood up for in gatherings and proclaimed in assemblies, giving the people the illusion that they are conveyers from Allah of what they have borne of His proofs, explainers to His servants of what He commanded them to explain, and deliverers to His creation of what He entrusted and charged them with. Yet they are the most abandoning of people in that, the furthest from its benefit, and the most disinterested in it.

Then He linked this sentence with another sentence that made it an explanation of their condition, a revealing of their faults, and a tearing away of their veils: that they committed this shameful act and this atrocious trait with knowledge and awareness of the Book that was revealed to them and constant recitation of it. In that they are, as al-Ma'arri said:

"The reader of the Torah carried it only for the gain of its benefits, not for love of recitations."

Then he moved with them from one rebuke to another rebuke, and from one reproach to another reproach, saying: "Even if you were not among the people of knowledge, the bearers of proof, and the students of the Books of Allah, the mere fact that you are among those who understand would be a barrier between you and that, repelling you from it and restraining you from it. So how have you neglected what reason requires after neglecting what knowledge necessitates?"

Al-'aql (reason) in the original linguistic sense means restraint. From it comes "iqal al-ba'ir" (the camel's hobble), because it restrains it from movement. From it also comes "al-'aql" in blood money (diyah), because it restrains the guardian of the slain from killing the offender.

Al-'aql is the opposite of ignorance. The interpretation of what is in this verse may be given in terms of the original linguistic meaning of al-'aql among the lexicographers, that is: will you not restrain yourselves from engaging in this disgraceful state? It may also be that the meaning of the verse is: will you not look with your intellects, which Allah has given you, in that you did not benefit from the knowledge you possess?

His saying ﴿And seek help through patience﴾. Al-sabr (patience) in linguistic usage means restraint. "Sabartu nafsi 'ala al-shay'" means I restrained my soul upon something.

From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"She remained patient, knowing that, a free woman who stays firm when the soul of the coward rises up."

The intent here is: seek help by restraining your souls from desires and confining them to acts of obedience, in order to repel what comes upon you of hardships. It was said that patience here is specifically patience upon the obligations of the prayer.

The one who said this used as evidence His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. But there is nothing in this specific patience of this verse that negates what the definite article attached to "al-sabr" indicates of comprehensiveness, just as what is meant by "al-salah" here is everything to which the legal prayer applies, without distinction between obligatory and voluntary prayer.

The exegetes differed concerning the return of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is difficult﴾. It was said that it refers to the prayer. Although the preceding mention was of patience and prayer, it is permissible to return the pronoun to one of the two matters mentioned before.

As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], when one of them is included within the other in some respect. From this is the saying of a poet:

"Indeed, the bloom of youth and black hair, if they are not dyed, are madness."

He did not say "if they are not dyed" (lam yu'da), but rather made the pronoun refer to youth, because black hair is included in it. It was also said that it refers to the prayer without considering that patience is included under it, because patience is upon it, as was said earlier. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the prayer, even though patience is intended along with it, but since it is more emphatic, more general in obligation, and greater in reward, the pronoun is used as a reference to it. From this is His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34]. Thus it was said. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the hoarded things. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they disperse toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], where He returned the pronoun here to the silver and the trade, since silver is more general in benefit and more abundant in existence, and trade is what drives them to disperse. The difference between this view and the first view is that patience there was made included under prayer, whereas here it was not included, although it is intended.

It was also said that what is intended is both patience and prayer, but the pronoun was returned to one of them, being sufficient by it from the other. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning: the son of Mary a sign and his mother a sign.

From this is the saying of a poet:

"And whoever has his dwelling in Medina, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

Another said:

"For every worry among worries there is a relief, but morning and evening, there is no success with them."

It was also said that the pronoun returned to both of them after interpreting them as worship. It was said that it returned to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from His saying "wa-sta'ini" (and seek help), which is seeking help. It was also said that it returned to all the matters which the Children of Israel were forbidden from.

The "kabirah" (difficult thing) is that whose matter is grave and whose affair is magnified upon the one who bears it, because of the hardship he finds when undertaking it and performing it. From this is ﴿It is difficult for the polytheists what you call them to﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

Al-khashi' (the humble one) is the one who is submissive, and al-khushu' is submissiveness.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said: "Al-khushu' is humility and calmness. From it is al-khushah, meaning a soft, sunken stretch of sand. As for al-khudu', it is gentleness and submission. From it: 'khada'at bi-qawlihā,' meaning when she softened him with her speech." End of quote.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The khashi' is the one upon whom the trace of humiliation and khushu' is seen, like the khushu' of a house after its strength is gone. A makan khashi' is a place that cannot be found. 'Khasha'at al-aswat' means the voices became silent. 'Khasha'a bi-basarihi' means when he lowered it. Al-khushah is a soft piece of land."

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "I asked al-A'mash about khushu', and he said: 'O Thawri, you want to be an imam for the people and you do not know khushu'? Khushu' is not eating coarse food, nor wearing coarse clothing, nor lowering the head. Rather, khushu' is that you see the noble and the lowly as equal in the truth, and that you humble yourself to Allah in every obligation that has been made obligatory upon you.'"

End.

How excellent is what some of the verifiers said in explaining its reality: it is a state in the soul that manifests in the limbs as stillness and humility. He, glory be to Him, made an exception for the khashi'un (the humble ones), despite their being, in terms of using their limbs in prayer, and their constant attention to the duties of khushu', which is the spirit of prayer, and their exhausting themselves greatly in the causes that bring about presence and submission, because they know the multiplication of reward, the abundance of recompense, and the attainment of what Allah has promised of great reward. These hardships become easy for them, and the difficulties they undertake become light for them. Rather, that becomes for them pure pleasure and entirely unmixed comfort. For a matter, the sufferings of the heat of swords at the clashing of ranks became easy for a people, and the desire for martyrdom became to them the taste of death, until one of them said:

"I do not care, when I am killed as a Muslim, on whichever side my fall is, for the sake of Allah."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 44–46 (part 2 of 2):

Among the majority of scholars, *al-zann* (assumption) here means *al-yaqin* (certainty). From this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], and His words: (p-٥٥)﴿and they were certain that they would be plunged into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. From this is also the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

*"I said to them, 'Be certain of two thousand armored men, their chiefs with the black Persian [spears].'"*

It has been said that *al-zann* in the verse retains its original meaning, and that the phrase "*bi-dhunubihim*" (with their sins) is implied in the speech, so that they expected to meet Him as sinners. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Mawardi, but the first view is preferable.

The original meaning of *al-zann* is doubt together with inclination toward one of the two sides, and it may be used in the place of certainty in various contexts, of which this verse is one.

The meaning of His words ﴿who will meet their Lord﴾ is "who will meet the reward of Him." The form *mufa'alah* (the reciprocal pattern) here is not on its proper pattern, and I see no harm in interpreting it according to its original meaning without supposing an omitted genitive.

Together with what follows it, His words ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾ affirm the Resurrection and what Allah has promised concerning the Last Day.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His words "*wa-rka'u*" (and bow), that he said: "Pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from Muqatil, regarding His words ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾, that he said: "He commanded them to bow with the community of Muhammad. He means: be among them and with them."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His words "Do you enjoin righteousness on the people" ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were the People of the Book. They used to enjoin righteousness on the people and forget themselves, while they recite the Book and do not benefit from what is in it."

Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah. A man among them would say to his in-law, to his relative, and to one who had a foster-relationship with him from among the Muslims: 'Remain upon the religion you are on, and do not let this man (meaning Muhammad (ﷺ)) command you otherwise, for his command is true.' They would command the people to this, but would not do it themselves."

Ibn Jarir related from him, regarding His words "Do you enjoin righteousness on the people," that he said: "By entering the religion of Muhammad."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding the verse, that he said: "You forbid the people from disbelief, by what you have of prophethood and the covenant from the Torah, while you yourselves disbelieve in what it contains of My covenant to you concerning the confirmation of My messengers?"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu al-Darda', regarding the verse, that he said: "A man does not comprehend the full understanding until he detests the people for the sake of Allah, then returns to himself and detests it even more."

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw men whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire; whenever they were cut, they returned. I said to Jibril: 'Who are these?' He said: 'These are preachers from your community who used to enjoin righteousness on the people and forget themselves, while they recite the Book. Do they not understand?'"

It is established in the two *Sahih*s from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out, and he will go around with them as a donkey goes around with its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is wrong with you? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good but would not do it myself, and forbid you from evil but would do it myself.'"

There are other hadiths on this subject, among them one from Jabir, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet, in al-Khatib and Ibn al-Najjar; and one from al-Walid ibn Uqbah, raised to the Prophet, in al-Tabarani and al-Khatib with a weak chain; and one in Abd Allah ibn Ahmad's *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* from him as a statement of his own (*mawquf*). Their meaning altogether is that a group of the people of Paradise will look down upon a group of the people of the Fire and say to them: "Why did you enter the Fire, when we entered Paradise only through your teaching?" They will say: "We used to command you, but we did not act."

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* and al-Asbahani in *al-Targhib* related with a good chain from Jundab ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The example of the scholar who teaches the people good but does not act upon it is like a lamp that gives light to the people while burning itself."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* related something similar from him.

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Abu Barzah, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Qani' in his *Mu'jam* and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Sulaik, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Woe to him who does not know once, and if Allah had willed He would have taught him; and woe seven times to him who knows and does not act."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related something like it from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

How excellent is what Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* and Ibn Asakir related from Ibn Abbas: that a man came to him and said: "O son of Abbas, I want to command good and forbid evil." He said: "Have you achieved that?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "If you do not fear being exposed by three letters in the Book of Allah, then do it." He said: "And what are they?" He said: "The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the second letter: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the third letter: the words of the righteous servant Shu'ayb: ﴿I do not intend to differ from you in what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then begin with yourself."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His words the Exalted: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾, that he said: "They are two aids from Allah, so seek help through them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Sabr*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Thawab* and al-Daylami in *Musnad al-Firdaws* have related from Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Patience is of three kinds: patience in the face of calamity, patience in obedience, and patience in refraining from disobedience."

Many hadiths have been transmitted in praise of patience, in encouragement toward it, and concerning the reward for those who are patient. We have not mentioned them here, because they are not specific to this verse but relate to patience in general. Al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, has mentioned a good portion of them here. In the Mighty Book there is much praise of this and encouragement toward it, and it is excellent.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Jarir related from Hudhayfah, who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer." Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban related from Suhayb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "They [meaning the Prophets] would turn to prayer whenever they were distressed."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir related from Abu al-Darda', raised to the Prophet, something like the hadith of Hudhayfah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (p-٥٦) related from Ibn Abbas that he was on a journey when news reached him of the death of a son of his. He dismounted, prayed two rak'ahs, then said the words of return (*istirja'*), and said: "We have done as Allah commanded us," and He said: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related something similar from him when news reached him of the death of his brother Qutham.

Something similar has been related from a number of the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, regarding His words "and indeed it is hard," that he said: "It is heavy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The true believers."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The fearful."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: "Every instance of *zann* in the Qur'an means certainty." This does not hold in verses such as ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28] and ﴿Indeed, some assumption is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. Perhaps he means the *zann* related to matters of the Hereafter, as Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah, who said: "Whatever is *zann* about the Hereafter is knowledge."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾, that he said: "They are certain that they will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the meaning and derivation of establishing the prayer (iqamat al-salah) has already preceded. Here, what is meant is the well-known prayer (al-salah al-ma'hudah), which is the prayer of the Muslims, with the definite article being for specification (al-'ahd). It is also permissible for it to be for the category (al-jins). Likewise is zakah (obligatory almsgiving).

And al-iytha' (giving) means al-i'ta' (bestowing). It is said: "ataytuhu," meaning "a'taytuhu" (I gave him).

Zakah is derived from al-zakah, which is growth. "Zaka al-shay'" means when a thing grows and increases. A "rajul zaki" means a man abundant in goodness. The removal of a portion of wealth is called zakah, meaning increase, even though it is a reduction from it, because it multiplies its blessing by this, or multiplies the reward of its owner. It is also said that zakah is derived from purification (al-tathir), as one says "zaka fulan," meaning he became pure.

Apparently, salah, zakah, hajj, sawm (fasting) and similar terms have been transferred by the Shari'ah (the revealed law) to specific legal meanings, which are the ones intended wherever they are mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah.

The scholars have discussed this at length, in a manner that the context does not allow to be expanded upon.

The scholars have differed regarding what is meant by zakah here. It is said that it means the obligatory zakah, because it is linked with the prayer. It is said that it means the zakat al-fitr (charity of fast-breaking). The apparent meaning is that what is intended is more general than that.

Ruku' (bowing) linguistically means bending, and every one who bends is "rakI'" (bowing). Labid said:

"I relate the reports of past generations, I walk, as if I, whenever I stand, am bowing."

It is said that bending includes both ruku' and sujud (prostration). Ruku' is also used metaphorically for a decline in rank. A poet said:

"Do not belittle the poor, lest you [one day] bow [in humiliation], while time has raised him."

The reason the ruku' is specifically mentioned here is that the Jews have no ruku' in their prayer. It is also said that it is because it was burdensome upon the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period). It is also said that by ruku' is meant all the pillars (arkan) of the prayer.

The Shari'ah definition of ruku' is that a man bends, stretches his back and neck, spreads the fingers of his hands, grips his knees, and then settles calmly in ruku', remembering Allah with the prescribed dhikr.

His saying ﴿with those who bow﴾ contains guidance to attend congregational prayer (jama'ah) and to go out to the mosques.

Regarding this, there are authentic hadiths, established in the Two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, that are well known.

Some scholars have made attendance at the congregation obligatory, with disagreement among them over whether it is an individual obligation (ayn) or a communal obligation (kifayah). The majority (al-jumhur) held that it is a strongly emphasized sunnah, encouraged but not obligatory, and this is the truth, due to the authentic hadiths narrated from a group of the Companions, that congregational prayer surpasses the prayer of an individual by twenty-five degrees, or twenty-seven degrees.

It is established in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The one who prays with the imam is better than the one who prays alone and then sleeps."

The discussion is long in its ramifications and abundant in its reports.

The hamzah in His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾ is for interrogation together with rebuke of the addressees. The intent is not to rebuke them for the very act of enjoining righteousness, for that is a good deed which is recommended. Rather, the rebuke is because of leaving off the performance of righteousness, which is understood from His saying ﴿and forget yourselves﴾, together with purifying themselves by praising their own souls and standing in the position of callers of creation to the truth, giving the people the illusion and deceiving them, as Abu al-'Atahiyah said:

"You described piety until it seemed as if you were pious, while the scent of sins rises from your garments."

Al-birr (righteousness) means obedience and righteous deeds. Al-birr also means abundance of good and kindness; al-birr means truthfulness; al-birr means the young of the fox; al-birr means driving sheep. From its application to obedience is the saying of a poet:

"O Lord, may those who are beneath You, who obey You [in the sense of "birruka"] and disobey You [in the sense of "yafjuruna"]..." Meaning: they obey You and disobey You.

Al-nisyan (forgetting), with a kasrah on the nun, here means abandonment, i.e., ﴿and you abandon yourselves﴾. Originally it means the opposite of remembrance and retention, that is, the disappearance of the image that was preserved from the perceiver and the retainer.

Al-nafs (self, soul) means the spirit (al-ruh). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], meaning the spirits.

Abu Khirash said:

"Salim escaped, and the soul (of the one who was after him) was in his jaws."

Al-nafs also means blood. From this is the saying: "his nafs flowed," meaning his blood flowed. A poet said:

"Our souls flow along the edge of swords, and they flow only upon the tips [of spears]."

Al-nafs also means the body. From this is:

"I was informed that the Banu Suhaym entered their tents with the tha'mur (the blood, or essence) of the self of al-Mundhir."

Al-ta'mur means the body.

His saying ﴿while you recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hal) containing the greatest reproach, the most severe rebuke, and the most eloquent condemnation.

That is: how do you abandon righteousness, which you command the people to, while you are among the people of knowledge, who know the ugliness of this act and the severity of the threat against it, as you see it in the Book that you recite and the verses that you read from the Torah?

Al-tilawah (recitation) means reading, and that is what is intended here. Its original meaning is following. One says "talawtuhu," meaning when I followed him. The reciter is called "tali," and the recitation is called "tilawah," because he follows some speech with other speech in the order in which it is arranged.

His saying ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is an interrogation of denial against them and a reproach to them. It is stronger than the first. The strongest rebuke Allah made in this place is against one who commands good and does not do it, from among the scholars who do not act upon their knowledge. So He first denounced their commanding the people to righteousness while forgetting themselves in that matter, the matter which they stood up for in gatherings and proclaimed in assemblies, giving the people the illusion that they are conveyers from Allah of what they have borne of His proofs, explainers to His servants of what He commanded them to explain, and deliverers to His creation of what He entrusted and charged them with. Yet they are the most abandoning of people in that, the furthest from its benefit, and the most disinterested in it.

Then He linked this sentence with another sentence that made it an explanation of their condition, a revealing of their faults, and a tearing away of their veils: that they committed this shameful act and this atrocious trait with knowledge and awareness of the Book that was revealed to them and constant recitation of it. In that they are, as al-Ma'arri said:

"The reader of the Torah carried it only for the gain of its benefits, not for love of recitations."
