Then he moved with them from one rebuke to another rebuke, and from one reproach to another reproach, saying: "Even if you were not among the people of knowledge, the bearers of proof, and the students of the Books of Allah, the mere fact that you are among those who understand would be a barrier between you and that, repelling you from it and restraining you from it. So how have you neglected what reason requires after neglecting what knowledge necessitates?"

Al-'aql (reason) in the original linguistic sense means restraint. From it comes "iqal al-ba'ir" (the camel's hobble), because it restrains it from movement. From it also comes "al-'aql" in blood money (diyah), because it restrains the guardian of the slain from killing the offender.

Al-'aql is the opposite of ignorance. The interpretation of what is in this verse may be given in terms of the original linguistic meaning of al-'aql among the lexicographers, that is: will you not restrain yourselves from engaging in this disgraceful state? It may also be that the meaning of the verse is: will you not look with your intellects, which Allah has given you, in that you did not benefit from the knowledge you possess?

His saying ﴿And seek help through patience﴾. Al-sabr (patience) in linguistic usage means restraint. "Sabartu nafsi 'ala al-shay'" means I restrained my soul upon something.

From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"She remained patient, knowing that, a free woman who stays firm when the soul of the coward rises up."

The intent here is: seek help by restraining your souls from desires and confining them to acts of obedience, in order to repel what comes upon you of hardships. It was said that patience here is specifically patience upon the obligations of the prayer.

The one who said this used as evidence His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. But there is nothing in this specific patience of this verse that negates what the definite article attached to "al-sabr" indicates of comprehensiveness, just as what is meant by "al-salah" here is everything to which the legal prayer applies, without distinction between obligatory and voluntary prayer.

The exegetes differed concerning the return of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is difficult﴾. It was said that it refers to the prayer. Although the preceding mention was of patience and prayer, it is permissible to return the pronoun to one of the two matters mentioned before.

As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], when one of them is included within the other in some respect. From this is the saying of a poet:

"Indeed, the bloom of youth and black hair, if they are not dyed, are madness."

He did not say "if they are not dyed" (lam yu'da), but rather made the pronoun refer to youth, because black hair is included in it. It was also said that it refers to the prayer without considering that patience is included under it, because patience is upon it, as was said earlier. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the prayer, even though patience is intended along with it, but since it is more emphatic, more general in obligation, and greater in reward, the pronoun is used as a reference to it. From this is His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34]. Thus it was said. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the hoarded things. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they disperse toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], where He returned the pronoun here to the silver and the trade, since silver is more general in benefit and more abundant in existence, and trade is what drives them to disperse. The difference between this view and the first view is that patience there was made included under prayer, whereas here it was not included, although it is intended.

It was also said that what is intended is both patience and prayer, but the pronoun was returned to one of them, being sufficient by it from the other. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning: the son of Mary a sign and his mother a sign.

From this is the saying of a poet:

"And whoever has his dwelling in Medina, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

Another said:

"For every worry among worries there is a relief, but morning and evening, there is no success with them."

It was also said that the pronoun returned to both of them after interpreting them as worship. It was said that it returned to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from His saying "wa-sta'ini" (and seek help), which is seeking help. It was also said that it returned to all the matters which the Children of Israel were forbidden from.

The "kabirah" (difficult thing) is that whose matter is grave and whose affair is magnified upon the one who bears it, because of the hardship he finds when undertaking it and performing it. From this is ﴿It is difficult for the polytheists what you call them to﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

Al-khashi' (the humble one) is the one who is submissive, and al-khushu' is submissiveness.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said: "Al-khushu' is humility and calmness. From it is al-khushah, meaning a soft, sunken stretch of sand. As for al-khudu', it is gentleness and submission. From it: 'khada'at bi-qawlihā,' meaning when she softened him with her speech." End of quote.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The khashi' is the one upon whom the trace of humiliation and khushu' is seen, like the khushu' of a house after its strength is gone. A makan khashi' is a place that cannot be found. 'Khasha'at al-aswat' means the voices became silent. 'Khasha'a bi-basarihi' means when he lowered it. Al-khushah is a soft piece of land."

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "I asked al-A'mash about khushu', and he said: 'O Thawri, you want to be an imam for the people and you do not know khushu'? Khushu' is not eating coarse food, nor wearing coarse clothing, nor lowering the head. Rather, khushu' is that you see the noble and the lowly as equal in the truth, and that you humble yourself to Allah in every obligation that has been made obligatory upon you.'"

End.

How excellent is what some of the verifiers said in explaining its reality: it is a state in the soul that manifests in the limbs as stillness and humility. He, glory be to Him, made an exception for the khashi'un (the humble ones), despite their being, in terms of using their limbs in prayer, and their constant attention to the duties of khushu', which is the spirit of prayer, and their exhausting themselves greatly in the causes that bring about presence and submission, because they know the multiplication of reward, the abundance of recompense, and the attainment of what Allah has promised of great reward. These hardships become easy for them, and the difficulties they undertake become light for them. Rather, that becomes for them pure pleasure and entirely unmixed comfort. For a matter, the sufferings of the heat of swords at the clashing of ranks became easy for a people, and the desire for martyrdom became to them the taste of death, until one of them said:

"I do not care, when I am killed as a Muslim, on whichever side my fall is, for the sake of Allah."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 44–46 (part 2 of 2):

Among the majority of scholars, *al-zann* (assumption) here means *al-yaqin* (certainty). From this is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], and His words: (p-٥٥)﴿and they were certain that they would be plunged into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. From this is also the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

*"I said to them, 'Be certain of two thousand armored men, their chiefs with the black Persian [spears].'"*

It has been said that *al-zann* in the verse retains its original meaning, and that the phrase "*bi-dhunubihim*" (with their sins) is implied in the speech, so that they expected to meet Him as sinners. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Mawardi, but the first view is preferable.

The original meaning of *al-zann* is doubt together with inclination toward one of the two sides, and it may be used in the place of certainty in various contexts, of which this verse is one.

The meaning of His words ﴿who will meet their Lord﴾ is "who will meet the reward of Him." The form *mufa'alah* (the reciprocal pattern) here is not on its proper pattern, and I see no harm in interpreting it according to its original meaning without supposing an omitted genitive.

Together with what follows it, His words ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾ affirm the Resurrection and what Allah has promised concerning the Last Day.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His words "*wa-rka'u*" (and bow), that he said: "Pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from Muqatil, regarding His words ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾, that he said: "He commanded them to bow with the community of Muhammad. He means: be among them and with them."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His words "Do you enjoin righteousness on the people" ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were the People of the Book. They used to enjoin righteousness on the people and forget themselves, while they recite the Book and do not benefit from what is in it."

Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Jews of Madinah. A man among them would say to his in-law, to his relative, and to one who had a foster-relationship with him from among the Muslims: 'Remain upon the religion you are on, and do not let this man (meaning Muhammad (ﷺ)) command you otherwise, for his command is true.' They would command the people to this, but would not do it themselves."

Ibn Jarir related from him, regarding His words "Do you enjoin righteousness on the people," that he said: "By entering the religion of Muhammad."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding the verse, that he said: "You forbid the people from disbelief, by what you have of prophethood and the covenant from the Torah, while you yourselves disbelieve in what it contains of My covenant to you concerning the confirmation of My messengers?"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu al-Darda', regarding the verse, that he said: "A man does not comprehend the full understanding until he detests the people for the sake of Allah, then returns to himself and detests it even more."

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw men whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire; whenever they were cut, they returned. I said to Jibril: 'Who are these?' He said: 'These are preachers from your community who used to enjoin righteousness on the people and forget themselves, while they recite the Book. Do they not understand?'"

It is established in the two *Sahih*s from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out, and he will go around with them as a donkey goes around with its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is wrong with you? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good but would not do it myself, and forbid you from evil but would do it myself.'"

There are other hadiths on this subject, among them one from Jabir, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet, in al-Khatib and Ibn al-Najjar; and one from al-Walid ibn Uqbah, raised to the Prophet, in al-Tabarani and al-Khatib with a weak chain; and one in Abd Allah ibn Ahmad's *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* from him as a statement of his own (*mawquf*). Their meaning altogether is that a group of the people of Paradise will look down upon a group of the people of the Fire and say to them: "Why did you enter the Fire, when we entered Paradise only through your teaching?" They will say: "We used to command you, but we did not act."

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* and al-Asbahani in *al-Targhib* related with a good chain from Jundab ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The example of the scholar who teaches the people good but does not act upon it is like a lamp that gives light to the people while burning itself."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* related something similar from him.

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Abu Barzah, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Qani' in his *Mu'jam* and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Sulaik, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Woe to him who does not know once, and if Allah had willed He would have taught him; and woe seven times to him who knows and does not act."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related something like it from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

How excellent is what Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* and Ibn Asakir related from Ibn Abbas: that a man came to him and said: "O son of Abbas, I want to command good and forbid evil." He said: "Have you achieved that?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "If you do not fear being exposed by three letters in the Book of Allah, then do it." He said: "And what are they?" He said: "The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the second letter: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the third letter: the words of the righteous servant Shu'ayb: ﴿I do not intend to differ from you in what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then begin with yourself."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His words the Exalted: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾, that he said: "They are two aids from Allah, so seek help through them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Sabr*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Thawab* and al-Daylami in *Musnad al-Firdaws* have related from Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Patience is of three kinds: patience in the face of calamity, patience in obedience, and patience in refraining from disobedience."

Many hadiths have been transmitted in praise of patience, in encouragement toward it, and concerning the reward for those who are patient. We have not mentioned them here, because they are not specific to this verse but relate to patience in general. Al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, has mentioned a good portion of them here. In the Mighty Book there is much praise of this and encouragement toward it, and it is excellent.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Jarir related from Hudhayfah, who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer." Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban related from Suhayb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "They [meaning the Prophets] would turn to prayer whenever they were distressed."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir related from Abu al-Darda', raised to the Prophet, something like the hadith of Hudhayfah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (p-٥٦) related from Ibn Abbas that he was on a journey when news reached him of the death of a son of his. He dismounted, prayed two rak'ahs, then said the words of return (*istirja'*), and said: "We have done as Allah commanded us," and He said: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related something similar from him when news reached him of the death of his brother Qutham.

Something similar has been related from a number of the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, regarding His words "and indeed it is hard," that he said: "It is heavy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The true believers."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The fearful."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: "Every instance of *zann* in the Qur'an means certainty." This does not hold in verses such as ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28] and ﴿Indeed, some assumption is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. Perhaps he means the *zann* related to matters of the Hereafter, as Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah, who said: "Whatever is *zann* about the Hereafter is knowledge."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾, that he said: "They are certain that they will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the meaning and derivation of establishing the prayer (iqamat al-salah) has already preceded. Here, what is meant is the well-known prayer (al-salah al-ma'hudah), which is the prayer of the Muslims, with the definite article being for specification (al-'ahd). It is also permissible for it to be for the category (al-jins). Likewise is zakah (obligatory almsgiving).

And al-iytha' (giving) means al-i'ta' (bestowing). It is said: "ataytuhu," meaning "a'taytuhu" (I gave him).

Zakah is derived from al-zakah, which is growth. "Zaka al-shay'" means when a thing grows and increases. A "rajul zaki" means a man abundant in goodness. The removal of a portion of wealth is called zakah, meaning increase, even though it is a reduction from it, because it multiplies its blessing by this, or multiplies the reward of its owner. It is also said that zakah is derived from purification (al-tathir), as one says "zaka fulan," meaning he became pure.

Apparently, salah, zakah, hajj, sawm (fasting) and similar terms have been transferred by the Shari'ah (the revealed law) to specific legal meanings, which are the ones intended wherever they are mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah.

The scholars have discussed this at length, in a manner that the context does not allow to be expanded upon.

The scholars have differed regarding what is meant by zakah here. It is said that it means the obligatory zakah, because it is linked with the prayer. It is said that it means the zakat al-fitr (charity of fast-breaking). The apparent meaning is that what is intended is more general than that.

Ruku' (bowing) linguistically means bending, and every one who bends is "rakI'" (bowing). Labid said:

"I relate the reports of past generations, I walk, as if I, whenever I stand, am bowing."

It is said that bending includes both ruku' and sujud (prostration). Ruku' is also used metaphorically for a decline in rank. A poet said:

"Do not belittle the poor, lest you [one day] bow [in humiliation], while time has raised him."

The reason the ruku' is specifically mentioned here is that the Jews have no ruku' in their prayer. It is also said that it is because it was burdensome upon the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period). It is also said that by ruku' is meant all the pillars (arkan) of the prayer.

The Shari'ah definition of ruku' is that a man bends, stretches his back and neck, spreads the fingers of his hands, grips his knees, and then settles calmly in ruku', remembering Allah with the prescribed dhikr.

His saying ﴿with those who bow﴾ contains guidance to attend congregational prayer (jama'ah) and to go out to the mosques.

Regarding this, there are authentic hadiths, established in the Two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and others, that are well known.

Some scholars have made attendance at the congregation obligatory, with disagreement among them over whether it is an individual obligation (ayn) or a communal obligation (kifayah). The majority (al-jumhur) held that it is a strongly emphasized sunnah, encouraged but not obligatory, and this is the truth, due to the authentic hadiths narrated from a group of the Companions, that congregational prayer surpasses the prayer of an individual by twenty-five degrees, or twenty-seven degrees.

It is established in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The one who prays with the imam is better than the one who prays alone and then sleeps."

The discussion is long in its ramifications and abundant in its reports.

The hamzah in His saying ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾ is for interrogation together with rebuke of the addressees. The intent is not to rebuke them for the very act of enjoining righteousness, for that is a good deed which is recommended. Rather, the rebuke is because of leaving off the performance of righteousness, which is understood from His saying ﴿and forget yourselves﴾, together with purifying themselves by praising their own souls and standing in the position of callers of creation to the truth, giving the people the illusion and deceiving them, as Abu al-'Atahiyah said:

"You described piety until it seemed as if you were pious, while the scent of sins rises from your garments."

Al-birr (righteousness) means obedience and righteous deeds. Al-birr also means abundance of good and kindness; al-birr means truthfulness; al-birr means the young of the fox; al-birr means driving sheep. From its application to obedience is the saying of a poet:

"O Lord, may those who are beneath You, who obey You [in the sense of "birruka"] and disobey You [in the sense of "yafjuruna"]..." Meaning: they obey You and disobey You.

Al-nisyan (forgetting), with a kasrah on the nun, here means abandonment, i.e., ﴿and you abandon yourselves﴾. Originally it means the opposite of remembrance and retention, that is, the disappearance of the image that was preserved from the perceiver and the retainer.

Al-nafs (self, soul) means the spirit (al-ruh). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], meaning the spirits.

Abu Khirash said:

"Salim escaped, and the soul (of the one who was after him) was in his jaws."

Al-nafs also means blood. From this is the saying: "his nafs flowed," meaning his blood flowed. A poet said:

"Our souls flow along the edge of swords, and they flow only upon the tips [of spears]."

Al-nafs also means the body. From this is:

"I was informed that the Banu Suhaym entered their tents with the tha'mur (the blood, or essence) of the self of al-Mundhir."

Al-ta'mur means the body.

His saying ﴿while you recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hal) containing the greatest reproach, the most severe rebuke, and the most eloquent condemnation.

That is: how do you abandon righteousness, which you command the people to, while you are among the people of knowledge, who know the ugliness of this act and the severity of the threat against it, as you see it in the Book that you recite and the verses that you read from the Torah?

Al-tilawah (recitation) means reading, and that is what is intended here. Its original meaning is following. One says "talawtuhu," meaning when I followed him. The reciter is called "tali," and the recitation is called "tilawah," because he follows some speech with other speech in the order in which it is arranged.

His saying ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ is an interrogation of denial against them and a reproach to them. It is stronger than the first. The strongest rebuke Allah made in this place is against one who commands good and does not do it, from among the scholars who do not act upon their knowledge. So He first denounced their commanding the people to righteousness while forgetting themselves in that matter, the matter which they stood up for in gatherings and proclaimed in assemblies, giving the people the illusion that they are conveyers from Allah of what they have borne of His proofs, explainers to His servants of what He commanded them to explain, and deliverers to His creation of what He entrusted and charged them with. Yet they are the most abandoning of people in that, the furthest from its benefit, and the most disinterested in it.

Then He linked this sentence with another sentence that made it an explanation of their condition, a revealing of their faults, and a tearing away of their veils: that they committed this shameful act and this atrocious trait with knowledge and awareness of the Book that was revealed to them and constant recitation of it. In that they are, as al-Ma'arri said:

"The reader of the Torah carried it only for the gain of its benefits, not for love of recitations."

Then he moved with them from one rebuke to another rebuke, and from one reproach to another reproach, saying: "Even if you were not among the people of knowledge, the bearers of proof, and the students of the Books of Allah, the mere fact that you are among those who understand would be a barrier between you and that, repelling you from it and restraining you from it. So how have you neglected what reason requires after neglecting what knowledge necessitates?"

Al-'aql (reason) in the original linguistic sense means restraint. From it comes "iqal al-ba'ir" (the camel's hobble), because it restrains it from movement. From it also comes "al-'aql" in blood money (diyah), because it restrains the guardian of the slain from killing the offender.

Al-'aql is the opposite of ignorance. The interpretation of what is in this verse may be given in terms of the original linguistic meaning of al-'aql among the lexicographers, that is: will you not restrain yourselves from engaging in this disgraceful state? It may also be that the meaning of the verse is: will you not look with your intellects, which Allah has given you, in that you did not benefit from the knowledge you possess?

His saying ﴿And seek help through patience﴾. Al-sabr (patience) in linguistic usage means restraint. "Sabartu nafsi 'ala al-shay'" means I restrained my soul upon something.

From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"She remained patient, knowing that, a free woman who stays firm when the soul of the coward rises up."

The intent here is: seek help by restraining your souls from desires and confining them to acts of obedience, in order to repel what comes upon you of hardships. It was said that patience here is specifically patience upon the obligations of the prayer.

The one who said this used as evidence His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. But there is nothing in this specific patience of this verse that negates what the definite article attached to "al-sabr" indicates of comprehensiveness, just as what is meant by "al-salah" here is everything to which the legal prayer applies, without distinction between obligatory and voluntary prayer.

The exegetes differed concerning the return of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is difficult﴾. It was said that it refers to the prayer. Although the preceding mention was of patience and prayer, it is permissible to return the pronoun to one of the two matters mentioned before.

As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], when one of them is included within the other in some respect. From this is the saying of a poet:

"Indeed, the bloom of youth and black hair, if they are not dyed, are madness."

He did not say "if they are not dyed" (lam yu'da), but rather made the pronoun refer to youth, because black hair is included in it. It was also said that it refers to the prayer without considering that patience is included under it, because patience is upon it, as was said earlier. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the prayer, even though patience is intended along with it, but since it is more emphatic, more general in obligation, and greater in reward, the pronoun is used as a reference to it. From this is His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34]. Thus it was said. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the hoarded things. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they disperse toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], where He returned the pronoun here to the silver and the trade, since silver is more general in benefit and more abundant in existence, and trade is what drives them to disperse. The difference between this view and the first view is that patience there was made included under prayer, whereas here it was not included, although it is intended.

It was also said that what is intended is both patience and prayer, but the pronoun was returned to one of them, being sufficient by it from the other. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning: the son of Mary a sign and his mother a sign.

From this is the saying of a poet:

"And whoever has his dwelling in Medina, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

Another said:

"For every worry among worries there is a relief, but morning and evening, there is no success with them."

It was also said that the pronoun returned to both of them after interpreting them as worship. It was said that it returned to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from His saying "wa-sta'ini" (and seek help), which is seeking help. It was also said that it returned to all the matters which the Children of Israel were forbidden from.

The "kabirah" (difficult thing) is that whose matter is grave and whose affair is magnified upon the one who bears it, because of the hardship he finds when undertaking it and performing it. From this is ﴿It is difficult for the polytheists what you call them to﴾ [al-Shura: 13].

Al-khashi' (the humble one) is the one who is submissive, and al-khushu' is submissiveness.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said: "Al-khushu' is humility and calmness. From it is al-khushah, meaning a soft, sunken stretch of sand. As for al-khudu', it is gentleness and submission. From it: 'khada'at bi-qawlihā,' meaning when she softened him with her speech." End of quote.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The khashi' is the one upon whom the trace of humiliation and khushu' is seen, like the khushu' of a house after its strength is gone. A makan khashi' is a place that cannot be found. 'Khasha'at al-aswat' means the voices became silent. 'Khasha'a bi-basarihi' means when he lowered it. Al-khushah is a soft piece of land."

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "I asked al-A'mash about khushu', and he said: 'O Thawri, you want to be an imam for the people and you do not know khushu'? Khushu' is not eating coarse food, nor wearing coarse clothing, nor lowering the head. Rather, khushu' is that you see the noble and the lowly as equal in the truth, and that you humble yourself to Allah in every obligation that has been made obligatory upon you.'"

End.

How excellent is what some of the verifiers said in explaining its reality: it is a state in the soul that manifests in the limbs as stillness and humility. He, glory be to Him, made an exception for the khashi'un (the humble ones), despite their being, in terms of using their limbs in prayer, and their constant attention to the duties of khushu', which is the spirit of prayer, and their exhausting themselves greatly in the causes that bring about presence and submission, because they know the multiplication of reward, the abundance of recompense, and the attainment of what Allah has promised of great reward. These hardships become easy for them, and the difficulties they undertake become light for them. Rather, that becomes for them pure pleasure and entirely unmixed comfort. For a matter, the sufferings of the heat of swords at the clashing of ranks became easy for a people, and the desire for martyrdom became to them the taste of death, until one of them said:

"I do not care, when I am killed as a Muslim, on whichever side my fall is, for the sake of Allah."

I said to Jibril: 'Who are these?' He said: 'These are preachers from your community who used to enjoin righteousness on the people and forget themselves, while they recite the Book. Do they not understand?'"

It is established in the two *Sahih*s from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his entrails will spill out, and he will go around with them as a donkey goes around with its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is wrong with you? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good but would not do it myself, and forbid you from evil but would do it myself.'"

There are other hadiths on this subject, among them one from Jabir, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet, in al-Khatib and Ibn al-Najjar; and one from al-Walid ibn Uqbah, raised to the Prophet, in al-Tabarani and al-Khatib with a weak chain; and one in Abd Allah ibn Ahmad's *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* from him as a statement of his own (*mawquf*). Their meaning altogether is that a group of the people of Paradise will look down upon a group of the people of the Fire and say to them: "Why did you enter the Fire, when we entered Paradise only through your teaching?" They will say: "We used to command you, but we did not act."

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* and al-Asbahani in *al-Targhib* related with a good chain from Jundab ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The example of the scholar who teaches the people good but does not act upon it is like a lamp that gives light to the people while burning itself."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* related something similar from him.

Al-Tabarani and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Abu Barzah, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Qani' in his *Mu'jam* and al-Khatib in *al-Iqtida'* related something similar from Sulaik, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Woe to him who does not know once, and if Allah had willed He would have taught him; and woe seven times to him who knows and does not act."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related something like it from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

How excellent is what Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* and Ibn Asakir related from Ibn Abbas: that a man came to him and said: "O son of Abbas, I want to command good and forbid evil." He said: "Have you achieved that?" He said: "I hope so." He said: "If you do not fear being exposed by three letters in the Book of Allah, then do it." He said: "And what are they?" He said: "The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the second letter: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then the third letter: the words of the righteous servant Shu'ayb: ﴿I do not intend to differ from you in what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88]. Have you put this verse into practice?" He said: "No." He said: "Then begin with yourself."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, regarding His words the Exalted: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾, that he said: "They are two aids from Allah, so seek help through them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Sabr*, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Thawab* and al-Daylami in *Musnad al-Firdaws* have related from Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Patience is of three kinds: patience in the face of calamity, patience in obedience, and patience in refraining from disobedience."

Many hadiths have been transmitted in praise of patience, in encouragement toward it, and concerning the reward for those who are patient. We have not mentioned them here, because they are not specific to this verse but relate to patience in general. Al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, has mentioned a good portion of them here. In the Mighty Book there is much praise of this and encouragement toward it, and it is excellent.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Jarir related from Hudhayfah, who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer." Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban related from Suhayb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "They [meaning the Prophets] would turn to prayer whenever they were distressed."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir related from Abu al-Darda', raised to the Prophet, something like the hadith of Hudhayfah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* (p-٥٦) related from Ibn Abbas that he was on a journey when news reached him of the death of a son of his. He dismounted, prayed two rak'ahs, then said the words of return (*istirja'*), and said: "We have done as Allah commanded us," and He said: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related something similar from him when news reached him of the death of his brother Qutham.

Something similar has been related from a number of the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, regarding His words "and indeed it is hard," that he said: "It is heavy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The true believers."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, that he said: "The fearful."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: "Every instance of *zann* in the Qur'an means certainty." This does not hold in verses such as ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28] and ﴿Indeed, some assumption is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. Perhaps he means the *zann* related to matters of the Hereafter, as Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah, who said: "Whatever is *zann* about the Hereafter is knowledge."

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾, that he said: "They are certain that they will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection."

His words: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. Its explanation has already preceded. He, glory be to Him, repeated this only to emphasise the proof against them and to warn them against abandoning the following of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then He linked it to a warning, which is His words: ﴿And fear a Day﴾, and His words: ﴿and that I preferred you﴾, which is conjoined to the object of "remember". That is: remember My favour and My preferring you over the worlds. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the worlds" is the world of their time. It has also been said: over all the worlds, through the prophets He placed among them.

In al-Kashshaf he said: over a great multitude of people, like His words: ﴿We blessed therein for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 71]. It is said: "I saw a world (ʿalam) of people," meaning a great number. End of quote.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: This is weak, because the word ʿalam is derived from ʿalam (sign), which is evidence, and everything that is evidence for God is a sign and is part of the ʿalam (world).

This is the verification of the saying of the theologians: the ʿalam is every existent other than God, and on this basis it is not possible to restrict the word ʿalam to some of the created things. End of quote.

I say: this objection is baseless. Firstly, the claim that it is derived from ʿalam has no proof. Secondly, even if we grant the correctness of this derivation, the meaning would exist in whatever yields the concept of evidence for God, whose name as a sign may be applied to it, and it is present in every individual of the created things by which one infers the Creator. Its furthest implication is that the plural ʿalamin requires that they be preferred over many created things. As for their being preferred over all created things in every age, the wording does not indicate this, nor does its derivation point to it. As for whoever takes ʿalam to mean the people of an era, its furthest implication is that they are preferred over the people of certain eras, not over the people of every era. This does not require their preference over the people of the era in which our Prophet (ﷺ) was, nor over those after it. Such a statement should be borne in mind when interpreting His words, exalted is He: ﴿When He placed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. If it is said: the definite article in "the worlds" indicates that it encompasses every world.

I say: even if the matter were so, that would not imply that they are better than the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), because of His words: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al ʿImran: 110]. For this verse and its like would specify those verses.

His words: ﴿and fear a Day﴾ is an imperative whose meaning is a warning, and the meaning of taqwa has already preceded.

The intended "Day" is the Day of Resurrection, that is, its punishment.

His words: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ are in the accusative position as an attribute of "Day", and the returning pronoun is omitted. The Basrans said regarding this and similar cases that its estimated form is "in it" (fihi). Al-Kisai said: this is an error; rather the estimate is "will not avail it" (la tajzihi), because omitting the adverbial of time is not permitted, while omitting the pronoun alone is permitted. It has been narrated from Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj that both are permitted.

The meaning of "will not avail" (la tajzi) is "will not suffice and will not discharge." It is said: "jaza ʿannī hādhā al-amr yajzī," meaning: it discharged it. And "ijtazaʾtu bi-l-shayʾ ajtazi," meaning: I was content with it. From this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed treachery among peoples is a shame, and indeed the free man is satisfied with the lowly (kurāʿ)."

The meaning is that on this Day no soul will discharge anything on behalf of another soul, nor suffice for it. The indefiniteness of "shayʾan" conveys belittling: that is, a small, paltry thing. It is in the accusative either as an object, or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: that is, a paltry recompense.

Intercession (shafaʿah) is derived from shafʿ, which means a pair. You say: "istashfaʿtuhu," meaning: I asked him to intercede for me, that is, to join his standing with your standing before the one interceded with, so that benefit reaches the one interceded for. It was named shufʿah (pre-emption) because you join your partner's share to your share.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-tuqbalu" with the feminine ta', because intercession is feminine. The rest read it with the masculine ya', because it means "the intercessor." al-Akhfash said: the masculine is better.

The pronoun in "minhā" refers to the soul mentioned second, that is: if it comes with the intercession of an intercessor. It is also permissible that it refers to the soul mentioned first, that is: if it interceded, nothing from it would be accepted.

ʿAdl with an open ʿayn means ransom, and with a kasra it means equivalent.
It is said: ʿadl and ʿadīl for the one who is equal in weight and measure.
Ibn Jarir related that among the Arabs there are some who use a kasra on the ʿayn with the meaning of ransom.

Al-nasr means help, and al-anṣār means helpers, and "intaṣara al-rajul" means he took revenge. The pronoun, that is "they" (hum), refers to the souls implied by the indefinite noun in the context of negation. The soul is treated as masculine or feminine.

His words: ﴿when We delivered you﴾ are connected to His words "remember". Al-najāh (deliverance) is al-najwah, meaning a raised part of the ground, and then every one who succeeds is called najī (delivered).

"Āl Fir'awn" means his people. The origin of āl is ahl (family), as shown by its diminutive ʾuhayl. It has been said other than this. It is attached to people of high rank.
al-Akhfash said: it is only said of the greatest leader, such as "āl Muhammad."
It is not attached to countries, so one does not say "āl al-Madīnah." 
Al-Akhfash also said: We have heard it used with countries; they say "āl al-Madīnah."
They differed as to whether it may be attached to a pronoun. Some forbade it, and others permitted it, and this is the correct view. From it is the saying of ʿAbd al-Muttalib:

"And help against the family of al-Ṣalīb and its worshippers today, against your family."

Fir'awn: it is said that it is the name of that very king. It is also said that it is a name for every king among the kings of the ʿAmalaqah, just as whoever ruled Persia was called Kisra, whoever ruled Rome was called Caesar, and whoever ruled Abyssinia was called al-Najashi.

The name of the Pharaoh of Moses mentioned here is Qabus according to the People of the Book. Wahb said: his name is al-Walid ibn Musʿab ibn al-Rayyan.

Al-Mas'udi said: no Arabic explanation of "Fir'awn" is known.

Al-Jawhari said: every tyrant is called Fir'awn, and one has become "tafarʿana," and he is "dhū farʿanah," meaning cunning and deceit.

In al-Kashshaf he said: "tafarʿana fulān" means when he became a tyrant and oppressor.

The meaning of His words: ﴿they inflicted upon you﴾ (yasumūnakum) is: they governed you. Abu ʿUbaydah said this. It has also been said: they made you taste and imposed it upon you. The origin of sawm is continuity, and from it comes "sāʾimah al-ghanam" (grazing sheep), because they continuously graze. It is said: "sāmahu khuṭṭata khasfin," meaning: he gave him an ignominious position.

In al-Kashshaf he said: its origin is from "sāma al-silʿah," when one seeks it, as if it means: they seek to inflict upon you the worst of punishment and want you to submit to it. End of quote.

"Sūʾ al-ʿadhāb" means its severest form. It is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: that is, they inflict upon you a torment of the worst kind. It is also permissible that it is a second object. This sentence is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permissible that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while they were governing you.

His words: ﴿they slaughter﴾ and what follows it are a substitute for His words "they inflict upon you." Al-Farra' said: it is an explanation of what precedes it. The majority read it with the doubled consonant (yudhabbihūna), and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (yadhbahūna).

Al-dhabh (slaughter) originally means cutting, which is severing the jugular veins of the slaughtered animal.

The meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they spare your women﴾ is that they leave them alive to employ and humiliate them. He only commanded the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the daughters because the soothsayers informed him that a child would be born whose destruction would be at his hands. He expressed the daughters with the term "women" because it is a genus that applies to daughters.

A group said: he commanded the killing of men, and they used as evidence His words "your women." The first view is more correct, by the testimony of the cause. It is not hidden what is involved in killing the sons and sparing the daughters for service and the like, of bringing humiliation upon them and attaching extreme disgrace to all of them, because of the shame in it.

The demonstrative in His words "and in that" refers to the whole matter.

The word balāʾ is applied sometimes to good and sometimes to evil. If it is meant here as evil, then the demonstrative in His words "and in that is a trial" refers to the vengeance that befell them through the slaughter and the like. If it is meant as good, then the demonstrative refers to the favour God bestowed upon them through deliverance, and what was mentioned before it of His preferring them over the worlds.

The early scholars and those after them differed as to what the demonstrative refers to. The majority preferred the first view, and others preferred the other.

Ibn Jarir said: most often one says for evil "baliytuhu abluhu balāʾan," and for good "ablīhi ibla'an wa-balāʾan." Zuhayr said:

"May God reward with goodness what they did for you, and bestowed upon them the best of the trial which tests."

He said: he combined the two usages, because he meant: He bestowed upon them the best of the favours by which He tests His servants.

His words: ﴿and when We divided﴾ are connected to what preceded of His words "remember." "Farraqnā" means "faraqnā" (We split). The origin of farq is separation, and from it is "farq al-shaʿr" (parting of hair). al-Zuhri read "farraqnā" with doubling. The ba' in His words "bikum" is said to mean the lām, that is "for you." It is also said to be the causal ba', that is: We split it because of you. It is also said that the prepositional phrase is in the circumstantial position: that is, We split it while you were involved in it. What is meant here is that the splitting of the sea was because of them, that is, because of their entering it. When they were between the two waters, the splitting took place with them.

The original meaning of "baḥr" in the language is expansion. It is applied to the sea, which is the opposite of land, because of its expansiveness relative to the river and the gulf. It is also applied to salt water, and from it "abḥara al-mā'" means the water became salty. Nusayb said:

"The land's water has returned to being sea, and it has increased me in my sickness, that the sweet drinking water has become salty."

His words: ﴿then We saved you﴾, that is, We brought you out of it. ﴿And We drowned the family of Pharaoh﴾ in it.

His words: ﴿while you were looking on﴾ are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while you were looking at them with your eyes. It has also been said that its meaning is: while you were looking, that is, one of you was looking at another of those travelling in the sea. It has been said: they looked at themselves being saved, and at the family of Pharaoh drowning.

The intended "family of Pharaoh" here is him, his people, and his followers.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that whenever he recited ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, he would say: "The people have passed away," and he meant by it only you.

Ibn Jarir related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah that he said regarding His words "remember My favour": it is God's graces and His days.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid that he said: the favour of God which He bestowed upon the Children of Israel is in what He named and in what is other than that: He made the rock gush forth for them, sent down upon them the manna and the quails, and delivered them from the servitude of the family of Pharaoh.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ that he said: They were preferred over the world in which they were, and for every age there is a world.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related similarly from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding His words: ﴿I preferred you over the worlds﴾ that he said: by what they were given of kingship, messengers, and books over those who were in that age, for every age has its world.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His words: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ that he said: no believing soul will avail a disbelieving soul with any benefit.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Mula'i, "from a man of the Banu Umayyah from the people of Syria," praising him highly, that he said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is ʿadl?" He said: "ʿAdl is the ransom."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was also narrated from Abu Malik, al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas something similar to that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from ʿAli regarding the explanation of "al-sarf and al-ʿadl" that he said: voluntary acts and obligatory acts.

Ibn Kathir said: This statement is strange here, and the first statement is more evident in the explanation of this verse.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The soothsayers (al-kahanah) said to Pharaoh, "A boy will be born in this year who will take away your kingdom." So Pharaoh appointed over every thousand women one hundred men, over every hundred ten, and over every ten one man, and said, "Look at every pregnant woman in the city. When she gives birth, if it is a male, slaughter him, and if it is a female, leave her alive." This is His saying: ﴿They slaughter your sons and spare your women﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾ that he said: Pharaoh ruled them for four hundred years.

The soothsayers said to him, "A boy will be born this year in Egypt whose hand will bring about your destruction." So he sent midwives (qawabil) throughout the people of Egypt. Whenever a woman gave birth to a boy, he was brought to Pharaoh, who killed him, and he spared the girls.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾ that he said: it means a punishment (niqmah).

Waki' reported from Mujahid something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ that he said: Yes, by Allah, He split the sea between them until it became a dry path they walked through. Allah rescued them and drowned the family of Pharaoh, their enemy.

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, i.e., the authentic collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina and saw the Jews fasting on the day of 'Ashura'. He said, "What is this day?" They said, "This is a righteous day, the day on which Allah rescued the Children of Israel from their enemy, so Musa fasted it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "We have a greater claim to Musa than you do." So he fasted it and commanded that it be fasted.

Al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that Heraclius (Hiraql) wrote to Mu'awiyah asking him about several matters, among them the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour. Mu'awiyah wrote to Ibn 'Abbas, and he answered him regarding those matters and said: As for the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour of the day, it is the sea that parted for the Children of Israel.

Perhaps, if Allah the Exalted wills, there will be more on this beyond what is mentioned here when we reach His saying ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

His words: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. Its explanation has already preceded. He, glory be to Him, repeated this only to emphasise the proof against them and to warn them against abandoning the following of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then He linked it to a warning, which is His words: ﴿And fear a Day﴾, and His words: ﴿and that I preferred you﴾, which is conjoined to the object of "remember". That is: remember My favour and My preferring you over the worlds. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the worlds" is the world of their time. It has also been said: over all the worlds, through the prophets He placed among them.

In al-Kashshaf he said: over a great multitude of people, like His words: ﴿We blessed therein for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 71]. It is said: "I saw a world (ʿalam) of people," meaning a great number. End of quote.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: This is weak, because the word ʿalam is derived from ʿalam (sign), which is evidence, and everything that is evidence for God is a sign and is part of the ʿalam (world).

This is the verification of the saying of the theologians: the ʿalam is every existent other than God, and on this basis it is not possible to restrict the word ʿalam to some of the created things. End of quote.

This does not require their preference over the people of the era in which our Prophet (ﷺ) was, nor over those after it. Such a statement should be borne in mind when interpreting His words, exalted is He: ﴿When He placed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. If it is said: the definite article in "the worlds" indicates that it encompasses every world.

The intended "Day" is the Day of Resurrection, that is, its punishment.

His words: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ are in the accusative position as an attribute of "Day", and the returning pronoun is omitted. The Basrans said regarding this and similar cases that its estimated form is "in it" (fihi). Al-Kisai said: this is an error; rather the estimate is "will not avail it" (la tajzihi), because omitting the adverbial of time is not permitted, while omitting the pronoun alone is permitted. It has been narrated from Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj that both are permitted.

The meaning of "will not avail" (la tajzi) is "will not suffice and will not discharge." It is said: "jaza ʿannī hādhā al-amr yajzī," meaning: it discharged it. And "ijtazaʾtu bi-l-shayʾ ajtazi," meaning: I was content with it. From this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed treachery among peoples is a shame, and indeed the free man is satisfied with the lowly (kurāʿ)."

It is in the accusative either as an object, or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: that is, a paltry recompense.

Intercession (shafaʿah) is derived from shafʿ, which means a pair. You say: "istashfaʿtuhu," meaning: I asked him to intercede for me, that is, to join his standing with your standing before the one interceded with, so that benefit reaches the one interceded for. It was named shufʿah (pre-emption) because you join your partner's share to your share.

It is said: ʿadl and ʿadīl for the one who is equal in weight and measure.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: This is weak, because the word ʿalam is derived from ʿalam (sign), which is evidence, and everything that is evidence for God is a sign and is part of the ʿalam (world).

This is the verification of the saying of the theologians: the ʿalam is every existent other than God, and on this basis it is not possible to restrict the word ʿalam to some of the created things. End of quote.

As for their being preferred over all created things in every age, the wording does not indicate this, nor does its derivation point to it. As for whoever takes ʿalam to mean the people of an era, its furthest implication is that they are preferred over the people of certain eras, not over the people of every era. This does not require their preference over the people of the era in which our Prophet (ﷺ) was, nor over those after it.
