He said, "What is this day?" They said, "This is a righteous day, the day on which Allah rescued the Children of Israel from their enemy, so Musa fasted it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "We have a greater claim to Musa than you do." So he fasted it and commanded that it be fasted.

Al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that Heraclius (Hiraql) wrote to Mu'awiyah asking him about several matters, among them the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour. Mu'awiyah wrote to Ibn 'Abbas, and he answered him regarding those matters and said: As for the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour of the day, it is the sea that parted for the Children of Israel.

Perhaps, if Allah the Exalted wills, there will be more on this beyond what is mentioned here when we reach His saying ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

His words: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. Its explanation has already preceded. He, glory be to Him, repeated this only to emphasise the proof against them and to warn them against abandoning the following of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then He linked it to a warning, which is His words: ﴿And fear a Day﴾, and His words: ﴿and that I preferred you﴾, which is conjoined to the object of "remember". That is: remember My favour and My preferring you over the worlds. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the worlds" is the world of their time. It has also been said: over all the worlds, through the prophets He placed among them.

In al-Kashshaf he said: over a great multitude of people, like His words: ﴿We blessed therein for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 71]. It is said: "I saw a world (ʿalam) of people," meaning a great number. End of quote.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: This is weak, because the word ʿalam is derived from ʿalam (sign), which is evidence, and everything that is evidence for God is a sign and is part of the ʿalam (world).

This is the verification of the saying of the theologians: the ʿalam is every existent other than God, and on this basis it is not possible to restrict the word ʿalam to some of the created things. End of quote.

I say: this objection is baseless. Firstly, the claim that it is derived from ʿalam has no proof. Secondly, even if we grant the correctness of this derivation, the meaning would exist in whatever yields the concept of evidence for God, whose name as a sign may be applied to it, and it is present in every individual of the created things by which one infers the Creator. Its furthest implication is that the plural ʿalamin requires that they be preferred over many created things. As for their being preferred over all created things in every age, the wording does not indicate this, nor does its derivation point to it. As for whoever takes ʿalam to mean the people of an era, its furthest implication is that they are preferred over the people of certain eras, not over the people of every era. This does not require their preference over the people of the era in which our Prophet (ﷺ) was, nor over those after it. Such a statement should be borne in mind when interpreting His words, exalted is He: ﴿When He placed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [al-Dukhan: 32], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. If it is said: the definite article in "the worlds" indicates that it encompasses every world.

I say: even if the matter were so, that would not imply that they are better than the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), because of His words: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al ʿImran: 110]. For this verse and its like would specify those verses.

His words: ﴿and fear a Day﴾ is an imperative whose meaning is a warning, and the meaning of taqwa has already preceded.

The intended "Day" is the Day of Resurrection, that is, its punishment.

His words: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ are in the accusative position as an attribute of "Day", and the returning pronoun is omitted. The Basrans said regarding this and similar cases that its estimated form is "in it" (fihi). Al-Kisai said: this is an error; rather the estimate is "will not avail it" (la tajzihi), because omitting the adverbial of time is not permitted, while omitting the pronoun alone is permitted. It has been narrated from Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj that both are permitted.

The meaning of "will not avail" (la tajzi) is "will not suffice and will not discharge." It is said: "jaza ʿannī hādhā al-amr yajzī," meaning: it discharged it. And "ijtazaʾtu bi-l-shayʾ ajtazi," meaning: I was content with it. From this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed treachery among peoples is a shame, and indeed the free man is satisfied with the lowly (kurāʿ)."

The meaning is that on this Day no soul will discharge anything on behalf of another soul, nor suffice for it. The indefiniteness of "shayʾan" conveys belittling: that is, a small, paltry thing. It is in the accusative either as an object, or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: that is, a paltry recompense.

Intercession (shafaʿah) is derived from shafʿ, which means a pair. You say: "istashfaʿtuhu," meaning: I asked him to intercede for me, that is, to join his standing with your standing before the one interceded with, so that benefit reaches the one interceded for. It was named shufʿah (pre-emption) because you join your partner's share to your share.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-tuqbalu" with the feminine ta', because intercession is feminine. The rest read it with the masculine ya', because it means "the intercessor." al-Akhfash said: the masculine is better.

The pronoun in "minhā" refers to the soul mentioned second, that is: if it comes with the intercession of an intercessor. It is also permissible that it refers to the soul mentioned first, that is: if it interceded, nothing from it would be accepted.

ʿAdl with an open ʿayn means ransom, and with a kasra it means equivalent.
It is said: ʿadl and ʿadīl for the one who is equal in weight and measure.
Ibn Jarir related that among the Arabs there are some who use a kasra on the ʿayn with the meaning of ransom.

Al-nasr means help, and al-anṣār means helpers, and "intaṣara al-rajul" means he took revenge. The pronoun, that is "they" (hum), refers to the souls implied by the indefinite noun in the context of negation. The soul is treated as masculine or feminine.

His words: ﴿when We delivered you﴾ are connected to His words "remember". Al-najāh (deliverance) is al-najwah, meaning a raised part of the ground, and then every one who succeeds is called najī (delivered).

"Āl Fir'awn" means his people. The origin of āl is ahl (family), as shown by its diminutive ʾuhayl. It has been said other than this. It is attached to people of high rank.
al-Akhfash said: it is only said of the greatest leader, such as "āl Muhammad."
It is not attached to countries, so one does not say "āl al-Madīnah." 
Al-Akhfash also said: We have heard it used with countries; they say "āl al-Madīnah."
They differed as to whether it may be attached to a pronoun. Some forbade it, and others permitted it, and this is the correct view. From it is the saying of ʿAbd al-Muttalib:

"And help against the family of al-Ṣalīb and its worshippers today, against your family."

Fir'awn: it is said that it is the name of that very king. It is also said that it is a name for every king among the kings of the ʿAmalaqah, just as whoever ruled Persia was called Kisra, whoever ruled Rome was called Caesar, and whoever ruled Abyssinia was called al-Najashi.

The name of the Pharaoh of Moses mentioned here is Qabus according to the People of the Book. Wahb said: his name is al-Walid ibn Musʿab ibn al-Rayyan.

Al-Mas'udi said: no Arabic explanation of "Fir'awn" is known.

Al-Jawhari said: every tyrant is called Fir'awn, and one has become "tafarʿana," and he is "dhū farʿanah," meaning cunning and deceit.

In al-Kashshaf he said: "tafarʿana fulān" means when he became a tyrant and oppressor.

The meaning of His words: ﴿they inflicted upon you﴾ (yasumūnakum) is: they governed you. Abu ʿUbaydah said this. It has also been said: they made you taste and imposed it upon you. The origin of sawm is continuity, and from it comes "sāʾimah al-ghanam" (grazing sheep), because they continuously graze. It is said: "sāmahu khuṭṭata khasfin," meaning: he gave him an ignominious position.

In al-Kashshaf he said: its origin is from "sāma al-silʿah," when one seeks it, as if it means: they seek to inflict upon you the worst of punishment and want you to submit to it. End of quote.

"Sūʾ al-ʿadhāb" means its severest form. It is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: that is, they inflict upon you a torment of the worst kind. It is also permissible that it is a second object. This sentence is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permissible that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while they were governing you.

His words: ﴿they slaughter﴾ and what follows it are a substitute for His words "they inflict upon you." Al-Farra' said: it is an explanation of what precedes it. The majority read it with the doubled consonant (yudhabbihūna), and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (yadhbahūna).

Al-dhabh (slaughter) originally means cutting, which is severing the jugular veins of the slaughtered animal.

The meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they spare your women﴾ is that they leave them alive to employ and humiliate them. He only commanded the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the daughters because the soothsayers informed him that a child would be born whose destruction would be at his hands. He expressed the daughters with the term "women" because it is a genus that applies to daughters.

A group said: he commanded the killing of men, and they used as evidence His words "your women." The first view is more correct, by the testimony of the cause. It is not hidden what is involved in killing the sons and sparing the daughters for service and the like, of bringing humiliation upon them and attaching extreme disgrace to all of them, because of the shame in it.

The demonstrative in His words "and in that" refers to the whole matter.

The word balāʾ is applied sometimes to good and sometimes to evil. If it is meant here as evil, then the demonstrative in His words "and in that is a trial" refers to the vengeance that befell them through the slaughter and the like. If it is meant as good, then the demonstrative refers to the favour God bestowed upon them through deliverance, and what was mentioned before it of His preferring them over the worlds.

The early scholars and those after them differed as to what the demonstrative refers to. The majority preferred the first view, and others preferred the other.

Ibn Jarir said: most often one says for evil "baliytuhu abluhu balāʾan," and for good "ablīhi ibla'an wa-balāʾan." Zuhayr said:

"May God reward with goodness what they did for you, and bestowed upon them the best of the trial which tests."

He said: he combined the two usages, because he meant: He bestowed upon them the best of the favours by which He tests His servants.

His words: ﴿and when We divided﴾ are connected to what preceded of His words "remember." "Farraqnā" means "faraqnā" (We split). The origin of farq is separation, and from it is "farq al-shaʿr" (parting of hair). al-Zuhri read "farraqnā" with doubling. The ba' in His words "bikum" is said to mean the lām, that is "for you." It is also said to be the causal ba', that is: We split it because of you. It is also said that the prepositional phrase is in the circumstantial position: that is, We split it while you were involved in it. What is meant here is that the splitting of the sea was because of them, that is, because of their entering it. When they were between the two waters, the splitting took place with them.

The original meaning of "baḥr" in the language is expansion. It is applied to the sea, which is the opposite of land, because of its expansiveness relative to the river and the gulf. It is also applied to salt water, and from it "abḥara al-mā'" means the water became salty. Nusayb said:

"The land's water has returned to being sea, and it has increased me in my sickness, that the sweet drinking water has become salty."

His words: ﴿then We saved you﴾, that is, We brought you out of it. ﴿And We drowned the family of Pharaoh﴾ in it.

His words: ﴿while you were looking on﴾ are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, while you were looking at them with your eyes. It has also been said that its meaning is: while you were looking, that is, one of you was looking at another of those travelling in the sea. It has been said: they looked at themselves being saved, and at the family of Pharaoh drowning.

The intended "family of Pharaoh" here is him, his people, and his followers.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that whenever he recited ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, he would say: "The people have passed away," and he meant by it only you.

Ibn Jarir related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah that he said regarding His words "remember My favour": it is God's graces and His days.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid that he said: the favour of God which He bestowed upon the Children of Israel is in what He named and in what is other than that: He made the rock gush forth for them, sent down upon them the manna and the quails, and delivered them from the servitude of the family of Pharaoh.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ that he said: They were preferred over the world in which they were, and for every age there is a world.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related similarly from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding His words: ﴿I preferred you over the worlds﴾ that he said: by what they were given of kingship, messengers, and books over those who were in that age, for every age has its world.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His words: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ that he said: no believing soul will avail a disbelieving soul with any benefit.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Mula'i, "from a man of the Banu Umayyah from the people of Syria," praising him highly, that he said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is ʿadl?" He said: "ʿAdl is the ransom."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was also narrated from Abu Malik, al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas something similar to that.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from ʿAli regarding the explanation of "al-sarf and al-ʿadl" that he said: voluntary acts and obligatory acts.

Ibn Kathir said: This statement is strange here, and the first statement is more evident in the explanation of this verse.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The soothsayers (al-kahanah) said to Pharaoh, "A boy will be born in this year who will take away your kingdom." So Pharaoh appointed over every thousand women one hundred men, over every hundred ten, and over every ten one man, and said, "Look at every pregnant woman in the city. When she gives birth, if it is a male, slaughter him, and if it is a female, leave her alive." This is His saying: ﴿They slaughter your sons and spare your women﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾ that he said: Pharaoh ruled them for four hundred years.

The soothsayers said to him, "A boy will be born this year in Egypt whose hand will bring about your destruction." So he sent midwives (qawabil) throughout the people of Egypt. Whenever a woman gave birth to a boy, he was brought to Pharaoh, who killed him, and he spared the girls.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾ that he said: it means a punishment (niqmah).

Waki' reported from Mujahid something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ that he said: Yes, by Allah, He split the sea between them until it became a dry path they walked through. Allah rescued them and drowned the family of Pharaoh, their enemy.

It is firmly established in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, i.e., the authentic collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina and saw the Jews fasting on the day of 'Ashura'. He said, "What is this day?" They said, "This is a righteous day, the day on which Allah rescued the Children of Israel from their enemy, so Musa fasted it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "We have a greater claim to Musa than you do." So he fasted it and commanded that it be fasted.

Al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that Heraclius (Hiraql) wrote to Mu'awiyah asking him about several matters, among them the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour. Mu'awiyah wrote to Ibn 'Abbas, and he answered him regarding those matters and said: As for the patch of ground that the sun touched only for an hour of the day, it is the sea that parted for the Children of Israel.

Perhaps, if Allah the Exalted wills, there will be more on this beyond what is mentioned here when we reach His saying ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 51–54:

Abu 'Amr read ﴿وَعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna*, "We appointed") without an alif. Abu 'Ubayda preferred this reading and rejected ﴿وَاعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna* with an alif, "We made a appointment"). He said: "Mu'ada (mutual promising) occurs only among humans. When it comes from God, it is only the sole giving of a promise. On this basis, we find the Qur'an uses ﴿وَعَدَكُمْ وَعْدَ الْحَقِّ﴾ [Ibrahim 14:22] and His saying ﴿وَإِذْ يَعِدُكُمُ اللَّهُ إِحْدَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ﴾ [al-Anfal 8:7], and similar verses." Abu Hatim and Makki said the same. They took this view by considering the basic meaning of the *mufa'ala* form (the form with an alif, which implies participation), namely that it indicates sharing in the action, with each of the parties to the promise being involved. However, the form may also be used for one party in the speech of the Arabs, as in their sayings: *dawaytu al-'alil* (I treated the sick person), *'aqabtu al-liss* (I punished the thief), and *tara'tu al-na'l* (I repaired the sandal). Such usage is common in their speech.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وَاعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna*, with the alif). Al-Nahhas said: "This reading is better and more excellent. The saying of God ﴿وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:9] has nothing to do with this, because *wa'adna Musa* belongs to the category of *muwafat* (arranging a meeting at a set time and place). It is not from *wa'd* and *wa'id* (promise and threat) at all. It comes from your saying: *mau'iduka yawm al-jum'a* (your appointment is Friday) and *mau'iduka mawdi' kadha* (your appointment is at such-and-such a place). The eloquent form in this sense is to say *wa'adtuhu*."

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Wa'adna* with the alif here is good, because obedience in acceptance is equivalent to the mutual agreement. So from God, glorified is He, comes the promise, and from Musa comes the acceptance."

As for God's saying ﴿أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ (forty nights), al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is the completion of forty nights." According to most exegetes (mufassirun), these were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. The reason the nights are specifically mentioned rather than the days is that the night precedes the day in time, so it comes before it in rank.

The meaning of God's saying ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ (then you took the calf) is: you made the calf a god after him, that is, after Musa had gone up to Mount Tur.

Some exegetes mention that they counted twenty days and twenty nights. They said: "His appointment was altered, and so they took the calf." This is not far-fetched from them, for they followed paths of stubbornness that lay outside the rules of reason and contradicted what they were addressed with, even what they witnessed with their own eyes. It cannot be asked, "How could you count the days and nights in that manner, when it was explicitly stated to them that the period was forty nights?" God called them *zalimin* (wrongdoers) because they associated partners with God and opposed the appointment of their prophet, peace be upon him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

God's saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ (after that) means: after your worship of the calf. The calf was named *'ijl* because of their haste (*isti'jal*) in worshipping it, as has been said. But this is not valid, because the Arabs use this name for a young cow.

The calf was made for them by al-Samiri, in the form of a calf.

God's saying ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ (so that you may give thanks) means: so that you may thank God for what He has bestowed upon you, namely His pardon for your great sin into which you had fallen.

The root meaning of *shukr* (thankfulness) in the language is "manifestation." It comes from the saying: *dabbatun shakur* (a thriving beast) when fat appears on it beyond what it is given in fodder.

Al-Jawhari said: *Shukr* is praise of a benefactor for the kindness he has conferred, one says *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*, with the preposition *lam* being more eloquent. Its meaning has been mentioned before. *Shukran* is the opposite of *kufran* (ingratitude).

The Book (al-Kitab) is the Torah, by the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the exegetes.

They differed concerning al-Furqan (the Criterion). Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: the meaning is "We gave Musa the Torah and Muhammad the Furqan." It has been said: this is an error, which they fell into because they assumed that al-Furqan is specific to the Qur'an, but it is not so, for God the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى وَهَارُونَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Furqan is the Book, mentioned again for emphasis. Something similar is related from al-Farra'. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

*Greetings to you from a ruin whose time has long passed, it has become desolate and empty after Umm al-Haytham.*

It has been said: the waw (and) is connective, and the meaning is: "We gave Musa the Book, the Furqan," and the waw is sometimes added in descriptions, as in the saying of the poet:

*To the mighty king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded melee.*

It has been said: the meaning is that this revelation combines being a Book and separating between truth and falsehood. This is like His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ تَمَامًا عَلَى الَّذِي أَحْسَنَ وَتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-An'am 6:154]. (p-59) It has been said: al-Furqan is the distinction between them (the Israelites) and the people of Pharaoh: He rescued these and drowned those. Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea. It has been said: al-Furqan is relief from distress. It has been said: it is the proof and clarity through the signs God gave him, such as the staff, the hand, and others. This last view is preferable and more likely, and the conjunction would then remain in its proper function, as if He had said: "We gave Musa the Torah and the signs with which We sent him as a miracle for him."

God's saying ﴿يَا قَوْمِ﴾ (O my people). The word *qawm* is sometimes used for men only, to the exclusion of women. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I do not know, and soon I will think I know: are the family of Hisn men or women?*

And from it is God's saying: ﴿لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِنْ قَوْمٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11], then He said: ﴿وَلَا نِسَاءٌ مِنْ نِسَاءٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11]. And from it: ﴿وَلُوطًا إِذْ قَالَ لِقَوْمِهِ﴾ [al-A'raf 7:80; al-Naml 27:54; al-'Ankabut 29:28], meaning the men. It is also used for the whole group, as in God's saying: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَى قَوْمِهِ﴾ [Nuh 71:1]. The intended meaning of *qawm* here is the worshippers of the calf.

Al-Bari' means the Creator. It has been said that al-Bari' here points to the enormity of their crime, meaning: "Repent to the One who created you, when you worshipped another alongside Him."

The fa' in God's saying ﴿فَتُوبُوا﴾ (so repent) indicates causation, that is, the repentance results from wrongdoing. The fa' in ﴿فَاقْتُلُوا﴾ (then kill) indicates sequence, meaning: make the killing follow the repentance.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that each one of the calf-worshippers was not commanded to kill himself with his own hand. It has been said: they stood in two rows, and some of them killed others. It has also been said: those who worshipped the calf stood still, and those who had not worshipped it came upon them with weapons and killed them.

God's saying ﴿فَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (and He turned to you in forgiveness). It has been said there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "You killed yourselves, and so He turned to you," that is, to those of you who remained.

It has been said: it is the answer to an omitted condition, as if He had said: "If you do so, then He has turned to you."

As for what the author of al-Kashshaf said, that it is permissible for it to be an address from God to them in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of speech), so that the meaning would be "you did what Musa commanded you, and so your Creator turned to you," this is very far-fetched, as is not hidden.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliya concerning God's saying ﴿أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ that he said: "Dhu al-Qa'da and ten from Dhu al-Hijja."

Ibn Jarir also related from him concerning God's saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ that he said: "After you took the calf."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 51–54:

Abu 'Amr read ﴿وَعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna*, "We appointed") without an alif. Abu 'Ubayda preferred this reading and rejected ﴿وَاعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna* with an alif, "We made a appointment"). He said: "Mu'ada (mutual promising) occurs only among humans. When it comes from God, it is only the sole giving of a promise. On this basis, we find the Qur'an uses ﴿وَعَدَكُمْ وَعْدَ الْحَقِّ﴾ [Ibrahim 14:22] and His saying ﴿وَإِذْ يَعِدُكُمُ اللَّهُ إِحْدَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ﴾ [al-Anfal 8:7], and similar verses." Abu Hatim and Makki said the same. They took this view by considering the basic meaning of the *mufa'ala* form (the form with an alif, which implies participation), namely that it indicates sharing in the action, with each of the parties to the promise being involved. However, the form may also be used for one party in the speech of the Arabs, as in their sayings: *dawaytu al-'alil* (I treated the sick person), *'aqabtu al-liss* (I punished the thief), and *tara'tu al-na'l* (I repaired the sandal). Such usage is common in their speech.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وَاعَدْنَا﴾ (*wa'adna*, with the alif). Al-Nahhas said: "This reading is better and more excellent. The saying of God ﴿وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:9] has nothing to do with this, because *wa'adna Musa* belongs to the category of *muwafat* (arranging a meeting at a set time and place). It is not from *wa'd* and *wa'id* (promise and threat) at all. It comes from your saying: *mau'iduka yawm al-jum'a* (your appointment is Friday) and *mau'iduka mawdi' kadha* (your appointment is at such-and-such a place). The eloquent form in this sense is to say *wa'adtuhu*."

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Wa'adna* with the alif here is good, because obedience in acceptance is equivalent to the mutual agreement. So from God, glorified is He, comes the promise, and from Musa comes the acceptance."

As for God's saying ﴿أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ (forty nights), al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is the completion of forty nights." According to most exegetes (mufassirun), these were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. The reason the nights are specifically mentioned rather than the days is that the night precedes the day in time, so it comes before it in rank.

The meaning of God's saying ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ (then you took the calf) is: you made the calf a god after him, that is, after Musa had gone up to Mount Tur.

Some exegetes mention that they counted twenty days and twenty nights. They said: "His appointment was altered, and so they took the calf." This is not far-fetched from them, for they followed paths of stubbornness that lay outside the rules of reason and contradicted what they were addressed with, even what they witnessed with their own eyes. It cannot be asked, "How could you count the days and nights in that manner, when it was explicitly stated to them that the period was forty nights?" God called them *zalimin* (wrongdoers) because they associated partners with God and opposed the appointment of their prophet, peace be upon him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

God's saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ (after that) means: after your worship of the calf. The calf was named *'ijl* because of their haste (*isti'jal*) in worshipping it, as has been said. But this is not valid, because the Arabs use this name for a young cow.

The calf was made for them by al-Samiri, in the form of a calf.

God's saying ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ (so that you may give thanks) means: so that you may thank God for what He has bestowed upon you, namely His pardon for your great sin into which you had fallen.

The root meaning of *shukr* (thankfulness) in the language is "manifestation." It comes from the saying: *dabbatun shakur* (a thriving beast) when fat appears on it beyond what it is given in fodder.

Al-Jawhari said: *Shukr* is praise of a benefactor for the kindness he has conferred, one says *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*, with the preposition *lam* being more eloquent. Its meaning has been mentioned before. *Shukran* is the opposite of *kufran* (ingratitude).

The Book (al-Kitab) is the Torah, by the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the exegetes.

They differed concerning al-Furqan (the Criterion). Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: the meaning is "We gave Musa the Torah and Muhammad the Furqan." It has been said: this is an error, which they fell into because they assumed that al-Furqan is specific to the Qur'an, but it is not so, for God the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى وَهَارُونَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Furqan is the Book, mentioned again for emphasis. Something similar is related from al-Farra'. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

*Greetings to you from a ruin whose time has long passed, it has become desolate and empty after Umm al-Haytham.*

It has been said: the waw (and) is connective, and the meaning is: "We gave Musa the Book, the Furqan," and the waw is sometimes added in descriptions, as in the saying of the poet:

*To the mighty king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded melee.*

It has been said: the meaning is that this revelation combines being a Book and separating between truth and falsehood. This is like His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ تَمَامًا عَلَى الَّذِي أَحْسَنَ وَتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-An'am 6:154]. (p-59) It has been said: al-Furqan is the distinction between them (the Israelites) and the people of Pharaoh: He rescued these and drowned those. Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea. It has been said: al-Furqan is relief from distress. It has been said: it is the proof and clarity through the signs God gave him, such as the staff, the hand, and others. This last view is preferable and more likely, and the conjunction would then remain in its proper function, as if He had said: "We gave Musa the Torah and the signs with which We sent him as a miracle for him."

God's saying ﴿يَا قَوْمِ﴾ (O my people). The word *qawm* is sometimes used for men only, to the exclusion of women. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I do not know, and soon I will think I know: are the family of Hisn men or women?*

And from it is God's saying: ﴿لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِنْ قَوْمٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11], then He said: ﴿وَلَا نِسَاءٌ مِنْ نِسَاءٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11]. It is also used for the whole group, as in God's saying: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَى قَوْمِهِ﴾ [Nuh 71:1]. The intended meaning of *qawm* here is the worshippers of the calf.

Al-Bari' means the Creator. It has been said that al-Bari' here points to the enormity of their crime, meaning: "Repent to the One who created you, when you worshipped another alongside Him."

It has been said: it is the answer to an omitted condition, as if He had said: "If you do so, then He has turned to you."

As for what the author of al-Kashshaf said, that it is permissible for it to be an address from God to them in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of speech), so that the meaning would be "you did what Musa commanded you, and so your Creator turned to you," this is very far-fetched, as is not hidden.

It comes from your saying: *mau'iduka yawm al-jum'a* (your appointment is Friday) and *mau'iduka mawdi' kadha* (your appointment is at such-and-such a place). The eloquent form in this sense is to say *wa'adtuhu*."

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Wa'adna* with the alif here is good, because obedience in acceptance is equivalent to the mutual agreement. So from God, glorified is He, comes the promise, and from Musa comes the acceptance."

As for God's saying ﴿أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ (forty nights), al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is the completion of forty nights." According to most exegetes (mufassirun), these were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. The reason the nights are specifically mentioned rather than the days is that the night precedes the day in time, so it comes before it in rank.

The meaning of God's saying ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ (then you took the calf) is: you made the calf a god after him, that is, after Musa had gone up to Mount Tur.

Some exegetes mention that they counted twenty days and twenty nights. They said: "His appointment was altered, and so they took the calf." This is not far-fetched from them, for they followed paths of stubbornness that lay outside the rules of reason and contradicted what they were addressed with, even what they witnessed with their own eyes. It cannot be asked, "How could you count the days and nights in that manner, when it was explicitly stated to them that the period was forty nights?" God called them *zalimin* (wrongdoers) because they associated partners with God and opposed the appointment of their prophet, peace be upon him. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

God's saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ (after that) means: after your worship of the calf. The calf was named *'ijl* because of their haste (*isti'jal*) in worshipping it, as has been said. But this is not valid, because the Arabs use this name for a young cow.

The calf was made for them by al-Samiri, in the form of a calf.

God's saying ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ (so that you may give thanks) means: so that you may thank God for what He has bestowed upon you, namely His pardon for your great sin into which you had fallen.

The root meaning of *shukr* (thankfulness) in the language is "manifestation." It comes from the saying: *dabbatun shakur* (a thriving beast) when fat appears on it beyond what it is given in fodder.

Al-Jawhari said: *Shukr* is praise of a benefactor for the kindness he has conferred, one says *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*, with the preposition *lam* being more eloquent. Its meaning has been mentioned before. *Shukran* is the opposite of *kufran* (ingratitude).

The Book (al-Kitab) is the Torah, by the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the exegetes.

They differed concerning al-Furqan (the Criterion). Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: the meaning is "We gave Musa the Torah and Muhammad the Furqan." It has been said: this is an error, which they fell into because they assumed that al-Furqan is specific to the Qur'an, but it is not so, for God the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى وَهَارُونَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Furqan is the Book, mentioned again for emphasis. Something similar is related from al-Farra'. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

*Greetings to you from a ruin whose time has long passed, it has become desolate and empty after Umm al-Haytham.*

It has been said: the waw (and) is connective, and the meaning is: "We gave Musa the Book, the Furqan," and the waw is sometimes added in descriptions, as in the saying of the poet:

*To the mighty king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded melee.*

It has been said: the meaning is that this revelation combines being a Book and separating between truth and falsehood. This is like His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ تَمَامًا عَلَى الَّذِي أَحْسَنَ وَتَفْصِيلًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-An'am 6:154]. (p-59) It has been said: al-Furqan is the distinction between them (the Israelites) and the people of Pharaoh: He rescued these and drowned those. Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea. It has been said: al-Furqan is relief from distress. It has been said: it is the proof and clarity through the signs God gave him, such as the staff, the hand, and others. This last view is preferable and more likely, and the conjunction would then remain in its proper function, as if He had said: "We gave Musa the Torah and the signs with which We sent him as a miracle for him."

God's saying ﴿يَا قَوْمِ﴾ (O my people). The word *qawm* is sometimes used for men only, to the exclusion of women. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*I do not know, and soon I will think I know: are the family of Hisn men or women?*

And from it is God's saying: ﴿لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِنْ قَوْمٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11], then He said: ﴿وَلَا نِسَاءٌ مِنْ نِسَاءٍ﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11]. And from it: ﴿وَلُوطًا إِذْ قَالَ لِقَوْمِهِ﴾ [al-A'raf 7:80; al-Naml 27:54; al-'Ankabut 29:28], meaning the men. It is also used for the whole group, as in God's saying: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا نُوحًا إِلَى قَوْمِهِ﴾ [Nuh 71:1]. The intended meaning of *qawm* here is the worshippers of the calf.

Al-Bari' means the Creator. It has been said that al-Bari' here points to the enormity of their crime, meaning: "Repent to the One who created you, when you worshipped another alongside Him."

The fa' in God's saying ﴿فَتُوبُوا﴾ (so repent) indicates causation, that is, the repentance results from wrongdoing. The fa' in ﴿فَاقْتُلُوا﴾ (then kill) indicates sequence, meaning: make the killing follow the repentance.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that each one of the calf-worshippers was not commanded to kill himself with his own hand. It has been said: they stood in two rows, and some of them killed others. It has also been said: those who worshipped the calf stood still, and those who had not worshipped it came upon them with weapons and killed them.

God's saying ﴿فَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (and He turned to you in forgiveness). It has been said there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "You killed yourselves, and so He turned to you," that is, to those of you who remained.

It has been said: it is the answer to an omitted condition, as if He had said: "If you do so, then He has turned to you."

As for what the author of al-Kashshaf said, that it is permissible for it to be an address from God to them in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of speech), so that the meaning would be "you did what Musa commanded you, and so your Creator turned to you," this is very far-fetched, as is not hidden.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliya concerning God's saying ﴿أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾ that he said: "Dhu al-Qa'da and ten from Dhu al-Hijja."

Ibn Jarir also related from him concerning God's saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ that he said: "After you took the calf."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning God's saying ﴿وَإِذْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ وَالْفُرْقَانَ﴾ that he said: "The Book is the Furqan; it separates between truth and falsehood."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The Furqan is the collective name for the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "Musa commanded his people, by the command of their Lord, to kill themselves. Those who had clung to the calf sat down and hid, while those who had not clung to the calf stood up and took daggers in their hands. A severe darkness came upon them, and they began to kill one another, until the darkness lifted from them, and seventy thousand had been slain. Everyone who was killed had repentance, and everyone who remained had repentance."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ali that he said: "They said to Musa: 'What is our repentance?' He said: 'Let some of you kill others.' So they took knives, and a man would kill his brother, his father, and his son, not caring whom he killed, until seventy thousand of them were killed. Then God revealed to Musa: 'Command them to raise their hands. Those who were killed are forgiven, and those who remain are forgiven.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatada, and Ahmad in al-Zuhd (Asceticism) and Ibn Jarir related from al-Zuhri, something similar to what has preceded.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliya concerning God's saying ﴿إِلَى بَارِئِكُمْ﴾ (to your Creator) that he said: "Your Creator."

The verb in ﴿وإذ قلتم﴾ ("And when you said") is conjoined to the preceding clause. The apparent context indicates that the speakers of this statement were the people of Musa, and it was said that they were the seventy whom he chose.

When they heard the speech of Allah, they uttered this statement after that, so Allah sent down fire upon them and it burned them.

Then Musa supplicated to his Lord and they were revived, as the Exalted says here: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. This will come in al-A'raf, Allah willing.

Al-jahrah means direct witnessing (mu'ayanah), and its root meaning is manifestness. From it come al-jahr bi-l-qira'ah (reciting aloud) and al-mujaharah bi-l-ma'asi (openly committing sins). One says "I saw the matter jahratan and jihaaran," meaning not concealed by anything. It is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as a circumstantial state (hal).

Ibn 'Abbas recited "jahratan" with a fatha on the ha', and both are two dialectal forms, like zahrah and zahrah. It is possible that on this reading it is the plural of jahir.

As for al-sa'iqah, its explanation has already been given. Umar, Uthman and Ali recited "al-sa'qah," and this is the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin. The meaning of "the seizing by the sa'iqah" is that it struck them.

﴿And you were looking﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning of this looking that occurred from them is that they looked at the first signs of the thunderbolt descending upon them and striking them, not at its final end by which they died. It was said that the meaning of the sa'iqah is death, and this was argued from His saying: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. But there is no reason to resort to this interpretation, because one struck by lightning may indeed die, as in this verse, and may also faint and then recover, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious, and when he recovered﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. What necessitates this is His saying: ﴿And you were looking﴾, for if the sa'iqah were an expression for death, this clause would have no great meaning. Rather, it may be said that it is not correct to say "you looked at death descending upon you," unless the meaning is looking at the causes that produce death.

The meaning of His saying ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ is the reviving of them, since it occurred after death. The root meaning of ba'th is stirring a thing from its place. One says "I stirred the she-camel" (ba'thtu al-naqah), meaning I roused her. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And brothers of truth, whom I roused at dawn, and they stood all together between the mounted and the drunken."

And the saying of 'Antarah:

"And companions with proud noses, whom I roused at night, when sleep had inclined over their shade."

They were punished with the seizing of the sa'iqah because they asked for what Allah had not permitted, namely seeing Him in this world.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) and those who followed them went to deny seeing Allah both in this world and in the Hereafter, while others went to the permissibility of it in this world and in the Hereafter, and its occurrence in the Hereafter.

The sound hadiths have been transmitted in mass-transmission (tawatur) that the servants will see their Lord in the Hereafter, and this is decisive in its indication (qat'i al-dalalah). It is not fitting for a fair-minded person to hold, against it, to those kalam principles that the early Mu'tazilah brought, claiming that reason had judged by them. That claim is built upon the edge of a crumbling precipice, and they are principles that none is deceived by except one who has not obtained a share of beneficial knowledge. The proofs from the Qur'an that they relied upon will come to you, Allah willing, with their explanation; all of them lie outside the place of dispute and far from the point of argument, and this is not the place for discussing this question.

His saying ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ means: We did it like a canopy.

Al-ghamam is the plural of ghamamah, like sahabah and sahab. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to say ghama'im.

The exegetes mention that this occurred in the wilderness (al-tih) between Egypt and Syria, when they refused to enter the city of the tyrants (al-Jabbarin).

Al-mann: it was said it is al-tarankjabin (a sweet exudation). Al-Nahhas said: it is with a shadda on the ra' and sukun on the nun, and it is said al-tarankjabin with a ta'. Most exegetes hold this view. It is a dew that descends from the sky upon a tree or a stone, becomes sweet, solidifies into honey, and dries like gum. Its meaning is mentioned in al-Qamus. It was also said that al-mann is honey, and it was said it is a sweet drink, and it was said it is thin bread (khubz al-ruqaq). It was also said that it is a verbal noun encompassing everything Allah bestowed upon His servants without toil or cultivation. From this is what is established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim from the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn Zayd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The mushroom (kam'ah) is from the manna that was sent down upon Musa."

A similar hadith has been established from Abu Hurayrah in Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, and from Jabir, Abu Sa'id and Ibn 'Abbas in al-Nasa'i.

Al-salwa: it was said it is al-sumani, like the bustard (hubara), a bird which they slaughtered and ate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-salwa is a bird by the consensus of the exegetes. The Hudhali erred when he said:

"And he swore by Allah with full effort that you two are sweeter than al-salwa when its honey (ashuruha) is tasted."

He thought that al-salwa is honey.

Al-Qurtubi said: what he claimed as consensus is not valid.

Al-Mu'arrij, one of the scholars of language and tafsir, said: it is honey, and he relied on the Hudhali's verse, and mentioned that it is so in the dialect of Kinanah, and recited:

"If I had drunk al-salwa, I would not have forgotten, but I have no sufficiency from you, even if I am sufficient."

Al-Jawhari said: al-salwa is honey.

Al-Akhfash said: al-salwa has no singular from its own form, like al-khayr and al-sharr, and it resembles that its singular is salwa.

Al-Khalil said: its singular is salwah, and he recited:

"Indeed, the remembrance of you stirs in me a salwah, as the salwah shakes when the rain has passed through it."

Al-Kisa'i said: al-salwa is singular, and its plural is salawa.

His saying "kulu" (eat) means: We said to them, "Eat." There is an elision in the speech, and the estimate is: We said, "Eat," but they disobeyed and did not meet the blessings with gratitude, so they wronged themselves and did not wrong Us. This was elided because of the indication of ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾. The fronting of "themselves" here conveys exclusivity (ikhtisas).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿until we see Allah openly﴾, that he said: "manifestly."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Anas, who said: They were the seventy whom Musa chose. ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: he said, "They died." ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾: he said, "They were raised after death so that they might complete their terms."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ something similar.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ that he said: "A cloud cooler and sweeter than this, which is the one in which Allah comes on the Day of Resurrection, and which the angels came in on the day of Badr, and it was with them in the wilderness."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ that he said: "This cloud was in the desert, shading them from the sun. It fed them manna and salwa when they came out into the desert. The manna would fall upon them in their camp like snow, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. It would fall upon them from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun, and a man would take what sufficed him for that day. If he exceeded that, what remained with him would spoil. But when it was the sixth day, the day of their Friday, he took what would suffice him for the sixth and seventh days, and it remained with him, because it was a day of festivity on which one did not set out for the matters of livelihood or for seeking anything." All of this was in the desert.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah, who said: "The manna is something Allah sent down upon them like dew, and the salwa is a bird larger than a sparrow."

Waki', 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "The manna is a gum, and the salwa is a bird."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: They said, "O Musa, how will we manage with what is here? Where is the food?" So Allah sent down upon them the manna, and upon the tree there would fall the tarankjabin.

And they transmitted from Wahb that he was asked: "What is the manna?" He said: "Thin bread like corn, or like the purest flour."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "The manna is a drink that was sent down upon them like honey, and they would mix it with water and then drink it."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The manna would descend upon them at night on the trees, and they would go out to it and eat from it whatever they wished. The salwa is a bird resembling the sumani, and they would eat from it whatever they wished."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him something similar.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions regarding the salwa something similar.

Something similar has been related from a group of the Successors and those after them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ that he said: "We are too mighty to be wronged."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ that he said: "They were harming (yadurruna) themselves."

It fed them manna and salwa when they came out into the desert. The manna would fall upon them in their camp like snow, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. It would fall upon them from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun, and a man would take what sufficed him for that day. If he exceeded that, what remained with him would spoil. But when it was the sixth day, the day of their Friday, he took what would suffice him for the sixth and seventh days, and it remained with him, because it was a day of festivity on which one did not set out for the matters of livelihood or for seeking anything." All of this was in the desert.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrimah, who said: "The manna is something Allah sent down upon them like dew, and the salwa is a bird larger than a sparrow."

Waki', 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "The manna is a gum, and the salwa is a bird."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: They said, "O Musa, how will we manage with what is here? Where is the food?" So Allah sent down upon them the manna, and upon the tree there would fall the tarankjabin.

And they transmitted from Wahb that he was asked: "What is the manna?" He said: "Thin bread like corn, or like the purest flour."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "The manna is a drink that was sent down upon them like honey, and they would mix it with water and then drink it."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The manna would descend upon them at night on the trees, and they would go out to it and eat from it whatever they wished. The salwa is a bird resembling the sumani, and they would eat from it whatever they wished."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him something similar.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions regarding the salwa something similar.

Something similar has been related from a group of the Successors and those after them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ that he said: "We are too mighty to be wronged."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ that he said: "They were harming (yadurruna) themselves."

The verb in ﴿وإذ قلتم﴾ ("And when you said") is conjoined to the preceding clause. The apparent context indicates that the speakers of this statement were the people of Musa, and it was said that they were the seventy whom he chose.

When they heard the speech of Allah, they uttered this statement after that, so Allah sent down fire upon them and it burned them.

Then Musa supplicated to his Lord and they were revived, as the Exalted says here: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. This will come in al-A'raf, Allah willing.

Al-jahrah means direct witnessing (mu'ayanah), and its root meaning is manifestness. From it come al-jahr bi-l-qira'ah (reciting aloud) and al-mujaharah bi-l-ma'asi (openly committing sins). One says "I saw the matter jahratan and jihaaran," meaning not concealed by anything. It is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as a circumstantial state (hal).

Ibn 'Abbas recited "jahratan" with a fatha on the ha', and both are two dialectal forms, like zahrah and zahrah. It is possible that on this reading it is the plural of jahir.

As for al-sa'iqah, its explanation has already been given. Umar, Uthman and Ali recited "al-sa'qah," and this is the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin. The meaning of "the seizing by the sa'iqah" is that it struck them.

﴿And you were looking﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning of this looking that occurred from them is that they looked at the first signs of the thunderbolt descending upon them and striking them, not at its final end by which they died. It was said that the meaning of the sa'iqah is death, and this was argued from His saying: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. But there is no reason to resort to this interpretation, because one struck by lightning may indeed die, as in this verse, and may also faint and then recover, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious, and when he recovered﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. What necessitates this is His saying: ﴿And you were looking﴾, for if the sa'iqah were an expression for death, this clause would have no great meaning. Rather, it may be said that it is not correct to say "you looked at death descending upon you," unless the meaning is looking at the causes that produce death.

The meaning of His saying ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ is the reviving of them, since it occurred after death. The root meaning of ba'th is stirring a thing from its place. One says "I stirred the she-camel" (ba'thtu al-naqah), meaning I roused her. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And brothers of truth, whom I roused at dawn, and they stood all together between the mounted and the drunken."

And the saying of 'Antarah:

"And companions with proud noses, whom I roused at night, when sleep had inclined over their shade."

They were punished with the seizing of the sa'iqah because they asked for what Allah had not permitted, namely seeing Him in this world.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) and those who followed them went to deny seeing Allah both in this world and in the Hereafter, while others went to the permissibility of it in this world and in the Hereafter, and its occurrence in the Hereafter.

The sound hadiths have been transmitted in mass-transmission (tawatur) that the servants will see their Lord in the Hereafter, and this is decisive in its indication (qat'i al-dalalah). It is not fitting for a fair-minded person to hold, against it, to those kalam principles that the early Mu'tazilah brought, claiming that reason had judged by them. That claim is built upon the edge of a crumbling precipice, and they are principles that none is deceived by except one who has not obtained a share of beneficial knowledge. The proofs from the Qur'an that they relied upon will come to you, Allah willing, with their explanation; all of them lie outside the place of dispute and far from the point of argument, and this is not the place for discussing this question.

His saying ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ means: We did it like a canopy.

Al-ghamam is the plural of ghamamah, like sahabah and sahab. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to say ghama'im.

The exegetes mention that this occurred in the wilderness (al-tih) between Egypt and Syria, when they refused to enter the city of the tyrants (al-Jabbarin).

Al-mann: it was said it is al-tarankjabin (a sweet exudation). Al-Nahhas said: it is with a shadda on the ra' and sukun on the nun, and it is said al-tarankjabin with a ta'. Most exegetes hold this view. It is a dew that descends from the sky upon a tree or a stone, becomes sweet, solidifies into honey, and dries like gum. Its meaning is mentioned in al-Qamus. It was also said that al-mann is honey, and it was said it is a sweet drink, and it was said it is thin bread (khubz al-ruqaq). It was also said that it is a verbal noun encompassing everything Allah bestowed upon His servants without toil or cultivation. From this is what is established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim from the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn Zayd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The mushroom (kam'ah) is from the manna that was sent down upon Musa."

A similar hadith has been established from Abu Hurayrah in Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, and from Jabir, Abu Sa'id and Ibn 'Abbas in al-Nasa'i.

Al-salwa: it was said it is al-sumani, like the bustard (hubara), a bird which they slaughtered and ate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-salwa is a bird by the consensus of the exegetes. The Hudhali erred when he said:

"And he swore by Allah with full effort that you two are sweeter than al-salwa when its honey (ashuruha) is tasted."

He thought that al-salwa is honey.

Al-Qurtubi said: what he claimed as consensus is not valid.

Al-Mu'arrij, one of the scholars of language and tafsir, said: it is honey, and he relied on the Hudhali's verse, and mentioned that it is so in the dialect of Kinanah, and recited:

"If I had drunk al-salwa, I would not have forgotten, but I have no sufficiency from you, even if I am sufficient."

Al-Jawhari said: al-salwa is honey.

Al-Akhfash said: al-salwa has no singular from its own form, like al-khayr and al-sharr, and it resembles that its singular is salwa.

Al-Khalil said: its singular is salwah, and he recited:

"Indeed, the remembrance of you stirs in me a salwah, as the salwah shakes when the rain has passed through it."

Al-Kisa'i said: al-salwa is singular, and its plural is salawa.

His saying "kulu" (eat) means: We said to them, "Eat." There is an elision in the speech, and the estimate is: We said, "Eat," but they disobeyed and did not meet the blessings with gratitude, so they wronged themselves and did not wrong Us. This was elided because of the indication of ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾. The fronting of "themselves" here conveys exclusivity (ikhtisas).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿until we see Allah openly﴾, that he said: "manifestly."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Anas, who said: They were the seventy whom Musa chose. ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: he said, "They died." ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾: he said, "They were raised after death so that they might complete their terms."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ something similar.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ that he said: "A cloud cooler and sweeter than this, which is the one in which Allah comes on the Day of Resurrection, and which the angels came in on the day of Badr, and it was with them in the wilderness."

It fed them manna and salwa when they came out into the desert. The manna would fall upon them in their camp like snow, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. It would fall upon them from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun, and a man would take what sufficed him for that day. If he exceeded that, what remained with him would spoil. But when it was the sixth day, the day of their Friday, he took what would suffice him for the sixth and seventh days, and it remained with him, because it was a day of festivity on which one did not set out for the matters of livelihood or for seeking anything." All of this was in the desert.

(p-61)

The majority of the commentators (*mufassirun*) said: The town is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said that it is Ariha, a town among the towns of Bayt al-Maqdis. And it was said that it is one of the towns of al-Sham (Syria).

His saying, ﴿kulu﴾ ("eat"), is a command of permission. ﴿Raghadan﴾ means abundant and wide. It is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning "eating in abundance." It is also permissible for it to be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and its explanation has already been given.

The gate they were commanded to enter is a gate in Bayt al-Maqdis known today as Bab Hittah (the Gate of Hittah). It was also said that it is the gate of the dome where Musa and the Children of Israel used to pray.

Prostration (*sujud*) has already been explained. It was also said that here it means bowing (*al-inhina'*), and it was said that it means humility and submission. They cited as evidence for this that if the intended meaning of prostration were the literal one, which is placing the forehead on the ground, then the entry commanded would be impossible, because one cannot enter while in literal prostration.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: They were commanded to prostrate upon reaching the gate, as thanks to Allah and as humility.

Abu Hayyan objected to this in *al-Nahr al-Madd*, saying: They were not commanded to prostrate. Rather, it is a restriction on the occurrence of the commanded act, which is the entering. States (*ahwal*) are restrictive relations (*nisab taqyidiyya*), while commands are predicative relations (*nisab isnadiyya*). End of quote.

This objection can be answered: a command to do something in a specified manner is a command to the qualifier itself. Whoever says, "Go out hastily," is commanding going out in this manner. If someone went out without haste, the people of the language (*ahl al-lisan*) would consider him to be in violation of the command.

This does not conflict with the fact that states are restrictive relations, because being characterized as qualifiers that are commanded is something beyond mere restriction.

His saying, ﴿hittatun﴾ ("forgiveness" / "remission"), is in the nominative case in the reading of the majority, as the omitted subject of a nominal sentence (*idmar mubtada'*). Al-Akhfash said: It has also been read in the accusative, *hittatan*, meaning "Remove from us our sins, a removal." It was also said that its meaning is seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*), and from this is the poet's line:

*He succeeded through the forgiveness (hittah) which Allah commanded,*
*the sin of His servant being forgiven.*

Ibn Faris said in *al-Mujmal*: *Hittah* is a word they were commanded to say, and if they had said it, their burdens would have been removed.

Al-Razi said in his *Tafsir*: He commanded them to say what indicates repentance, because repentance is a state of the heart, so others cannot perceive it. However, if the sin became well known and the person was held to account for it, and then repented afterward, it would be necessary for him to relate his repentance to those who witnessed his sin, because repentance is not complete without that. End of quote.

That repentance is not complete without this has no evidence. Rather, merely resolving in the heart is sufficient, whether or not people become aware of his sin. Indeed, concealing one's repentance in a way that only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, perceives is perhaps more beloved to Allah and closer to His forgiveness.

As for removing what people hold of the belief that he remains in disobedience, that is a separate matter.

His saying, ﴿yughfar lakum﴾ ("your sins will be forgiven"), was read by Nafi' with a yā' (ي) that is marked with a dammah on top, meaning the verb is in the third person. Ibn Amir read it with a tā' (ت) marked with a dammah, meaning the second person. The rest read it with a nūn (ن), and this reading is preferable.

*Khataya* is the plural of *khati'ah* with a hamzah, and the scholars of Arabic have spoken about this at length in what is known in the books of morphology (*sarf*).

His saying, ﴿wa-sanazidu al-muhsinin﴾ ("and We will increase the good-doers"), means: We will increase them in goodness beyond their earlier goodness. *Muhsin* is an active participle (*ism fa'il*) from *ahsana*.

It is established in the authentic collections that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about *ihsan* (excellence), and he said: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

His saying, ﴿fa-baddala alladhina zalamu qawlan ghayra alladhi qila lahum﴾ ("But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than what had been said to them"), it was said that they said *hintah* (wheat). It was said otherwise.

The correct view is that they said *habbatun fi sha'rah* (a grain in a hair), as will come later, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying, ﴿fa-anzalna ala alladhina zalamu﴾ ("So We sent down upon those who did wrong"), is the placing of an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun for a specific rhetorical purpose, as established in the science of rhetoric (*ilm al-bayan*). Here its purpose is to magnify the matter against them and to denounce their act. From this is the saying of Adi ibn Zayd:

*I do not see that death precedes death by anything,*
*death has troubled the wealthy and the poor alike.*

So he repeated *al-mawt* (death) three times in the line, to terrify concerning its matter and to magnify its importance.

His saying, ﴿rijzan﴾ ("a punishment"), is read with a kasrah on the *ra'* by all except Ibn Muhaysin, who read it with a dammah on the *ra'*.

*Rijz* means punishment (*al-adhab*).

*Fisq* (defiant disobedience) has already been explained.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, regarding His saying, ﴿Enter this town﴾, that he said: It is Bayt al-Maqdis.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd that he said: It is Ariha, a town of Bayt al-Maqdis.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying, ﴿Enter the gate﴾, that he said: A narrow gate. ﴿Prostrating﴾: he said, bowing (*rukka'an*).

Regarding His saying, ﴿hittah﴾, he said: It means forgiveness. "They entered from their buttocks (*astahim*) and said *hintah* (wheat) mockingly." He said: That is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than what had been said to them﴾.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The gate is one of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is called the Gate of Hittah.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: It was said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," so they entered with their heads covered, and they said *hintah*: a red grain in which there is a barley-grain.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah regarding His saying, ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, that he said: Lower your heads, and say *hittah*. He said: Say, "There is no god but Allah."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying, "Say *hittah*," that he said: "There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: The gate was facing the *qiblah*.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It was said to the Children of Israel: Enter the gate prostrating, and say *hittah*. But they changed it, and they entered crawling on their buttocks, and they said *habbatun fi sha'rah* (a grain in a hair)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, who both said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They entered the gate they were commanded to enter prostrating, crawling on their buttocks, while saying *hintah fi shu'ayrah* (wheat in a barley-grain)." The first is more preferable because it is in the two Sahihs.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related it along with those two, the other hadith: I mean the one reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ali that he said: Our likeness in this *ummah* is like the Ark of Nuh, and like the Gate of Hittah among the Children of Israel.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: Everything in the Book of Allah concerning *rijz* means by it punishment.

Muslim and others related from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, Sa'd ibn Malik, and Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, this plague is a *rijz* and a remnant of punishment with which some people before you were punished. So if it is in a land and you are in it, do not leave it; and if you hear that it is in a land, do not enter it."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: It was said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," so they entered with their heads covered, and they said *hintah*: a red grain in which there is a barley-grain.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah regarding His saying, ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, that he said: Lower your heads, and say *hittah*. He said: Say, "There is no god but Allah."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying, "Say *hittah*," that he said: "There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: The gate was facing the *qiblah*.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It was said to the Children of Israel: Enter the gate prostrating, and say *hittah*. But they changed it, and they entered crawling on their buttocks, and they said *habbatun fi sha'rah* (a grain in a hair)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, who both said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They entered the gate they were commanded to enter prostrating, crawling on their buttocks, while saying *hintah fi shu'ayrah* (wheat in a barley-grain)." The first is more preferable because it is in the two Sahihs.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related it along with those two, the other hadith: I mean the one reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ali that he said: Our likeness in this *ummah* is like the Ark of Nuh, and like the Gate of Hittah among the Children of Israel.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: Everything in the Book of Allah concerning *rijz* means by it punishment.

Muslim and others related from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, Sa'd ibn Malik, and Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, this plague is a *rijz* and a remnant of punishment with which some people before you were punished. So if it is in a land and you are in it, do not leave it; and if you hear that it is in a land, do not enter it."

In this there is evidence that each group drank from its own spring, and no others shared it with them.

It has been said: each tribe had one of those springs which it did not exceed to another. Al-asbat (الأسباط) are the descendants of the twelve sons of Ya'qub.

As for His saying ﴿كُلُوا﴾ (kulu, "eat"), it means: We said to them, "Eat the manna and the quails, and drink the water gushing from the rock."

'Atha (عثا) yai'tha 'athyan, 'atha ya'thu 'athwan, and 'aatha ya'iitu 'aythan are dialectal forms, meaning "to corrupt."

As for His saying ﴿مُفْسِدِينَ﴾ (mufsidin, "causing corruption"), it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah).

In al-Qamus: 'Athiya (like ramiya), sa'a and radiya, 'athyan and 'atayanan, and 'atha ya'thu 'athwan mean "to corrupt." In al-Kashshaf: al-'athy is the most severe corruption.

So it was said to them: Do not persist in corruption while you are in a state of corruption, because they were persisting in it. End of quote.

"Indeed the wretched one is attached to wretchedness; he cannot refuse it when it comes."

It is possible that this was not from them out of longing for what they had been in, or out of consideration for the luxurious life they had come to. Rather, it is a door of their obstinacy and a branch of their arrogance, as is their habit and constant way in most of what has been related to us of their accounts.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: They were people of leeks, onions and lentils, so they yearned for their former ways, meaning their origin of evil stock, and their natures longed for what their habits had been accustomed to, so they said: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾. The "one food" intended is the manna and the quails. Although these were two foods, since they used to eat one with the other, they treated them as one food.

It has been said: because they recurred each day and no other food existed with them or as a substitute.

As for min (مِن) in His saying ﴿مِمّا تُنْبِتُ﴾ ("of what the earth produces"), meaning "brings forth," al-Akhfash said it is extra (za'idah). Sibawayh disagreed, because it is not added in an affirmative statement.

Al-Nahhas said: al-Akhfash was prompted to this because he did not find an object for (yukhrij), so he wanted to make "ma" the object. The better view is that the object is omitted, indicated by the context of the speech, meaning: "brings forth for us something to eat."

As for His saying ﴿مِن بَقْلِها﴾ ("from its herbs"), it is a substitute (badal) for "ma," with the preposition repeated. Al-baql is every plant that has no stalk, while al-shajar is that which has a stalk.

In al-Kashshaf: al-baql is what the earth produces of greens, and what is meant is the choicest herbs that people eat, such as mint, celery, leeks and the like. End of quote.

Al-qithha' (القثاء) is pronounced with a kasra or a fatha on the qaf.

The first is the reading of the majority (al-jumhur).

The second is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and it is well known.

Al-fum (الفوم): it has been said it is garlic (al-thawm), and Ibn Mas'ud read it with the letter thā' (ثوم).

Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that al-fum is wheat, and most of the exegetes went to this view, as al-Qurtubi said.

Ibn al-Nahhas preferred this view.

"I used to think myself the richest of men, one who had left Medina from cultivating wheat."

"Their dwellings were then evident, in them were the farādīs, the fūmāt and onions."

That is, garlic (al-thum).

Hassan said:

"You are a people of base origins; your food is fum and haqal."

He means garlic and onions.

It has been said that al-fum is the ear of grain; it has been said that it is chickpeas; and it has been said that al-fum is every grain that is baked into bread.

Al-'adas (lentils) and al-basal (onions) are both well known.

Al-Hasan, Aban ibn Taghlib and Talhah ibn Musarrif read it without tanwin, and it is so in the codices of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud.

"The spider has struck upon you with its web, and the revealed Book has decreed upon you."

This is an eloquent form of satire, just as when it is used in praise it has an elevated status.

From this is the poet's saying:

"Indeed manliness, courage and generosity are in a tent struck over the son of al-Hashraj."

"Ba'a fulan bi-fulan" means one is worthy of being put to death in return for him because of equality with him. From this is the poet's saying:

"Will not kings desist from us and fear our fighters? Blood does not stand against blood."

What is meant in the verse is that they returned with anger from God, or became deserving of His anger. The explanation of anger has already been given.

The indication in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ ("that") refers to what preceded of the matter of humiliation and what follows it, because of their disbelief in God and their killing of His prophets without right, a matter which obliges them to follow and act upon what is required. Rather, what is meant is to censure this matter upon them and to magnify it, and that it is pure injustice in reality.

They killed them while knowing and believing that they were wrongdoers.

The repetition of the indication is for the purpose of emphasis, magnifying the matter upon them and making it terrifying. The whole of what follows the first indication and the second indication is the cause of the imposition of humiliation and what follows it. It has been said that the second indication may refer to disbelief and killing, so that what follows becomes a cause of the cause, and this is very far-fetched. Al-i'tida' is transgressing the limit in everything.
