'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah and Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Juwaybir, something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and do not act wickedly in the earth﴾ that he said: do not strive in the earth to cause corruption.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, who said: meaning, do not walk in sins.

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, who said: do not travel in the earth as corrupters.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ that he said: the manna and quails; they exchanged for them the herbs and what is mentioned with them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and its fum﴾ that he said: bread. In another wording: wheat (al-burr). In another wording: al-hintah (wheat).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: al-fum is garlic (al-thum).

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "wa-thumiha" (with thā'). Ibn Abi al-Dunya related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: my recitation is the recitation of Zayd, and I take up about ten letters from the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, of which this is one: "min baqlihā wa-qithā'ihā wa-thūmihā."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿that which is inferior﴾ that he said: worse (ardi').

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Go down to a city﴾ that he said: a city among cities.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah that it is the city of Pharaoh.

Ibn Abi Dawud and Ibn al-Anbari related something similar from al-A'mash.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and humiliation and wretchedness were imposed upon them﴾ that he said: they are the people of the jizya.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah and al-Hasan, who said: humiliation and wretchedness were imposed upon them, meaning they pay the jizya by hand while they are humbled.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: al-maskanah is poverty (al-faqah).

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿and they returned with anger from God﴾ that he said: they deserved the anger of God.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿and they returned﴾ that he said: they turned back.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Children of Israel would kill three hundred prophets in a single day, and then they would set up their vegetable market at the end of the day.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and do not act wickedly in the earth﴾ that he said: do not strive in the earth to cause corruption.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, who said: meaning, do not walk in sins.

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, who said: do not travel in the earth as corrupters.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ that he said: the manna and quails; they exchanged for them the herbs and what is mentioned with them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and its fum﴾ that he said: bread. In another wording: wheat (al-burr). In another wording: al-hintah (wheat).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: al-fum is garlic (al-thum).

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited "wa-thumiha" (with thā'). Ibn Abi al-Dunya related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: my recitation is the recitation of Zayd, and I take up about ten letters from the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, of which this is one: "min baqlihā wa-qithā'ihā wa-thūmihā."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿that which is inferior﴾ that he said: worse (ardi').

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Go down to a city﴾ that he said: a city among cities.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah that it is the city of Pharaoh.

Ibn Abi Dawud and Ibn al-Anbari related something similar from al-A'mash.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and humiliation and wretchedness were imposed upon them﴾ that he said: they are the people of the jizya.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah and al-Hasan, who said: humiliation and wretchedness were imposed upon them, meaning they pay the jizya by hand while they are humbled.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: al-maskanah is poverty (al-faqah).

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak regarding His saying ﴿and they returned with anger from God﴾ that he said: they deserved the anger of God.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿and they returned﴾ that he said: they turned back.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Children of Israel would kill three hundred prophets in a single day, and then they would set up their vegetable market at the end of the day.

It was said: the intended meaning of "those who believe" is the hypocrites, as indicated by their being grouped with the Jews, Christians and Sabians, that is, they believed outwardly.

The better view is that the intended meaning is those who affirmed the Prophet (ﷺ) and became among his followers. It seems that Allah, exalted is He, wanted to make clear that the condition of this Islamic community and of the communities before it, among all the other religions, returns to one thing: whoever among them believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds deserves the reward that Allah mentioned, and whoever misses that misses all good, and the reward, both small and great.

The meaning of faith (*iman*) here is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained when Gabriel asked him about faith. He said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the decree, its good and its evil." This faith is attributed only to one who enters the Islamic religion. Whoever does not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) or in the Qur'an is not a believer, and whoever believes in both becomes a Muslim believer and is no longer a Jew, a Christian or a Magian.

His saying ﴿hādū﴾ means they became Jews. It was said that it is a relative form ascribing them to Yahudha, son of Ya'qub, with the dhal pointed, but the Arabs changed it to an unpointed dal. It was also said that the meaning of *hādū* is "they repented," because of their repentance from worshipping the calf, and from this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], meaning "we have repented." It was also said that its meaning is calm and mutual peace.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: its meaning is that they entered Judaism.

[p. 64] As for *al-Nasara* (the Christians), Sibawayh said: its singular is *Nasran* and *Nasranah*, like *Nadman* and *Nadmanah*. He cited as evidence on this the verse of the poet:

*You see him, when he visits the evening, lightly dressed, and in the morning he is with him, a Christian, a sunbather.*

And another said:

*Both of them fell, and she bowed her head, as a Christian woman bows without bending.*

He said: but it is only used with the *ya* of relation, so one says: a Christian man (*rajul nasrani*) and a Christian woman (*imra'ah nasraniyyah*).

Al-Khalil said: the singular of the Christians is *Nasri*.

Al-Jawhari said: *Nasran* is a village in Syria from which the Christians are named, and it is said *Nasirah*, and according to this the *ya* is for relation.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: the *ya* is for emphasis, like the one in *ahmari* (reddish), and they were named so because they helped (*nasaru*) the Messiah.

As for *al-Sabi'in*, it is the plural of *sabi*, and it was said *sabin*.

The readers differed concerning it: they all pronounced the hamza except Nafi', so whoever pronounced the hamza took it from *sabi'at al-nujum*, when the stars rose, and *sabi'at thaniyyat al-ghulam*, when the boy's front tooth came out.

Whoever did not pronounce the hamza took it from *saba yasbu*, when one inclines. In the language, the *sabi* is one who leaves a religion and inclines to another religion. For this reason, the Arabs used to say of one who became Muslim: "he has become a *sabi*." They named this sect *Sabi'ah* because it departed from the religion of the Jews and the Christians and worshipped the angels.

His saying ﴿man āmana billāh﴾ ("whoever believes in Allah") is in the accusative position as a substitute for ﴿alladhina amanu﴾ ("those who believe") and what follows it. The meaning of faith has already been explained. The predicate of *inna* would be his saying ﴿fa-lahum ajruhum﴾ ("then they shall have their reward"). It is also permissible that ﴿man āmana billāh﴾ be in the nominative position, as a subject whose predicate is his saying "then they shall have their reward," and both together are the predicate of *inna*, with the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*) understood in the first clause, meaning "whoever of them believes." The *fa'* was introduced into the predicate because the subject includes the meaning of a condition.

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] has already passed.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Salman, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about a religion whose people I had been with, and I mentioned their prayer and worship, and then ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ was revealed, to the end of the verse.

Al-Wahidi transmitted similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, in mentioning the occasion of revelation, something similar to what preceded, and he related a long story.

Abu Dawud, in *al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh* (the abrogating and abrogated), and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ that he said: after this Allah revealed ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be in the Hereafter among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali, who said: the Jews were only named so because they said ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156].

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: We know best from where the Jews were named Jews by their word, from the words of Musa (peace be upon him): "Indeed, we have turned back to You." And why the Christians were named Christians by their word, from the words of 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿Be helpers of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 14]. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted something similar from him.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah: they were only named Christians after a village called Nasirah.

Ibn Sa'd in his *Tabaqat* and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Christians were only named so because the village of 'Isa was called Nasirah.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said: the Sabians are a sect between the Jews, the Christians and the Magians, who have no religion of their own.

'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from him, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: and he mentioned something similar.

Other than this has been related concerning the explanation of the Sabians.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 63–66:

His saying: ﴿And when We took﴾ is in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by an implied verb, which is "remember," as has been mentioned more than once.

The meaning of the covenant (mithaq, a binding pledge) has already been explained. The intended meaning is that God, glorified is He, took from them a covenant to act upon what He had prescribed for them in the Torah, and upon what is more general than that or more specific.

Al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which God spoke to Musa (peace be upon him), and on which He sent down the Torah to him. It has been said that it is the name of every mountain in Syriac.

Many exegetes have mentioned that when Musa came to the Children of Israel from God with the tablets, he said to them: "Take them and hold fast to them." They said: "No, unless God speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless, then they were revived. He said to them: "Take them and hold fast to them." They said: "No." So God commanded the angels, and they uprooted a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh (about three miles) by the same measure, and their camp was like that. It was placed over them like a canopy, and a sea was brought from behind them and a fire from in front of their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you shall not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to God and took the Torah with the covenant.

Ibn Jarir reported from some of the scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them."

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "What cannot be authentically upheld other than this is that God, glorified is He, created faith at the time of their prostration, not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace," end of quote.

This is a baseless forced interpretation, driven by his preservation of the doctrinal principles that had become fixed in his mind, as they had in the minds of others. Every intelligent person knows that there is no cause of compulsion stronger than this, or more severe than it.

We say: God compelled them to faith, so they believed under compulsion, and He lifted punishment from them by this faith. This is similar to what is established in our law regarding the lifting of the sword from one who utters the word of Islam while the sword is drawn and its bearer has raised it over his head.

It is established in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to one who had killed a man who had uttered the word of Islam, excusing his killing by saying that he had said it out of taqiyya (concealment of belief under fear), and it was not from a sound intention: "Did you search his heart?" and he said: "I was not commanded to probe the hearts of people."

His saying "take" means: and We said to you, ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾. Determination (quwwa) means effort and diligence. The intended meaning of "remember what is in it" is that it should be preserved among them so that they may act upon it.

His saying: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. The original meaning of tawalli is turning one's back on a thing and turning away physically. Then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from matters, religions and beliefs. The intended meaning here is their turning away from the covenant taken from them. His saying ﴿after that﴾ means after the proof was given to them and after being terrified by the most severe thing that minds can conceive and imaginations can picture, which is the lifting of the mountain above their heads as though it were a canopy over them.

His saying: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you﴾, by His gentleness and mercy coming to your aid until you showed repentance, ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾.

Al-Fadl means increase.

Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: al-fadl is increase and goodness, and al-ifdal is benevolence. End of quote.

Al-khusran means loss, and its explanation has been given before.

In the original language, al-sabt means cutting, because things were completed on it and work ceased. It has also been said that it is derived from al-sabut, which is rest and ease.

In al-Kashshaf it says: al-sabt is a verbal noun from "the Jews observed the Sabbath" (sabatat al-yahud), when they glorified the day of Sabbath. End of quote.

A group of exegetes have mentioned that the Jews split into two factions. One faction transgressed regarding the Sabbath, that is, they exceeded what God had commanded them regarding work on it, and they hunted fish which God had forbidden them to hunt on it. The other faction divided into two groups: one group openly forbade it and withdrew, and another group did not agree with the transgressors, nor did they hunt with them, but they sat with them and did not openly forbid them, nor did they withdraw from them. So God transformed them all, and none were saved except the first faction alone.

This is among the trials by which God tested those who had gone to extremes in arrogance and opposed their prophets. At every station they continued to display their foolishness, the feebleness of their minds, and their obstinacy, a kind of distortion and a branch of artificiality. For fish used to come on the Sabbath day, as God, glorified is He, described in His saying: ﴿When their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them.﴾ So they devised a scheme to catch them. They dug pits and cut channels, so the fish would enter them on the Sabbath, and they would catch them on Sunday. They gained nothing from this false trick.

Al-khasi' means one who is driven away. It is said: "I drove him away, so he withdrew, and he was driven off and was driven away." That is: I expelled him, so he went far away.

From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled (khasi'an)﴾, that is, driven away.

His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised (khasi'in)﴾, that is, withdraw with the withdrawal of wrath. Al-khasi' may also mean humiliated.

The intended meaning here: be between transformation into the forms of apes while being expelled and humiliated.

So qiradatan (apes) is the predicate of the verb "be," and (khasi'in) is another predicate. It has been said that it is an attribute of qiradatan, but the first is more evident.

There is disagreement about the referent of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿So We made it﴾ and in His saying: ﴿as a warning for what lay before it and what lay after it﴾. It has been said: the punishment; it has been said: the nation; it has been said: the town; it has been said: the apes; it has been said: the fish. The first is more evident.

Al-nakal means deterrence and punishment. Al-nikl means a fetter, because it prevents its owner, and the bridle of an animal is called nikl because it restrains it. Al-maw'iza (admonition) is derived from ittiʿaz (taking warning) and inzijar (restraint), and al-waʿz means intimidation.

Al-Khalil said: al-waʿz is reminder with goodness.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: al-Tur is the mountain on which the Torah was sent down, and the Children of Israel were beneath it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported similarly from Qatada.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: al-Tur is what grows of the mountains, and what does not grow is not a tur.

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾ that he said: that is, with diligence.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-ʿAliya regarding His saying: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ that he said: read what is in the Torah and act upon it.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿So that you may be God-fearing﴾ that he said: so that you may desist from what you are upon.

Ibn Jarir reported from him, he said: "And you certainly knew" (wa-laqad ʿalimtum), that is, you recognized, and "transgressed" (iʿtadaw) means: they dared on the Sabbath to hunt fish, so God transformed them into apes for their disobedience, and no transformed creature ever lived beyond three days, and it did not eat or drink, and it did not reproduce.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, he said: the apes and the pigs are from the offspring of those who were transformed. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan who said: that offspring was cut off.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid who said: their hearts were transformed, and they were not transformed into apes; it is only a parable which God struck for them, like His saying: ﴿The likeness of the donkey which carries books﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada regarding the verse that he said: the fish were made lawful for them and forbidden to them on the Sabbath day, so that God might know who among them obeyed Him from those who disobeyed Him. There were three categories among them, and he mentioned something similar to what we have previously cited from the exegetes.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: the young men of the people became apes, and the elders became pigs.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿khasi'in﴾ that he said: humiliated.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him regarding His saying "khasi'in" that he said: despised.

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it﴾ [of the towns] ﴿and what lay after it﴾ [of the towns] ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, those who came after them until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding ﴿So We made it﴾, meaning the fish, ﴿a deterrent for what lay before it and what lay after it﴾ [of the sins they committed before and after]. 

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding ﴿So We made it﴾, he said: We made that punishment, namely the transformation, a deterrent, a punishment ﴿for what lay before it﴾, meaning: so that those after them would beware of My punishment, ﴿and what lay after it﴾, meaning: for those who were with them, ﴿and an admonition﴾, he said: a reminder and a lesson for the God-fearing.

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding ﴿So We made it﴾, meaning the fish, ﴿a deterrent for what lay before it and what lay after it﴾ [of the sins they committed before and after]. 

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding ﴿So We made it﴾, he said: We made that punishment, namely the transformation, a deterrent, a punishment ﴿for what lay before it﴾, meaning: so that those after them would beware of My punishment, ﴿and what lay after it﴾, meaning: for those who were with them, ﴿and an admonition﴾, he said: a reminder and a lesson for the God-fearing.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 63–66:

His saying: ﴿And when We took﴾ is in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by an implied verb, which is "remember," as has been mentioned more than once.

The meaning of the covenant (mithaq, a binding pledge) has already been explained. The intended meaning is that God, glorified is He, took from them a covenant to act upon what He had prescribed for them in the Torah, and upon what is more general than that or more specific.

Al-Tur is the name of the mountain on which God spoke to Musa (peace be upon him), and on which He sent down the Torah to him. It has been said that it is the name of every mountain in Syriac.

Many exegetes have mentioned that when Musa came to the Children of Israel from God with the tablets, he said to them: "Take them and hold fast to them." They said: "No, unless God speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless, then they were revived. He said to them: "Take them and hold fast to them." They said: "No." So God commanded the angels, and they uprooted a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh (about three miles) by the same measure, and their camp was like that. It was placed over them like a canopy, and a sea was brought from behind them and a fire from in front of their faces. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you shall not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you." So they prostrated in repentance to God and took the Torah with the covenant.

Ibn Jarir reported from some of the scholars: "If they had taken it the first time, there would have been no covenant upon them."

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "What cannot be authentically upheld other than this is that God, glorified is He, created faith at the time of their prostration, not that they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at peace," end of quote.

This is a baseless forced interpretation, driven by his preservation of the doctrinal principles that had become fixed in his mind, as they had in the minds of others. Every intelligent person knows that there is no cause of compulsion stronger than this, or more severe than it.

We say: God compelled them to faith, so they believed under compulsion, and He lifted punishment from them by this faith. This is similar to what is established in our law regarding the lifting of the sword from one who utters the word of Islam while the sword is drawn and its bearer has raised it over his head.

It is established in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to one who had killed a man who had uttered the word of Islam, excusing his killing by saying that he had said it out of taqiyya (concealment of belief under fear), and it was not from a sound intention: "Did you search his heart?" and he said: "I was not commanded to probe the hearts of people."

His saying "take" means: and We said to you, ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾. Determination (quwwa) means effort and diligence. The intended meaning of "remember what is in it" is that it should be preserved among them so that they may act upon it.

His saying: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. The original meaning of tawalli is turning one's back on a thing and turning away physically. Then it was used, by extension and metaphor, for turning away from matters, religions and beliefs. The intended meaning here is their turning away from the covenant taken from them. His saying ﴿after that﴾ means after the proof was given to them and after being terrified by the most severe thing that minds can conceive and imaginations can picture, which is the lifting of the mountain above their heads as though it were a canopy over them.

His saying: ﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you﴾, by His gentleness and mercy coming to your aid until you showed repentance, ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾.

Al-Fadl means increase.

Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: al-fadl is increase and goodness, and al-ifdal is benevolence. End of quote.

Al-khusran means loss, and its explanation has been given before.

In the original language, al-sabt means cutting, because things were completed on it and work ceased. It has also been said that it is derived from al-sabut, which is rest and ease.

In al-Kashshaf it says: al-sabt is a verbal noun from "the Jews observed the Sabbath" (sabatat al-yahud), when they glorified the day of Sabbath. End of quote.

A group of exegetes have mentioned that the Jews split into two factions. One faction transgressed regarding the Sabbath, that is, they exceeded what God had commanded them regarding work on it, and they hunted fish which God had forbidden them to hunt on it. The other faction divided into two groups: one group openly forbade it and withdrew, and another group did not agree with the transgressors, nor did they hunt with them, but they sat with them and did not openly forbid them, nor did they withdraw from them. So God transformed them all, and none were saved except the first faction alone.

This is among the trials by which God tested those who had gone to extremes in arrogance and opposed their prophets. At every station they continued to display their foolishness, the feebleness of their minds, and their obstinacy, a kind of distortion and a branch of artificiality. For fish used to come on the Sabbath day, as God, glorified is He, described in His saying: ﴿When their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them.﴾ So they devised a scheme to catch them. They dug pits and cut channels, so the fish would enter them on the Sabbath, and they would catch them on Sunday. They gained nothing from this false trick.

Al-khasi' means one who is driven away. It is said: "I drove him away, so he withdrew, and he was driven off and was driven away." That is: I expelled him, so he went far away.

From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled (khasi'an)﴾, that is, driven away.

His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised (khasi'in)﴾, that is, withdraw with the withdrawal of wrath. Al-khasi' may also mean humiliated.

The intended meaning here: be between transformation into the forms of apes while being expelled and humiliated.

So qiradatan (apes) is the predicate of the verb "be," and (khasi'in) is another predicate. It has been said that it is an attribute of qiradatan, but the first is more evident.

There is disagreement about the referent of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿So We made it﴾ and in His saying: ﴿as a warning for what lay before it and what lay after it﴾. It has been said: the punishment; it has been said: the nation; it has been said: the town; it has been said: the apes; it has been said: the fish. The first is more evident.

Al-Khalil said: al-waʿz is reminder with goodness.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported similarly from Qatada.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-ʿAliya regarding His saying: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ that he said: read what is in the Torah and act upon it.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿So that you may be God-fearing﴾ that he said: so that you may desist from what you are upon.

Ibn Jarir reported from him, he said: "And you certainly knew" (wa-laqad ʿalimtum), that is, you recognized, and "transgressed" (iʿtadaw) means: they dared on the Sabbath to hunt fish, so God transformed them into apes for their disobedience, and no transformed creature ever lived beyond three days, and it did not eat or drink, and it did not reproduce.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, he said: the apes and the pigs are from the offspring of those who were transformed. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan who said: that offspring was cut off.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 67–71 (part 1 of 2):**

It has been said: the story of the slaughtering of the cow mentioned here is placed earlier in recitation but later in meaning than His saying, ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾. It is also possible that His saying "you killed" came earlier in revelation, and the command to slaughter came later. It is also possible that the order of their revelation follows the order of their recitation, so that it is as if Allah commanded them to slaughter the cow, and they slaughtered it, and then the matter of the killing occurred, so they were commanded to strike the body with a part of it. This is on the assumption that the particle *wa* (and) implies sequence, but it has been established in the science of Arabic (ʿilm al-ʿArabiyyah) that it merely denotes joining, without sequence or simultaneity. The full discussion of this will come in the story of the killing. *Al-baqarah* is a name for the female, and the male is called *thawr*. It has also been said that it applies to both. Its root is from *al-baqar*, which means splitting, because it splits the earth by plowing. Al-Azhari said: *al-baqar* is a collective noun (ism jins), and its plural is *baqir*. ʿIkrimah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar recited ﴿Indeed, the cows look alike to us﴾. As for His saying, *huzuwan* (mockery), *al-huzu* here means play and ridicule, and its explanation has already been given.

Only people of ignorance do such a thing, because it is a kind of frivolity that sensible people do not engage in. For this reason Musa answered them by seeking refuge in Allah, the Glorified, from ignorance.

His saying, ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us﴾, is a form of their familiar obstinacy. They used to pursue these paths concerning most of what Allah commanded them. Had they left off the difficulty and the far-fetched questions, a cow of the common kind would have sufficed them. But they made it difficult, so Allah made it difficult for them, as its explanation will come.

*Al-fariḍ* is the aged one, and its meaning in the language is "the wide" or "the broad." Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "It may be that she was called *fariḍ* because she had cut (*faraḍat*) her teeth, meaning she had cut them and reached their end." End of quotation. The word is also used of something old, and from this is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*O Lord, of one who bears a grudge against me, an old enemy, who has a hollow like the hollow of a menstruating woman.*

That is, old. It has also been said: *al-fariḍ* is the one that has given birth to many litters, so that her womb has become wide.

*Al-bikr* is the young one that has not yet carried. It is applied to female animals and to human females to refer to one who has not been mounted by a male. It is also applied to the first of offspring, and from this is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*O firstborn of two firstborns, and O firm-hearted one, you have become from me like the forearm from the upper arm.*

*Al-ʿawan* is the one in the middle between the age of the aged and the young, who has given birth to one or two litters. It is also said: she is the one who has given birth time after time. The indication in His saying, ﴿between that﴾, refers to the aged and the young. Although both are feminine, they are referred to by a masculine form in accordance with the interpretation of "the one mentioned," as if He said: "between that which was mentioned." The use of *bayna* (between), which normally requires two items, is permissible because what was mentioned is more than one.

His saying, ﴿So do it﴾, is a renewal and a reinforcement of the command, and a rebuke to them against obstinacy. But this did not benefit them, nor did it take effect on them. Rather they returned to their nature, reverted to their deceit, and continued in their familiar habit, so they said: "Call upon your Lord for us."

*Al-lawn* is the singular of the colors. The majority of the commentators hold that all of it was yellow. Some said: even its horn and hoof. Al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it was yellow only in its horn and hoof, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. The intended meaning of "yellow" here is the well-known yellow. It is related from al-Hasan that *ṣafrāʾ* means black. This is one of the strange and rejected interpretations. I wonder how the black color, which is the ugliest of colors, could be described as one that pleases the beholders, and how it could be described as *fāqiʿ* (bright, pure), which everyone who knows the language of the Arabs knows does not apply to black in any way. For they describe black with words such as *ḥālik*, *ḥalkūk*, *dajūjī*, and *ghirbīb*.

Al-Kisai said: it is said, "Its color fasa'a (became pure), yafqaʿu fuqūʿan," when its yellowness became unmixed. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-fuqūʿ* is the most intense and purest form of yellow.

The meaning of ﴿pleasing the beholders﴾ is that it brings joy to those who look at it, because of their admiration for it and their approval of its color.

Wahb said: it was as if the rays of the sun were coming out of its skin.

Then they did not desist from their error, nor did they refrain from their folly and ignorance. Rather they returned to their obstinacy and said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for indeed the cows look alike to us." That is, the species of cows is confused for them because of the many that are described as middle-aged, bright yellow, and pure. They promised on their own behalf that they would be guided to what He pointed out to them and would comply with what they were commanded.

*Al-dhalūl* is the one that work has not tamed, that is, one that is not made docile by work and not broken in for it.

His saying, ﴿plowing﴾ (*tuthīr*), is in the position of a nominative as an attribute of *baqarah*. That is: it is a cow that is not tame, plowing. Likewise His saying, ﴿nor irrigates the tilth﴾, is in the position of a nominative because it is an attribute of it. That is: it is not one of the water-drawing camels by which crops are irrigated. The second negative particle is an emphasis of the first. That is: it is a cow not tamed for plowing or for drawing water. For this reason al-Hasan said: the cow was wild.

Some said: His saying, *tuthīr*, is a new verb (fiʿl mustaʾnaf), and the meaning is: making plowing and irrigating obligatory upon it. The first view is preferable, because if it were plowing and irrigating, it would be tame and broken in, and Allah has negated that about it.

His saying, ﴿sound﴾ (*musallamah*), is in the nominative as one of the attributes of the cow. It is also permissible for it to be nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "it is sound." The clause is in the position of a nominative as an attribute. *Al-musallamah* is the one without defect. It has been said: sound from work, but this is weak, because Allah, the Glorified, has already negated that about it. Establishing a new meaning is better than emphasis, and providing information is preferable to repetition.

*Al-shiyah* originally is *wishiyah*; the *waw* was dropped as it was dropped from *yashi*, and its original is *yawshi*. Its parallels are *al-zinah*, *al-ʿidah*, and *al-silah*. It is derived from *wushiya al-thawb*, when a garment is woven with two different colors. A bull that is *muwashsha* has markings on its face and its legs are black.

The intended meaning is that this cow was purely yellow, with no gleam of another color on its body.

When they heard these attributes, after which no doubt remains, and which the listener cannot entertain any suspicion about, and which admit no sharing in any respect, they desisted from their error, woke from their slumber, and recognized the extent to which their obstinacy had brought upon themselves the narrowing of the matter. The clause is in the position of a nominative as an attribute. *Al-musallamah* is the one without defect. It has been said: sound from work, but this is weak, because Allah, the Glorified, has already negated that about it. Establishing a new meaning is better than emphasis, and providing information is preferable to repetition.

*Al-shiyah* originally is *wishiyah*; the *waw* was dropped as it was dropped from *yashi*, and its original is *yawshi*. Its parallels are *al-zinah*, *al-ʿidah*, and *al-silah*. It is derived from *wushiya al-thawb*, when a garment is woven with two different colors. A bull that is *muwashsha* has markings on its face and its legs are black.

The intended meaning is that this cow was purely yellow, with no gleam of another color on its body.

When they heard these attributes, after which no doubt remains, and which the listener cannot entertain any suspicion about, and which admit no sharing in any respect, they desisted from their error, woke from their slumber, and recognized the extent to which their obstinacy had brought upon themselves the narrowing of the matter. They said: "Now you have brought the truth." That is: you have clarified the description for us and made clear the reality at which one must stop. So they obtained that cow described with those attributes, slaughtered it, and carried out the command which had been easy but which they made difficult, and which had been wide but which they narrowed. ﴿But they almost did not do it﴾, meaning the command they were given, because of the hesitation and obstinacy that had come from them and their lack of haste. So this was a context for amazement and a place for a phrase indicating the hesitation that existed among them. It has also been said: they almost did not do it because they could not find a cow with these attributes. It has also been said: because of its high price. It has also been said: for fear that the matter of the slain man would be exposed. The first view is preferable.

Several commentators and jurists have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of abrogation (*naskh*) before the act is possible. But this is not correct in my view, for two reasons.

First: these added attributes, which came because of repeated questioning, belong to the category of specification (*taqyīd*) of what is commanded, not to the category of abrogation (*naskh*). Between the two categories there is a great distance, as is established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence.

Second: even if we grant that this is of the category of abrogation and not of specification, it would not be evidence for what they claimed. For it was possible for them, after the first command, to choose a cow of the common kind and slaughter it; and likewise after the description of it as middle-aged and yellow. There is no evidence that this exchange between them and Musa, peace be upon him, took place in a single moment. Rather the apparent meaning is that they would coordinate these obstinate questions, discuss the matter among themselves, and then raise them. At the very least, this is a possibility that undermines the argument.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from ʿUbaydah al-Salmani, who said: A man from the Children of Israel was sterile and had no children, and he had much wealth, and his nephew was his heir. The nephew killed him, then carried him at night and placed him at the door of a man from among them. Then in the morning he accused them of it, until they armed themselves and some of them rode against others. A man of judgment among them said: "Why do some of you kill others, when this is the Messenger of Allah among you?" So they came to Musa and told him of this. He said: ﴿Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, to the end of the verse. If they had not objected, any cow would have sufficed them. But they made it difficult, so it was made difficult for them, until they reached the cow they were commanded to slaughter, and they found it with a man who had no other cow. He said: "By Allah, I will not sell it except for its hide filled with gold." So they took it for its hide filled with gold, and they slaughtered it and struck him with a part of it, and he rose up. They said: "Who killed you?" He said: "This one," meaning his nephew. Then he fell dead. He was not given any of his wealth, and no killer was inherited from after him.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, in *Kitab man ʿAsha baʿda al-Mawt*, transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that the slain man was found between two villages, and that the cow belonged to a man who was dutiful to his father, so they bought it for its weight in gold.

Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from him, but did not mention what preceded about the cow.

Various stories have been related about this, and not much benefit depends upon them.

al-Bazzar transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If the Children of Israel had taken any cow at all, it would have sufficed them, or it would have sufficed for them."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Had it not been that the Children of Israel said: ﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided﴾, they would never have been given it. And had they taken any cow of the cows and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them. But they made it difficult, so Allah made it difficult for them."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from ʿIkrimah, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from Ibn Jurayj, raising it to the Prophet.

Ibn Jarir also transmitted it from Qatadah, raising it as well.

These three are *mursal* (with a missing companion in the chain).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: *al-fāriḍ* is the decrepit one, *al-bikr* is the young one, and *al-ʿawān* is the middle one.

He transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying, ﴿middle-aged, between that﴾, that he said: between the young and the old, and it is at its strongest and best.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying, ﴿yellow, its color bright﴾, that he said: intensely yellow, so that from its yellowness it almost turns white.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His saying, *ṣafrāʾ* (yellow), that he said: yellow of the hoof. "Its color bright" he said: pure.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "Its color bright" means pure. ﴿Pleasing the beholders﴾ means: it pleases.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Hasan regarding His saying, ﴿yellow, its color bright﴾, that he said: black, intensely black.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu al-ʿAliyah regarding His saying, *lā dhalūl* (not tame), meaning: work has not made it tame, it does not plow the earth, meaning it is not tame so as to plow the earth, ﴿nor irrigates the tilth﴾, he says: nor does it labor in the tilth. *Musallamah* (sound), he said: free from defects.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

And he said: *lā shiyata fīhā* (no marking on it), meaning no whiteness on it and no blackness.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: *musallamah* (sound), free from blemish (*ʿawār*).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿They said, "Now you have brought the truth"﴾: they said, "Now you have made it clear to us." ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b regarding His words ﴿though they had almost not done so﴾: because of its high price.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on 2:72–74:

What I mentioned earlier concerning the story of the slaughter of the cow has already passed. So the sense of the speech is: "When you killed a soul and disputed about it, and Allah is bringing forth what you were concealing." Then Musa said to his people: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ to the end of the story. After it comes ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it"﴾ and the verse.

Al-Razi said in his *tafsir*: Know that the occurrence of the killing must have preceded His command to slaughter. As for the report of that killing, and that the slain person must be struck with part of that cow, it is not necessary that it precede the report of the story of the cow. So the saying of whoever says, "This story must come before the first one in recitation," is an error. This is because the story in itself must come before the first one in existence, but precedence in mention is not obligatory, since sometimes the cause is mentioned before the ruling, and sometimes the reverse. So when that incident befell them, Allah commanded them to slaughter the cow, and when they had slaughtered it, He said: ﴿And when you killed a soul earlier﴾, and He attributed the killing to them because the killer was one of them. The original of *idaraʾtum* (ادّارَأْتُمْ) is *tadāraʾtum*, then the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *dāl*. Since beginning with an assimilated quiescent letter is not permitted, they added the *alif al-waṣl* (the connecting alif). The meaning of *idaraʾtum* is "you differed and disputed," because disputants push (*yadraʾu*) one another away, i.e., repel one another. The meaning of *mukhrijun* (مُخْرِجٌ) is "making manifest," i.e., what you concealed among yourselves of the matter of the killing, Allah makes it manifest to His servants and clarifies it for them. This clause is a parenthetical insertion between the parts of the speech (p-68), i.e., "you disputed concerning it, so We said."

Scholars differed about specifying the part with which they were commanded to strike the slain man. There is no need for that, given what it entails of speaking without knowledge. It suffices us to say: Allah commanded them to strike him with part of it. Whatever part they struck him with, they have done what they were commanded. Anything beyond this is among the superfluous details of knowledge, when no proof has been brought for it.

His saying ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ contains an ellipsis. The implied sense is: "So We said, 'Strike him with part of it,' and Allah brought him to life. ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾," i.e., a revival like this revival.

﴿And He shows you His signs﴾, i.e., His indications and proofs that point to the perfection of His power. This may be addressed to those who were present at the story, and it may be addressed to those present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an.

*Al-qaswa* (القَسْوَةُ) is hardness and dryness. It is an expression for the heart's being devoid of turning in repentance and submission to the signs of Allah, despite the presence of what calls for the opposite of this hardness: the revival of the slain man, his speaking, and his naming of his killer. The reference in His saying ﴿after that﴾ is to the signs mentioned earlier, which necessitate softness and tenderness of hearts.

It has been said: *aw* (أو) in His saying ﴿or harder in hardness﴾ carries the meaning of *wa* (and), as in His saying: ﴿a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ (76:24). It has also been said: it means *bal* (بَلْ, "rather"). And it has been said: *aw* retains its original meaning, or means *wa*, and the conjunction is upon His saying "like stones," i.e., these hearts are like stones, or they are harder than them. So compare them with whichever of the two you wish, for you are correct in this comparison.

Al-Razi, in his *tafsir*, answered the question of why *aw* occurs here, although it denotes choice (*al-tardid*), i.e., it is not fitting for the Knower of the unseen, with eight aspects. He arrived at the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) by means of *ashadd* (أشدّ, "harder"), though it would be valid to say *wa-aqsā min al-ḥijāra* (وأقسى مِنَ الحِجارَةِ), because it is clearer and more indicative of extreme hardness, as he said in *al-Kashshaf*.

Al-A'mash read *aw ashadda* (أوْ أشَدَّ) with a *fatḥah* on the *dāl*, and it seems he made it a conjunction upon "stones," so *ashadd* would be in the genitive with the *fatḥah*.

As for His saying ﴿And indeed among stones﴾ to its end, al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: it is an explanation of the superiority of their hearts over stones in intensity of hardness, and a confirmation of His saying ﴿or harder in hardness﴾, end of quote.

But in this there is the point that an explanation coming with *wa* is neither known nor customary. The better option is to treat what follows the *wa* as a concluding remark (*tadhyīl*) or as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

*Al-tafajjur* (التَّفَجُّرُ) is splitting open, and its explanation has already preceded.

The original of *yashsharru* (يَشَّقَّقُ) is *yatashaqqaqu*, and the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *shīn*. Al-A'mash read *yatashaqqaqu* according to the original form.

Ibn Musarrif read *yanshaqqu* (يَنْشَقُّ) with a *nūn*. *Al-shaqq* is one of the cracks (*shuqūq*), and it may be lengthwise or widthwise, unlike *al-infijār*, which is opening from one place with the widening of the breach.

The meaning is that water comes out of the stones from the places of bursting and splitting. And among stones is that which descends (*yahbiṭu*), i.e., drops down from the place where it is to a place below it, out of the fear of Allah that enters it and dwells in it. It has been said: the descent is a metaphor for humility from them and the modesty present in them in submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is like His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from the fear of Allah﴾ (59:21). Ibn Jarir reported from a group that the fear attributed to the stones is figurative, just as "wanting" is figuratively attributed to a wall, and as the poet said:

*When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains were humbled.*

Al-Jahiz mentioned that the pronoun in His saying "and indeed among them" refers to the hearts, not to the stones, and this is corrupt. The purpose of the context of this speech is to declare that the hearts of these people have reached in hardness and extreme dryness, which necessitate not accepting the truth nor being affected by admonitions, to a degree that stones have not reached, although stones are the most solid of bodies and the greatest in firmness. For they return to a kind of softness, which is their bursting with water, their splitting open because of it, and their acceptance of what the fear of Allah requires of humility and submission, unlike those hearts.

In His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ there is a threat and an intensifying of warning that is not hidden, for when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows what they do, sees it, and is not unaware of it, He is on watch for their recompense.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾ that he said: "You differed about it." ﴿And Allah brings forth what you were concealing﴾: "What you were hiding."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, reported from al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', who said: "No man does a good deed within seven houses except that Allah makes it manifest, and no man does an evil deed within seven houses except that Allah makes it manifest." The confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is ﴿And Allah brings forth what you were concealing﴾.

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Sa'd who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man performed a deed on a solid rock with no door or window to it, his deed would come out to the people, whatever it was."

Al-Bayhaqi reported from the hadith of Uthman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a good or bad secret, Allah will cast over him a cloak by which he will be known." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it similarly as a statement of Uthman, and he said: "The stopped (*mawquf*) version is more authentic."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Anas, as a raised (*marfu'*) report, a lengthy hadith with this meaning, and its meaning is that Allah clothes every doer with his deed until people speak of it and add to it, even if he did it inside a house, within seventy houses, each house having an iron door. Its chain has weakness.

Ibn 'Adi reported from the hadith of Anas, also as a raised report: "Indeed Allah dresses every person in the cloak of his deed."

A number of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*) have statements that convey this meaning.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it"﴾ that he said: "He was struck with the bone that is adjacent to the cartilage."

Ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that they struck him with its thigh.

Ibn Jarir reported the like of it from 'Ikrima.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: "He was struck with the piece between the two shoulders."

Ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh, in *al-'Azama*, reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih a lengthy story concerning the cow and its owner. There is no need to lengthen by mentioning it, and it has been fully reported in *al-Durr al-Manthur*.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾ that he said: "After Allah showed them the revival of the dead, and after He showed them the matter of the slain man, ﴿they were like stones or harder in hardness﴾." Then Allah excused the stones and did not excuse (p-69) the wretched children of Adam, so He said: ﴿And indeed among stones is that from which rivers burst forth﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Indeed, among stones are those that are softer than your hearts in regard to the truth to which you are called."

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Indeed a stone falls to the ground, and even if a crowd of people gathered upon it they could not move it, yet it descends out of the fear of Allah."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Indeed, among stones are those that are softer than your hearts in regard to the truth to which you are called."

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "Indeed a stone falls to the ground, and even if a crowd of people gathered upon it they could not move it, yet it descends out of the fear of Allah."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on 2:72–74:

What I mentioned earlier concerning the story of the slaughter of the cow has already passed. So the sense of the speech is: "When you killed a soul and disputed about it, and Allah is bringing forth what you were concealing." Then Musa said to his people: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ to the end of the story. After it comes ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it"﴾ and the verse.

Al-Razi said in his *tafsir*: Know that the occurrence of the killing must have preceded His command to slaughter. As for the report of that killing, and that the slain person must be struck with part of that cow, it is not necessary that it precede the report of the story of the cow. So the saying of whoever says, "This story must come before the first one in recitation," is an error. This is because the story in itself must come before the first one in existence, but precedence in mention is not obligatory, since sometimes the cause is mentioned before the ruling, and sometimes the reverse. So when that incident befell them, Allah commanded them to slaughter the cow, and when they had slaughtered it, He said: ﴿And when you killed a soul earlier﴾, and He attributed the killing to them because the killer was one of them. The original of *idaraʾtum* (ادّارَأْتُمْ) is *tadāraʾtum*, then the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *dāl*. Since beginning with an assimilated quiescent letter is not permitted, they added the *alif al-waṣl* (the connecting alif). The meaning of *idaraʾtum* is "you differed and disputed," because disputants push (*yadraʾu*) one another away, i.e., repel one another. The meaning of *mukhrijun* (مُخْرِجٌ) is "making manifest," i.e., what you concealed among yourselves of the matter of the killing, Allah makes it manifest to His servants and clarifies it for them. This clause is a parenthetical insertion between the parts of the speech (p-68), i.e., "you disputed concerning it, so We said."

Scholars differed about specifying the part with which they were commanded to strike the slain man. There is no need for that, given what it entails of speaking without knowledge. It suffices us to say: Allah commanded them to strike him with part of it. Whatever part they struck him with, they have done what they were commanded. Anything beyond this is among the superfluous details of knowledge, when no proof has been brought for it.

His saying ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ contains an ellipsis. The implied sense is: "So We said, 'Strike him with part of it,' and Allah brought him to life. ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾," i.e., a revival like this revival.

﴿And He shows you His signs﴾, i.e., His indications and proofs that point to the perfection of His power. This may be addressed to those who were present at the story, and it may be addressed to those present at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an.

*Al-qaswa* (القَسْوَةُ) is hardness and dryness. It is an expression for the heart's being devoid of turning in repentance and submission to the signs of Allah, despite the presence of what calls for the opposite of this hardness: the revival of the slain man, his speaking, and his naming of his killer. The reference in His saying ﴿after that﴾ is to the signs mentioned earlier, which necessitate softness and tenderness of hearts.

It has been said: *aw* (أو) in His saying ﴿or harder in hardness﴾ carries the meaning of *wa* (and), as in His saying: ﴿a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ (76:24). It has also been said: it means *bal* (بَلْ, "rather"). And it has been said: *aw* retains its original meaning, or means *wa*, and the conjunction is upon His saying "like stones," i.e., these hearts are like stones, or they are harder than them. So compare them with whichever of the two you wish, for you are correct in this comparison.

Al-Razi, in his *tafsir*, answered the question of why *aw* occurs here, although it denotes choice (*al-tardid*), i.e., it is not fitting for the Knower of the unseen, with eight aspects. He arrived at the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) by means of *ashadd* (أشدّ, "harder"), though it would be valid to say *wa-aqsā min al-ḥijāra* (وأقسى مِنَ الحِجارَةِ), because it is clearer and more indicative of extreme hardness, as he said in *al-Kashshaf*.

Al-A'mash read *aw ashadda* (أوْ أشَدَّ) with a *fatḥah* on the *dāl*, and it seems he made it a conjunction upon "stones," so *ashadd* would be in the genitive with the *fatḥah*.

As for His saying ﴿And indeed among stones﴾ to its end, al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: it is an explanation of the superiority of their hearts over stones in intensity of hardness, and a confirmation of His saying ﴿or harder in hardness﴾, end of quote.

But in this there is the point that an explanation coming with *wa* is neither known nor customary. The better option is to treat what follows the *wa* as a concluding remark (*tadhyīl*) or as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

*Al-tafajjur* (التَّفَجُّرُ) is splitting open, and its explanation has already preceded.

The original of *yashsharru* (يَشَّقَّقُ) is *yatashaqqaqu*, and the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *shīn*. Al-A'mash read *yatashaqqaqu* according to the original form.

Ibn Musarrif read *yanshaqqu* (يَنْشَقُّ) with a *nūn*. *Al-shaqq* is one of the cracks (*shuqūq*), and it may be lengthwise or widthwise, unlike *al-infijār*, which is opening from one place with the widening of the breach.

The meaning is that water comes out of the stones from the places of bursting and splitting. And among stones is that which descends (*yahbiṭu*), i.e., drops down from the place where it is to a place below it, out of the fear of Allah that enters it and dwells in it. It has been said: the descent is a metaphor for humility from them and the modesty present in them in submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is like His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from the fear of Allah﴾ (59:21). Ibn Jarir reported from a group that the fear attributed to the stones is figurative, just as "wanting" is figuratively attributed to a wall, and as the poet said:

*When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains were humbled.*

Al-Jahiz mentioned that the pronoun in His saying "and indeed among them" refers to the hearts, not to the stones, and this is corrupt. The purpose of the context of this speech is to declare that the hearts of these people have reached in hardness and extreme dryness, which necessitate not accepting the truth nor being affected by admonitions, to a degree that stones have not reached, although stones are the most solid of bodies and the greatest in firmness. For they return to a kind of softness, which is their bursting with water, their splitting open because of it, and their acceptance of what the fear of Allah requires of humility and submission, unlike those hearts.

In His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ there is a threat and an intensifying of warning that is not hidden, for when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows what they do, sees it, and is not unaware of it, He is on watch for their recompense.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾ that he said: "You differed about it." ﴿And Allah brings forth what you were concealing﴾: "What you were hiding."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, reported from al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', who said: "No man does a good deed within seven houses except that Allah makes it manifest, and no man does an evil deed within seven houses except that Allah makes it manifest." The confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is ﴿And Allah brings forth what you were concealing﴾.

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Sa'd who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man performed a deed on a solid rock with no door or window to it, his deed would come out to the people, whatever it was."

Al-Bayhaqi reported from the hadith of Uthman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a good or bad secret, Allah will cast over him a cloak by which he will be known." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it similarly as a statement of Uthman, and he said: "The stopped (*mawquf*) version is more authentic."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Anas, as a raised (*marfu'*) report, a lengthy hadith with this meaning, and its meaning is that Allah clothes every doer with his deed until people speak of it and add to it, even if he did it inside a house, within seventy houses, each house having an iron door. Its chain has weakness.

Ibn 'Adi reported from the hadith of Anas, also as a raised report: "Indeed Allah dresses every person in the cloak of his deed."

A number of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*) have statements that convey this meaning.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it"﴾ that he said: "He was struck with the bone that is adjacent to the cartilage."

Ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that they struck him with its thigh.

Ibn Jarir reported the like of it from 'Ikrima.

Ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: "He was struck with the piece between the two shoulders."

Ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh, in *al-'Azama*, reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih a lengthy story concerning the cow and its owner. There is no need to lengthen by mentioning it, and it has been fully reported in *al-Durr al-Manthur*.

Then Allah excused the stones and did not excuse (p-69) the wretched children of Adam, so He said: ﴿And indeed among stones is that from which rivers burst forth﴾ to the end of the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 75–77:

His saying: (Afatatma'una) This interrogation carries the sense of denial, as if he had despaired them of the faith of this group of the Jews.

The address is either to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, or to him and them together.

And (yu'minu lakum) means "for your sake," or it is by way of the verb āmana being construed with the meaning of istajāba (to respond), i.e., "Do you hope that they will respond to you?"

Al-Fariq is a collective noun (ism jam') that has no singular from its own form.

And (kalama Allah) means the Torah. It is said that they heard God's address to Musa when He spoke to him, and on this view al-Fariq would be the seventy whom Musa chose. Al-A'mash read "kalima Allah."

The meaning of tahrif (distortion) is that they deliberately went to what they had heard of the Torah and made its permissible things forbidden, or something similar to that, of what agrees with their desires, such as their distortion of the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ and their dropping of the prescribed punishments from their nobles. Or they heard the words of God to Musa and added to them and subtracted from them. This is an report of their persistence in disbelief and a rebuke against whoever hoped for their faith, while their state is this state; that is, they have predecessors who distorted the words of God and changed His laws, and they are imitators of them, following their path.

The meaning of His saying: (min ba'di ma 'aqaluhu) is: after they had understood it with their intellects, while knowing that what they did was a distortion contrary to what God had commanded them, namely to convey His laws as they are. So they fell into disobedience knowingly, and that is more severe for their punishment and clearer as evidence of their misguidance.

(Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu) means: when the hypocrites meet those who believe, (qalu amanna). (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) means: when those who were not hypocrites are alone with the hypocrites, they say to them, reproaching them, (Atuhaddithunahum bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) — that is, what God has decreed against you of punishment. This is because some Jews had embraced Islam and then became hypocrites, and they would tell the believing Arabs about the punishment with which their forefathers had been punished. It is also said that what is meant is what God opened up for them in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad. The meaning of (khala) has already been mentioned.

Al-fath (opening) in the usage of the Arabs means judgment and ruling; al-fattah means the judge in the dialect of Yemen; and al-fath means victory. Among its uses is God's saying: (yastaftihuna 'ala alladhina kafaru) and His saying: (in tastaftihu faqadja'akumu al-fath). And from the first sense is: (thumma yaftahu baynana bi'l-haqq), that is, the best of judges, i.e., the judges. The fath may also mean separating one thing from another. Al-muhajja is the presentation of proof. That is: do not inform them of what God has decreed against you of punishment, for that would be a proof for them against you, so they would say: "We are more honored by God than you, and more deserving of good from Him."

Al-hujjah is the upright speech; and "haajajtu fulanan fahajajtuhu" means I overcame him with proof.

(Afala ta'qilun) — will you not consider the harm to you from this speech of yours to them?

Then God, glorified is He, rebuked them: (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirrruna wa ma yu'linun) — of all kinds of secrecy and kinds of openness, and among that is their concealing of disbelief and their proclaiming of faith.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Then God said to His Prophet and those with him of the believers, despairing them of them: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum wa qad kana fariqun minhum yasma'una kalama Allah). It is not His saying "yasma'una" (they heard) the Torah; all of them had heard it, but they are the ones who asked Musa to see their Lord, and the thunderbolt seized them for it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah concerning His saying: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum), the verse, he said: They are the Jews, who used to hear the word of God and then distort it after they had heard it and understood it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum), the verse, he said: Those who distort it and those who write it are their scholars, and those who cast the Book of God behind their backs — all of these are Jews.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: (yasma'una kalama Allah), he said: It is the Torah, which they distorted.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: (Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu qalu amanna), that is, in your companion, the Messenger of God ﷺ, but only to you specifically. (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) they said: Do not tell the Arabs about this, for you used to seek victory over them through it. Among them was (liyuhajjukum bihi 'inda rabbikum), that is, you acknowledge that he is a prophet, and you know that the covenant was taken from you to follow him, and he informs them that he is the prophet who was awaited, and we find him in our book. Deny him and do not acknowledge him.

Ibn Jarir related from him that this verse concerns the hypocritical Jews, and His saying (bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) means: with what God has honored you with.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: This verse was revealed concerning some Jews who believed and then became hypocrites, and they would tell the believing Arabs about the punishment with which they had been punished. Some of them said to others: "Do you tell them what God has opened against you of punishment, so that they may say: we are more beloved to God than you and more honored by God than you?"

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let no one enter upon us in the outskirts of Madinah except a believer." So the Jews would show faith, enter, and return to their people with news. The believers would say to them: "Did not God say in the Torah such and such?" They would say: "Yes." Then when they returned to their people, (they said: Do you tell them what God has opened up for you) — the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that the occasion of revelation was: that the Prophet ﷺ stood before the tribe of Qurayzah beneath their fortresses and said: "O brothers of the apes and the swine, and O worshippers of the taghut!" They said: "Who told Muhammad this matter? This matter came out only from among you." (Atuhaddithunahum bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) — that is, with what God has decreed, so that it would be a proof for them against you.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah that the cause of the revelation of the verse was: "A Jewish woman committed an indecency, and they came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking his ruling, hoping for leniency. The Messenger of God ﷺ summoned their scholar, who was Ibn Suriya, and said to him: 'Judge.' He said: They humiliated him (tajbiyah), and tajbiyah means they put him on a donkey with his face toward the donkey's tail. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Did you judge by the command of God?' He said: 'No, but our women were beautiful, so our men hastened to them, so we changed the ruling.' And concerning this was revealed (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd), the verse."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah concerning His saying: (Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu qalu amanna), he said: They are the Jews, who, when they met those who believed, said: "We believe," flattering them so that they would be pleased with them. (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) some of them forbade others from telling what God had opened to them and made clear to them in His Book about the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, his description and his prophethood. They said: "If you do that, they will argue against you with it before your Lord. Will you not reason?" (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirruna wa ma yu'linun) he said: what they proclaim of their affair and speech when they meet those who believe, and what they conceal when they are alone with one another, of their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and their denial of him, while they find him written in their possession.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying: (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirruna wa ma yu'linun), meaning of their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and their lying, and what they proclaim when they say to the believers "We believe." A group of the early scholars also said the like of this.
