Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 75–77:

His saying: (Afatatma'una) This interrogation carries the sense of denial, as if he had despaired them of the faith of this group of the Jews.

The address is either to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, or to him and them together.

And (yu'minu lakum) means "for your sake," or it is by way of the verb āmana being construed with the meaning of istajāba (to respond), i.e., "Do you hope that they will respond to you?"

Al-Fariq is a collective noun (ism jam') that has no singular from its own form.

And (kalama Allah) means the Torah. It is said that they heard God's address to Musa when He spoke to him, and on this view al-Fariq would be the seventy whom Musa chose. Al-A'mash read "kalima Allah."

The meaning of tahrif (distortion) is that they deliberately went to what they had heard of the Torah and made its permissible things forbidden, or something similar to that, of what agrees with their desires, such as their distortion of the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ and their dropping of the prescribed punishments from their nobles. Or they heard the words of God to Musa and added to them and subtracted from them. This is an report of their persistence in disbelief and a rebuke against whoever hoped for their faith, while their state is this state; that is, they have predecessors who distorted the words of God and changed His laws, and they are imitators of them, following their path.

The meaning of His saying: (min ba'di ma 'aqaluhu) is: after they had understood it with their intellects, while knowing that what they did was a distortion contrary to what God had commanded them, namely to convey His laws as they are. So they fell into disobedience knowingly, and that is more severe for their punishment and clearer as evidence of their misguidance.

(Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu) means: when the hypocrites meet those who believe, (qalu amanna). (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) means: when those who were not hypocrites are alone with the hypocrites, they say to them, reproaching them, (Atuhaddithunahum bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) — that is, what God has decreed against you of punishment. This is because some Jews had embraced Islam and then became hypocrites, and they would tell the believing Arabs about the punishment with which their forefathers had been punished. It is also said that what is meant is what God opened up for them in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad. The meaning of (khala) has already been mentioned.

Al-fath (opening) in the usage of the Arabs means judgment and ruling; al-fattah means the judge in the dialect of Yemen; and al-fath means victory. Among its uses is God's saying: (yastaftihuna 'ala alladhina kafaru) and His saying: (in tastaftihu faqadja'akumu al-fath). And from the first sense is: (thumma yaftahu baynana bi'l-haqq), that is, the best of judges, i.e., the judges. The fath may also mean separating one thing from another. Al-muhajja is the presentation of proof. That is: do not inform them of what God has decreed against you of punishment, for that would be a proof for them against you, so they would say: "We are more honored by God than you, and more deserving of good from Him."

Al-hujjah is the upright speech; and "haajajtu fulanan fahajajtuhu" means I overcame him with proof.

(Afala ta'qilun) — will you not consider the harm to you from this speech of yours to them?

Then God, glorified is He, rebuked them: (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirrruna wa ma yu'linun) — of all kinds of secrecy and kinds of openness, and among that is their concealing of disbelief and their proclaiming of faith.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Then God said to His Prophet and those with him of the believers, despairing them of them: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum wa qad kana fariqun minhum yasma'una kalama Allah). It is not His saying "yasma'una" (they heard) the Torah; all of them had heard it, but they are the ones who asked Musa to see their Lord, and the thunderbolt seized them for it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah concerning His saying: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum), the verse, he said: They are the Jews, who used to hear the word of God and then distort it after they had heard it and understood it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: (Afatatma'una an yu'minu lakum), the verse, he said: Those who distort it and those who write it are their scholars, and those who cast the Book of God behind their backs — all of these are Jews.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: (yasma'una kalama Allah), he said: It is the Torah, which they distorted.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: (Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu qalu amanna), that is, in your companion, the Messenger of God ﷺ, but only to you specifically. (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) they said: Do not tell the Arabs about this, for you used to seek victory over them through it. Among them was (liyuhajjukum bihi 'inda rabbikum), that is, you acknowledge that he is a prophet, and you know that the covenant was taken from you to follow him, and he informs them that he is the prophet who was awaited, and we find him in our book. Deny him and do not acknowledge him.

Ibn Jarir related from him that this verse concerns the hypocritical Jews, and His saying (bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) means: with what God has honored you with.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: This verse was revealed concerning some Jews who believed and then became hypocrites, and they would tell the believing Arabs about the punishment with which they had been punished. Some of them said to others: "Do you tell them what God has opened against you of punishment, so that they may say: we are more beloved to God than you and more honored by God than you?"

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let no one enter upon us in the outskirts of Madinah except a believer." So the Jews would show faith, enter, and return to their people with news. The believers would say to them: "Did not God say in the Torah such and such?" They would say: "Yes." Then when they returned to their people, (they said: Do you tell them what God has opened up for you) — the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that the occasion of revelation was: that the Prophet ﷺ stood before the tribe of Qurayzah beneath their fortresses and said: "O brothers of the apes and the swine, and O worshippers of the taghut!" They said: "Who told Muhammad this matter? This matter came out only from among you." (Atuhaddithunahum bima fataha Allahu 'alaykum) — that is, with what God has decreed, so that it would be a proof for them against you.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah that the cause of the revelation of the verse was: "A Jewish woman committed an indecency, and they came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking his ruling, hoping for leniency. The Messenger of God ﷺ summoned their scholar, who was Ibn Suriya, and said to him: 'Judge.' He said: They humiliated him (tajbiyah), and tajbiyah means they put him on a donkey with his face toward the donkey's tail. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Did you judge by the command of God?' He said: 'No, but our women were beautiful, so our men hastened to them, so we changed the ruling.' And concerning this was revealed (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd), the verse."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah concerning His saying: (Wa idha laqu alladhina amanu qalu amanna), he said: They are the Jews, who, when they met those who believed, said: "We believe," flattering them so that they would be pleased with them. (Wa idha khala ba'duhum ila ba'd) some of them forbade others from telling what God had opened to them and made clear to them in His Book about the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, his description and his prophethood. They said: "If you do that, they will argue against you with it before your Lord. Will you not reason?" (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirruna wa ma yu'linun) he said: what they proclaim of their affair and speech when they meet those who believe, and what they conceal when they are alone with one another, of their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and their denial of him, while they find him written in their possession.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying: (Awa la ya'lamuna anna Allaha ya'lamu ma yusirruna wa ma yu'linun), meaning of their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and their lying, and what they proclaim when they say to the believers "We believe." A group of the early scholars also said the like of this.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 78–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And among them" — i.e., among the Jews.

The ummi (ummī) is related to the ummī nation (al-ummah al-ummiyyah), which is, in its original state at birth, as its mothers bore it: it has not learned writing and does not skillfully read what is written. From this is the hadith: "We are an ummī nation; we do not write and we do not calculate." Abu 'Ubaydah said: they were called ummiyyun only because the Book was revealed to them, as if they were ascribed to Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book). So it is as if He said: "And among them are the People of the Book." It has also been said: they are the Magians, and other things have been said, but the strongest view is the first.

The meaning of ﴿they know not the Book, except wishful thinking (amani)﴾ is that they have no knowledge of it except what they hold of wishful thinkings, which they wish for and with which they deceive themselves.

Amani is the plural of umniyyah, which is what a person wishes for himself. These people have no knowledge of the Book, which is the Torah, because of their condition of being forgiven by what they claim for themselves of good deeds, or by what they have from the pious predecessors in their belief. It has also been said that amani means lies, as will come from Ibn 'Abbas.

From this is the saying of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: "I have not wished (tamanneitu) since I embraced Islam," i.e., I have not lied. Al-Qurtubi related this from him in his tafsir. It has also been said that amani means recitation, and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except when he wishes (tamannā), Satan casts into his wish (umniyyatihi)﴾, i.e., when he recites, Satan casts into his recitation. That is, they have no knowledge except the bare recitation without understanding and reflection. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"He wished for the Book of God at the first night and its last, and met the death-sentence of the decrees."

And another said:

"He wished for the Book of God in the last night, wishing as Dawud wished for the Psalms with their chants."

It has also been said that amani means decree.

Al-Jawhari said: it is said "munniya lahu," i.e., it was decreed for him. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Do not feel safe even if you are in a sanctuary, until you meet what the Decreer has decreed for you."

i.e., the Decreer decrees for you.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: the derivation is from munniya when it was decreed, because the one who wishes decrees in his soul and allows what he wishes; likewise the one who fabricates and the reader decrees that such-and-such a word comes after such-and-such. End of quotation.

As for "in" in His saying: ﴿and they only conjecture (in hum illa yazunnun)﴾, it is negating, i.e., they are not. Zann is the probable doubt between the two sides of belief that is not decisive. So says al-Qamus: i.e., they only waver without certainty or conviction. It has also been said that zann here means lying, and it has been said that it is mere guesswork.

When God, glorified is He, mentioned among them the people of knowledge, saying that they do not act, but rather distort the words of God after they had understood them while they knew, He mentioned among them the ignorant, saying that they rely on wishful thinking and depend on conjecture, which they do not take from anything other than their imitation and do not obtain anything else.

Al-Wayl (woe) means destruction.

Al-Farra' said: the origin of wayl is wai, i.e., grief, as you say "wai li-fulan," i.e., grief for him; the Arabs connected it with the lam. Al-Khalil said: we have heard it in no form except wai, wais, wayh, wayk, and wayb, all close in meaning. Some have distinguished between them. They are verbal nouns whose verbs the Arabs did not utter, and it is permissible to begin with it even though it is indefinite, because it carries the meaning of supplication.

Writing is well known, and what is meant is that they write the distorted Book and do not clarify it, nor do they denounce it against its author.

His saying: "with their hands" (bi-aydihim) is an emphasis, because writing is not except by the hand, so it is like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ and His saying: ﴿they say with their mouths﴾. Ibn Siraj said: it is a metonymy meaning that it is from their own devising, without its being sent down to them.

And in it: that it has indicated that it is from their own devising by His saying: ﴿who write the Book﴾, for ascribing the writing to them conveys that.

Purchase (al-ishtira') is exchange (al-istibdal), and the discussion of it has already passed. He described it as little either because it is perishable, having no reward in it, or because it is unlawful, in which blessing does not dwell. These scribes did not suffice with distortion, nor with writing that distorted thing, until they proclaimed in the assemblies that it is from God, so that by these repeated sins they might obtain this paltry gain and this contemptible reward.

His saying: ﴿for what they earn﴾ — it has been said: from bribes and the like; it has been said: from sins. He repeated "woe" as an intensification against them, a magnification of their deed, and an unveiling of their concealments.

And they said — i.e., the Jews — ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾, the verse.

The occasion of the revelation of the verse has been disputed, as will come with its explanation.

What is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with God?﴾ is rebuke against them for what proceeded from them of this false claim that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days. That is: no covenant was previously made with you by God regarding this, nor have you sent ahead any righteous deeds that would confirm this claim, so that fulfilling it and not breaking the covenant would be required. That is: if you have taken a covenant with God, then God will not break His covenant; or do you say about God what you do not know?

Al-Kashshaf says: "am" (or) is either equalizing, meaning "whichever of the two matters is the case," as a form of affirmation, since knowledge is attached to the occurrence of one of them; or it may be disjunctive. End of quotation. This is a severe rebuke for them.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: the covenant in this place runs in the manner of a promise, and His report, glorified is He, was named a covenant because His report is more emphatic than emphasized covenants.

His saying: "Bala" (Yes) is an affirmation after a negation, i.e., yes, the touching of you will be, not in the manner you mentioned of being for a number of days.

As for al-sayyi'ah (evil deed), what is meant by it here is the genus, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the recompense of an evil deed is an evil like it﴾ and ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾. Then He, glorified is He, clarified that the mere earning of an evil deed does not necessitate eternal abiding in the Fire, but rather there must be an evil deed encompassing him. It has been said: it is shirk; and it has been said: a major sin.

Its interpretation as shirk is preferable, because it is established in the Sunnah by mass transmission that the sinners among the monotheists will come out of the Fire. This is supported by its being revealed concerning the Jews, although the consideration is by the generality of the wording and not by the particularity of the occasion.

Nafi' read khatiyatuhu in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular. The explanation of khulud (eternal abiding) has already passed.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book﴾ he said: they do not know what is in it. ﴿and they only conjecture﴾ he said: and they deny your prophethood by conjecture.

Ibn Jarir related from him, he said: the ummiyyun are a people who neither confirmed a messenger sent by God nor a book sent down by God; so they wrote a book with their own hands, then said to a base, ignorant people: "This is from God."

He has informed that they write with their hands, then named them ummiyyin because of their denial of the books of God and His messengers.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Nakha'i, he said: among them is one who does not know how to write.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "except wishful thinking (amani)," he said: the hadiths.

Ibn Jarir related from him that it is falsehood.

Likewise 'Abd ibn Humayd related the same from Mujahid, and added, concerning ﴿and they only conjecture﴾: "they only lie."

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their hands﴾ he said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and he authenticated it, related from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "Wayl is a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever plunges for forty autumns before reaching its bottom."

Ibn Jarir related from the hadith of 'Uthman, marfu', who said: "Wayl is a mountain in the Fire."

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, marfu', that it is a stone in the Fire.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their hands﴾ he said: they are the rabbis of the Jews, who found the description of the Prophet ﷺ written in the Torah: antimony-eyed, of medium stature, curly-haired, handsome of face. When they found him in the Torah, they erased it out of envy and transgression. Then a group from Quraysh came to them and said: "Do you find in the Torah a prophet who is unlettered?" They said: "Yes, we find him tall, blue-eyed, straight-haired." Quraysh denied this and said: "This is not one of us."

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning His saying: "a small price" (thamanan qalilan), he said: "a commodity from the commodities of the world," so "woe to them" — he said: the punishment upon them is from what they wrote with their hands of that falsehood. ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾ — he says: for what they eat thereby of the wealth of the base people and others.

The owner of al-Durr al-Manthur mentioned reports from a group of the predecessors that they disliked selling mushafs, citing this verse as evidence, though there is no indication in it of that. Then he mentioned reports from a group of them that they permitted it and did not dislike it.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Wahidi related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Jews used to say: the duration of the world is seven thousand years, and we are punished for one day in Hell for every thousand years of the days of the world, and these are only seven numbered days; then the punishment ends. So God revealed concerning that: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us...﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, he said: the People of the Book found the distance between the two extremes of Hell to be forty (years), and they said: "The people of the Fire will be punished only for the measure of forty." When the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be bridled in the Fire and will walk in it until they reach Saqar, in which is the tree of Zaqqum, until the last day of the numbered days. The guardians of the Fire will say to them: "O enemies of God, you claimed you would be punished in the Fire only for numbered days; the count has ended and eternity remains." Then they will be taken to ascend, and they will be dragged upon their faces.

Ibn Jarir related from him that the Jews said: "The Fire will not touch us except forty nights," the duration of the worship of the calf.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related «from 'Ikrimah, who said: the Jews gathered one day and disputed with the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days, forty days, after which people will succeed us in it." They pointed to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, placing his hands upon his head: "You lie; rather you are eternal, abiding forever therein. We will not succeed you therein, God willing, ever." Concerning them this verse was revealed: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us...﴾»

Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam, marfu', something similar.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Darimi and al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah «that the Prophet ﷺ asked the Jews of Khaybar: "Who are the people of the Fire?" They said: "We will be in it a little while, then you will succeed us in it." The Messenger of God ﷺ said to them: "Begone! By God, we will never succeed you in it, ever."»

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with God?﴾, i.e., a binding pledge from God that it is as you say.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained the covenant here as their saying: "There is no god but God," they did not associate anything with Him and did not disbelieve.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿or do you say about God what you do not know?﴾, he said: the people said falsehood and vanity. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, he said: shirk.

'Abd ibn Humayd related the like from Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah concerning His saying: "and his sin has encompassed him," he said: his shirk has encompassed him.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related concerning His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, i.e., whoever does the like of your deeds and disbelieves with the like of what you disbelieved, until his disbelief encompasses what good he has; ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever. And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, i.e., whoever believes in what you disbelieved in and acts by what you abandoned of His religion, for them is Paradise, abiding therein forever.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah concerning His words, "and his sin has encompassed him," that he said: it is the grave sin that makes its people deserving of the Fire.

Waki' and Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan that he said: everything for which Allah has promised the Fire is a sin (khati'ah).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabi' ibn Khaythum that he said: it is the one who dies in his sin before repenting. And Ibn Jarir related the like of it from al-A'mash.

It has been said: it is shirk; and it has been said: a major sin.

Ibn Jarir related from the hadith of 'Uthman, marfu', who said: "Wayl is a mountain in the Fire."

Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam, marfu', something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 83–86:

The explanation of the covenant (mithaq) taken from the Children of Israel has already been given earlier.

Makki said: The covenant that Allah took from them here is what He took from them in their lifetime through the tongues of their prophets, and it is His saying: ﴿You shall worship none but Allah.﴾ Worship of Allah means affirming His tawhid (oneness), believing in His messengers, and acting upon what He revealed in His books.

Sibawayh said: His saying ﴿You shall worship none but Allah﴾ is the answer to an oath (jawab qasam). The meaning is: "We made them swear by Allah that you shall worship none but Allah." It was also said: it is an informative statement with the meaning of a command. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud, "lā ta'budū" (do not worship), in the prohibitive form. It is also supported by what is conjoined to it: "and say" and "establish" and "give."

Qutrub and al-Mubarrad said: His saying "you worship" (lā ta'budūna) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya), meaning: "We took their covenant while they were monotheists, or not opposers."

Al-Qurtubi said: This only fits the reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, "ya'budūna" with the yā' (third person).

Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and a group said: its meaning is: "We took your covenant that you would not worship except Allah, that you would be good to the two parents, and that you would not shed blood." Then the particle "an" (that) was deleted, so the verb became marfū' (in the nominative) because of its removal.

Al-Mubarrad said: This is an error, because everything that is elided in Arabic still operates as if it were pronounced.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is not an error; rather both are two valid options. He cited in support of them the verse:

"Ah, you who reproach me for attending battle, and for witnessing pleasures, will you make me immortal?"

It is in the naṣb (accusative) because of his saying "that I attend" (aḥḍura), and in the rafʿ (nominative) as well.

Good treatment of the two parents (iḥsān ilā al-wālidayn) means: living with them kindly, showing humility toward them, obeying their command, and all the other rights that Allah has made obligatory on a child toward his parents.

Al-qurbā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like al-rujʿā and al-ʿuqbā. It refers to relatives. Good treatment of them means: maintaining ties with them and attending to what they need according to one's capacity and to the extent of one's ability.

Al-yatāmā is the plural of yatīm (orphan). Among human beings, the yatīm is one who has lost his father. Among the rest of the animals, it is one who has lost his mother.

Its root meaning is isolation (infirād). It is said: "a yatīm child," meaning one who is separated from his father.

Al-masākīn is the plural of miskīn (the needy). He is one whom need has rendered quiet and humbled. According to most lexicographers and many jurists, he is in greater need than the faqīr (the poor).

It is narrated from al-Shafi'i that the faqīr is in a worse condition than the miskīn.

The people of knowledge have mentioned evidences for this question, fully treated in their proper places.

The meaning of His saying ﴿And speak to people kindly﴾ is: say to them a good word. It is an adjective of an elided verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf). That verbal noun is like bushrā (glad tidings). Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ḥasanan with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the sīn.

Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

Al-Akhfash said: both forms have one meaning, like al-bukhl and al-bakhal, and al-rushd and al-rashad. Al-Akhfash also transmitted ḥusnā without tanwīn (nunation), in the pattern fuʿlā.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya regarding His saying ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾: that some of you do not kill others, ﴿nor expel yourselves from your homes﴾: that some of you do not expel others from the homes, ﴿then you acknowledged﴾ this covenant, ﴿while you bore witness﴾: while you were witnesses.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (p-74) regarding His saying ﴿Then you acknowledged﴾: that this is a truth from My covenant upon you. ﴿Then you are these who kill yourselves﴾: meaning the people of polytheism, until you shed your blood along with them. ﴿And expel a faction of you from their homes﴾: he said: you expel them from their homes along with them. ﴿You support one another against them in sin and aggression﴾: so whenever there was war between the Aws and the Khazraj, the Banu Qaynuqa' would go out with the Khazraj, and al-Nadir and Qurayza with the Aws, and each of the two groups would support their allies against their brothers until they shed each other's blood. When the war laid down its burdens, they would ransom their captives, in confirmation of what is in the Torah. ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾, and you know that this is obligatory for you in your religion. ﴿And it is forbidden for you﴾ in your Book: their expulsion. ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ Do you ransom them while believing in that, and expel them while disbelieving in that?

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter﴾: he said: they preferred the little of this world over the abundance of the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 87–88:**

*Al-Kitab* (the Book): the Torah (al-Tawrah). *Al-Taqfiyah* means following and succeeding, derived from *al-qafa*, which is the back of the neck. One says *istaqfaytuhu* when one comes up behind him. From this the rhyme of a poem (*qafiyat al-shi'r*) is so named, because it follows the rest of the speech.

The meaning is that God, glorified is He, sent after it messengers who followed it. They were the prophets of the Children of Israel who were sent after Moses.

*Al-bayyinat* (the clear proofs): the proofs that God mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran and Surat al-Ma'idah.

*Al-ta'yid* means strengthening.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read *"wa-ayyadnahu"* with the long vowel (*al-madd*), and both are two dialectal forms of the same word.

*Ruh al-Qudus* is an attributive construction, meaning "the holy spirit," i.e., the spirit that is sacred.

*Al-Quds* means purity, and *al-muqaddas* means the purified. It was said that it is Gabriel, with whom God strengthened Jesus. From this is the verse of Hassan:

*"And Gabriel, the trustworthy of God among us, and the Holy Spirit, about which there is no concealment."*

Al-Nahhas said: Gabriel was called "spirit" and was attributed to *al-Quds* because he came into being by God's command without birth. It was also said: *al-Quds* is God, the Mighty and Majestic, and His spirit is Gabriel. It was also said: the intended meaning of *Ruh al-Qudus* is the Name by which Jesus used to revive the dead. It was said: the intended meaning is the Gospel (*al-Injil*). It was said: the intended meaning is the spirit that was breathed into him, with which God strengthened him because of the power in it.

His words, *"with what your souls do not desire"* (﴿بِما لا تَهْوى أنْفُسُكُمُ﴾), mean: with what does not agree with them and suit them. The root of *al-hawa* is inclination toward a thing.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-hawa* was so named because it throws its owner down into the Fire.

God rebuked them with this statement, introduced by the interrogative particle of rebuke, saying: *"Is it that whenever a messenger comes to you"* (﴿أفَكُلَّما جاءَكم رَسُولٌ﴾) from among you with what does not agree with what you desire, *"you grew arrogant"* (﴿اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ﴾) and refused to respond to him, belittling the messengers and considering the message far-fetched. The *fa'* in His words *"afakullama"* is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause, meaning: We gave you, O Children of Israel, prophets, and what We gave you [was given]. *Afakullama jaakum rasul*.

*Fariqan* (a group) is in the accusative, governed by the verb that follows it, and the *fa'* is for detailing. Among the group that were denied were Jesus and Muhammad, and among the group that were killed were Yahya and Zakariyya.

*Al-ghulf* is the plural of *aghlaf*. What is meant here is one who has a covering that prevents speech from reaching him. From it comes *ghallaftu al-sayf*, meaning I put a sheath on the sword.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: it is a metaphor taken from the uncircumcised man (*al-aghlaf alladhi lam yukhtan*), like His words: *"Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to"* (﴿قُلُوبُنا في أكِنَّةٍ مِمّا تَدْعُونا إلَيْهِ﴾). It was also said: *ghulf* is the plural of *ghilaf* (sheath), like *himar* and *humr* (donkey and donkeys). That is, our hearts are containers for knowledge, so why do they not understand from you, when we have preserved much knowledge? God replied to them with what they had said, saying: *"Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief"* (﴿بَلْ لَعَنَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾). The root of *al-la'n* in the speech of the Arabs is expulsion and distancing. From it is the verse of al-Shammakh:

*"I startled the sand grouse with it, and I drove away from it the station of the wolf, like a cursed man."*

That is, like a man who is expelled.

The meaning is: God has distanced them from His mercy. *Qalilan* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning *iman qalilan ma yu'minun* (they believe very little). The *ma* is superfluous. He described their faith as scant because they are the ones whom God has related to us in their obstinacy, their haughtiness, their intense stubbornness, and their distance from answering the messengers, which He has recounted. Among the totality of that is that they believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part of it.

Ma'mar said: the meaning is that they do not believe except a little of what is in their hands, and they disbelieve in most of it. On this view, *qalilan* is accusative by removal of the preposition.

Al-Waqidi said: its meaning is that they do not believe, little or much.

Al-Kisa'i said: the Arabs say, "We passed by a land that rarely produces leeks and onions," meaning it produces nothing.

Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: *"And We certainly gave Moses the Book"* (﴿ولَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ﴾): he means by it the Torah, all at once, detailed and firm. *"And We followed after him with messengers"* (﴿وقَفَّيْنا مِن بَعْدِهِ بِالرُّسُلِ﴾): he means a messenger called Samuel son of Babel, a messenger called Manshabil, a messenger called Sha'ya, a messenger called Hizqil, a messenger called Irmiya, who is al-Khidr, a messenger called Dawud, who is the father of Sulayman, and a messenger called the Messiah Jesus son of Mary. These messengers God raised up and chose from the community after Moses. So We took from them a binding covenant that they would convey to their community the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the description of his community.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His words: *"And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs"* (﴿وآتَيْنا عِيسى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ البَيِّناتِ﴾) that he said: they are the signs that were placed at his hands: the reviving of the dead, the creating from clay of the likeness of a bird, the healing of diseases, the reporting of many unseen matters, and what came down to them of the Torah and the Gospel, which God revealed to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His words, *"and We strengthened him"* (*wa-ayyadnahu*), that he said: "We made him strong."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: *"a spirit from the Holy"* (*ruhun min al-quds*) is the Name with which Jesus used to revive the dead.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: *al-Quds* is God, exalted is He.

He transmitted the like of it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

He transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: *al-Quds* is purity.

He transmitted from al-Suddi that he said: *al-Quds* is blessing.

He transmitted from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid that *Ruh al-Quds* is Gabriel.

He transmitted the like of it from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Ruh al-Quds is Gabriel."

It is established in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, strengthen Hassan with the Holy Spirit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His words, *"a group"* (*fariqan*), that he said: a party.

He transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the heart was only named *qalb* because of its *taqallub* (its turning and fluctuation).

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* transmitted from him that he used to recite *"qulubuna ghullun"* with a doubled letter (*muthaqqalah*), meaning: how do we learn when our hearts are full (*ghullun*) with wisdom, that is, containers for wisdom?

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His words, *"And they said: our hearts are ghulf"* (﴿وقالُوا قُلُوبُنا غُلْفٌ﴾), that it means: filled with knowledge, not needing the knowledge of Muhammad or anyone else.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His words, *"Our hearts are ghulf"*, that he said: in a covering. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: in enclosures.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: they are the hearts upon which a seal has been set.

Waki' transmitted from 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Jarir from Mujahid, something similar to it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah that he said: they are the hearts that do not understand.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Ikhlas*, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Hudhayfah that he said: "The hearts are four: a heart that is ghulf, and that is the heart of the disbeliever; a heart that is musaffah (polished or bound with a lid-like sheet), and that is the heart of the hypocrite; a heart that is ajrad, in which is something like a lamp, and that is the heart of the believer; and a heart in which there is both faith and hypocrisy. The likeness of faith is like a tree watered with good water, and the likeness of the hypocrite is like a sore fed by pus and blood."

Ahmad transmitted with a good chain from Abu Sa'id that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The hearts are four: a heart that is ajrad, in which is something like a lamp that shines; a heart that is aghlaf, bound over its sheath; a heart that is mankus (inverted); and a heart that is musaffah. As for the ajrad heart, it is the heart of the believer, its lamp is in it, and its light is in it. As for the aghlaf heart, it is the heart of the disbeliever. As for the mankus heart, it is the heart of the hypocrite, who recognized and then denied. As for the musaffah heart, it is a heart in which there is faith and hypocrisy: the likeness of faith in it is like the likeness of the herb fed by good water, and the likeness of hypocrisy in it is like the likeness of the sore fed by pus. Whichever of the two substances overcomes the other, it is overcome by it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Salman al-Farisi the like of it, identically, as a statement of his own (mawquf).

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words, *"Then little is what they believe"* (﴿فَقَلِيلًا ما يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾), that he said: only a few of them believe.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 89–92:

﴿When there came to them﴾ i.e., the Jews, "a Book" i.e., the Qur'an, "confirming" is a description of it, and it is in the codex of Abu Mansur, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), even though its governing noun is indefinite, because it has been made specific by its description with His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾. And its confirming what is with them of the Torah and the Gospel means that it informs them of what is in them, and confirms it, and does not contradict it.

And al-istiftāḥ (seeking victory, istinṣār), i.e., they used to ask Allah for victory over their enemies through the Prophet described at the end of time, whose description they find with them in the Torah. It was also said: al-istiftāḥ here means al-fatḥ (opening), i.e., they would inform them that he would be sent, and make them aware of that. The answer to "lammā" in His saying: ﴿And when there came to them a Book﴾ is said to be His saying: ﴿so when there came to them what they recognised﴾ and what follows it. It was also said: it is omitted, i.e., "they disbelieved" or the like, as al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said.

Al-Mubarrad said: the answer to the first "lammā" is His saying: "disbelieved," and the second "lammā" was repeated because of the length of the speech. The lām in "the disbelievers" is for the genus.

It is permissible that it be for the specific (ʿahd), and that this would be placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, but the first is more evident.

The "mā" in His saying: "How evil" (bi'samā) is either a relative (mawṣūlah) or a descriptive (mawṣūfah), i.e., "how evil is the thing" or "a thing," ﴿for which they have sold themselves﴾. This is what Sibawayh said.

Al-Akhfash said: "mā" is in the position of the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), like your saying: "how evil a man is Zayd."

Al-Farra' said: "bi'samā" together, as a whole, is one thing, composed like "ḥabbadhā."

Al-Kisa'i said: "mā" and "ishtarawā" are in the status of one independent noun, and the estimate is: "how evil is their buying that they disbelieve."

His saying: ﴿that they disbelieve﴾ is in the position of the nominative as the subject (mubtada') according to Sibawayh, and its predicate is what precedes it.

Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: if you wish, it is in the position of the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "bihi" (by it): i.e., they sold themselves by [their] disbelieving.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: "mā" is an indefinite in the accusative, explaining the subject of "bi'sa," in the sense of "a thing for which they sold themselves," and the one specified for dispraise is "that they disbelieve," and "ishtarawā" means "sold."

His saying: "out of envy" (baghyan), i.e., out of jealousy.

Al-Asma'i said: al-baghy is derived from their saying: "the wound has baghā" when it has festered. It was also said: its origin is seeking, and for this reason the adulteress is called baghiyy.

It is the cause (ʿillah) of His saying: "they sold," and His saying: "that Allah should send down" is the cause of His saying "baghyan," i.e., because Allah should send down.

The meaning: they sold themselves for this wretched price out of envy and rivalry, ﴿that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin read "an yunzila" with lightening (the verb in the form of ʾanzala).

So "fa-bā'ū" means they returned and became deserving of ﴿wrath upon wrath﴾. The meaning of "bā'ū" and of "ghaḍab" has already been mentioned. It was said: the first wrath was for their worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in Muhammad. It was said: their disbelief in Jesus, then their disbelief in Muhammad. It was said: their disbelief in Muhammad, then their transgression against him. Other things were also said.

Al-muhīn is derived from humiliation (hawān). It was said: it is that which necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire.

This sentence, i.e., "and they disbelieve," is in the position of the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, i.e., they said: "We believe in what was sent down to us" while being disbelievers in what is beyond it, together with the fact that this which is beyond what they believe in is the truth.

His saying: "confirming" (muṣaddiqan) is a confirmatory circumstantial qualifier. These circumstances are interlocking: his saying "and they disbelieve," and his saying "and it is the truth," and his saying "confirming." Then Allah, glorified is He, rebuked them when they said: "We believe in what was sent down to us," with this sentence containing an interrogation that conveys reproach, i.e., if you believe in what was sent down to you, then why do you kill the prophets when you were forbidden from killing them in what was sent down to you? Although this address is directed at the Jews present, what is meant is their forefathers, but since they were content with the deeds of their predecessors, they were like them.

The lām in His saying: "And indeed" is the answer to an implied oath.

"The clear signs" (al-bayyināt) may be intended as the Torah, or the nine signs referred to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾. It is also permissible that all of them be intended. Then you took the calf for worship after looking at those clear signs, while you were wrongdoers by this worship which proceeded from you in obstinacy after the proof had been established against you.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming﴾, he said: it is the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with them﴾ of the Torah and the Gospel.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi, both in al-Dala'il, narrated through the chain of 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn Qatadah al-Ansari, who said: "Some of our elders told me: No one among the Arabs was more knowledgeable about the affair of the Messenger of Allah ﴾ﷺ﴿ than us, because there were Jews with us, and they were People of the Book, while we were idolaters. Whenever what we did displeased them, they would say: A prophet is about to be sent now, his time has drawn near, we will follow him and kill you with him, a killing like that of 'Ad and Iram. When the Messenger of Allah ﴾ﷺ﴿ was sent, we followed him, and they disbelieved in him. So by Allah, concerning us and them Allah revealed: ﴿And they had previously been seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, they said: The Arabs used to pass by the Jews, and they would harm them, and they found Muhammad in the Torah, so they would ask Allah to send him as a prophet so that they might fight the Arabs alongside him. When Muhammad came, they disbelieved in him because he was not from the Children of Israel.

Something similar has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas through more than one route with different wording, and their meanings are close.

Something similar has also been narrated from others among the early generations.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿How evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾, he said: They are the Jews, who disbelieved in what Allah sent down and in Muhammad ﴾ﷺ﴿, out of baghy and envy toward the Arabs. ﴿So they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾, he said: Allah became angry with them twice: for their disbelief in the Gospel and in Jesus, and for their disbelief in the Qur'an and in Muhammad.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿out of baghy that Allah should send down﴾, i.e., that Allah made it from someone other than them, ﴿so they returned with wrath﴾, by their disbelief in this Prophet, upon a wrath that was upon them for what they had done with the Torah.

Ibn Jarir also narrated the same from 'Ikrimah.

He also narrated its meaning from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His saying: ﴿and they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾, he said: in what is after it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, he said: "what is beyond it" means the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 2, verses 93–96:

The explanation of the taking of the covenant and the lifting of Mount Sinai has already passed.

The command to "listen" (al-sam‘) means obedience and acceptance, and it does not mean merely perceiving with the sense of hearing. From this comes the saying "Allah hears the one who praises Him" (sami‘a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning He accepts and responds. From this also is the poet's verse:

*"I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say"*

meaning, would not accept it. As for their answer, "We heard" (sami‘na), it is on its literal meaning and also on its figurative meaning: that is, "We heard your words with the sense of hearing, and we disobey you," meaning, "We do not accept what you command us." It is also possible that by their saying "We heard" they meant what was habitual from their trickery and their use of deception when addressing their prophets, by taking His words, "and listen" (wa-sma‘u), in their literal sense, namely hearing with the sense.

Then they answered, "We heard," meaning, "We perceived that with our ears, acting upon what You command." But since they knew that this was not what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended, and that His intention by the command to listen was the command to obey and accept, they did not confine themselves to this deception. Rather, they added to it what they considered the answer, and so they said, "and we disobey" (wa-‘asayna).

In His words "and they were made to drink" (wa-usribu) there is an eloquent metaphor, meaning: their hearts were made as if they drank the calf, because the love of the calf had taken firm hold in them. A similar expression is the verse of Zuhayr:

*"So I awoke from her after an inward love, and love is a disease that makes your heart drink it."*

He expressed the love of the calf by "drinking" rather than "eating" because the drinking of water penetrates the limbs until it reaches their inner parts, whereas food passes over them and does not penetrate them. The preposition "bi" in His words "bi-kufrihim" (because of their disbelief) is causal, meaning that this happened because of their disbelief, as a punishment for them and as abandonment (by Allah).

As for His words, "Say: Evil is that which your faith commands you" (qul bi'sama ya'murukum bihi iman-ukum), it means: your faith which you claim, that you believe in what was revealed to you and disbelieve in what is beyond it. For this act, which is your saying "We hear and we disobey," is in response to what you were commanded in your own Book, and the covenant was taken from you regarding it. The one who calls out to you with the most eloquent call is opposed to what you claim. Likewise, what has occurred from you of worshipping the calf and the descent of its love into your hearts in the manner of a drink is among the greatest things that show you are liars in your saying, "We believe in what was revealed to us," and not truthful. If you claim that your Book, in which you believed, commanded you this, then evil is that which your faith in your Book commands you. In this there is a mockery of them that is not hidden.

As for His words, "Say: If the abode of the Hereafter is for you alone (in-kanat lakumu al-dar al-akhirah)," it is a refutation of them, since they claimed that they would enter Paradise and that no one else would share their entry, and it is a binding argument against them by which it becomes clear that they are lying in that claim and that it issues from them without any proof. (p. 77) "Khalisatan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and the predicate of *kana* is "‘inda Allah" (with Allah). Or the predicate of *kana* is "khalisatan." The meaning of "khulus" (exclusivity) is that no one else shares it with them, if the *lam* in His words "min dun al-nas" (apart from the people) is for the genus. Or it means that the Muslims do not share it with them, if the *lam* is for a specific known group.

This is more likely, because of their saying in another verse: "And they said: None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." He commanded them to wish for death because whoever believes that he is among the people of Paradise would love death more than life. Since this was from them merely a claim, they held back.

For this reason He, Glorified is He, said: "But they will never wish for it, ever." The *ma* in His words "bi-ma qaddamat aydihim" (because of what their hands have sent forth) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: because of the sins that they sent forth, whose doer is not secure from punishment, but is not even hopeful of entering Paradise, let alone being certain of it, let alone it being exclusively theirs and specific to them. It was also said that Allah, Glorified is He, turned them away from wishing so that this would be a sign for His Prophet ﷺ.

What is meant by "wishing" here is the uttering of what indicates it, not merely its passing through the heart and the inclination of the soul toward it, for that is not intended in a situation of debate, in the places of dispute and the positions of challenge. In their abstaining from wishing, or their being turned away from it, there is a miracle for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for they used to adopt arrogance and boldness toward Allah and toward His prophets through false claims in many places, as the Revelation has related about them. So they left off their habit here only because of what had been established among them: that if they made that wish, death would descend upon them, either because of a matter they knew, or because of a turning away (*sarfah*) from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It may be said: It is established that the Prophet ﷺ forbade wishing for death, so how did Allah command him to tell them what is forbidden in his law?

The answer is that what is meant here is establishing the proof against them and the presenting of evidence for the falsity of their claim.

As for His words, "And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers," it is a threat to them and a recording against them that they are like that.

The *lam* in His words "wa-latajidanna-hum" (you will surely find them) is the answer to an implied oath, and the indefiniteness of "hayat" (life) is for belittling, meaning: they are the most eager of people for the most contemptible life and the least duration in this world. How then (would they be) with a long life and an extended stay? In the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) it says that he intended by the indefiniteness a specific life, namely the long-lasting life, and al-Razi followed him in that in his *Tafsir*.

As for His words "and from those who associated partners" (wa-min alladhina ashraku), it was said: it is a new independent sentence, and the implied meaning is: "and from those who associated partners are people, one of whom wishes..." It was also said: it is coordinated with "al-nas" (the people), meaning "most eager of people, and more eager than those who associated partners." On this view, His words "one of whom wishes" refer to the Jews, as an explanation of the increase in their eagerness for life. The reason for mentioning "those who associated partners" after "the people," although they are included among them, is to indicate the greater eagerness of the polytheists among the Arabs and those who resembled them from others.

So whoever is more eager than them, and they are the Jews, has gone to an extreme of eagerness whose measure cannot be estimated.

They reached this extreme of eagerness that exceeds the eagerness of the polytheists only because they know what punishment awaits them in the Hereafter. Unlike the polytheists among the Arabs and their like, they do not acknowledge that. Their eagerness for life was less than the eagerness of the Jews.

Although the first view involves a shift in the discourse from the Jews to others among the Arab polytheists, it is more likely because it does not entail imposing obligation, and there is no harm in digressing to mention the eagerness of the polytheists after mentioning the eagerness of the Jews.

Al-Razi said: the second view is more likely, so that this would be more forceful in nullifying their claim and in showing their lying in their saying that the abode of the Hereafter is ours and not for others. End.

It is answered that what he considered the preferred view has already been conveyed by His words, "And you will surely find them the most eager of people," and beginning a new discourse about the polytheists does not require that they not be among the people. The alif (of the number "a thousand") was singled out for mention because the Arabs used to mention it when intending exaggeration.

The origin of *sanah* (year) is *sanahah*, and it was said *sanawah*.

They differed regarding the pronoun in His words "wa-ma huwa bi-muzahzihi" (and it is not one who will remove him). It was said: it refers to "ahadihim" (one of them), and the implied meaning is: "and none of them will remove him from the punishment by being granted long life." On this view, "an yu‘ammar" (that he be granted long life) is the subject of *muzahzih*. It was also said: it refers to what is indicated by "yu‘ammar" (be granted long life) from its verbal noun, meaning "and the granting of long life will not remove him," and "an yu‘ammar" is then an appositive for it.

Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: "huwa" is a supporting pronoun (‘imad). It was also said: "huwa" is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha’n*). It was also said: "ma" is the Hijazi *ma* (the negation operating like *laysa*), its noun is the pronoun, and what follows it is its predicate. The first view is more likely, and so is the second. The third is very weak, because the supporting pronoun occurs only between two things, which is why they call it the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*). The fourth has the objection that the pronoun of the matter is explained by a full sentence free of a preposition, as Ibn ‘Atiyyah related from the grammarians.

*Al-zahzahah* means removing, as one says: "I pushed him and he moved away," meaning I moved him and he withdrew and went far off. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"O You who seize the soul from a body that has disobeyed for a time, and O Forgiver of sins, push me away from the Fire."*

*Al-basir* is one who knows a thing and is expert in it. From this is the saying: "So-and-so is *basir* in such-and-such," meaning expert in it. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"If you ask me about women, then I am an expert in women's ailments, a physician."*

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words, "And the calf was made to sink into their hearts," that he said: they were made to drink its love until that reached their hearts.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-‘Aliyah that when the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian," (and so on), the words of Allah, Exalted is He, were revealed: "Say: If the abode of the Hereafter is for you alone..." (and so on).

Ibn Jarir related the like of it from Qatadah.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala’il* related from Ibn ‘Abbas that His words "khalisatan min dun al-nas" (exclusively for you, apart from the people) mean the believers, and "fa-tamannaw al-mawt" (then wish for death) that the Messenger of Allah said to them: "If you are truthful in your statement, then say: O Allah, cause us to die. By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you will say it except that he will choke on his saliva and die in his place."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His words "fa-tamannaw al-mawt" that it means: invoke death against whichever of the two groups is the liar. But they refused that. Had they wished for it on the day he said that, not a Jew would have remained on the earth except that he died.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu Nu‘aym related from him that he said: "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of it from him.

Al-Bukhari and others related from his narration, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "If the Jews had wished, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim (p. 78) and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him regarding His words "and you will surely find them the most eager of people for life": he said, "The Jews." "And of those who associated partners": he said, "That is because the polytheists do not hope for resurrection after death, so he loves a long life. And the Jew knows what disgrace awaits him, because he wasted what knowledge he had." "And he is not one to remove him": he said, "one to remove him (from it)."

Sa‘id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from him regarding His words "one of them would love to be granted a thousand years" that he said: it is the saying of the non-Arabs when one of them sneezes: "*dh-h-z-arsal*," meaning "Live a thousand years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 2, verses 93–96:

The explanation of the taking of the covenant and the lifting of Mount Sinai has already passed.

The command to "listen" (al-sam‘) means obedience and acceptance, and it does not mean merely perceiving with the sense of hearing. From this comes the saying "Allah hears the one who praises Him" (sami‘a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning He accepts and responds. From this also is the poet's verse:

*"I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say"*

meaning, would not accept it. As for their answer, "We heard" (sami‘na), it is on its literal meaning and also on its figurative meaning: that is, "We heard your words with the sense of hearing, and we disobey you," meaning, "We do not accept what you command us." It is also possible that by their saying "We heard" they meant what was habitual from their trickery and their use of deception when addressing their prophets, by taking His words, "and listen" (wa-sma‘u), in their literal sense, namely hearing with the sense.

Then they answered, "We heard," meaning, "We perceived that with our ears, acting upon what You command." But since they knew that this was not what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended, and that His intention by the command to listen was the command to obey and accept, they did not confine themselves to this deception. Rather, they added to it what they considered the answer, and so they said, "and we disobey" (wa-‘asayna).

In His words "and they were made to drink" (wa-usribu) there is an eloquent metaphor, meaning: their hearts were made as if they drank the calf, because the love of the calf had taken firm hold in them. A similar expression is the verse of Zuhayr:

*"So I awoke from her after an inward love, and love is a disease that makes your heart drink it."*

He expressed the love of the calf by "drinking" rather than "eating" because the drinking of water penetrates the limbs until it reaches their inner parts, whereas food passes over them and does not penetrate them. The preposition "bi" in His words "bi-kufrihim" (because of their disbelief) is causal, meaning that this happened because of their disbelief, as a punishment for them and as abandonment (by Allah).

As for His words, "Say: Evil is that which your faith commands you" (qul bi'sama ya'murukum bihi iman-ukum), it means: your faith which you claim, that you believe in what was revealed to you and disbelieve in what is beyond it. For this act, which is your saying "We hear and we disobey," is in response to what you were commanded in your own Book, and the covenant was taken from you regarding it. The one who calls out to you with the most eloquent call is opposed to what you claim. Likewise, what has occurred from you of worshipping the calf and the descent of its love into your hearts in the manner of a drink is among the greatest things that show you are liars in your saying, "We believe in what was revealed to us," and not truthful. If you claim that your Book, in which you believed, commanded you this, then evil is that which your faith in your Book commands you. In this there is a mockery of them that is not hidden.

As for His words, "Say: If the abode of the Hereafter is for you alone (in-kanat lakumu al-dar al-akhirah)," it is a refutation of them, since they claimed that they would enter Paradise and that no one else would share their entry, and it is a binding argument against them by which it becomes clear that they are lying in that claim and that it issues from them without any proof. (p. 77) "Khalisatan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and the predicate of *kana* is "‘inda Allah" (with Allah). Or the predicate of *kana* is "khalisatan." The meaning of "khulus" (exclusivity) is that no one else shares it with them, if the *lam* in His words "min dun al-nas" (apart from the people) is for the genus. Or it means that the Muslims do not share it with them, if the *lam* is for a specific known group.

This is more likely, because of their saying in another verse: "And they said: None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." He commanded them to wish for death because whoever believes that he is among the people of Paradise would love death more than life. Since this was from them merely a claim, they held back.

For this reason He, Glorified is He, said: "But they will never wish for it, ever." The *ma* in His words "bi-ma qaddamat aydihim" (because of what their hands have sent forth) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: because of the sins that they sent forth, whose doer is not secure from punishment, but is not even hopeful of entering Paradise, let alone being certain of it, let alone it being exclusively theirs and specific to them. It was also said that Allah, Glorified is He, turned them away from wishing so that this would be a sign for His Prophet ﷺ.

What is meant by "wishing" here is the uttering of what indicates it, not merely its passing through the heart and the inclination of the soul toward it, for that is not intended in a situation of debate, in the places of dispute and the positions of challenge. In their abstaining from wishing, or their being turned away from it, there is a miracle for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for they used to adopt arrogance and boldness toward Allah and toward His prophets through false claims in many places, as the Revelation has related about them. So they left off their habit here only because of what had been established among them: that if they made that wish, death would descend upon them, either because of a matter they knew, or because of a turning away (*sarfah*) from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It may be said: It is established that the Prophet ﷺ forbade wishing for death, so how did Allah command him to tell them what is forbidden in his law?

The answer is that what is meant here is establishing the proof against them and the presenting of evidence for the falsity of their claim.

As for His words, "And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers," it is a threat to them and a recording against them that they are like that.

The *lam* in His words "wa-latajidanna-hum" (you will surely find them) is the answer to an implied oath, and the indefiniteness of "hayat" (life) is for belittling, meaning: they are the most eager of people for the most contemptible life and the least duration in this world. How then (would they be) with a long life and an extended stay? In the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) it says that he intended by the indefiniteness a specific life, namely the long-lasting life, and al-Razi followed him in that in his *Tafsir*.

As for His words "and from those who associated partners" (wa-min alladhina ashraku), it was said: it is a new independent sentence, and the implied meaning is: "and from those who associated partners are people, one of whom wishes..." It was also said: it is coordinated with "al-nas" (the people), meaning "most eager of people, and more eager than those who associated partners." On this view, His words "one of whom wishes" refer to the Jews, as an explanation of the increase in their eagerness for life. The reason for mentioning "those who associated partners" after "the people," although they are included among them, is to indicate the greater eagerness of the polytheists among the Arabs and those who resembled them from others.

So whoever is more eager than them, and they are the Jews, has gone to an extreme of eagerness whose measure cannot be estimated.

They reached this extreme of eagerness that exceeds the eagerness of the polytheists only because they know what punishment awaits them in the Hereafter. Unlike the polytheists among the Arabs and their like, they do not acknowledge that. Their eagerness for life was less than the eagerness of the Jews.

Although the first view involves a shift in the discourse from the Jews to others among the Arab polytheists, it is more likely because it does not entail imposing obligation, and there is no harm in digressing to mention the eagerness of the polytheists after mentioning the eagerness of the Jews.

Al-Razi said: the second view is more likely, so that this would be more forceful in nullifying their claim and in showing their lying in their saying that the abode of the Hereafter is ours and not for others. End.

It is answered that what he considered the preferred view has already been conveyed by His words, "And you will surely find them the most eager of people," and beginning a new discourse about the polytheists does not require that they not be among the people. The alif (of the number "a thousand") was singled out for mention because the Arabs used to mention it when intending exaggeration.

The origin of *sanah* (year) is *sanahah*, and it was said *sanawah*.

They differed regarding the pronoun in His words "wa-ma huwa bi-muzahzihi" (and it is not one who will remove him). It was said: it refers to "ahadihim" (one of them), and the implied meaning is: "and none of them will remove him from the punishment by being granted long life." On this view, "an yu‘ammar" (that he be granted long life) is the subject of *muzahzih*. It was also said: it refers to what is indicated by "yu‘ammar" (be granted long life) from its verbal noun, meaning "and the granting of long life will not remove him," and "an yu‘ammar" is then an appositive for it.

Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: "huwa" is a supporting pronoun (‘imad). It was also said: "huwa" is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha’n*). It was also said: "ma" is the Hijazi *ma* (the negation operating like *laysa*), its noun is the pronoun, and what follows it is its predicate. The first view is more likely, and so is the second. The third is very weak, because the supporting pronoun occurs only between two things, which is why they call it the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*). The fourth has the objection that the pronoun of the matter is explained by a full sentence free of a preposition, as Ibn ‘Atiyyah related from the grammarians.

*Al-zahzahah* means removing, as one says: "I pushed him and he moved away," meaning I moved him and he withdrew and went far off. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"O You who seize the soul from a body that has disobeyed for a time, and O Forgiver of sins, push me away from the Fire."*

*Al-basir* is one who knows a thing and is expert in it. From this is the saying: "So-and-so is *basir* in such-and-such," meaning expert in it. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"If you ask me about women, then I am an expert in women's ailments, a physician."*

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words, "And the calf was made to sink into their hearts," that he said: they were made to drink its love until that reached their hearts.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-‘Aliyah that when the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian," (and so on), the words of Allah, Exalted is He, were revealed: "Say: If the abode of the Hereafter is for you alone..." (and so on).

Ibn Jarir related the like of it from Qatadah.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala’il* related from Ibn ‘Abbas that His words "khalisatan min dun al-nas" (exclusively for you, apart from the people) mean the believers, and "fa-tamannaw al-mawt" (then wish for death) that the Messenger of Allah said to them: "If you are truthful in your statement, then say: O Allah, cause us to die. By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you will say it except that he will choke on his saliva and die in his place."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ‘Abbas regarding His words "fa-tamannaw al-mawt" that it means: invoke death against whichever of the two groups is the liar. But they refused that. Had they wished for it on the day he said that, not a Jew would have remained on the earth except that he died.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu Nu‘aym related from him that he said: "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of it from him.

Al-Bukhari and others related from his narration, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "If the Jews had wished, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim (p. 78) and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him regarding His words "and you will surely find them the most eager of people for life": he said, "The Jews." "And of those who associated partners": he said, "That is because the polytheists do not hope for resurrection after death, so he loves a long life. And the Jew knows what disgrace awaits him, because he wasted what knowledge he had." "And he is not one to remove him": he said, "one to remove him (from it)."

Sa‘id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from him regarding His words "one of them would love to be granted a thousand years" that he said: it is the saying of the non-Arabs when one of them sneezes: "*dh-h-z-arsal*," meaning "Live a thousand years."
