This is supported by the fact that Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan read "al-malikayni" with a kasra under the lam. Perhaps the reason for holding firmly to this interpretation, despite its distance and the evident strain in it, is to declare Allah free of sending sorcery down to His earth as a trial for His servants through the tongues of His angels.

But in my view there is no reason for this forced reading, which contradicts what is apparent. Allah, glorified is He, may test His servants with whatever He wills, as He tested them with the river of Talut. For this reason the two angels say: ﴿We are only a trial﴾. Ibn Jarir said: Many of the early scholars held that the two were angels from heaven, sent down to earth, and what happened to them happened. As for Babylon, it was said: it is Iraq; it was said: Nahawand; it was said: Nasibin; it was said: the West.

Harut and Marut are two non-Arabic names that take no nunation.

His words "And they do not teach anyone until they say": al-Zajjaj said: it is teaching of warning about sorcery, not teaching that calls to it. He said: this is what most scholars of language and analysis hold. Its meaning is that they teach it as a prohibition, saying to them: "Do not do such and such." The "min" in His words "from anyone" is extra for emphasis. It has been said that the word "yu'allimani" is from informing (i'lam), not from teaching (ta'lim). Tu'allamu, meaning "to inform," has come in Arabic speech, as transmitted by Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn al-A'rabi, and it is frequent in their poetry, such as the words of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You know, Messenger of Allah, that you will overtake me, and that your threat is like seizing by the hand."

And al-Qatami said:

"You know that after error there is guidance, and that for that error there is clearing."

His words "We are only a trial" are to be taken literally. That is: we are only a test and examination from Allah for His servants. It was also said that it is a mockery from them both, because they only say it to one whose misguidance they are certain of. In their words "So do not disbelieve" is the most eloquent warning and the greatest caution, meaning: this is a sin, and whoever commits it is a disbeliever; so do not disbelieve. In it is evidence that learning sorcery is disbelief, and its apparent meaning makes no distinction between one who believes in it and one who does not, nor between one who learns it in order to become a sorcerer and one who learns it in order to be able to repel it.

His words "from them they learn that by which they separate a man from his wife": the ascription of separation to the sorcerers, and making sorcery the cause of it, is evidence that sorcery has effect upon hearts through love and hatred, union and division, closeness and distance.

A group of scholars held that the sorcerer cannot do more than what Allah has mentioned of separation, since Allah mentioned this in the context of blaming sorcery and explained what is its ultimate purpose in being taught; so if he could do more than that, He would have mentioned it.

Another group said that this came out in the manner of what is most usual, and that the sorcerer can do other than what is specifically mentioned. It was also said: sorcery has no effect in itself at all, on the basis of His words: ﴿And they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission﴾. The truth is that there is no contradiction between His words "they learn from them what they separate by it between a man and his wife" and His words "and they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission," for what is derived from all of this is that sorcery has an effect in itself, but it causes harm only to those upon whom Allah has permitted its effect.

The people of knowledge have agreed that it has an effect in itself and a real established existence. Only the Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa disagreed, as has been mentioned.

His words "and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them" are an explicit statement that sorcery does not return to its practitioner with any benefit, nor does it bring him any gain; rather it is pure harm and utter loss.

The "lam" in His words "And they had certainly known" is the answer to an omitted oath. In His words "for whoever purchases it" the lam is for emphasis, and "man" is a relative pronoun in a nominative place as the subject, and the predicate is His words "he has no share in the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said that it is conditional for requital. Al-Zajjaj said: this is not a place for a condition, and he preferred that it is a relative as we have mentioned.

By "purchase" here is meant exchange, that is: whoever exchanged what the devils recite for the Book of Allah.

"Khalaq" (share), according to the lexicographers, means portion; so said al-Zajjaj.

By His words "for which they sold their souls" is meant: they sold them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 2 of 3):

Allah affirmed knowledge for them in His saying: ﴿And they had certainly known﴾, and negated it from them in His saying: ﴿if only they knew﴾. The scholars differed over how this is to be understood. Qutrub and al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) said: the intended subject of His saying ﴿And they had certainly known﴾ is the devils (al-shayatin), and the intended subject of His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾ is mankind (al-ins).

Al-Zajjaj said: the first [occurrence] refers to the two angels, even though it is in the plural form, and it is like the saying of the Arabs: "al-Zaydan qamu" (the two Zayds stood up, using plural verbs for a dual subject).

The second refers to the scholars of the Jews, and He said ﴿if only they knew﴾ because they abandoned acting upon their knowledge.

His saying ﴿And if only they had believed﴾ means: in the Prophet (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Qur'an, ﴿and had been mindful of Allah﴾, [and] avoided what they had fallen into of sorcery and disbelief. The lam in His saying ﴿a reward﴾ (lamathubatun) is the answer to "law" (if), and al-mathubah means the reward (al-thawab).

Al-Akhfash said: the answer is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "And if they had believed and been mindful of Allah, they would surely have been rewarded," and it was omitted because His saying ﴿a reward﴾ indicates it. (p-81) As for His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾, it is either to indicate that they have no knowledge, or to treat their knowledge, when accompanied by no action, as if it were nonexistent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas: "Ibn Suriya said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, you have brought us nothing that is recognised, and Allah has sent down to you no clear sign,' so Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾." And Malik ibn al-Sayf said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent and [the Prophet] reminded them of the covenant that had been taken from them and what had been enjoined upon them concerning Muhammad: "By Allah, no covenant was ever made with us concerning Muhammad, and nothing was taken from us," so Allah revealed: ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾ [the verse].

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding His saying "clear signs": "You recite it to them, and you inform them of it morning and evening and in between, while you are among them an unlettered man who has not read the Book, and you inform them of what is in their hands exactly as it is. In that is a lesson for them and a proof against them ﴿if only they knew﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying "[one] threw it away," he said: "he broke it."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿confirming what was with them﴾, he said: "When Muhammad came to them, they opposed him with the Torah, and the Torah and the Qur'an agreed, so they threw the Torah away and took up the Book of Asif and the sorcery of Harut and Marut, as if they did not know what was in the Torah of the command to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and to confirm him."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The devils used to eavesdrop on the heaven, and whenever one of them heard a word of truth, he would add to it a thousand lies. These were absorbed into the hearts of people, and they made them into registers (dawawin). Allah informed Sulayman ibn Dawud of this, so he seized them and buried them beneath the throne. When Sulayman died, a devil stood up on the road and said: 'Shall I direct you to the treasure of Sulayman, of which no one has a treasure like it, the guarded one?' They said: 'Yes,' so they dug it up, and behold, it was sorcery. So the nations copied it (fatanasakhat al-umam)."

And Allah revealed the excuse of Sulayman regarding what they had said of sorcery, so He said: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ [the verse].

An-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "Asif was the scribe of Sulayman, and he knew the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). He used to write everything on Sulayman's command and bury it beneath his throne. When Sulayman died, the devils brought it out, and they wrote between every two lines sorcery and disbelief, and said: 'This is what Sulayman used to practise.' The ignorant among the people disbelieved him and reviled him, and their scholars stood aside. Their ignorant ones continued to revile him until Allah sent down to Muhammad: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "When Sulayman wished to enter the privy or attend to some matter of his, he would give his ring to al-Jaradah, who was his wife. One day, when Allah willed to test Sulayman with what He tested him with, he gave al-Jaradah his ring, and the devil came in the form of Sulayman and said to her: 'Give me my ring,' and he took it and put it on. When he put it on, the devils, the jinn and mankind submitted to him. Then Sulayman came and said: 'Give me my ring,' and she said: 'You lie, you are not Sulayman.' So he knew that it was a trial with which he had been tested. The devils then went and wrote books during those days, containing sorcery and disbelief, then buried them beneath the throne of Sulayman, then dug them up and recited them to the people, saying: 'Sulayman only overcame the people by these books.' So the people disassociated themselves from Sulayman and accused him of disbelief, until Allah sent Muhammad and revealed to him: ﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they follow."

He also transmitted from Ata' regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they bring about (nura-hu ma tuhdith)."

He also transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾, he said: "during the kingdom of Sulayman."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "This is another sorcery with which they disputed. The speech of the angels among themselves, if mankind learned it and it was made and acted upon, would be sorcery."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "Allah did not send down sorcery."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, who said: "They are two angels from among the angels of heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from him through another route, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet).

Al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, meaning Jibril and Mika'il, ﴿at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾, who teach people sorcery.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza that he used to recite it: "and what was sent down to the two kings, Dawud and Sulayman."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "They are two men (ilj) from the people of Babylon."

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels looked down upon the world and saw the children of Adam disobeying, so they said: 'O Lord, how ignorant these people are, how little they know of Your greatness!' Allah said: 'If you were in their places, you would have disobeyed Me.' They said: 'How could that be, when we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?' He said: 'Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. Then they were sent down to the earth, and the desires of the children of Adam were placed in them, and a woman was presented to them, and they did not resist until they committed the sin. Allah said: 'Choose between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'What do you say?' He said: 'I say that the punishment of this world ends, and the punishment of the Hereafter does not end.' So they chose the punishment of this world. They are the two whom Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾" [the verse].

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Umar that he used to say: "Has al-Hamra' risen yet?" and when he saw it, he said: "No welcome." Then he said: "Two angels, Harut and Marut, asked Allah to send them down to the earth, so they were sent down to the earth and judged between the people. When evening came, they spoke words and ascended with them to heaven. A woman of the most beautiful women was appointed for them, and desire was cast upon them, and they began to delay her, and it was cast into their hearts. They continued doing so until she promised them a rendezvous. She came to them at the appointed time and said: 'Teach me the word with which you ascend.' So they taught her the word, and she spoke it and ascended to heaven, and she was transformed and made into what you see. When they came at evening and spoke the word, they did not ascend. Then it was sent to them: 'If you wish, [it is] the punishment of the Hereafter, and if you wish, [it is] the punishment of this world until the Hour rises, on condition that you meet Allah; if He wills, He will punish you, and if He wills, He will (p-82) have mercy on you.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'Rather, we choose the punishment of this world, a thousand thousand times,' so they are punished until the Day of Resurrection."

This story has been narrated from Ibn Umar in various wordings. In some versions, Ibn Umar narrates it from Ka'b al-Ahbar, as Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab (al-Iman) transmitted through al-Thawri, from Musa ibn Uqba, from Salim, from Ibn Umar, from Ka'b, who said: "The angels mentioned the deeds of the children of Adam and the sins they commit, so it was said to them: 'If you were in their place, you would commit the same as they commit. Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. He said to them: 'I am sending messengers to the children of Adam, but there is no messenger between Me and you. Descend, do not associate anything with Me, do not commit adultery, and do not drink wine.' Ka'b said: 'By Allah, they had not yet reached evening on the day they were sent down until they had committed everything they had been forbidden.'"

Ibn Kathir said: "This is more authentic," meaning of the two chains of transmission he mentioned before it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "This star, the Arabs call it al-Zuhrah, and the non-Arabs call it Anahid." He mentioned something similar to the earlier narration from Ibn Umar in al-Hakim.

Ibn Kathir said: "The men of this chain are trustworthy (thiqat), but it is extremely strange (gharib jiddan)."

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Zuhrah was a woman."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from him: "The woman with whom the two angels were tempted was transformed, and she is this red constellation, meaning al-Zuhrah."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab transmitted from him, and he mentioned a long story, in which there is an explicit statement that the two angels drank wine, committed adultery with the woman, and killed her.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas this story, and both said: "The Zuhrah was sent down to them in the form of a woman, and they fell into the sin."

Many long stories and varied narrations have been related on this subject, which al-Suyuti compiled fully in al-Durr al-Manthur. Ibn Kathir mentioned some of them in his Tafsir, then said: "The story of Harut and Marut has been related from a group of the Followers (tabi'un) such as Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Zuhri, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and others, and many of the exegetes, earlier and later, have recounted it."

Its substance, in its details, goes back to the reports of the Children of Israel (isra'iliyyat), for there is no sound marfu' hadith in it with a connected chain (isnad) to the truthful, believed one (al-sadiq al-masdduq), the infallible, who does not speak from desire. The apparent context of the Qur'an is a summary of the story without elaboration or lengthy detail. So we believe in what came in the Qur'an as Allah intended it, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi, after quoting some of this, said: "We say: all of this is weak and far from Ibn Umar and others; nothing of it is authentic, for it is a claim that the principles (usul) of the religion reject concerning the angels, who are the trustees of Allah over His revelation and His messengers to His prophets, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded." Then he mentioned something to the effect that reason permits such a thing to happen from them, but the occurrence of this permissible matter is not known except through revelation (al-sam'), and it has not been authenticated. End of quote.

I say: this is merely an assumption of improbability. The Mighty Book has come in this place with what you see, and there is no basis for taking it out of its apparent meaning through these strained interpretations. As for his claim that the principles reject this, even if these principles exist, they are specified by what occurred in this story, and there is no basis for refusing such a specification. Iblis himself held a great station and became the most evil of creatures and the most disbelieving of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿We are only a trial﴾, he said: "a test (bala')."

Al-Bazzar with a sound chain and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) or a sorcerer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was sent down to Muhammad."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Bazzar narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever practises augury (tiyarah) or has it practised for him, or practises soothsaying (kahanah) or has it practised for him, or practises sorcery (sihr) or has it practised for him, and whoever ties a knot (for sorcery), and whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) and believes what he says, has indeed disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Safwan ibn Sulaym, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever learns anything of sorcery, little or much, will have his last share from Allah (i.e., he will be deprived of Allah's mercy)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, "from any share (min khalaq)," that he said: "Min khalaq means min qiwam (a portion/sustenance)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: "Min khalaq means min nasib (a share)." Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿They will have no share of it in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "He has no religion."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His words, ﴿And how evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾, that he said: "They sold."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His words, "a reward (lamathubah)," that he said: "A reward (thawab)."

The pronoun in His words "to you" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: We sent down clear signs indicating your prophethood.

His words "except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)" have already had their interpretation given. The apparent meaning is that the intended reference is the category of the defiantly disobedient, though it is also possible that the Jews are meant, since the discourse is addressed to them.

The "wa" (and) in His words "Awa-kullama" (Is it then that every time) is a conjunction, and the interrogative hamza has entered upon it, just as it enters upon the fa'. Among examples of this are His words, exalted is He: ﴿Afa-hukma al-jahiliyyati yabghun﴾ ("Is it the judgment of the time of ignorance that they seek?"), ﴿Afa-anta tusmi'u al-summ﴾ ("Then can you make the deaf hear?"), ﴿Afa-tattakhidhunahu wa-dhurriyyatahu﴾ ("Will you then take him and his offspring?"). And it enters upon thumma (then), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Athumma idha ma waqa'a﴾ ("Then, when it has occurred?"). This is the view of Sibawayh.

Al-Akhfash said: the wa is extra (zaʾida).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is originally "aw" (or), and the wa was vocalized for ease of pronunciation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: all of this is far-fetched (mutakallif), and the correct view is the opinion of Sibawayh, with the conjoined element omitted. The intended meaning is: "Did they disbelieve in the clear signs, and every time they made a covenant...?"

His words "a party of them threw away" (nabadha fariq): Ibn Jarir said: the root meaning of nabdh is to cast away and throw down, and from it the foundling is called manbudh (cast-off), and from it nabidh is named, which is dates and raisins when put into water. Abu al-Aswad said:

"You looked at its title and cast it aside, as you cast aside a sandal that has worn out from your shoes."

Another said:

"Those whom you commanded to act justly have cast aside your Book, and what is forbidden has been made lawful."

His words "behind their backs" (wara'a zuhurihim) mean behind their backs. This is a proverbial expression used for one who makes light of a matter and does not act upon it. The Arabs say: "Make this behind your back, and behind your ear, and under your foot," meaning: leave it and turn away from it. Among such usage is what al-Farra' recited:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, let not my need be behind (bi-zahr), so that its answer does not weary me."

His words "the Book of Allah" means the Torah, because when they disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) and in what was revealed to him, after Allah had taken from them in the Torah the covenant of faith in him, of confirming him, following him, and had explained to them his attributes, that was from them a casting away of the Torah, a breaking of it, and a rejection of what is in it. It is also possible that "the Book" here means the Qur'an, that is: when there came to them a messenger of Allah from Allah, confirming what they had with them of the Torah, they cast away the Book of Allah which this messenger brought. This is more evident than the first interpretation.

His words "as if they did not know" are a comparison of them to one who knows nothing, although they knew with certain knowledge from the Torah what was obligatory upon them of faith in this Prophet. But since they did not act upon knowledge, rather they acted as one who does not know, by casting away the Book of Allah behind their backs, they were in the position of one who does not know.

His words "and they followed what the devils recited" are conjoined to His words "cast away", meaning: they cast away the Book of Allah and followed what the devils recited of sorcery and the like.

Al-Tabari said: "followed" (ittaba'u) means "did."

The meaning of "recited" (tatlu) is "made up and read." "Over the kingdom of Sulayman" means "in the time of the kingdom of Sulayman," as said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: the meaning is "in the kingdom of Sulayman," that is, in his stories, attributes and reports. Al-Farra' said: "ʿala" and "fi" are both suitable in this place, though the first is more evident.

They used to think that this was the knowledge of Sulayman, and that he permitted it and taught it. Allah refuted this for them and said: ﴿Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾. Nobody had previously attributed disbelief to Sulayman, but when the Jews attributed sorcery to him, they became like those who attributed disbelief to him, because sorcery necessitates that. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, affirmed the disbelief of the devils, saying: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾, meaning: by teaching it.

His words "teaching people sorcery" are in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it may be in a place of nominative as a second predicate after a predicate.

Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans other than 'Asim read "wa-lakini al-shayatinu" with the lightened "lakin" and the nominative "al-shayatin," while the rest read with the doubled and accusative form.

Sihr (sorcery): it is what the sorcerer does of tricks and imaginings, through which there arises in the bewitched person the corrupt impressions resembling what happens to one who sees a mirage and thinks it water, and what the rider of a ship or beast imagines, that the mountains are moving. It is derived from "sahartu al-sabiyy," meaning: when you deceive him. It was said: its root is concealment, for the sorcerer does it secretly. It was said: its root is diversion, because sorcery is turned away from its course. It was said: its root is seduction, because whoever bewitches you has won you over.

Al-Jawhari said: sihr is seizure (akhdha), and everything that is subtle and fine is sihr. One says "sahara-hu yasharu-hu sihran," and the sahir is the knowledgeable one; "sahara-hu" also means "deceived him."

It has been disputed whether it has a real existence or not. The Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa held that it is deception with no basis and no reality. Others held that it has a real, effective existence.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) was bewitched: Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, bewitched him until it seemed to him that he was doing a thing when he had not done it. Then Allah, glorified is He, healed him. The discussion of this is lengthy.

His words "and what was sent down to the two angels": meaning, and they taught people what was sent down to the two angels, so it is conjoined to sorcery. It was also said: it is conjoined to His words "what the devils recited," meaning: they followed what Allah sent down to the two angels.

It was also said: the "ma" in His words "and what was sent down to the two angels" is a negation, and the wa is conjunctive to His words "Sulayman did not disbelieve," and there is inversion in the speech; the intended sense is: "Sulayman did not disbelieve, nor was what was sent down to the two angels [disbelief], but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babylon, Harut and Marut." So Harut and Marut is a substitution (badal) for the devils in His words "but the devils disbelieved." Ibn Jarir mentioned this and said: if someone asks us, "How is this arrangement?", it is said: the arrangement is that it be said: they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman, and Sulayman did not disbelieve, and what Allah sent down to the two angels, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Then "the two angels" means Jibril and Mika'il, because the Jewish sorcerers, as is mentioned, claimed that Allah sent down sorcery through the tongue of Jibril and Mika'il to Sulayman son of Dawud. So Allah refuted them in that, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that Jibril and Mika'il did not descend with sorcery, cleared Sulayman of what they attributed to him of sorcery, and informed them that sorcery is the work of the devils, and that they teach people this at Babylon, and that the ones who teach them are two men, one named Harut and the other Marut. So on this interpretation Harut and Marut are a translation (tarjama) for "the people" and a refutation of them. End.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir, after relating the meaning of this statement and preferring that Harut and Marut are a substitution for the devils, the following: "This is the best that the verse can be taken to mean, and the most sound of what has been said about it, and nothing else should be considered." So sorcery is drawn from the devils because of the subtlety of their substance and the fineness of their understanding, and most of what is practised among humans is done by women, especially during their menstruation. Allah says: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Then he said: If it is said, how can two be a substitute for a plural, when the substitute must conform to the substituted? He answered that by saying that two may be called a plural, or that they were singled out for mention rather than others because of their rebelliousness. This is supported by the fact that Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan read "al-malikayni" with a kasra under the lam. Perhaps the reason for holding firmly to this interpretation, despite its distance and the evident strain in it, is to declare Allah free of sending sorcery down to His earth as a trial for His servants through the tongues of His angels.

But in my view there is no reason for this forced reading, which contradicts what is apparent. Allah, glorified is He, may test His servants with whatever He wills, as He tested them with the river of Talut. For this reason the two angels say: ﴿We are only a trial﴾. Ibn Jarir said: Many of the early scholars held that the two were angels from heaven, sent down to earth, and what happened to them happened. As for Babylon, it was said: it is Iraq; it was said: Nahawand; it was said: Nasibin; it was said: the West.

Harut and Marut are two non-Arabic names that take no nunation.

His words "And they do not teach anyone until they say": al-Zajjaj said: it is teaching of warning about sorcery, not teaching that calls to it. He said: this is what most scholars of language and analysis hold. Its meaning is that they teach it as a prohibition, saying to them: "Do not do such and such." The "min" in His words "from anyone" is extra for emphasis. It has been said that the word "yu'allimani" is from informing (i'lam), not from teaching (ta'lim). Tu'allamu, meaning "to inform," has come in Arabic speech, as transmitted by Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn al-A'rabi, and it is frequent in their poetry, such as the words of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You know, Messenger of Allah, that you will overtake me, and that your threat is like seizing by the hand."

And al-Qatami said:

"You know that after error there is guidance, and that for that error there is clearing."

His words "We are only a trial" are to be taken literally. That is: we are only a test and examination from Allah for His servants. It was also said that it is a mockery from them both, because they only say it to one whose misguidance they are certain of. In their words "So do not disbelieve" is the most eloquent warning and the greatest caution, meaning: this is a sin, and whoever commits it is a disbeliever; so do not disbelieve. In it is evidence that learning sorcery is disbelief, and its apparent meaning makes no distinction between one who believes in it and one who does not, nor between one who learns it in order to become a sorcerer and one who learns it in order to be able to repel it.

His words "from them they learn that by which they separate a man from his wife": the ascription of separation to the sorcerers, and making sorcery the cause of it, is evidence that sorcery has effect upon hearts through love and hatred, union and division, closeness and distance.

A group of scholars held that the sorcerer cannot do more than what Allah has mentioned of separation, since Allah mentioned this in the context of blaming sorcery and explained what is its ultimate purpose in being taught; so if he could do more than that, He would have mentioned it.

Another group said that this came out in the manner of what is most usual, and that the sorcerer can do other than what is specifically mentioned. It was also said: sorcery has no effect in itself at all, on the basis of His words: ﴿And they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission﴾. The truth is that there is no contradiction between His words "they learn from them what they separate by it between a man and his wife" and His words "and they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission," for what is derived from all of this is that sorcery has an effect in itself, but it causes harm only to those upon whom Allah has permitted its effect.

The people of knowledge have agreed that it has an effect in itself and a real established existence. Only the Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa disagreed, as has been mentioned.

His words "and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them" are an explicit statement that sorcery does not return to its practitioner with any benefit, nor does it bring him any gain; rather it is pure harm and utter loss.

The "lam" in His words "And they had certainly known" is the answer to an omitted oath. In His words "for whoever purchases it" the lam is for emphasis, and "man" is a relative pronoun in a nominative place as the subject, and the predicate is His words "he has no share in the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said that it is conditional for requital. Al-Zajjaj said: this is not a place for a condition, and he preferred that it is a relative as we have mentioned.

By "purchase" here is meant exchange, that is: whoever exchanged what the devils recite for the Book of Allah.

"Khalaq" (share), according to the lexicographers, means portion; so said al-Zajjaj.

By His words "for which they sold their souls" is meant: they sold them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 2 of 3):

Allah affirmed knowledge for them in His saying: ﴿And they had certainly known﴾, and negated it from them in His saying: ﴿if only they knew﴾. The scholars differed over how this is to be understood. Qutrub and al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) said: the intended subject of His saying ﴿And they had certainly known﴾ is the devils (al-shayatin), and the intended subject of His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾ is mankind (al-ins).

Al-Zajjaj said: the first [occurrence] refers to the two angels, even though it is in the plural form, and it is like the saying of the Arabs: "al-Zaydan qamu" (the two Zayds stood up, using plural verbs for a dual subject).

The second refers to the scholars of the Jews, and He said ﴿if only they knew﴾ because they abandoned acting upon their knowledge.

His saying ﴿And if only they had believed﴾ means: in the Prophet (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Qur'an, ﴿and had been mindful of Allah﴾, [and] avoided what they had fallen into of sorcery and disbelief. The lam in His saying ﴿a reward﴾ (lamathubatun) is the answer to "law" (if), and al-mathubah means the reward (al-thawab).

Al-Akhfash said: the answer is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "And if they had believed and been mindful of Allah, they would surely have been rewarded," and it was omitted because His saying ﴿a reward﴾ indicates it. (p-81) As for His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾, it is either to indicate that they have no knowledge, or to treat their knowledge, when accompanied by no action, as if it were nonexistent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas: "Ibn Suriya said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, you have brought us nothing that is recognised, and Allah has sent down to you no clear sign,' so Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾." And Malik ibn al-Sayf said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent and [the Prophet] reminded them of the covenant that had been taken from them and what had been enjoined upon them concerning Muhammad: "By Allah, no covenant was ever made with us concerning Muhammad, and nothing was taken from us," so Allah revealed: ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾ [the verse].

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding His saying "clear signs": "You recite it to them, and you inform them of it morning and evening and in between, while you are among them an unlettered man who has not read the Book, and you inform them of what is in their hands exactly as it is. In that is a lesson for them and a proof against them ﴿if only they knew﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying "[one] threw it away," he said: "he broke it."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿confirming what was with them﴾, he said: "When Muhammad came to them, they opposed him with the Torah, and the Torah and the Qur'an agreed, so they threw the Torah away and took up the Book of Asif and the sorcery of Harut and Marut, as if they did not know what was in the Torah of the command to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and to confirm him."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The devils used to eavesdrop on the heaven, and whenever one of them heard a word of truth, he would add to it a thousand lies. These were absorbed into the hearts of people, and they made them into registers (dawawin). Allah informed Sulayman ibn Dawud of this, so he seized them and buried them beneath the throne. When Sulayman died, a devil stood up on the road and said: 'Shall I direct you to the treasure of Sulayman, of which no one has a treasure like it, the guarded one?' They said: 'Yes,' so they dug it up, and behold, it was sorcery. So the nations copied it (fatanasakhat al-umam)."

And Allah revealed the excuse of Sulayman regarding what they had said of sorcery, so He said: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ [the verse].

An-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "Asif was the scribe of Sulayman, and he knew the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). He used to write everything on Sulayman's command and bury it beneath his throne. When Sulayman died, the devils brought it out, and they wrote between every two lines sorcery and disbelief, and said: 'This is what Sulayman used to practise.' The ignorant among the people disbelieved him and reviled him, and their scholars stood aside. Their ignorant ones continued to revile him until Allah sent down to Muhammad: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "When Sulayman wished to enter the privy or attend to some matter of his, he would give his ring to al-Jaradah, who was his wife. One day, when Allah willed to test Sulayman with what He tested him with, he gave al-Jaradah his ring, and the devil came in the form of Sulayman and said to her: 'Give me my ring,' and he took it and put it on. When he put it on, the devils, the jinn and mankind submitted to him. Then Sulayman came and said: 'Give me my ring,' and she said: 'You lie, you are not Sulayman.' So he knew that it was a trial with which he had been tested. The devils then went and wrote books during those days, containing sorcery and disbelief, then buried them beneath the throne of Sulayman, then dug them up and recited them to the people, saying: 'Sulayman only overcame the people by these books.' So the people disassociated themselves from Sulayman and accused him of disbelief, until Allah sent Muhammad and revealed to him: ﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they follow."

He also transmitted from Ata' regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they bring about (nura-hu ma tuhdith)."

He also transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾, he said: "during the kingdom of Sulayman."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "This is another sorcery with which they disputed. The speech of the angels among themselves, if mankind learned it and it was made and acted upon, would be sorcery."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "Allah did not send down sorcery."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, who said: "They are two angels from among the angels of heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from him through another route, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet).

Al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, meaning Jibril and Mika'il, ﴿at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾, who teach people sorcery.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza that he used to recite it: "and what was sent down to the two kings, Dawud and Sulayman."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "They are two men (ilj) from the people of Babylon."

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels looked down upon the world and saw the children of Adam disobeying, so they said: 'O Lord, how ignorant these people are, how little they know of Your greatness!' Allah said: 'If you were in their places, you would have disobeyed Me.' They said: 'How could that be, when we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?' He said: 'Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. Then they were sent down to the earth, and the desires of the children of Adam were placed in them, and a woman was presented to them, and they did not resist until they committed the sin. Allah said: 'Choose between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'What do you say?' He said: 'I say that the punishment of this world ends, and the punishment of the Hereafter does not end.' So they chose the punishment of this world. They are the two whom Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾" [the verse].

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Umar that he used to say: "Has al-Hamra' risen yet?" and when he saw it, he said: "No welcome." Then he said: "Two angels, Harut and Marut, asked Allah to send them down to the earth, so they were sent down to the earth and judged between the people. When evening came, they spoke words and ascended with them to heaven. A woman of the most beautiful women was appointed for them, and desire was cast upon them, and they began to delay her, and it was cast into their hearts. They continued doing so until she promised them a rendezvous. She came to them at the appointed time and said: 'Teach me the word with which you ascend.' So they taught her the word, and she spoke it and ascended to heaven, and she was transformed and made into what you see. When they came at evening and spoke the word, they did not ascend. Then it was sent to them: 'If you wish, [it is] the punishment of the Hereafter, and if you wish, [it is] the punishment of this world until the Hour rises, on condition that you meet Allah; if He wills, He will punish you, and if He wills, He will (p-82) have mercy on you.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'Rather, we choose the punishment of this world, a thousand thousand times,' so they are punished until the Day of Resurrection."

This story has been narrated from Ibn Umar in various wordings. In some versions, Ibn Umar narrates it from Ka'b al-Ahbar, as Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab (al-Iman) transmitted through al-Thawri, from Musa ibn Uqba, from Salim, from Ibn Umar, from Ka'b, who said: "The angels mentioned the deeds of the children of Adam and the sins they commit, so it was said to them: 'If you were in their place, you would commit the same as they commit. Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. He said to them: 'I am sending messengers to the children of Adam, but there is no messenger between Me and you. Descend, do not associate anything with Me, do not commit adultery, and do not drink wine.' Ka'b said: 'By Allah, they had not yet reached evening on the day they were sent down until they had committed everything they had been forbidden.'"

Ibn Kathir said: "This is more authentic," meaning of the two chains of transmission he mentioned before it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "This star, the Arabs call it al-Zuhrah, and the non-Arabs call it Anahid." He mentioned something similar to the earlier narration from Ibn Umar in al-Hakim.

Ibn Kathir said: "The men of this chain are trustworthy (thiqat), but it is extremely strange (gharib jiddan)."

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Zuhrah was a woman."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from him: "The woman with whom the two angels were tempted was transformed, and she is this red constellation, meaning al-Zuhrah."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab transmitted from him, and he mentioned a long story, in which there is an explicit statement that the two angels drank wine, committed adultery with the woman, and killed her.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas this story, and both said: "The Zuhrah was sent down to them in the form of a woman, and they fell into the sin."

Many long stories and varied narrations have been related on this subject, which al-Suyuti compiled fully in al-Durr al-Manthur. Ibn Kathir mentioned some of them in his Tafsir, then said: "The story of Harut and Marut has been related from a group of the Followers (tabi'un) such as Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Zuhri, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and others, and many of the exegetes, earlier and later, have recounted it."

Its substance, in its details, goes back to the reports of the Children of Israel (isra'iliyyat), for there is no sound marfu' hadith in it with a connected chain (isnad) to the truthful, believed one (al-sadiq al-masdduq), the infallible, who does not speak from desire. The apparent context of the Qur'an is a summary of the story without elaboration or lengthy detail. So we believe in what came in the Qur'an as Allah intended it, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi, after quoting some of this, said: "We say: all of this is weak and far from Ibn Umar and others; nothing of it is authentic, for it is a claim that the principles (usul) of the religion reject concerning the angels, who are the trustees of Allah over His revelation and His messengers to His prophets, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded." Then he mentioned something to the effect that reason permits such a thing to happen from them, but the occurrence of this permissible matter is not known except through revelation (al-sam'), and it has not been authenticated. End of quote.

I say: this is merely an assumption of improbability. The Mighty Book has come in this place with what you see, and there is no basis for taking it out of its apparent meaning through these strained interpretations. As for his claim that the principles reject this, even if these principles exist, they are specified by what occurred in this story, and there is no basis for refusing such a specification. Iblis himself held a great station and became the most evil of creatures and the most disbelieving of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿We are only a trial﴾, he said: "a test (bala')."

Al-Bazzar with a sound chain and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) or a sorcerer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was sent down to Muhammad."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Bazzar narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever practises augury (tiyarah) or has it practised for him, or practises soothsaying (kahanah) or has it practised for him, or practises sorcery (sihr) or has it practised for him, and whoever ties a knot (for sorcery), and whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) and believes what he says, has indeed disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Safwan ibn Sulaym, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever learns anything of sorcery, little or much, will have his last share from Allah (i.e., he will be deprived of Allah's mercy)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, "from any share (min khalaq)," that he said: "Min khalaq means min qiwam (a portion/sustenance)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: "Min khalaq means min nasib (a share)." Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿They will have no share of it in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "He has no religion."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His words, ﴿And how evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾, that he said: "They sold."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His words, "a reward (lamathubah)," that he said: "A reward (thawab)."

The pronoun in His words "to you" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: We sent down clear signs indicating your prophethood.

His words "except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)" have already had their interpretation given. The apparent meaning is that the intended reference is the category of the defiantly disobedient, though it is also possible that the Jews are meant, since the discourse is addressed to them.

The "wa" (and) in His words "Awa-kullama" (Is it then that every time) is a conjunction, and the interrogative hamza has entered upon it, just as it enters upon the fa'. Among examples of this are His words, exalted is He: ﴿Afa-hukma al-jahiliyyati yabghun﴾ ("Is it the judgment of the time of ignorance that they seek?"), ﴿Afa-anta tusmi'u al-summ﴾ ("Then can you make the deaf hear?"), ﴿Afa-tattakhidhunahu wa-dhurriyyatahu﴾ ("Will you then take him and his offspring?"). And it enters upon thumma (then), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Athumma idha ma waqa'a﴾ ("Then, when it has occurred?"). This is the view of Sibawayh.

Al-Akhfash said: the wa is extra (zaʾida).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is originally "aw" (or), and the wa was vocalized for ease of pronunciation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: all of this is far-fetched (mutakallif), and the correct view is the opinion of Sibawayh, with the conjoined element omitted. The intended meaning is: "Did they disbelieve in the clear signs, and every time they made a covenant...?"

His words "a party of them threw away" (nabadha fariq): Ibn Jarir said: the root meaning of nabdh is to cast away and throw down, and from it the foundling is called manbudh (cast-off), and from it nabidh is named, which is dates and raisins when put into water. Abu al-Aswad said:

"You looked at its title and cast it aside, as you cast aside a sandal that has worn out from your shoes."

Another said:

"Those whom you commanded to act justly have cast aside your Book, and what is forbidden has been made lawful."

His words "behind their backs" (wara'a zuhurihim) mean behind their backs. This is a proverbial expression used for one who makes light of a matter and does not act upon it. The Arabs say: "Make this behind your back, and behind your ear, and under your foot," meaning: leave it and turn away from it. Among such usage is what al-Farra' recited:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, let not my need be behind (bi-zahr), so that its answer does not weary me."

His words "the Book of Allah" means the Torah, because when they disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) and in what was revealed to him, after Allah had taken from them in the Torah the covenant of faith in him, of confirming him, following him, and had explained to them his attributes, that was from them a casting away of the Torah, a breaking of it, and a rejection of what is in it. It is also possible that "the Book" here means the Qur'an, that is: when there came to them a messenger of Allah from Allah, confirming what they had with them of the Torah, they cast away the Book of Allah which this messenger brought. This is more evident than the first interpretation.

His words "as if they did not know" are a comparison of them to one who knows nothing, although they knew with certain knowledge from the Torah what was obligatory upon them of faith in this Prophet. But since they did not act upon knowledge, rather they acted as one who does not know, by casting away the Book of Allah behind their backs, they were in the position of one who does not know.

His words "and they followed what the devils recited" are conjoined to His words "cast away", meaning: they cast away the Book of Allah and followed what the devils recited of sorcery and the like.

Al-Tabari said: "followed" (ittaba'u) means "did."

The meaning of "recited" (tatlu) is "made up and read." "Over the kingdom of Sulayman" means "in the time of the kingdom of Sulayman," as said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: the meaning is "in the kingdom of Sulayman," that is, in his stories, attributes and reports. Al-Farra' said: "ʿala" and "fi" are both suitable in this place, though the first is more evident.

They used to think that this was the knowledge of Sulayman, and that he permitted it and taught it. Allah refuted this for them and said: ﴿Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾. Nobody had previously attributed disbelief to Sulayman, but when the Jews attributed sorcery to him, they became like those who attributed disbelief to him, because sorcery necessitates that. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, affirmed the disbelief of the devils, saying: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾, meaning: by teaching it.

His words "teaching people sorcery" are in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it may be in a place of nominative as a second predicate after a predicate.

Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans other than 'Asim read "wa-lakini al-shayatinu" with the lightened "lakin" and the nominative "al-shayatin," while the rest read with the doubled and accusative form.

Sihr (sorcery): it is what the sorcerer does of tricks and imaginings, through which there arises in the bewitched person the corrupt impressions resembling what happens to one who sees a mirage and thinks it water, and what the rider of a ship or beast imagines, that the mountains are moving. It is derived from "sahartu al-sabiyy," meaning: when you deceive him. It was said: its root is concealment, for the sorcerer does it secretly. It was said: its root is diversion, because sorcery is turned away from its course. It was said: its root is seduction, because whoever bewitches you has won you over.

Al-Jawhari said: sihr is seizure (akhdha), and everything that is subtle and fine is sihr. One says "sahara-hu yasharu-hu sihran," and the sahir is the knowledgeable one; "sahara-hu" also means "deceived him."

It has been disputed whether it has a real existence or not. The Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa held that it is deception with no basis and no reality. Others held that it has a real, effective existence.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) was bewitched: Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, bewitched him until it seemed to him that he was doing a thing when he had not done it. Then Allah, glorified is He, healed him. The discussion of this is lengthy.

His words "and what was sent down to the two angels": meaning, and they taught people what was sent down to the two angels, so it is conjoined to sorcery. It was also said: it is conjoined to His words "what the devils recited," meaning: they followed what Allah sent down to the two angels.

It was also said: the "ma" in His words "and what was sent down to the two angels" is a negation, and the wa is conjunctive to His words "Sulayman did not disbelieve," and there is inversion in the speech; the intended sense is: "Sulayman did not disbelieve, nor was what was sent down to the two angels [disbelief], but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babylon, Harut and Marut." So Harut and Marut is a substitution (badal) for the devils in His words "but the devils disbelieved." Ibn Jarir mentioned this and said: if someone asks us, "How is this arrangement?", it is said: the arrangement is that it be said: they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman, and Sulayman did not disbelieve, and what Allah sent down to the two angels, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Then "the two angels" means Jibril and Mika'il, because the Jewish sorcerers, as is mentioned, claimed that Allah sent down sorcery through the tongue of Jibril and Mika'il to Sulayman son of Dawud. So Allah refuted them in that, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that Jibril and Mika'il did not descend with sorcery, cleared Sulayman of what they attributed to him of sorcery, and informed them that sorcery is the work of the devils, and that they teach people this at Babylon, and that the ones who teach them are two men, one named Harut and the other Marut. So on this interpretation Harut and Marut are a translation (tarjama) for "the people" and a refutation of them. End.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir, after relating the meaning of this statement and preferring that Harut and Marut are a substitution for the devils, the following: "This is the best that the verse can be taken to mean, and the most sound of what has been said about it, and nothing else should be considered." So sorcery is drawn from the devils because of the subtlety of their substance and the fineness of their understanding, and most of what is practised among humans is done by women, especially during their menstruation. Allah says: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Then he said: If it is said, how can two be a substitute for a plural, when the substitute must conform to the substituted? He answered that by saying that two may be called a plural, or that they were singled out for mention rather than others because of their rebelliousness. This is supported by the fact that Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan read "al-malikayni" with a kasra under the lam. Perhaps the reason for holding firmly to this interpretation, despite its distance and the evident strain in it, is to declare Allah free of sending sorcery down to His earth as a trial for His servants through the tongues of His angels.

But in my view there is no reason for this forced reading, which contradicts what is apparent. Allah, glorified is He, may test His servants with whatever He wills, as He tested them with the river of Talut. For this reason the two angels say: ﴿We are only a trial﴾. Ibn Jarir said: Many of the early scholars held that the two were angels from heaven, sent down to earth, and what happened to them happened. As for Babylon, it was said: it is Iraq; it was said: Nahawand; it was said: Nasibin; it was said: the West.

Harut and Marut are two non-Arabic names that take no nunation.

His words "And they do not teach anyone until they say": al-Zajjaj said: it is teaching of warning about sorcery, not teaching that calls to it. He said: this is what most scholars of language and analysis hold. Its meaning is that they teach it as a prohibition, saying to them: "Do not do such and such." The "min" in His words "from anyone" is extra for emphasis. It has been said that the word "yu'allimani" is from informing (i'lam), not from teaching (ta'lim). Tu'allamu, meaning "to inform," has come in Arabic speech, as transmitted by Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn al-A'rabi, and it is frequent in their poetry, such as the words of Ka'b ibn Malik:

"You know, Messenger of Allah, that you will overtake me, and that your threat is like seizing by the hand."

And al-Qatami said:

"You know that after error there is guidance, and that for that error there is clearing."

His words "We are only a trial" are to be taken literally. That is: we are only a test and examination from Allah for His servants. It was also said that it is a mockery from them both, because they only say it to one whose misguidance they are certain of. In their words "So do not disbelieve" is the most eloquent warning and the greatest caution, meaning: this is a sin, and whoever commits it is a disbeliever; so do not disbelieve. In it is evidence that learning sorcery is disbelief, and its apparent meaning makes no distinction between one who believes in it and one who does not, nor between one who learns it in order to become a sorcerer and one who learns it in order to be able to repel it.

His words "from them they learn that by which they separate a man from his wife": the ascription of separation to the sorcerers, and making sorcery the cause of it, is evidence that sorcery has effect upon hearts through love and hatred, union and division, closeness and distance.

A group of scholars held that the sorcerer cannot do more than what Allah has mentioned of separation, since Allah mentioned this in the context of blaming sorcery and explained what is its ultimate purpose in being taught; so if he could do more than that, He would have mentioned it.

Another group said that this came out in the manner of what is most usual, and that the sorcerer can do other than what is specifically mentioned. It was also said: sorcery has no effect in itself at all, on the basis of His words: ﴿And they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission﴾. The truth is that there is no contradiction between His words "they learn from them what they separate by it between a man and his wife" and His words "and they could not harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission," for what is derived from all of this is that sorcery has an effect in itself, but it causes harm only to those upon whom Allah has permitted its effect.

The people of knowledge have agreed that it has an effect in itself and a real established existence. Only the Mu'tazila and Abu Hanifa disagreed, as has been mentioned.

His words "and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them" are an explicit statement that sorcery does not return to its practitioner with any benefit, nor does it bring him any gain; rather it is pure harm and utter loss.

The "lam" in His words "And they had certainly known" is the answer to an omitted oath. In His words "for whoever purchases it" the lam is for emphasis, and "man" is a relative pronoun in a nominative place as the subject, and the predicate is His words "he has no share in the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said that it is conditional for requital. Al-Zajjaj said: this is not a place for a condition, and he preferred that it is a relative as we have mentioned.

By "purchase" here is meant exchange, that is: whoever exchanged what the devils recite for the Book of Allah.

"Khalaq" (share), according to the lexicographers, means portion; so said al-Zajjaj.

By His words "for which they sold their souls" is meant: they sold them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 2 of 3):

Allah affirmed knowledge for them in His saying: ﴿And they had certainly known﴾, and negated it from them in His saying: ﴿if only they knew﴾. The scholars differed over how this is to be understood. Qutrub and al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) said: the intended subject of His saying ﴿And they had certainly known﴾ is the devils (al-shayatin), and the intended subject of His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾ is mankind (al-ins).

Al-Zajjaj said: the first [occurrence] refers to the two angels, even though it is in the plural form, and it is like the saying of the Arabs: "al-Zaydan qamu" (the two Zayds stood up, using plural verbs for a dual subject).

The second refers to the scholars of the Jews, and He said ﴿if only they knew﴾ because they abandoned acting upon their knowledge.

His saying ﴿And if only they had believed﴾ means: in the Prophet (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Qur'an, ﴿and had been mindful of Allah﴾, [and] avoided what they had fallen into of sorcery and disbelief. The lam in His saying ﴿a reward﴾ (lamathubatun) is the answer to "law" (if), and al-mathubah means the reward (al-thawab).

Al-Akhfash said: the answer is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "And if they had believed and been mindful of Allah, they would surely have been rewarded," and it was omitted because His saying ﴿a reward﴾ indicates it. (p-81) As for His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾, it is either to indicate that they have no knowledge, or to treat their knowledge, when accompanied by no action, as if it were nonexistent.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas: "Ibn Suriya said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, you have brought us nothing that is recognised, and Allah has sent down to you no clear sign,' so Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾." And Malik ibn al-Sayf said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent and [the Prophet] reminded them of the covenant that had been taken from them and what had been enjoined upon them concerning Muhammad: "By Allah, no covenant was ever made with us concerning Muhammad, and nothing was taken from us," so Allah revealed: ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾ [the verse].

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding His saying "clear signs": "You recite it to them, and you inform them of it morning and evening and in between, while you are among them an unlettered man who has not read the Book, and you inform them of what is in their hands exactly as it is. In that is a lesson for them and a proof against them ﴿if only they knew﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying "[one] threw it away," he said: "he broke it."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿confirming what was with them﴾, he said: "When Muhammad came to them, they opposed him with the Torah, and the Torah and the Qur'an agreed, so they threw the Torah away and took up the Book of Asif and the sorcery of Harut and Marut, as if they did not know what was in the Torah of the command to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and to confirm him."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The devils used to eavesdrop on the heaven, and whenever one of them heard a word of truth, he would add to it a thousand lies. These were absorbed into the hearts of people, and they made them into registers (dawawin). Allah informed Sulayman ibn Dawud of this, so he seized them and buried them beneath the throne. When Sulayman died, a devil stood up on the road and said: 'Shall I direct you to the treasure of Sulayman, of which no one has a treasure like it, the guarded one?' They said: 'Yes,' so they dug it up, and behold, it was sorcery. So the nations copied it (fatanasakhat al-umam)."

And Allah revealed the excuse of Sulayman regarding what they had said of sorcery, so He said: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ [the verse].

An-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "Asif was the scribe of Sulayman, and he knew the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). He used to write everything on Sulayman's command and bury it beneath his throne. When Sulayman died, the devils brought it out, and they wrote between every two lines sorcery and disbelief, and said: 'This is what Sulayman used to practise.' The ignorant among the people disbelieved him and reviled him, and their scholars stood aside. Their ignorant ones continued to revile him until Allah sent down to Muhammad: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "When Sulayman wished to enter the privy or attend to some matter of his, he would give his ring to al-Jaradah, who was his wife. One day, when Allah willed to test Sulayman with what He tested him with, he gave al-Jaradah his ring, and the devil came in the form of Sulayman and said to her: 'Give me my ring,' and he took it and put it on. When he put it on, the devils, the jinn and mankind submitted to him. Then Sulayman came and said: 'Give me my ring,' and she said: 'You lie, you are not Sulayman.' So he knew that it was a trial with which he had been tested. The devils then went and wrote books during those days, containing sorcery and disbelief, then buried them beneath the throne of Sulayman, then dug them up and recited them to the people, saying: 'Sulayman only overcame the people by these books.' So the people disassociated themselves from Sulayman and accused him of disbelief, until Allah sent Muhammad and revealed to him: ﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved﴾."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they follow."

He also transmitted from Ata' regarding His saying ﴿what they recite﴾, he said: "what they bring about (nura-hu ma tuhdith)."

He also transmitted from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾, he said: "during the kingdom of Sulayman."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "This is another sorcery with which they disputed. The speech of the angels among themselves, if mankind learned it and it was made and acted upon, would be sorcery."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, he said: "Allah did not send down sorcery."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, who said: "They are two angels from among the angels of heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from him through another route, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet).

Al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾, meaning Jibril and Mika'il, ﴿at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾, who teach people sorcery.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza that he used to recite it: "and what was sent down to the two kings, Dawud and Sulayman."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "They are two men (ilj) from the people of Babylon."

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from the hadith of Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels looked down upon the world and saw the children of Adam disobeying, so they said: 'O Lord, how ignorant these people are, how little they know of Your greatness!' Allah said: 'If you were in their places, you would have disobeyed Me.' They said: 'How could that be, when we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?' He said: 'Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. Then they were sent down to the earth, and the desires of the children of Adam were placed in them, and a woman was presented to them, and they did not resist until they committed the sin. Allah said: 'Choose between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'What do you say?' He said: 'I say that the punishment of this world ends, and the punishment of the Hereafter does not end.' So they chose the punishment of this world. They are the two whom Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾" [the verse].

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Umar that he used to say: "Has al-Hamra' risen yet?" and when he saw it, he said: "No welcome." Then he said: "Two angels, Harut and Marut, asked Allah to send them down to the earth, so they were sent down to the earth and judged between the people. When evening came, they spoke words and ascended with them to heaven. A woman of the most beautiful women was appointed for them, and desire was cast upon them, and they began to delay her, and it was cast into their hearts. They continued doing so until she promised them a rendezvous. She came to them at the appointed time and said: 'Teach me the word with which you ascend.' So they taught her the word, and she spoke it and ascended to heaven, and she was transformed and made into what you see. When they came at evening and spoke the word, they did not ascend. Then it was sent to them: 'If you wish, [it is] the punishment of the Hereafter, and if you wish, [it is] the punishment of this world until the Hour rises, on condition that you meet Allah; if He wills, He will punish you, and if He wills, He will (p-82) have mercy on you.' One of them looked at his companion and said: 'Rather, we choose the punishment of this world, a thousand thousand times,' so they are punished until the Day of Resurrection."

This story has been narrated from Ibn Umar in various wordings. In some versions, Ibn Umar narrates it from Ka'b al-Ahbar, as Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab (al-Iman) transmitted through al-Thawri, from Musa ibn Uqba, from Salim, from Ibn Umar, from Ka'b, who said: "The angels mentioned the deeds of the children of Adam and the sins they commit, so it was said to them: 'If you were in their place, you would commit the same as they commit. Choose two of your number,' so they chose Harut and Marut. He said to them: 'I am sending messengers to the children of Adam, but there is no messenger between Me and you. Descend, do not associate anything with Me, do not commit adultery, and do not drink wine.' Ka'b said: 'By Allah, they had not yet reached evening on the day they were sent down until they had committed everything they had been forbidden.'"

Ibn Kathir said: "This is more authentic," meaning of the two chains of transmission he mentioned before it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "This star, the Arabs call it al-Zuhrah, and the non-Arabs call it Anahid." He mentioned something similar to the earlier narration from Ibn Umar in al-Hakim.

Ibn Kathir said: "The men of this chain are trustworthy (thiqat), but it is extremely strange (gharib jiddan)."

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Zuhrah was a woman."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from him: "The woman with whom the two angels were tempted was transformed, and she is this red constellation, meaning al-Zuhrah."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab transmitted from him, and he mentioned a long story, in which there is an explicit statement that the two angels drank wine, committed adultery with the woman, and killed her.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas this story, and both said: "The Zuhrah was sent down to them in the form of a woman, and they fell into the sin."

Many long stories and varied narrations have been related on this subject, which al-Suyuti compiled fully in al-Durr al-Manthur. Ibn Kathir mentioned some of them in his Tafsir, then said: "The story of Harut and Marut has been related from a group of the Followers (tabi'un) such as Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Zuhri, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and others, and many of the exegetes, earlier and later, have recounted it."

Its substance, in its details, goes back to the reports of the Children of Israel (isra'iliyyat), for there is no sound marfu' hadith in it with a connected chain (isnad) to the truthful, believed one (al-sadiq al-masdduq), the infallible, who does not speak from desire. The apparent context of the Qur'an is a summary of the story without elaboration or lengthy detail. So we believe in what came in the Qur'an as Allah intended it, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi, after quoting some of this, said: "We say: all of this is weak and far from Ibn Umar and others; nothing of it is authentic, for it is a claim that the principles (usul) of the religion reject concerning the angels, who are the trustees of Allah over His revelation and His messengers to His prophets, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded." Then he mentioned something to the effect that reason permits such a thing to happen from them, but the occurrence of this permissible matter is not known except through revelation (al-sam'), and it has not been authenticated. End of quote.

I say: this is merely an assumption of improbability. The Mighty Book has come in this place with what you see, and there is no basis for taking it out of its apparent meaning through these strained interpretations. As for his claim that the principles reject this, even if these principles exist, they are specified by what occurred in this story, and there is no basis for refusing such a specification. Iblis himself held a great station and became the most evil of creatures and the most disbelieving of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿We are only a trial﴾, he said: "a test (bala')."

Al-Bazzar with a sound chain and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) or a sorcerer and believes what he says has disbelieved in what was sent down to Muhammad."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 99–103 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Bazzar narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever practises augury (tiyarah) or has it practised for him, or practises soothsaying (kahanah) or has it practised for him, or practises sorcery (sihr) or has it practised for him, and whoever ties a knot (for sorcery), and whoever comes to a soothsayer (kahin) and believes what he says, has indeed disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad."

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Safwan ibn Sulaym, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever learns anything of sorcery, little or much, will have his last share from Allah (i.e., he will be deprived of Allah's mercy)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, "from any share (min khalaq)," that he said: "Min khalaq means min qiwam (a portion/sustenance)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: "Min khalaq means min nasib (a share)." Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid.
