Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿They will have no share of it in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "He has no religion."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His words, ﴿And how evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾, that he said: "They sold."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His words, "a reward (lamathubah)," that he said: "A reward (thawab)."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 104–105:

His saying: ﴿Do not say "Ra‘ina"﴾. That is, "Watch over us and preserve us." The form of mufa‘alah (the verbal pattern expressing mutual action) indicates that the meaning of "Ra‘ina" is: "Watch over us, and we will watch over you; preserve us, and we will preserve you; keep us in view, and we will keep you in view." It is also permissible that it derives from "arina sam‘aka" (give your hearing to us), meaning: empty your hearing for our speech.

The reason for the prohibition is that this expression, in the language of the Jews, was an insult. It was said that in their language it meant "listen, may you not hear," and it was said that it meant other than this. When they heard the Muslims saying to the Prophet ﷺ "Ra‘ina," requesting from him that he show them consideration (from *al-mura‘ah*, consideration), they seized the opportunity. They would say this to the Prophet ﷺ in the same way, displaying that they intended the Arabic meaning, while concealing that they intended the insult which is the meaning of this expression in their language.

In this there is evidence that one should avoid words which may be understood as insult or disparagement, even if the speaker does not intend by them the meaning that conveys abuse, as a means of blocking the pretext (*sadd al-dhari‘ah*, blocking the means to harm), averting the avenue, and cutting off the source of corruption and the path to it.

Then Allah commanded them to address the Prophet ﷺ with what does not admit disparagement and is not suitable for allusion to insult. So He said: ﴿But say "Unzurna" (look upon us)﴾. That is: turn toward us and look at us. It is therefore of the type of omission and transitivity (*al-hadhf wa’l-iysal*), as the poet said:

*"Radiant in beauty and loveliness, they gaze*
*as the gazelles gaze upon the arak trees."*

That is, gaze upon the arak trees.

It was also said that its meaning is: "Wait for us and be patient with us." From this is the saying of the poet:

*"For if you two give me respite a while*
*of time, it will benefit me with Umm Jundab."*

Al-A‘mash recited "Anzirna" with a hamzah (an-zirna, causative form) and a kasrah on the ẓā’, meaning: delay us and give us time until we understand from you. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"O Abu Hind, do not hasten against us,*
*and grant us respite; we will inform you of the certainty."*

Al-Hasan recited "Ra‘inan" with tanwin (nunation) and said: "Ar-ra‘in (the one who says ra‘ina) is from the speech of mockery directed at him." End of quotation.

After this prohibition and command, He commanded them with another matter, which is His saying: ﴿And listen﴾. That is: listen to what you are commanded and forbidden. Its meaning is: obey Allah by leaving off addressing the Prophet ﷺ with that expression, and address him with what you have been commanded. It may also be that its meaning is: listen to what the Messenger addresses you with of the Sharia, so that what you seek is obtained for you without the request for consideration.

Then He threatened the Jews with His saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment﴾. It may also be that this is a threat encompassing the whole category of disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir said: The correct view with us on this matter is that Allah forbade the believers from saying to His Prophet ﷺ "Ra‘ina," because it is a word which Allah disliked that they should say to His Prophet ﷺ, like what is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Do not say to the vine 'al-karm,' but say 'al-hublah'; and do not say 'my slave' (*‘abdi*), but say 'my young man' (*fataya*)," and what is similar to that.

His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, wish that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord﴾, the verse. In it is a demonstration of the severity of the enmity of the disbelievers toward the Muslims, in that they do not wish that good be sent down upon them from Allah, glorified is He. Then Allah, glorified is He, refuted that for them, saying: ﴿But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills﴾, the verse.

His saying: "an yunazzila" (that He send down) is in a place of nasb (accusative) as an object. The "min" in His saying "min khayr" (of any good) is extra (*za’idah*), as said by al-Nahhas. In al-Kashshaf, the "min" in His saying "min ahl al-kitab" is explicative (*bayaniyyah*); the "min" in His saying "min khayr" is extra, for the encompassment of all good; and the "min" in His saying "min rabbikum" is for the starting point of the end (*ibtida’ al-ghayah*). It has been said that the good is revelation, and it has been said other than that. The apparent meaning is that they do not wish that any good at all be sent down upon the Muslims, so it is not restricted to a specific kind, as is indicated by the occurrence of this indefinite noun in the context of negation and the emphasis of generality through the addition of the extra "min" upon it. Even if some kinds of good are greater than others, that does not necessitate restriction.

As for the mercy, it has been said that it is the Qur'an, and it has been said that it is prophethood, and it has been said that it is the category of mercy without specification, as the attribution to His pronoun indicates. His saying: ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, that is, the Possessor of great bounty. So how is it that you do not wish that He specially select for His mercy whom He wills of His servants?

Sa‘id ibn Mansur related in his Sunan, and Ahmad in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu‘aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu‘ab, from Ibn Mas‘ud: that a man came to him and said: "Advise me." He said: "When you hear Allah saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾, then give it your hearing, for it is either good that He commands you with, or evil that He forbids you from."

Abu Nu‘aym related in al-Dala’il from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: "Ra‘ina" in the language of the Jews is a foul insult. The Jews would say that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ secretly. When they heard his Companions saying it, they made it public, and they would say it and laugh among themselves. So Allah revealed the verse.

Abu Nu‘aym related in al-Dala’il from him, that he said: The believers, after this verse, said: "Whoever you hear saying it, strike his neck." So the Jews desisted after that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Suddi, who said: There were two men of the Jews, Malik ibn al-Sayf and Rifa‘ah ibn Zayd, who, when they met the Prophet ﷺ and were speaking to him, would say to him, "Ra‘ina sam‘aka" (give us your attention) and "Isma‘ ghayra musma‘" (hear, may you not be heard). The Muslims thought that this was something the People of the Book used to exalt their prophets, so they said it to the Prophet ﷺ. So Allah revealed the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Sakhr, who said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away, whoever among the believers had a need would call out to him, and they would say: 'Ra‘ina sam‘aka.' So Allah magnified His Messenger from having this said to him, and commanded them to say: 'Unzurna,' so that they would honour and revere the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu Nu‘aym related from Qatadah that the Jews used to say that as mockery, so Allah disliked for the believers that they should say the same as their saying.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: "Al-rahmah" is the Qur'an and Islam.

The abrogation (naskh) in the language of the Arabs has two meanings. The first is transcription, like copying a book from another. On this meaning, the entire Qur'an is "abrogated," namely from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so this meaning has no place in this verse. From this sense comes His saying: ﴿Indeed, We used to have recorded what you were doing﴾, meaning: We used to order its copying.

The second meaning is annulment and removal, and this is the one intended here.

According to the linguists, this second meaning divides into two types. The first is the annulment of a thing and its disappearance, with another thing set in its place. From this comes the expression "the sun abrogated (nasakhat) the shade," when it removes it and takes its place. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾. In Sahih Muslim there is the report: "Prophethood never existed except that it was transformed (tanasakhat)," meaning it changed from one state to another.

The second is the removal of a thing without another taking its place, as in their saying: "The wind abrogated the trace," and from this meaning is His saying: ﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts﴾, meaning He removes it.

It is narrated from Abu 'Ubayd that this used to occur during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): a surah would descend upon him, then it would be lifted, so it was neither recited nor written.

Am hādhihi hiya al-munqati'ah allatī bi-ma'nā bal, ay bal turīdūn, wa fī hādhā tawbīkh wa taqrī'. Wa al-kāf fī qawlihi: ﴿kamā su'ila﴾ fī mawḍi' naṣb na't li-maṣdar maḥdhūf, ay su'ālan mithla mā su'ila Mūsā min qabl, ḥaythu sa'alūhu an yurīhimu Allāh jahratan, wa sa'alū Muḥammadan (ﷺ) an ya'tiya bi-Allāh wa al-malā'ikati qabīlan.

Wa qawluhu: sawā' huwa al-wasaṭu min kulli shay', qālahu Abū 'Ubaydah, wa minhu qawluhu ta'ālā: ﴿fī sawā'i al-jaḥīm﴾, wa minhu qawlu Ḥassān yarthī al-Nabiyya (ﷺ):

Yā wayḥa aṣḥābi al-Nabiyyi wa rahṭihi ba'da al-mughayyabi fī sawā'i al-mulḥad

Wa qāla al-Farrā': al-sawā'u: al-qaṣd, ay dhahaba 'an qaṣdi al-ṭarīqi wa samtihi, ay ṭarīqi ṭā'ati Allāh.

Wa qawluhu ta'ālā: ﴿wadda kathīrun min ahli al-kitāb﴾ fīhi ikhbāru al-muslimīna biḥirṣi al-yahūd 'alā fitnatihim wa raddihim 'ani al-Islām wa al-tashkīki 'alayhim fī dīnihim.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿law yaruddūnakum﴾ fī maḥall naṣb 'alā annahu maf'ūl lil-fi'l al-madhkūr.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿min 'indi anfusihim﴾ yuḥtamalu an yata'allaqa bi-qawlihi wadda, ay waddū dhālika min 'indi anfusihim, wa yuḥtamalu an yata'allaqa bi-qawlihi: ḥasadan, ay ḥasadan nāshi'an min 'indi anfusihim, wa huwa 'illatun li-qawlihi: wadda.

Wa al-'afw: tark al-mu'ākhadhah bi-al-dhanb.

Wa al-ṣafḥ: izālat atharihi min al-nafs, ṣafaḥtu 'an fulānin: idhā a'raḍta 'an dhanbihi, wa qad ḍarabtu 'anhu ṣafḥan: idhā a'raḍta 'anhu, wa fīhi al-targhību fī dhālika wa al-irshādu ilayhi, wa qad nusikha dhālika bi-al-amri bi-al-qitāl, qālahu Abū 'Ubaydah.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿ḥattā ya'tiya Allāhu bi-amrihi﴾ huwa ghāyatu mā amara Allāhu subḥānahu bihi mina al-'afwi wa al-ṣafḥ, ay if'alū dhālika ilā an ya'tiya ilaykumu al-amru mina Allāhi subḥānahu fī sha'nihim bi-mā yakhtāruhu wa yashā'uhu, wa mā qad qaḍā bihi fī sābiqi 'ilmihi, wa huwa qatlu man qutila minhum, wa ijlā'u man ujliya, wa ḍarbu al-jizyati 'alā man ḍuribat 'alayhi, wa islāmu man aslama.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿wa aqīmū al-ṣalāh﴾ ḥathththun min Allāhi subḥānahu lahum 'alā al-ishtighāli bi-mā yanfa'uhum wa ya'ūdu 'alayhim bi-al-maṣlaḥah, min iqāmati al-ṣalāh wa itā'i al-zakāh wa taqdīmi al-khayri alladhī yuthābūna 'alayhi, ḥattā yumakkina Allāhu lahum wa yanṣurahum 'alā al-mukhālifīna lahum.

Wa qad akhraja Ibn Isḥāq wa Ibn Jarīr wa Ibn Abī Ḥātim 'an Ibn 'Abbās annahu qāla: «Qāla Rāfi' ibn Ḥuraymilah wa Wahb ibn Zayd li-Rasūli Allāh (ﷺ): Yā Muḥammad, i'tinā bi-kitābin yanzilu 'alaynā mina al-samā' naqra'uhu, aw fajjir lanā anhāran nattabi'ka wa nuṣaddiqka, fa-anzala Allāh fī dhālika ﴿am turīdūna an tas'alū rasūlakum﴾ ilā qawlihi ﴿sawā'a al-sabīl﴾, wa kāna Ḥuyayyu ibn Akhṭab min ashaddi al-yahūdi ḥasadan lil-'Arab idh khaṣṣahumu Allāh bi-rasūlihi, wa kānā jāhidayni fī radd al-nās 'ani al-Islām mā istaṭā'ā, fa-anzala Allāh fīhimā ﴿wadda kathīrun min ahli al-kitāb﴾» al-āyah.

Wa akhraja Ibn Jarīr wa Ibn al-Mundhir wa Ibn Abī Ḥātim 'ani al-Suddī qāla: «Sa'alati al-'Arabu Muḥammadan (ﷺ) an ya'tiyahum bi-Allāh fa-yarawhu jahratan, fa-nazalat hādhihi al-āyah».

Wa akhraja Ibn Jarīr wa Ibn Abī Ḥātim wa Ibn Mardawayh wa al-Bayhaqī fī al-Dalā'il 'an Ibn 'Abbās fī qawlihi: ﴿fa-'fū waṣfaḥū﴾ wa qawlihi: ﴿wa a'riḍ 'ani al-mushrikīn﴾ wa naḥw hādhā fī al-'afwi 'ani al-mushrikīn qāla: nusikha dhālika kulluhu bi-qawlihi: ﴿qātilū alladhīna lā yu'minūna bi-Allāh﴾ (p-86) al-āyah, wa qawlihi: ﴿faqtulū al-mushrikīna ḥaythu wajadtumūhum﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 111–113:

His saying: "hudan" (Hūdan). Al-Farrā' said: it is permissible that "hūdan" means "yahūdiyyan" (Jews), and that it is the plural of "hā'id" (one who repents and returns).

Al-Akhfash said: the singular pronoun in "kāna" (was) is according to the wording of "man" (whoever), and the plural in His saying "hūdan" is according to the meaning of "man." It has been said that there is an ellipsis (ḥadhf) in this statement, and its original form is: "The Jews said: None will enter Paradise except he who is a Jew, and the Christians said: None will enter Paradise except he who is a Christian."

Thus said many of the exegetes, and some of the early generation (salaf) preceded them in this.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, uttered this statement, and that they are singled out for it to the exclusion of others. The justification for saying that there is an ellipsis is what is known from the fact that each of these two groups misguides the other and denies that the other is upon anything of the religion, let alone of entering Paradise, as in this context. God has related of the Jews that they said: "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians said: "The Jews are not upon anything." The wishful thinkings (amānī) have already been explained, and the reference in His saying "those" (tilka) is to the wishful thinkings previously mentioned for them, the last of which is that none but they will enter Paradise.

It has also been said that the reference is to this last wishful thinking, and the estimate is "their wishful thinkings are like those wishful thinkings," with the omission of the modifier (muḍāf) so that "their wishful thinkings" agrees.

His saying: "hātū" (bring). Its original form is "hātūyū"; the ḍamma was dropped because of its heaviness, then the yā' was dropped because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. It is said to the masculine singular "hāt" and to the feminine "hātī," and it is an interjection (ṣawt) meaning "come forward/present yourself."

And "al-burhān" (proof): the evidence by which certainty is attained.

Ibn Jarīr said: the demand for evidence here requires the establishment of reflection (naẓar) and refutes those who deny it.

His saying: "in kuntum ṣādiqīn" (if you are truthful), i.e., in those bare wishful thinkings and false claims.

Then He answered them, saying: "Balā, man aslama" (Yes! Whoever submits), and this is an affirmation of what they denied concerning others entering Paradise, meaning: it is not as they say; rather, whoever submits his face to God will enter it.

The meaning of "aslama" is: surrendered (istaslama); it has also been said: sincerely devoted (akhlaṣa).

The face (wajh) was singled out for mention because it is the most noble part of a person that is seen, and because it is the locus of the apparent senses, and in it honour and humiliation appear. It has also been said that the Arabs refer to the face in speaking of the whole of a thing, and that the meaning here is the face and other than it. It has also been said that by "face" is meant here the aim (maqṣid), i.e., whoever sincerely directs his aim.

His saying: "wa-huwa muḥsin" (while he is a doer of good) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The pronoun in His saying "wajhahu" and "lahu" is according to the wording of "man," and in His saying "'alayhim" it is according to its meaning.

His saying: "man" — if it is the relative (mawṣūlah), then it is the subject of an elided verb, meaning: "Yes, whoever submits will enter it."

His saying: "fa-lahu" is coordinated with "man aslama." If "man" is conditional (shartiyyah), then His saying "fa-lahu" is the response (jazā'), and the whole of the condition and response is a refutation of the People of the Book and a nullification of that claim.

His saying: "wa-qālati al-yahūdu" and what follows it contains that each group denies goodness to the other, and this implies its affirmation for itself, restricting God's mercy.

Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: "shay'" (thing) is that which is valid and is regarded as having worth. He said: this is a great exaggeration, because the impossible and the non-existent may be called "a thing," and when the application of the name "thing" to it is negated, it has been exaggerated in disregarding it to the utmost degree; and likewise is the saying "less than nothing."

His saying: "wa-hum yatlūna al-kitāb" (while they recite the Book), i.e., the Torah and the Gospel; the clause is circumstantial. It has been said that the intended meaning is the genus of the Book. In this is the greatest rebuke and the sharpest reproach, because falling into false claims and speaking without evidence is, though ugly in general, even uglier and more heinous in sin and graver in offence for those who are people of knowledge and study of God's books.

His saying: "kadhālika qāla alladhīna lā ya'lamūn" (Likewise said those who do not know): the intended ones are the pagan Arabs who had no Book; they said the like of the Jews' statement, imitating them, because they are ignorant and cannot do other than follow blindly whoever they believe to be a person of knowledge. It has also been said that the intended ones are a group of Jews and Christians who have no knowledge.

Then God, glorified is He, informed us that He is the one who decides this dispute over which disagreement occurred, upon return to Him: He punishes whoever deserves punishment and saves whoever deserves salvation.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Abū al-'Āliyah concerning His saying: "Wa-qālū lan yadkhula al-jannata" (and they said: none will enter Paradise), to the end of the verse, he said: The Jews said: None will enter Paradise except he who is a Jew, and the Christians said: None will enter Paradise except he who is a Christian. "Tilka amānīyuhum" (those are their wishful thinkings): he said: wishes they desire of God without right. "Qul hātū burhānakum" (say: bring your proof): he said: your argument. "In kuntum ṣādiqīn" (if you are truthful) in what you say, that it is as you say. "Balā man aslama wajhahu lillāh" (Yes, whoever submits his face to God): he says: sincerely devoted to God.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Mujāhid concerning His saying: "Qul hātū burhānakum," he said: your argument.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: "Balā man aslama wajhahu," he said: sincerely devoted his religion.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbās, who said: "When the delegation of Najrān of the Christians came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the rabbis of the Jews came to them, and they disputed in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Rāfi' ibn Ḥuraymilah said: 'You are not upon anything,' and he disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel. A man from the people of Najrān said to him: 'You are not upon anything,' and he denied the prophethood of Moses and disbelieved in the Torah." He said: So God revealed concerning that: "Wa-qālati al-yahūdu laysati al-naṣārā 'alā shay'in wa-qālati al-naṣārā laysati al-yahūdu 'alā shay'in wa-hum yatlūna al-kitāb," meaning: each recites in his book the confirmation of the one he disbelieves in.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Aṭā': "Who are those who do not believe?" He said: They are nations that existed before the Jews and the Christians.

Ibn Jarīr transmitted from al-Suddī, who said: They are the Arabs; they said: "Muḥammad is not upon anything."

(p-87) This interrogative carries the most emphatic indication that this wrongdoing has reached its extreme, and that it is of such a degree that no other kind of wrongdoing should be attached to it; that is, there is no one more wrongful than the one who prevents the mosques of Allah. The interrogative particle is in the position of nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "azlamu" (more wrongful) is its predicate (khabar).

As for His saying, ﴿that His name be mentioned in them﴾: it has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for "masajid" (mosques). It has also been said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with the implied meaning "out of aversion to His name being mentioned." It has also been said that the original phrasing is "min an yudhkara" (from His name being mentioned), and then the preposition was deleted because the sentence is long. It has also been said that it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of the verb "mana'a" (prevented). The meaning of preventing the mosques from His name being mentioned in them is preventing those who come to them for prayer, recitation, remembrance and teaching of it.

By "striving for their ruin" is meant striving to demolish them and to lift their structures. It is also permissible that the ruin meant is their being left idle from the acts of worship for which they were established, in which case it is more general than His saying ﴿that His name be mentioned in them﴾, and it includes everything prevented of the matters for which mosques were built, such as the learning and teaching of knowledge, sitting for i'tikaf (spiritual retreat), and awaiting prayer. It is also permissible that what is meant is something more general than both matters, by way of the generality of metaphor (ʿumum al-majaz), as has been said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Only those who believe in Allah maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾; that is, it was not fitting for them to enter them except in a state of fear.

In this there is guidance from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the servants that they should prevent the mosques of Allah from the people of disbelief, without distinction between one mosque and another, or between one disbeliever and another, as the generality of the wording indicates; and the specific occasion of revelation does not negate this. They should also cause them to be in a state where, whenever they wish to enter, they are fearful and apprehensive lest any of the Muslims perceive them, so that the Muslims inflict upon them what entails humiliation and abasement. There is no permission in it for us to enable them to do so in a state of fear; rather, it is a metaphor (kinaya) for preventing them from us from entering our mosques.

As for "khizy" (disgrace): it has been said that it is the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) upon them and their humiliation; and it has been said otherwise. Its explanation has already been given.

"Al-mashriq" is the place of sunrise. "Al-maghrib" is the place of sunset; that is, both belong to Allah, and what lies between them of directions and created things, so it includes the whole earth.

As for His saying ﴿Wherever you turn﴾: that is, whatever direction you face, there is the Face of Allah, meaning the place which He is pleased for you to face. This occurs when the direction of the qibla becomes unclear, the qibla to which He, glorified is He, commanded us to turn by His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. In al-Kashshaf he said: The meaning is that when you are prevented from praying in the Sacred Mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis, then the earth has been made a mosque for you, so pray in whatever place of its places you wish, and perform the turning (to the qibla) in it, for turning is possible in every place; it is not restricted to particular places, in one mosque rather than another, nor in one place rather than another. End of quotation.

This restriction has no basis, for the wording is broader than it. However, if the intent is to state the cause (of revelation), there is no harm.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ contains guidance to the vastness of His mercy, and that He makes things easy for His servants in their religion and does not burden them with what is beyond their capacity. It has been said that "wasi'" (All-Encompassing) means that His knowledge encompasses everything, as He said: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. Al-Farra' said: "al-Wasi'" is the Generous whose giving encompasses everything.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Quraysh prevented the Prophet ﷺ from praying at the Ka'bah in the Sacred Mosque, so Allah revealed: ﴿And who is more wrongful than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: "They are the Christians."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Suddi that he said: "They are the Romans, who had aided Bukhtnassar in the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis."

Regarding His saying: ﴿Those, it was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾, he said: "There is no Roman in the earth who enters it today except that he is fearful that his neck will be struck, and he has been made afraid by paying the jizya, so he pays it."

Regarding His saying: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, he said: "As for their disgrace in this world, when the Mahdi arises and Constantinople is conquered, he will kill them, and that is the disgrace."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah that they are the Romans.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "They are the polytheists when they barred the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the House on the day of al-Hudaybiyah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Abu Salih that he said: "The polytheists are not permitted to enter the mosque except in fear."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ that he said: "They give the jizya willingly while they are humbled."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The first of the Qur'an to be abrogated, as far as we have been told, and Allah knows best, concerned the qibla. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾ (the verse), so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ faced and prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis and left the Ancient House. Then Allah turned him toward the Ancient House and abrogated it, saying: ﴿And from wherever you go out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾."

Then Ibn ʿUmar recited this verse: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾, and said: "This verse was revealed concerning this."

Ibn Jarir, al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) transmitted something similar from him.

It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Jabir, "that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray on his mount facing the east; when he wished to pray the obligatory prayer, he would dismount, face the qibla and pray."

Something similar has been related from the hadith of Anas, raised to the Prophet ﷺ. It was transmitted by Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Dawud.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who declared it weak), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from ʿAmir ibn Rabiʿah that he said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a dark, pitch-black night, and we alighted at a station, and a man began taking stones and making a mosque and praying in it. When morning came, we found that we had prayed facing other than the qibla. So we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we prayed this whole night facing other than the qibla.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ (the verse)," (p-88) and he said: "Your prayer has passed."

al-Daraqutni, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Jabir, raised to the Prophet ﷺ, something similar, except that it mentions that they drew lines (as markers for the direction).

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar with a weak chain from Ibn ʿAbbas, raised.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted something similar from ʿAta', raising it, and it is mursal.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Then there is the Face of Allah﴾ that he said: "A qibla belonging to Allah, wherever you turn, east or west."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi transmitted something similar from ʿUmar.

(p-87) This interrogative carries the most emphatic indication that this wrongdoing has reached its extreme, and that it is of such a degree that no other kind of wrongdoing should be attached to it; that is, there is no one more wrongful than the one who prevents the mosques of Allah. The interrogative particle is in the position of nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "azlamu" (more wrongful) is its predicate (khabar).

As for His saying, ﴿that His name be mentioned in them﴾: it has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for "masajid" (mosques). It has also been said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with the implied meaning "out of aversion to His name being mentioned." It has also been said that the original phrasing is "min an yudhkara" (from His name being mentioned), and then the preposition was deleted because the sentence is long. It has also been said that it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of the verb "mana'a" (prevented). The meaning of preventing the mosques from His name being mentioned in them is preventing those who come to them for prayer, recitation, remembrance and teaching of it.

By "striving for their ruin" is meant striving to demolish them and to lift their structures. It is also permissible that the ruin meant is their being left idle from the acts of worship for which they were established, in which case it is more general than His saying ﴿that His name be mentioned in them﴾, and it includes everything prevented of the matters for which mosques were built, such as the learning and teaching of knowledge, sitting for i'tikaf (spiritual retreat), and awaiting prayer. It is also permissible that what is meant is something more general than both matters, by way of the generality of metaphor (ʿumum al-majaz), as has been said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Only those who believe in Allah maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾; that is, it was not fitting for them to enter them except in a state of fear.

In this there is guidance from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the servants that they should prevent the mosques of Allah from the people of disbelief, without distinction between one mosque and another, or between one disbeliever and another, as the generality of the wording indicates; and the specific occasion of revelation does not negate this. They should also cause them to be in a state where, whenever they wish to enter, they are fearful and apprehensive lest any of the Muslims perceive them, so that the Muslims inflict upon them what entails humiliation and abasement. There is no permission in it for us to enable them to do so in a state of fear; rather, it is a metaphor (kinaya) for preventing them from us from entering our mosques.

As for "khizy" (disgrace): it has been said that it is the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) upon them and their humiliation; and it has been said otherwise. Its explanation has already been given.

"Al-mashriq" is the place of sunrise. "Al-maghrib" is the place of sunset; that is, both belong to Allah, and what lies between them of directions and created things, so it includes the whole earth.

As for His saying ﴿Wherever you turn﴾: that is, whatever direction you face, there is the Face of Allah, meaning the place which He is pleased for you to face. This occurs when the direction of the qibla becomes unclear, the qibla to which He, glorified is He, commanded us to turn by His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. In al-Kashshaf he said: The meaning is that when you are prevented from praying in the Sacred Mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis, then the earth has been made a mosque for you, so pray in whatever place of its places you wish, and perform the turning (to the qibla) in it, for turning is possible in every place; it is not restricted to particular places, in one mosque rather than another, nor in one place rather than another. End of quotation.

This restriction has no basis, for the wording is broader than it. However, if the intent is to state the cause (of revelation), there is no harm.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 116–118:

His saying: "And they say" refers to the Jews and the Christians. It is also said that it refers to the Jews, meaning they said: ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾. It is also said that it refers to the Christians, meaning they said: ﴿The Messiah is the son of God﴾. It is also said that it refers to the idolaters of the Arabs, meaning they said: the angels are the daughters of God.

His saying: "Glory be to Him" has already had its meaning explained. What is intended here is God's declaring Himself free of what they attributed to Him of taking a son.

His saying: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a refutation of those who claimed that He has taken a son. That is, rather, He is the Owner of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and these sayers are included within His dominion. A son is of the same kind as them, not of the same kind as Him, and a son can only be of the same kind as the father.

Al-qanit (the obedient, the one who submits): the one who obeys and humbles himself. That is, everyone in the heavens and the earth is obedient to Him, humble before His greatness, and submissive to His majesty. Qunut, in its original linguistic sense, means standing.

Al-Zajjaj said: "So all creation is qanitun," meaning standing in servitude, either by acknowledgment or otherwise, since the effect of the creation is clear upon them. It is also said that its origin is obedience, and from this comes ﴿the obedient men and the obedient women﴾. It is also said that it means stillness, and from this comes His saying: ﴿And stand before God in qunut﴾. For this reason Zayd ibn Arqam said: "We used to speak during prayer until there was revealed ﴿And stand before God in qunut﴾, so we were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak." It is also said that qunut means prayer, and from this comes the saying of the poet:

Devout to God, reciting His books,
And he withdrew from people deliberately.

The more appropriate view is that qunut is a term shared among many meanings. It has been said there are thirteen meanings, and they are clarified. Some scholars have versified them, as I explained in my commentary on ʿIlm al-Muntaqa.

The word (Badi'): it is a fa'il in the intensive form (mubalaghah), and it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Originator of His heavens and His earth. Abda'a al-shay': he brought it into existence without a model. Whoever creates what has not been created before is called mubdi'.

His saying: ﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾ means He establishes it and perfects it.

Al-Azhari said: qada in the language has several uses, all of which go back to the ending or completion of a thing. It has been said that it is shared among several meanings. It is used in the sense of creating, and from this: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾. It is used in the sense of informing, and from this: ﴿And We made known to the Children of Israel in the Scripture﴾. It is used in the sense of commanding, and from this: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. It is used in the sense of obligating, and from this: the judge ruled against him. It is used in the sense of fulfilling, and from this: ﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾. It is used in the sense of intending, and from this: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

Al-amr: the singular of "affairs" (umur).

It has occurred in the Qur'an in fourteen meanings:

First: religion, and from this: ﴿until the truth came and the command of God appeared﴾.

Second: speech, and from this: ﴿and when Our command came﴾.

Third: punishment, and from this: ﴿when the matter was decided﴾.

Fourth: ʿIsa, and from this: ﴿and when He decrees a matter﴾, meaning He brought ʿIsa, upon him be peace, into existence.

Fifth: killing, and from this: ﴿and when the command of God came﴾.

Sixth: the conquest of Makkah, and from this: ﴿so wait until God brings about His command﴾.

Seventh: the killing of Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir, and from this: ﴿so pardon and overlook until God brings about His command﴾.

Eighth: the Resurrection, and from this: ﴿the command of God has come﴾.

Ninth: judgment, and from this: ﴿He manages the affair﴾.

Tenth: revelation, and from this: ﴿the command descends among them﴾.

Eleventh: the affair of creatures, and from this: ﴿Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned﴾.

Twelfth: victory, and from this: ﴿Do we have anything to do with the affair?﴾.

Thirteenth: sin, and from this: ﴿so she tasted the evil of her affair﴾.

Fourteenth: the matter or affair, and from this: ﴿and the affair of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾.

Thus did some exegetes list these meanings at greater length than this, and there is not much benefit under that. Its application to the various affairs is valid because the name "amr" truly applies to them.

His saying: ﴿So He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: the apparent meaning in this context is the literal meaning, that He, glory be to Him, says this word. There is no impediment to that, and nothing has come that requires interpreting it otherwise. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. And He said: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. And He said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾. From this is the saying of the poet:

When God intends a matter,
He only says to it "Be," and His word is what is.

It has also been said that this is metaphorical, that there is no actual speech, but only a decree He decrees, which is expressed as speech. From this is the saying of the poet, who is ʿUmar ibn Hummah al-Dawsi:

So I became like the eagle whose chicks have flown away,
When it tries to fly, it is told: "Stay!"

Another said:

His two wings said to his two legs: "Hold fast,
And save yourselves for your judgment, lest you be torn apart."

His saying: ﴿And those who do not know said﴾: what is intended is the Jews. It has also been said that it is the Christians, and Ibn Jarir preferred this because they are the ones mentioned in the verse. It has also been said that it is the idolaters of the Arabs. Lawla is a particle of urging, meaning: why does God not ﴿speak to us﴾ with the prophethood of Muhammad, so that we would know that he is a prophet, or ﴿a sign come to us﴾ as evidence of his prophethood?

(p-89)

What is intended by His saying: ﴿Those before them said﴾ has been said to be the Jews and the Christians according to the view of those who take ﴿those who do not know﴾ to be the idolaters of the Arabs; or the earlier nations according to the view of those who take ﴿those who do not know﴾ to be the Jews and the Christians; or the Jews according to the view of those who take ﴿those who do not know﴾ to be the Christians. ﴿They are alike﴾, that is, in obstinacy and in making demands. Al-Farra' said: they are alike in their agreement upon disbelief.

﴿We have certainly made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾: that is, who acknowledge the truth, are fair in speech, submit to the commands of God, glory be to Him, because they believe Him to be true, believe in His signs, and follow what He has legislated for them.

Al-Bukhari has related from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "God, the Exalted, said: 'The son of Adam has denied Me and reviled Me. As for his denying Me, he claims that I cannot bring him back as he was. As for his reviling Me, he says: "I have a son." Glory be to Me, that I should take a consort or a son.'"

He also related something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and there are other hadiths on this subject.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Glory be to God﴾, that he said: it is God's declaring Himself free of evil.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Musa ibn Talhah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he was asked about tasbih, that a person says "Subhan Allah," and he said: "The clearing of God from evil."

al-Hakim related it and authenticated it, as did Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi, by way of Talhah ibn Yahya ibn Talhah, from his father, from his grandfather Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the explanation of 'Subhan Allah,' and he said: it is God's declaring Himself free of every evil."

Ibn Mardawayh related it from him by another route as a marfu' report.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "Every letter in the Qur'an in which qunut is mentioned means obedience."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿All are qanitun to Him﴾, that he said: obedient.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah, concerning His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: He originated their creation, and no one shared with Him in creating them.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Rafi' ibn Huraymilah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: 'O Muhammad, if you are a messenger from God as you say, then tell God to speak to us so that we may hear His speech.' So God revealed concerning that: ﴿And those who do not know said﴾, the verse."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah that they were the idolaters of the Arabs.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, who said: they are the Christians, and "those before them" are the Jews.

It is also said that it refers to the idolaters of the Arabs, meaning they said: the angels are the daughters of God.

His saying: "Glory be to Him" has already had its meaning explained. What is intended here is God's declaring Himself free of what they attributed to Him of taking a son.

His saying: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a refutation of those who claimed that He has taken a son. That is, rather, He is the Owner of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and these sayers are included within His dominion. A son is of the same kind as them, not of the same kind as Him, and a son can only be of the same kind as the father.

And he withdrew from people deliberately.

His saying: ﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾ means He establishes it and perfects it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 119–121:

His saying: ﴿bashīran wa-nadhīran﴾ ("as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner") may be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and it may be an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: We sent you for the sake of giving glad tidings and warning.

His saying: ﴿wa-lā tus'alu﴾ ("and you will not be questioned") was read by the majority (al-Jumhūr) with a raised final vowel and in the passive voice, meaning: while you are not being questioned. It was also read with the raised vowel in the active voice.

Al-Akhfash said: It may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, coordinated with ﴿bashīran wa-nadhīran﴾, meaning: while you are not asking about them, because God's knowledge of their disbelief after your warning makes your asking about them unnecessary. Nafi' read ﴿wa-lā tas'al﴾ with the jussive, meaning: there should not proceed from you a question about these people, or a question about those among them who died in their disbelief and disobedience, magnifying their condition and emphasizing its gravity, that is, this is a dreadful matter and a monstrous calamity, such that the speaker is awed to let it pass his tongue, or the hearer is awed to hear it.

His saying: ﴿wa-lan tarḍā ʿanka al-yahūd﴾ ("the Jews will never be pleased with you") and the verse that follows: that is, their aim and the extent of their approval is not what they propose to you of signs and what they raise of obstinate challenges. Even if you were to bring them everything they propose and answer every obstinate challenge, they would not be pleased with you. Then He informed him that they would never be pleased with him until he entered their religion and followed their creed.

The milla (creed) is the name for what God has prescribed for His servants in His books through the tongues of His prophets, and likewise the sharīʿa (law). Then He, glorified be He, refuted them, commanding him to say to them: ﴿Indeed, the guidance of God is the (true) guidance﴾, not what you hold of the abrogated law and the corrupted books. Then He followed this with a severe warning to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) should he follow their desires, seek their approval, and exhaust himself in pursuing what agrees with them. It may also be an indirect address to his community and a warning to them not to fall into any of that, or to enter into the desires of the people of the other creeds and seek the approval of the people of innovation.

In this verse there is a severe warning that makes hearts tremble and hearts split apart, which obliges the people of knowledge who bear the proofs of God, glorified be He, and who stand in explaining His laws, to abandon flattery (al-dihān) toward the people of innovation who adhere to evil doctrines, who abandon acting by the Book and the Sunna, and who prefer mere opinion over them both. For most of these people, though they show acceptance and display gentleness in their manners, are not satisfied except by following their innovation, entering its avenues, and falling into its snares. If the scholar does this after God has taught him the knowledge by which he learns that the guidance of God is what is in His Book and the Sunna of His Messenger, and not what they hold of those innovations, which are pure error, manifest ignorance, collapsing opinion, and imitation on the edge of a crumbling precipice, then at that point he has no protector or helper from God. Whoever is like this is certainly forsaken and undoubtedly ruined, without any doubt or ambiguity.

His saying: ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾ ("those to whom We gave the Book"). It was said: they are the Muslims, and the Book is the Qur'an. It was also said: those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam. The meaning of His saying ﴿yatlūnahu﴾ ("they recite it") is that they act upon what is in it, so they make lawful what it makes lawful and prohibit what it prohibits. Thus it comes from talāhu, yatlūhu, meaning "to follow it", as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿wa-l-qamari idhā talāhā﴾ ("and the moon when it follows it"), i.e., follows it, as it is said. It may also be from recitation (tilāwa), meaning they recite it with its true recitation, not distorting it or altering it.

His saying: ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿yatlūnahu﴾ (p-90), or the predicate is His saying ﴿ulā'ika﴾ together with what follows it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what has become of my parents," and then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. So he did not mention them until God took him.

Al-Suyuti said: This is a mursal narration with a weak chain.

Then he related it through the route of Ibn Jarir from Dawud ibn Abi ʿAsim, raised to the Prophet, and said: It is mu'dal in its chain, weak; neither it nor the preceding one may be used as proof.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, who said: al-Jahīm is what is greatest of the fire.

Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran used to hope that the Prophet (ﷺ) would pray toward their qibla. When God turned the qibla to the Kaʿba, this grieved them, and they despaired of his agreeing with their religion.

So God revealed: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾, the verse.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾, he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They make lawful its lawful and prohibit its unlawful, and do not distort it from its places.

They also related from him as well, he said: They follow it with the true following. Then they recited: ﴿wa-l-qamari idhā talāhā﴾, he says: it follows it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾: when he passes a mention of Paradise, he asks God for Paradise, and when he passes a mention of the Fire, he seeks refuge in God from the Fire.

Al-Khatib, in Kitab al-Ruwat, with a chain containing unknown narrators (majahil), related from Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They follow it with the true following. Al-Qurtubi likewise said in his tafsir that its chain contains unknown narrators, but its meaning is sound.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir, through several routes, related from Ibn Masʿud concerning his tafsir of this verse, the same as what preceded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: they make lawful its lawful, to the end.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: They speak it as it was revealed, and do not conceal it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada concerning this verse, he said: They are the companions of Muhammad. Then he related something similar from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.

Waki' and Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They act by its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous verses, and refer what is unclear to them to its Knower.

Thus it comes from talāhu, yatlūhu, meaning "to follow it", as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿wa-l-qamari idhā talāhā﴾ ("and the moon when it follows it"), i.e., follows it, as it is said. It may also be from recitation (tilāwa), meaning they recite it with its true recitation, not distorting it or altering it.

His saying: ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿yatlūnahu﴾ (p-90), or the predicate is His saying ﴿ulā'ika﴾ together with what follows it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have related from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what has become of my parents," and then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. So he did not mention them until God took him.

Al-Suyuti said: This is a mursal narration with a weak chain.

Then he related it through the route of Ibn Jarir from Dawud ibn Abi ʿAsim, raised to the Prophet, and said: It is mu'dal in its chain, weak; neither it nor the preceding one may be used as proof.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, who said: al-Jahīm is what is greatest of the fire.

Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran used to hope that the Prophet (ﷺ) would pray toward their qibla. When God turned the qibla to the Kaʿba, this grieved them, and they despaired of his agreeing with their religion.

So God revealed: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾, the verse.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾, he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They make lawful its lawful and prohibit its unlawful, and do not distort it from its places.

They also related from him as well, he said: They follow it with the true following. Then they recited: ﴿wa-l-qamari idhā talāhā﴾, he says: it follows it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾: when he passes a mention of Paradise, he asks God for Paradise, and when he passes a mention of the Fire, he seeks refuge in God from the Fire.

Al-Khatib, in Kitab al-Ruwat, with a chain containing unknown narrators (majahil), related from Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They follow it with the true following. Al-Qurtubi likewise said in his tafsir that its chain contains unknown narrators, but its meaning is sound.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir, through several routes, related from Ibn Masʿud concerning his tafsir of this verse, the same as what preceded from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: they make lawful its lawful, to the end.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: They speak it as it was revealed, and do not conceal it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada concerning this verse, he said: They are the companions of Muhammad. Then he related something similar from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.

Waki' and Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning His saying ﴿yatlūnahu ḥaqqa tilāwatihi﴾, he said: They act by its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous verses, and refer what is unclear to them to its Knower.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 119–121:

His saying: ﴿bashīran wa-nadhīran﴾ ("as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner") may be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and it may be an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: We sent you for the sake of giving glad tidings and warning.

His saying: ﴿wa-lā tus'alu﴾ ("and you will not be questioned") was read by the majority (al-Jumhūr) with a raised final vowel and in the passive voice, meaning: while you are not being questioned. It was also read with the raised vowel in the active voice.

Al-Akhfash said: It may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, coordinated with ﴿bashīran wa-nadhīran﴾, meaning: while you are not asking about them, because God's knowledge of their disbelief after your warning makes your asking about them unnecessary. Nafi' read ﴿wa-lā tas'al﴾ with the jussive, meaning: there should not proceed from you a question about these people, or a question about those among them who died in their disbelief and disobedience, magnifying their condition and emphasizing its gravity, that is, this is a dreadful matter and a monstrous calamity, such that the speaker is awed to let it pass his tongue, or the hearer is awed to hear it.

His saying: ﴿wa-lan tarḍā ʿanka al-yahūd﴾ ("the Jews will never be pleased with you") and the verse that follows: that is, their aim and the extent of their approval is not what they propose to you of signs and what they raise of obstinate challenges. Even if you were to bring them everything they propose and answer every obstinate challenge, they would not be pleased with you. Then He informed him that they would never be pleased with him until he entered their religion and followed their creed.

The milla (creed) is the name for what God has prescribed for His servants in His books through the tongues of His prophets, and likewise the sharīʿa (law). Then He, glorified be He, refuted them, commanding him to say to them: ﴿Indeed, the guidance of God is the (true) guidance﴾, not what you hold of the abrogated law and the corrupted books. Then He followed this with a severe warning to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) should he follow their desires, seek their approval, and exhaust himself in pursuing what agrees with them. It may also be an indirect address to his community and a warning to them not to fall into any of that, or to enter into the desires of the people of the other creeds and seek the approval of the people of innovation.

In this verse there is a severe warning that makes hearts tremble and hearts split apart, which obliges the people of knowledge who bear the proofs of God, glorified be He, and who stand in explaining His laws, to abandon flattery (al-dihān) toward the people of innovation who adhere to evil doctrines, who abandon acting by the Book and the Sunna, and who prefer mere opinion over them both. For most of these people, though they show acceptance and display gentleness in their manners, are not satisfied except by following their innovation, entering its avenues, and falling into its snares. If the scholar does this after God has taught him the knowledge by which he learns that the guidance of God is what is in His Book and the Sunna of His Messenger, and not what they hold of those innovations, which are pure error, manifest ignorance, collapsing opinion, and imitation on the edge of a crumbling precipice, then at that point he has no protector or helper from God. Whoever is like this is certainly forsaken and undoubtedly ruined, without any doubt or ambiguity.

His saying: ﴿alladhīna ātaynāhumu al-kitāb﴾ ("those to whom We gave the Book"). It was said: they are the Muslims, and the Book is the Qur'an. It was also said: those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam.
