Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. Something similar has already occurred at the beginning of the surah, and its tafsir (exegesis) has already been given. The reason for the repetition is to urge following the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet. Ibn Kathir mentioned its meaning in his tafsir.

Al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: "When the discussion grew long in cataloguing their reminders of blessings, then in explaining their defects and exposing their secrets, and it concluded with a warning against the ruin of their religion through their deeds, states and words, He repeated what He had opened their story with, the reminder of blessings and the warning against the coming of retribution on the Day when the nations are gathered, a Day in which regret will last for whoever has slipped. This is so that it is known that this is the summation (fadhlakah) of the story, and the primary purpose is to urge seizing the opportunity." End of quote.

I say: This is not anything of substance. For if the cause of the repetition were what he mentioned, namely the length of the span and that He returned to what He had opened their story with, then the more fitting thing to be repeated, and the more deserving of being restated, would be His words, glorified is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant, and fear Me﴾. This verse, although it is the first speech addressed to them and the address to them in this surah, is also more worthy of being restated and repeated, because of what it contains of the command to remember the blessings, to fulfil the covenant, and to hold awe of God, glorified is He. By this you will know the soundness of what we presented to you when explaining the law of God, glorified is He, in the address to the Children of Israel in this surah, so refer back to it.

Then al-Biqa'i, after his previous speech, related from al-Hawali that he said: "He, exalted is He, repeated it to manifest the intent that the end of the address harmonises with its beginning, and so that this clarification and instruction may become a principle for what may come of its kind elsewhere in the Qur'an. So when the address reaches the limit of its conclusion, the heart must by itself take note of that limit and recite what follows it, so that in its recitation it combines both extremes of praise, and in its understanding it combines the meanings of both extremes." End of quote.

I say: If this were the cause of the repetition, then the more fitting explanation would be what we have made known to you.

As for his saying, "and so that this is taken as a principle for what recurs of repetition elsewhere in the Qur'an", it is well known that the establishment of this matter in minds and its settling in understandings is not confined to the repetition of one particular verse at which this purpose begins. Therefore the subtle point in repeating these two particular verses is not complete. God alone possesses the far-reaching wisdom which understandings cannot reach and minds cannot grasp. There is nothing in forcing these strained correspondences except what we made known to you there, so reflect.

His saying: ﴿And when He tested﴾. Al-ibtila' (testing) means trial and examination; that is, He tested him with what He commanded him. "Ibrahim" means in Syriac "a merciful father", so said al-Mawardi.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "Its meaning in Arabic is also that."

Al-Suhayli said: "Agreement between Syriac and Arabic is very frequent."

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) raised here a question about the pronoun referring back to Ibrahim while his grammatical position is later (i.e., the pronoun precedes its referent in rank), and he answered that he had already been mentioned explicitly, so the pronoun refers back to him. The matter in this is clearer than that it needs to be occupied with mentioning, or that questions should be raised regarding it, or that the face of the paper should be blackened with its clarification.

His saying: ﴿with words﴾. The scholars differed over determining them. It was said: they are the laws of Islam. It was said: the slaughter of his son. It was said: the conveying of the message. It was said: they are the characteristics of the natural disposition (fitrah). It was said: they are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾. It was said: they are purification, as its explanation will come.

Al-Zajjaj said: "These sayings are not contradictory, for all of this is what Ibrahim was tested with." End of quote.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic composition is that the words are His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ and what follows it, and that this would be an explanation of the words. What will come from some of the early generation (salaf) agrees with this, and from others is what opposes it.

On this basis, His saying ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ would be a new independent sentence, as if it were said: what did He say to him?

Ibn Jarir said, the gist of which is: It is permissible that the intended meaning of "the words" is all of that, and it is permissible that it is some of that. It is not permissible to assert definitively that any of them is the one intended specifically, except by a hadith or a consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). Nothing has been authentically reported on this, neither by a single transmitter nor by the group of transmitters whose report must be accepted. Then he said: "If someone said that what Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said is closer to the correct view," meaning that the words are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾ and His saying: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim...﴾ and what follows it.

Ibn Kathir preferred that they include all that was mentioned, and the explicit statement of what is true will come after the mention of what was transmitted from the righteous predecessors.

His saying: ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, meaning: he upheld them with the utmost completeness, and carried them out in the most perfect manner.

Al-imam (the leader) is that which is followed (yu'tamm bihi). From this it was said of a road that it is an imam, and of a building that it is an imam, because it is followed in that way, that is, the traveller is guided by it. Since the imam is the model for people, as they follow him and are guided by his way, this term was applied to him.

His saying: ﴿And from my offspring﴾ may be a supplication from Ibrahim, meaning: "and make from my offspring leaders." It may also be that this is from Ibrahim with the intent of a question, even though it is not in its grammatical form, meaning: "And what will be from my offspring, O Lord?" So He informed him that among them are the disobedient and the wrongdoers, and that they are not fit for that and will not undertake it, and that the covenant of God, glorified is He, will not reach them.

Al-dhurriyyah (offspring) is derived from al-dharr (scattering), because God brought forth creation from the loins of Adam when He made them testify against themselves, like atoms (dharr). It was also said: it is derived from dhara'a Allah al-khalq, yadhra'uhum, when He created them. In the Noble Book: ﴿so it became stubble, which the winds scatter﴾. In al-Sihah it says: the wind scattered (dharrat) the clouds and other things, scatters them (tadhruhu and tadhri), dharwan and dhar'an, meaning it blew them away. Al-Khalil said: they were only called dhurriyyah because God scattered them over the earth as the sower scatters the seed.

The meaning of the covenant has been disputed. It was said: the imamate. It was said: prophethood. It was said: the covenant of God is His command. It was said: safety from the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj preferred this, but the first is most apparent, as the context indicates.

A group of the people of knowledge have used this verse to show that the imam must be one of the people of justice and of acting by the law, as has been reported, because if he deviates from that he is a wrongdoer.

It is possible to consider what the term "covenant" truly applies to, and what the idafah (genitive construction) conveys of generality, so it includes all of that, taking into account the generality of the wording without looking to the occasion of revelation (sabab) or to the context. Thus it is used as evidence for the requirement of being free of the attribute of wrongdoing in everyone entrusted with religious affairs.

Ibn Jarir chose that this verse, although it is apparent as a report that the covenant of God regarding the imamate does not reach a wrongdoer, contains an informing from God to Ibrahim the Friend that there will be among his offspring someone who is a wrongdoer to himself.

End of quote.

It is not hidden from you that there is no benefit in this statement of his.

The better view is to say: this report carries the meaning of a command to His servants that they should not entrust the affairs of the law to a wrongdoer. We say it carries the meaning of a command because His reports, exalted is He, cannot be contrary to what they state, and we know that His covenant has in fact reached many wrongdoers, in the imamate and other things.

His saying: ﴿And when We made the House﴾. It is the Ka'bah, which became its specific name, just as al-najm (the star) became the specific name for al-Thurayya. And ﴿mathabah﴾ is a verbal noun from thaba, yathubu, mathaban and mathabah, meaning a place to which pilgrims return after dispersing from it. From this is the saying of Waraqah ibn Nawfal about the Ka'bah:

A return for the nape of every tribe, to which the lean, swift camels hasten.

Al-A'mash read "mathabat" (plural). It was said: mathabah is from thawab (reward), meaning they are rewarded there.

Mujahid said: the intent is that they never fulfil their need from it. The poet said:

The House was made a place of return for them,
Never do they fulfil their desire from it, through all time.

Al-Akhfash said: the ta' marbutah entered because of how many return to it, so it is like 'allamah and nassabah (intensive forms). Others said: it is for the feminine, not for emphasis.

His saying: ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ is a noun of place, meaning a place of security.

A group of the people of knowledge used this as evidence that the prescribed punishment (hadd) is not carried out against one who takes refuge in it. His saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾. It was also said that this is abrogated (mansukh).

His saying: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read with a fathah on the kha', as a past tense verb, meaning: We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary, and they took it as a place of prayer.

The rest read it in the imperative form, coordinated with ﴿remember﴾ mentioned at the beginning of the verses, or with the implied ﴿remember﴾ which governs ﴿and when﴾. It is also permissible that it is under the assumption of a verb of saying, meaning: and We said, "take."

Al-maqam (station) linguistically means the place of standing. Al-Nahhas said: it derives from qama, yaqumu, and it can be a verbal noun and a noun for a place, and maqam of one who stands (aqama). This is not the sense in the poet's words:

Among them are fine stations, their faces, and assemblies where speech and deed are exchanged.

Because its meaning is "people of stations."

There has been disagreement over determining the maqam in several views. The most sound is that it is the stone which people know and at which they pray the two rak'ahs of tawaf. It was said: the maqam is the entire Hajj. This was reported from 'Ata' and Mujahid. It was said: 'Arafah and Muzdalifah, also reported from 'Ata'.

Al-Sha'bi said: the entire sanctuary (haram) is the station of Ibrahim.

It was reported from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord﴾, that he said: God tested him with purification: five in the head and five in the body. In the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling water into the nose, the siwak, and parting the hair. In the body: cutting the nails, shaving the pubic area, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing the place of excrement and urine with water.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir related similar from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir related from him that he said: "No one was tested with this religion and carried it out entirely except Ibrahim." He recited this verse, and it was asked of him: what are the words? He said: "The arrows of Islam are thirty arrows: ten in (Surat) Bara'ah: ﴿those who repent, who worship...﴾ to the end of the verse; ten at the beginning of Surat 'Qad aflaha' and 'Sa'ala sa'il': ﴿and those who believe in the Day of Recompense...﴾ the verses; and ten in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, the Muslims...﴾ to the end of the verse. ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, all of them, so he was granted an acquittal." He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from him that he said: "Among them are the rites of Hajj."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "The words are ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾, ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations﴾, and the signs concerning the rites, the station that was made for Ibrahim, the provision given to the residents of the House, and the sending of Muhammad from their offspring."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words﴾, that he said: "He was tested with the signs that come after it."

Both of them also related similar from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The words with which Ibrahim was tested and fulfilled them were: his separation from his people for God's sake when he was commanded to part from them; his argument with Nimrud for God's sake when he made him stand before what he made him stand before, of the gravity of the matter in which they disagreed; his patience at their throwing him into the fire to burn him for God's sake; the emigration after that from his homeland and country when He commanded him to leave them; what he was commanded of hospitality and patience in it; and what he was tested with of sacrificing his son. When he had completed all of that, God said to him: ﴿Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.﴾"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "He tested him with the star, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the moon, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the sun, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with emigration (hijrah), and he was pleased with him; He tested him with circumcision, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with his son, and he was pleased with him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿fa-atammahunna﴾ (﴿and he fulfilled them﴾), that he said: "He performed them (fa-addahunna)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ata', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of the fitrah (natural disposition) of Ibrahim is the siwak (tooth-cleaning stick)." I say: Even if its chain up to Ata' is sound, this is a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), which does not establish proof, and it is not permissible to rely on the like of it in the tafsir (exegesis) of the words of Allah, the Exalted. Likewise, it is not permissible to rely on what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Of the fitrah of Ibrahim is washing the private parts and the joints (al-baraajim)," nor on what Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated in his Musannaf from him, who said: "Six are of the fitrah of Ibrahim: trimming the moustache, the siwak, parting the hair, cutting the nails, istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself), and shaving the pubic hair." He said: "Three are on the head and three are on the body."

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the Sahih and elsewhere, through a number of Companions, that these ten practices are prescribed for this Ummah. However, it has not been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that these are the words with which Ibrahim was tested. The best that has been transmitted from him is what al-Tirmidhi narrated and graded as hasan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to trim or take from his moustache. He said: The Khalil of the Most Merciful, Ibrahim, used to do it."

It is not hidden from you that the Khalil (Ibrahim) doing something does not necessitate that it is one of the words with which he was tested. Since nothing has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and nothing has come to us through a channel that establishes proof, specifying those words, we have no option but to say: they are what Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in His Book with His words ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ through to the end of the verses. This would then be an explanation of the words, or else one remains silent and leaves the knowledge of that to Allah, the Exalted.

As for what has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and similar reports from the Companions and those after them concerning their specification, firstly these are sayings of Companions, which do not establish proof, let alone the sayings of those who came after them. Even if we suppose there is no room for ijtihad (independent reasoning) in this matter, and that such reports have the status of being traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), they differ in specifying them to such an extent that it is impossible to act upon some of what has been narrated from them to the exclusion of the others. Indeed, the reports from one and the same person among them differ, as we have already mentioned from Ibn Abbas. How then could it be permissible to act upon this? By this you will recognise the weakness of the view of one who says: the matter is to be taken in its general sense, and it is said that those words are all of what we have mentioned here. This would necessitate interpreting the words of Allah with what is weak, contradictory, and what does not establish proof.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾: "to be followed in your religion, your guidance and your sunnah." ﴿He said: And from my offspring﴾: an imam for others than my offspring. ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾: that they be followed in their religion, their guidance and their sunnah.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: Allah said to Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people,﴾ he said: ﴿And from my offspring,﴾ so He refused to do so, then said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "This is with Allah on the Day of Resurrection: His covenant does not reach a wrongdoer. As for in this world, they did attain His covenant, so they inherited from the Muslims through it, fought them, and intermarried with them. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah restricts His covenant and His honour to His friends (awliya')."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, regarding the interpretation of the verse, that he said: "I will not make a wrongdoer an imam to be followed."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "He informs him that if there is a wrongdoer among his offspring, he will not attain His covenant, and it is not appropriate for him to appoint him to any of his affairs."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "A wrongdoer has no covenant upon you in disobedience to Allah."

Waki' ibn Mardawayh has narrated, from a hadith of Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers,﴾ that he said: "There is no obedience except in what is right (ma'ruf)." Its chain as given by Ibn Mardawayh is as follows: He said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Hamid narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Abd Allah ibn Sa'd al-Asadi narrated to us; Sulaym ibn Sa'id al-Damaghani narrated to us; Waki' narrated to us from al-A'mash, from Sa'd ibn Ubaydah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from a hadith of Imran ibn Husayn, "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: There is no obedience to any created being in disobedience to Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of the verse: "A wrongdoer has no covenant; even if you make a covenant with him, break it."

Ibn Kathir said: Similar to this has been narrated from Mujahid, Ata', Muqatil and Ibn Hibban.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿a place of return for the people and a security﴾ that he said: "They return to it, then they go back."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "They never finish their need of it; they come to it, then return to their families, then come back to it again."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and a security﴾ that he said: "A security for the people."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated, from a hadith of Anas, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters, and my Lord agreed with me in three. I said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer. Then this was revealed: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾ I also said: O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon your wives, so if only you would command them to veil. Then the verse of hijab (veiling) was revealed. And the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered together in jealousy, so I said to them: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾; and it was revealed in this manner."

Muslim and others narrated it in abridged form from the hadith of Ibn Umar, from him.

Muslim and others narrated, from a hadith of Jabir, "that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ramal (hastened walking) for three circuits and walked for four. When he finished, he went to the Station of Ibrahim and prayed two rak'ahs behind it, then recited: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾"

Regarding the Station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, there are many hadiths, fully recorded in the major collections and elsewhere. The sound hadiths indicate that the Station of Ibrahim is the stone upon which Ibrahim used to stand to build the Ka'bah when the wall had risen; Isma'il brought it to him so that he could stand upon it, as in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. It is the stone that was attached to the wall of the Ka'bah.

The first person to move it was Umar ibn al-Khattab, as narrated by Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi with a sound chain, and by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh through various routes.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from a hadith of Jabir describing the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) had performed tawaf, Umar said to him: 'Is this the Station of Ibrahim?' He said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar to it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. Something similar has already occurred at the beginning of the surah, and its tafsir (exegesis) has already been given. The reason for the repetition is to urge following the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet. Ibn Kathir mentioned its meaning in his tafsir.

Al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: "When the discussion grew long in cataloguing their reminders of blessings, then in explaining their defects and exposing their secrets, and it concluded with a warning against the ruin of their religion through their deeds, states and words, He repeated what He had opened their story with, the reminder of blessings and the warning against the coming of retribution on the Day when the nations are gathered, a Day in which regret will last for whoever has slipped. This is so that it is known that this is the summation (fadhlakah) of the story, and the primary purpose is to urge seizing the opportunity." End of quote.

I say: This is not anything of substance. For if the cause of the repetition were what he mentioned, namely the length of the span and that He returned to what He had opened their story with, then the more fitting thing to be repeated, and the more deserving of being restated, would be His words, glorified is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant, and fear Me﴾. This verse, although it is the first speech addressed to them and the address to them in this surah, is also more worthy of being restated and repeated, because of what it contains of the command to remember the blessings, to fulfil the covenant, and to hold awe of God, glorified is He. By this you will know the soundness of what we presented to you when explaining the law of God, glorified is He, in the address to the Children of Israel in this surah, so refer back to it.

Then al-Biqa'i, after his previous speech, related from al-Hawali that he said: "He, exalted is He, repeated it to manifest the intent that the end of the address harmonises with its beginning, and so that this clarification and instruction may become a principle for what may come of its kind elsewhere in the Qur'an. So when the address reaches the limit of its conclusion, the heart must by itself take note of that limit and recite what follows it, so that in its recitation it combines both extremes of praise, and in its understanding it combines the meanings of both extremes." End of quote.

I say: If this were the cause of the repetition, then the more fitting explanation would be what we have made known to you.

As for his saying, "and so that this is taken as a principle for what recurs of repetition elsewhere in the Qur'an", it is well known that the establishment of this matter in minds and its settling in understandings is not confined to the repetition of one particular verse at which this purpose begins. Therefore the subtle point in repeating these two particular verses is not complete. God alone possesses the far-reaching wisdom which understandings cannot reach and minds cannot grasp. There is nothing in forcing these strained correspondences except what we made known to you there, so reflect.

His saying: ﴿And when He tested﴾. Al-ibtila' (testing) means trial and examination; that is, He tested him with what He commanded him. "Ibrahim" means in Syriac "a merciful father", so said al-Mawardi.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "Its meaning in Arabic is also that."

Al-Suhayli said: "Agreement between Syriac and Arabic is very frequent."

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) raised here a question about the pronoun referring back to Ibrahim while his grammatical position is later (i.e., the pronoun precedes its referent in rank), and he answered that he had already been mentioned explicitly, so the pronoun refers back to him. The matter in this is clearer than that it needs to be occupied with mentioning, or that questions should be raised regarding it, or that the face of the paper should be blackened with its clarification.

His saying: ﴿with words﴾. The scholars differed over determining them. It was said: they are the laws of Islam. It was said: the slaughter of his son. It was said: the conveying of the message. It was said: they are the characteristics of the natural disposition (fitrah). It was said: they are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾. It was said: they are purification, as its explanation will come.

Al-Zajjaj said: "These sayings are not contradictory, for all of this is what Ibrahim was tested with." End of quote.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic composition is that the words are His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ and what follows it, and that this would be an explanation of the words. What will come from some of the early generation (salaf) agrees with this, and from others is what opposes it.

On this basis, His saying ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ would be a new independent sentence, as if it were said: what did He say to him?

Ibn Jarir said, the gist of which is: It is permissible that the intended meaning of "the words" is all of that, and it is permissible that it is some of that. It is not permissible to assert definitively that any of them is the one intended specifically, except by a hadith or a consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). Nothing has been authentically reported on this, neither by a single transmitter nor by the group of transmitters whose report must be accepted. Then he said: "If someone said that what Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said is closer to the correct view," meaning that the words are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾ and His saying: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim...﴾ and what follows it.

Ibn Kathir preferred that they include all that was mentioned, and the explicit statement of what is true will come after the mention of what was transmitted from the righteous predecessors.

His saying: ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, meaning: he upheld them with the utmost completeness, and carried them out in the most perfect manner.

Al-imam (the leader) is that which is followed (yu'tamm bihi). From this it was said of a road that it is an imam, and of a building that it is an imam, because it is followed in that way, that is, the traveller is guided by it. Since the imam is the model for people, as they follow him and are guided by his way, this term was applied to him.

His saying: ﴿And from my offspring﴾ may be a supplication from Ibrahim, meaning: "and make from my offspring leaders." It may also be that this is from Ibrahim with the intent of a question, even though it is not in its grammatical form, meaning: "And what will be from my offspring, O Lord?" So He informed him that among them are the disobedient and the wrongdoers, and that they are not fit for that and will not undertake it, and that the covenant of God, glorified is He, will not reach them.

Al-dhurriyyah (offspring) is derived from al-dharr (scattering), because God brought forth creation from the loins of Adam when He made them testify against themselves, like atoms (dharr). It was also said: it is derived from dhara'a Allah al-khalq, yadhra'uhum, when He created them. In the Noble Book: ﴿so it became stubble, which the winds scatter﴾. In al-Sihah it says: the wind scattered (dharrat) the clouds and other things, scatters them (tadhruhu and tadhri), dharwan and dhar'an, meaning it blew them away. Al-Khalil said: they were only called dhurriyyah because God scattered them over the earth as the sower scatters the seed.

The meaning of the covenant has been disputed. It was said: the imamate. It was said: prophethood. It was said: the covenant of God is His command. It was said: safety from the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj preferred this, but the first is most apparent, as the context indicates.

A group of the people of knowledge have used this verse to show that the imam must be one of the people of justice and of acting by the law, as has been reported, because if he deviates from that he is a wrongdoer.

It is possible to consider what the term "covenant" truly applies to, and what the idafah (genitive construction) conveys of generality, so it includes all of that, taking into account the generality of the wording without looking to the occasion of revelation (sabab) or to the context. Thus it is used as evidence for the requirement of being free of the attribute of wrongdoing in everyone entrusted with religious affairs.

Ibn Jarir chose that this verse, although it is apparent as a report that the covenant of God regarding the imamate does not reach a wrongdoer, contains an informing from God to Ibrahim the Friend that there will be among his offspring someone who is a wrongdoer to himself.

End of quote.

It is not hidden from you that there is no benefit in this statement of his.

The better view is to say: this report carries the meaning of a command to His servants that they should not entrust the affairs of the law to a wrongdoer. We say it carries the meaning of a command because His reports, exalted is He, cannot be contrary to what they state, and we know that His covenant has in fact reached many wrongdoers, in the imamate and other things.

His saying: ﴿And when We made the House﴾. It is the Ka'bah, which became its specific name, just as al-najm (the star) became the specific name for al-Thurayya. And ﴿mathabah﴾ is a verbal noun from thaba, yathubu, mathaban and mathabah, meaning a place to which pilgrims return after dispersing from it. From this is the saying of Waraqah ibn Nawfal about the Ka'bah:

A return for the nape of every tribe, to which the lean, swift camels hasten.

Al-A'mash read "mathabat" (plural). It was said: mathabah is from thawab (reward), meaning they are rewarded there.

Mujahid said: the intent is that they never fulfil their need from it. The poet said:

The House was made a place of return for them,
Never do they fulfil their desire from it, through all time.

Al-Akhfash said: the ta' marbutah entered because of how many return to it, so it is like 'allamah and nassabah (intensive forms). Others said: it is for the feminine, not for emphasis.

His saying: ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ is a noun of place, meaning a place of security.

A group of the people of knowledge used this as evidence that the prescribed punishment (hadd) is not carried out against one who takes refuge in it. His saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾. It was also said that this is abrogated (mansukh).

His saying: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read with a fathah on the kha', as a past tense verb, meaning: We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary, and they took it as a place of prayer.

The rest read it in the imperative form, coordinated with ﴿remember﴾ mentioned at the beginning of the verses, or with the implied ﴿remember﴾ which governs ﴿and when﴾. It is also permissible that it is under the assumption of a verb of saying, meaning: and We said, "take."

Al-maqam (station) linguistically means the place of standing. Al-Nahhas said: it derives from qama, yaqumu, and it can be a verbal noun and a noun for a place, and maqam of one who stands (aqama). This is not the sense in the poet's words:

Among them are fine stations, their faces, and assemblies where speech and deed are exchanged.

Because its meaning is "people of stations."

There has been disagreement over determining the maqam in several views. The most sound is that it is the stone which people know and at which they pray the two rak'ahs of tawaf. It was said: the maqam is the entire Hajj. This was reported from 'Ata' and Mujahid. It was said: 'Arafah and Muzdalifah, also reported from 'Ata'.

Al-Sha'bi said: the entire sanctuary (haram) is the station of Ibrahim.

It was reported from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord﴾, that he said: God tested him with purification: five in the head and five in the body. In the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling water into the nose, the siwak, and parting the hair. In the body: cutting the nails, shaving the pubic area, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing the place of excrement and urine with water.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir related similar from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir related from him that he said: "No one was tested with this religion and carried it out entirely except Ibrahim." He recited this verse, and it was asked of him: what are the words? He said: "The arrows of Islam are thirty arrows: ten in (Surat) Bara'ah: ﴿those who repent, who worship...﴾ to the end of the verse; ten at the beginning of Surat 'Qad aflaha' and 'Sa'ala sa'il': ﴿and those who believe in the Day of Recompense...﴾ the verses; and ten in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, the Muslims...﴾ to the end of the verse. ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, all of them, so he was granted an acquittal." He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from him that he said: "Among them are the rites of Hajj."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "The words are ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾, ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations﴾, and the signs concerning the rites, the station that was made for Ibrahim, the provision given to the residents of the House, and the sending of Muhammad from their offspring."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words﴾, that he said: "He was tested with the signs that come after it."

Both of them also related similar from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The words with which Ibrahim was tested and fulfilled them were: his separation from his people for God's sake when he was commanded to part from them; his argument with Nimrud for God's sake when he made him stand before what he made him stand before, of the gravity of the matter in which they disagreed; his patience at their throwing him into the fire to burn him for God's sake; the emigration after that from his homeland and country when He commanded him to leave them; what he was commanded of hospitality and patience in it; and what he was tested with of sacrificing his son. When he had completed all of that, God said to him: ﴿Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.﴾"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "He tested him with the star, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the moon, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the sun, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with emigration (hijrah), and he was pleased with him; He tested him with circumcision, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with his son, and he was pleased with him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿fa-atammahunna﴾ (﴿and he fulfilled them﴾), that he said: "He performed them (fa-addahunna)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ata', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of the fitrah (natural disposition) of Ibrahim is the siwak (tooth-cleaning stick)." I say: Even if its chain up to Ata' is sound, this is a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), which does not establish proof, and it is not permissible to rely on the like of it in the tafsir (exegesis) of the words of Allah, the Exalted. Likewise, it is not permissible to rely on what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Of the fitrah of Ibrahim is washing the private parts and the joints (al-baraajim)," nor on what Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated in his Musannaf from him, who said: "Six are of the fitrah of Ibrahim: trimming the moustache, the siwak, parting the hair, cutting the nails, istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself), and shaving the pubic hair." He said: "Three are on the head and three are on the body."

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the Sahih and elsewhere, through a number of Companions, that these ten practices are prescribed for this Ummah. However, it has not been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that these are the words with which Ibrahim was tested. The best that has been transmitted from him is what al-Tirmidhi narrated and graded as hasan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to trim or take from his moustache. He said: The Khalil of the Most Merciful, Ibrahim, used to do it."

It is not hidden from you that the Khalil (Ibrahim) doing something does not necessitate that it is one of the words with which he was tested. Since nothing has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and nothing has come to us through a channel that establishes proof, specifying those words, we have no option but to say: they are what Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in His Book with His words ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ through to the end of the verses. This would then be an explanation of the words, or else one remains silent and leaves the knowledge of that to Allah, the Exalted.

As for what has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and similar reports from the Companions and those after them concerning their specification, firstly these are sayings of Companions, which do not establish proof, let alone the sayings of those who came after them. Even if we suppose there is no room for ijtihad (independent reasoning) in this matter, and that such reports have the status of being traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), they differ in specifying them to such an extent that it is impossible to act upon some of what has been narrated from them to the exclusion of the others. Indeed, the reports from one and the same person among them differ, as we have already mentioned from Ibn Abbas. How then could it be permissible to act upon this? By this you will recognise the weakness of the view of one who says: the matter is to be taken in its general sense, and it is said that those words are all of what we have mentioned here. This would necessitate interpreting the words of Allah with what is weak, contradictory, and what does not establish proof.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾: "to be followed in your religion, your guidance and your sunnah." ﴿He said: And from my offspring﴾: an imam for others than my offspring. ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾: that they be followed in their religion, their guidance and their sunnah.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: Allah said to Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people,﴾ he said: ﴿And from my offspring,﴾ so He refused to do so, then said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "This is with Allah on the Day of Resurrection: His covenant does not reach a wrongdoer. As for in this world, they did attain His covenant, so they inherited from the Muslims through it, fought them, and intermarried with them. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah restricts His covenant and His honour to His friends (awliya')."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, regarding the interpretation of the verse, that he said: "I will not make a wrongdoer an imam to be followed."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "He informs him that if there is a wrongdoer among his offspring, he will not attain His covenant, and it is not appropriate for him to appoint him to any of his affairs."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "A wrongdoer has no covenant upon you in disobedience to Allah."

Waki' ibn Mardawayh has narrated, from a hadith of Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers,﴾ that he said: "There is no obedience except in what is right (ma'ruf)." Its chain as given by Ibn Mardawayh is as follows: He said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Hamid narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Abd Allah ibn Sa'd al-Asadi narrated to us; Sulaym ibn Sa'id al-Damaghani narrated to us; Waki' narrated to us from al-A'mash, from Sa'd ibn Ubaydah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from a hadith of Imran ibn Husayn, "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: There is no obedience to any created being in disobedience to Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of the verse: "A wrongdoer has no covenant; even if you make a covenant with him, break it."

Ibn Kathir said: Similar to this has been narrated from Mujahid, Ata', Muqatil and Ibn Hibban.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿a place of return for the people and a security﴾ that he said: "They return to it, then they go back."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "They never finish their need of it; they come to it, then return to their families, then come back to it again."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and a security﴾ that he said: "A security for the people."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated, from a hadith of Anas, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters, and my Lord agreed with me in three. I said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer. Then this was revealed: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾ I also said: O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon your wives, so if only you would command them to veil. Then the verse of hijab (veiling) was revealed. And the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered together in jealousy, so I said to them: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾; and it was revealed in this manner."

Muslim and others narrated it in abridged form from the hadith of Ibn Umar, from him.

Muslim and others narrated, from a hadith of Jabir, "that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ramal (hastened walking) for three circuits and walked for four. When he finished, he went to the Station of Ibrahim and prayed two rak'ahs behind it, then recited: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾"

Regarding the Station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, there are many hadiths, fully recorded in the major collections and elsewhere. The sound hadiths indicate that the Station of Ibrahim is the stone upon which Ibrahim used to stand to build the Ka'bah when the wall had risen; Isma'il brought it to him so that he could stand upon it, as in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. It is the stone that was attached to the wall of the Ka'bah.

The first person to move it was Umar ibn al-Khattab, as narrated by Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi with a sound chain, and by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh through various routes.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from a hadith of Jabir describing the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) had performed tawaf, Umar said to him: 'Is this the Station of Ibrahim?' He said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar to it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. Something similar has already occurred at the beginning of the surah, and its tafsir (exegesis) has already been given. The reason for the repetition is to urge following the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet. Ibn Kathir mentioned its meaning in his tafsir.

Al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: "When the discussion grew long in cataloguing their reminders of blessings, then in explaining their defects and exposing their secrets, and it concluded with a warning against the ruin of their religion through their deeds, states and words, He repeated what He had opened their story with, the reminder of blessings and the warning against the coming of retribution on the Day when the nations are gathered, a Day in which regret will last for whoever has slipped. This is so that it is known that this is the summation (fadhlakah) of the story, and the primary purpose is to urge seizing the opportunity." End of quote.

I say: This is not anything of substance. For if the cause of the repetition were what he mentioned, namely the length of the span and that He returned to what He had opened their story with, then the more fitting thing to be repeated, and the more deserving of being restated, would be His words, glorified is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant, and fear Me﴾. This verse, although it is the first speech addressed to them and the address to them in this surah, is also more worthy of being restated and repeated, because of what it contains of the command to remember the blessings, to fulfil the covenant, and to hold awe of God, glorified is He. By this you will know the soundness of what we presented to you when explaining the law of God, glorified is He, in the address to the Children of Israel in this surah, so refer back to it.

Then al-Biqa'i, after his previous speech, related from al-Hawali that he said: "He, exalted is He, repeated it to manifest the intent that the end of the address harmonises with its beginning, and so that this clarification and instruction may become a principle for what may come of its kind elsewhere in the Qur'an. So when the address reaches the limit of its conclusion, the heart must by itself take note of that limit and recite what follows it, so that in its recitation it combines both extremes of praise, and in its understanding it combines the meanings of both extremes." End of quote.

I say: If this were the cause of the repetition, then the more fitting explanation would be what we have made known to you.

As for his saying, "and so that this is taken as a principle for what recurs of repetition elsewhere in the Qur'an", it is well known that the establishment of this matter in minds and its settling in understandings is not confined to the repetition of one particular verse at which this purpose begins. Therefore the subtle point in repeating these two particular verses is not complete. God alone possesses the far-reaching wisdom which understandings cannot reach and minds cannot grasp. There is nothing in forcing these strained correspondences except what we made known to you there, so reflect.

His saying: ﴿And when He tested﴾. Al-ibtila' (testing) means trial and examination; that is, He tested him with what He commanded him. "Ibrahim" means in Syriac "a merciful father", so said al-Mawardi.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "Its meaning in Arabic is also that."

Al-Suhayli said: "Agreement between Syriac and Arabic is very frequent."

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) raised here a question about the pronoun referring back to Ibrahim while his grammatical position is later (i.e., the pronoun precedes its referent in rank), and he answered that he had already been mentioned explicitly, so the pronoun refers back to him. The matter in this is clearer than that it needs to be occupied with mentioning, or that questions should be raised regarding it, or that the face of the paper should be blackened with its clarification.

His saying: ﴿with words﴾. The scholars differed over determining them. It was said: they are the laws of Islam. It was said: the slaughter of his son. It was said: the conveying of the message. It was said: they are the characteristics of the natural disposition (fitrah). It was said: they are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾. It was said: they are purification, as its explanation will come.

Al-Zajjaj said: "These sayings are not contradictory, for all of this is what Ibrahim was tested with." End of quote.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic composition is that the words are His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ and what follows it, and that this would be an explanation of the words. What will come from some of the early generation (salaf) agrees with this, and from others is what opposes it.

On this basis, His saying ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am making you...﴾ would be a new independent sentence, as if it were said: what did He say to him?

Ibn Jarir said, the gist of which is: It is permissible that the intended meaning of "the words" is all of that, and it is permissible that it is some of that. It is not permissible to assert definitively that any of them is the one intended specifically, except by a hadith or a consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). Nothing has been authentically reported on this, neither by a single transmitter nor by the group of transmitters whose report must be accepted. Then he said: "If someone said that what Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said is closer to the correct view," meaning that the words are His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾ and His saying: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim...﴾ and what follows it.

Ibn Kathir preferred that they include all that was mentioned, and the explicit statement of what is true will come after the mention of what was transmitted from the righteous predecessors.

His saying: ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, meaning: he upheld them with the utmost completeness, and carried them out in the most perfect manner.

Al-imam (the leader) is that which is followed (yu'tamm bihi). From this it was said of a road that it is an imam, and of a building that it is an imam, because it is followed in that way, that is, the traveller is guided by it. Since the imam is the model for people, as they follow him and are guided by his way, this term was applied to him.

His saying: ﴿And from my offspring﴾ may be a supplication from Ibrahim, meaning: "and make from my offspring leaders." It may also be that this is from Ibrahim with the intent of a question, even though it is not in its grammatical form, meaning: "And what will be from my offspring, O Lord?" So He informed him that among them are the disobedient and the wrongdoers, and that they are not fit for that and will not undertake it, and that the covenant of God, glorified is He, will not reach them.

Al-dhurriyyah (offspring) is derived from al-dharr (scattering), because God brought forth creation from the loins of Adam when He made them testify against themselves, like atoms (dharr). It was also said: it is derived from dhara'a Allah al-khalq, yadhra'uhum, when He created them. In the Noble Book: ﴿so it became stubble, which the winds scatter﴾. In al-Sihah it says: the wind scattered (dharrat) the clouds and other things, scatters them (tadhruhu and tadhri), dharwan and dhar'an, meaning it blew them away. Al-Khalil said: they were only called dhurriyyah because God scattered them over the earth as the sower scatters the seed.

The meaning of the covenant has been disputed. It was said: the imamate. It was said: prophethood. It was said: the covenant of God is His command. It was said: safety from the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj preferred this, but the first is most apparent, as the context indicates.

A group of the people of knowledge have used this verse to show that the imam must be one of the people of justice and of acting by the law, as has been reported, because if he deviates from that he is a wrongdoer.

It is possible to consider what the term "covenant" truly applies to, and what the idafah (genitive construction) conveys of generality, so it includes all of that, taking into account the generality of the wording without looking to the occasion of revelation (sabab) or to the context. Thus it is used as evidence for the requirement of being free of the attribute of wrongdoing in everyone entrusted with religious affairs.

Ibn Jarir chose that this verse, although it is apparent as a report that the covenant of God regarding the imamate does not reach a wrongdoer, contains an informing from God to Ibrahim the Friend that there will be among his offspring someone who is a wrongdoer to himself.

End of quote.

It is not hidden from you that there is no benefit in this statement of his.

The better view is to say: this report carries the meaning of a command to His servants that they should not entrust the affairs of the law to a wrongdoer. We say it carries the meaning of a command because His reports, exalted is He, cannot be contrary to what they state, and we know that His covenant has in fact reached many wrongdoers, in the imamate and other things.

His saying: ﴿And when We made the House﴾. It is the Ka'bah, which became its specific name, just as al-najm (the star) became the specific name for al-Thurayya. And ﴿mathabah﴾ is a verbal noun from thaba, yathubu, mathaban and mathabah, meaning a place to which pilgrims return after dispersing from it. From this is the saying of Waraqah ibn Nawfal about the Ka'bah:

A return for the nape of every tribe, to which the lean, swift camels hasten.

Al-A'mash read "mathabat" (plural). It was said: mathabah is from thawab (reward), meaning they are rewarded there.

Mujahid said: the intent is that they never fulfil their need from it. The poet said:

The House was made a place of return for them,
Never do they fulfil their desire from it, through all time.

Al-Akhfash said: the ta' marbutah entered because of how many return to it, so it is like 'allamah and nassabah (intensive forms). Others said: it is for the feminine, not for emphasis.

His saying: ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ is a noun of place, meaning a place of security.

A group of the people of knowledge used this as evidence that the prescribed punishment (hadd) is not carried out against one who takes refuge in it. His saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾. It was also said that this is abrogated (mansukh).

His saying: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read with a fathah on the kha', as a past tense verb, meaning: We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary, and they took it as a place of prayer.

The rest read it in the imperative form, coordinated with ﴿remember﴾ mentioned at the beginning of the verses, or with the implied ﴿remember﴾ which governs ﴿and when﴾. It is also permissible that it is under the assumption of a verb of saying, meaning: and We said, "take."

Al-maqam (station) linguistically means the place of standing. Al-Nahhas said: it derives from qama, yaqumu, and it can be a verbal noun and a noun for a place, and maqam of one who stands (aqama). This is not the sense in the poet's words:

Among them are fine stations, their faces, and assemblies where speech and deed are exchanged.

Because its meaning is "people of stations."

There has been disagreement over determining the maqam in several views. The most sound is that it is the stone which people know and at which they pray the two rak'ahs of tawaf. It was said: the maqam is the entire Hajj. This was reported from 'Ata' and Mujahid. It was said: 'Arafah and Muzdalifah, also reported from 'Ata'.

Al-Sha'bi said: the entire sanctuary (haram) is the station of Ibrahim.

It was reported from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan have related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord﴾, that he said: God tested him with purification: five in the head and five in the body. In the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling water into the nose, the siwak, and parting the hair. In the body: cutting the nails, shaving the pubic area, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing the place of excrement and urine with water.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir related similar from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir related from him that he said: "No one was tested with this religion and carried it out entirely except Ibrahim." He recited this verse, and it was asked of him: what are the words? He said: "The arrows of Islam are thirty arrows: ten in (Surat) Bara'ah: ﴿those who repent, who worship...﴾ to the end of the verse; ten at the beginning of Surat 'Qad aflaha' and 'Sa'ala sa'il': ﴿and those who believe in the Day of Recompense...﴾ the verses; and ten in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, the Muslims...﴾ to the end of the verse. ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾, all of them, so he was granted an acquittal." He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from him that he said: "Among them are the rites of Hajj."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "The words are ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾, ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations﴾, and the signs concerning the rites, the station that was made for Ibrahim, the provision given to the residents of the House, and the sending of Muhammad from their offspring."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words﴾, that he said: "He was tested with the signs that come after it."

Both of them also related similar from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The words with which Ibrahim was tested and fulfilled them were: his separation from his people for God's sake when he was commanded to part from them; his argument with Nimrud for God's sake when he made him stand before what he made him stand before, of the gravity of the matter in which they disagreed; his patience at their throwing him into the fire to burn him for God's sake; the emigration after that from his homeland and country when He commanded him to leave them; what he was commanded of hospitality and patience in it; and what he was tested with of sacrificing his son. When he had completed all of that, God said to him: ﴿Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.﴾"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 122–124 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "He tested him with the star, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the moon, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with the sun, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with emigration (hijrah), and he was pleased with him; He tested him with circumcision, and he was pleased with him; He tested him with his son, and he was pleased with him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿fa-atammahunna﴾ (﴿and he fulfilled them﴾), that he said: "He performed them (fa-addahunna)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ata', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of the fitrah (natural disposition) of Ibrahim is the siwak (tooth-cleaning stick)." I say: Even if its chain up to Ata' is sound, this is a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), which does not establish proof, and it is not permissible to rely on the like of it in the tafsir (exegesis) of the words of Allah, the Exalted. Likewise, it is not permissible to rely on what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Of the fitrah of Ibrahim is washing the private parts and the joints (al-baraajim)," nor on what Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated in his Musannaf from him, who said: "Six are of the fitrah of Ibrahim: trimming the moustache, the siwak, parting the hair, cutting the nails, istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself), and shaving the pubic hair." He said: "Three are on the head and three are on the body."

It has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the Sahih and elsewhere, through a number of Companions, that these ten practices are prescribed for this Ummah. However, it has not been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that these are the words with which Ibrahim was tested. The best that has been transmitted from him is what al-Tirmidhi narrated and graded as hasan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to trim or take from his moustache. He said: The Khalil of the Most Merciful, Ibrahim, used to do it."

It is not hidden from you that the Khalil (Ibrahim) doing something does not necessitate that it is one of the words with which he was tested. Since nothing has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and nothing has come to us through a channel that establishes proof, specifying those words, we have no option but to say: they are what Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in His Book with His words ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ through to the end of the verses. This would then be an explanation of the words, or else one remains silent and leaves the knowledge of that to Allah, the Exalted.

As for what has been narrated from Ibn Abbas and similar reports from the Companions and those after them concerning their specification, firstly these are sayings of Companions, which do not establish proof, let alone the sayings of those who came after them. Even if we suppose there is no room for ijtihad (independent reasoning) in this matter, and that such reports have the status of being traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), they differ in specifying them to such an extent that it is impossible to act upon some of what has been narrated from them to the exclusion of the others. Indeed, the reports from one and the same person among them differ, as we have already mentioned from Ibn Abbas. How then could it be permissible to act upon this? By this you will recognise the weakness of the view of one who says: the matter is to be taken in its general sense, and it is said that those words are all of what we have mentioned here. This would necessitate interpreting the words of Allah with what is weak, contradictory, and what does not establish proof.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾: "to be followed in your religion, your guidance and your sunnah." ﴿He said: And from my offspring﴾: an imam for others than my offspring. ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾: that they be followed in their religion, their guidance and their sunnah.

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: Allah said to Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people,﴾ he said: ﴿And from my offspring,﴾ so He refused to do so, then said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "This is with Allah on the Day of Resurrection: His covenant does not reach a wrongdoer. As for in this world, they did attain His covenant, so they inherited from the Muslims through it, fought them, and intermarried with them. But when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah restricts His covenant and His honour to His friends (awliya')."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, regarding the interpretation of the verse, that he said: "I will not make a wrongdoer an imam to be followed."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "He informs him that if there is a wrongdoer among his offspring, he will not attain His covenant, and it is not appropriate for him to appoint him to any of his affairs."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "A wrongdoer has no covenant upon you in disobedience to Allah."

Waki' ibn Mardawayh has narrated, from a hadith of Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers,﴾ that he said: "There is no obedience except in what is right (ma'ruf)." Its chain as given by Ibn Mardawayh is as follows: He said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Hamid narrated to us; Ahmad ibn Abd Allah ibn Sa'd al-Asadi narrated to us; Sulaym ibn Sa'id al-Damaghani narrated to us; Waki' narrated to us from al-A'mash, from Sa'd ibn Ubaydah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned it.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from a hadith of Imran ibn Husayn, "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: There is no obedience to any created being in disobedience to Allah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the interpretation of the verse: "A wrongdoer has no covenant; even if you make a covenant with him, break it."

Ibn Kathir said: Similar to this has been narrated from Mujahid, Ata', Muqatil and Ibn Hibban.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿a place of return for the people and a security﴾ that he said: "They return to it, then they go back."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "They never finish their need of it; they come to it, then return to their families, then come back to it again."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿and a security﴾ that he said: "A security for the people."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated, from a hadith of Anas, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters, and my Lord agreed with me in three. I said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer. Then this was revealed: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾ I also said: O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon your wives, so if only you would command them to veil. Then the verse of hijab (veiling) was revealed. And the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered together in jealousy, so I said to them: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾; and it was revealed in this manner."

Muslim and others narrated it in abridged form from the hadith of Ibn Umar, from him.

Muslim and others narrated, from a hadith of Jabir, "that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ramal (hastened walking) for three circuits and walked for four. When he finished, he went to the Station of Ibrahim and prayed two rak'ahs behind it, then recited: ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer.﴾"

Regarding the Station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, there are many hadiths, fully recorded in the major collections and elsewhere. The sound hadiths indicate that the Station of Ibrahim is the stone upon which Ibrahim used to stand to build the Ka'bah when the wall had risen; Isma'il brought it to him so that he could stand upon it, as in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. It is the stone that was attached to the wall of the Ka'bah.

The first person to move it was Umar ibn al-Khattab, as narrated by Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi with a sound chain, and by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh through various routes.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from a hadith of Jabir describing the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) had performed tawaf, Umar said to him: 'Is this the Station of Ibrahim?' He said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar to it.

He said: "‘Ahida" here means: commanded and made obligatory.

His saying: ﴿an ṭahhirā﴾ (that you two purify) is in a place of accusative by removal of the preposition (naz‘ al-khāfid), meaning "bi-an ṭahhirā" (with [the meaning] that you purify). This is the view of the Kufan grammarians. Sibawayh said it is with the explanatory "ay" (that is) implied, meaning "an ṭahhirā," so it has no place in the i‘rab (grammatical analysis). By purification is meant: it was said, from idols; it was said, from calamities and doubts; it was said, from disbelievers; it was said, from impurities, and from the circumambulation of one who is junub (in major ritual impurity) and of a menstruating woman, and from every filth.

The apparent meaning is that it is not restricted to one of these types, and that whatever truly falls under the meaning of purification is included in it, either comprehensively or by way of substitution. The idafa (possessive construction) in His saying ﴿bayti﴾ (My House) is for honour and dignity. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, the people of Madina, Hisham and Hafs read "bayti" with a fatha on the ya’, and the others read it with it sukun.

Al-ṭā’if (the one who circumambulates) is the one who goes around it; it was said: the stranger who arrives at Makka.

Al-‘ākif is the one who resides. The root meaning of al-‘ukūf in the language is adhering to and devoting oneself to something. It was said: it refers to the one who is a neighbour (resident by settlement) and not to the native resident of its people.

By His saying ﴿al-rukka‘ al-sujūd﴾ (those who bow and prostrate) is meant those who pray. He singled out these two pillars for mention because they are the most noble pillars of the prayer.

His saying ﴿wa-idh qāla Ibrāhīm﴾ (And when Ibrahim said): the ahadith indicating that Ibrahim is the one who made Makka sacred will come, and the ahadith indicating that Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth; the reconciliation between these ahadith will be discussed in this section.

His saying ﴿baladan āminan﴾ (a secure land) means Makka. The intent is a supplication for its people, from his descendants and others, like His saying ﴿‘īshatin rāḍiyah﴾ (a pleasing life), meaning one whose possessor is pleased (rāḍin ṣāḥibuhā).

His saying ﴿man āmana﴾ (whoever believes) is a substitute for "ahlahu" (its people), meaning: provide for whoever among its people believes, but not for whoever disbelieves.

His saying ﴿wa-man kafara﴾ (and whoever disbelieves): the apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of Allah, Glorified is He, as a rebuttal to Ibrahim when he requested provision for the believers only, meaning: "And I shall provide for whoever disbelieves, so I shall let him enjoy [provision] for a little, then I shall compel him to the torment of the Fire." It is possible that it is an independent statement explaining the state of the disbeliever, and that it is in the sense of informing about the state of the disbelievers by this conditional sentence, meaning: whoever disbelieves, I shall let him enjoy in this world what he needs of provision, ﴿then I shall compel him﴾ after this enjoyment ﴿to the torment of the Fire﴾. So He, Glorified is He, informed that the disbelievers attain no good except their enjoyment in this world, and that for them after that there is nothing but what is pure evil, which is the torment of the Fire.
