The governing element of the first "idh" (when) is the meaning of witnessing, and the second "idh" is a substitute (badal) for the first. The intended sense of the presence of death is the presence of its preliminaries. The word "ma" rather than "man" is used in His saying ﴿what you worship﴾ because most of the things worshipped besides Allah are inanimate, such as idols, fire, the sun and the stars.

The meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is: after my death.

His saying ﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿your fathers﴾. Isma'il, although he was the paternal uncle of Ya'qub, is included because the Arabs call an uncle "father". His saying ﴿one God﴾ is a substitute for ﴿your God﴾. Although it is indefinite, this is permissible, especially after it has been specified by the attribute which is His saying ﴿One﴾, since the purpose of the substitution has been achieved through this attribute.

It has been said that ﴿a god﴾ is in the accusative on the basis of specification (ikhtisas), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a fine view, because the aim is to establish the state of oneness.

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read ﴿and the God of your father﴾. It has been said that they meant Abraham alone, and His saying ﴿Isma'il﴾ is then a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "your father", and likewise Ishaq, even though he was in fact his father, and Ibrahim was his grandfather; but Ibrahim has a special distinction. It has also been said that His saying "abika" (your father) is a plural, as is related from Sibawayh, that "abin" is a sound plural, and similarly "abun", and from this is the saying of the poet:

"When they distinguished our voices, they wept, and they ransomed us with their fathers."

His saying ﴿and we are to Him submitting﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: we worship Him in the state of our submission to Him. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah), according to his view that parenthetical clauses may occur at the end of speech.

The reference of His saying ﴿That﴾ is to Abraham and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons. ﴿A community﴾ is a substitute for it, and its predicate is ﴿has passed away﴾; or "a community" is the predicate, and ﴿has passed away﴾ is a qualifier (na't) of "a community". His saying ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾ is an explanation of the condition of that community and of the addressed people: each of the two groups has its own earnings. The deeds of another do not benefit him, nothing of them reaches him, and the sin of another does not harm him. In this is a refutation of one who relies upon the deeds of his predecessors and beguiles himself with false hopes. From this is what is reported in the hadith: "Whoever is held back by his deeds, his lineage will not hasten him forward." The meaning is: you will not benefit from their good deeds, nor will you be held accountable for their bad deeds, nor will you be questioned about their actions, just as they will not be questioned about your actions. Similar to this is His saying ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾.

When the Jews and Christians claimed that guidance is in their hands and that goodness is confined to them, Allah refuted this claim by His saying ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad, this statement. "Millata" (religion) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, meaning: we follow. It has been said that the estimate is: we are the followers of the religion of Abraham, that is, its people; and it has been said: rather, we are guided by the religion of Abraham, and when the preposition was removed it became accusative.

Al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "millatu" in the nominative, meaning: rather, the guidance is the religion of Abraham.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth. In its original linguistic sense, it is one whose feet incline, each toward the other.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: we follow the religion of Abraham in the state of his being a hanif.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative by the estimate of "a'ni" (I mean), and the circumstantial state is an error, just as it is not permissible to say: the boy of Hind came to me hastening.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: it is a circumstantial state of the genitive-attached noun (al-mudaf ilayh), as in your saying: I saw the face of Hind standing.

Some people said: al-hanaf means uprightness, so the religion of Abraham was called hanif because of his uprightness, and the one whose legs are bent is called ahnaf, optimistically, in hope of uprightness, just as the stung one is called "salim" (safe) and the place of destruction is called "mafazah" (place of safety).

Whoever argued that hanif in the language means one who inclines, not one who is upright, relied upon the saying of the poet:

"When the shadow turns in the evening, you see it hanif, and at the height of the forenoon it becomes Christian."

That is, the chameleon faces the qibla in the evening, and faces the east in the morning, and the east is the qibla of the Christians. From this is the saying of the poet:

"By Allah, were it not for a hanaf in his leg, there would not be among your men one like him."

His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ contains an allusion (ta'rid) against the Jews for their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, and against the Christians for their saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. That is: Abraham was not in the condition in which you are, of associating partners with Allah; so how can you claim concerning him that he was upon Judaism or Christianity?

His saying ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ is an address to the Muslims and a command to them to say this statement. It has been said that it is an address to the disbelievers, that they should say likewise so that they may be upon the truth. The first is more evident.

The "asbat" (tribes) are the sons of Ya'qub, and they are twelve sons, and each of them has among his offspring a group. The "sibt" among the Children of Israel is in the position of the tribe among the Arabs. They were called "asbat" from "sabt", which is continuity, so they are groups in succession. It has been said that the root is from "sabat" with a vowel, which is a tree, meaning that in their multiplicity they are like trees. It has been said that the "asbat" are the grandchildren of Ya'qub, that is, the children of his children, not his own children, because the multiplicity was among them and not among Ya'qub's own children, who were individuals and not tribes.

His saying ﴿We do not make a distinction between any of them﴾: al-Farra' said its meaning is: we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "ahad" (any one) here has the sense of a group, and for this reason it is correct for "bayn" (between) to govern it.

His saying ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾: this address is also to the Muslims, meaning: if the People of the Book and others believe in the like of what you believed in, of all (p. 97) the Books of Allah and His messengers, and do not make a distinction between any of them, then they have been guided. On this view, "mithl" (like) is redundant, as in His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ and the saying of the poet:

"So be like chewed straw."

It has been said that the likeness occurs between the two beliefs, meaning: if they believe in a belief like your belief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from the mode of rebuke, because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam. He said: that is, if they acquire another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and rectitude, then they have been guided. It has been said that the "ba'" (with) is redundant and emphatic, and it has been said that it is for assistance.

"Shiqaq" (opposition) is originally from "shaqq" (split), which is a side, as if each of the two groups is on a side other than the side on which the other is. It has been said that it is derived from doing what is difficult and hard, so each of the two groups is eager to do what is difficult for its opponent. The verse can be taken to mean either of the two meanings, and likewise the saying of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in opposition."

And the saying of another:

"How long will the scholars accept by force, and boast of opposition and hypocrisy?"

His saying ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ is a promise from Allah Most High to His Prophet that He will suffice him against whoever opposes and contradicts him among those who turn away. He fulfilled His promise to him by sending down His might upon Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'.

His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾: al-Akhfash and others said: that is, the religion of Allah. He said: it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) from "millah" (religion), as Al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad) in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, just as ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is accusative governed by what precedes it. It is a form of the verb "sabagha" like "jilsah" from "jalasa", and it is the state in which the dyeing takes place. The meaning is the purification of Allah, because faith is the purification of souls. End of quotation. Sibawayh also said this, that is, that it is an emphatic verbal noun.

The commentators have mentioned that the origin of this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water, which is what they call the baptism (ma'mudiyyah), and they regarded this as purification for them. When they did this they would say: now he has become truly a Christian. So Allah responded to them with His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾, that is, Islam, and He called it "sibgha" as a metaphor. From this is the saying of one of the poets of Hamdan:

"Every people has a dye of their own, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes.

We have dyed our children upon that, so how excellent is our dye among dyes."

It has been said that "sibgha" is immersion for one who wishes to enter Islam, in place of the Christian baptism; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Jawhari said: "Sibghat Allah" is His religion, and this supports what was previously stated from al-Farra'. It has been said that "sibgha" is circumcision.

His saying ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah﴾, that is: do you argue with us concerning Allah, meaning concerning His religion, nearness to Him and favour with Him? This is like their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read "atuhajjunana" with assimilation (idgham) because of the meeting of two identical letters.

His saying ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: that is, we and you share in His lordship over us and our servitude to Him. So how do you claim that you have more right to Him than we do, and dispute with us about that?

His saying ﴿For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾: that is, for us are deeds and for you are deeds, so you are not nearer to Allah than we are. This is like His saying Most High: ﴿Say: For me is my deed and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.﴾

His saying ﴿And we are to Him sincere﴾: that is, we are the people of sincerity in worship, not you. This is the criterion by which superiority is determined, and the quality by which its possessor has more right to Allah, Glorified is He, than others. So how do you claim for yourselves what we have more right to and are more worthy of than you? In this is a rebuke to them and a cutting off of what they brought of argument and debate.

His saying ﴿Or do they say﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "taqulun" with the second-person ta'. On this reading, "am" here is equivalent to the hamza in His saying ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾, meaning: do you dispute with us concerning Allah, or do you say that these prophets were upon your religion? On the reading with the third-person ya', "am" is disjunctive, meaning: rather, they say. His saying ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ contains reproach and rebuke, that is: Allah has informed us that they were neither Jews nor Christians, while you claim that they were Jews or Christians. So are you more knowing, or is Allah, Glorified is He?

His saying ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogative, meaning: no one is more unjust ﴿than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah﴾. It may be intended by this a censure of the People of the Book, that they know these prophets were neither Jews nor Christians but were upon the Islamic religion, so they wronged themselves by concealing this testimony, and indeed by claiming what is contrary to it. This is more grave in sin than one who merely conceals, and no one is more unjust than him. It may also be that the intended meaning is that if the Muslims were to conceal this testimony, no one would be more unjust than they, and the intended sense would then be an allusion to the People of the Book. It has also been said that what is meant here is what they concealed of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a severe warning and a threat beyond which there is no further threat, and an announcement that Allah, Glorified is He, will not leave their punishment for this injustice and this hideous sin.

He repeated His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ to the end of the verse, because it includes the meaning of threat and intimidation, which is the purpose in this context.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ that it means the People of the Book.

Al-Hasan commented on His words ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾, saying: He means that neither the Jews, nor the Christians, nor any of the people witnessed Ya'qub (Jacob) when death came to him and he took a covenant from his sons: "Do not worship anyone except Allah." They affirmed this, and He (Allah) bore witness against them that they had affirmed their worship, that they are Muslims.

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: "The grandfather is a father," and he would recite the verse.

He also narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding the verse, who said: "The paternal uncle was called a father."

He also narrated something similar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Guidance is only what we are upon, so follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided.' The Christians said the same. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say: Be Jews﴾ and the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾ (upright), who said: "Followers" (muttaba'an).

They also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, who said: "Pilgrims" (ḥājjan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "The ḥanīf is the upright one."

He also narrated from Khusayf, who said: "The ḥanīf is the sincere one."

He also narrated from Abu Qilaba, who said: "The ḥanīf is one who believes in all the messengers, from the first of them to the last."

Ahmad narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the tolerant ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith)."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which religion is most beloved to Allah?' He said: 'The tolerant ḥanīfiyya.'"

al-Hakim in his History and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from the hadith of As'ad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Malik al-Khuza'i, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the first of the two rak'as of the dawn prayer the verse of al-Baqara ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ in its entirety, and in the second ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in Allah,' and the verse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The al-Asbat are the sons of Ya'qub; they were twelve men, each of whom fathered a nation of people."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from al-Suddi, and Ibn Kathir related it in his tafsir from Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi' and Qatada.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do not say: ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾, for Allah has no like. Rather say: 'If they believe in that which you believe in.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif and al-Khatib in his History narrated from Abu Jamra, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas used to recite ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His words ﴿they are in schism﴾, who said: "Separation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "The religion of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "The fitra of Allah upon which He created people."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Children of Israel said: 'O Musa, does your Lord dye?' He said: 'Fear Allah.' Then his Lord called to him: 'O Musa, they asked you whether your Lord dyes; so say: Yes, I dye the colours: red, white and black, and all colours are in My colouring.'" And Allah revealed to His Prophet: ﴿The colouring of Allah; and who is better than Allah in colouring?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada, who said: "The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians. The colouring of Allah is Islam; there is no colouring better than the colouring of Islam, nor purer. It is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and those prophets after him."

Ibn al-Najjar in the History of Baghdad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "Whiteness."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Do you argue with us﴾, who said: "Do you dispute with us?"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: "Do you debate with us?"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada regarding His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾ and the verse, who said: "They are the People of the Book, who concealed Islam while knowing that it is the religion of Allah, and adopted Judaism and Christianity, and concealed Muhammad while knowing that he is the Messenger of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada and al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, who said: "He means Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the al-Asbat."

It has been said that the "ba'" (with) is redundant and emphatic, and it has been said that it is for assistance.

"Shiqaq" (opposition) is originally from "shaqq" (split), which is a side, as if each of the two groups is on a side other than the side on which the other is. It has been said that it is derived from doing what is difficult and hard, so each of the two groups is eager to do what is difficult for its opponent. The verse can be taken to mean either of the two meanings, and likewise the saying of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in opposition."

And the saying of another:

"How long will the scholars accept by force, and boast of opposition and hypocrisy?"

His saying ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ is a promise from Allah Most High to His Prophet that He will suffice him against whoever opposes and contradicts him among those who turn away. He fulfilled His promise to him by sending down His might upon Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'.

His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾: al-Akhfash and others said: that is, the religion of Allah. He said: it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) from "millah" (religion), as Al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad) in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, just as ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is accusative governed by what precedes it. It is a form of the verb "sabagha" like "jilsah" from "jalasa", and it is the state in which the dyeing takes place. The meaning is the purification of Allah, because faith is the purification of souls. End of quotation. Sibawayh also said this, that is, that it is an emphatic verbal noun.

The commentators have mentioned that the origin of this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water, which is what they call the baptism (ma'mudiyyah), and they regarded this as purification for them. When they did this they would say: now he has become truly a Christian. So Allah responded to them with His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾, that is, Islam, and He called it "sibgha" as a metaphor. From this is the saying of one of the poets of Hamdan:

"Every people has a dye of their own, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes.

We have dyed our children upon that, so how excellent is our dye among dyes."

It has been said that "sibgha" is immersion for one who wishes to enter Islam, in place of the Christian baptism; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Jawhari said: "Sibghat Allah" is His religion, and this supports what was previously stated from al-Farra'. It has been said that "sibgha" is circumcision.

His saying ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah﴾, that is: do you argue with us concerning Allah, meaning concerning His religion, nearness to Him and favour with Him? This is like their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read "atuhajjunana" with assimilation (idgham) because of the meeting of two identical letters.

His saying ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: that is, we and you share in His lordship over us and our servitude to Him. So how do you claim that you have more right to Him than we do, and dispute with us about that?

His saying ﴿For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾: that is, for us are deeds and for you are deeds, so you are not nearer to Allah than we are. This is like His saying Most High: ﴿Say: For me is my deed and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.﴾

His saying ﴿And we are to Him sincere﴾: that is, we are the people of sincerity in worship, not you. This is the criterion by which superiority is determined, and the quality by which its possessor has more right to Allah, Glorified is He, than others. So how do you claim for yourselves what we have more right to and are more worthy of than you? In this is a rebuke to them and a cutting off of what they brought of argument and debate.

His saying ﴿Or do they say﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "taqulun" with the second-person ta'. On this reading, "am" here is equivalent to the hamza in His saying ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾, meaning: do you dispute with us concerning Allah, or do you say that these prophets were upon your religion? On the reading with the third-person ya', "am" is disjunctive, meaning: rather, they say. His saying ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ contains reproach and rebuke, that is: Allah has informed us that they were neither Jews nor Christians, while you claim that they were Jews or Christians. So are you more knowing, or is Allah, Glorified is He?

His saying ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogative, meaning: no one is more unjust ﴿than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah﴾. It may be intended by this a censure of the People of the Book, that they know these prophets were neither Jews nor Christians but were upon the Islamic religion, so they wronged themselves by concealing this testimony, and indeed by claiming what is contrary to it. This is more grave in sin than one who merely conceals, and no one is more unjust than him. It may also be that the intended meaning is that if the Muslims were to conceal this testimony, no one would be more unjust than they, and the intended sense would then be an allusion to the People of the Book. It has also been said that what is meant here is what they concealed of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a severe warning and a threat beyond which there is no further threat, and an announcement that Allah, Glorified is He, will not leave their punishment for this injustice and this hideous sin.

He repeated His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ to the end of the verse, because it includes the meaning of threat and intimidation, which is the purpose in this context.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ that it means the People of the Book.

Al-Hasan commented on His words ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾, saying: He means that neither the Jews, nor the Christians, nor any of the people witnessed Ya'qub (Jacob) when death came to him and he took a covenant from his sons: "Do not worship anyone except Allah." They affirmed this, and He (Allah) bore witness against them that they had affirmed their worship, that they are Muslims.

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: "The grandfather is a father," and he would recite the verse.

He also narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding the verse, who said: "The paternal uncle was called a father."

He also narrated something similar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Guidance is only what we are upon, so follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided.' The Christians said the same. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say: Be Jews﴾ and the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾ (upright), who said: "Followers" (muttaba'an).

They also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, who said: "Pilgrims" (ḥājjan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "The ḥanīf is the upright one."

He also narrated from Khusayf, who said: "The ḥanīf is the sincere one."

He also narrated from Abu Qilaba, who said: "The ḥanīf is one who believes in all the messengers, from the first of them to the last."

Ahmad narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the tolerant ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith)."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which religion is most beloved to Allah?' He said: 'The tolerant ḥanīfiyya.'"

al-Hakim in his History and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from the hadith of As'ad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Malik al-Khuza'i, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the first of the two rak'as of the dawn prayer the verse of al-Baqara ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ in its entirety, and in the second ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in Allah,' and the verse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The al-Asbat are the sons of Ya'qub; they were twelve men, each of whom fathered a nation of people."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from al-Suddi, and Ibn Kathir related it in his tafsir from Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi' and Qatada.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do not say: ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾, for Allah has no like. Rather say: 'If they believe in that which you believe in.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif and al-Khatib in his History narrated from Abu Jamra, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas used to recite ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His words ﴿they are in schism﴾, who said: "Separation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "The religion of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "The fitra of Allah upon which He created people."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Children of Israel said: 'O Musa, does your Lord dye?' He said: 'Fear Allah.' Then his Lord called to him: 'O Musa, they asked you whether your Lord dyes; so say: Yes, I dye the colours: red, white and black, and all colours are in My colouring.'" And Allah revealed to His Prophet: ﴿The colouring of Allah; and who is better than Allah in colouring?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada, who said: "The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians. The colouring of Allah is Islam; there is no colouring better than the colouring of Islam, nor purer. It is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and those prophets after him."

Ibn al-Najjar in the History of Baghdad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "Whiteness."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Do you argue with us﴾, who said: "Do you dispute with us?"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: "Do you debate with us?"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada regarding His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾ and the verse, who said: "They are the People of the Book, who concealed Islam while knowing that it is the religion of Allah, and adopted Judaism and Christianity, and concealed Muhammad while knowing that he is the Messenger of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada and al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, who said: "He means Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the al-Asbat."

(p. 96) His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾. Here "am" (أمْ) is said by some to be the disjunctive (munqati'ah), and by others the connective (muttasilah). The interrogative hamza carries the sense of denial, which conveys reproach and rebuke. The address is to the Jews and Christians who attribute to Abraham and his sons that they were upon Judaism and Christianity. Allah rejected this claim against them and said to them: Were you present when Ya'qub (Jacob) was dying, and did you know what he enjoined upon his sons, so that you claim this on the basis of knowledge? Or were you not present? Rather, you are fabricators.

The word "shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of shahid, and it is not declined because it contains the feminine alif of the plural of groups. The governing element of the first "idh" (when) is the meaning of witnessing, and the second "idh" is a substitute (badal) for the first. The intended sense of the presence of death is the presence of its preliminaries. The word "ma" rather than "man" is used in His saying ﴿what you worship﴾ because most of the things worshipped besides Allah are inanimate, such as idols, fire, the sun and the stars.

The meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is: after my death.

His saying ﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿your fathers﴾. Isma'il, although he was the paternal uncle of Ya'qub, is included because the Arabs call an uncle "father". His saying ﴿one God﴾ is a substitute for ﴿your God﴾. Although it is indefinite, this is permissible, especially after it has been specified by the attribute which is His saying ﴿One﴾, since the purpose of the substitution has been achieved through this attribute.

It has been said that ﴿a god﴾ is in the accusative on the basis of specification (ikhtisas), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a fine view, because the aim is to establish the state of oneness.

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read ﴿and the God of your father﴾. It has been said that they meant Abraham alone, and His saying ﴿Isma'il﴾ is then a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "your father", and likewise Ishaq, even though he was in fact his father, and Ibrahim was his grandfather; but Ibrahim has a special distinction. It has also been said that His saying "abika" (your father) is a plural, as is related from Sibawayh, that "abin" is a sound plural, and similarly "abun", and from this is the saying of the poet:

"When they distinguished our voices, they wept, and they ransomed us with their fathers."

His saying ﴿and we are to Him submitting﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: we worship Him in the state of our submission to Him. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah), according to his view that parenthetical clauses may occur at the end of speech.

The reference of His saying ﴿That﴾ is to Abraham and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons. ﴿A community﴾ is a substitute for it, and its predicate is ﴿has passed away﴾; or "a community" is the predicate, and ﴿has passed away﴾ is a qualifier (na't) of "a community". His saying ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾ is an explanation of the condition of that community and of the addressed people: each of the two groups has its own earnings. The deeds of another do not benefit him, nothing of them reaches him, and the sin of another does not harm him. In this is a refutation of one who relies upon the deeds of his predecessors and beguiles himself with false hopes. From this is what is reported in the hadith: "Whoever is held back by his deeds, his lineage will not hasten him forward." The meaning is: you will not benefit from their good deeds, nor will you be held accountable for their bad deeds, nor will you be questioned about their actions, just as they will not be questioned about your actions. Similar to this is His saying ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾.

When the Jews and Christians claimed that guidance is in their hands and that goodness is confined to them, Allah refuted this claim by His saying ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad, this statement. "Millata" (religion) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, meaning: we follow. It has been said that the estimate is: we are the followers of the religion of Abraham, that is, its people; and it has been said: rather, we are guided by the religion of Abraham, and when the preposition was removed it became accusative.

Al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "millatu" in the nominative, meaning: rather, the guidance is the religion of Abraham.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth. In its original linguistic sense, it is one whose feet incline, each toward the other.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: we follow the religion of Abraham in the state of his being a hanif.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative by the estimate of "a'ni" (I mean), and the circumstantial state is an error, just as it is not permissible to say: the boy of Hind came to me hastening.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: it is a circumstantial state of the genitive-attached noun (al-mudaf ilayh), as in your saying: I saw the face of Hind standing.

Some people said: al-hanaf means uprightness, so the religion of Abraham was called hanif because of his uprightness, and the one whose legs are bent is called ahnaf, optimistically, in hope of uprightness, just as the stung one is called "salim" (safe) and the place of destruction is called "mafazah" (place of safety).

Whoever argued that hanif in the language means one who inclines, not one who is upright, relied upon the saying of the poet:

"When the shadow turns in the evening, you see it hanif, and at the height of the forenoon it becomes Christian."

That is, the chameleon faces the qibla in the evening, and faces the east in the morning, and the east is the qibla of the Christians. From this is the saying of the poet:

"By Allah, were it not for a hanaf in his leg, there would not be among your men one like him."

His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ contains an allusion (ta'rid) against the Jews for their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, and against the Christians for their saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. That is: Abraham was not in the condition in which you are, of associating partners with Allah; so how can you claim concerning him that he was upon Judaism or Christianity?

His saying ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ is an address to the Muslims and a command to them to say this statement. It has been said that it is an address to the disbelievers, that they should say likewise so that they may be upon the truth. The first is more evident.

The "asbat" (tribes) are the sons of Ya'qub, and they are twelve sons, and each of them has among his offspring a group. The "sibt" among the Children of Israel is in the position of the tribe among the Arabs. They were called "asbat" from "sabt", which is continuity, so they are groups in succession. It has been said that the root is from "sabat" with a vowel, which is a tree, meaning that in their multiplicity they are like trees. It has been said that the "asbat" are the grandchildren of Ya'qub, that is, the children of his children, not his own children, because the multiplicity was among them and not among Ya'qub's own children, who were individuals and not tribes.

His saying ﴿We do not make a distinction between any of them﴾: al-Farra' said its meaning is: we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "ahad" (any one) here has the sense of a group, and for this reason it is correct for "bayn" (between) to govern it.

His saying ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾: this address is also to the Muslims, meaning: if the People of the Book and others believe in the like of what you believed in, of all (p. 97) the Books of Allah and His messengers, and do not make a distinction between any of them, then they have been guided. On this view, "mithl" (like) is redundant, as in His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ and the saying of the poet:

"So be like chewed straw."

It has been said that the likeness occurs between the two beliefs, meaning: if they believe in a belief like your belief.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which religion is most beloved to Allah?' He said: 'The tolerant ḥanīfiyya.'"

al-Hakim in his History and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from the hadith of As'ad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Malik al-Khuza'i, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the first of the two rak'as of the dawn prayer the verse of al-Baqara ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ in its entirety, and in the second ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in Allah,' and the verse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The al-Asbat are the sons of Ya'qub; they were twelve men, each of whom fathered a nation of people."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from al-Suddi, and Ibn Kathir related it in his tafsir from Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi' and Qatada.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do not say: ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾, for Allah has no like. Rather say: 'If they believe in that which you believe in.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif and al-Khatib in his History narrated from Abu Jamra, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas used to recite ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His words ﴿they are in schism﴾, who said: "Separation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "The religion of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "The fitra of Allah upon which He created people."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Children of Israel said: 'O Musa, does your Lord dye?' He said: 'Fear Allah.' Then his Lord called to him: 'O Musa, they asked you whether your Lord dyes; so say: Yes, I dye the colours: red, white and black, and all colours are in My colouring.'" And Allah revealed to His Prophet: ﴿The colouring of Allah; and who is better than Allah in colouring?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada, who said: "The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians. The colouring of Allah is Islam; there is no colouring better than the colouring of Islam, nor purer. It is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and those prophets after him."

Ibn al-Najjar in the History of Baghdad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "Whiteness."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Do you argue with us﴾, who said: "Do you dispute with us?"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: "Do you debate with us?"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada regarding His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾ and the verse, who said: "They are the People of the Book, who concealed Islam while knowing that it is the religion of Allah, and adopted Judaism and Christianity, and concealed Muhammad while knowing that he is the Messenger of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada and al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, who said: "He means Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the al-Asbat."

(p. 96) His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾. Here "am" (أمْ) is said by some to be the disjunctive (munqati'ah), and by others the connective (muttasilah). The interrogative hamza carries the sense of denial, which conveys reproach and rebuke. The address is to the Jews and Christians who attribute to Abraham and his sons that they were upon Judaism and Christianity. Allah rejected this claim against them and said to them: Were you present when Ya'qub (Jacob) was dying, and did you know what he enjoined upon his sons, so that you claim this on the basis of knowledge? Or were you not present? Rather, you are fabricators.

The word "shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of shahid, and it is not declined because it contains the feminine alif of the plural of groups. The governing element of the first "idh" (when) is the meaning of witnessing, and the second "idh" is a substitute (badal) for the first. The intended sense of the presence of death is the presence of its preliminaries. The word "ma" rather than "man" is used in His saying ﴿what you worship﴾ because most of the things worshipped besides Allah are inanimate, such as idols, fire, the sun and the stars.

The meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is: after my death.

His saying ﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿your fathers﴾. Isma'il, although he was the paternal uncle of Ya'qub, is included because the Arabs call an uncle "father". His saying ﴿one God﴾ is a substitute for ﴿your God﴾. Although it is indefinite, this is permissible, especially after it has been specified by the attribute which is His saying ﴿One﴾, since the purpose of the substitution has been achieved through this attribute.

It has been said that ﴿a god﴾ is in the accusative on the basis of specification (ikhtisas), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a fine view, because the aim is to establish the state of oneness.

Al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read ﴿and the God of your father﴾. It has been said that they meant Abraham alone, and His saying ﴿Isma'il﴾ is then a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "your father", and likewise Ishaq, even though he was in fact his father, and Ibrahim was his grandfather; but Ibrahim has a special distinction. It has also been said that His saying "abika" (your father) is a plural, as is related from Sibawayh, that "abin" is a sound plural, and similarly "abun", and from this is the saying of the poet:

"When they distinguished our voices, they wept, and they ransomed us with their fathers."

His saying ﴿and we are to Him submitting﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: we worship Him in the state of our submission to Him. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah), according to his view that parenthetical clauses may occur at the end of speech.

The reference of His saying ﴿That﴾ is to Abraham and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons. ﴿A community﴾ is a substitute for it, and its predicate is ﴿has passed away﴾; or "a community" is the predicate, and ﴿has passed away﴾ is a qualifier (na't) of "a community". His saying ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾ is an explanation of the condition of that community and of the addressed people: each of the two groups has its own earnings. The deeds of another do not benefit him, nothing of them reaches him, and the sin of another does not harm him. In this is a refutation of one who relies upon the deeds of his predecessors and beguiles himself with false hopes. From this is what is reported in the hadith: "Whoever is held back by his deeds, his lineage will not hasten him forward." The meaning is: you will not benefit from their good deeds, nor will you be held accountable for their bad deeds, nor will you be questioned about their actions, just as they will not be questioned about your actions. Similar to this is His saying ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾.

When the Jews and Christians claimed that guidance is in their hands and that goodness is confined to them, Allah refuted this claim by His saying ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad, this statement. "Millata" (religion) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, meaning: we follow. It has been said that the estimate is: we are the followers of the religion of Abraham, that is, its people; and it has been said: rather, we are guided by the religion of Abraham, and when the preposition was removed it became accusative.

Al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "millatu" in the nominative, meaning: rather, the guidance is the religion of Abraham.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth. In its original linguistic sense, it is one whose feet incline, each toward the other.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: we follow the religion of Abraham in the state of his being a hanif.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative by the estimate of "a'ni" (I mean), and the circumstantial state is an error, just as it is not permissible to say: the boy of Hind came to me hastening.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: it is a circumstantial state of the genitive-attached noun (al-mudaf ilayh), as in your saying: I saw the face of Hind standing.

Some people said: al-hanaf means uprightness, so the religion of Abraham was called hanif because of his uprightness, and the one whose legs are bent is called ahnaf, optimistically, in hope of uprightness, just as the stung one is called "salim" (safe) and the place of destruction is called "mafazah" (place of safety).

Whoever argued that hanif in the language means one who inclines, not one who is upright, relied upon the saying of the poet:

"When the shadow turns in the evening, you see it hanif, and at the height of the forenoon it becomes Christian."

That is, the chameleon faces the qibla in the evening, and faces the east in the morning, and the east is the qibla of the Christians. From this is the saying of the poet:

"By Allah, were it not for a hanaf in his leg, there would not be among your men one like him."

His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ contains an allusion (ta'rid) against the Jews for their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, and against the Christians for their saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. That is: Abraham was not in the condition in which you are, of associating partners with Allah; so how can you claim concerning him that he was upon Judaism or Christianity?

His saying ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ is an address to the Muslims and a command to them to say this statement. It has been said that it is an address to the disbelievers, that they should say likewise so that they may be upon the truth. The first is more evident.

The "asbat" (tribes) are the sons of Ya'qub, and they are twelve sons, and each of them has among his offspring a group. The "sibt" among the Children of Israel is in the position of the tribe among the Arabs. They were called "asbat" from "sabt", which is continuity, so they are groups in succession. It has been said that the root is from "sabat" with a vowel, which is a tree, meaning that in their multiplicity they are like trees. It has been said that the "asbat" are the grandchildren of Ya'qub, that is, the children of his children, not his own children, because the multiplicity was among them and not among Ya'qub's own children, who were individuals and not tribes.

His saying ﴿We do not make a distinction between any of them﴾: al-Farra' said its meaning is: we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "ahad" (any one) here has the sense of a group, and for this reason it is correct for "bayn" (between) to govern it.

His saying ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾: this address is also to the Muslims, meaning: if the People of the Book and others believe in the like of what you believed in, of all (p. 97) the Books of Allah and His messengers, and do not make a distinction between any of them, then they have been guided. On this view, "mithl" (like) is redundant, as in His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ and the saying of the poet:

"So be like chewed straw."

It has been said that the likeness occurs between the two beliefs, meaning: if they believe in a belief like your belief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from the mode of rebuke, because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam. He said: that is, if they acquire another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and rectitude, then they have been guided. It has been said that the "ba'" (with) is redundant and emphatic, and it has been said that it is for assistance.

"Shiqaq" (opposition) is originally from "shaqq" (split), which is a side, as if each of the two groups is on a side other than the side on which the other is. It has been said that it is derived from doing what is difficult and hard, so each of the two groups is eager to do what is difficult for its opponent. The verse can be taken to mean either of the two meanings, and likewise the saying of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in opposition."

And the saying of another:

"How long will the scholars accept by force, and boast of opposition and hypocrisy?"

His saying ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ is a promise from Allah Most High to His Prophet that He will suffice him against whoever opposes and contradicts him among those who turn away. He fulfilled His promise to him by sending down His might upon Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'.

His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾: al-Akhfash and others said: that is, the religion of Allah. He said: it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) from "millah" (religion), as Al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad) in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, just as ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is accusative governed by what precedes it. It is a form of the verb "sabagha" like "jilsah" from "jalasa", and it is the state in which the dyeing takes place. The meaning is the purification of Allah, because faith is the purification of souls. End of quotation. Sibawayh also said this, that is, that it is an emphatic verbal noun.

The commentators have mentioned that the origin of this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water, which is what they call the baptism (ma'mudiyyah), and they regarded this as purification for them. When they did this they would say: now he has become truly a Christian. So Allah responded to them with His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾, that is, Islam, and He called it "sibgha" as a metaphor. From this is the saying of one of the poets of Hamdan:

"Every people has a dye of their own, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes.

We have dyed our children upon that, so how excellent is our dye among dyes."

It has been said that "sibgha" is immersion for one who wishes to enter Islam, in place of the Christian baptism; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Jawhari said: "Sibghat Allah" is His religion, and this supports what was previously stated from al-Farra'. It has been said that "sibgha" is circumcision.

His saying ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah﴾, that is: do you argue with us concerning Allah, meaning concerning His religion, nearness to Him and favour with Him? This is like their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read "atuhajjunana" with assimilation (idgham) because of the meeting of two identical letters.

His saying ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: that is, we and you share in His lordship over us and our servitude to Him. So how do you claim that you have more right to Him than we do, and dispute with us about that?

His saying ﴿For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾: that is, for us are deeds and for you are deeds, so you are not nearer to Allah than we are. This is like His saying Most High: ﴿Say: For me is my deed and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.﴾

His saying ﴿And we are to Him sincere﴾: that is, we are the people of sincerity in worship, not you. This is the criterion by which superiority is determined, and the quality by which its possessor has more right to Allah, Glorified is He, than others. So how do you claim for yourselves what we have more right to and are more worthy of than you? In this is a rebuke to them and a cutting off of what they brought of argument and debate.

His saying ﴿Or do they say﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "taqulun" with the second-person ta'. On this reading, "am" here is equivalent to the hamza in His saying ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾, meaning: do you dispute with us concerning Allah, or do you say that these prophets were upon your religion? On the reading with the third-person ya', "am" is disjunctive, meaning: rather, they say. His saying ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ contains reproach and rebuke, that is: Allah has informed us that they were neither Jews nor Christians, while you claim that they were Jews or Christians. So are you more knowing, or is Allah, Glorified is He?

His saying ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogative, meaning: no one is more unjust ﴿than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah﴾. It may be intended by this a censure of the People of the Book, that they know these prophets were neither Jews nor Christians but were upon the Islamic religion, so they wronged themselves by concealing this testimony, and indeed by claiming what is contrary to it. This is more grave in sin than one who merely conceals, and no one is more unjust than him. It may also be that the intended meaning is that if the Muslims were to conceal this testimony, no one would be more unjust than they, and the intended sense would then be an allusion to the People of the Book. It has also been said that what is meant here is what they concealed of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a severe warning and a threat beyond which there is no further threat, and an announcement that Allah, Glorified is He, will not leave their punishment for this injustice and this hideous sin.

He repeated His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ to the end of the verse, because it includes the meaning of threat and intimidation, which is the purpose in this context.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ that it means the People of the Book.

Al-Hasan commented on His words ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾, saying: He means that neither the Jews, nor the Christians, nor any of the people witnessed Ya'qub (Jacob) when death came to him and he took a covenant from his sons: "Do not worship anyone except Allah." They affirmed this, and He (Allah) bore witness against them that they had affirmed their worship, that they are Muslims.

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: "The grandfather is a father," and he would recite the verse.

He also narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding the verse, who said: "The paternal uncle was called a father."

He also narrated something similar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Guidance is only what we are upon, so follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided.' The Christians said the same. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say: Be Jews﴾ and the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾ (upright), who said: "Followers" (muttaba'an).

They also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, who said: "Pilgrims" (ḥājjan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "The ḥanīf is the upright one."

He also narrated from Khusayf, who said: "The ḥanīf is the sincere one."

He also narrated from Abu Qilaba, who said: "The ḥanīf is one who believes in all the messengers, from the first of them to the last."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: "Do you debate with us?"
