His saying ﴿and we are to Him submitting﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: we worship Him in the state of our submission to Him. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah), according to his view that parenthetical clauses may occur at the end of speech.

The reference of His saying ﴿That﴾ is to Abraham and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons. ﴿A community﴾ is a substitute for it, and its predicate is ﴿has passed away﴾; or "a community" is the predicate, and ﴿has passed away﴾ is a qualifier (na't) of "a community". His saying ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾ is an explanation of the condition of that community and of the addressed people: each of the two groups has its own earnings. The deeds of another do not benefit him, nothing of them reaches him, and the sin of another does not harm him. In this is a refutation of one who relies upon the deeds of his predecessors and beguiles himself with false hopes. From this is what is reported in the hadith: "Whoever is held back by his deeds, his lineage will not hasten him forward." The meaning is: you will not benefit from their good deeds, nor will you be held accountable for their bad deeds, nor will you be questioned about their actions, just as they will not be questioned about your actions. Similar to this is His saying ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾.

When the Jews and Christians claimed that guidance is in their hands and that goodness is confined to them, Allah refuted this claim by His saying ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad, this statement. "Millata" (religion) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, meaning: we follow. It has been said that the estimate is: we are the followers of the religion of Abraham, that is, its people; and it has been said: rather, we are guided by the religion of Abraham, and when the preposition was removed it became accusative.

Al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "millatu" in the nominative, meaning: rather, the guidance is the religion of Abraham.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth. In its original linguistic sense, it is one whose feet incline, each toward the other.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: we follow the religion of Abraham in the state of his being a hanif.

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is in the accusative by the estimate of "a'ni" (I mean), and the circumstantial state is an error, just as it is not permissible to say: the boy of Hind came to me hastening.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: it is a circumstantial state of the genitive-attached noun (al-mudaf ilayh), as in your saying: I saw the face of Hind standing.

Some people said: al-hanaf means uprightness, so the religion of Abraham was called hanif because of his uprightness, and the one whose legs are bent is called ahnaf, optimistically, in hope of uprightness, just as the stung one is called "salim" (safe) and the place of destruction is called "mafazah" (place of safety).

Whoever argued that hanif in the language means one who inclines, not one who is upright, relied upon the saying of the poet:

"When the shadow turns in the evening, you see it hanif, and at the height of the forenoon it becomes Christian."

That is, the chameleon faces the qibla in the evening, and faces the east in the morning, and the east is the qibla of the Christians. From this is the saying of the poet:

"By Allah, were it not for a hanaf in his leg, there would not be among your men one like him."

His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ contains an allusion (ta'rid) against the Jews for their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾, and against the Christians for their saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. That is: Abraham was not in the condition in which you are, of associating partners with Allah; so how can you claim concerning him that he was upon Judaism or Christianity?

His saying ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ is an address to the Muslims and a command to them to say this statement. It has been said that it is an address to the disbelievers, that they should say likewise so that they may be upon the truth. The first is more evident.

The "asbat" (tribes) are the sons of Ya'qub, and they are twelve sons, and each of them has among his offspring a group. The "sibt" among the Children of Israel is in the position of the tribe among the Arabs. They were called "asbat" from "sabt", which is continuity, so they are groups in succession. It has been said that the root is from "sabat" with a vowel, which is a tree, meaning that in their multiplicity they are like trees. It has been said that the "asbat" are the grandchildren of Ya'qub, that is, the children of his children, not his own children, because the multiplicity was among them and not among Ya'qub's own children, who were individuals and not tribes.

His saying ﴿We do not make a distinction between any of them﴾: al-Farra' said its meaning is: we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "ahad" (any one) here has the sense of a group, and for this reason it is correct for "bayn" (between) to govern it.

His saying ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you believed in﴾: this address is also to the Muslims, meaning: if the People of the Book and others believe in the like of what you believed in, of all (p. 97) the Books of Allah and His messengers, and do not make a distinction between any of them, then they have been guided. On this view, "mithl" (like) is redundant, as in His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ and the saying of the poet:

"So be like chewed straw."

It has been said that the likeness occurs between the two beliefs, meaning: if they believe in a belief like your belief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from the mode of rebuke, because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam. He said: that is, if they acquire another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and rectitude, then they have been guided. It has been said that the "ba'" (with) is redundant and emphatic, and it has been said that it is for assistance.

"Shiqaq" (opposition) is originally from "shaqq" (split), which is a side, as if each of the two groups is on a side other than the side on which the other is. It has been said that it is derived from doing what is difficult and hard, so each of the two groups is eager to do what is difficult for its opponent. The verse can be taken to mean either of the two meanings, and likewise the saying of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors, as long as we remain in opposition."

And the saying of another:

"How long will the scholars accept by force, and boast of opposition and hypocrisy?"

His saying ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ is a promise from Allah Most High to His Prophet that He will suffice him against whoever opposes and contradicts him among those who turn away. He fulfilled His promise to him by sending down His might upon Qurayzah, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'.

His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾: al-Akhfash and others said: that is, the religion of Allah. He said: it is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) from "millah" (religion), as Al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad) in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, just as ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is accusative governed by what precedes it. It is a form of the verb "sabagha" like "jilsah" from "jalasa", and it is the state in which the dyeing takes place. The meaning is the purification of Allah, because faith is the purification of souls. End of quotation. Sibawayh also said this, that is, that it is an emphatic verbal noun.

The commentators have mentioned that the origin of this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water, which is what they call the baptism (ma'mudiyyah), and they regarded this as purification for them. When they did this they would say: now he has become truly a Christian. So Allah responded to them with His saying ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾, that is, Islam, and He called it "sibgha" as a metaphor. From this is the saying of one of the poets of Hamdan:

"Every people has a dye of their own, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes.

We have dyed our children upon that, so how excellent is our dye among dyes."

It has been said that "sibgha" is immersion for one who wishes to enter Islam, in place of the Christian baptism; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Jawhari said: "Sibghat Allah" is His religion, and this supports what was previously stated from al-Farra'. It has been said that "sibgha" is circumcision.

His saying ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah﴾, that is: do you argue with us concerning Allah, meaning concerning His religion, nearness to Him and favour with Him? This is like their saying ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read "atuhajjunana" with assimilation (idgham) because of the meeting of two identical letters.

His saying ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: that is, we and you share in His lordship over us and our servitude to Him. So how do you claim that you have more right to Him than we do, and dispute with us about that?

His saying ﴿For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾: that is, for us are deeds and for you are deeds, so you are not nearer to Allah than we are. This is like His saying Most High: ﴿Say: For me is my deed and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do.﴾

His saying ﴿And we are to Him sincere﴾: that is, we are the people of sincerity in worship, not you. This is the criterion by which superiority is determined, and the quality by which its possessor has more right to Allah, Glorified is He, than others. So how do you claim for yourselves what we have more right to and are more worthy of than you? In this is a rebuke to them and a cutting off of what they brought of argument and debate.

His saying ﴿Or do they say﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "taqulun" with the second-person ta'. On this reading, "am" here is equivalent to the hamza in His saying ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾, meaning: do you dispute with us concerning Allah, or do you say that these prophets were upon your religion? On the reading with the third-person ya', "am" is disjunctive, meaning: rather, they say. His saying ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ contains reproach and rebuke, that is: Allah has informed us that they were neither Jews nor Christians, while you claim that they were Jews or Christians. So are you more knowing, or is Allah, Glorified is He?

His saying ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is an interrogative, meaning: no one is more unjust ﴿than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah﴾. It may be intended by this a censure of the People of the Book, that they know these prophets were neither Jews nor Christians but were upon the Islamic religion, so they wronged themselves by concealing this testimony, and indeed by claiming what is contrary to it. This is more grave in sin than one who merely conceals, and no one is more unjust than him. It may also be that the intended meaning is that if the Muslims were to conceal this testimony, no one would be more unjust than they, and the intended sense would then be an allusion to the People of the Book. It has also been said that what is meant here is what they concealed of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a severe warning and a threat beyond which there is no further threat, and an announcement that Allah, Glorified is He, will not leave their punishment for this injustice and this hideous sin.

He repeated His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ to the end of the verse, because it includes the meaning of threat and intimidation, which is the purpose in this context.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ that it means the People of the Book.

Al-Hasan commented on His words ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾, saying: He means that neither the Jews, nor the Christians, nor any of the people witnessed Ya'qub (Jacob) when death came to him and he took a covenant from his sons: "Do not worship anyone except Allah." They affirmed this, and He (Allah) bore witness against them that they had affirmed their worship, that they are Muslims.

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to say: "The grandfather is a father," and he would recite the verse.

He also narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding the verse, who said: "The paternal uncle was called a father."

He also narrated something similar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Guidance is only what we are upon, so follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided.' The Christians said the same. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say: Be Jews﴾ and the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾ (upright), who said: "Followers" (muttaba'an).

They also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, who said: "Pilgrims" (ḥājjan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "The ḥanīf is the upright one."

He also narrated from Khusayf, who said: "The ḥanīf is the sincere one."

He also narrated from Abu Qilaba, who said: "The ḥanīf is one who believes in all the messengers, from the first of them to the last."

Ahmad narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent with the tolerant ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith)."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which religion is most beloved to Allah?' He said: 'The tolerant ḥanīfiyya.'"

al-Hakim in his History and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from the hadith of As'ad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Malik al-Khuza'i, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the first of the two rak'as of the dawn prayer the verse of al-Baqara ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ in its entirety, and in the second ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾."

Al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in Allah,' and the verse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The al-Asbat are the sons of Ya'qub; they were twelve men, each of whom fathered a nation of people."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from al-Suddi, and Ibn Kathir related it in his tafsir from Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi' and Qatada.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Do not say: ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾, for Allah has no like. Rather say: 'If they believe in that which you believe in.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif and al-Khatib in his History narrated from Abu Jamra, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas used to recite ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His words ﴿they are in schism﴾, who said: "Separation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "The religion of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "The fitra of Allah upon which He created people."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Children of Israel said: 'O Musa, does your Lord dye?' He said: 'Fear Allah.' Then his Lord called to him: 'O Musa, they asked you whether your Lord dyes; so say: Yes, I dye the colours: red, white and black, and all colours are in My colouring.'" And Allah revealed to His Prophet: ﴿The colouring of Allah; and who is better than Allah in colouring?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada, who said: "The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians. The colouring of Allah is Islam; there is no colouring better than the colouring of Islam, nor purer. It is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and those prophets after him."

Ibn al-Najjar in the History of Baghdad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿the colouring of Allah﴾, who said: "Whiteness."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Do you argue with us﴾, who said: "Do you dispute with us?"

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: "Do you debate with us?"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada regarding His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾ and the verse, who said: "They are the People of the Book, who concealed Islam while knowing that it is the religion of Allah, and adopted Judaism and Christianity, and concealed Muhammad while knowing that he is the Messenger of Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada and al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, who said: "He means Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the al-Asbat."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 142–143:

His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. This is a report from Allah, glorified is He, to His Prophet ﷺ and to the believers that the foolish ones among the Jews and the hypocrites will say this statement when the qibla is changed from Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah.

It is also said that ﴿will say﴾ has the meaning of ﴿said﴾, and that He expressed the past with the future form to indicate the continuation and persistence of their saying it. It is also said that this report was given before the change to the Ka'bah, and that the benefit of this is that when a disliked matter is announced before it occurs, this lessens its shock, eases its dread, and breaks its force.

As for al-sufahā' (the foolish), it is the plural of safīh, which is the liar, the one who fabricates what is contrary to what is known, as some lexicographers have said.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: they are those of light minds, and the same is in al-Qamus.

What should be referred to has already been mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. The meaning of ﴿What turned them﴾ is: what diverted them ﴿from their qibla which they had been facing﴾, which is Bayt al-Maqdis. So Allah replied to them with His saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, so He may command facing whatever direction He wills.

His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ indicates that changing the qibla to Makkah is part of the guidance, for the Prophet ﷺ and the people of his community, to the straight path.

His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you﴾, i.e., We made you in the likeness of that appointment. It has been said its meaning is: just as the Ka'bah is at the center of the earth, so We have made you a justly balanced community (ummah wasatan).

Al-wasat means the best or the just, and the verse allows both meanings. Among what carries both is the saying of Zuhayr:

They are a wasat (center/best) whose judgment the people are content with, when one of the nights of calamity descends upon the great.

Similar is the saying of another:

You are the wasat (best/most just) of a tribe, known for [handling] small matters or one of the great ones.

It has been firmly established from the Prophet ﷺ that wasat is explained here as ʿadl (justice), as will come, so it is obligatory to return to that. From it is the saying of the rajiz:

Do not go to extremes in affairs,
nor ask excessively if you ask,
and be among the people, all of them, a wasat (moderate).

Since the wasat is far from exaggeration and negligence, it is praiseworthy; that is, this community did not exaggerate as the Christians exaggerated regarding ʿIsa, nor did it fall short as the Jews fell short regarding their prophets. It is said: so-and-so is the wasat of his people and their middle, meaning their best.

His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection you will bear witness for the prophets against their nations that they conveyed to them what Allah commanded them to convey. And the Messenger will be a witness over his community that they have done what he was commanded to convey to them. Similar is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ It has been said: His saying ﴿over you﴾ means ﴿for you﴾, i.e., he will testify in their favor regarding faith. It has been said: its meaning is he will testify against you regarding the conveying to you.

In al-Kashshaf it says: Since the witness is like the watcher and the guardian over the one for whom testimony is borne, the word denoting elevation (ʿalā) was used. Similar is His saying: ﴿And Allah is witness over all things﴾, and ﴿You were the watcher over them, and You are witness over all things﴾. End.

A group said: the meaning of the verse is that some of you bear witness over others after death. It has been said: the intended meaning is that you be witnesses over people in this world concerning matters that are not valid except by the testimony of upright witnesses.

What will come from the marfu' (traced to the Prophet) that explains the meaning of the verse will come, if Allah wills. The word ʿalā was placed later in the testimony of the community over the people, and placed earlier in the testimony of the Messenger over them, because the purpose, as the author of al-Kashshaf said in the first case, is to establish their testimony over the nations, and in the second, to single them out by the Messenger being a witness over them.

His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you had been facing﴾. It has been said: the intended qibla here is Bayt al-Maqdis, i.e., We did not make it except so that We would know who follows and who turns back. This is supported by His saying ﴿which you had been facing﴾, if the revelation of this verse came after the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah. It has been said: the intended qibla is the Ka'bah, i.e., We did not make the qibla which you are now facing, after it had been Bayt al-Maqdis, except for that purpose, and ﴿had been﴾ would then mean the present state. It has been said: the intended qibla is that which he faced before facing Bayt al-Maqdis, for he used to face the Ka'bah in Makkah. Then, when he emigrated, he turned toward Bayt al-Maqdis to win over the Jews, and then he was turned back to the Ka'bah.

His saying: ﴿except that We might know﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of knowing here is seeing. It has been said: the intended meaning is: except that you might know that We know that the hypocrites were in doubt. It has been said: so that the Prophet would know. It has been said: the intended meaning is that We would know that as existing and actual. Likewise, whatever comes attributed to the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He, must be interpreted in this manner, like His saying: ﴿And that Allah may distinguish those who believe and take from among you martyrs﴾.

His saying: ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾, i.e., it was nothing but a great thing, as al-Farra' said regarding ʾan and in that they mean "mā" and "illā."

The Basrans said: it is the heavy form (inna) lightened, and the pronoun in kānat refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you had been facing﴾, namely the turning, or the turning away, or the making, or the apostasy. This meaning was mentioned by al-Akhfash. There is no obstacle to the pronoun referring to the qibla mentioned, i.e., "and indeed the qibla, [described as one] you had been facing, was a great thing, except for those whom Allah guided to faith, so their hearts expanded to accept your truth, and their minds accepted what you brought." This exception is complete (mufarragh), because what precedes it has the force of negation, i.e., it is not light nor easy except for those whom Allah guided.

His saying: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that it was revealed concerning one who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis. Then he said: He called the prayer faith because it combines intention, speech, and action. It has been said: the intended meaning is the steadfastness of the believers upon faith at the change of the qibla, and their not doubting as others doubted.

The first is the one that must be held to and adopted, because of what will come of the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the verse in this sense.

Al-Ra'uf is one who has much ra'fah (tenderness), and ra'fah is stronger than rahmah (mercy).

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: ra'fah is greater than rahmah, though the meaning is close.

Abu Ja'far ibn Yazid ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ recited "la-raʾuf" without hamza, and this is the dialect of Banu Asad. From it is the saying of al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah:

The worst of the victors, so do not be like him, who fights his paternal uncle, the tender, the merciful.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from al-Bara' that: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he first came to Madinah, stayed with his maternal uncles from the Ansar, and he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and it pleased him that his qibla be toward the House. The first prayer he prayed (in the new direction) was ʿAsr, and a people prayed with him. A man from among those who had prayed with him went out and passed by the people of the mosque while they were bowing, and said: 'I bear witness by Allah that I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing the Ka'bah,' and they turned as they were, facing the House. The Jews had been pleased when he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, as had the People of the Book; but when he turned his face toward the House, they denied that. Men had died or been killed while facing the qibla before it was changed toward the House, and we did not know what to say about them, so Allah revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost; indeed Allah is Kind and Merciful to the people﴾." It has other chains and close wordings.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The first thing abrogated in the Qur'an was the qibla."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The Prophet ﷺ used to pray in Makkah facing Bayt al-Maqdis with the Ka'bah between his hands; and after he moved to Madinah, for sixteen months, then Allah turned him to the Ka'bah."

There are many hadiths in this chapter with the meaning of what has preceded, and likewise hadiths were transmitted about the time when facing the qibla was revealed, and about how the worshippers turned when they received the news while they were in prayer. We will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Isma'ili in his Sahih, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾ that he said: "Just (ʿadl)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, the like of it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of it.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Nuh will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Did you convey?' He will say: 'Yes.' Then his people will be called and it will be said to them: 'Did he convey to you?' They will say: 'No warner came to us, and no one came to us.' Then it will be said to Nuh: 'Who will bear witness for you?' He will say: 'Muhammad and his community.' That is His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾ — he said — and the wasat is the just. So you will be called and will bear witness for him that he conveyed, and I will bear witness over you."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated the like of it from Abu Sa'id.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "I and my community on the Day of Resurrection will be upon a hill overlooking the creation. No person will be there but he wishes that he were of us, and no prophet whose people denied him, but we will bear witness that he conveyed the message of his Lord."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Sa'id concerning His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾: that the messengers had conveyed, ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ concerning what you did.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "They passed by a funeral, and good was said about it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is due, it is due, it is due.' Then they passed by another funeral, and bad was said about it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is due, it is due, it is due.' ʿUmar asked him, and he said: 'Whomever you praise with good, Paradise is due to him, and whomever you praise with evil, Hellfire is due to him. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth, you are the witnesses of Allah on earth, you are the witnesses of Allah on earth.'" al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi added: "Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾, the verse."

There are hadiths in this chapter, among them from Jabir marfu' in Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim (who graded it sound); among them from ʿUmar marfu' in Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i; among them from Abu Zuhayr al-Thaqafi marfu' in Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan; among them from Abu Hurayrah marfu' in Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim; and among them from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' marfu' in Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani.

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿAta' concerning His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you had been facing﴾ that he said: "It means Bayt al-Maqdis." ﴿Except that We might know﴾: "We test them so that We know who submits to His command."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿except that We might know﴾: "To distinguish the people of certainty from the people of doubt." ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾: "meaning its change upon the polytheists and the doubters."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: "It reached me that some who had embraced Islam turned back and said: 'Once here and once there.'"

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was turned to the qibla, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about those who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?' So Allah revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost.﴾"

The hadith of al-Bara' has already been mentioned.

There are many hadiths in this chapter, and reports from the early scholars.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 142–143:

His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. This is a report from Allah, glorified is He, to His Prophet ﷺ and to the believers that the foolish ones among the Jews and the hypocrites will say this statement when the qibla is changed from Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah.

It is also said that ﴿will say﴾ has the meaning of ﴿said﴾, and that He expressed the past with the future form to indicate the continuation and persistence of their saying it. It is also said that this report was given before the change to the Ka'bah, and that the benefit of this is that when a disliked matter is announced before it occurs, this lessens its shock, eases its dread, and breaks its force.

As for al-sufahā' (the foolish), it is the plural of safīh, which is the liar, the one who fabricates what is contrary to what is known, as some lexicographers have said.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: they are those of light minds, and the same is in al-Qamus.

What should be referred to has already been mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. The meaning of ﴿What turned them﴾ is: what diverted them ﴿from their qibla which they had been facing﴾, which is Bayt al-Maqdis. So Allah replied to them with His saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, so He may command facing whatever direction He wills.

His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ indicates that changing the qibla to Makkah is part of the guidance, for the Prophet ﷺ and the people of his community, to the straight path.

His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you﴾, i.e., We made you in the likeness of that appointment. It has been said its meaning is: just as the Ka'bah is at the center of the earth, so We have made you a justly balanced community (ummah wasatan).

Al-wasat means the best or the just, and the verse allows both meanings. Among what carries both is the saying of Zuhayr:

They are a wasat (center/best) whose judgment the people are content with, when one of the nights of calamity descends upon the great.

Similar is the saying of another:

You are the wasat (best/most just) of a tribe, known for [handling] small matters or one of the great ones.

It has been firmly established from the Prophet ﷺ that wasat is explained here as ʿadl (justice), as will come, so it is obligatory to return to that. From it is the saying of the rajiz:

Do not go to extremes in affairs,
nor ask excessively if you ask,
and be among the people, all of them, a wasat (moderate).

Since the wasat is far from exaggeration and negligence, it is praiseworthy; that is, this community did not exaggerate as the Christians exaggerated regarding ʿIsa, nor did it fall short as the Jews fell short regarding their prophets. It is said: so-and-so is the wasat of his people and their middle, meaning their best.

His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection you will bear witness for the prophets against their nations that they conveyed to them what Allah commanded them to convey. And the Messenger will be a witness over his community that they have done what he was commanded to convey to them. Similar is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ It has been said: His saying ﴿over you﴾ means ﴿for you﴾, i.e., he will testify in their favor regarding faith. It has been said: its meaning is he will testify against you regarding the conveying to you.

In al-Kashshaf it says: Since the witness is like the watcher and the guardian over the one for whom testimony is borne, the word denoting elevation (ʿalā) was used. Similar is His saying: ﴿And Allah is witness over all things﴾, and ﴿You were the watcher over them, and You are witness over all things﴾. End.

A group said: the meaning of the verse is that some of you bear witness over others after death. It has been said: the intended meaning is that you be witnesses over people in this world concerning matters that are not valid except by the testimony of upright witnesses.

What will come from the marfu' (traced to the Prophet) that explains the meaning of the verse will come, if Allah wills. The word ʿalā was placed later in the testimony of the community over the people, and placed earlier in the testimony of the Messenger over them, because the purpose, as the author of al-Kashshaf said in the first case, is to establish their testimony over the nations, and in the second, to single them out by the Messenger being a witness over them.

His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you had been facing﴾. It has been said: the intended qibla here is Bayt al-Maqdis, i.e., We did not make it except so that We would know who follows and who turns back. This is supported by His saying ﴿which you had been facing﴾, if the revelation of this verse came after the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah. It has been said: the intended qibla is the Ka'bah, i.e., We did not make the qibla which you are now facing, after it had been Bayt al-Maqdis, except for that purpose, and ﴿had been﴾ would then mean the present state. It has been said: the intended qibla is that which he faced before facing Bayt al-Maqdis, for he used to face the Ka'bah in Makkah. Then, when he emigrated, he turned toward Bayt al-Maqdis to win over the Jews, and then he was turned back to the Ka'bah.

His saying: ﴿except that We might know﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of knowing here is seeing. It has been said: the intended meaning is: except that you might know that We know that the hypocrites were in doubt. It has been said: so that the Prophet would know. It has been said: the intended meaning is that We would know that as existing and actual. Likewise, whatever comes attributed to the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He, must be interpreted in this manner, like His saying: ﴿And that Allah may distinguish those who believe and take from among you martyrs﴾.

His saying: ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾, i.e., it was nothing but a great thing, as al-Farra' said regarding ʾan and in that they mean "mā" and "illā."

The Basrans said: it is the heavy form (inna) lightened, and the pronoun in kānat refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you had been facing﴾, namely the turning, or the turning away, or the making, or the apostasy. This meaning was mentioned by al-Akhfash. There is no obstacle to the pronoun referring to the qibla mentioned, i.e., "and indeed the qibla, [described as one] you had been facing, was a great thing, except for those whom Allah guided to faith, so their hearts expanded to accept your truth, and their minds accepted what you brought." This exception is complete (mufarragh), because what precedes it has the force of negation, i.e., it is not light nor easy except for those whom Allah guided.

His saying: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that it was revealed concerning one who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis. Then he said: He called the prayer faith because it combines intention, speech, and action. It has been said: the intended meaning is the steadfastness of the believers upon faith at the change of the qibla, and their not doubting as others doubted.

The first is the one that must be held to and adopted, because of what will come of the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the verse in this sense.

Al-Ra'uf is one who has much ra'fah (tenderness), and ra'fah is stronger than rahmah (mercy).

Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: ra'fah is greater than rahmah, though the meaning is close.

Abu Ja'far ibn Yazid ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ recited "la-raʾuf" without hamza, and this is the dialect of Banu Asad. From it is the saying of al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah:

The worst of the victors, so do not be like him, who fights his paternal uncle, the tender, the merciful.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from al-Bara' that: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he first came to Madinah, stayed with his maternal uncles from the Ansar, and he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and it pleased him that his qibla be toward the House. The first prayer he prayed (in the new direction) was ʿAsr, and a people prayed with him. A man from among those who had prayed with him went out and passed by the people of the mosque while they were bowing, and said: 'I bear witness by Allah that I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing the Ka'bah,' and they turned as they were, facing the House. The Jews had been pleased when he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, as had the People of the Book; but when he turned his face toward the House, they denied that. Men had died or been killed while facing the qibla before it was changed toward the House, and we did not know what to say about them, so Allah revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost; indeed Allah is Kind and Merciful to the people﴾." It has other chains and close wordings.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The first thing abrogated in the Qur'an was the qibla."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The Prophet ﷺ used to pray in Makkah facing Bayt al-Maqdis with the Ka'bah between his hands; and after he moved to Madinah, for sixteen months, then Allah turned him to the Ka'bah."

There are many hadiths in this chapter with the meaning of what has preceded, and likewise hadiths were transmitted about the time when facing the qibla was revealed, and about how the worshippers turned when they received the news while they were in prayer. We will not lengthen by mentioning them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Isma'ili in his Sahih, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾ that he said: "Just (ʿadl)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, the like of it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of it.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Nuh will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Did you convey?' He will say: 'Yes.' Then his people will be called and it will be said to them: 'Did he convey to you?' They will say: 'No warner came to us, and no one came to us.' Then it will be said to Nuh: 'Who will bear witness for you?' He will say: 'Muhammad and his community.' That is His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾ — he said — and the wasat is the just. So you will be called and will bear witness for him that he conveyed, and I will bear witness over you."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated the like of it from Abu Sa'id.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "I and my community on the Day of Resurrection will be upon a hill overlooking the creation. No person will be there but he wishes that he were of us, and no prophet whose people denied him, but we will bear witness that he conveyed the message of his Lord."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Sa'id concerning His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾: that the messengers had conveyed, ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ concerning what you did.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "They passed by a funeral, and good was said about it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is due, it is due, it is due.' Then they passed by another funeral, and bad was said about it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It is due, it is due, it is due.' ʿUmar asked him, and he said: 'Whomever you praise with good, Paradise is due to him, and whomever you praise with evil, Hellfire is due to him. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth, you are the witnesses of Allah on earth, you are the witnesses of Allah on earth.'" al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi added: "Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And thus We have made you an ummah wasatan﴾, the verse."

There are hadiths in this chapter, among them from Jabir marfu' in Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim (who graded it sound); among them from ʿUmar marfu' in Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i; among them from Abu Zuhayr al-Thaqafi marfu' in Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan; among them from Abu Hurayrah marfu' in Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim; and among them from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' marfu' in Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani.

So Allah revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost.﴾"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 144–147:**

His saying: ﴿We see the turning of your face﴾. Al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis): The scholars said: this verse was revealed before His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. The meaning of "qad" here is the frequency of seeing, as stated by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). The meaning of ﴿the turning of your face﴾ is the turning of your face toward the sky, as stated by Qutrub.

Al-Zajjaj said: "the turning of your eyes" in looking toward the sky. The meanings are close.

His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you﴾ may be from *al-wilaya* (authority), meaning We will surely give you that, or from *al-tawalli* (turning), meaning We will surely make you turn toward it. The latter is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.

The word *shatr* here means the side and the direction, and it is in the accusative as an adverb of place. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I say to Umm Zinbaʿ: "Make the camels' chests face toward the Banu Tamim."*

And from it also is the saying of another:

*Is there none to convey to ʿAmr a message, and does a message avail toward ʿAmr?*

*Shatr* may also mean half, as in "wudu (ablution) is half of faith," and as in the saying of ʿAntara:

*I am a man of the best lineage among ʿAbs, my half is noble, and I defend the rest with the sword.*

He said this because his father was one of the chiefs of ʿAbs, while his mother was a slave woman.

It also comes in the sense of a part in general.

There is no disagreement that what is meant by *shatr al-masjid* here is the Kaʿba.

Al-Qurtubi related consensus that facing the very Kaʿba is obligatory for one who can see it, and that one who cannot see it faces its direction, deriving the direction by whatever evidence is available to him. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to what the discourse indicates, namely the turning toward the direction of the Kaʿba. The knowledge of the People of the Book of this is either because it had reached them from their prophets, or because they found in the Books of God revealed to them that this Prophet would face the Kaʿba, or because they knew from their books or their prophets that abrogation (*naskh*) would occur in this law, and that this would make it obligatory for them to enter Islam and follow the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾. Its meaning has already been mentioned.

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read ﴿ta'malun﴾ with the second-person (taʾ), addressing the People of the Book or the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The rest read it with the third-person (yaʾ).

His saying: ﴿And if you were to bring﴾: this *lam* is the preface to an oath, and the implied meaning is: "By God, if you were to bring…"

His saying: ﴿they would not follow﴾ is the answer to the implied oath. Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: the answer of *la-in* (if) is given the answer of *law* (if, counterfactual), because the meaning is "and if you had brought." A similar example is His saying: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely remain﴾, meaning "and if We had sent." They said so because *la-in* is the opposite of *law*: the first requires in its answer the past and actuality, while *la-in* requires in its answer the future.

Sibawayh said: the meaning of *la-in* differs from the meaning of *law*, so one of them does not enter upon the other. The meaning is: ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾.

Sibawayh said: and the meaning of ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow﴾ is "they would surely remain." End of quote.

In this verse there is a great emphasis, containing consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and easing of his heart, because every sign does not affect these people, and they do not return to the truth even if every proof came to them, let alone a single proof. That is because they did not abandon following the truth due to evidence they have or due to a doubt that arose for them, so that they would weigh what they have against what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought and give up their error when the truth is clear. Rather, their abandoning of the truth was rebellion and obstinacy, while knowing that they are not on anything. Whoever is like this does not benefit from proof ever.

His saying: ﴿And you are not one who follows their qibla﴾. This statement can be understood as a prohibition from God, Glorified is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: do not follow their qibla, O Muhammad. It can also be understood literally, as a rebuff of the hopes of the People of the Book and a cutting off of what they hoped for, namely his return (ﷺ) to the qibla he had been facing.

His saying: ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾ contains information that the Jews and the Christians, despite their eagerness to win over the Messenger (ﷺ) to what they have, disagree about their religion even in this specific ruling which God, Glorified is He, related to His Messenger. For some of them do not follow the others in facing their qibla.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: That is because the Jews face the House of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), and the Christians face the rising of the sun. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ to the end of the verse contains a great threat and an eloquent rebuke that makes the skins shudder and the hearts tremble. If inclining toward the desires of those who oppose this noble law and honored religion is obligatory for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the master of the children of Adam, and far be it from him to be among the wrongdoers, then what is your opinion of others from his community? God has protected this Islamic group, after the foothold of Islam became firm and its minaret rose, from inclining toward anything of the desires of the People of the Book. Only a satanic trickery and a tyrannical means remain, which is the inclination of some of those who bear the proofs of God toward the desires of some sects of innovators, for what they hope for from fleeting worldly wealth from their hands, or status with them, if they have a state among the people or were of those with power. This inclination is no less than that inclination. Rather, following the desires of innovators resembles following the desires of the People of the Book, as water resembles water, an egg resembles an egg, and a date resembles a date. The harm of following the desires of innovators may be greater for this religion than the harm of following the desires of the people of other religions, because innovators claim affiliation with Islam and show the people that they support the religion and follow its best. But they are the opposite of that and the contrary of what they claim. They keep moving those who incline to their desires from one innovation to another and push them from one abomination to another until they strip them from the religion and take them out of it, while he thinks he is firmly within it, and that the path he is on is the straight path. This is if he is among the negligent and of the ignorant. If he is of the people of knowledge and understanding who distinguish between truth and falsehood, then his following of their desires is like one whom God has led astray with knowledge and sealed upon his heart, and he becomes a calamity upon the servants of God and a disaster that God pours upon the negligent. For they believe that he, in his knowledge and understanding, inclines only toward the truth and follows only the correct, so they go astray by his error, and upon him will be his sin and the sin of whoever follows him until the Day of Resurrection. We ask God for gentleness, safety and guidance.

His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it﴾. It is said: the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning they recognize his prophethood. This was related from Mujahid, Qatada and a group of scholars. It was also said: they recognize the change of the qibla from the House of Jerusalem to the Kaʿba by the way we have already mentioned. This was said by a group of exegetes. Al-Zamakhshari preferred the first.

In my view, the preferred opinion is the other, as the context to which these verses were brought indicates.

His saying: ﴿they conceal the truth﴾: according to the people of the first view, it is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); according to the people of the second view, it is facing the Kaʿba.

His saying: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ may mean by it the first truth, and it may mean the category of truth, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is His saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: the truth is that which is from your Lord, not from anyone else.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib read *al-haqqa* (the truth) in the accusative, as a substitute for the first, or as an accusative of exhortation, meaning: hold fast to the truth.

His saying: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). *Imtira'* means doubt. God, Glorified is He, forbade him from doubting that it is the truth from his Lord, or from doubting that their concealing of the truth is with their knowledge. According to the first, it is an indirect address to the community, meaning: let none of his community be among the doubters, because he (ﷺ) does not doubt that this is the truth from God, Glorified is He.

Ibn Majah related from al-Bara' who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) facing the House of Jerusalem for eighteen months, and the qibla was turned to the Kaʿba two months after his entering Medina. The Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he prayed facing the House of Jerusalem, would often turn his face toward the sky. God knew from the heart of His Prophet that he loved the Kaʿba, so Gabriel ascended, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept following him with his gaze as he ascended between the sky and the earth, looking at what would come to him from Him. So God revealed: ﴿We see the turning of your face in the sky﴾, the verse. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: O Gabriel, what is our state in our prayer toward the House of Jerusalem? **Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 144–147:**

His saying: ﴿We see the turning of your face﴾. Al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis): The scholars said: this verse was revealed before His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. The meaning of "qad" here is the frequency of seeing, as stated by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). The meaning of ﴿the turning of your face﴾ is the turning of your face toward the sky, as stated by Qutrub.

Al-Zajjaj said: "the turning of your eyes" in looking toward the sky. The meanings are close.

His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you﴾ may be from *al-wilaya* (authority), meaning We will surely give you that, or from *al-tawalli* (turning), meaning We will surely make you turn toward it. The latter is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.

The word *shatr* here means the side and the direction, and it is in the accusative as an adverb of place. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I say to Umm Zinbaʿ: "Make the camels' chests face toward the Banu Tamim."*

And from it also is the saying of another:

*Is there none to convey to ʿAmr a message, and does a message avail toward ʿAmr?*

*Shatr* may also mean half, as in "wudu (ablution) is half of faith," and as in the saying of ʿAntara:

*I am a man of the best lineage among ʿAbs, my half is noble, and I defend the rest with the sword.*

He said this because his father was one of the chiefs of ʿAbs, while his mother was a slave woman.

It also comes in the sense of a part in general.

There is no disagreement that what is meant by *shatr al-masjid* here is the Kaʿba.

Al-Qurtubi related consensus that facing the very Kaʿba is obligatory for one who can see it, and that one who cannot see it faces its direction, deriving the direction by whatever evidence is available to him. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to what the discourse indicates, namely the turning toward the direction of the Kaʿba. The knowledge of the People of the Book of this is either because it had reached them from their prophets, or because they found in the Books of God revealed to them that this Prophet would face the Kaʿba, or because they knew from their books or their prophets that abrogation (*naskh*) would occur in this law, and that this would make it obligatory for them to enter Islam and follow the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾. Its meaning has already been mentioned.

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read ﴿ta'malun﴾ with the second-person (taʾ), addressing the People of the Book or the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The rest read it with the third-person (yaʾ).

His saying: ﴿And if you were to bring﴾: this *lam* is the preface to an oath, and the implied meaning is: "By God, if you were to bring…"

His saying: ﴿they would not follow﴾ is the answer to the implied oath. Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: the answer of *la-in* (if) is given the answer of *law* (if, counterfactual), because the meaning is "and if you had brought." A similar example is His saying: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely remain﴾, meaning "and if We had sent." They said so because *la-in* is the opposite of *law*: the first requires in its answer the past and actuality, while *la-in* requires in its answer the future.

Sibawayh said: the meaning of *la-in* differs from the meaning of *law*, so one of them does not enter upon the other. The meaning is: ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾.

Sibawayh said: and the meaning of ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow﴾ is "they would surely remain." End of quote.

In this verse there is a great emphasis, containing consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and easing of his heart, because every sign does not affect these people, and they do not return to the truth even if every proof came to them, let alone a single proof. That is because they did not abandon following the truth due to evidence they have or due to a doubt that arose for them, so that they would weigh what they have against what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought and give up their error when the truth is clear. Rather, their abandoning of the truth was rebellion and obstinacy, while knowing that they are not on anything. Whoever is like this does not benefit from proof ever.

His saying: ﴿And you are not one who follows their qibla﴾. This statement can be understood as a prohibition from God, Glorified is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: do not follow their qibla, O Muhammad. It can also be understood literally, as a rebuff of the hopes of the People of the Book and a cutting off of what they hoped for, namely his return (ﷺ) to the qibla he had been facing.

His saying: ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾ contains information that the Jews and the Christians, despite their eagerness to win over the Messenger (ﷺ) to what they have, disagree about their religion even in this specific ruling which God, Glorified is He, related to His Messenger. For some of them do not follow the others in facing their qibla.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: That is because the Jews face the House of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), and the Christians face the rising of the sun. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ to the end of the verse contains a great threat and an eloquent rebuke that makes the skins shudder and the hearts tremble. If inclining toward the desires of those who oppose this noble law and honored religion is obligatory for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the master of the children of Adam, and far be it from him to be among the wrongdoers, then what is your opinion of others from his community? God has protected this Islamic group, after the foothold of Islam became firm and its minaret rose, from inclining toward anything of the desires of the People of the Book. Only a satanic trickery and a tyrannical means remain, which is the inclination of some of those who bear the proofs of God toward the desires of some sects of innovators, for what they hope for from fleeting worldly wealth from their hands, or status with them, if they have a state among the people or were of those with power. This inclination is no less than that inclination. Rather, following the desires of innovators resembles following the desires of the People of the Book, as water resembles water, an egg resembles an egg, and a date resembles a date. The harm of following the desires of innovators may be greater for this religion than the harm of following the desires of the people of other religions, because innovators claim affiliation with Islam and show the people that they support the religion and follow its best. But they are the opposite of that and the contrary of what they claim. They keep moving those who incline to their desires from one innovation to another and push them from one abomination to another until they strip them from the religion and take them out of it, while he thinks he is firmly within it, and that the path he is on is the straight path. This is if he is among the negligent and of the ignorant. If he is of the people of knowledge and understanding who distinguish between truth and falsehood, then his following of their desires is like one whom God has led astray with knowledge and sealed upon his heart, and he becomes a calamity upon the servants of God and a disaster that God pours upon the negligent. For they believe that he, in his knowledge and understanding, inclines only toward the truth and follows only the correct, so they go astray by his error, and upon him will be his sin and the sin of whoever follows him until the Day of Resurrection. We ask God for gentleness, safety and guidance.

This was related from Mujahid, Qatada and a group of scholars. It was also said: they recognize the change of the qibla from the House of Jerusalem to the Kaʿba by the way we have already mentioned. Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh*, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "*shatrahu*" means "toward it."

Al-Bayhaqi related from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-ʿAliya who said: "*shatra al-masjid al-haram*" means "facing it."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The whole House is a qibla, and the qibla of the House is the door."

Al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from him, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The House is a qibla for the people of the Mosque, the Mosque is a qibla for the people of the Sanctuary, and the Sanctuary is a qibla for the people of the earth in its east and west, from my community."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book﴾ that he said: "That was revealed concerning the Jews."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿they surely know that it is the truth﴾ that he said: "By that is meant the qibla."

Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh* and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-ʿAliya something similar.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾ that he said: "The Jews do not follow the qibla of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qibla of the Jews."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ that he said: "The Jews and the Christians." ﴿They recognize it﴾: he said, "They recognize the Messenger of God in their Book." ﴿as they recognize their sons﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from him concerning His saying: ﴿they recognize it﴾, meaning they recognize that the Sacred House is the qibla.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Rabiʿ the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed a party of them surely conceal the truth while they know﴾ that he said: "They conceal Muhammad, while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel."

Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh* and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-ʿAliya who said: "God said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾," meaning: "Do not be in doubt, O Muhammad, that the Kaʿba is your qibla, and it was the qibla of the prophets before you."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 144–147:**

His saying: ﴿We see the turning of your face﴾. Al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis): The scholars said: this verse was revealed before His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. The meaning of "qad" here is the frequency of seeing, as stated by the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). The meaning of ﴿the turning of your face﴾ is the turning of your face toward the sky, as stated by Qutrub.

Al-Zajjaj said: "the turning of your eyes" in looking toward the sky. The meanings are close.

His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you﴾ may be from *al-wilaya* (authority), meaning We will surely give you that, or from *al-tawalli* (turning), meaning We will surely make you turn toward it. The latter is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.

The word *shatr* here means the side and the direction, and it is in the accusative as an adverb of place. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I say to Umm Zinbaʿ: "Make the camels' chests face toward the Banu Tamim."*

And from it also is the saying of another:

*Is there none to convey to ʿAmr a message, and does a message avail toward ʿAmr?*

*Shatr* may also mean half, as in "wudu (ablution) is half of faith," and as in the saying of ʿAntara:

*I am a man of the best lineage among ʿAbs, my half is noble, and I defend the rest with the sword.*

He said this because his father was one of the chiefs of ʿAbs, while his mother was a slave woman.

It also comes in the sense of a part in general.

There is no disagreement that what is meant by *shatr al-masjid* here is the Kaʿba.

Al-Qurtubi related consensus that facing the very Kaʿba is obligatory for one who can see it, and that one who cannot see it faces its direction, deriving the direction by whatever evidence is available to him. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to what the discourse indicates, namely the turning toward the direction of the Kaʿba. The knowledge of the People of the Book of this is either because it had reached them from their prophets, or because they found in the Books of God revealed to them that this Prophet would face the Kaʿba, or because they knew from their books or their prophets that abrogation (*naskh*) would occur in this law, and that this would make it obligatory for them to enter Islam and follow the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾. Its meaning has already been mentioned.

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read ﴿ta'malun﴾ with the second-person (taʾ), addressing the People of the Book or the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The rest read it with the third-person (yaʾ).

His saying: ﴿And if you were to bring﴾: this *lam* is the preface to an oath, and the implied meaning is: "By God, if you were to bring…"

His saying: ﴿they would not follow﴾ is the answer to the implied oath. Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: the answer of *la-in* (if) is given the answer of *law* (if, counterfactual), because the meaning is "and if you had brought." A similar example is His saying: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely remain﴾, meaning "and if We had sent." They said so because *la-in* is the opposite of *law*: the first requires in its answer the past and actuality, while *la-in* requires in its answer the future.

Sibawayh said: the meaning of *la-in* differs from the meaning of *law*, so one of them does not enter upon the other. The meaning is: ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾.

Sibawayh said: and the meaning of ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow﴾ is "they would surely remain." End of quote.

In this verse there is a great emphasis, containing consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and easing of his heart, because every sign does not affect these people, and they do not return to the truth even if every proof came to them, let alone a single proof. That is because they did not abandon following the truth due to evidence they have or due to a doubt that arose for them, so that they would weigh what they have against what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought and give up their error when the truth is clear. Rather, their abandoning of the truth was rebellion and obstinacy, while knowing that they are not on anything. Whoever is like this does not benefit from proof ever.

His saying: ﴿And you are not one who follows their qibla﴾. This statement can be understood as a prohibition from God, Glorified is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: do not follow their qibla, O Muhammad. It can also be understood literally, as a rebuff of the hopes of the People of the Book and a cutting off of what they hoped for, namely his return (ﷺ) to the qibla he had been facing.

His saying: ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾ contains information that the Jews and the Christians, despite their eagerness to win over the Messenger (ﷺ) to what they have, disagree about their religion even in this specific ruling which God, Glorified is He, related to His Messenger. For some of them do not follow the others in facing their qibla.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: That is because the Jews face the House of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), and the Christians face the rising of the sun. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ to the end of the verse contains a great threat and an eloquent rebuke that makes the skins shudder and the hearts tremble. If inclining toward the desires of those who oppose this noble law and honored religion is obligatory for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the master of the children of Adam, and far be it from him to be among the wrongdoers, then what is your opinion of others from his community? God has protected this Islamic group, after the foothold of Islam became firm and its minaret rose, from inclining toward anything of the desires of the People of the Book. Only a satanic trickery and a tyrannical means remain, which is the inclination of some of those who bear the proofs of God toward the desires of some sects of innovators, for what they hope for from fleeting worldly wealth from their hands, or status with them, if they have a state among the people or were of those with power. This inclination is no less than that inclination. Rather, following the desires of innovators resembles following the desires of the People of the Book, as water resembles water, an egg resembles an egg, and a date resembles a date. The harm of following the desires of innovators may be greater for this religion than the harm of following the desires of the people of other religions, because innovators claim affiliation with Islam and show the people that they support the religion and follow its best. But they are the opposite of that and the contrary of what they claim. They keep moving those who incline to their desires from one innovation to another and push them from one abomination to another until they strip them from the religion and take them out of it, while he thinks he is firmly within it, and that the path he is on is the straight path. This is if he is among the negligent and of the ignorant. If he is of the people of knowledge and understanding who distinguish between truth and falsehood, then his following of their desires is like one whom God has led astray with knowledge and sealed upon his heart, and he becomes a calamity upon the servants of God and a disaster that God pours upon the negligent. For they believe that he, in his knowledge and understanding, inclines only toward the truth and follows only the correct, so they go astray by his error, and upon him will be his sin and the sin of whoever follows him until the Day of Resurrection. We ask God for gentleness, safety and guidance.

His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it﴾. It is said: the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning they recognize his prophethood. This was related from Mujahid, Qatada and a group of scholars. It was also said: they recognize the change of the qibla from the House of Jerusalem to the Kaʿba by the way we have already mentioned. This was said by a group of exegetes. Al-Zamakhshari preferred the first.

In my view, the preferred opinion is the other, as the context to which these verses were brought indicates.

His saying: ﴿they conceal the truth﴾: according to the people of the first view, it is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); according to the people of the second view, it is facing the Kaʿba.

His saying: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ may mean by it the first truth, and it may mean the category of truth, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is His saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: the truth is that which is from your Lord, not from anyone else.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib read *al-haqqa* (the truth) in the accusative, as a substitute for the first, or as an accusative of exhortation, meaning: hold fast to the truth.

His saying: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). *Imtira'* means doubt. God, Glorified is He, forbade him from doubting that it is the truth from his Lord, or from doubting that their concealing of the truth is with their knowledge. According to the first, it is an indirect address to the community, meaning: let none of his community be among the doubters, because he (ﷺ) does not doubt that this is the truth from God, Glorified is He.

Ibn Majah related from al-Bara' who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) facing the House of Jerusalem for eighteen months, and the qibla was turned to the Kaʿba two months after his entering Medina. The Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he prayed facing the House of Jerusalem, would often turn his face toward the sky. God knew from the heart of His Prophet that he loved the Kaʿba, so Gabriel ascended, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept following him with his gaze as he ascended between the sky and the earth, looking at what would come to him from Him. So God revealed: ﴿We see the turning of your face in the sky﴾, the verse. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: O Gabriel, what is our state in our prayer toward the House of Jerusalem? So God revealed: ﴿And God would not have let your faith be lost﴾."

Al-Tabarani related it from the hadith of Muʿadh in brief, but he said: "seventeen months."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr concerning His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qibla you will be pleased with﴾ that he said: "the qibla of Abraham, toward the spout (*al-mizab*)."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Bara' concerning His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ that he said: "in front of it."
