**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 148–152**

His statement "wa-li-kullin" (ولِكُلٍّ, "and for each"), with the noun it governs omitted, is because the tanwin (التنوين, the nunation ending) indicates that omission. That is, "for every people of a religion there is a direction" (وِجْهَةٌ, wijhah). The wijhah is a fi'lah (فِعْلَة, a noun of the form "fi'lah") from al-muwajahah (المُواجَهَة, "facing"). Its synonyms include al-jihah (الجِهَة) and al-wajh (الوَجْه). What is meant is the qiblah (القِبْلَة, the direction of prayer). That is, they do not follow your qiblah, and you do not follow their qiblah. ﴿And for each there is a direction﴾, either in truth or in falsehood. The pronoun in His words ﴿he is facing it (muwalliha)﴾ refers to the word kull (كُلٍّ, "each").

The ha' (الهاء) in ﴿muwalliha﴾ is the first object (al-maf'ul al-awwal), and the second object is omitted. That is, "facing it his face" (وجْهَهُ).

The meaning is: for every adherent of a religious community there is a qiblah, and the owner of the qiblah faces it. Or, if the address is to the Muslims, then: for each of you, O community of Muhammad, there is a qiblah toward which you pray, from east or west or south or north. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to God, may He be glorified, even though He has not been mentioned, since it is known that God is the one who does this. The meaning then is: for every adherent of a religious community there is a qiblah, toward which God makes him face.

Al-Tabari reports that some people read ﴿wa-li-kulli wijhatin﴾ (وِجْهَةٍ) with the genitive (bi-l-idafah, بِالإضافَةِ, "as an annexed construction"), and Abu 'Amr al-Dani (أبو عمرو الداني) attributes this reading to Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: the meaning is "and every direction God makes him face," so the lam (اللّام) was added to introduce the object first, as in your saying: "As for Zayd, I struck (him)" (لَزَيْدٌ ضَرَبْتُ), and "As for Zayd, his father struck him" (لَزَيْدٌ أبُوهُ ضارِبُهُ). End of quotation.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿muwallaha﴾ (مُوَلّاها) in the passive form (ما لم يُسَمَّ فاعِلُهُ, "the form whose agent is not named"). Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in this reading refers to one (لواحد), meaning: for each one of the people there is a qiblah, and the one (who is) turned toward it (muwallaha), that is, directed toward it.

His words ﴿so race to the good things﴾ (فاستبقوا الخيرات) mean: race toward the good things, with the preposition omitted and the verb connected directly (على الحذف والإيصال). That is: hasten to what God has commanded you concerning facing the Sacred House (al-Masjid al-Haram), as the context indicates. Although the apparent sense is a command to race toward every thing that qualifies as good, as the generality derived from the definite plural "the good things" indicates, racing toward the facing (of the qiblah) means racing toward the prayer at the beginning of its time.

The meaning of His words ﴿wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾ (أينما تكونوا يأت بكم الله) is: in whichever of the different directions you are, God will bring you forth for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection, or He will gather you all together and make your prayers in the different directions appear as though they were toward one direction.

His words ﴿and from wherever you set out﴾ (ومن حيث خرجت): God, may He be glorified, repeated this to emphasize the command to face the Ka'bah and to give it importance, because the matter of the change (of qiblah) was something they cared about deeply. It was also said that the purpose of the repetition is that abrogation (al-naskh, النسخ, "replacement of a ruling by a later one") is a site of trial and a place of doubt, so when they hear it again and again they remain steadfast, and what troubles their hearts is dispelled. It was also said that He repeated this ruling because its causes are multiple. He, may He be glorified, mentioned three causes for the change: the first is seeking His pleasure; the second is the divine custom that every people of a religion and every bearer of a call should be directed toward a direction they hold to; the third is repelling the arguments of the opponents. He thus attached to each cause its effect. It was also said that He meant by the first: "Turn your face toward the Ka'bah when you pray, facing it." Then He said: "And wherever you are, O assembly of Muslims, in all mosques in Medina and elsewhere, turn your faces toward it." Then He said: "And from wherever you set out," meaning the obligation to face it during journeys. So this was a command to face the Ka'bah in all places and in all regions of the earth.

His words ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ (لئلا يكون للناس عليكم حجة): it was said that the meaning is that the Jews should have no argument against you, except for the obstinate among them, who say: "He did not abandon our qiblah for the Ka'bah except out of inclination toward the religion of his people." According to this, the ones who wronged (الذين ظلموا) are the obstinate among the People of the Book. It was also said that they are the polytheists of the Arabs, whose argument is their saying: "He has reverted to our qiblah." It was also said that the meaning is: so that people will have no argument against you, so that they will not say to you: "You were commanded to face the Ka'bah, and you do not see it."

Abu 'Ubayda said: the particle illa (إلّا) here means "and" (بمعنى الواو), that is, "and those who wronged." So it is an exception in the sense of "and." From this is the poet's verse:

*"In Medina there is no house other than one: the house of the caliph, except the house of Marwan."*

As if he said: "the house of the caliph and the house of Marwan." Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', استثناء مُنْقَطِع), that is: "but those among them who wronged, for they argue," and the meaning is: "except one who wrongs through his argument concerning what has become clear to him," as you say: "You have no argument against me except that you wrong me," that is: "You have no argument against me at all, but you are wronging me." He called his wrongdoing an argument because the one who argues with it calls it an argument, even though it is futile.

Qutrub said: it is possible that the meaning is: "so that people will have no argument against you except those who wronged," so that "those who" (الذين) is an apposition (بدل) for the kaf and mim in "against you" (عليكم).

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred that the exception is connected (متصل). He said: God denied that anyone could have an argument against the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions regarding their facing the Ka'bah. The meaning is: no one has an argument against you except the futile argument, namely their saying that He (Muhammad) has been diverted, and their saying: "Muhammad is confused in his religion, and he turned toward our qiblah only because we are more rightly guided than he." He said: and other sayings that arose only from a worshipper of idols, or a Jew, or a hypocrite. He said: "The argument (al-hujjah, الحُجّة) here means the act of arguing (al-muhajjah, المُحاجَّة), which is dispute and contention, and God called it an argument and judged it invalid because it came from a wrongdoer."

Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred that the exception is disjunctive, as al-Zajjaj said. Al-Qurtubi said: this is on the basis that the intended people (al-nas) are the Jews, and then He excepted the disbelievers of the Arabs, as if He said: "But those who wronged in their saying: 'Muhammad has returned to our qiblah, and he will return to our religion entirely.'"

His words ﴿so do not fear them﴾ (فلا تخشوهم) mean: they refers to the people. That is: do not fear their attacks, for they are futile and false and cannot harm you.

His words ﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾ (ولأتم نعمتي عليكم) are conjoined to ﴿so that ... not be﴾ (لئلا يكون), that is, "and in order that I complete." This was said by al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is cut off from what precedes it (مقطوع عما قبله), in a nominative position as a beginning (مبتدأ), with an implied predicate (خبر مضمر). The estimate is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you, I have made you know My qiblah." This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said that it is conjoined to an implied cause, as if it were said: "fear Me so that I may guide you, and that I may complete My favor upon you."

Completing the favor is guidance to the qiblah. It was also said that it is entering Paradise.

His words ﴿as We sent﴾ (كما أرسلنا): the kaf (الكاف) is in a accusative position as an adjective (نعت) for an omitted verbal noun (مصدر محذوف). The meaning is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you with a completion like what We sent." This was said by al-Farra', and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred it.

It was also said that the kaf is in an accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (حال), and the meaning is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you in this state," and the comparison falls on the point that the favor in the qiblah is like the favor in the messengership.

It was also said that the meaning of the sentence is by inversion (على التقديم والتأخير), that is: "remember Me as We sent," said by al-Zajjaj.

His words ﴿so remember Me, I will remember you﴾ (فاذكروني أذكركم) are an imperative and its response, and it carries the sense of a conditional (فيه معنى المجازاة).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of the verse is: remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness. Al-Qurtubi related this from him in his tafsir, and 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir took it from him. Something similar has also been reported as a marfu' hadith, as will come.

His words ﴿and be thankful to Me﴾ (واشكروا لي): al-Farra' said: "He thanked you" (شكر لك) and "He thanked you" (شكرك).

Thanks (al-shukr, الشُّكْر) is recognizing a favor and speaking of it. Its origin in the language is: purity (الطَّهُور). This has already been discussed.

His words ﴿and do not disbelieve Me﴾ (ولا تكفرون) are a prohibition, and for this reason the nun of the plural (نون الجماعة) was dropped. The nun present in the verb is the nun of the first-person speaker (نون المتكلم). The ya' (الياء) was dropped because it is the end of a verse (رأس آية), and keeping it is good outside the Qur'an.

Disbelief (al-kufr, الكفر) here means concealing a favor, not denial. This has already been discussed.

The meaning is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you with a completion like what We sent." This was said by al-Farra', and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred it.

It was also said that the meaning is: so that people will have no argument against you, so that they will not say to you: "You were commanded to face the Ka'bah, and you do not see it."

Abu 'Ubayda said: the particle illa (إلّا) here means "and" (بمعنى الواو), that is, "and those who wronged." So it is an exception in the sense of "and." From this is the poet's verse:

*"In Medina there is no house other than one: the house of the caliph, except the house of Marwan."*

As if he said: "the house of the caliph and the house of Marwan." Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', استثناء مُنْقَطِع), that is: "but those among them who wronged, for they argue," and the meaning is: "except one who wrongs through his argument concerning what has become clear to him," as you say: "You have no argument against me except that you wrong me," that is: "You have no argument against me at all, but you are wronging me." He called his wrongdoing an argument because the one who argues with it calls it an argument, even though it is futile.

Qutrub said: it is possible that the meaning is: "so that people will have no argument against you except those who wronged," so that "those who" (الذين) is an apposition (بدل) for the kaf and mim in "against you" (عليكم).

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred that the exception is connected (متصل). He said: God denied that anyone could have an argument against the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions regarding their facing the Ka'bah. The meaning is: no one has an argument against you except the futile argument, namely their saying that He (Muhammad) has been diverted, and their saying: "Muhammad is confused in his religion, and he turned toward our qiblah only because we are more rightly guided than he." He said: and other sayings that arose only from a worshipper of idols, or a Jew, or a hypocrite. He said: "The argument (al-hujjah, الحُجّة) here means the act of arguing (al-muhajjah, المُحاجَّة), which is dispute and contention, and God called it an argument and judged it invalid because it came from a wrongdoer."

Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred that the exception is disjunctive, as al-Zajjaj said. Al-Qurtubi said: this is on the basis that the intended people (al-nas) are the Jews, and then He excepted the disbelievers of the Arabs, as if He said: "But those who wronged in their saying: 'Muhammad has returned to our qiblah, and he will return to our religion entirely.'"

His words ﴿so do not fear them﴾ (فلا تخشوهم) mean: they refers to the people. That is: do not fear their attacks, for they are futile and false and cannot harm you.

His words ﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾ (ولأتم نعمتي عليكم) are conjoined to ﴿so that ... not be﴾ (لئلا يكون), that is, "and in order that I complete." This was said by al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is cut off from what precedes it (مقطوع عما قبله), in a nominative position as a beginning (مبتدأ), with an implied predicate (خبر مضمر). The estimate is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you, I have made you know My qiblah." This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said that it is conjoined to an implied cause, as if it were said: "fear Me so that I may guide you, and that I may complete My favor upon you."

Completing the favor is guidance to the qiblah. It was also said that it is entering Paradise.

His words ﴿as We sent﴾ (كما أرسلنا): the kaf (الكاف) is in a accusative position as an adjective (نعت) for an omitted verbal noun (مصدر محذوف). The meaning is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you with a completion like what We sent." This was said by al-Farra', and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred it.

It was also said that the kaf is in an accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (حال), and the meaning is: "and that I may complete My favor upon you in this state," and the comparison falls on the point that the favor in the qiblah is like the favor in the messengership.

It was also said that the meaning of the sentence is by inversion (على التقديم والتأخير), that is: "remember Me as We sent," said by al-Zajjaj.

His words ﴿so remember Me, I will remember you﴾ (فاذكروني أذكركم) are an imperative and its response, and it carries the sense of a conditional (فيه معنى المجازاة).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of the verse is: remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness. Al-Qurtubi related this from him in his tafsir, and 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir took it from him. Something similar has also been reported as a marfu' hadith, as will come.

His words ﴿and be thankful to Me﴾ (واشكروا لي): al-Farra' said: "He thanked you" (شكر لك) and "He thanked you" (شكرك).

Thanks (al-shukr, الشُّكْر) is recognizing a favor and speaking of it. Its origin in the language is: purity (الطَّهُور). This has already been discussed.

His words ﴿and do not disbelieve Me﴾ (ولا تكفرون) are a prohibition, and for this reason the nun of the plural (نون الجماعة) was dropped. The nun present in the verb is the nun of the first-person speaker (نون المتكلم). The ya' (الياء) was dropped because it is the end of a verse (رأس آية), and keeping it is good outside the Qur'an.

Disbelief (al-kufr, الكفر) here means concealing a favor, not denial. This has already been discussed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿For each there is a direction, He is facing it﴾ that he said: by this He means the people of religions, saying: for each there is a qiblah they are content with.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said concerning this verse: "Pray toward the Bayt al-Maqdis once, and toward the Ka'bah another time."

Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (ناسخه) related from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Jarir related from Qatada concerning His words ﴿so race to the good things﴾ that he said: "Do not be overcome concerning your qiblah."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd concerning His words ﴿so race to the good things﴾ that he said: "the righteous deeds."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His words ﴿so race to the good things﴾ that he said: "hasten toward the good things," ﴿wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾, he said: "on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir related through the route of al-Suddi, from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned toward the Ka'bah after his prayer toward the Bayt al-Maqdis, the polytheists of Mecca said: 'Muhammad's religion has become confused; he has turned his qiblah toward you, and he knows that you are more rightly guided in the way than he is, and he will soon enter your religion.' So God revealed: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those among them who wronged. So do not fear them, but fear Me.﴾"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada concerning His words ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾ that he said: "By this He means the People of the Book, when the Prophet of God was turned toward the Ka'bah. They said: 'The man has longed for his father's house and his people's religion.'"

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that he said: "Their argument is their saying: 'He has loved our qiblah.'"

Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada and Mujahid concerning His words: "﴿except those among them who wronged﴾" that he said: "Those among them who wronged are the polytheists of Quraysh, who said that they would argue with this against you, and they argued against the Prophet of God concerning his turning toward the Sacred House, and they said: 'He will return to our religion just as he returned to our qiblah.' So God revealed about all of that: ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer; surely God is with the patient.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His words ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from among you﴾ that he means Muhammad (ﷺ).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from among you﴾ that he said: "as I did, so remember Me."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Daylami related through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾ "He says: remember Me, O assembly of servants, through My obedience, and I will remember you with My forgiveness."

Al-Daylami and Ibn 'Asakir related something similar as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Abu Hind al-Dari, and added: "Whoever remembers Me while he is obedient, it is incumbent upon Me to remember him with My forgiveness, and whoever remembers Me while he is disobedient to Me, it is incumbent upon Me to remember him with censure (maqt)."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn 'Abbas: God says: "My remembrance of you is better than your remembrance of Me."

Numerous hadiths have been transmitted about the excellence of the remembrance of God in general and the excellence of gratitude.

[p. 103]

(p-104) When Allah, glorified is He, finished guiding His servants to remember Him and give thanks to Him, He followed that with guiding them to seek help through patience (al-sabr) and prayer (al-salah). Whoever combines the remembrance of Allah with thanking Him, and seeks help through patience and prayer in carrying out what Allah has commanded and in repelling the trials that befall him, has been guided to what is right and granted success in good. This companionship, which Allah clarified with His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾, contains the strongest encouragement for His servants to hold firmly to patience in the face of the calamities that befall them. Whoever has Allah with him will not fear any terror, however great it may be, like mountains.

The words ﴿amwat﴾ (dead) and ﴿ahya'﴾ (alive) are in the nominative because each is the predicate of an omitted subject. The meaning is: "Do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, 'They are dead'; rather, they are alive. But you do not perceive this life when you look at their bodies after their souls have been taken, because you judge them to be dead in outward appearance, according to what your knowledge reaches, which, compared with the knowledge of Allah, is like what a bird takes up in its beak from the water of the sea. In reality, they are not as you think; rather, they are alive in the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection)."

In the verse is evidence for the existence of the punishment of the grave. Anyone who disagrees on this is not to be considered. The sound hadiths concerning it are mutually reinforcing (mutawatir), and the Qur'anic verses point to it. Similar to this verse is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And never think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾.

Al-bala' (trial) originally means ordeal. The meaning of ﴿nabluwannakum﴾ (We will surely test you) is: We will try you in order to examine you, to see whether you will be patient with the decree (al-qada') or not. The indefinite ﴿shay'﴾ (something) is for minimization, meaning: with something small from these matters.

Al-Dahhak read ﴿bi-ashya'﴾ (with things).

By fear is meant what occurs to one who dreads harm coming to him from an enemy or from something else.

By hunger is meant the famine that occurs during drought and dearth.

By loss of wealth is meant what happens to property through calamities, and what Allah has made obligatory in it, such as zakah (obligatory alms) and similar things.

By loss of lives is meant death and being killed in jihad.

By loss of fruits is meant the blights that strike them. This is the mention of a specific part after a general category, since wealth includes fruits and other things. It has also been said that the loss of fruits means the death of children.

The saying ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to give good tidings. The meaning of glad tidings (al-bishara) has already been explained.

Patience (al-sabr) originally means restraint. He described them as those who say "istirja'" (the formula of return) at the time of calamity, because that is submission and contentment.

The musibah (calamity) is the singular of masa'ib (calamities): it is the misfortune by which a person is hurt, however small it may be.

The saying ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾ shows that these words are a refuge for those afflicted and a safeguard for those tested, for they combine affirmation of servitude to Allah with acknowledgment of resurrection and rising.

The meaning of "prayers" (al-salawat) here is forgiveness and good praise, as said by al-Zajjaj.

According to this, the mention of mercy is for the purpose of emphasis.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Salah means mercy and tenderness, so it is used in place of compassion, and it is combined with mercy, like His saying: ﴿compassion and mercy﴾ and ﴿Kind and merciful﴾. The meaning is: upon them is compassion after compassion, and mercy after mercy." End of quote.

It has also been said that the meaning of mercy is the removal of distress and the fulfillment of needs.

The word ﴿al-muhtadun﴾ (the guided) has already had its meaning explained. They are described with this here because they did what leads to the path of what is right, namely istirja' (saying "Inna lillah...") and submission.

Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf fell into a faint during his illness, a faint in which they thought his soul had departed. They got up from beside him and covered him with a cloth. Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah, his wife, went out to the mosque, seeking help through the patience and prayer she had been commanded to use. They waited for a while while he was still unconscious, then he recovered.

Ibn Mandah related in al-Ma'rifah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Umayr ibn al-Humam was killed at Badr, and this verse and others were revealed concerning him and others: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, 'They are dead'﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "﴿In the way of Allah﴾ means in obedience to Allah, in fighting the polytheists."

Hadiths have come down that the souls of martyrs are in the bodies of green birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise.

Among them is one from Ka'b ibn Malik, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), in the collections of Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

It is also reported that the souls of martyrs are in the forms of white birds, as related by 'Abd al-Razzaq from Qatadah, who said: "We have been told," and then mentioned that. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related it also from him with similar wording. It is reported that they are in the forms of green birds, as related by Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman from Abu al-'Aliyah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related it in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur from Ka'b.

Hannad ibn al-Sari related it from Hudhayl.

'Abd al-Razzaq related it in al-Musannaf from him, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, traced back to the Prophet.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from 'Ata', concerning His saying ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾, that he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "Allah informed the believers that this world is a house of trial, and that He will test them in it. He commanded them to be patient and gave them good tidings, saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾. He also informed them that when the believer submits to the command of Allah, returns to Him, and says istirja' at the time of calamity, Allah writes for him three kinds of good: prayers from Allah, mercy, and the easing of the path to guidance."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says istirja' at the time of calamity, Allah will remedy his calamity, grant him a better outcome, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Raja' ibn Haywah concerning His saying ﴿and loss of fruits﴾ that he said: "A time will come upon people when the date palm will bear only one date."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My community has been given something that no other nation has been given: that they say at the time of calamity, 'Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return.'" Many hadiths have been reported about the merit of istirja' at the time of calamity.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 158:

The root of "al-Safa" (aṣ-Ṣafā) in the lexicon is the smooth stone, and here it is the proper name of one of the mountains of Makkah, well known. Likewise "al-Marwah" (al-Marwa) is the proper name of a mountain in Makkah, well known. Its root in the lexicon is the singular of al-marwā (marwā), meaning small stones that have some softness in them.

It has been said: those that have hardness. It has also been said: it covers the whole category (of stones).

Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Until I am, for calamities, like a marwah (stone) struck every day on the rock of al-Mushharraq (aṣ-Ṣafā al-Mushharraq)."

It has been said: they are the white, shining stones. It has also been said: they are the black stones.

Ash-shaʿā'ir (ash-shaʿāʾir) is the plural of shaʿīrah, which means a sign, i.e., one of the markers of its rites.

What is meant by them are the places of worship that Allah has marked out as signs for the people: the standing place (ʿArafah), the sa'y (running between al-Safa and al-Marwah), and the place of sacrifice. From this comes ish'ar al-hady (marking the sacrificial animal), meaning making it known by piercing a piece of iron into its hump. From this is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"We kill them generation after generation; you see them as sacrificial signs by which one draws near (to God)."

Hajj al-Bayt (ḥajj al-bayt) in the lexicon means intending it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And I witness from ʿAwf many tribes who go to the turban of az-Zibriqan, the saffron-dyed one."

As-sabb means the turban.

In the sacred law (ash-sharʿ), it means performing the rites of the Hajj that Allah, glory be to Him, has prescribed.

And ʿUmrah in the lexicon means visiting.

In the sacred law, it means performing the known rite in its established form.

And al-janāḥ (jināḥ) is originally from al-junūḥ, which is inclination, and from it come al-jawāniḥ (the ribs), because of their curvature.

His saying "yaṭṭawwaf" (yaṭṭawwafa) originally is yatatawwafa, and it was assimilated (idghām).

It is also read "an yaṭūfa". The lifting of blame (raf al-junāḥ) indicates that it is not obligatory, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions, and ath-Thawri.

Az-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, reported from Abu Hanifah that he said: it is obligatory, but it is not a pillar, and whoever abandons it must offer a sacrifice (dam).

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn az-Zubayr, Anas ibn Malik and Ibn Sirin held that it is not obligatory.

Among the things that strengthen the indication of this verse that it is not obligatory is His saying, exalted is He, at the end of the verse: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing﴾.

The majority held that the sa'y is obligatory and a rite among the rites, and they cited what al-Shaykhan and others transmitted from ʿĀ'ishah: that ʿUrwah said to her, "Have you considered the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs ʿUmrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾? I do not see that there is blame on anyone for not going around between them." ʿĀ'ishah said: "What a bad thing you have said, nephew. If it were as you interpreted it, it would be: there is no blame upon him for not going around between them. Rather, it was revealed because the Ansar, before they embraced Islam, used to make the talbiyah for Manat, the idol they worshipped, and whoever made the talbiyah for it would feel uneasy about going around between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah. So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾, the verse." ʿĀ'ishah said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the going around between them, so no one has the right to abandon going around between them."

Muslim and others also transmitted from her that she said: "By my life, Allah has not completed the Hajj or ʿUmrah of one who does not perform the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾."

al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, and he said: "Indeed Allah has prescribed for you the sa'y, so run (sa'aw)."

Ahmad in his Musnad, ash-Shafiʿi, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Qani' and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Habibah bint Abi Tajrah, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) going around between al-Safa and al-Marwah, with the people in front of him while he was behind them, running, until I could see his knees from the intensity of the running, his waist-wrap turning around him, and he was saying: 'Run, for indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has prescribed for you the sa'y.'" It is in the Musnad of Ahmad by the route of his teacher ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal, from ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah, from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, from her. He also narrated it by another route from ʿAbd al-Razzaq: Ma'mar informed us, from Wasil, the mawla of Abu ʿUyaynah, from Musa ibn ʿUbaydah, from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, that a woman informed her, and he mentioned it.

This is supported by the hadith: "Take your rites from me" (khudhu ʿannī manāsikakum).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ to the end of the verse. It contains a report that whoever conceals this is cursed. They differed over who is meant. It was said: the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews and the monks (ruhbān) of the Christians who concealed the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: everyone who conceals the truth and leaves off explaining what God has made obligatory to explain. This is the stronger view, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh). So even if the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) was the concealment by Jews and Christians, that does not preclude this verse from covering everyone who conceals the truth.

In this verse there is a severe warning whose extent cannot be measured. For whomever God curses, and whomever among His servants who is capable of cursing curses, has reached such a degree of wretchedness and loss that its depth cannot be grasped or reached.

In His saying: ﴿from the clear proofs and the guidance﴾ there is evidence that it is permissible to conceal other than that. As Abū Hurayrah said: "I memorised two receptacles (wiʿāʾ) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for one of them, I spread it out; as for the other, if I spread it out, this throat would be cut." Related by al-Bukhari.

The pronoun in His saying: ﴿after We have made it clear﴾ refers to ﴿what We have sent down﴾. "The Book" is a generic noun (ism jins), and its definite article indicates that it includes all the books. It was also said that what is meant by it is the Torah.

Al-laʿn (cursing) means distancing and expelling.

What is meant by His saying: ﴿those who curse﴾ is the angels and the believers, as said by al-Zajjaj and others, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah preferred this. It was also said: everyone who is capable of cursing, so that the jinn enter into this. It was also said: they are the insects and the beasts.

His saying: ﴿and all people﴾ — it was said: this is on the Day of Resurrection. As for in this world, among people there are Muslims and disbelievers, and those who know of the sinner and his sin and those who do not know; so cursing him by all people is not possible. It was also said: it refers to this world, and what is meant is that most people curse him, or everyone among them who knows of his sin.

His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ means in the Fire. It was also said: in the curse.

Al-inẓār means respite (imhāl). It was also said that the meaning of ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾ is: God does not look at them, so it is from looking (naẓar). It was also said it is from waiting (intiẓār), meaning they will not be waited for so that they may make excuses.

The explanation of ﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ has already passed.

His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ contains guidance to monotheism (tawḥīd) and the severing of the ties of polytheism (shirk), and an indication that the first thing that must be made clear and whose concealment is forbidden is the matter of monotheism.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim have reported "from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: Muʿādh ibn Jabal, brother of the Banū Salamah, and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, brother of the Banū al-Ashhal, and Kharijah ibn Zayd, brother of the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn al-Khazraj, asked a group of the rabbis of the Jews about some of what is in the Torah, but they concealed it from them and refused to inform them. So God revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down﴾ the verse."

It has been narrated from a group of the early scholars that the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book for their concealment of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Mājah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib who said: "We were at a funeral with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed the disbeliever is struck a blow between his eyes, and every beast hears it except the two weighty ones (the jinn and humankind), and every beast that hears his voice curses him.' That is God's saying: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾, meaning the beasts of the earth."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿAṭāʾ who said: the jinn and the humans and every beast.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Īmān reported that he said concerning the explanation of the verse: "The beasts of the earth, the scorpions and the beetles say: 'We were only withheld the rain because of their sins,' so they curse them."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿIkrimah something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Abū Jaʿfar who said: everything curses them, even the beetle.

Many hadiths have come concerning the prohibition of concealing knowledge and the warning against the one who does it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah concerning His saying: ﴿except those who repent and set right﴾ that he said: "They set right what is between them and God, and they made clear what came to them from God and did not conceal it or deny it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿I relent toward them﴾ that it means: I overlook them.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah who said: "The disbeliever will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection, and God curses him, then the angels curse him, then all people curse him."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah who said: by "all people" is meant the believers.

Ibn Jarīr reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah concerning His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ that he said: abiding in Jahannam, in the curse.

He said concerning His saying: ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾: that they will not be given time to make excuses.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾ that he said: they will not be delayed.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Dārimī, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mājah reported from Asmāʾ bint Yazīd ibn al-Sakan that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Greatest Name of God is in these two verses: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, and ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. God—there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾."

Al-Daylami reported from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is nothing more severe upon the rebellious jinn than these verses in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿And your God is one God﴾, the two verses."

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ to the end of the verse. It contains a report that whoever conceals this is cursed. They differed over who is meant. It was said: the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews and the monks (ruhbān) of the Christians who concealed the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: everyone who conceals the truth and leaves off explaining what God has made obligatory to explain. This is the stronger view, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh). So even if the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl) was the concealment by Jews and Christians, that does not preclude this verse from covering everyone who conceals the truth.

In this verse there is a severe warning whose extent cannot be measured. For whomever God curses, and whomever among His servants who is capable of cursing curses, has reached such a degree of wretchedness and loss that its depth cannot be grasped or reached.

In His saying: ﴿from the clear proofs and the guidance﴾ there is evidence that it is permissible to conceal other than that. As Abū Hurayrah said: "I memorised two receptacles (wiʿāʾ) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for one of them, I spread it out; as for the other, if I spread it out, this throat would be cut." Related by al-Bukhari.

The pronoun in His saying: ﴿after We have made it clear﴾ refers to ﴿what We have sent down﴾. "The Book" is a generic noun (ism jins), and its definite article indicates that it includes all the books. It was also said that what is meant by it is the Torah.

Al-laʿn (cursing) means distancing and expelling.

What is meant by His saying: ﴿those who curse﴾ is the angels and the believers, as said by al-Zajjaj and others, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah preferred this. It was also said: everyone who is capable of cursing, so that the jinn enter into this. It was also said: they are the insects and the beasts.

His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾ etc. contains an exception for those who repent and who set right what has been corrupted of their deeds, and who make clear to people what God has made clear in His books and on the tongues of His messengers.

His saying: ﴿and they die while they are disbelievers﴾: this clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah). It has been used as evidence that it is not permissible to curse a specific disbeliever, because his state at the time of death is not known. This does not contradict what is established from him (ﷺ) of cursing specific groups of disbelievers by name, because he knows by revelation what we do not know. It was also said: it is permissible to curse him, acting on the apparent state, just as it is permissible to fight him.

His saying: ﴿those—upon them is the curse of God﴾ etc. has been used as evidence for the permissibility of cursing disbelievers in general.

Al-Qurṭubi said: there is no disagreement on this.

He said: cursing a disbeliever is not by way of deterring him from disbelief; rather it is a recompense for disbelief and a display of the ugliness of his disbelief, whether the disbeliever is sane or insane.

Some of the early scholars (salaf) said: there is no benefit in cursing one of them who has gone mad or died, neither by way of recompense nor by way of deterrence.

He said: what supports this view is that the verse reports, about God, the angels and people, that they curse them, (p-106) and does not command cursing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 164:

When He, glorified is He, mentioned monotheism with His words, ﴿And your God is One God﴾, He followed it with the proof that points to it, namely these matters, which are among the greatest works of the Wise Creator. Every intelligent person knows that none of the gods which the disbelievers affirmed is able to produce any of them, or to have power over them or over some of them: the creation of the heavens, the creation of the earth, the alternation of the night and the day, the running of the ship in the sea, the sending down of rain from the sky, the reviving of the earth by it, the dispersing of animals upon it by means of it, and the directing of the winds. Whoever looks closely at any one of them and applies his thought to it is dazzled by it, and his mind is too narrow to conceive its reality.

It becomes necessary for him to affirm that its Maker is Allah, glorified is He. He used the plural for the heavens because they are different kinds, each heaven being of a kind other than the kind of the others, and he used the singular for the earth because it is all of one kind, which is dirt.

What is meant by the alternation of the night and the day is their succession, with the coming of one and the going of the other, and the illumination of one and the darkening of the other.

Al-Nahar (the day) is what lies between the break of dawn and the setting of the sun.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the beginning of the day is the rising of the sun, and what precedes that is not counted as part of the day.

Tha'lab said likewise, and he cited the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

﻿The sun rises every last night red, its color becoming rosy at dawn.

Al-Zajjaj also said likewise.

Ibn al-Anbari divided time into three parts: a part which he made pure night, which is from the setting of the sun to the break of dawn;

a part which he made pure day, which is from the rising of the sun to its setting;

and a part which he made shared between day and night, which is what lies between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun, due to the remnants of the darkness of the night and the beginnings of the light of the day.

This is according to the terminology of the people of language.

As for the sharia, the discussion on that is well known.

Al-Fulk (the ships): these are boats, and its singular and plural are with one form, and it is masculine and feminine.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿in the laden ship﴾ and ﴿and the ships that run in the sea﴾ (p-107) and He said: ﴿until when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾. It was also said: its singular is falak, with a vowel on the second letter, like usud and asad.

His words ﴿with that which benefits mankind﴾: "ma" may be a relative pronoun, meaning "with that which benefits them," or a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning "with their benefit." What is meant by "that which Allah sends down from the sky" is the rain, by which the life of the world, the growth of plants, and provisions come about.

Al-Batth means dispersal. The apparent meaning is that His words "and He dispersed in it" are conjoined to His words "and revived," because they are two matters caused by the sending down of rain.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf that the apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to "sent down."

What is meant by the directing of the winds is sending them as barren winds, fertilizing winds, cold winds, winds of victory, winds of destruction, hot winds, cold winds, gentle winds, and violent winds. It was also said: their directing is sending them as the south wind, the north wind, the west wind, and the east wind, and the mixed winds, which come between the directions of two winds. It was also said: their directing is that they come to large ships by the measure that carries them, and to small ships likewise. There is no barrier to taking "directing" to cover all that has been mentioned.

Al-Sahab (the clouds) was named sahab because it is drawn (insihab) through the air. I dragged my garment (sahbtu dhayli sahban), and so-and-so dragged himself over so-and-so: he dared.

Al-Musakhkhar: the subjugated, the made submissive. "Sakhkharahu" means he sent it from one place to another. It was also said that its subjugation is its being fixed between the sky and the earth without pillars or ties. The first is more apparent.

The signs (al-ayat) are the indications of His oneness, glorified is He, for whoever looks with his sight and reflects with his intellect.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Ask Allah to make Safa gold for us, so that we may strengthen ourselves with it against our enemy. Allah revealed to him: I will give them, so I will make Safa gold for them, but if they disbelieve after that, I will punish them with a punishment that I will not inflict upon anyone among the worlds. He said: My Lord, leave me and my people, and I will call them day by day. So Allah revealed this verse."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Waki', al-Firyabi, Adam ibn Abi Iyas, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu al-Duha, who said: "When ﴿And your God is One God﴾ was revealed, the polytheists were amazed and said: Muhammad says, ﴿And your God is One God﴾; let him bring us a sign if he is among the truthful. So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ata' something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azama narrated from Sulayman, who said: "The night is entrusted to an angel called Sharahil. When the time of night arrives, he takes a black bead and lowers it from the direction of the west. When the sun sees it, it sets in less than the blink of an eye. The sun has been commanded not to set until it sees the bead. When it sets, the night comes, and the bead remains suspended until another angel called Harahil comes with a white bead and suspends it from the direction of the east. When Sharahil sees it, he extends his bead to it, and the sun sees the white bead, so it rises, and it had been commanded not to rise until it sees it. When it rises, the day comes."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, regarding His words ﴿and the ships﴾, that he said: "the boat."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "Batth means He created."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His words ﴿and the directing of the winds﴾, that he said: "When He wills, He makes them a mercy, fertilizing the clouds and heralding glad tidings before His mercy; and when He wills, He makes them a punishment, a barren wind that does not fertilize."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Everything in the Qur'an concerning winds (al-riyah) is mercy, and everything in the Qur'an concerning wind (al-rih) in the singular is punishment."

Numerous hadiths have been related prohibiting cursing the wind and its attributes, but they have no connection to the verse.

When God (glorified is He) finished with the proof of His oneness, He informed that alongside this clear proof, which shows His great dominion and sublime power and His being the sole Creator, there are among people those who take for Him, glorified is He, rivals (andad, sing. nidd) that they worship from among the idols.

The explanation of the rivals (andad) has already passed. These disbelievers did not confine themselves to merely worshipping the rivals. Rather, they loved them greatly and went to extremes in this to a considerable degree, so that their love for these idols and the like became firmly established in their hearts, just as the love of the believers for God (glorified is He) is firmly established. Thus the verbal noun in His saying ﴿as the love of God﴾ is in the genitive as the object of the verbal noun, and its subject is omitted, which is "the believers."

It is also possible that the intended meaning is "as their love for God," that is, the worshippers of idols. This was said by Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj.

It is also possible that this verbal noun belongs to the passive form, meaning "as God is loved."

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿but those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾. This is a correction of what the comparison implies of equality, meaning that the love of the believers for God is stronger than the love of the disbelievers for the rivals, because the believers single out God (glorified is He) in worship and supplication, whereas the disbelievers do not single out their idols in this way, but associate others with God, and they acknowledge that they worship their idols only so that the idols may bring them near to God. It is also possible to make this, that is His saying ﴿but those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, a proof for the second interpretation, because when the believers are stronger in love for God, the love of the disbelievers for the rivals is not like the love of the believers for God. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "rivals" here is the leaders, that is, they obey them in acts of disobedience to God. The pronoun in their saying ﴿they love them﴾ supports this, since it is used for those who have reason. It is also supported by His saying (glorified is He) right after it: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾, and so on.

As for His saying ﴿if only those who did wrong could see﴾, the reading of the people of Makkah, Kufah and Abu 'Amr is with the yaa' (third person, "they see"). This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

The reading of the people of Madinah and the people of Sham is with the taa' (second person, "you see"). The meaning according to the first reading is: if only those who did wrong in the world could see the punishment of the Hereafter, they would know, when they see it, that power belongs to God entirely. This was said by Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Nahhas said: "This is the view on which the people of tafsir (exegesis of the Qur'an) rely." End of quote.

According to this, the seeing is visual, not of the heart.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad that he said: "This explanation which Abu 'Ubayd gave is far-fetched, and his expression in it is not good (p. 108), because it would be taken as: if only those who did wrong could see the punishment, which makes it something doubtful, while God has made it certain. Rather, the better estimation is: if only those who did wrong could see that power belongs to God, with 'see' meaning 'know,' that is, if only they knew the reality of God's power and the severity of His punishment."

He said: The answer to "if only" (law) is omitted, meaning: they would have made clear the harm of taking the gods, just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ and ﴿if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. As for the one who reads with the taa', the estimation is: if only you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong while they see the punishment and are terrified of it, you would know that power belongs to God entirely.

The Prophet (ﷺ) already knew this, but he was addressed with this address, and what is meant is his community. It has also been said that the phrase "that power belongs to God" is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, meaning "because power belongs to God," as the poet said:

"I overlook the faults of the noble, saving them for later, and turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity."

That is, for the sake of saving them. The meaning is: if only you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong while they are seeing the punishment, because power belongs to God, you would know the extent of their chastisement. The word "when" (idh), which is for the past, has entered upon these future verbs to bring the matter near and to affirm its occurrence.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿when they see﴾ with a damma on the yaa', and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub and Abu Ja'far read ﴿that power﴾ and ﴿that God﴾ with a kasra on the hamza in both, as a new sentence, and on the assumption of a verb of saying.

His saying ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ is a substitute for His saying ﴿when they see the punishment﴾. Its meaning is that the leaders and chiefs disowned those who followed them in disbelief.

His saying ﴿and they see the punishment﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is, the followers and the followed. It has been said: at the moment of witnessing it in the world. It has been said: at the time of the presentation and questioning in the Hereafter.

It is possible to say that both apply together, since there is nothing preventing that.

His saying ﴿and their ties are cut off from them﴾: "ties" (asbab) is the plural of sabab. Its original meaning in the language is the rope with which a thing is tied and pulled, then everything that draws something is called a sabab. What is meant by it here are the bonds by which they used to connect with one another in the world, such as kinship and others. It has also been said that they are deeds.

Karrah means return and going back to a state that once existed. The "law" here carries the meaning of wishing, as if it were said: "If only we had a return," and for this reason the fa' appears in the answer.

The meaning is that the followers said: if only we were sent back to the world so that we could do righteous deeds and disown them as they disowned us.

The kaf in His saying ﴿as they disowned us﴾ is in the accusative position as a description of an omitted verbal noun. It has also been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, but I do not think this is correct.

His saying ﴿thus God shows them﴾ is in the nominative position: that is, the matter is thus, meaning that just as God shows them the punishment, He shows them their deeds. If this seeing is visual, then His saying ﴿as regrets﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. If it is of the heart, then it is the third object, and the meaning is that God shows them their corrupt deeds, so they become regrets for them, or He shows them the righteous deeds which He had made obligatory upon them, but they abandoned them, so that becomes a regret for them.

His saying ﴿and they will not come out of the Fire﴾ contains evidence for the eternity of the disbelievers in the Fire. The apparent sense of this structure conveys exclusivity, and al-Zamakhshari made it for emphasis for a purpose of his own that relates to his school of thought. The discussion of this would be lengthy.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿and among people are those who take rivals besides God﴾ that he said: "Out of vanity and in order to harm the truth with the rivals," ﴿and those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, he said: "than the disbelievers' love for their gods."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Zayd regarding this verse that he said: "These polytheists, their rivals are their gods whom they worship alongside God. They love them as those who believe love God, ﴿and those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, than their love for their gods."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "The rivals are men whom they obey just as they obey God. When they command them, they obey them and disobey God."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Ikrimah something similar to what Ibn Zayd said.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zubayri regarding His saying ﴿if only those who did wrong could see﴾ that he said: "If only you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong against themselves by taking besides Me rivals whom they love as you love Me, when they witness My punishment on the Day of Resurrection which I have prepared for them, you would know that all power belongs to Me and not to the rivals, and the gods will not avail them anything there, nor will they repel from them a punishment I have sent down upon them. I have made certain to them that My punishment is severe for whoever disbelieves in Me and claims alongside Me another god besides Me."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ that he said: "They are the tyrants, the leaders and the heads in polytheism," ﴿from those who followed﴾, he said: "They are the devils who disowned mankind."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and their ties are cut off from them﴾ that he said: "It is affection."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "It is the stations."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "It is the kinship ties."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Mujahid that he said: "It is the bonds that existed between them in the world, and the affection."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih that he said: "It is the deeds."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Rabi' that he said: "It is the stations."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿if only we had a return﴾ that he said: "A return to the world."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His saying ﴿as regrets﴾ that he said: "Their wicked deeds became a regret for them on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿and they will not come out of the Fire﴾ that he said: "Those are its people, who are its people."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Thabit ibn Ma'bad that he said: "The people of the Fire continued to hope to come out of it, until this was revealed: ﴿and they will not come out of the Fire﴾."

When God (glorified is He) finished with the proof of His oneness, He informed that alongside this clear proof, which shows His great dominion and sublime power and His being the sole Creator, there are among people those who take for Him, glorified is He, rivals (andad, sing. nidd) that they worship from among the idols.

The explanation of the rivals (andad) has already passed. These disbelievers did not confine themselves to merely worshipping the rivals. Rather, they loved them greatly and went to extremes in this to a considerable degree, so that their love for these idols and the like became firmly established in their hearts, just as the love of the believers for God (glorified is He) is firmly established. Thus the verbal noun in His saying ﴿as the love of God﴾ is in the genitive as the object of the verbal noun, and its subject is omitted, which is "the believers."

It is also possible that the intended meaning is "as their love for God," that is, the worshippers of idols. This was said by Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj.

It is also possible that this verbal noun belongs to the passive form, meaning "as God is loved."

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿but those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾. This is a correction of what the comparison implies of equality, meaning that the love of the believers for God is stronger than the love of the disbelievers for the rivals, because the believers single out God (glorified is He) in worship and supplication, whereas the disbelievers do not single out their idols in this way, but associate others with God, and they acknowledge that they worship their idols only so that the idols may bring them near to God. It is also possible to make this, that is His saying ﴿but those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, a proof for the second interpretation, because when the believers are stronger in love for God, the love of the disbelievers for the rivals is not like the love of the believers for God. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "rivals" here is the leaders, that is, they obey them in acts of disobedience to God. The pronoun in their saying ﴿they love them﴾ supports this, since it is used for those who have reason. It is also supported by His saying (glorified is He) right after it: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾, and so on.

As for His saying ﴿if only those who did wrong could see﴾, the reading of the people of Makkah, Kufah and Abu 'Amr is with the yaa' (third person, "they see"). This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

The reading of the people of Madinah and the people of Sham is with the taa' (second person, "you see"). The meaning according to the first reading is: if only those who did wrong in the world could see the punishment of the Hereafter, they would know, when they see it, that power belongs to God entirely. This was said by Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Nahhas said: "This is the view on which the people of tafsir (exegesis of the Qur'an) rely." End of quote.

According to this, the seeing is visual, not of the heart.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad that he said: "This explanation which Abu 'Ubayd gave is far-fetched, and his expression in it is not good (p. 108), because it would be taken as: if only those who did wrong could see the punishment, which makes it something doubtful, while God has made it certain. Rather, the better estimation is: if only those who did wrong could see that power belongs to God, with 'see' meaning 'know,' that is, if only they knew the reality of God's power and the severity of His punishment."

He said: The answer to "if only" (law) is omitted, meaning: they would have made clear the harm of taking the gods, just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ and ﴿if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. As for the one who reads with the taa', the estimation is: if only you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong while they see the punishment and are terrified of it, you would know that power belongs to God entirely.

The Prophet (ﷺ) already knew this, but he was addressed with this address, and what is meant is his community. It has also been said that the phrase "that power belongs to God" is in the accusative position as an object of purpose, meaning "because power belongs to God," as the poet said:

"I overlook the faults of the noble, saving them for later, and turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity."

That is, for the sake of saving them. The meaning is: if only you could see, O Muhammad, those who did wrong while they are seeing the punishment, because power belongs to God, you would know the extent of their chastisement. The word "when" (idh), which is for the past, has entered upon these future verbs to bring the matter near and to affirm its occurrence.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿when they see﴾ with a damma on the yaa', and the rest read it with a fatha.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub and Abu Ja'far read ﴿that power﴾ and ﴿that God﴾ with a kasra on the hamza in both, as a new sentence, and on the assumption of a verb of saying.

His saying ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ is a substitute for His saying ﴿when they see the punishment﴾. Its meaning is that the leaders and chiefs disowned those who followed them in disbelief.

His saying ﴿and they see the punishment﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is, the followers and the followed. It has been said: at the moment of witnessing it in the world. It has been said: at the time of the presentation and questioning in the Hereafter.

It is possible to say that both apply together, since there is nothing preventing that.

His saying ﴿and their ties are cut off from them﴾: "ties" (asbab) is the plural of sabab. Its original meaning in the language is the rope with which a thing is tied and pulled, then everything that draws something is called a sabab. What is meant by it here are the bonds by which they used to connect with one another in the world, such as kinship and others. It has also been said that they are deeds.

Karrah means return and going back to a state that once existed. The "law" here carries the meaning of wishing, as if it were said: "If only we had a return," and for this reason the fa' appears in the answer.

The meaning is that the followers said: if only we were sent back to the world so that we could do righteous deeds and disown them as they disowned us.

The kaf in His saying ﴿as they disowned us﴾ is in the accusative position as a description of an omitted verbal noun. It has also been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, but I do not think this is correct.

His saying ﴿thus God shows them﴾ is in the nominative position: that is, the matter is thus, meaning that just as God shows them the punishment, He shows them their deeds. If this seeing is visual, then His saying ﴿as regrets﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. If it is of the heart, then it is the third object, and the meaning is that God shows them their corrupt deeds, so they become regrets for them, or He shows them the righteous deeds which He had made obligatory upon them, but they abandoned them, so that becomes a regret for them.

His saying ﴿and they will not come out of the Fire﴾ contains evidence for the eternity of the disbelievers in the Fire. The apparent sense of this structure conveys exclusivity, and al-Zamakhshari made it for emphasis for a purpose of his own that relates to his school of thought. The discussion of this would be lengthy.

(p. 109) His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾. It was said that it was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'a, and Banu Mudlij regarding what they had forbidden to themselves of the cattle.

Al-Qurtubi transmitted this in his tafsir. However, the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

His saying: (ḥalālan, "lawful") is either an object (maf'ul) or a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The lawful (ḥalāl) was named ḥalāl because the knot of prohibition is untied from it (inḥilāl).

The ṭayyib here is what is pleasant (al-mustaladhdh), as al-Shafi'i and others said.

Malik and others said: it is the lawful (ḥalāl), so it is an emphasis (ta'kīd) of his saying "lawful."

The "min" in His saying ﴿of what is in the earth﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), because it is certain that there is in the earth what is unlawful.

(Khuṭuwāt, "steps") is the plural of khuṭwa, which is pronounced with a fatḥa or a ḍamma. With a fatḥa it means a single step, and with a ḍamma it means the distance between the two feet.

Al-Farra' read khaṭu'āt with a fatḥa on the kha'. Abu Simak read it with a fatḥa on both the kha' and the ṭa'. 'Ali, Qatada, al-A'raj, 'Amr ibn Maymun, and al-A'mash read khuṭu'āt with a ḍamma on the kha' and the ṭa', and a hamza in place of the waw.

Al-Akhfash said: They took this reading to be the plural of khaṭiyya, from error (khaṭa'), not from stepping (khaṭw).

Al-Jawhari said: The khaṭwa with a fatḥa is one single step, and its plural is khuṭuwāt and khuṭan. End of quote.

The meaning according to the reading of the majority: do not follow the trail of the Shaytan and his deeds. Whatever the sacred law (shar') has not sanctioned is attributed to the Shaytan. It was said: they are vows and sins. The better view is generalization, and not restricting it to one individual or one category.

His saying ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ means: manifest in enmity. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a misleading, clear enemy﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾.

His saying (bi-l-sū', "evil") — evil (sū') was named sū' because it harms its doer through its bad outcome. It is the verbal noun of sā'ahu, yasū'uhu, sau' and masā'a, meaning: when it grieves him.

Fāḥisha originally means ugliness of appearance, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not ugly."

Then it was used for what is repulsive in meanings. It was said: sū' is what is ugly, and fāḥisha is exceeding the limit in ugliness. It was said: sū' is what has no limit (ḥadd) in it, and fāḥisha is what has a limit (ḥadd) in it. It was said: fāḥisha is adultery. It was said: everything the sacred law (al-shar'ah) has forbidden is of fāḥisha.

His saying ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: He means what they forbade of the baḥīra, the sā'iba, and similar things, which they made into law (shar'). It was said: it is their saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" without knowledge.

The apparent meaning is that it applies to everything that is said in the sacred law without knowledge.

In this verse there is evidence that every matter concerning which there is no text or apparent indication regarding the existing things on earth, its origin is permissibility (al-ḥill) until a proof is found that requires its prohibition. The clearest indication of this from this verse is His saying: ﴿He is the One who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ refers to the people, because the disbelievers are among them, and they are the ones intended here. It was said: it refers specifically to the disbelieving Arabs. Their saying alfaynā means wajadnā ("we found"). The alif in His saying ﴿Even though their fathers﴾ is interrogative, and the waw was given a fatḥa because it is the conjunctive waw (wāw al-'aṭf).

In this verse there is blame for the blind followers (muqallidūn), and a rebuke for their gross ignorance and corrupt belief, to a degree that cannot be measured. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon"﴾, to the end of the verse. In that is evidence for the ugliness of taqlīd (blind imitation) and its prohibition. The discussion of this would be lengthy.

I have devoted a separate independent work to it, which I named [The Beneficial Word on the Ruling on Taqlīd], and I have fully exhausted the discussion of it in [The Etiquette of the Seeker and the Ultimate Aim].
