Likewise is the disbeliever: if you command him to good, or forbid him from evil, or admonish him, he does not understand what you say except that he hears your voice.

Something similar was narrated from Mujahid, transmitted by 'Abd ibn Humayd, and from 'Ikrima, transmitted by Waki'.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that he said: 'Ata' said to me concerning this verse: They are the Jews, about whom Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾, to His saying ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾.

(p. 109) His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾. It was said that it was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'a, and Banu Mudlij regarding what they had forbidden to themselves of the cattle.

Al-Qurtubi transmitted this in his tafsir. However, the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

His saying: (ḥalālan, "lawful") is either an object (maf'ul) or a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The lawful (ḥalāl) was named ḥalāl because the knot of prohibition is untied from it (inḥilāl).

The ṭayyib here is what is pleasant (al-mustaladhdh), as al-Shafi'i and others said.

Malik and others said: it is the lawful (ḥalāl), so it is an emphasis (ta'kīd) of his saying "lawful."

The "min" in His saying ﴿of what is in the earth﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), because it is certain that there is in the earth what is unlawful.

(Khuṭuwāt, "steps") is the plural of khuṭwa, which is pronounced with a fatḥa or a ḍamma. With a fatḥa it means a single step, and with a ḍamma it means the distance between the two feet.

Al-Farra' read khaṭu'āt with a fatḥa on the kha'. Abu Simak read it with a fatḥa on both the kha' and the ṭa'. 'Ali, Qatada, al-A'raj, 'Amr ibn Maymun, and al-A'mash read khuṭu'āt with a ḍamma on the kha' and the ṭa', and a hamza in place of the waw.

Al-Akhfash said: They took this reading to be the plural of khaṭiyya, from error (khaṭa'), not from stepping (khaṭw).

Al-Jawhari said: The khaṭwa with a fatḥa is one single step, and its plural is khuṭuwāt and khuṭan. End of quote.

The meaning according to the reading of the majority: do not follow the trail of the Shaytan and his deeds. Whatever the sacred law (shar') has not sanctioned is attributed to the Shaytan. It was said: they are vows and sins. The better view is generalization, and not restricting it to one individual or one category.

His saying ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ means: manifest in enmity. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a misleading, clear enemy﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾.

His saying (bi-l-sū', "evil") — evil (sū') was named sū' because it harms its doer through its bad outcome. It is the verbal noun of sā'ahu, yasū'uhu, sau' and masā'a, meaning: when it grieves him.

Fāḥisha originally means ugliness of appearance, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not ugly."

Then it was used for what is repulsive in meanings. It was said: sū' is what is ugly, and fāḥisha is exceeding the limit in ugliness. It was said: sū' is what has no limit (ḥadd) in it, and fāḥisha is what has a limit (ḥadd) in it. It was said: fāḥisha is adultery. It was said: everything the sacred law (al-shar'ah) has forbidden is of fāḥisha.

His saying ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: He means what they forbade of the baḥīra, the sā'iba, and similar things, which they made into law (shar'). It was said: it is their saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" without knowledge.

The apparent meaning is that it applies to everything that is said in the sacred law without knowledge.

In this verse there is evidence that every matter concerning which there is no text or apparent indication regarding the existing things on earth, its origin is permissibility (al-ḥill) until a proof is found that requires its prohibition. The clearest indication of this from this verse is His saying: ﴿He is the One who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ refers to the people, because the disbelievers are among them, and they are the ones intended here. It was said: it refers specifically to the disbelieving Arabs. Their saying alfaynā means wajadnā ("we found"). The alif in His saying ﴿Even though their fathers﴾ is interrogative, and the waw was given a fatḥa because it is the conjunctive waw (wāw al-'aṭf).

In this verse there is blame for the blind followers (muqallidūn), and a rebuke for their gross ignorance and corrupt belief, to a degree that cannot be measured. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon"﴾, to the end of the verse. In that is evidence for the ugliness of taqlīd (blind imitation) and its prohibition. The discussion of this would be lengthy.

I have devoted a separate independent work to it, which I named [The Beneficial Word on the Ruling on Taqlīd], and I have fully exhausted the discussion of it in [The Etiquette of the Seeker and the Ultimate Aim].

His saying ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾: in it is a comparison of the preacher of the disbelievers, and their caller, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), to the shepherd who shouts to sheep or camels, so they hear nothing but calling and shouting and do not understand what he says. Thus did al-Zajjaj, al-Farra', and Sibawayh interpret it, and a group of the early generations (al-salaf) said the same.

Sibawayh said: They were not compared to the one who shouts; rather they were compared to the one being shouted at. The meaning is: your likeness, O Muhammad, and the likeness of those who disbelieve, is like the likeness of the one who shouts and the one shouted at among the animals that do not understand. So it was omitted because the meaning indicates it.

Qutrub said: The meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon what does not understand, meaning the idols, is like the likeness of a shepherd when he shouts to his sheep while he does not know where they are. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari also said this.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon the lifeless gods is like the likeness of one who cries out in the middle of the night, and the echo (ṣadā) answers him. He shouts at what does not hear, and what has no reality answers him.

Al-Na'iq is driving sheep and shouting at them. It is said: nā'iq al-rā'ī bi-ghanamihi, yanʿiqu, naʿīqan and nu'āqan, meaning he shouted at them and drove them. The Arabs use the shepherd of sheep as a proverb for ignorance, and they say: "More ignorant than the shepherd of sheep."

His saying (ṣumm, "deaf") and what follows are predicates (akhbār) of an omitted subject, meaning: they are deaf, dumb, and blind.

The explanation of this has already been given.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "This verse was recited in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾. Then Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas stood and said: O Messenger of Allah, invoke Allah to make me one whose supplication is answered. He said: O Sa'd, make your food good, and you will be one whose supplication is answered. By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, indeed a man who puts a forbidden morsel into his stomach, nothing from him is accepted for forty days. Any servant whose flesh grew from what is unlawfully gained (suḥt) and interest (ribā), the Fire is more deserving of him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His saying ﴿and do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ that he said: his deed.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: Whatever opposes the Qur'an is of the steps of Satan.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that he said: his footsteps.

They both also transmitted from 'Ikrima that he said: They are the incitements (nazaghāt) of Satan.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: They are the embellishment (tazyīn) of Satan.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatada that he said: Every act of disobedience to Allah is of the steps of Satan.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Whatever oath or vow is made in anger is of the steps of Satan, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he was brought a udder and salt, and began to eat. A man from the people withdrew, so Ibn Mas'ud said: Offer your companion some. He said: I do not want it. He said: (p. 110) Are you fasting? He said: No. He said: Then what is your matter? He said: I have forbidden myself to eat udder. Ibn Mas'ud said: This is of the steps of Satan. Eat, and expiate for your oath.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from 'Uthman ibn Ghiyath that he said: I asked Jabir ibn Zayd about a man who vowed to put a ring of gold in his nose. He said: It is of the steps of Satan, and he remains disobedient to Allah, so let him expiate for his oath.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from al-Hasan that he made the oath of one who swears to perform Hajj crawling (ḥabwan) to be of the steps of Satan.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Mijlaz that he said: They are vows in acts of disobedience.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Suddi concerning His saying ﴿He only commands you to evil﴾ that he said: disobedience (al-ma'ṣiya). ﴿And immorality (al-faḥshā')﴾: he said: adultery.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam and encouraged them to it, and warned them of the punishment and vengeance of Allah. Rafi' ibn Kharija and Malik ibn 'Awf said to him: Rather, we will follow, O Muhammad, what we found our fathers upon, for they were more knowledgeable and better than us. So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿And when it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has revealed,' they say, 'Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon.'﴾"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' and Qatada concerning His saying alfaynā that both said: wajadnā ("we found").

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: It is like the likeness of cattle, a donkey, and a sheep: if you speak to one of them, it does not know what you say except that it hears your voice. Likewise is the disbeliever: if you command him to good, or forbid him from evil, or admonish him, he does not understand what you say except that he hears your voice.

Something similar was narrated from Mujahid, transmitted by 'Abd ibn Humayd, and from 'Ikrima, transmitted by Waki'.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that he said: 'Ata' said to me concerning this verse: They are the Jews, about whom Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾, to His saying ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 172–173:

His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ This is an emphasis of the first command, namely His saying: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾. The Qur'an specified the believers here because they are the best kind of people. It has been said: what is meant by eating is benefiting (from), and it has been said: what is meant by it is the customary eating, and this is the apparent meaning.

His saying: ﴿And be grateful to Allah﴾ It has already been mentioned that one says shakara-hu and shakara la-hu (both forms), it being transitive by itself and by a preposition.

And His saying: ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾, i.e., you single Him out for worship, as the fronting of the object indicates.

His saying: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾. Abu Ja'far read ḥurrima (in the passive form). And (innamā) is a word laid down for restriction: it establishes what the address encompasses and negates whatever is other than it.

Here, the prohibition has been restricted to the matters mentioned after it.

His saying: (carrion, al-maytah): Ibn 'Abalah read it in the nominative case. The reasoning for this is that he makes "mā" in (innamā) a separate relative pronoun (written separately in the script), and al-maytah and what follows it are the predicate of the relative clause. The reading of all the others is with the accusative.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read (al-mayyitah) with a doubled yāʾ. The lexicographers have mentioned that for mayyit both lightening and doubling are permissible.

Al-maytah is that from which the soul has departed without slaughter (dhakāh).

This general statement has been specified by such a hadith as: "Two dead animals and two bloods have been made lawful for us." Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ibn 'Umar as a marfu' report; and like the hadith of Jabir concerning the ʿanbar (ambergris/whale) which is established in the two Sahihs, together with His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾. So what is meant by carrion here is the carrion of land animals, not the carrion of the sea.

Most scholars have held that it is permissible to eat all sea animals, whether alive or dead.

Some scholars said: it is forbidden from sea animals what is forbidden of their likeness on land. Ibn Habib hesitated regarding the water-pig (khinzīr al-māʾ). Ibn al-Qasim said: "I avoid it and do not consider it forbidden."

His saying: (and blood): The scholars have agreed that blood is forbidden. In the other verse: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾, so the absolute is interpreted in light of the qualified, because what is mixed with meat is not forbidden. Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus.

ʿĀʾishah narrated that she used to cook meat, and the yellow film would rise upon the cooking pot from the blood, and the Prophet ﷺ would eat that and not object to it.

His saying: ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾. The apparent meaning of this verse and of the other verse, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine﴾, is that what is forbidden is only the flesh itself.

The community has agreed on the prohibition of its fat, as al-Qurtubi related in his tafsir.

A group of scholars have mentioned that fat falls under the term "flesh."

Al-Qurtubi also related consensus that the whole of the swine is forbidden except its bristles, for it is permissible to sew with them.

His saying: ﴿and what has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾. Al-ihlal means raising the voice; one says: ahalla bi-kadhā, i.e., he raised his voice (with it).

A poet describing a desert waste said:

"It makes the riders on it raise their voices with the Farqad, as the pilgrim in ihram raises his voice."

And al-Nabighah said:

"Or a pearl of the oyster-shell whose diver is delighted; whenever he sees it, he raises his voice and prostrates."

From it comes the ihlal of the infant and its istihlal, which is its crying at birth.

What is meant here is: that over which the name of other than Allah has been mentioned, such as al-Lat and al-ʿUzza, when the slaughterer is an idolater; and fire, when the slaughterer is a Magian.

There is no disagreement about the prohibition of this and its like. Similar to it is what occurs from those who hold beliefs about the dead, of slaughtering upon their graves, for that is among what is dedicated to other than Allah, and there is no difference between it and slaughtering for an idol.

His saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾. It has been read with a damma on the nun for the sake of following, and with a kasra according to the original form for the meeting of two sukun. Within it there is an ellipsis, i.e., whoever is compelled to something of these forbidden things.

Ibn Muhaysin read with assimilation of the dad into the ta'.

Abu al-Sammak read with a kasra on the ta'.

What is meant is one whom hunger and want have driven to the necessity of carrion.

His saying: ﴿not desiring nor transgressing﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

It has been said: what is meant by the bāghi (desiring) is one who eats beyond his need, and the ʿādi (transgressing) is one who eats these forbidden things while finding an alternative to them. It has been said: "not desiring" against the Muslims and "transgressing" against them, so this includes highway robbers, those who rebel against the ruler, those who sever the ties of kinship, and the like. It has been said: what is meant is: not desiring against another person in necessity, nor transgressing by exceeding what satisfies the hunger.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ that he said: "of the lawful."

Ibn Sa'd narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz that what is meant by it in the verse is good earnings, not good food.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak that it is lawful provision.

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah is good and accepts only what is good, and Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾." Then he mentioned the man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, who stretches his hands toward the sky: "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful—so how would he be answered?

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿and what has been dedicated﴾ that he said: "slaughtered."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: ﴿and what has been dedicated to it﴾ means "to the idols (ṭawāghīt)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid that he said: "what is slaughtered for other than Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: "what over which the name of other than Allah has been mentioned."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿not desiring nor transgressing﴾ that he said: "Whoever eats any of these while compelled, there is no blame; and whoever eats it while not compelled has desired and transgressed."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: "not desiring," he said: "in the carrion"; "nor transgressing," he said: "in the eating."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿not desiring nor transgressing﴾ that he said: "not desiring against the Muslims, nor transgressing against them. So whoever goes out to sever kinship, or to cut off the road, or to cause corruption in the land, or who separates from the community and the leaders, or who goes out in disobedience to Allah and is compelled to carrion, it is not lawful for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "The transgressor (al-ʿādī) is the one who cuts the road."

His saying: ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning in his eating, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, forgiving toward whoever ate of the unlawful, merciful toward him, since He made the unlawful lawful for him in the state of necessity.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿But whoever is compelled, not desiring nor transgressing﴾: "not desiring in his eating, nor transgressing by going beyond the lawful to the unlawful while finding from it a sufficiency and an alternative."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: "not desiring," he said: "in the carrion"; "nor transgressing," he said: "in the eating."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿not desiring nor transgressing﴾ that he said: "not desiring against the Muslims, nor transgressing against them. So whoever goes out to sever kinship, or to cut off the road, or to cause corruption in the land, or who separates from the community and the leaders, or who goes out in disobedience to Allah and is compelled to carrion, it is not lawful for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "The transgressor (al-ʿādī) is the one who cuts the road."

His saying: ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning in his eating, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, forgiving toward whoever ate of the unlawful, merciful toward him, since He made the unlawful lawful for him in the state of necessity.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿But whoever is compelled, not desiring nor transgressing﴾: "not desiring in his eating, nor transgressing by going beyond the lawful to the unlawful while finding from it a sufficiency and an alternative."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 174–176:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾. It was said: the intended people in this verse are the scholars of the Jews, because they concealed what Allah had sent down in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The word "ishtira'" (purchasing) here means "istibdal" (exchanging), and its verification has already been given before. He called it "qalil" (little) because its period is cut off and its end is evil. Although this cause is specific, the consideration is by the generality of the wording, and it includes everyone who conceals what Allah has legislated and takes a bribe for it. He mentioned "the bellies" as an indication and emphasis that this eating is literal, since it may be used figuratively in such expressions as: "So-and-so ate his land," and the like.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: the meaning of "in their bellies" is "filling their bellies." He said: One says, "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "he ate in part of his belly." End.

His saying: "except the Fire," meaning that it necessitates for them the punishment of the Fire. So He called what they ate "fire" because it leads them to it. This is what most of the exegetes said. It was also said: they will be punished for their concealment by eating fire in Hell literally. Similar to it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾. His saying: ﴿and Allah will not speak to them﴾ contains a metaphor for the descent of Allah's anger upon them and His not being pleased with them. It is said: "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so" when he is angry with him.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the meaning is that He will not speak to them with what they love, but not with what they hate,

like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be driven away therein, and do not speak to Me﴾.

His saying: "and will not purify them" means: He will not praise them with good.

Al-Zajjaj said: It was also said its meaning is: He will not set right their evil deeds so as to purify them.

His saying: ﴿they have purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾. Its meaning has already been verified.

His saying: ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ The majority, including al-Hasan and Mujahid, held that its meaning is wonderment.

The intended meaning is to make the created beings marvel at the state of those who engaged in the causes of the punishment of the Fire, as though by this engagement in the causes they endured punishment in the Fire of Hell.

Al-Zajjaj related that the meaning is: "What has kept them upon the Fire," from the saying: "What has made so-and-so patient upon the imprisonment," meaning what has kept him in it. It was also said the meaning is: How little is their impatience from the Fire, making little impatience "patience."

Al-Kisa'i and Qutrub said: that is, how constant they are in the work of the people of the Fire. It was also said: "ma" is interrogative, and its meaning is rebuke, i.e., what is it that makes them patient upon the work of the Fire.

This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and Abu 'Ubayda.

﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth﴾. The demonstrative refers to the matter, i.e., that matter, which is the punishment. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Akhfash said: the predicate of the demonstrative is omitted, and the estimate is: "That is known."

The intended "Book" here is the Qur'an.

"with the truth" means with sincerity; it was also said: with proof.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾. It was said: the intended "Book" here is the Torah. The Christians claimed that the description of Jesus is in it and the Jews denied it. It was also said: they opposed what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and differed concerning it. It was also said: the intended is the Qur'an, and those who differed are the disbelievers of Quraysh; some of them say it is magic, some say it is the myths of the ancients, and some say otherwise.

"is in extreme dissension," meaning a disagreement far from the truth. The meaning of "shiqaq" has already been given before.

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrima concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down﴾ that he said: it was revealed concerning the Jews.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi who said: they concealed the name of Muhammad (ﷺ) and took for it a little gain out of greed.

Ibn Jarir also related similarly from Abu al-'Aliya.

(p-112) al-Tha'labi related from Ibn Abbas through two weak chains that it was revealed concerning the Jews.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliya concerning His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ that he said: they chose error over guidance and punishment over forgiveness. ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ He said: how bold they are upon the work of the Fire.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ that he said: how knowledgeable they are of the deeds of the people of the Fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related concerning His saying: ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ that he said: By Allah, they have no patience for it, but it says: how bold they are upon the Fire.

Ibn Jarir related similarly from Qatada.

Ibn Jarir also related from al-Suddi concerning the verse that he said: this is in the form of a question: "What is it that has made them patient for the Fire?" His saying: ﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾ he said: they are the Jews and the Christians. ﴿are in far-reaching dissension﴾ he said: in far-reaching enmity.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 177:**

His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ Ḥamzah and Ḥafs read it in the accusative (*naṣb*), making it the predicate (*khabar*) of *laysa* (the negating verb "is not"), with the subject being *an tuwallū* (that you turn). The rest read it in the nominative (*rafʿ*), making it the subject. It was said: this verse was revealed in response to the Jews and Christians, when they spoke at length about the matter of the qiblah (direction of prayer) at the time the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned toward the Kaaba. It was also said: the cause of its revelation was that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this will come at the end of the discussion, God willing.

His saying: ﴿toward the east and the west﴾ It was said: by mentioning the east, He (glorified is He) indicated the qiblah of the Christians, because they face the rising of the sun; and by mentioning the west, He indicated the qiblah of the Jews, because they face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which at that time lay to the west of them.

His saying: ﴿but righteousness is﴾ *Al-birr* is a comprehensive term for goodness, and its predicate is omitted; its estimated (implied) form is: "the righteousness of him who believes [in Allah]." This was stated by al-Farrāʾ, Quṭrub and al-Zajjāj. It was also said that the estimated form is: "but the one possessing righteousness is him who believes." The reason for this estimation is to avoid reporting a concrete entity (*ism al-ʿayn*) as the subject of an abstract noun (*ism al-maʿnā*). It is also permissible for *al-birr* to mean *al-bārr* (the one who is righteous), since the verbal noun is frequently used in the sense of the active participle; from this in the revelation is ﴿if your water should become sunk (*ghawran*)﴾, meaning "sunk (*ghāʾiran*)." This is the view preferred by Abū ʿUbayda.

The word "the Book" here means the category (of books) or the Qur'an. The pronoun in His saying *ʿalā ḥubbihi* ("out of love for it") refers to the wealth. It was also said that it refers to the giving (*al-itāʾ*) indicated by His saying ﴿and gives wealth﴾. And it was said that it refers to Allah (glorified is He), meaning "out of love for Allah." The meaning on the first view is that he gives wealth while loving it and being stingy with it; from this is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾. The meaning on the second view is that he loves giving wealth and his soul is content with it. The meaning on the third view is that he gives to those included in the verse purely out of love for Allah (mighty and majestic), not for any other purpose. It is like His saying: ﴿and they give food out of love for it﴾. Similar to it is the verse of Zuhayr:

*Indeed the generous man, despite his afflictions, grows old.*

He placed the near kin first, because giving wealth to them is both charity (*ṣadaqah*) and kinship-support (*ṣilah*) when they are poor. Likewise, poor orphans have greater claim to charity than poor people who are not orphans, because they lack the ability to earn.

*Al-miskīn* (the needy): the one who relies on what is in people's hands because he finds nothing.

*Ibn al-sabīl* (the wayfarer): the traveler who is cut off; he was called "son of the road" because he constantly accompanies it.

His saying: ﴿and for the captives (*fī al-riqāb*)﴾ means: in assisting the slaves whom their owners have agreed to free by contract. It was also said that the meaning is purchasing slaves and freeing them, and it was said that the meaning is the release of prisoners of war.

His saying: ﴿and gives the zakāt﴾ In this is evidence that the giving mentioned earlier is voluntary charity (*ṣadaqat al-taṭawwuʿ*), not obligatory charity (*ṣadaqat al-farīḍah*).

His saying: *wal-mūfūn* ("and those who fulfill"): it was said that it is coordinated (*maʿṭūf*) with *man āmana* ("he who believes"), as if it were said: "but righteousness is [the attribute of] the believers and those who fulfill." This was stated by al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is in the nominative by way of inception (*mubtadaʾ*), with its predicate omitted. It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who fulfill." It was also said that it is coordinated with the pronoun in *āmana*, but Abū ʿAlī rejected this and said: "the meaning does not go that way."

His saying: *waṣ-ṣābirīn* ("and the patient") is in the accusative by way of praise (*al-madḥ*), like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾. From this is what Abū ʿUbayda recited:

*Let not my people be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughter-camels (*al-juzur*),*

*who alight in every battle-field, and who are good in tying the waistcloths (*al-uzur*).*

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is coordinated with *dhawī al-qurbā* ("the near kin"), as if he said: "and gave to the patient." Al-Naḥḥās said: this is an error.

Al-Kisāʾī said: and this is the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd): *wal-mūfīna wal-ṣābirīn*. Al-Naḥḥās said: on this reading both would be coordinated with *dhawī al-qurbā*, or they would be in the accusative by way of praise.

Yaʿqūb and al-Aʿmash read *wal-mūfūna* and *wal-ṣābirūna* with the nominative in both.

*Al-basāʾ* means hardship and poverty. *Al-ḍarrāʾ* means illness and chronic affliction. *Wa-ḥīn al-baʾs* ("and at the time of battle"): it was said that it means the time of war. *Al-basāʾ* and *al-ḍarrāʾ* are nouns built on the pattern *faʿlāʾ* and have no verb-form of their own, because they are nouns and not adjectives.

His saying: *ṣadaqū* ("they are sincere"): He described them with truthfulness and piety in their affairs, and with fulfilling them, and that they were earnest. It was said that the meaning is that they were truthful in facing combat; but the first is preferable.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, who also graded it sound, reported from Abū Dharr that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about faith, and he recited ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ until he finished it. Then he asked him again, and he recited it again. Then he asked him again, and he recited it again. He said: "When you do a good deed, your heart loves it; and when you do an evil deed, your heart hates it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Mardawayh reported from al-Qāsim ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: A man came to Abū Dharr and said: "What is faith?" So he recited to him this verse, then mentioned to him something similar to the preceding hadith.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning this verse, that he said: "It means: it is not righteousness that you pray and do not act. This was when he turned from Makkah to Madinah and the obligatory duties were revealed."

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him that he said: "This verse was revealed in Madinah. It means: it is not righteousness that you pray; rather, righteousness is what is firmly established in the heart of obedience to Allah."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatādah, who said: "It has been related to us that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness, so Allah revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ to the end of the verse." / 50

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah, who said: "The Jews used to pray facing the west, and the Christians facing the east, so ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ to the end of the verse was revealed."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah something similar.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan reported from Ibn Masʿūd concerning His saying: ﴿and gives wealth out of love for it﴾ that he said: "He gives while he is healthy and stingy, hoping to live long and fearing poverty."

He also reported it from him as a raised (*marfūʿ*) report, similar to it.

al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab reported from al-Muṭṭalib that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is giving wealth out of love for it? For all of us love it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You give it at the time you give it while your soul tells you of long life and poverty."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿and gives wealth out of love for it﴾ that it means: out of love for wealth.

He also reported from him concerning His saying: "the near kin," that it means his relatives.

It is firmly established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Charity given to a needy person is [simply] charity, but to a kinsperson it is two: charity and kinship-support." Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it good), al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan reported it from the hadith of Salmān ibn ʿĀmir al-Ḍabbī. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from the hadith of Zaynab, the wife of Ibn Masʿūd, that she asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Does spending on my husband and on orphans in my care count for me as charity?" He said: "You have two rewards: the reward of charity and the reward of kinship."

al-Ṭabarānī and al-Ḥākim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan reported from the hadith of Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best charity is that given to a kinsperson who is hostile to you."

Aḥmad, al-Dārimī and al-Ṭabarānī reported from the hadith of Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Ibn al-sabīl is the guest who stops at the homes of Muslims."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid, who said: "It is the one who passes by you while he is traveling."

Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿIkrimah concerning His saying: *wal-sāʾilīn* ("and the beggars"), who said: "The beggar is the one who asks you."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿and for the captives﴾ that he said: "it means freeing captives."

He also reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿and establishes prayer﴾, that it means: and completes the prescribed prayer; ﴿and gives the zakāt﴾ means: the obligatory zakāt.

al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn ʿAdī, al-Dāraquṭnī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Fāṭimah bint Qays, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is a right in wealth besides zakāt." Then he recited: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah concerning His saying: ﴿and those who fulfill their covenant﴾ that he said: "Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and then breaks it, Allah will take vengeance on him; and whoever gives the protection (*dhimmah*) of the Prophet (ﷺ) and then betrays it, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be his adversary."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾ that it means: among themselves and among people.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, and al-Ḥākim (who graded it sound) reported from Ibn Masʿūd concerning the verse that he said: "*al-basāʾ* is poverty, *al-ḍarrāʾ* is sickness, and *ḥīn al-baʾs* is the time of fighting."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿those are the ones who are sincere﴾ that he said: "They did what Allah mentioned in this verse."

Ibn Jarīr reported from al-Rabīʿ concerning His saying: ﴿those are the ones who are sincere﴾, that he said: "They spoke words of faith, and the reality of the deed was that they were sincere to Allah."

He said: al-Ḥasan used to say: "This is a statement of faith, and its reality is action; if there is no action along with the statement, then there is nothing."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 178–179:**

His saying: *kutiba* (ﷻ "it is prescribed") means *furida* (it is made obligatory) and *uthbita* (it is established). From this is the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

*"Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,*
*and for the coquettish women, trailing their skirts."*

This is a report from Allah, glorified is He, to His servants that He has legislated this for them. It has also been said that *kutiba* here refers to what the Pen has written on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

As for *al-qisas* (retaliation), its root meaning is *qass al-athar*, that is, following the trail. From it comes *al-qass* (the storyteller), because he traces accounts. And *qass al-sha'r* means following its trace. So it is as if the killer takes a path of killing and follows its traces. From this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿So they both returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ (18:64). It has also been said that *al-qisas* is derived from *al-qass*, which means cutting. One says *qasasta ma baynahuma*, meaning "I cut what was between them."

This verse has been used as evidence by those who hold that a free person is not killed for a slave, and they are the majority (al-jumhur).

Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla and Dawud held that a free person is killed for him.

Al-Qurtubi said: This has been reported from Ali and Ibn Mas'ud.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatada and al-Hakam ibn Utayba also said so, and they cited the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ (5:45). The earlier scholars (al-awwalun) answered this argument by saying that the Exalted's saying ﴿the free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ explains His saying ﴿the life for the life﴾. They also said: His saying ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾ indicates that this is a report of what Allah legislated for the Children of Israel in the Torah.

Among what the latter scholars cited is his saying ﷺ (ﷺ): "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafa'u dima'uhum)." This is answered by saying that it is general (mujmal) and the verse is explanatory (mubayyina). Yet it may be said that the Exalted's saying ﴿the free for the free, and the slave for the slave﴾ only indicates by its explicit wording (mantuq) that a free person is killed for a free person and a slave for a slave. It contains nothing that indicates that a free person is not killed for a slave except through the implicit meaning (mafhum). Whoever relies on this kind of implicit meaning is bound to say so here, and whoever does not rely on such implicit meaning is not bound to say so here. The discussion of this is established in the science of usul al-fiqh (legal theory).

This verse has been used as evidence by those who hold that a Muslim is killed for a disbeliever. They are the Kufans and al-Thawri, because the word "free" includes the disbeliever just as it includes the Muslim, and likewise the words "slave" and "female" include the disbeliever just as they include the Muslim.

They also cited the Exalted's saying ﴿that the life is for the life﴾, because "life" applies to a disbelieving soul just as it applies to a Muslim soul.

The majority held that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever. They cited what was transmitted from the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ: "A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever." This explains what is intended in the two verses. The discussion of this is lengthy.

This verse has been used as evidence by those who hold that a man is not killed for a woman. They established the implication in the same way as above, except that if the woman's guardians agree to pay the excess over the woman's blood-money from the man's blood-money.

This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Thawri and Abu Thawr.

The majority held that a man is killed for a woman without any excess, and this is the truth.

We have expanded on this discussion in *Sharh al-Muntaqa*, so let the reader refer to it.

His saying: ﴿But if anything is remitted to him by his brother﴾. Here "whoever" (man) refers to the killer.

By "brother" is meant either the slain person or the guardian (al-wali), and "anything" refers to the blood. The meaning is that if the killer or the offender is pardoned by the victim or the guardian, the blood that he incurred from him, on condition that he takes something from it as blood-money (diyah) or compensation (arsh), then the victim should follow the guardian by claiming it from the one who owes the blood, by what he takes from him, with fair following (ittiba' bi'l-ma'ruf). And the offender should pay what is due from the blood-money or compensation to the victim or the guardian, paying with goodness (ada' bi-ihsan).

It has also been said that "whoever" (man) refers to the guardian, and "brother" refers to the killer, and "anything" refers to the blood-money. The meaning is that if the guardian inclines to pardon retaliation in exchange for the blood-money, then the killer has the choice between giving it or surrendering himself to retaliation. This was reported from Malik, that the killer has the right of choice in this. The others held that he is not given a choice, but rather when the heirs are content with the blood-money, the killer has no choice, and he is obliged to hand it over.

It has also been said that the meaning of *ufiya* (is remitted) is *bdu'ila* (is offered), that is, whoever is offered something of the blood-money should accept it and follow with fairness.

It has also been said that the intention is that whoever among the two groups has something of the blood-money in excess over the other, then *ufiya* means *fadala* (is in excess).

On all these interpretations, the indefinite *shay'* (anything) is for minimization, so it includes the pardon of a small amount of blood-money and the pardon issued by one individual among the heirs.

His saying: *fa-ittiba'un* (then following) is in the nominative by an implied verb, that is, let there be following from him (falyakun minhu ittiba'), or it is the predicate of an implied subject, that is, the matter is following (fa-al-amr ittiba'). Likewise His saying: ﴿and payment to him with goodness﴾.

His saying: ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾ refers to the pardon and the blood-money. That is, Allah legislated for this Ummah pardon without compensation or with compensation, and He did not restrict them as He restricted the Jews. He made retaliation obligatory for them, with no pardon. And He restricted the Christians, for He made pardon obligatory for them, with no blood-money.

His saying: ﴿Then whoever transgresses after that﴾, that is, after the lightening. For example, he takes the blood-money and then kills the killer, or he pardons and then exacts retaliation.

The people of knowledge have differed concerning whoever kills the killer after taking the blood-money.

A group, including Malik and al-Shafi'i, said: He is like one who kills from the start. If the guardian wishes, he kills him, and if he wishes, he pardons him.

Qatada, Ikrima, al-Suddi and others said: His punishment is that he must be killed without fail, and the ruler does not permit the guardian to pardon.

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: His matter is for the imam to deal with as he sees fit.

His saying: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾, that is, in this ruling which Allah has legislated for you there is life for you. For when a man knows that he will be killed in retaliation if he kills another, he restrains himself from killing and refrains from rushing into it and falling into it. So this is like life for human souls.

This is a eloquent kind of rhetoric and a sublime kind of eloquence, for He made retaliation, which is death, a life in consideration of what it leads to, namely people restraining from killing one another, preserving their own souls and perpetuating their lives. He directed this address to *ulu al-albab* (people of understanding), because they are the ones who consider consequences and avoid what carries delayed harm. As for one who is afflicted with folly, recklessness and levity, he does not look at consequences at the surge of his anger and the boiling of the cauldrons of his recklessness, nor does he think about a future matter, as one of their brigands said:

*"I will wash the shame from myself with the sword, bringing*
*upon myself what Allah decrees, whatever it brings."*

Then the Glorified explained this ruling which He legislated for His servants by His saying: ﴿so that you may have taqwa (be mindful)﴾, that is, that you may avoid killing by preserving retaliation, and this will be a cause of taqwa.

Abu al-Jawza' recited *wa-lakum fi al-qasas hayat* (in the "qasas"). It has been said he meant by *al-qasas* the Qur'an, that is, in the Book of Allah in which He legislated retaliation there is life for you, meaning salvation. It has also been said he meant the life of hearts. It has also been said it is a verbal noun meaning retaliation. All of these are weak, and the recitation with it is unacceptable (munkara).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Two Arab tribes fought one another in the Jahiliyyah shortly before Islam. Between them there was killing and wounding, until they killed slaves and women, and one of them did not take retaliation from the other until they embraced Islam. One of the two tribes boasted over the other in numbers and wealth. So they swore that they would not be content until a free man of theirs is killed for a slave of ours, and a man of theirs is killed for a woman of ours. So this verse was revealed.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported similarly from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: They did not kill a man for a woman, but they killed a man for a man and a woman for a woman. So Allah revealed ﴿the life for the life﴾, and He made free persons equal in retaliation among themselves in intentional killing, men and women alike, regarding the soul and regarding what is less than the soul. And He made slaves equal in intentional killing, regarding the soul and regarding what is less than the soul, men and women alike.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Malik, who said: There was fighting between two Ansari tribes, in which one of them had superiority over the other. It was as if they sought excess, so the Prophet ﷺ came to reconcile between them, and this verse was revealed: ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Then the verse ﴿the life for the life﴾ abrogated it (fa-nasakhathu).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿But if anything is remitted to him﴾ that he said: It is intentional killing where its people are content with the pardon.

﴿Then following with fairness﴾: He commanded the claimant (talib) to do so. ﴿And payment to him with goodness﴾ is from the one who pays. He said: He pays the one sought with goodness.

﴿That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾ (pp. 115): from what was prescribed for the Children of Israel.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported something similar from him through another chain.

Al-Bukhari and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: Among the Children of Israel there was retaliation, but there was no blood-money among them. So Allah said to this Ummah: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ up to His saying ﴿But if anything is remitted to him by his brother﴾. So pardon means that you accept blood-money for intentional killing. ﴿Then following with fairness and payment to him with goodness. That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾ from what was prescribed for those before you. ﴿Then whoever transgresses after that﴾: it is said, after accepting the blood-money. ﴿For him is a painful punishment.﴾

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: The people of the Torah had only retaliation or pardon, with no compensation between them. The people of the Gospel were only commanded to pardon. Allah made for this Ummah killing, pardon and blood-money, if they wished. He made it lawful for them, and it had not been for any nation before them.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is afflicted by killing or by injury (khabal), he chooses one of three: either he exacts retaliation, or he pardons, or he takes the blood-money. If he wants a fourth, then restrain him. And whoever transgresses after that, for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatada that if one kills after taking the blood-money, for him is a great punishment. He said: So he must be killed, and the blood-money is not accepted from him.

He said: It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood-money."

Samuwayh in his Fawa'id reported from Samura, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ikrima that he said: He is killed. Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾: He said: Allah placed in retaliation life, deterrence and admonition, so that when the wrongdoing transgressor remembers it, he restrains from killing.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿so that you may have taqwa﴾: He said: Perhaps you will fear that you would kill him and thus be killed for him.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿O people of understanding﴾: He said: Whoever has understanding remembers retaliation, and the fear of retaliation restrains him from killing. ﴿So that you may have taqwa﴾: He said: So that you may guard against bloodshed out of fear of retaliation.

So Allah said to this Ummah: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ up to His saying ﴿But if anything is remitted to him by his brother﴾. So pardon means that you accept blood-money for intentional killing. ﴿Then following with fairness and payment to him with goodness. That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾ from what was prescribed for those before you. ﴿Then whoever transgresses after that﴾: it is said, after accepting the blood-money. ﴿For him is a painful punishment.﴾

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: The people of the Torah had only retaliation or pardon, with no compensation between them. The people of the Gospel were only commanded to pardon. Allah made for this Ummah killing, pardon and blood-money, if they wished. He made it lawful for them, and it had not been for any nation before them.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is afflicted by killing or by injury (khabal), he chooses one of three: either he exacts retaliation, or he pardons, or he takes the blood-money. If he wants a fourth, then restrain him. And whoever transgresses after that, for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatada that if one kills after taking the blood-money, for him is a great punishment. He said: So he must be killed, and the blood-money is not accepted from him.

He said: It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood-money."

Samuwayh in his Fawa'id reported from Samura, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ikrima that he said: He is killed. Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾: He said: Allah placed in retaliation life, deterrence and admonition, so that when the wrongdoing transgressor remembers it, he restrains from killing.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿so that you may have taqwa﴾: He said: Perhaps you will fear that you would kill him and thus be killed for him.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿O people of understanding﴾: He said: Whoever has understanding remembers retaliation, and the fear of retaliation restrains him from killing. ﴿So that you may have taqwa﴾: He said: So that you may guard against bloodshed out of fear of retaliation.

Jarir also said:

> "I am the death of whom you have been told, so there is no escape for the one who flees from me."

God, glory be to Him, made the condition for the bequest He prescribed that the testator leave "khayr" (wealth). Scholars disagreed about what the answer to this condition is. Two views are transmitted from al-Akhfash: the first is that the implied meaning is "If he leaves wealth, then there is a bequest," and the fa' (then) was omitted, as the poet said:

> "Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them, and evil with evil is equal in the sight of God."

The second is that its answer is implied before it, meaning: "A bequest is prescribed for the parents and the relatives if he leaves wealth."

The scholars differed about the amount of khayr. It was said: what exceeds seven hundred dinars; it was said: a thousand dinars; and it was said: what exceeds five hundred dinars.

The wasiyya (bequest), originally, is an expression for commanding something and binding oneself to it, during life and after death. Here it is an expression for commanding something to take effect after death.

The scholars have agreed that a bequest is obligatory upon one who owes a debt, or holds a deposit (wadī'a), or the like.

As for one who is not in such a situation, most of them held that it is not obligatory for him, whether he is poor or rich. A group said it is obligatory.

God, glory be to Him, did not specify here the amount with which He prescribed the bequest for the parents and the relatives. It was said: a fifth; it was said: a quarter; it was said: a third.

The scholars disagreed about whether this verse is muḥkam (definitive, not abrogated) or mansūkh (abrogated, naskh being abrogation). A group held that it is muḥkam, and they said: although it is general in wording, its meaning is specific.

By the parents is meant those who do not inherit, such as non-Muslim parents, and those who are in slavery; and by the relatives is meant those other than the heirs among them.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars whom we know have agreed that the bequest to the parents who do not inherit and to the relatives who do not inherit is permissible.

Many scholars said: it has been abrogated by the verse of inheritance, together with his, ṣallā Allāh ʿalayhi wa-sallam, saying: "There is no bequest to an heir." This is a ḥadīth that some scholars of ḥadīth authenticated, and it was transmitted through more than one chain.

Some scholars said: it abrogated the obligation and removed the recommendation (nadb). This is transmitted from al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and Malik.

His saying "bi-l-maʿrūf" means: with justice, without deficiency or excess.

God has permitted the deceased to bequeath up to a third, and not more than that.

His saying "ḥaqqan" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose meaning is establishment and obligation.

His saying: "fa-man baddalahu" (then whoever alters it): this pronoun refers to the bequest understood from the wasiyya. The same applies to the pronoun in "sami'ahu" (he heard it). Tabdīl means taghyīr (change). The pronoun in "fa-innamā ithmuhu" (its sin is only upon him) refers to the alteration understood from "baddalahu." This is a warning to whoever changes a bequest that accords with the truth, one in which there is no jani (deviation) or harm, and that he will bear the sin, while the testator is free of any of that, having been relieved of what was upon him by the bequest.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement that if someone bequeaths what is not permitted, such as wine, pork, or any of the sins, it is permissible to alter it, and it is not permissible to carry it out, just as it is not permissible to carry out what exceeds a third.

This is what Abu 'Umar said, and it ends there.

Al-janaf: excess, from janifa yajnafu, meaning "he exceeded," as al-Nahhas said. It was said: al-janaf is inclination (mayl). From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

> "Turn aside from the stone of Yamama, O youth, and I did not seek from its people anything other than you."

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ, it says: al-janaf is inclination, and likewise in al-Kashshāf.

Labid said:

> "I am a man whose noble lineage of 'Amir has protected my dignity, though my adversaries have inclined against me."

His saying "fa-aṣlaḥa baynahum" (then makes peace among them) means: he reconciles what has occurred among the heirs of discord and disorder because of the bequest, by annulling what contains harm and opposes what God has legislated, and by establishing what is right, such as a bequest to relatives who are not heirs. The pronoun in "baynahum" refers to the heirs, even though no mention of them has preceded, because it is known from the context that they are the intended ones. It was also said that it refers to the beneficiaries of the bequest, who are the parents and the relatives.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever does not leave sixty dinars has not left khayr."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from 'Urwa that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib entered upon a freedman of theirs who was dying and who had seven hundred or six hundred dirhams, and he said: "Shall I not bequeath?" He said: "No. God only said: 'If he leaves khayr,' and you do not have much wealth, so leave your property to your heirs."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from 'Aisha that a man said to her: "I want to bequeath." She said: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." They also both transmitted from Tawus that he said: "Whoever bequeaths to a people and names them, and leaves his close relatives in need, the bequest is taken from them and returned to his relatives."

Abu Dawud in his Sunan and al-Bayhaqi transmitted similar to it from him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: "janafan aw ithman" (deviation or sin) that he said: "Error or intention."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from him that he said: "Janaf in the bequest, and harming through it, is among the major sins."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 183–184:

The meaning of "kutiba" (prescribed) has already been explained. There is no disagreement among all Muslims that the fasting of Ramadan is an obligation (fard) which Allah, glorified is He, has enjoined upon this Ummah.

Linguistically, the root meaning of al-siyam (fasting) is restraint (al-imsak) and abstaining from moving from one state to another. Silence is also called sawm, because it is a restraint from speech. From this usage is the verse ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾, meaning a restraint from speech. From this usage is also the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Horses that are restrained (siyam), and horses that are not restrained, under the dust, and horses that chew their bits."

That is, horses that are holding back from running and movement.

In the Shari'ah, it is restraint from the things that break the fast (al-muftirat), together with the intention (niyyah) accompanying it, from the break of dawn (fajr) until the sunset.

As for His saying "kama kutiba" (as it was prescribed): that is, a fast as it was prescribed. The kaf (like) is then in a position of nasb (accusative) as a qualifier (na't). Or the meaning is: "It has been prescribed for you, the fasting, resembling what was prescribed," and the kaf is in a position of nasb as a circumstantial (hal).

Some grammarians said: the kaf is in a position of raf' (nominative) as a qualifier of al-siyam, but this is weak, because al-siyam is definite by the article (al-), and the hidden pronoun in His saying "kama kutiba" refers back to "ma" (what).

The exegetes differed concerning the aspect of the resemblance (wajh al-tashbih), what it is. It was said: it is the amount and the time of the fast, for Allah prescribed the fasting of Ramadan upon the Jews and the Christians, and they altered it. It was said: it is the obligation itself, for Allah obligated fasting upon the nations. It was said: it is the attribute, that is, abstaining from eating, drinking and the like during a period of time. According to the first view, the meaning is: Allah prescribed the fasting of Ramadan upon this Ummah as He prescribed it upon those before them. According to the second: Allah obligated fasting upon this Ummah as He obligated it upon those before them. According to the third: Allah, glorified is He, obligated upon this Ummah restraint from the things that break the fast as He obligated it upon those before them.

As for His, exalted is He, saying ﴿la'allakum tattaqun﴾ (so that you may become God-conscious): by preserving it. It was also said: you guard against sins through this act of worship, because it breaks desire and weakens the incitements to sin, as is related in the hadith that it is "a shield" (junnah) and that it is "a castration" (wija') [i.e., a means of curbing desire].

As for His saying "ayyaman" (days): it is in the accusative as a second object of "kutiba", as said by al-Farra'. It was also said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: fasting was prescribed for you on days.

As for His saying "ma'dudat" (numbered): that is, specified by a known number. It is possible that the use of this plural form, being of the plurals of paucity (jumu' al-qillah), indicates the fewness of the days.

As for His saying ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: it was said that the sick person has two states. If he cannot endure the fast, then breaking it is a firm obligation (‘azimah). If he can endure it with harm and hardship, then it is a concession (rukhsah). The majority held this view. As for His saying "'ala safar" (on a journey), the people of knowledge differed concerning the journey that permits breaking the fast. It was said: the distance for shortening the prayer, and the disagreement about its measure is well known; the majority held this view, while others gave measures for which there is no evidence.

The truth is that whatever qualifies as the designation of a journey is the one in which breaking the fast is permitted, and likewise whatever qualifies as the designation of illness is the one in which breaking the fast is permitted.

There is consensus on breaking the fast during a journey of obedience (safar al-ta'ah).

They differed concerning permissible journeys, and the truth is that the concession is established in them. Likewise they differed concerning a journey of disobedience (safar al-ma'siyah).

As for His saying ﴿fa'iddatun﴾ (then a number): that is, then upon him is a number (of days), or the ruling is a number, or the obligation is a number. The 'iddah is a form (fi'lah) from the numbering, and it carries the meaning of the counted.

As for His saying ﴿min ayyamin ukhar﴾ (of other days): Sibawayh said: it is not declined (lam yanṣarif) because it is diverted (ma'dul) from its original form al-ākhar, since the usual pattern of this category is to take the definite article al-. Al-Kisa'i said: it is diverted from ākhar; and it was said: it is the plural of ukhra.

There is nothing in the verse that indicates the obligation of consecutiveness in making up the missed days.

As for His saying ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾: the reading of the majority is with a kasrah on the ta' and a sukun on the ya', and its origin is (yuṭawwiqūnahu); the kasrah was transferred to the ta', and the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it.

Ḥumayd read it according to the original form without phonetic change.

Ibn 'Abbas read it with a fatha on the ta' lightened and a shaddah on the waw, meaning yukallafūnahu (they are burdened with it).

Ibn al-Anbari related from Ibn 'Abbas "yaṭṭayyaqūnahu" with a fatha on the ya' and shaddah on the ta' and the ya' both fatha, meaning yuṭīqūnahu.

It is related from 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Amr ibn Dinar and Tawus that they read (yaṭṭayqūnahu) with a fatha on the ya' and a shaddah on the ta' with a fatha.

The people of Madinah and Syria read "fidyatu ta'am" as an idafah (construct), and they also read "masakin" (plural). Ibn 'Abbas read "ta'amu miskin" (singular), which is the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i.

The people of knowledge have differed concerning this verse, whether it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or mansukh (abrogated). It was said: it is abrogated, and it was only a concession at the beginning of the prescription of fasting, because it was hard upon them; so whoever fed a poor person each day and abandoned the fast, while being able to fast, [was excused]. Then this was abrogated. This is the view of the majority.

It is related from some people of knowledge that it was not abrogated, and that it is a concession specifically for the elderly men and women who cannot fast except with hardship. This fits the reading with the shaddah, i.e., "yukallafūnahu," as already mentioned.

The abrogating verse of this verse, according to the majority, is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾.

They differed concerning the amount of the fidyah. It was said: one ṣā' of other than wheat each day, and half a ṣā' of it. It was said: only one mudd.

As for His saying ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾:

Ibn Shihab said: its meaning is that he intended feeding together with fasting.

Mujahid said: its meaning is that whoever increases in feeding beyond the mudd. It was said: whoever feeds another poor person along with the first poor person.

'Isa ibn 'Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaṭṭawwa'" with a shaddah and a jazm on the verb, according to the meaning "yatatawwa'"; the rest read with a lightened ta' as a past verb.

As for His saying ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾: its meaning is that fasting is better for them than breaking it along with the fidyah, and this was before the abrogation. It was also said: its meaning is that you fast during a journey and in illness that is not burdensome.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The prayer was transferred through three states, and the fasting was transferred through three states," and he mentioned the states of the prayer, then said: "As for the states of fasting, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madinah and began fasting three days each month, and he fasted 'Ashura'. Then Allah, glorified is He, made fasting obligatory upon him and revealed ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ until His saying ﴿And for those who are able to do it, a fidyah: the feeding of a poor person﴾. So whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a poor person, and that sufficed him. Then Allah revealed the other verse ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, so Allah confirmed fasting for the resident healthy person, and granted concession for the sick and the traveler, and the feeding was maintained for the elderly who cannot fast." Then he mentioned the rest of the hadith.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿as it was prescribed to those before you﴾: he said: by this is meant the People of the Book.

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh and al-Tabarani related from Daghfal ibn Handhalah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The fasting of the month of Ramadan was upon the Christians. Their king fell ill, so they said: If Allah cures him, we will add ten [days]. Then another came and ate meat, and his mouth was injured. He said: If Allah cures him, he will add seven. Then there was another king over them, who said: We will not leave any of these three days without completing them, and we will make our fast in spring. So he did, and it became fifty days."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi concerning His saying ﴿so that you may become God-conscious﴾: he said: you guard yourselves from food, drink and women, just as they guarded themselves.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas something similar to what preceded from Mu'adh.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The fasting of Ramadan, Allah prescribed it upon the nations before you."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from 'A'ishah, who said: "'Ashura' was a fast, and when Ramadan was revealed, whoever wished fasted and whoever wished broke it."

'Abd ibn Humayd related that Ibn 'Abbas said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾ has been abrogated.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, and added that its abrogating verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾, the verse.

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh related something similar from him.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related something similar from him as well.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And for those who are able to do it, a fidyah: the feeding of a poor person﴾, whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished to break it and pay the fidyah did so, until the following verse was revealed and abrogated it: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾."

Al-Bukhari related from Ibn Abi Layla, who said: "The companions of Muhammad related to us," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His saying ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾: he said: the old man who cannot fast, so he breaks it and feeds a poor person in place of each day.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi related that Anas ibn Malik weakened in fasting a year before his death, so he prepared a bowl of tharid and invited thirty poor people and fed them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Daraqutni (who authenticated it) related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said to a mother of a child of his who was pregnant or nursing: "You are in the position of those who cannot fast; upon you is food, and there is no making up upon you."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni related from Ibn 'Umar that one of his daughters sent to ask him about fasting Ramadan while pregnant. He said: "She breaks it and feeds a poor person each day." Something similar has also been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

'Abd ibn Humayd related from 'Ikrimah concerning His saying ﴿So whoever volunteers good﴾: he said: he fed two poor people.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Tawus concerning His saying ﴿So whoever volunteers good﴾: he said: feeding poor people.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Shihab concerning His saying ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾: that fasting is better for you than the fidyah.

There are many hadiths concerning the virtue of fasting.
