Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Shihab concerning His saying ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾: that fasting is better for you than the fidyah.

There are many hadiths concerning the virtue of fasting.

Ramadan is derived from *ramiḍa al-ṣā'im yarmaḍu* (رَمِضَ الصّائِمُ يَرْمَضُ), meaning the fasting person's insides are burned from intense thirst. *Al-ramḍā'* (الرَّمْضاءُ), with a long vowel, means intense heat. From this is the established hadith in the Sahih (the authentic collection): "The prayer of the ones who turn back in repentance (al-awwābīn) is when the young camels are scorched (ramiḍat al-fiṣāl)," meaning the scorching sand burns their bellies.

Al-Jawhari said: The month of Ramadan is pluralized as *ramaḍānāt* and *armiḍā'*. It is said that when they adopted the names of the months from the ancient language, they named them after the seasons in which they fell. This month coincided with the days of heat, so it was named accordingly. It is also said that Ramadan was named so because it burns (*yarmiḍu*) sins, that is, it burns them away through righteous deeds.

Al-Mawardi said: Its name in the pre-Islamic period was *Nātiq*. Al-Mufaddal recited:

"And in Nātiq, the Khath'am horsemen were routed at the thick of battle, and they turned their backs and fled."

They named it so because it "plucked" (*yantiquhum*) them, due to its severity upon them. The word "month" (*shahr*) is in the nominative in the reading of the majority, as a subject whose predicate is ﴿the one in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the fasting of the month of Ramadan is obligatory upon you. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for the fasting mentioned in His words, ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾.

Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab read *al-shahr* in the accusative. Harun al-A'war transmitted it from Abu 'Amr, and it is in the accusative by the implied verb *ilzamū* ("observe") or *ṣūmū* ("fast").

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: It is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "fasting has been prescribed for you" and "that you fast." Al-Nahhas rejected this and said it is in the accusative by way of *al-ighrā'* (urging/admonition).

Al-Akhfash said: It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and it is not declined because of the added *alif* and *nūn*.

His words ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾: It was said that it was sent down from the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*) to the lowest heaven, and then Jibril used to bring it down piece by piece.

It was also said: its beginning was sent down in it. It was also said: the Qur'an was sent down concerning its matter. This verse is more general than His words ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾, which refers to the Night of Decree.

*Al-Qur'ān* (the Qur'an) is the name for the speech of God Most High. It carries the meaning of "that which is recited," like *al-mashrūb* (the drink) being called *sharāb*, and *al-maktūb* (the written) being called *kitāb*. It was also said that it is the verbal noun of *qara'a yaqra'u* (to recite). The poet said:

"They sacrificed a grey-streaked one, whose mark is prostration, who passes the night in glorification and recitation (qur'ān)."

That is, recitation. From this is His words ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾, meaning the recitation of dawn.

His words ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), meaning: guiding them.

His words ﴿and clear proofs of guidance﴾ are an example of specific following general (*'aṭf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm*), to show the nobility of what is coordinated by singling it out for mention, because the Qur'an encompasses both its clear (*muḥkam*) and allegorical (*mutashābih*) verses, while the "clear proofs" are specific to its clear verses.

*Al-Furqān* (the criterion) is that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood, that is, it separates them.

His words ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ mean: whoever is present and not on a journey but resident. "The month" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it cannot be an object.

A group of the earlier and later scholars (*al-salaf wa-al-khalaf*) said: whoever is reached by the month of Ramadan while residing and not traveling is obligated to fast it, whether he travels afterward or remains, based on this verse.

The majority said: if he travels, he breaks his fast, because the meaning of the verse is: if he is present for the month from its beginning to its end, not if he is present for part of it and then travels. In that case, he is only bound to fast the part he was present for. This is the truth, and authentic evidences from the Sunnah support it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to go out during Ramadan and break his fast.

His words ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾ have already been explained.

His words ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ indicate that this is one of the objectives of the Lord, Glorified is He, and one of His intentions in all matters of religion. Similar to it is His words ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾. It is established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he would guide toward ease and forbid making things difficult, as in his saying (ﷺ): "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give good news and do not drive people away," and it is in the Sahih.

*Al-yusr* (ease) is the facility in which there is no difficulty.

His words ﴿and that you complete the period﴾: apparently it is coordinated with His words ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾, meaning: He intends ease for you, and He intends for you to complete the period and to magnify Him. It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element, its implied meaning being: He granted you this concession so that you may complete the period, and prescribed fasting for whoever witnesses the month so that you may complete the period.

The Basrans held the first view, saying: the implied meaning is "He intends in order that you complete the period," like the statement of Kathir ibn Sakhr:

"I wish to forget her, but it is as though she appears to me at night along every path."

The Kufans held the second view. It was said: the *wāw* is superfluous (*muqḥama*). It was also said: this *lām* is the *lām* of command, and the *wāw* coordinates the following clause with the preceding clause.

In *al-Kashshāf* (a Qur'an commentary by al-Zamakhshari), it is said: His words ﴿that you complete the period﴾ are the reason for the command to observe the period. ﴿and that you magnify﴾ is the reason for what is known of the manner of making up fasts and being released from the obligation of breaking the fast. ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾ is the reason for the concession and facilitation. The meaning of "magnifying" here is the saying of one who says: "Allahu Akbar."

The majority said: its meaning is urging the glorification of God at the end of Ramadan. There has been disagreement about its time. It was narrated from some of the earlier scholars that they used to glorify God on the night of Eid al-Fitr. It was also said: when they saw the crescent of Shawwal, they would glorify God until the end of the sermon. It was also said: until the imam came out. And it was also said: it is the glorification on the day of Eid al-Fitr.

Malik said: it begins from the time one leaves his house until the imam comes out, and al-Shafi'i said likewise.

Abu Hanifa said: one glorifies God on Eid al-Adha and does not glorify on Eid al-Fitr.

His words ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾ have already been explained.

Abu Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn 'Adi, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Abu Hurayra, both as a marfū' (attributed to the Prophet) and as a mawqūf (attributed to a companion), that he said: "Do not say 'Ramadan,' for Ramadan is one of the names of Allah Most High; rather say 'the month of Ramadan.'"

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." And it is established from him that he said: "Whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." And it is established from him that he said: "Two months of Eid will not decrease: Ramadan and Dhu al-Hijja." And he said: "When Ramadan begins, the gates of Paradise are opened." All of this is in the Sahih.

It is also established from him in many hadiths other than these that he would say "Ramadan" without mentioning "the month."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Asbahani in *al-Targhib* transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It was named Ramadan because Ramadan burns (*yarmiḍu*) sins."

Both of them also transmitted similar from 'Aisha, as a marfū'.

Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted something similar from Ibn 'Umar.

Many hadiths about the virtue of Ramadan have been reported.

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from Wathila ibn al-Asqa' that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Psalms (*al-Zabur*) were sent down on the eighteenth night of Ramadan, and God sent down the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth night of Ramadan."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the same from Jabir, but he said: "and the Psalms were sent down on the twelfth," and he added: "and the Torah was sent down on the sixth night of Ramadan, and the Gospel was sent down on the eighteenth night of Ramadan."

Muhammad ibn Nasr transmitted from 'Aisha something similar to the saying of Jabir, except that she did not mention the descent of the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Miqsam who said: 'Atiyya ibn al-Aswad asked Ibn 'Abbas, saying: "Doubt has entered my heart concerning God's words ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was sent down during the Night of Decree, in Ramadan, and during a blessed night, all at once. Then after that it was sent down in parts, according to the positions of the stars, in months and days."

Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Qur'an was sent down all at once on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan, and it was placed in the House of Honor (*Bayt al-'Izza*) in the lowest heaven. Then Jibril began to bring it down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in gradual recitation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "The Night of Decree is the blessed night, and it is in Ramadan. The Qur'an was sent down all at once from the Remembrance (*al-dhikr*) to the House that is Frequented (*al-Bayt al-Ma'mūr*)."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning His words ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ that he said: "They are guided by it." Concerning ﴿and clear proofs of guidance﴾, he said: "In it are the lawful and the unlawful, and the prescribed limits."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ that he said: "It refers to his sighting of the crescent in his home."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali who said: "Whoever is reached by Ramadan while residing, and then travels, the fast has become obligatory for him, because God says: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur transmitted something similar from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾ that he said: "Ease is breaking the fast while traveling, and hardship is fasting while traveling."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' concerning His words ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ that he said: "The period of the month of Ramadan."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "The period of what the sick or traveling person broke their fast over (and must make up)."

It has been authentically reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Fast when you see the crescent, and break the fast when you see it. If it is hidden from you by clouds, then complete the period as thirty days."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "It is binding upon those who fast, when they look at the month of Shawwal, to glorify God until they finish their festival, because God says: ﴿and that you complete the period, and that you magnify God for what He has guided you to﴾."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Shayba transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to glorify: "Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa-Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, wa-lillahi al-hamd."

Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to glorify: "Allahu Akbar kabīran, Allahu Akbar kabīran, Allahu Akbar, wa-lillahi al-hamd wa-ajall, Allahu Akbar 'alā mā hadānā."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 186:

His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me﴾ It is possible that the question concerns nearness and distance, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, I am near﴾. It is also possible that the question concerns the answering of supplication, as His saying indicates: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. It is also possible that the question concerns what is more general than that, and this is the apparent meaning, setting aside the cause that will be explained later.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am near﴾ It has been said: by answering; it has been said: by knowledge; it has been said: by bestowing favour.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: it is a figurative image of His readiness to answer whoever calls upon Him and the swiftness with which He grants the need of one who asks Him, by likening it to one who is near in place: when he is called, his response comes quickly.

The meaning of "answering" is the same as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾. It has also been said that its meaning is: I accept the worship of the one who worships Me by supplication, based on what is established from him (ﷺ) that "supplication is worship," as Abu Dawud and others narrated from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir. The apparent meaning is that the answering here remains on its linguistic meaning, and that supplication being a form of worship does not necessitate that answering means acceptance of the supplication, i.e., making it accepted worship; rather, answering is a matter other than the acceptance of this worship. (p-120)

The meaning is that He, Glorified is He, answers as He wills and in the manner He wills: the sought thing may come near, or it may come far; and He may ward off from the supplicant some affliction he does not know of because of his supplication. This is restricted to the supplicant not transgressing in his supplication, as in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾. Among transgression is that one seeks what he does not deserve and is not fit for, such as one who asks for a station in Paradise equal to the stations of the prophets or above them.

His saying: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ That is: as I have responded to them when they call upon Me, so let them respond to Me in what I have called them to of faith and acts of obedience. It has also been said that its meaning is: they seek the answering of Allah, Glorified is He, to their supplication by their responding to Him, that is: by carrying out what He commanded them and abstaining from what He forbade them.

Rushd (rectitude) is the opposite of ghayy (error); rashida, yarshudu, rushdan and rashadan.

Al-Harawi said: al-rushd, al-rashad and al-rashad mean guidance and uprightness.

He said: and this verse is among its instances.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of al-Salt ibn Hakim, from a man of the Ansar, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near so that we confide to Him, or distant so that we call out to Him? The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, and then this verse was revealed."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan who said: The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) asked: Where is our Lord? So Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas that "a Bedouin asked the Prophet (ﷺ): Where is our Lord?" So it was revealed.

Ibn Asakir narrated in his History from Ali who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not be incapable of supplication, for Allah revealed to me: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, does our Lord hear supplication, or how is that?" So Allah revealed this verse.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ata' that it reached him that when ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ was revealed, they said: "If only we knew at what hour we should call!" So this verse was revealed.

It is established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim calls upon Allah with a supplication that contains no sin or severing of kinship, but that Allah gives him one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an evil equal to it."

It is also established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of you is answered so long as he does not hasten, saying: I supplicated but I was not answered."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾, he said: "Let them call upon Me," ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾, that is, that when they call upon Me, I answer them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid who said: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ means: let them obey Me.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning His saying: ﴿that they may be rightly guided﴾, he said: "that they may be guided."

His saying, ﴿It has been made lawful for you﴾, indicates that what Allah has made lawful was previously forbidden to them. This is how it was, as the occasion of the revelation of the verse indicates, and it will come.

Al-rafath (sexual talk or intercourse, rendered here as "intercourse") is a metaphor for intercourse (jima').

Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-rafath is a comprehensive word for everything a man desires from his wife." Al-Azhari said the same. From this is the poet's saying:

*"They show, from the closeness of talk, [their] glances, and from them there is a refusal of men's sexual advances."*

It has also been said that al-rafath originally means obscene speech; one says rafatha and arfatha when he speaks indecently. But this is not what is meant here. Al-rafath is construed with ilā (to) because it is included in the sense of "going forth" (imḍā'). He made women a garment (libās) for men and men a garment for them, because each of the two mingles with the other during intercourse, like the mingling between a garment and the one who wears it.

Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "A woman is called libās, firāsh (bedding) and izār (wrapper)."

It has also been said: he made each of them a garment for the other because it covers the other during intercourse from people's eyes.

His saying, ﴿you betray yourselves﴾, means: you betray yourselves by physical contact (mubāshara) during the nights of fasting. It is said khāna and ikhtāna have the same meaning, and both are from khiyāna (betrayal).

Al-Qutaybi said: "The origin of khiyāna is that a man is entrusted with something and does not fulfil the trust in it." End.

He called them traitors to themselves because the harm of that returns to them. His saying, ﴿So He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾, may bear two meanings: one, the acceptance of repentance for their betrayal of themselves; the other, lightening the burden on them by a concession and permission, as in His saying, ﴿He knew that you could not keep count, so He turned to you﴾, meaning He lightened [the burden] on you; and as in His saying, ﴿So whoever does not find [the means], [let him fast] three days... [and] seven [when you return]... ﴾ and ﴿whoever does not find [it], then fasting for two consecutive months as a repentance from Allah﴾, meaning a lightening. Likewise His saying, ﴿and He pardoned you﴾, may mean pardon from sin, and may mean widening and facilitation.

His saying, ﴿and seek﴾: it has been said this is the child, meaning: seek through physical contact with your wives the attainment of what is the greatest aim of marriage, namely the attainment of offspring. It has also been said that what is meant is: seek what Allah has prescribed in the Qur'an by what He has permitted you therein. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. It has also been said: seek the concession and the widening. It has been said: seek what He has written for you of female slaves and wives. And other things have been said which the Qur'anic wording does not indicate, nor does any other evidence point to them.

Al-Hasan al-Basri recited "wa-ittabi'ū" (and follow) with the letter ʿayn, from ittibāʿ (following).

His saying, ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾, is an eloquent metaphor. What is meant here by the white thread is that which stretches across the horizon, not that which is like the tail of a wolf, for the false dawn does not make anything lawful or unlawful.

What is meant by the black thread is the blackness of the night. Distinction (tabayyun) means that one of them separates from the other, and this happens only when the time of dawn enters.

His saying, ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ contains an explicit statement that the fast has a limit, which is the night. So when the night approaches from the east and the day recedes from the west, the fasting person breaks his fast, and eating, drinking and other things become lawful for him. (p-121)

His saying, ﴿And do not have physical contact with them while you are devoted [in retreat] in the mosques﴾: it has been said that what is meant by physical contact here is intercourse. It has also been said that it includes kissing and touching when they are done out of desire, but not when they are done without desire; in that case both are permissible, as ʿAṭāʾ, al-Shāfiʿī, Ibn al-Mundhir and others said. On this basis, the report of consensus (ijmā') narrated by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, that the one in retreat does not have physical contact or kiss, may be understood as restricted to cases done out of desire.

I'tikāf (retreat, spiritual seclusion in a mosque) linguistically means staying constant/attached to something; one says ʿakafa ʿalā al-shay' when he clings to it. From this is the poet's saying:

*"The daughters of the night stayed around me, devoted [to me], like the devotion of the wailing women around their fallen [man]."*

Since the one in retreat stays constantly in the mosque, he is called ʿākif in the mosque and muʿtakif in it, because he confines himself to this worship in the mosque.

I'tikāf in the Sharia is staying constant in a specific act of worship under specific conditions.

Consensus (ijmāʿ) has been reached that it is not obligatory, and that it is only in a mosque. The rulings on i'tikāf are fully set out in the books of jurisprudence and the commentaries on hadith.

His saying, ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾, means these rulings are the limits of Allah.

The origin of ḥadd (limit) is prevention. From this the doorkeeper and the jailer are called ḥaddād. The commands and prohibitions are called the limits of Allah because they prevent anything that is not part of them from entering them, and anything that is part of them from leaving them. For this reason the legal penalties (ḥudūd) are called ḥudūd, because they prevent their subjects from returning [to the offence].

The meaning of the prohibition of approaching them is the prohibition of transgressing them by opposing them. It has also been said: the limits of Allah are only His prohibitions. Among them are physical contact by one in retreat and breaking the fast in Ramadan without an excuse, and other things the prohibition of which has already preceded. On this view, the meaning of the prohibition of approaching them is clear.

His saying, ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs﴾, means: just as He made these limits clear to you, He makes clear to you the signs that guide to the truth.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others have related from al-Bara' ibn ʿĀzib, who said: "When one of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was fasting, and the time of breaking the fast came, and he slept before breaking it, he would not eat that night or the next day until evening. Qays ibn Ṣirma al-Anṣārī was fasting, and he was working on his land that day. When the time of breaking the fast came, he came to his wife and said, 'Do you have any food?' She said, 'No, but I will go and seek some for you.' His eyes overcame him and he slept. When his wife came and saw him asleep she said, 'Disappointment for you! You have slept!' When midday came he fainted. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿It has been made lawful for you on the night of the fast﴾ up to His saying ﴿from the dawn﴾, and they rejoiced at it with great joy."

Al-Bukhari also related from him: "When the fast of the month of Ramadan was prescribed, they did not approach women the whole of Ramadan. Men would betray themselves, so Allah revealed ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ up to the end of the verse."

Reports explaining the occasion of revelation of this verse have been narrated from a group of companions, similar to what al-Bara' said.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When people first embraced Islam, if one of them fasted, he would fast his day until evening, when he would eat food. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb came to his wife, then he came to the Messenger of Allah and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I apologise to Allah and to you for myself,' and he mentioned what had happened from him. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿It has been made lawful for you on the night of the fast﴾ up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: "The Muslims, during the month of Ramadan, when they had prayed the night prayer ('ishā'), women, food and drink became forbidden to them until the same time the next day. Then some Muslims had intercourse with women and ate food in Ramadan after the night prayer, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. They complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah revealed ﴿It has been made lawful for you on the night of the fast﴾ up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Al-rafath is intercourse."

Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Ibn ʿUmar.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Entering (al-dukhūl), covering (al-taghashshī), consummation (al-ifḍā'), physical contact (al-mubāshara), al-rafath, touching (al-lams) and contact (al-mass) — all of this is intercourse, except that Allah is Bashful and Generous, and He alludes by what He wills to what He wills."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying, ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: "They are a shelter for you and you are a shelter for them."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from Mujāhid concerning His saying, ﴿you betray yourselves﴾: "You wrong yourselves."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying, ﴿So now have physical contact with them﴾: "Marry them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from him concerning His saying, ﴿and seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾: "The child."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related the same from Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying, ﴿and seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾: "The night of Qadr."

Al-Bukhari in his History related the same from Anas.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq related from Qatāda: "And seek the concession which Allah has prescribed for you."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: "The verse ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ was revealed, and ﴿of the dawn﴾ was not yet revealed. So when some men wanted to fast, one of them would tie a white thread and a black thread to his feet, and he would not stop eating and drinking until he could distinguish them. Then Allah revealed ﴿of the dawn﴾, and they knew that it meant the night and the day."

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere, from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, that he placed under his pillow two threads, one white and one black, and kept looking at them, but the white did not become distinct to him from the black. So he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him. He said: "Your pillow is then wide indeed; that is only the whiteness of day from the blackness of night."

In a narration in al-Bukhari and elsewhere, he said to him: "You have a wide nape."

In a narration with Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim: "He laughed at him."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "They used to have intercourse while in retreat, until the verse ﴿And do not have physical contact with them while you are devoted in retreat in the mosques﴾ was revealed."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related similarly from Qatāda.

Ibn Jarir related similarly from al-Rabīʿ.

Ibn Jarir related similarly from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "If the one in retreat has intercourse, his retreat is void and he must start again."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying (p-122) ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: "It means the obedience to Allah."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "﴿The limits of Allah﴾ are the disobedience to Allah, meaning physical contact during retreat."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from Muqātil that they are intercourse.

He also related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying, ﴿Thus﴾: that is, "in this way Allah makes clear."

This covers the whole community and all property. Excluded from it is only what the revealed law (al-Shar') has shown to be permissible to take. Such property is taken by right, not by falsehood, and eaten lawfully, not sinfully, even if its owner is unwilling. Examples include paying a debt when the debtor refuses to pay, handing over what God has made obligatory in zakat (almsgiving) and the like, and providing maintenance for those whom the Shari'ah requires one to maintain.

The conclusion is that anything the Shari'ah does not permit one to take from its owner is eaten unlawfully, even if the owner is willing to give it. Examples are the earnings of a prostitute (mahr al-baghi), the fee of a soothsayer (hulwan al-kahin), and the price of wine.

Linguistically, al-batil (falsehood) means that which goes away and vanishes.

On His words, ﴿وَتُدْلُوا﴾ (and that you bring it down), this is in the jussive mood (majzum) as a conjunction with ﴿تَأْكُلُوا﴾ (that you consume), so it falls under the same prohibition. It is said: adla al-rajul bi-hujjatihi (a man "let down" his argument) or with the matter by which he hopes for success, as an image of one who lets down a bucket into a well; adla dalwahu means he lowered his bucket. The meaning is that you must not combine consuming property unlawfully with bringing it before the rulers through false arguments.

This verse is also evidence that a judge's ruling does not make lawful what is unlawful, nor make unlawful what is lawful, whether concerning property or intimate relations. So if a judge rules in someone's favour on the basis of false testimony (shahadat zur) or a perjured oath (yamin fujur), it is not lawful for that person to consume it, because this is eating people's property unlawfully. Likewise, if he bribes the judge and the judge rules for him contrary to the truth, it is eating people's property unlawfully. There is no disagreement among scholars that a judge's ruling does not make lawful what is unlawful or make unlawful what is lawful.

It has been narrated from Abu Hanifa something contrary to this, but it is rejected by the Book of God and by the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as in the hadith of Umm Salama, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps some of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I rule for him according to what I hear. Whomever I rule for, from the right of his brother, let him not take it, for I am only cutting for him a piece of Fire." It is in the two Sahihs and elsewhere.

On His words, ﴿فَرِيقًا﴾ (a portion), this means a piece, a part, or a group, and the word "fariq" is used to express that. The original sense of fariq is a piece of sheep that strays from the main flock.

It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence, and the intended meaning is: "that you may consume the property of a group of people with sin." The injustice and aggression are called "sin" because of their connection to the one who commits them.

On His words, ﴿وَأَنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (while you know), this means while you are aware that this is falsehood and has nothing of the truth in it. This makes their punishment more severe and their crime greater.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words, ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم﴾ (and do not consume your property) to the end of the verse, that he said: This refers to a man who owes property but has no evidence, so he denies the debt, brings the matter before the rulers, and knows that the right is against him.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid that he said: Its meaning is: Do not dispute while you know that you are a wrongdoer.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similarly from Qatada.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis and 'Abdan ibn Ashwa' al-Hadrami disputed over a piece of land, and Imru' al-Qays wanted to swear an oath, so the verse was revealed: ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم﴾ (and do not consume your property) to the end of the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 189:

His saying: ﴿They ask you﴾. The explanation of who the questioners were, to him ﷺ, will come later. Al-ahilla (the new moons) is the plural of hilal (crescent). Its plural is taken with regard to the crescent of each month, or each night, treating the differences of times as if they were differences of essences. Hilal is the name for what appears at the beginning of the month and at its end.

Al-Asma'i said: it is a hilal until it becomes full (istadara). It was also said: it is a hilal until it lights up the sky with its brightness, and that is on the night of the seventh.

It is called hilal because people raise their voices in announcing it when they see it. From this comes istahalla al-sabiyy (the child cried out), meaning when he wailed, and istahalla wajhuhu wa-tahallala (his face lit up and beamed), meaning when joy appeared in it.

His saying: ﴿Say: they are times for the people and for the Hajj﴾. In it is an explanation of the wisdom in the increase and decrease of the crescent, and that this is for the sake of showing the appointed times (mawaqit) by which people fix their acts of worship and their dealings: such as fasting, breaking the fast, the Hajj, the period of pregnancy, the waiting period ('iddah), leases (ijarat), oaths, and other things. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. Mawaqit is the plural of miqat (appointed time), which is the time.

The reading of the majority is wa-l-Hajji with a fatha on the ha'.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a kasra in all of the Qur'an.

Sibawayh said: al-Hajj with a fatha is like al-radd and al-shadd, and with a kasra is like al-dhikr; they are two verbal nouns with the same meaning. It was also said: with a fatha it is the verbal noun, and with a kasra it is the noun.

He, glorified is He, singled out the Hajj for mention because it is among the things in which knowledge of the time is needed, and it is not permissible to postpone it (al-nasi') from its time, and because of the great hardship upon one who is confused about the time of its rites, or who misses its time or the time of some of them.

Some scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani) have considered this answer, I mean His saying: ﴿Say: they are times﴾, to be of the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), which is receiving the addressee with something other than what he expects, as an alert that this is more deserving of attention. The reasoning is that they asked about the physical bodies of the crescents with regard to their increase and decrease, so they were answered with the wisdom for which that increase and decrease exist, because that is more fitting for the questioner to intend and more worthy of his seeking to know.

His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾. The connection of this with the question about the crescents and the answer that they are times for the people and the Hajj is that the Ansar, when they performed Hajj, would not enter through the doors of their houses if one of them returned to his house after entering the state of ihram before completing his Hajj, because they believed that the muhrim should not have anything between him and the sky. They would climb onto the roofs of their houses.

Abu 'Ubayda said: this is a figure of speech, and the meaning is: righteousness is not that you ask the ignorant, but righteousness is piety, and ask the scholars, as you say: I came to this matter through its door. It was also said: it is a metaphor for sexual intercourse, and that they were commanded to approach their women in the front passage (al-qubul) and not in the back passage (al-dubur), and other things were said.

Al-buyut is the plural of bayt (house), and it was read with a damma and a kasra on the ba'.

The explanation of taqwa (piety) and falah (success) has already been given, and it has also been mentioned earlier that the implied phrase in such a saying as: ﴿But righteousness is [the righteousness of] one who fears God﴾ is: but righteousness is the righteousness of one who is pious.

Ibn 'Asakir reported with a weak chain from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn 'Amah.

They are two men from the Ansar who said: O Messenger of God, what is the matter with the crescent that it appears and rises thin like a thread, then increases until it grows large and becomes full, then never ceases to decrease and become thin until it returns as it was, not being in one state? So it was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are times for the people﴾, for the lawfulness of their debts, for their fasting and their breaking of the fast, for the counting of their women, and for the conditions that are tied to a term.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that he said: they asked the Prophet ﷺ about the new moons, why were they made so? Then God revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾, the verse, and He made them for the fasting of the Muslims and their breaking of the fast, for their rites and their Hajj, for the counting of their women, and for the due date of their debts.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported similar to it from Abu al-'Aliyah.

Ibn Jarir reported similar to it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported similar to it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God made the new moons as times for the people, so fast when you see it and break your fast when you see it, and if it is cloudy over you, then complete thirty days."

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Adi and al-Daraqutni reported with a weak chain from Talq ibn 'Ali that he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar to the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.

al-Bukhari and others reported from al-Bara' that he said: In the Jahiliyyah, when they entered the state of ihram, they would come to the houses from their backs, so the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness...﴾, the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Jabir that he said: "Quraysh were called al-Hums, and they would enter through the doors while in ihram, while the Ansar and the rest of the Arabs did not enter through a door while in ihram. Then while the Messenger of God ﷺ was in a garden, he came out through its door, and Qutbah ibn 'Amir al-Ansari came out with him. They said: O Messenger of God, Qutbah ibn 'Amir is a wicked man, and he came out with you through the door. He said to him: What led you to what you did? He said: I saw you do it, so I did as you did. He said: I am a man of the Hums. He said: Then my religion is your religion. So God revealed the verse."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported similar to it from Ibn 'Abbas.

This meaning has been transmitted from a group of the Companions and the Followers.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 190–193:

There is no disagreement among the scholars ('ulama') that fighting was prohibited before the Hijra, based on His saying, Most High: ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾, and His saying: ﴿And forsake them with gracious forsaking﴾, and His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾, and His saying: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, and similar to that of what was revealed in Makkah. When he (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah, Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to fight, and this verse was revealed. It was also said: the first thing revealed was His saying, Most High: ﴿Permission [to fight] is given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged﴾. When this verse was revealed, he (ﷺ) would fight whoever fought him and refrain from those who refrained from him, until His saying, Most High, was revealed: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾, and His saying, Most High: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾.

A group among the early scholars (al-salaf) said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿those who fight you﴾ is other than women, children, monks and the like, and they considered this verse to be muhkam (definitive), not abrogated (mansukh). The meaning of "aggression" (i'tida') according to the people of the first view is fighting those among the disbelieving groups who fight.

What is meant by it according to the second view is exceeding the killing of those who deserve to be killed to the killing of those who do not deserve it, from among those previously mentioned.

His saying: ﴿wherever you find them﴾: it is said: thaqifa yathqafu thaqafan, and a man is thaqif when he is skilled in handling the matters he undertakes.

In al-Kashshaf it says: "Ath-thaqaf is attaining something by way of seizing and overpowering, and from it comes 'a thaqaf man': one quick to seize his opponents." End.

From it is the saying of Hassan:

"If he (Jadhima) overtakes the sons of Luayy, then killing them is a cure."

His saying: ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾, that is, Makkah.

Ibn Jarir said: the address is to the emigrants, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. End.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complied with the command of his Lord, and he expelled from Makkah those who had not embraced Islam when Allah granted him its conquest.

His saying: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾: that is, the fitnah that they wished to inflict upon you, which is your return to disbelief, is worse than killing. It was said: what is meant by fitnah is the trial that befalls a person in himself, his family, his property or his honour. It was also said: what is meant by fitnah is the shirk in which the polytheists were, because they used to regard killing in the Haram as grave, so Allah informed them that the shirk they were upon is graver than what they considered grave. It was said: what is meant is their fitnah of you by their barring you from the Sacred Mosque is worse than your killing of them in the Haram, or than their killing of you if they kill you.

The apparent meaning is that what is meant is fitnah in the religion by whatever cause and in whatever form it occurs, for it is worse than killing.

His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, the verse.

The scholars differed regarding this. A group held that it is muhkam, and that fighting in the Haram is not permitted unless they transgress by fighting therein, in which case it is permitted to repel them by fighting them. And this is the truth.

Another group said: this verse is abrogated by His saying, Most High: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. This argument is answered by the possibility of reconciling them by giving the general (ruling) precedence over the specific, so the polytheist is killed wherever he is found except within the Haram. Supporting this is his (ﷺ) saying: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day," and it is in the Sahih.

Those who argue for abrogation have cited his (ﷺ) killing of Ibn Khatal, who was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah; this is answered by saying that it occurred in that very hour which Allah had made lawful for His Messenger (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿But if they desist﴾, that is, (p-124) from fighting you and enter into Islam.

His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾: in it is the command to fight the polytheists up to a limit, which is that there be no fitnah and that religion be for Allah, which is entering Islam and leaving all other religions that oppose it. Whoever enters Islam and abandons shirk, his fighting is not permitted. It was said: what is meant by fitnah here is shirk, and the apparent meaning is that it is fitnah in religion in its generality, as has passed.

His saying: ﴿Then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾: that is, do not transgress except against those who did wrong, who are those who did not desist from fitnah and did not enter Islam. The recompense of the wrongdoers was called "aggression" only by way of correspondence, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

His saying: ﴿So whoever has assaulted you, then assault him in the same manner﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, the verse, that it was the first verse revealed about fighting in Madinah. When it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah would fight whoever fought him and refrain from whoever refrained from him, until the surah of (Bara'ah) was revealed.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Mujahid concerning this verse that he said: the companions of Muhammad were commanded to fight the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And do not transgress﴾ that he said: do not kill women, children, the elderly old man, nor whoever offers peace and withholds his hand; if you do so, you have transgressed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that he said: this verse concerns women and offspring. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His saying: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾ that he said: shirk is worse than killing.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: the apostasy of a believer back to idolatry is more grievous to him than being killed while in the right.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein﴾ that he said: until they begin the fighting; then it was abrogated after that when He said: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu Dawud in his Nasikh transmitted from Qatadah that His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ and His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting therein. Say: fighting therein is great﴾ remained so until both verses were abrogated together in (Bara'ah) by His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾, and ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿But if they desist﴾ that he said: if they repent.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ that he said: shirk with Allah, ﴿and religion be for Allah﴾, and that tawhid be made sincere for Allah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid concerning the verse, he said: it is shirk.

His saying: ﴿But if they desist, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾: he said: do not fight except whoever fights you.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: ﴿and religion be for Allah﴾ that he said: until you worship none but Allah.

He also transmitted from 'Ikrimah concerning His saying: ﴿then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾ that he said: they are those who refuse to say "There is no god but Allah."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah something similar.

It was also said: the first thing revealed was His saying, Most High: ﴿Permission [to fight] is given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged﴾. When this verse was revealed, he (ﷺ) would fight whoever fought him and refrain from those who refrained from him, until His saying, Most High, was revealed: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾, and His saying, Most High: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾.

A group among the early scholars (al-salaf) said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿those who fight you﴾ is other than women, children, monks and the like, and they considered this verse to be muhkam (definitive), not abrogated (mansukh). The meaning of "aggression" (i'tida') according to the people of the first view is fighting those among the disbelieving groups who fight.

What is meant by it according to the second view is exceeding the killing of those who deserve to be killed to the killing of those who do not deserve it, from among those previously mentioned.

His saying: ﴿wherever you find them﴾: it is said: thaqifa yathqafu thaqafan, and a man is thaqif when he is skilled in handling the matters he undertakes.

In al-Kashshaf it says: "Ath-thaqaf is attaining something by way of seizing and overpowering, and from it comes 'a thaqaf man': one quick to seize his opponents." End.

From it is the saying of Hassan:

His saying: ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾, that is, Makkah.

Ibn Jarir said: the address is to the emigrants, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. End.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complied with the command of his Lord, and he expelled from Makkah those who had not embraced Islam when Allah granted him its conquest.

His saying: ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾: that is, the fitnah that they wished to inflict upon you, which is your return to disbelief, is worse than killing. It was said: what is meant by fitnah is the trial that befalls a person in himself, his family, his property or his honour. It was also said: what is meant by fitnah is the shirk in which the polytheists were, because they used to regard killing in the Haram as grave, so Allah informed them that the shirk they were upon is graver than what they considered grave. His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, the verse.

Supporting this is his (ﷺ) saying: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day," and it is in the Sahih.

Those who argue for abrogation have cited his (ﷺ) killing of Ibn Khatal, who was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah; this is answered by saying that it occurred in that very hour which Allah had made lawful for His Messenger (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿But if they desist﴾, that is, (p-124) from fighting you and enter into Islam.
