His saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ means: if they fight you in the sacred month and violate its sanctity, you fight them in the sacred month as recompense for them and as a requital for their action.

﴿And the sacred things﴾ is the plural of ḥurmah (sanctity), like ẓulumāt (darknesses) being the plural of ẓulmah (darkness). He used the plural ḥurumāt because he meant the sacred month, the sacred city, and the sanctity of the state of iḥrām (ritual consecration). Ḥurmah is what the Sharia has forbidden violating.

Qiṣāṣ (retaliation) means equality. The meaning is that every sanctity admits of qiṣāṣ: whoever violates a sanctity against you, you may violate a sanctity against him in retaliation. It has been said that this was at the beginning of Islam and was then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revealed ruling) by fighting. It has also been said that it remains in force among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) and was not abrogated. Whoever is wronged in property or person may retaliate with the same as was done to him, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and others.

Others said: matters of qiṣāṣ are restricted to the rulers, and likewise property matters, on account of his (ﷺ) saying: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." Al-Daraqutni and others recorded it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, the majority of the Malikis, and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani. The first view is more preferred. It was held by Ibn al-Mundhir, chosen by Ibn al-ʿArabi and al-Qurtubi, and related by al-Dawudi from Malik. It is supported by his (ﷺ) permission to the wife of Abu Sufyan to take from his property what suffices her and her child, which is in the Ṣaḥīḥ. There is nothing more explicit and clear than the saying of Allah, Exalted, in this verse: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. This clause is in the sense of an emphasis of the first clause, namely His saying: ﴿And the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾. He called the requital "transgression" by way of mushākalah (rhetorical matching of terms), as has already been mentioned.

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out to perform ʿumrah in the sixth year after the Hijrah, the polytheists prevented him from entering and reaching the House, and they blocked him and those Muslims with him in Dhu al-Qaʿdah, which is a sacred month. He made a treaty with them that he would enter in the following year. He entered in the coming year, he and those Muslims who were with him, and Allah granted him retribution against them. This verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a similar report from Abu al-ʿĀliyah. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir recorded a similar report from Mujahid as well. The two of them also recorded a similar report from Qatadah. Ibn Jarir recorded a similar report from Ibn Jurayj.

Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (Nasikh), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you﴾ and the verse, and His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ and the verse, and His saying: ﴿And whoever retaliates after he has been wronged﴾ and the verse, and His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like﴾ and the verse. He said: "This and similar verses were revealed in Mecca when the Muslims were few and had no authority to subdue the polytheists. The polytheists used to insult them and harm them. So Allah commanded the Muslims who were to retaliate that they retaliate with the like of what was done to them, or that they be patient and forgive. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated to Medina and Allah strengthened his authority, Allah commanded the Muslims to refer their grievances to their authority, and not to transgress against one another as the people of Jahiliyyah (the time of ignorance before Islam) did. He said: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ and the verse, meaning: the authority supports him until he obtains justice against the one who wronged him. Whoever avenges himself without the authority is a sinner and a transgressor, having acted by the zeal of the Jahiliyyah and not having accepted the judgment of Allah, Exalted." End of quotation.

I say: this verse, which Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, took as abrogating, actually confirms and supports what the verses that he considered abrogated indicate, and emphasizes it. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿We have given his heir authority﴾ is that He gave the authority to him, meaning He gave him a power by which he may exercise authority over the killer. This is why He said: ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Then, even if we grant that the meaning of the verse is as he stated, this would be a specification (takhṣīṣ) of killing from the general scope of the mentioned verses, not an abrogation of them. This is because the verse mentions only killing explicitly, while those verses include it and other things. This is well known from the language of the Arabs, which is the reference in explaining the speech of Allah, glorified is He.

In this verse there is a command to spend in the way of God (*sabil Allah*), which is jihad, but the wording extends to anything that truly counts as being in the way of God. The **ba'** in the phrase ﴿with your hands﴾ (**bi-aydikum**) is *za'idah* (redundant, extra). The sense is: "and do not throw your hands" (**wa-la tulqu aydiyakum**). Similar is ﴿Does he not know that God sees?﴾ (96:14). Al-Mubarrad said: "﴿with your hands﴾ means with your selves, using a part to refer to the whole, as in His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ (42:30)." It was also said: this is a figurative expression (*mathal madrub*). One says, "So-and-so cast his hand into such-and-such a matter" when he surrenders, because the one who surrenders in battle throws down his weapon with his hands. Likewise is the act of every helpless person in whatever action he takes. Others said: the meaning is "and do not cast yourselves by your hands."

*Al-tahlukah* is a verbal noun from *halaka yahlaku halakan, hulkan, and tahlukatan*, meaning: do not engage in what destroys you.

The early scholars (*al-salaf*) have sayings on the meaning of the verse, whose explanation will come, as will the explanation of the occasion of its revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*).

The truth is that what matters is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion. So whatever truly counts as a ruin (*tahlukah*) in religion or in worldly life is included in this, and this is the view of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

Among what falls under the verse is that a man rushes into battle and charges at the army while unable to save himself and without any effect that would benefit the fighters. The objection of those who rejected this, from among those who looked only at the occasion of revelation, does not prevent this from being included under the verse. They thought the verse does not go beyond its occasion, but this assumption is refuted by the Arabic language.

His saying ﴿and do good﴾ (*wa-ahsinu*) means: in spending in obedience (to God), or: think well of God regarding His replacing what you spend.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from Hudhayfah concerning His saying ﴿And spend in the way of God and do not throw yourselves by your hands into ruin﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning spending.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning the verse that he said: it is leaving off spending in the way of God out of fear of poverty (*al-'aylah*).

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Ikrimah something similar too.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan something similar.

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from him that he said: it is stinginess (*al-bukhl*).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse that he said: there were men who went out with expeditions (*bu'uth*) which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) dispatched without provision, so either they were cut off from supplies, or they were dependents (*'iyal*). So God commanded them that they should spend from what God has provided them and not throw themselves by their hands into ruin.

And *al-tahlukah* is that men perish from hunger, thirst, and walking.

And He said to those who have surplus: ﴿And do good; indeed God loves the good-doers﴾ (2:195).

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, al-Baghawi in his *Mu'jam*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mani', and al-Tabarani related from al-Dahhak ibn Abi Jubayrah: that the Ansar used to spend in the way of God and give charity, then a year of hardship struck them, so their opinion of (God) worsened and they held back from that, so God revealed the verse.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from Aslam ibn Imran who said: We were at Constantinople, and over the people of Egypt was Uqbah ibn Amir, and over the people of Syria was Fudalah ibn Ubayd. A great line of the Romans came out, and we lined up against them. A man from the Muslims charged at the Roman line until he entered among them. The people cried out and said: "Glory be to God! He casts his hand into ruin!" Then Abu Ayyub, a companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), stood up and said: "O people, you are interpreting the verse in this way, but this verse was revealed concerning us, the group of the Ansar. When God made His religion mighty and its helpers increased, some of us said to others secretly, without the Messenger of God (ﷺ) (hearing): 'Indeed the wealth of the people has been lost, and God has made Islam mighty and its helpers have increased. So if we stayed at home with our wealth and repaired what had been lost from it?' So God revealed to His Prophet to answer us: ﴿And spend in the way of God and do not throw yourselves by your hands into ruin﴾ (2:195). So the ruin was staying at home with our wealth, repairing it, and abandoning the raid."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said concerning the explanation of the verse: it is the man who commits a sin and then throws down his hands, saying: "God will never forgive me."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir something similar.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related that he said concerning the explanation of the verse: it is despair (*al-qunut*).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-tahlukah" is the punishment of God.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth that they besieged Damascus, and a man rushed alone toward the enemy, so the Muslims criticized him for that. His report was raised to Amr ibn al-As, who sent for him and turned him back, and said: God said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves by your hands into ruin﴾ (2:195).

Ibn Jarir related from a man among the Companions concerning His saying ﴿and do good﴾ that he said: "Perform the obligatory duties (*al-fara'id*)."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu Ishaq something similar.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from (p-126) Ikrimah who said: "Think well of God."

**Ibn Kathir** no. Translation follows:

His words: ﴿And complete the Hajj﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning intended by completing the Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah) and the 'Umrah (lesser pilgrimage) for Allah. It was said: it means performing them and carrying them out without anything forbidden mingling with them, and without neglecting any condition or obligation, based on His words, Exalted is He: ﴿then fulfilled them﴾ and His words: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: completing them is that you set out for them alone and not for anything else. It was also said: completing them is that you perform each of them separately, without tamattu' (combining 'Umrah and Hajj in one journey) or qiran (performing both together under one state of ihram). Ibn Habib held this view.

Muqatil said: completing them is that they do not make lawful during them what is not proper for them. It was said: completing them is that one enters the state of ihram for them from the dwelling of one's family. It was said: it is that one spends on the journey of both only what is lawful and good. The occasion of revelation of the verse and what has been transmitted from the early generations concerning the meaning of completing them will come later.

This verse has been used as evidence that 'Umrah is obligatory, because the command to complete them is a command to perform it. This was the view of 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Tawus, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Masruq, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ibn al-Jahm from the Malikis.

Malik, al-Nakha'i, and the people of opinion (Hanafis), as Ibn al-Mundhir related from them, said: it is a sunnah (recommended practice, not obligatory).

It is related from Abu Hanifah that he held it to be obligatory.

Among those who said it is a sunnah were Ibn Mas'ud and Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.

Among what the first group used as evidence is what is established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih (authentic collection) that he said to his companions: "Whoever has a hady (sacrificial animal with him, let him enter the state of ihram for Hajj and 'Umrah."

It is also established from him in the Sahih that he said: "The 'Umrah has entered into the Hajj until the Day of Resurrection."

al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim narrated from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Hajj and the 'Umrah are two obligations; it does not harm you which of them you begin with."

The others used as evidence what al-Shafi'i narrated in (his commentary on) the verse, and 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih al-Hanafi who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hajj is jihad (struggle), and the 'Umrah is a voluntary act."

Ibn Majah narrated from Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and al-Tirmidhi narrated, and he graded it sahih, from Jabir: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the 'Umrah: Is it obligatory? He said: No, but if you perform it, it is better for you."

Those who held it obligatory answered regarding the verse and the hadiths explicitly stating that it is an obligation by interpreting that as referring to the fact that one has entered into it; and once one has begun it, it is obligatory without disagreement. Although this is a far-fetched interpretation, it must be adopted in order to reconcile the evidences, especially after his (ﷺ) explicit statement mentioned earlier in the hadith of Jabir that it is not obligatory. On this basis, whatever has been reported that indicates its obligation is to be understood accordingly, as al-Shafi'i narrated in al-Umm that in the letter which the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to 'Amr ibn Hazm: "Indeed the 'Umrah is the lesser Hajj."

Similarly, the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Bayhaqi's al-Shu'ab, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Advise me. He said: Worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakah, fast the month of Ramadan, perform Hajj and 'Umrah, listen and obey, be open (in your deeds), and beware of secrecy." In this manner, the hadiths which link Hajj and 'Umrah together, stating that they are among the best deeds, that they are an expiation for what lies between them, and that they demolish what came before them, and similar statements, should be understood.

His words: ﴿But if you are held back﴾. al-Hasr is al-habs (restraint, detention).

Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i, and al-Khalil said: it is said uhsira (passive) for illness, and husira for the enemy.

In al-Mujmal by Ibn Faris, the reverse is found: it is said uhsira for the enemy and husira for illness.

Ibn al-'Arabi preferred the first, and said: this is the opinion of most of the lexicographers.

al-Zajjaj said: it is so according to all the lexicographers.

al-Farra' said: both have the same meaning, whether for illness or for the enemy.

Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani agreed with him in this, saying: "hasarani al-shay' and ahsarani," meaning it detained me.

Because of this difference among the lexicographers, the jurists differed over the meaning of the verse. The Hanafiyyah said: the muhsar (one who is held back) is one who becomes prevented from Makkah after entering ihram, by illness, an enemy, or other causes.

The Shafi'iyyah and the people of Madinah said: the intended meaning of the verse is being held back by an enemy.

Most scholars held that one held back by an enemy is released from ihram where he is held back, slaughters his hady if he has one there, and shaves his head, as the Prophet (ﷺ) himself and his companions did at al-Hudaybiyah.

His words: ﴿then what is easy of the hady﴾. The word "ma" (what) is in the nominative position, as the subject or as the predicate, meaning: then what is required, or upon you. It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: then slaughter or offer what is easy, i.e., what is facilitated. It is said: yassara al-amr and istay'sara, just as it is said: sa''aba and istas''aba (both meaning to make something difficult or easy). Al-hady and al-hadi are two dialects, and both are the plural of hadiyyah, which is what is offered to the House, whether a camel or something else.

al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad pronounce al-hady with a light vowel, while Tamim and the lower Qays pronounce it with a heavy one.

The poet said:
"I swore by the Lord of the Ka'bah and the place of prayer, and by the necks of the hady adorned with garlands."

He said: the singular of al-hady is hadiyyah, and it is said that the plural of al-hadi is uhud.

The people of knowledge differed over what is meant by His words: ﴿what is easy﴾. The majority held that it is a sheep.

Ibn 'Umar, 'A'ishah, and Ibn al-Zubayr said: a camel or a cow.

al-Hasan said: the highest of the hady is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its lowest is a sheep.

His words: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. This is an address to the entire ummah (community), without distinction between one held back and one not held back, and a group of the people of knowledge went to this view. Another group held that it is addressed to the held-back only, meaning: do not come out of ihram until you know that the hady which you sent to the Haram has reached its place of sacrifice, which is the place where it is lawful to slaughter it.

They differed over identifying it. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is the place where one is held back, following the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was held back in the year of al-Hudaybiyah.

Abu Hanifah said: it is the Haram, based on His words: ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾. It was answered that what is addressed in that is one who is safe and able to reach the House. (p-127)

The Hanafiyyah answered regarding his (ﷺ) sacrifice at al-Hudaybiyah by saying that the part of al-Hudaybiyah which lies downward toward Makkah is part of the Haram. It was refuted by saying that the place where the sacrifice took place is not part of the Haram.

His words: ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾, the verse. The intended meaning of illness here is whatever truly fits the linguistic meaning of illness.

The intended meaning of an ailment (adha) of the head is what it has of lice, wounds, or the like. The meaning of the verse is that whoever is ill, or has an ailment of his head, and shaves, then upon him is a fidyah (compensation).

The Sunnah has clarified what is mentioned here generally regarding fasting, charity, and sacrifice. It is established in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah while he was in ihram and his lice were falling onto his face, and he said: "Do the vermin of your head harm you?" He said: "Yes." So he commanded him to shave and to feed six poor persons, or to offer a sheep, or to fast three days.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned that there is no disagreement among the scholars that the nusuk (act of worship/sacrifice) here is a sheep.

It is related from the majority that the fasting mentioned in the verse is three days, and the feeding is ten poor persons.

The authentic hadith mentioned earlier refutes them and nullifies their view.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and Dawud held that the feeding in this case is two mudds (a unit of measure) by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning for each poor person. al-Thawri said: half a sa' of wheat or a sa' of anything else. This was narrated from Abu Hanifah.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is an error, because in some reports of Ka'b it is stated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Give charity of three sa's of dates among six poor persons."

The narrations from Ahmad ibn Hanbal differed. It was narrated from him the like of Malik's and al-Shafi'i's view, and it was narrated from him that if one feeds wheat, then one mudd for each poor person, and if one feeds dates, then half a sa'.

They differed over the place of this fidyah. 'Ata' said: whatever is a blood sacrifice is in Makkah, and whatever is food or fasting is wherever one wishes. The people of opinion agreed with this.

Tawus and al-Shafi'i said: feeding and blood sacrifice may only be done in Makkah, while fasting may be done wherever one wishes.

Malik and Mujahid said: wherever one wishes in all cases, and this is the correct view, due to the absence of evidence specifying the place.

His words: ﴿Then when you are safe, whoever performs tamattu' (combining 'Umrah with Hajj) by 'Umrah until Hajj, then what is easy of the hady﴾. That is, when you are recovered from illness. It was also said: when you are safe from your fear of the enemy, according to the earlier difference. But safety from the enemy is more apparent than using "amintum" (you are safe) for the departure of illness, so this strengthens the view of those who said that His words: ﴿But if you are held back﴾ mean being held back by an enemy, just as His words: ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾ strengthen the view of those who hold that, by singling out the excuse of illness for mention.

A difference has occurred over whether the addressees of this are only the held-back, or the entire ummah, according to what has already passed. The intended meaning of tamattu' mentioned in the verse is that a man enters ihram for 'Umrah, then remains in a state of lawfulness in Makkah until he enters ihram for Hajj. Thus he has, by this, made lawful what is not lawful for one in ihram, and this is the meaning of tamattu' and istamta'.

There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge on the permissibility of tamattu'. Indeed, in my view it is the best type of Hajj, as I have set out in my commentary on al-Muntaqa.

The difference over the meaning of His words: ﴿what is easy of the hady﴾ has already passed.

His words: ﴿And whoever does not find (the means)﴾, the verse. That is, whoever does not find the hady, either for lack of wealth or for lack of livestock, then he fasts three days during Hajj, that is, during the days of Hajj, which run from the beginning of his entering ihram until the day of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). It was also said: he fasts one day before the day of Tarwiyah (8 Dhu al-Hijjah), the day of Tarwiyah, and the day of 'Arafah. It was said: it is what lies between his entering ihram for Hajj and the day of 'Arafah. It was said: he fasts them from the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. It was said: as long as he is in Makkah. It was also said: it is permissible for him to fast the three days before he enters ihram.

Some scholars permitted fasting the days of tashriq (11–13 Dhu al-Hijjah) for one who does not find the hady, while others forbade it.

His words: ﴿and seven when you return﴾. The majority read "sab'ah" (seven) in the genitive case. Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it in the accusative, on the basis that it is governed by an implied verb, meaning: and fast seven. It was also said: it is coordinated with "thalathah" (three), because although that is in the genitive in form, it is in the accusative position, as if it was said: then the fasting of three.

The meaning of "return" here is the return to one's homelands.

Ahmad and Ishaq said: fasting on the way is sufficient for him, and the obligation does not become binding on him except when he arrives at his homeland. This was also the view of al-Shafi'i, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, and others.

Malik said: if one returns from Mina, there is no harm in fasting. The first view is more correct.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not find (the hady), let him fast three days during Hajj, and seven when he returns to his family." Thus he (ﷺ) made clear that the return mentioned in the verse is the return to the family.

It is also established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas with the wording: "and seven when you return to your cities."

As for His words, Glorified is He: ﴿That is ten complete﴾, although everyone knows that three and seven make ten, it was said to remove the suspicion that someone might think there is an option between the three days during Hajj and the seven when one returns. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

al-Mubarrad said: this was mentioned to show that the count is complete, lest someone think that some part of it remains after mentioning the seven. It was also said: it is an emphasis, as you say: "I wrote with my own hand."

The Arabs used to employ this kind of summation for numbers lower than this, as in the saying of the poet:
"Three and two, so they are five, and a sixth inclining toward my arrows."

Likewise the saying of another:
"Three by count, and that is enough for me, and six when the night prayer overtakes me.
So that is nine in the day, and quenching is sufficient; but drinking beyond quenching is a sickness."

Its saying: ﴿كاملة﴾ ("complete") is another emphasis after the summary (al-fadhlaka), to add to the stress on fasting them and that nothing be reduced from their number.

Its saying: ﴿ذلك لمن لم يكن أهله حاضري المسجد الحرام﴾ ("That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque"). It is said that the reference of "that" (dhalika) is to tamattu' (performing 'umrah and then hajj in the same season, combining the two). On this view, there is no tamattu' for the residents of the Sacred Mosque, as Abu Hanifa and his companions say. They said: whoever among them does tamattu' must offer a dam, a penalty sacrifice (dam jinayah), of which he may not eat. It is also said that the reference is to the ruling, namely the obligation of the hady (sacrificial animal) and fasting, so that this is not obligatory for one who is among the residents of the Sacred Mosque, as al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him say.

What is meant by "whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque" is: one who does not reside in the Haram, or one who does not reside within the miqat (the boundary points for entering ihram) or closer to Mecca than them, on which there is a difference among the imams (p-128).

Its saying: ﴿واتقوا الله﴾ ("And fear Allah") means: regarding what He has obligated upon you in these rulings. It is also said that it is a general command to taqwa and a warning against the severity of Allah's punishment, glory be to Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid narrated from Ya'la ibn Umayya, who said: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was at al-Ji'ranah, wearing a robe and with traces of khaluq (a yellowish perfume) on him, and he said: 'How do you command me, O Messenger of Allah, to act in my 'umrah?' So Allah revealed: ﴿And complete the hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Where is the one who asked about 'umrah?' He said: 'Here I am.' He said: 'Take off the robe and wash off the traces of khaluq, then do in your 'umrah what you would do in your hajj.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated it from his hadith, but in them it says that the revelation came to him ﷺ after the question, and it does not mention what was revealed to him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Ali, regarding its saying: ﴿And complete the hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾, that he said: "It is that you enter ihram from the dwelling of your family (duwayrat ahlika)."

Ibn 'Adi and al-Bayhaqi narrated the like of it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Among its completion is that each of them be performed separately from the other, and that the 'umrah be performed outside the months of hajj."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The completion of hajj is on the day of nahr (sacrifice), when one throws the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and visits the House, then one has exited ihram. And the completion of 'umrah is when one circumambulates the House and performs sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then one has exited ihram."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the virtue of hajj and 'umrah, but this is not the place to mention them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding its saying: ﴿But if you are prevented (fa in uhsirtum)﴾, he said: "Whoever enters ihram for hajj or 'umrah and is then held back from the House by an illness that exhausts him, or by an enemy who restrains him, then upon him is the slaughter of what is easily obtainable of the hady, a sheep or more. If it was the obligatory hajj (hajjat al-Islam), then he must make it up (qada'). If it was after the obligatory hajj, then there is no qada' upon him."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding its saying: ﴿But if you are prevented﴾, he said: "A man who enters ihram for hajj and is then prevented sends what is easily obtainable of the hady. If he hastens before the hady reaches its place of sacrifice and shaves his head, or applies perfume, or treats himself with medicine, then upon him is a fidyah (compensation) of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice (nusuk). The fasting is three days, the charity is three sa' (measures) distributed among six needy persons, each needy person receiving half a sa', and the nusuk is a sheep."

﴿Then when you are secure (fa idha amintum)﴾, he said: "When he recovers and proceeds from that situation to the House, he exits ihram from his hajj by 'umrah, and the hajj becomes obligatory upon him in the following year. If he returns without completing the journey to the House from that situation, then upon him is a hajj and an 'umrah. If he returns performing tamattu' during the months of hajj, then upon him is what is easily obtainable of the hady, a sheep. If he does not find it, then fasting three days during hajj and seven when he returns."

Ibrahim said: "I mentioned this hadith to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and he said: 'Thus Ibn 'Abbas said in all of this hadith.'"

Malik, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'Ali regarding its saying: ﴿So what is easily obtainable of the hady﴾, that he said: "A sheep."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated the like of it from Ibn 'Abbas.

al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and al-Bayhaqi narrated ﴿So what is easily obtainable of the hady﴾ and he said: "A cow or a camel." It was said: "Would a sheep not suffice for him?" He said: "No."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said in the explanation of ﴿So what is easily obtainable﴾: "What he finds."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: "If he is wealthy, then from camels; otherwise from cattle; otherwise from sheep."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of al-Qasim from 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar that they did not consider what is easily obtainable of the hady to be anything but camels and cattle.

Ibn 'Abbas used to say: ﴿So what is easily obtainable of the hady﴾ is a sheep.

al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no ihsar (being prevented) except the ihsar of an enemy. As for one who is afflicted by an illness, pain, or getting lost, there is nothing upon him, for Allah only said: ﴿Then when you are secure﴾, and security is only from fear."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "There is no ihsar except from an enemy."

He also narrated the like of it from al-Zuhri.

He also narrated from 'Ata', who said: "There is no ihsar except from illness, an enemy, or a sudden matter."

He also narrated from 'Urwah, who said: "Everything that holds back the muhrim (one in ihram) is ihsar."

al-Bukhari narrated from al-Miswar that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slaughtered before he shaved, and he commanded his companions to do the same."

Abu Dawud in his al-Nasikh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding its saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice﴾, then he made an exception, saying: ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾, to the end of the verse.

al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, who said: "It was revealed concerning me, and it was meant for me: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an injury to his head﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾, that it means one whose illness is severe.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: "By illness is meant that he has an injury or sores on his head." ﴿Or has an injury to his head﴾: he said: "The injury is lice."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The nusuk mentioned in the verse is a sheep." It is also reported from 'Ali the like of it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding its saying: ﴿So whoever performs tamattu' with 'umrah until hajj﴾, that he said: "One who enters ihram for 'umrah during the months of hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated the like of it from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that al-Zubayr used to say: "Tamattu' is only for one who is prevented, and it is not for one whose path is left unobstructed."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is for one who is prevented and for one whose path is unobstructed."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ali regarding its saying: ﴿Then when you are secure, whoever performs tamattu' with 'umrah until hajj﴾, that he said: "If he delays the 'umrah until he combines it with hajj, then upon him is the hady."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding its saying: ﴿Then fasting three days﴾, that he said: "One day before al-Tarwiyah, the day of al-Tarwiyah, and the day of 'Arafah. If he misses them, he fasts them on the days of tashriq."

These, except Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, narrated from Ibn 'Umar the like of it, except that he said: "And if he misses them, he fasts the days of Mina, for they are part of hajj."

Ibn Jarir, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Umar the like of it, marfu'.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Alqamah, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr the like of it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The fasting for the mutamatti' is from the time of his ihram until the day of 'Arafah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse, who said: "If the mutamatti' with 'umrah does not find a hady, then upon him is fasting three days during hajj before the day of 'Arafah. If the day of 'Arafah is the third day, then his fasting is complete, and seven when he returns to his family."

al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'ishah: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever does not have a hady with him, let him fast three days before the day of nahr, and whoever has not fasted those three days, let him fast the days of tashriq.'"

He also narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded him, along with a group, to go around in Mina during the Farewell Hajj and proclaim: 'Indeed these are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah, so we do not fast during them except for fasting in lieu of a hady.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Ata' regarding the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, that he said: "Six villages: 'Arafah, 'Uranah, al-Raji', al-Nakhlatan, Marr al-Zahran, and Dajnan."

Mujahid said: "They are the people of the Haram."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They are the people of the Haram."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the like of it from Ibn 'Umar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 197–198 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ contains an ellipsis (ḥadhf). The estimated reading is: "The time of the Hajj is months," i.e., the time for performing the Hajj is months. It has also been said that the estimated reading is: "The Hajj is in months," and in this case the accusative (naṣb) would be required with the removal of the preposition, not the nominative (rafʿ).

Al-Farrāʾ said: "al-ashhur" is in the nominative, because its meaning is: "The time of the Hajj is well-known months." It has also been said that the estimate is: "The Hajj is the Hajj of well-known months."

There has been disagreement concerning the "well-known months." Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Rabīʿ, Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said: they are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and all of Dhū al-Ḥijja. This is also the view of Mālik.

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Shaʿbī and al-Nakhaʿī said: they are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijja. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and others.

It has also been narrated from Mālik.

The practical benefit of the disagreement appears in acts of the Hajj performed after the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr). Whoever says that all of Dhū al-Ḥijja is within the time does not impose the penalty for delay (damm al-taʾkhīr), and whoever says that only the ten days of it are (the time) says that the penalty for delay is required.

This verse has been used as evidence by those who say that it is not permissible to enter into ihram for the Hajj before the months of Hajj. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid, al-Awzāʿī, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Thawr. They said: whoever enters into ihram for the Hajj before them exits (ihram) with an ʿumra, and it does not suffice for him in place of the ihram of Hajj, like one who enters into prayer before its time, for it does not suffice for him.

Aḥmad and Abū Ḥanīfa said: it is only disliked (makrūh).

Something similar has been narrated from Mālik, but what is well known from him is the permissibility of entering into ihram for the Hajj throughout the whole year without disapproval.

Something similar has been narrated from Abū Ḥanīfa.

According to this view, one should consider the benefit of specifying the Hajj by the months mentioned in the verse.

It has been said that the explicit mention of them is for the increase of their merit.

The view permitting ihram throughout the entire year has been narrated from Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Thawrī and al-Layth ibn Saʿd. They argued with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times set for people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqara: 189], where He made all the crescents times for the Hajj and did not single out the three months. It is answered that this verse is general and that one is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Among what they argued with is analogy (qiyās) of Hajj upon ʿUmra: just as it is permissible to enter into ihram for ʿUmra throughout the whole year, so too it is permissible for Hajj. It is not hidden that this analogy contradicts the Qur'anic text, so it is invalid. The truth is what the earlier scholars held, if the months mentioned in His saying ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ are specifically the three mentioned, by explicit text or consensus. If it is not so, then "ashhur" is the plural of "shahr," and it is among the plurals of paucity (jumūʿ al-qilla), which ranges from three to ten, and the three is the certain minimum, so one must stop at it. The meaning of His saying ﴿well-known﴾ is that Hajj occurs once in the year in well-known months of its months, unlike ʿUmra. Or the meaning is: well-known through the explanation of the Prophet (ﷺ). Or: well-known to the addressees, so that it is not permissible to precede them or to delay beyond them.

His saying: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj therein﴾. The original meaning of "fard" in the language is cutting and severing, and from it comes "furḍat al-qaws" (the notch of the bow), and of the river and the mountain. So the obligation of Hajj is binding upon the free adult servant as the notch is binding upon the bow. It has also been said: the meaning of "faraḍa" is "abāna" (to separate), which also returns to cutting, because whoever cuts something has separated it from other things.

The meaning in the verse: whoever binds himself to Hajj therein by beginning it with intention, a hidden resolve, and by entering into ihram, an outward act, and by talbiya, an audible utterance.

Abū Ḥanīfa said: his binding himself is by talbiya or by garlanding the offering (hady) and driving it.

al-Shāfiʿī said: intention suffices for entering into ihram for Hajj.

Regarding al-rafath: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jarīr, al-Suddī, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, al-Zuhrī, Mujāhid and Mālik said: it is sexual intercourse.

Ibn ʿUmar, Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ and others said: al-rafath is obscene speech.

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-rafath is idle talk (lighāʾ) of speech, and he recited:
"And many a flock of pilgrims restrained from idle talk and the speech of rafath"
It is said: rafatha yarfuthu, with the fāʾ vowelled with kasra or ḍamma.

Al-fusūq: departing from the limits of the Sharīʿa. It has been said: it is sacrificing to idols; it has been said: mutual insulting by nicknames; it has been said: cursing.

Apparently it is not restricted to one specific sin; whoever restricted it to what was mentioned did so on the basis that this particular instance has been called "fusūq." As the Exalted said regarding sacrificing to idols: ﴿or a transgression (fisq) over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾. And He said regarding mutual insulting: ﴿Wretched is the name of fusūq﴾.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding cursing: "Cursing a Muslim is fusūq."

It is not hidden from one who knows that applying the name "fusūq" to one instance of sins does not necessitate restricting it to that.

Al-jidāl is derived from "jadal," which is killing, and what is meant here is disputation (mirāʾ). It has been said: cursing; it has been said: boasting about ancestors. The apparent is the first.

These three have been read with the accusative and nominative, the first two in the nominative and the third in the accusative, and the reverse. The meaning of negation for these matters is prohibition of them.

His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, God knows it﴾ is an exhortation to good after mention of evil, and to obedience after mention of disobedience. It also implies that everything they do of that sort is known to God, and nothing of it escapes Him.

His saying: ﴿And take provision﴾ contains a command to acquire provision, because some Arabs used to say: "How can we perform Hajj to the House of our Lord and He does not feed us?" So they would perform Hajj without provision, saying: "We rely upon God, the Exalted." It has also been said: the meaning is: take provision for your return of righteous deeds. ﴿For the best provision is taqwā﴾. The first is more preponderant, as the occasion of revelation of the verse indicates, and it will come.

His saying: ﴿For the best provision is taqwā﴾ is a statement that the best provision is guarding against what is forbidden. It is as if He said: fear God in carrying out what He commanded you regarding going out with provision, for the best provision is taqwā. It has been said: the meaning is: the best provision is that with which the traveler guards himself from perdition and from need of asking and begging.

His saying: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ specifies the people of understanding with address after exhorting all servants to taqwā, because the possessors of understanding are those who accept the commands of God and rise to fulfill them, and the kernel (lubb) of everything is its pure essence.

His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ grants a concession to whoever performs Hajj to engage in trade and similar activities by which some provision is obtained, and this is what is meant by "faḍl" here. From it is His saying: ﴿So disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 10]. That is, there is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord while traveling to fulfill what He has obligated upon you of Hajj.

His saying: ﴿So when you pour forth (afaḍtum)﴾ means you pushed forward (daffaʿtum). It is said: "fāḍa al-ināʾ" when the vessel is filled with water until it pours out from its sides; and "rajul fayyāḍ" means one whose hands pour forth with giving. Its meaning is: you poured yourselves forth, so the object is omitted, as it is omitted in their saying "daffaʿū min mawḍiʿ kadhā" (they pushed forward from such a place).

ʿArafāt: the name of that tract, i.e., the place of standing. The majority read it with tanwīn, and the tanwīn here is not for distinguishing what is diptote from what is triptote; rather it is like the nūn in "muslimīn."

al-Naḥḥās said: this is the good (reading).

Sībawayh related from the Arabs the omission of tanwīn from ʿArafāt, and said: when they made it a definite proper name, they omitted the tanwīn.

al-Akhfash and the Kufans related the vocalization of the tāʾ with fatḥa, likening it to the tāʾ of Fāṭima, and they recited:
"I looked upon them from Adhruʿāt, and its people in Yathrib, the nearest of its dwellings, a high sight."

In al-Kashshāf it is said: If you ask, why is it not prohibited from tanwīn, while it has two causes, definiteness and feminine form? I say: the feminine form is either by the tāʾ in its wording, or by an assumed tāʾ as in Suʿād. The tāʾ in its wording is not for femininity; rather it, together with the alif before it, is the sign of the feminine plural. It is not valid to assume a tāʾ in it, because this tāʾ, being specific to the feminine plural, prevents its assumption, just as the tāʾ of femininity is not assumed in bint, since the tāʾ which replaces a wāw is specific to the feminine like the tāʾ of femininity, so it refuses to be assumed. End of quote. It was named ʿArafāt because people recognize one another there (yataʿārafūn). It has been said: Adam and Eve met there and recognized one another. It has been said other than that.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the apparent is that it is a coined proper name like the names of other places. He used the verse as evidence for the obligation of standing at ʿArafa, because pouring forth does not occur except after it. The meaning of mention of God at al-mashʿar al-ḥarām is supplication to Him, including talbiya and takbīr. The mashʿar was named from "shiʿār," which is a sign, and supplication there is among the rites of Hajj. It is described as "ḥarām" because of its sanctity. It has been said: the meaning of the mention is the maghrib and ʿishāʾ prayers at Muzdalifa combined.

The people of knowledge have agreed that the sunna is for the pilgrim to combine the two there.

al-Mashʿar is the mountain of Quzaḥ on which the imam stands. It has been said: it is what lies between the two mountains of Muzdalifa, from the narrow passages of ʿArafa to the valley of Muḥassir.

His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾. The kāf is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, and mā is either a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle or a restrictive (kāffa) one, i.e., remember Him with a good remembrance, as He guided you with a good guidance. He repeated the command to remember for emphasis. It has been said: the first is a command to remember at al-mashʿar al-ḥarām, and the second is a command to remember in accordance with sincerity. It has been said: the second is meant to enumerate the blessing upon them. The "in" in His saying ﴿And indeed you were before it﴾ is light (mukhaffafa), as the entry of the lām into the predicate indicates. It has been said: it means "qad" (indeed), i.e., indeed you were. The pronoun in His saying ﴿before it﴾ refers to the guidance; it has been said: to the Qur'an.

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Umāma who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾: "Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and Dhū al-Ḥijja."

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ also narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, raised (marfūʿ), the like of it.

al-Khaṭīb narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, raised, the like of it too.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, as a statement of his own (mawqūf), the like of it.

al-Shāfiʿī in al-Umm, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, as a statement of his own, the like of it.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk the like of it.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, through several routes, narrated from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ that he said: Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijja.

They (the compilers) narrated, except al-Ḥākim, from Ibn Masʿūd the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās through several routes the like of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr the like of it too.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from al-Ḥasan, Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His saying: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj therein﴾ that he said: whoever enters into ihram therein with Hajj.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn Masʿūd who said: the fard is the ihram.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr who said: it is the ihlāl.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from him (Ibn al-Zubayr) who said: the fard of Hajj is the ihram.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: the fard is the ihlāl.

Something similar to this has been narrated from a group of the Successors (tābiʿūn).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 197–198 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is not proper for anyone to enter the state of ihram for Hajj except during the months of Hajj, because of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him something similar.

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "It is not proper for anyone to enter the state of ihram for Hajj except during the months of Hajj."

al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, nor disobedience, nor quarrelling during the Hajj﴾: 'Obscenity (rafath) is making advances to women with intercourse in mind; disobedience (fusuq) is all acts of sin; and quarrelling (jidal) is a man's quarrelling with his companion.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Isbahani in al-Targhib narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'Rafath' means intercourse; 'fusuq' means sins and lying."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: "Rafath is intercourse, fusuq is sins, and jidal is disputation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something similar from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "Rafath is approaching women, fusuq is abusive speech, and jidal is disputation."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him something similar.

Something similar to what has preceded has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un) in various wordings.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, saying: 'We rely upon Allah (mutawakkilun).' Then they would arrive and ask people for provisions. So Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: "Some people would leave their families without any provisions, saying: 'We perform the Hajj to the House of Allah; will He not feed us?' So the verse was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "When they entered the state of ihram while carrying their provisions, they would throw them away and take other provisions. So Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is taqwa﴾, and they were forbidden from that and were commanded to take ka'k (biscuit), flour and sawiq (roasted grain meal)."

al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The people used to rely upon one another for provisions, so Allah commanded them to take provisions."

Something similar to what has been narrated from the Companions has also been related from a group of the Successors.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They used to avoid buying, selling and trade during the season and the Hajj, saying: 'These are days of the remembrance of Allah.' So there was revealed ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ to the end of the verse."

Something similar has been narrated from him by al-Bukhari and others.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: "I said to Ibn Umar: 'We are people who hire out animals; is there a Hajj for us?' He said: 'Do you not circumambulate the House, go between al-Safa and al-Marwah, come to al-Mu'arraf, throw the pebbles at the jamarat, and shave your heads?' I said: 'Yes.' Ibn Umar said: 'A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about what you have asked me about, and he did not answer him until Jibril descended to him with this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) called him, recited the verse to him and said: "And you are pilgrims."'"

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ during the seasons of Hajj.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr that he recited it as Ibn Abbas did.

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif narrated that Ibn Mas'ud recited it in that manner.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "It was named 'Arafat because Jibril used to say to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he saw the rites: 'You have recognised (‘arafta).'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Ibn Umar.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ali.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Umar that he was asked about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he remained silent until, when the riding animals' feet descended at Muzdalifah, he said: "This is al-Mash'ar al-Haram."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from him that he said: "Al-Mash'ar al-Haram is all of Muzdalifah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from him that he said: "It is the mountain and what surrounds it."

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "Between the two mountains of Jam' is al-Mash'ar."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr concerning His words ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, that he said: "This is not general; this is for the people of the locality who used to depart from Jam' while the rest of the people departed from 'Arafat. Allah refused that for them, and revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199]."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Sufyan concerning His words ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾ that he said: "Before the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾ that he said: "Among the ignorant."

His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ contains an ellipsis (ḥadhf). The estimated reading is: "The time of the Hajj is months," i.e., the time for performing the Hajj is months. It has also been said that the estimated reading is: "The Hajj is in months," and in this case the accusative (naṣb) would be required with the removal of the preposition, not the nominative (rafʿ).

Al-Farrāʾ said: "al-ashhur" is in the nominative, because its meaning is: "The time of the Hajj is well-known months." It has also been said that the estimate is: "The Hajj is the Hajj of well-known months."

There has been disagreement concerning the "well-known months." Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Rabīʿ, Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said: they are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and all of Dhū al-Ḥijja. This is also the view of Mālik.

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Shaʿbī and al-Nakhaʿī said: they are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijja. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and others.

It has also been narrated from Mālik.
