Whoever says that all of Dhū al-Ḥijja is within the time does not impose the penalty for delay (damm al-taʾkhīr), and whoever says that only the ten days of it are (the time) says that the penalty for delay is required.

This verse has been used as evidence by those who say that it is not permissible to enter into ihram for the Hajj before the months of Hajj. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid, al-Awzāʿī, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Thawr. They said: whoever enters into ihram for the Hajj before them exits (ihram) with an ʿumra, and it does not suffice for him in place of the ihram of Hajj, like one who enters into prayer before its time, for it does not suffice for him.

Aḥmad and Abū Ḥanīfa said: it is only disliked (makrūh).

Something similar has been narrated from Mālik, but what is well known from him is the permissibility of entering into ihram for the Hajj throughout the whole year without disapproval.

Something similar has been narrated from Abū Ḥanīfa.

According to this view, one should consider the benefit of specifying the Hajj by the months mentioned in the verse.

It has been said that the explicit mention of them is for the increase of their merit.

The view permitting ihram throughout the entire year has been narrated from Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Thawrī and al-Layth ibn Saʿd. They argued with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times set for people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqara: 189], where He made all the crescents times for the Hajj and did not single out the three months. It is answered that this verse is general and that one is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Among what they argued with is analogy (qiyās) of Hajj upon ʿUmra: just as it is permissible to enter into ihram for ʿUmra throughout the whole year, so too it is permissible for Hajj. It is not hidden that this analogy contradicts the Qur'anic text, so it is invalid. The truth is what the earlier scholars held, if the months mentioned in His saying ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ are specifically the three mentioned, by explicit text or consensus. If it is not so, then "ashhur" is the plural of "shahr," and it is among the plurals of paucity (jumūʿ al-qilla), which ranges from three to ten, and the three is the certain minimum, so one must stop at it. The meaning of His saying ﴿well-known﴾ is that Hajj occurs once in the year in well-known months of its months, unlike ʿUmra. Or the meaning is: well-known through the explanation of the Prophet (ﷺ). Or: well-known to the addressees, so that it is not permissible to precede them or to delay beyond them.

His saying: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj therein﴾. The original meaning of "fard" in the language is cutting and severing, and from it comes "furḍat al-qaws" (the notch of the bow), and of the river and the mountain. So the obligation of Hajj is binding upon the free adult servant as the notch is binding upon the bow. It has also been said: the meaning of "faraḍa" is "abāna" (to separate), which also returns to cutting, because whoever cuts something has separated it from other things.

The meaning in the verse: whoever binds himself to Hajj therein by beginning it with intention, a hidden resolve, and by entering into ihram, an outward act, and by talbiya, an audible utterance.

Abū Ḥanīfa said: his binding himself is by talbiya or by garlanding the offering (hady) and driving it.

al-Shāfiʿī said: intention suffices for entering into ihram for Hajj.

Regarding al-rafath: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jarīr, al-Suddī, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, al-Zuhrī, Mujāhid and Mālik said: it is sexual intercourse.

Ibn ʿUmar, Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ and others said: al-rafath is obscene speech.

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-rafath is idle talk (lighāʾ) of speech, and he recited:
"And many a flock of pilgrims restrained from idle talk and the speech of rafath"
It is said: rafatha yarfuthu, with the fāʾ vowelled with kasra or ḍamma.

Al-fusūq: departing from the limits of the Sharīʿa. It has been said: it is sacrificing to idols; it has been said: mutual insulting by nicknames; it has been said: cursing.

Apparently it is not restricted to one specific sin; whoever restricted it to what was mentioned did so on the basis that this particular instance has been called "fusūq." As the Exalted said regarding sacrificing to idols: ﴿or a transgression (fisq) over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾. And He said regarding mutual insulting: ﴿Wretched is the name of fusūq﴾.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding cursing: "Cursing a Muslim is fusūq."

It is not hidden from one who knows that applying the name "fusūq" to one instance of sins does not necessitate restricting it to that.

Al-jidāl is derived from "jadal," which is killing, and what is meant here is disputation (mirāʾ). It has been said: cursing; it has been said: boasting about ancestors. The apparent is the first.

These three have been read with the accusative and nominative, the first two in the nominative and the third in the accusative, and the reverse. The meaning of negation for these matters is prohibition of them.

His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, God knows it﴾ is an exhortation to good after mention of evil, and to obedience after mention of disobedience. It also implies that everything they do of that sort is known to God, and nothing of it escapes Him.

His saying: ﴿And take provision﴾ contains a command to acquire provision, because some Arabs used to say: "How can we perform Hajj to the House of our Lord and He does not feed us?" So they would perform Hajj without provision, saying: "We rely upon God, the Exalted." It has also been said: the meaning is: take provision for your return of righteous deeds. ﴿For the best provision is taqwā﴾. The first is more preponderant, as the occasion of revelation of the verse indicates, and it will come.

His saying: ﴿For the best provision is taqwā﴾ is a statement that the best provision is guarding against what is forbidden. It is as if He said: fear God in carrying out what He commanded you regarding going out with provision, for the best provision is taqwā. It has been said: the meaning is: the best provision is that with which the traveler guards himself from perdition and from need of asking and begging.

His saying: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ specifies the people of understanding with address after exhorting all servants to taqwā, because the possessors of understanding are those who accept the commands of God and rise to fulfill them, and the kernel (lubb) of everything is its pure essence.

His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ grants a concession to whoever performs Hajj to engage in trade and similar activities by which some provision is obtained, and this is what is meant by "faḍl" here. From it is His saying: ﴿So disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 10]. That is, there is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord while traveling to fulfill what He has obligated upon you of Hajj.

His saying: ﴿So when you pour forth (afaḍtum)﴾ means you pushed forward (daffaʿtum). It is said: "fāḍa al-ināʾ" when the vessel is filled with water until it pours out from its sides; and "rajul fayyāḍ" means one whose hands pour forth with giving. Its meaning is: you poured yourselves forth, so the object is omitted, as it is omitted in their saying "daffaʿū min mawḍiʿ kadhā" (they pushed forward from such a place).

ʿArafāt: the name of that tract, i.e., the place of standing. The majority read it with tanwīn, and the tanwīn here is not for distinguishing what is diptote from what is triptote; rather it is like the nūn in "muslimīn."

al-Naḥḥās said: this is the good (reading).

Sībawayh related from the Arabs the omission of tanwīn from ʿArafāt, and said: when they made it a definite proper name, they omitted the tanwīn.

al-Akhfash and the Kufans related the vocalization of the tāʾ with fatḥa, likening it to the tāʾ of Fāṭima, and they recited:
"I looked upon them from Adhruʿāt, and its people in Yathrib, the nearest of its dwellings, a high sight."

In al-Kashshāf it is said: If you ask, why is it not prohibited from tanwīn, while it has two causes, definiteness and feminine form? I say: the feminine form is either by the tāʾ in its wording, or by an assumed tāʾ as in Suʿād. The tāʾ in its wording is not for femininity; rather it, together with the alif before it, is the sign of the feminine plural. It is not valid to assume a tāʾ in it, because this tāʾ, being specific to the feminine plural, prevents its assumption, just as the tāʾ of femininity is not assumed in bint, since the tāʾ which replaces a wāw is specific to the feminine like the tāʾ of femininity, so it refuses to be assumed. End of quote. It was named ʿArafāt because people recognize one another there (yataʿārafūn). It has been said: Adam and Eve met there and recognized one another. It has been said other than that.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the apparent is that it is a coined proper name like the names of other places. He used the verse as evidence for the obligation of standing at ʿArafa, because pouring forth does not occur except after it. The meaning of mention of God at al-mashʿar al-ḥarām is supplication to Him, including talbiya and takbīr. The mashʿar was named from "shiʿār," which is a sign, and supplication there is among the rites of Hajj. It is described as "ḥarām" because of its sanctity. It has been said: the meaning of the mention is the maghrib and ʿishāʾ prayers at Muzdalifa combined.

The people of knowledge have agreed that the sunna is for the pilgrim to combine the two there.

al-Mashʿar is the mountain of Quzaḥ on which the imam stands. It has been said: it is what lies between the two mountains of Muzdalifa, from the narrow passages of ʿArafa to the valley of Muḥassir.

His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾. The kāf is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, and mā is either a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle or a restrictive (kāffa) one, i.e., remember Him with a good remembrance, as He guided you with a good guidance. He repeated the command to remember for emphasis. It has been said: the first is a command to remember at al-mashʿar al-ḥarām, and the second is a command to remember in accordance with sincerity. It has been said: the second is meant to enumerate the blessing upon them. The "in" in His saying ﴿And indeed you were before it﴾ is light (mukhaffafa), as the entry of the lām into the predicate indicates. It has been said: it means "qad" (indeed), i.e., indeed you were. The pronoun in His saying ﴿before it﴾ refers to the guidance; it has been said: to the Qur'an.

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Umāma who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾: "Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and Dhū al-Ḥijja."

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ also narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, raised (marfūʿ), the like of it.

al-Khaṭīb narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, raised, the like of it too.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, as a statement of his own (mawqūf), the like of it.

al-Shāfiʿī in al-Umm, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, as a statement of his own, the like of it.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk the like of it.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, through several routes, narrated from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ that he said: Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda and ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijja.

They (the compilers) narrated, except al-Ḥākim, from Ibn Masʿūd the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās through several routes the like of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr the like of it too.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from al-Ḥasan, Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His saying: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj therein﴾ that he said: whoever enters into ihram therein with Hajj.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn Masʿūd who said: the fard is the ihram.

Ibn Abī Shayba narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr who said: it is the ihlāl.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Bayhaqī narrated from him (Ibn al-Zubayr) who said: the fard of Hajj is the ihram.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: the fard is the ihlāl.

Something similar to this has been narrated from a group of the Successors (tābiʿūn).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 197–198 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is not proper for anyone to enter the state of ihram for Hajj except during the months of Hajj, because of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him something similar.

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "It is not proper for anyone to enter the state of ihram for Hajj except during the months of Hajj."

al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, nor disobedience, nor quarrelling during the Hajj﴾: 'Obscenity (rafath) is making advances to women with intercourse in mind; disobedience (fusuq) is all acts of sin; and quarrelling (jidal) is a man's quarrelling with his companion.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Isbahani in al-Targhib narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'Rafath' means intercourse; 'fusuq' means sins and lying."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: "Rafath is intercourse, fusuq is sins, and jidal is disputation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something similar from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "Rafath is approaching women, fusuq is abusive speech, and jidal is disputation."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him something similar.

Something similar to what has preceded has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un) in various wordings.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, saying: 'We rely upon Allah (mutawakkilun).' Then they would arrive and ask people for provisions. So Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, who said: "Some people would leave their families without any provisions, saying: 'We perform the Hajj to the House of Allah; will He not feed us?' So the verse was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "When they entered the state of ihram while carrying their provisions, they would throw them away and take other provisions. So Allah revealed: ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is taqwa﴾, and they were forbidden from that and were commanded to take ka'k (biscuit), flour and sawiq (roasted grain meal)."

al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The people used to rely upon one another for provisions, so Allah commanded them to take provisions."

Something similar to what has been narrated from the Companions has also been related from a group of the Successors.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They used to avoid buying, selling and trade during the season and the Hajj, saying: 'These are days of the remembrance of Allah.' So there was revealed ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ to the end of the verse."

Something similar has been narrated from him by al-Bukhari and others.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: "I said to Ibn Umar: 'We are people who hire out animals; is there a Hajj for us?' He said: 'Do you not circumambulate the House, go between al-Safa and al-Marwah, come to al-Mu'arraf, throw the pebbles at the jamarat, and shave your heads?' I said: 'Yes.' Ibn Umar said: 'A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about what you have asked me about, and he did not answer him until Jibril descended to him with this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) called him, recited the verse to him and said: "And you are pilgrims."'"

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite ﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord﴾ during the seasons of Hajj.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr that he recited it as Ibn Abbas did.

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif narrated that Ibn Mas'ud recited it in that manner.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "It was named 'Arafat because Jibril used to say to Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he saw the rites: 'You have recognised (‘arafta).'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar from Ibn Umar.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ali.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Umar that he was asked about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he remained silent until, when the riding animals' feet descended at Muzdalifah, he said: "This is al-Mash'ar al-Haram."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from him that he said: "Al-Mash'ar al-Haram is all of Muzdalifah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from him that he said: "It is the mountain and what surrounds it."

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "Between the two mountains of Jam' is al-Mash'ar."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr concerning His words ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, that he said: "This is not general; this is for the people of the locality who used to depart from Jam' while the rest of the people departed from 'Arafat. Allah refused that for them, and revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199]."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Sufyan concerning His words ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾ that he said: "Before the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾ that he said: "Among the ignorant."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 132] It has been said: the address in His words ﴿Then depart [from where] the people depart﴾ is to the Hums (al-Hums, the group of Quraysh and those who followed their religion who considered themselves people of the sacred precinct) of Quraysh, because they did not stand at Arafat with the people. Rather, they would stand at Muzdalifah, which is within the Haram, so they were commanded to do this. On this view, "thumma" (then) is used to conjoin one clause to another, not to indicate sequence.

It has also been said that the address is to the whole Ummah, and that by "the people" is meant Ibrahim. That is, "Then depart from where Ibrahim departed." This allows that it is a command to them to depart from Arafat, or that it refers to another departure, which is the one from Muzdalifah. On this view, "thumma" retains its original meaning of sequence.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this last possibility. They were commanded to seek forgiveness because they were in places where mercy descends, in locations of acceptance, and in places where supplications are likely to be answered. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness for what contravened the Sunnah of Ibrahim, namely your standing at Muzdalifah rather than at Arafat.

By "the rites" (al-manasik) is meant the acts of Hajj. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take your rites from me" (khudhu 'anni manasikakum). That is: when you have finished the acts of Hajj, remember Allah. It has also been said that by "the rites" is meant the sacrificial slaughter. As for His saying ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, it is because the Arabs, when they finished their Hajj, would stand at the Jamrah and mention the glories of their fathers and the virtues of their ancestors. So Allah commanded them to remember Him in place of that remembrance, and to make it a remembrance like their remembrance of their fathers, or greater than their remembrance of their fathers.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿or greater﴾ are in the genitive position, coordinated with "dhikrikum" (your remembrance). The meaning is: "or as one greater in remembrance." It may also be in the accusative position: that is, "remember Him with a greater remembrance."

In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is coordinated with what the remembrance is attributed to in His words ﴿as your remembrance﴾, as you would say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance."

His words ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾ and so on: when Allah guided His servants to His remembrance, and supplication being a type of remembrance, He made the one who supplicates divided into two categories. One seeks the share of this world and does not turn to the share of the Hereafter. The other category seeks both together. The object of the verb, that is His words ﴿give us﴾, is omitted, meaning: "what we desire or what we seek." The waw in His words ﴿and he has not﴾ is the waw of circumstance, and the clause after it is in a circumstantial position.

Al-Khalaq means the portion. That is: this supplicant has no portion in the Hereafter, because his concern is confined to this world; he does not desire anything else and seeks nothing other than it.

In this report is the meaning of a prohibition against limiting oneself to seeking this world, and a censure of the one who makes it the ultimate goal of his desire and the greatest of his aims.

The two good things mentioned in the verse have been interpreted differently. It has been said that they are what the righteous seek in this world, such as well-being and the sustenance they need, and what they seek in the Hereafter, such as the bliss of Paradise and Allah's good pleasure. It has been said that the good of this world is a beautiful wife and the good of the Hereafter is the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). It has been said that the good of this world is knowledge and worship, and other views have been stated.

Al-Qurtubi said: What most scholars hold is that the two good things mean the bliss of this world and of the Hereafter.

He said: This is the correct view, for the wording implies all of this, since ﴿good﴾ is indefinite in the context of supplication, so it encompasses every good thing by way of substitution. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise, by consensus (ijma'). End of quote.

His words ﴿and protect us﴾: its original form is "awqina", the waw was deleted as it was deleted in "yaqi", because it lies between a ya' and a kasrah, like "ya'idu". This is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra).

The Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa) said: it was deleted to distinguish between the intransitive and the transitive verb.

His words ﴿Those﴾ refer to the second group. ﴿For them is a portion of﴾ what they earned of deeds, that is, of their reward. Among their deeds is supplication. So whatever good Allah gives them because of it is among what they earned. It has been said that the meaning of His words ﴿of what they earned﴾ is causal, that is, "because of what they earned," but this is far-fetched. It has also been said that His words ﴿those﴾ refer to both groups together. That is: the first have a portion of this world and no portion for them in the Hereafter; the latter have a portion of what they earned in this world and in the Hereafter.

"Sari'" (swift) is from "sara'a yasru'u," like " 'azuma ya'zumu," with the verbal noun "saraʿan" and "surʿatan." "Al-hisab" (the reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muhasabah." Its original meaning is counting. It is said: "hasaba yahsubu hisaban, wa hisabatan, wa husbanan, wa hasban."

Here "al-hisab" means "the thing reckoned," and it is named "reckoning" by calling the object by the verbal noun. The meaning is: His reckoning of His servants on the Day of Resurrection will come swiftly, so hasten to it with deeds of goodness. Or, He described Himself with swiftness in reckoning the creatures despite their great number, and that no matter distracts Him from another, so He reckons them in a single moment, as He said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28].

His words ﴿in numbered days﴾: Al-Qurtubi said: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the numbered days in this verse are the days of Mina, which are the days of Tashriq, and they are the days of stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar).

Al-Tha'labi said: Ibrahim said: "The numbered days are the days of the ten, and the known days are the days of sacrifice." This is also reported from Makki and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Qurtubi said: This cannot be sound, given the consensus (ijma') that he transmitted, as did Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others.

Al-Tahawi transmitted from Abu Yusuf that "the known days" are the days of sacrifice. He said: this is based on His words: ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided them of the cattle of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. Al-Karkhi transmitted from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that the known days are the three days of sacrifice: the day of Eid al-Adha and two days after it.

Ilkiya al-Tabari said: According to the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, there is no difference between "the known days" and "the numbered days," because the numbered days mentioned in the Qur'an are, without disagreement, the days of Tashriq.

It is transmitted from Malik that the numbered days and the known days together comprise four days: the day of sacrifice and three days after it. So the day of sacrifice is known but not numbered, the two days after it are known and numbered, and the fourth day is numbered but not known. This is also transmitted from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Zayd said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the days of Tashriq.

The one addressed by this address mentioned in the verse, that is, His words ﴿and remember Allah in numbered days﴾, is the pilgrim and others, as the majority hold. It has been said that it is specific to the pilgrim.

Scholars have differed about its time. It has been said: from the dawn prayer on the day of Arafat until the afternoon prayer on the last day of Tashriq. It has been said: from the morning of Arafat until the afternoon prayer of the last day of the sacrifice, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. It has been said: from the noon prayer on the day of sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last day of Tashriq, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i.

His words ﴿Whoever hastens﴾ and so on: the two days are the second day of sacrifice and its third day.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i said: whoever stones [the pillars] on the second of the numbered days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays until the third, there is no sin upon him. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It expressed this by this division for emphasis and affirmation, because among the Arabs some censured hastening and some censured delaying, so the verse came removing blame in both cases.

'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever hastens, he is forgiven, and whoever delays, he is forgiven. The verse indicates that both hastening and delaying are permissible.

His words ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾ mean that the option and the lifting of sin are established for the one who fears Allah, because the possessor of piety guards against everything that causes doubt, so he is most deserving of being singled out for this ruling.

Al-Akhfash said: the implied meaning is "that is for whoever fears Allah." It has been said: for whoever fears Allah after his departure from Hajj, against all sins. It has been said: for whoever fears killing game. It has been said: its meaning is safety for whoever fears Allah. It has been said: it is connected to the remembrance: that is, the remembrance is for whoever fears Allah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from 'A'ishah, who said: "Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called the Hums, while the rest of the Arabs stood at Arafat. When Islam came, Allah commanded His Prophet to come to Arafat, stand there, and then depart from it. This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted from her, as a statement from her own words (mawquf), something similar.

Reports with this meaning have come from the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "When it is the day of Arafat, Allah descends to the lowest heaven with the angels, and says to them: 'My servants have believed in My promise and affirmed My messengers; what is their reward?' It is said: 'That You forgive them.' This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾."

Many hadiths have been reported about the forgiveness of the people of Arafat, the descent of mercy upon them, and the answering of their supplications.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "your Hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "the shedding of blood (sacrifice)." ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, he said: "the boasting of the Arabs among themselves with the deeds of their fathers on the day of sacrifice when they finish, so they were commanded to remember Allah in place of that."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The polytheists used to sit during the Hajj and mention the days of their fathers and what they counted of their lineages, all day long. So Allah sent down to His Messenger: ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a greater remembrance﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir also transmitted something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾ that he said: "As children remember their fathers."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it was said to him regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾: "Indeed a man may pass a day and not mention his father." He said: "That is not the point, rather it means: be angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than you are angry when your father is spoken ill of."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Some of the Bedouins used to come to the standing place and say: 'O Allah, make this a year of rain, a year of abundance, and a year of good birth,' and they mentioned nothing of the matter of the Hereafter at all. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Among the people is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world, and he has no share in the Hereafter﴾. And there come after them others from the believers who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾."

Al-Tabarani transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when people stood at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), one of them would supplicate and say: 'O Allah, provide me with camels,' and another would say: 'O Allah, provide me with sheep.' So Allah sent down the verse."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas that they used to circumambulate the House naked, supplicating: "O Allah, give us rain, grant us victory over our enemy, and return us righteous to a righteous people." So the verse was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ that he said: "of what they did of good."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ that he said: "swift in counting."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali that he said: "The numbered days are three days: the day of Eid al-Adha and two days after it. Slaughter on whichever of them you wish, and the best of them is the first."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that they are the three days of Tashriq.

In another wording: "These three days after the day of sacrifice."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The known days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'lumat) are the days of the ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah), and the counted days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat, the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)."

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn al-Zubayr that, regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "They are the days of tashriq, in which Allah is remembered with tasbih (saying Subhan Allah), tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah), takbir (saying Allahu akbar) and tahmid (saying al-hamdu lillah)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The counted days are four days: the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the three days after it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to glorify Allah (make takbir) during those days at Mina and would say: "The takbir is obligatory," and he would interpret this verse, ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, as evidence.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to make takbir on the day of sacrifice and recite this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "The takbir is during the days of tashriq; one says after every prayer: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to make takbir three times after the prayers and would say: "La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir (There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent)."

Malik related from Yahya ibn Sa'id that it reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on the day after the day of sacrifice at Mina when the day had risen somewhat, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a second time on that same day after the sun had risen, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir, until their takbir reached the House (the Ka'bah). Then he went out a third time on that same day when the sun had passed its zenith, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to throw the pebbles (at the jamarat) and would make takbir with every pebble." 

Something similar has been related from the hadith of 'A'ishah in al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his hastening," and ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his delaying."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The departure (nafr) in two days is for the one who fears Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Whoever the sun sets upon on the day in which Allah said ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ while he is at Mina, let him not depart until he has thrown the pebbles on the next day."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears hunting while in the state of ihram."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say while he was standing at 'Arafat, when people from Makkah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the Hajj?' He said: 'The Hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever reaches Jam' (Muzdalifah) on the night before the dawn has reached (the Hajj). The days of Mina are three days. ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven. ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven.'"

Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj."

Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj, his past sins are forgiven."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "All his sin is removed, if he fears (Allah) in the remainder of his life."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 132] It has been said: the address in His words ﴿Then depart [from where] the people depart﴾ is to the Hums (al-Hums, the group of Quraysh and those who followed their religion who considered themselves people of the sacred precinct) of Quraysh, because they did not stand at Arafat with the people. Rather, they would stand at Muzdalifah, which is within the Haram, so they were commanded to do this. On this view, "thumma" (then) is used to conjoin one clause to another, not to indicate sequence.

It has also been said that the address is to the whole Ummah, and that by "the people" is meant Ibrahim. That is, "Then depart from where Ibrahim departed." This allows that it is a command to them to depart from Arafat, or that it refers to another departure, which is the one from Muzdalifah. On this view, "thumma" retains its original meaning of sequence.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this last possibility. They were commanded to seek forgiveness because they were in places where mercy descends, in locations of acceptance, and in places where supplications are likely to be answered. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness for what contravened the Sunnah of Ibrahim, namely your standing at Muzdalifah rather than at Arafat.

By "the rites" (al-manasik) is meant the acts of Hajj. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take your rites from me" (khudhu 'anni manasikakum). That is: when you have finished the acts of Hajj, remember Allah. It has also been said that by "the rites" is meant the sacrificial slaughter. As for His saying ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, it is because the Arabs, when they finished their Hajj, would stand at the Jamrah and mention the glories of their fathers and the virtues of their ancestors. So Allah commanded them to remember Him in place of that remembrance, and to make it a remembrance like their remembrance of their fathers, or greater than their remembrance of their fathers.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿or greater﴾ are in the genitive position, coordinated with "dhikrikum" (your remembrance). The meaning is: "or as one greater in remembrance." It may also be in the accusative position: that is, "remember Him with a greater remembrance."

In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is coordinated with what the remembrance is attributed to in His words ﴿as your remembrance﴾, as you would say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance."

His words ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾ and so on: when Allah guided His servants to His remembrance, and supplication being a type of remembrance, He made the one who supplicates divided into two categories. One seeks the share of this world and does not turn to the share of the Hereafter. The other category seeks both together. The object of the verb, that is His words ﴿give us﴾, is omitted, meaning: "what we desire or what we seek." The waw in His words ﴿and he has not﴾ is the waw of circumstance, and the clause after it is in a circumstantial position.

Al-Khalaq means the portion. That is: this supplicant has no portion in the Hereafter, because his concern is confined to this world; he does not desire anything else and seeks nothing other than it.

In this report is the meaning of a prohibition against limiting oneself to seeking this world, and a censure of the one who makes it the ultimate goal of his desire and the greatest of his aims.

The two good things mentioned in the verse have been interpreted differently. It has been said that they are what the righteous seek in this world, such as well-being and the sustenance they need, and what they seek in the Hereafter, such as the bliss of Paradise and Allah's good pleasure. It has been said that the good of this world is a beautiful wife and the good of the Hereafter is the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). It has been said that the good of this world is knowledge and worship, and other views have been stated.

Al-Qurtubi said: What most scholars hold is that the two good things mean the bliss of this world and of the Hereafter.

He said: This is the correct view, for the wording implies all of this, since ﴿good﴾ is indefinite in the context of supplication, so it encompasses every good thing by way of substitution. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise, by consensus (ijma'). End of quote.

His words ﴿and protect us﴾: its original form is "awqina", the waw was deleted as it was deleted in "yaqi", because it lies between a ya' and a kasrah, like "ya'idu". This is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra).

The Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa) said: it was deleted to distinguish between the intransitive and the transitive verb.

His words ﴿Those﴾ refer to the second group. ﴿For them is a portion of﴾ what they earned of deeds, that is, of their reward. Among their deeds is supplication. So whatever good Allah gives them because of it is among what they earned. It has been said that the meaning of His words ﴿of what they earned﴾ is causal, that is, "because of what they earned," but this is far-fetched. It has also been said that His words ﴿those﴾ refer to both groups together. That is: the first have a portion of this world and no portion for them in the Hereafter; the latter have a portion of what they earned in this world and in the Hereafter.

"Sari'" (swift) is from "sara'a yasru'u," like " 'azuma ya'zumu," with the verbal noun "saraʿan" and "surʿatan." "Al-hisab" (the reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muhasabah." Its original meaning is counting. It is said: "hasaba yahsubu hisaban, wa hisabatan, wa husbanan, wa hasban."

Here "al-hisab" means "the thing reckoned," and it is named "reckoning" by calling the object by the verbal noun. The meaning is: His reckoning of His servants on the Day of Resurrection will come swiftly, so hasten to it with deeds of goodness. Or, He described Himself with swiftness in reckoning the creatures despite their great number, and that no matter distracts Him from another, so He reckons them in a single moment, as He said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28].

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "The takbir is during the days of tashriq; one says after every prayer: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to make takbir three times after the prayers and would say: "La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir (There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent)."

Malik related from Yahya ibn Sa'id that it reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on the day after the day of sacrifice at Mina when the day had risen somewhat, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a second time on that same day after the sun had risen, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir, until their takbir reached the House (the Ka'bah). Then he went out a third time on that same day when the sun had passed its zenith, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to throw the pebbles (at the jamarat) and would make takbir with every pebble." 

Something similar has been related from the hadith of 'A'ishah in al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his hastening," and ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his delaying."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The departure (nafr) in two days is for the one who fears Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Whoever the sun sets upon on the day in which Allah said ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ while he is at Mina, let him not depart until he has thrown the pebbles on the next day."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears hunting while in the state of ihram."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say while he was standing at 'Arafat, when people from Makkah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the Hajj?' He said: 'The Hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever reaches Jam' (Muzdalifah) on the night before the dawn has reached (the Hajj). The days of Mina are three days. ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven. ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven.'"

Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj."

Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj, his past sins are forgiven."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "All his sin is removed, if he fears (Allah) in the remainder of his life."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 132] It has been said: the address in His words ﴿Then depart [from where] the people depart﴾ is to the Hums (al-Hums, the group of Quraysh and those who followed their religion who considered themselves people of the sacred precinct) of Quraysh, because they did not stand at Arafat with the people. Rather, they would stand at Muzdalifah, which is within the Haram, so they were commanded to do this. On this view, "thumma" (then) is used to conjoin one clause to another, not to indicate sequence.

It has also been said that the address is to the whole Ummah, and that by "the people" is meant Ibrahim. That is, "Then depart from where Ibrahim departed." This allows that it is a command to them to depart from Arafat, or that it refers to another departure, which is the one from Muzdalifah. On this view, "thumma" retains its original meaning of sequence.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this last possibility. They were commanded to seek forgiveness because they were in places where mercy descends, in locations of acceptance, and in places where supplications are likely to be answered. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness for what contravened the Sunnah of Ibrahim, namely your standing at Muzdalifah rather than at Arafat.

By "the rites" (al-manasik) is meant the acts of Hajj. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take your rites from me" (khudhu 'anni manasikakum). That is: when you have finished the acts of Hajj, remember Allah. It has also been said that by "the rites" is meant the sacrificial slaughter. As for His saying ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, it is because the Arabs, when they finished their Hajj, would stand at the Jamrah and mention the glories of their fathers and the virtues of their ancestors. So Allah commanded them to remember Him in place of that remembrance, and to make it a remembrance like their remembrance of their fathers, or greater than their remembrance of their fathers.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿or greater﴾ are in the genitive position, coordinated with "dhikrikum" (your remembrance). The meaning is: "or as one greater in remembrance." It may also be in the accusative position: that is, "remember Him with a greater remembrance."

In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is coordinated with what the remembrance is attributed to in His words ﴿as your remembrance﴾, as you would say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance."

His words ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾ and so on: when Allah guided His servants to His remembrance, and supplication being a type of remembrance, He made the one who supplicates divided into two categories. One seeks the share of this world and does not turn to the share of the Hereafter. The other category seeks both together. The object of the verb, that is His words ﴿give us﴾, is omitted, meaning: "what we desire or what we seek." The waw in His words ﴿and he has not﴾ is the waw of circumstance, and the clause after it is in a circumstantial position.

Al-Khalaq means the portion. That is: this supplicant has no portion in the Hereafter, because his concern is confined to this world; he does not desire anything else and seeks nothing other than it.

In this report is the meaning of a prohibition against limiting oneself to seeking this world, and a censure of the one who makes it the ultimate goal of his desire and the greatest of his aims.

The two good things mentioned in the verse have been interpreted differently. It has been said that they are what the righteous seek in this world, such as well-being and the sustenance they need, and what they seek in the Hereafter, such as the bliss of Paradise and Allah's good pleasure. It has been said that the good of this world is a beautiful wife and the good of the Hereafter is the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). It has been said that the good of this world is knowledge and worship, and other views have been stated.

Al-Qurtubi said: What most scholars hold is that the two good things mean the bliss of this world and of the Hereafter.

He said: This is the correct view, for the wording implies all of this, since ﴿good﴾ is indefinite in the context of supplication, so it encompasses every good thing by way of substitution. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise, by consensus (ijma'). End of quote.

His words ﴿and protect us﴾: its original form is "awqina", the waw was deleted as it was deleted in "yaqi", because it lies between a ya' and a kasrah, like "ya'idu". This is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra).

The Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa) said: it was deleted to distinguish between the intransitive and the transitive verb.

His words ﴿Those﴾ refer to the second group. ﴿For them is a portion of﴾ what they earned of deeds, that is, of their reward. Among their deeds is supplication. So whatever good Allah gives them because of it is among what they earned. It has been said that the meaning of His words ﴿of what they earned﴾ is causal, that is, "because of what they earned," but this is far-fetched. It has also been said that His words ﴿those﴾ refer to both groups together. That is: the first have a portion of this world and no portion for them in the Hereafter; the latter have a portion of what they earned in this world and in the Hereafter.

"Sari'" (swift) is from "sara'a yasru'u," like " 'azuma ya'zumu," with the verbal noun "saraʿan" and "surʿatan." "Al-hisab" (the reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muhasabah." Its original meaning is counting. It is said: "hasaba yahsubu hisaban, wa hisabatan, wa husbanan, wa hasban."

Here "al-hisab" means "the thing reckoned," and it is named "reckoning" by calling the object by the verbal noun. The meaning is: His reckoning of His servants on the Day of Resurrection will come swiftly, so hasten to it with deeds of goodness. Or, He described Himself with swiftness in reckoning the creatures despite their great number, and that no matter distracts Him from another, so He reckons them in a single moment, as He said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28].

His words ﴿in numbered days﴾: Al-Qurtubi said: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the numbered days in this verse are the days of Mina, which are the days of Tashriq, and they are the days of stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar).

Al-Tha'labi said: Ibrahim said: "The numbered days are the days of the ten, and the known days are the days of sacrifice." This is also reported from Makki and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Qurtubi said: This cannot be sound, given the consensus (ijma') that he transmitted, as did Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others.

Al-Tahawi transmitted from Abu Yusuf that "the known days" are the days of sacrifice. He said: this is based on His words: ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided them of the cattle of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. Al-Karkhi transmitted from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that the known days are the three days of sacrifice: the day of Eid al-Adha and two days after it.

Ilkiya al-Tabari said: According to the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, there is no difference between "the known days" and "the numbered days," because the numbered days mentioned in the Qur'an are, without disagreement, the days of Tashriq.

It is transmitted from Malik that the numbered days and the known days together comprise four days: the day of sacrifice and three days after it. So the day of sacrifice is known but not numbered, the two days after it are known and numbered, and the fourth day is numbered but not known. This is also transmitted from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Zayd said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the days of Tashriq.

The one addressed by this address mentioned in the verse, that is, His words ﴿and remember Allah in numbered days﴾, is the pilgrim and others, as the majority hold. It has been said that it is specific to the pilgrim.

Scholars have differed about its time. It has been said: from the dawn prayer on the day of Arafat until the afternoon prayer on the last day of Tashriq. It has been said: from the morning of Arafat until the afternoon prayer of the last day of the sacrifice, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. It has been said: from the noon prayer on the day of sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last day of Tashriq, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i.

His words ﴿Whoever hastens﴾ and so on: the two days are the second day of sacrifice and its third day.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i said: whoever stones [the pillars] on the second of the numbered days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays until the third, there is no sin upon him. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It expressed this by this division for emphasis and affirmation, because among the Arabs some censured hastening and some censured delaying, so the verse came removing blame in both cases.

'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever hastens, he is forgiven, and whoever delays, he is forgiven. The verse indicates that both hastening and delaying are permissible.

His words ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾ mean that the option and the lifting of sin are established for the one who fears Allah, because the possessor of piety guards against everything that causes doubt, so he is most deserving of being singled out for this ruling.

Al-Akhfash said: the implied meaning is "that is for whoever fears Allah." It has been said: for whoever fears Allah after his departure from Hajj, against all sins. It has been said: for whoever fears killing game. It has been said: its meaning is safety for whoever fears Allah. It has been said: it is connected to the remembrance: that is, the remembrance is for whoever fears Allah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from 'A'ishah, who said: "Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called the Hums, while the rest of the Arabs stood at Arafat. When Islam came, Allah commanded His Prophet to come to Arafat, stand there, and then depart from it. This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted from her, as a statement from her own words (mawquf), something similar.

Reports with this meaning have come from the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "When it is the day of Arafat, Allah descends to the lowest heaven with the angels, and says to them: 'My servants have believed in My promise and affirmed My messengers; what is their reward?' It is said: 'That You forgive them.' This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾."

Many hadiths have been reported about the forgiveness of the people of Arafat, the descent of mercy upon them, and the answering of their supplications.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "your Hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "the shedding of blood (sacrifice)." ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, he said: "the boasting of the Arabs among themselves with the deeds of their fathers on the day of sacrifice when they finish, so they were commanded to remember Allah in place of that."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The polytheists used to sit during the Hajj and mention the days of their fathers and what they counted of their lineages, all day long. So Allah sent down to His Messenger: ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a greater remembrance﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir also transmitted something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾ that he said: "As children remember their fathers."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it was said to him regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾: "Indeed a man may pass a day and not mention his father." He said: "That is not the point, rather it means: be angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than you are angry when your father is spoken ill of."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Some of the Bedouins used to come to the standing place and say: 'O Allah, make this a year of rain, a year of abundance, and a year of good birth,' and they mentioned nothing of the matter of the Hereafter at all. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Among the people is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world, and he has no share in the Hereafter﴾. And there come after them others from the believers who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾."

Al-Tabarani transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when people stood at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), one of them would supplicate and say: 'O Allah, provide me with camels,' and another would say: 'O Allah, provide me with sheep.' So Allah sent down the verse."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas that they used to circumambulate the House naked, supplicating: "O Allah, give us rain, grant us victory over our enemy, and return us righteous to a righteous people." So the verse was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ that he said: "of what they did of good."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ that he said: "swift in counting."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali that he said: "The numbered days are three days: the day of Eid al-Adha and two days after it. Slaughter on whichever of them you wish, and the best of them is the first."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that they are the three days of Tashriq.

In another wording: "These three days after the day of sacrifice."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The known days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'lumat) are the days of the ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah), and the counted days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat, the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say while he was standing at 'Arafat, when people from Makkah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the Hajj?' "Sari'" (swift) is from "sara'a yasru'u," like " 'azuma ya'zumu," with the verbal noun "saraʿan" and "surʿatan." "Al-hisab" (the reckoning) is a verbal noun like "al-muhasabah." Its original meaning is counting. It is said: "hasaba yahsubu hisaban, wa hisabatan, wa husbanan, wa hasban."

Here "al-hisab" means "the thing reckoned," and it is named "reckoning" by calling the object by the verbal noun. The meaning is: His reckoning of His servants on the Day of Resurrection will come swiftly, so hasten to it with deeds of goodness. Or, He described Himself with swiftness in reckoning the creatures despite their great number, and that no matter distracts Him from another, so He reckons them in a single moment, as He said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28].

His words ﴿in numbered days﴾: Al-Qurtubi said: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the numbered days in this verse are the days of Mina, which are the days of Tashriq, and they are the days of stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar).

Al-Tha'labi said: Ibrahim said: "The numbered days are the days of the ten, and the known days are the days of sacrifice." This is also reported from Makki and al-Mahdawi.

Al-Qurtubi said: This cannot be sound, given the consensus (ijma') that he transmitted, as did Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others.

Al-Tahawi transmitted from Abu Yusuf that "the known days" are the days of sacrifice. He said: this is based on His words: ﴿and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided them of the cattle of livestock﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. Al-Karkhi transmitted from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that the known days are the three days of sacrifice: the day of Eid al-Adha and two days after it.

Ilkiya al-Tabari said: According to the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, there is no difference between "the known days" and "the numbered days," because the numbered days mentioned in the Qur'an are, without disagreement, the days of Tashriq.

It is transmitted from Malik that the numbered days and the known days together comprise four days: the day of sacrifice and three days after it. So the day of sacrifice is known but not numbered, the two days after it are known and numbered, and the fourth day is numbered but not known. This is also transmitted from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Zayd said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the days of Tashriq.

The one addressed by this address mentioned in the verse, that is, His words ﴿and remember Allah in numbered days﴾, is the pilgrim and others, as the majority hold. It has been said that it is specific to the pilgrim.

Scholars have differed about its time. It has been said: from the dawn prayer on the day of Arafat until the afternoon prayer on the last day of Tashriq. It has been said: from the morning of Arafat until the afternoon prayer of the last day of the sacrifice, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. It has been said: from the noon prayer on the day of sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last day of Tashriq, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i.

His words ﴿Whoever hastens﴾ and so on: the two days are the second day of sacrifice and its third day.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i said: whoever stones [the pillars] on the second of the numbered days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays until the third, there is no sin upon him. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It expressed this by this division for emphasis and affirmation, because among the Arabs some censured hastening and some censured delaying, so the verse came removing blame in both cases.

'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever hastens, he is forgiven, and whoever delays, he is forgiven. The verse indicates that both hastening and delaying are permissible.

His words ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾ mean that the option and the lifting of sin are established for the one who fears Allah, because the possessor of piety guards against everything that causes doubt, so he is most deserving of being singled out for this ruling.

Al-Akhfash said: the implied meaning is "that is for whoever fears Allah." It has been said: for whoever fears Allah after his departure from Hajj, against all sins. It has been said: for whoever fears killing game. It has been said: its meaning is safety for whoever fears Allah. It has been said: it is connected to the remembrance: that is, the remembrance is for whoever fears Allah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from 'A'ishah, who said: "Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called the Hums, while the rest of the Arabs stood at Arafat. When Islam came, Allah commanded His Prophet to come to Arafat, stand there, and then depart from it. This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also transmitted from her, as a statement from her own words (mawquf), something similar.

Reports with this meaning have come from the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "When it is the day of Arafat, Allah descends to the lowest heaven with the angels, and says to them: 'My servants have believed in My promise and affirmed My messengers; what is their reward?' It is said: 'That You forgive them.' This is His saying: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾."

Many hadiths have been reported about the forgiveness of the people of Arafat, the descent of mercy upon them, and the answering of their supplications.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "your Hajj."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿and when you have completed your rites﴾ that he said: "the shedding of blood (sacrifice)." ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, he said: "the boasting of the Arabs among themselves with the deeds of their fathers on the day of sacrifice when they finish, so they were commanded to remember Allah in place of that."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The polytheists used to sit during the Hajj and mention the days of their fathers and what they counted of their lineages, all day long. So Allah sent down to His Messenger: ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a greater remembrance﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted something similar from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir also transmitted something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾ that he said: "As children remember their fathers."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it was said to him regarding His words ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾: "Indeed a man may pass a day and not mention his father." He said: "That is not the point, rather it means: be angrier for Allah when He is disobeyed than you are angry when your father is spoken ill of."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Some of the Bedouins used to come to the standing place and say: 'O Allah, make this a year of rain, a year of abundance, and a year of good birth,' and they mentioned nothing of the matter of the Hereafter at all. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Among the people is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world, and he has no share in the Hereafter﴾. And there come after them others from the believers who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. So Allah sent down about them: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning﴾."

Al-Tabarani transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "In the Jahiliyyah, when people stood at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), one of them would supplicate and say: 'O Allah, provide me with camels,' and another would say: 'O Allah, provide me with sheep.' So Allah sent down the verse."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas that they used to circumambulate the House naked, supplicating: "O Allah, give us rain, grant us victory over our enemy, and return us righteous to a righteous people." So the verse was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words ﴿those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ that he said: "of what they did of good."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ that he said: "swift in counting."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that they are the three days of Tashriq.

In another wording: "These three days after the day of sacrifice."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The known days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'lumat) are the days of the ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah), and the counted days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat, the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)."

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn al-Zubayr that, regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "They are the days of tashriq, in which Allah is remembered with tasbih (saying Subhan Allah), tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah), takbir (saying Allahu akbar) and tahmid (saying al-hamdu lillah)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The counted days are four days: the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the three days after it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to glorify Allah (make takbir) during those days at Mina and would say: "The takbir is obligatory," and he would interpret this verse, ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, as evidence.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to make takbir on the day of sacrifice and recite this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "The takbir is during the days of tashriq; one says after every prayer: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to make takbir three times after the prayers and would say: "La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir (There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent)."

Malik related from Yahya ibn Sa'id that it reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on the day after the day of sacrifice at Mina when the day had risen somewhat, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a second time on that same day after the sun had risen, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir, until their takbir reached the House (the Ka'bah). Then he went out a third time on that same day when the sun had passed its zenith, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to throw the pebbles (at the jamarat) and would make takbir with every pebble." 

Something similar has been related from the hadith of 'A'ishah in al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his hastening," and ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his delaying."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The departure (nafr) in two days is for the one who fears Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Whoever the sun sets upon on the day in which Allah said ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ while he is at Mina, let him not depart until he has thrown the pebbles on the next day."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears hunting while in the state of ihram."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say while he was standing at 'Arafat, when people from Makkah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the Hajj?' He said: 'The Hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever reaches Jam' (Muzdalifah) on the night before the dawn has reached (the Hajj). The days of Mina are three days. ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven. ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven.'"

Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj."

Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj, his past sins are forgiven."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "All his sin is removed, if he fears (Allah) in the remainder of his life."

On this view, "thumma" retains its original meaning of sequence.

They were commanded to seek forgiveness because they were in places where mercy descends, in locations of acceptance, and in places where supplications are likely to be answered. It has also been said that the meaning is: seek forgiveness for what contravened the Sunnah of Ibrahim, namely your standing at Muzdalifah rather than at Arafat.
