Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 199–203 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The known days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'lumat) are the days of the ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah), and the counted days (al-Ayyam al-Ma'dudat) are the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat, the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)."

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn al-Zubayr that, regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "They are the days of tashriq, in which Allah is remembered with tasbih (saying Subhan Allah), tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah), takbir (saying Allahu akbar) and tahmid (saying al-hamdu lillah)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The counted days are four days: the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the three days after it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to glorify Allah (make takbir) during those days at Mina and would say: "The takbir is obligatory," and he would interpret this verse, ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, as evidence.

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to make takbir on the day of sacrifice and recite this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding His words ﴿And remember Allah during counted days﴾, he said: "The takbir is during the days of tashriq; one says after every prayer: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar that he used to make takbir three times after the prayers and would say: "La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir (There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent)."

Malik related from Yahya ibn Sa'id that it reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on the day after the day of sacrifice at Mina when the day had risen somewhat, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a second time on that same day after the sun had risen, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir, until their takbir reached the House (the Ka'bah). Then he went out a third time on that same day when the sun had passed its zenith, and he made takbir, and the people made takbir with his takbir.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to throw the pebbles (at the jamarat) and would make takbir with every pebble." 

Something similar has been related from the hadith of 'A'ishah in al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his hastening," and ﴿and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, he said: "in his delaying."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The departure (nafr) in two days is for the one who fears Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "Whoever the sun sets upon on the day in which Allah said ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ while he is at Mina, let him not depart until he has thrown the pebbles on the next day."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears hunting while in the state of ihram."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur al-Dili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say while he was standing at 'Arafat, when people from Makkah came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the Hajj?' He said: 'The Hajj is 'Arafat. Whoever reaches Jam' (Muzdalifah) on the night before the dawn has reached (the Hajj). The days of Mina are three days. ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven. ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ (he said): he is forgiven.'"

Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "for whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj."

Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: whoever fears (Allah) in his Hajj, his past sins are forgiven."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears (Allah)﴾, he said: "All his sin is removed, if he fears (Allah) in the remainder of his life."

When Allah (glorified is He) mentioned the two groups of Muslims by His saying, ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾, He followed this with mention of the group of hypocrites, who display faith and conceal disbelief.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, as its explanation will come.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It was never established that al-Akhnas embraced Islam. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of the hypocrites. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, or falsehood and displays with his tongue the opposite of it.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and he pleases you﴾ is clear.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ is that he swears to that, saying: "Allah bears witness to what is in my heart of love for you," or "to what is in my heart of Islam," or he says: "Allah knows that I speak the truth and that I am sincere in what I say to you."

Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa-yashhadu Allah" with a fatha on the letter of the present tense and the noble Name in the nominative as the subject, and the meaning is: "and Allah knows from him the opposite of what he said." Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. The reading of the majority is more emphatic in censure.

Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa-Allahu yashhadu 'ala ma fi qalbihi." Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-yastashhidu Allaha 'ala ma fi qalbihi."

His saying ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is connected either to the speech or to "pleases you." On the first, the speech issues in the life of this world; on the second, the pleasing issues in it.

Al-alad means: the most intense in contention.

It is said: a man is alad, and a woman is laddaa. "Laddahu yaludduhu" means: when you argue with him and overcome him. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And a contentious one, with deviation against me, as though the enmity of his breast were boiling in a cauldron."

Al-khisam is the verbal noun of "khasama," as al-Khalil said. It has been said that it is a plural of khasm, as al-Zajjaj said, like kalb and kilab, sa'b and si'ab, dakhm and dikhám.

The meaning is: he is the most intense of the contenders in contention, due to the abundance of his disputing and the strength of his arguing. The annexing of alad to khisam is in the sense of "in": i.e., most contentious in the dispute; or khisam is made alad as an intensification.

His saying ﴿and when he turns away﴾ means: he turns his back and departs from you, O Muhammad. It has been said that it means: he goes astray and becomes angry. It has also been said that it means governance: i.e., if he is in authority, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the land.

The striving mentioned may be understood as striving with the feet toward what is corruption in the land, such as highway robbery and warring against the Muslims. It may also be understood as working at corruption, even if there is no striving with the feet, such as plotting against the Muslims to harm them, and employing tricks against them. Every action a person performs with his limbs or senses is called striving, and this is the apparent meaning of this verse.

His saying ﴿and destroy﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿to corrupt﴾. In Ubayy's reading it is "wa-li-yuhlika."

Qatadah read it in the nominative.

It was narrated from Ibn Kathir: "wa-yahlik" with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the kaf, and "al-harth wa-al-nasl" in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin.

By al-harth is meant crops, and by al-nasl, offspring. It has been said: al-harth means women.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is because hypocrisy leads to the division of the word and the outbreak of fighting, and in it is the destruction of creation. It has been said: the meaning is that the wrongdoer corrupts the land, so Allah withholds the rain, and the crops and offspring perish.

The original meaning of harth in the language is: tilling/splitting, from which comes al-mihrath, the implement by which the earth is split. Harth also means earning and gathering wealth.

The original meaning of nasl in the language is: emergence and falling out, from which comes "the hair's nasl," and also His saying, ﴿they come forth from every mound﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], and His saying, ﴿to their Lord they hasten﴾ [Ya-Sin: 51]. And whatever comes out of any female is called nasl because of its emergence from her.

His saying ﴿and Allah does not love corruption﴾ encompasses every kind of it, without distinction between what involves corruption of religion and what involves corruption of worldly affairs.

Al-'izzah means strength and dominance, from 'azzahu ya'uzzuhu, when he overcame him. From it is His saying, ﴿and he has overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. It has been said that al-'izzah here means zeal and pride. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Pride seized him from his ignorance, so he turned away angry, like one vexed."

It has also been said that al-'izzah here means protection and intensity of self.

The meaning of ﴿pride takes him to sin﴾ is: pride drives him to sin. From your saying, "akhadhtuhu bi-kadha," when you drive him to it and bind him to it. It has been said: pride took him by what makes him sinful, i.e., he committed disbelief out of pride. From it is His saying, ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2]. It has been said that the ba' in "bi-al-ithm" has the sense of lam: i.e., pride and zeal seized him from accepting admonition because of the sin that was in his heart, which is hypocrisy. It has been said that the ba' has the sense of ma'a: i.e., pride seized him along with the sin.

His saying ﴿then Hell is sufficient for him﴾ means: it is enough as requital and punishment, as you say to a man, "Let what has befallen you suffice you," while you magnify for him what has befallen him.

Al-mihad is the plural of mahd, which is the place prepared for sleep, and from it comes the cradle of a child. Hell is called a mihad because it is the resting place of the disbelievers. It has been said that the meaning is that it is a replacement for them in place of a bed, like His saying, ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], and the saying of the poet:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Yashri means yabi': i.e., he sells his soul in seeking Allah's pleasure, such as by jihad and by enjoining good and forbidding evil. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. Its original meaning is exchange. From it is His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for them is Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. From it is the saying of the poet:

"I bought a cloak, would that I had, after the cloak, been a skull."

And from it is the saying of another:

"He offers a price for it, yet he withholds it, and his companion says: Will you not buy?"

Al-mardah means al-rida: one says, "radiya yarda, ridan wa-mardatan."

The reason for mentioning kindness (ra'fah) here is that He obligated upon them what He obligated, so that He might reward and recompense them for it, and that was kindness toward them and gentleness to them.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the expedition in which 'Asim and Marthad were was struck, some men of the hypocrites said: "Woe to these slain who perished thus! They neither stayed among their families nor delivered the message of their companion!" So Allah revealed: ﴿Among the people is one whose speech pleases you in the life of this world﴾, i.e., what he displays of Islam with his tongue, ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾, that he opposes what he says with his tongue, ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾, i.e., full of disputation when he speaks to you and argues with you, ﴿and when he turns away﴾, he leaves your presence, ﴿he strives in the land to corrupt therein and destroy crops and offspring, and Allah does not love corruption﴾, i.e., He does not love his deed and does not approve of it. ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾, those who sell their souls to Allah by jihad in His way and upholding His right, until they perished in that; meaning this expedition.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying, ﴿Among the people is one who pleases you﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, ally of Banu Zuhrah, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Madinah and said: "I came desiring Islam, and Allah knows that I am truthful." This pleased the Prophet (ﷺ) from him, and that is His saying, ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾.

Then he left the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), passed by a field of crops belonging to some Muslims and some donkeys, burned the crops and hamstrung the donkeys. So Allah revealed, ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾, the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying, ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾, that he said: He is intense in contention.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying, ﴿and when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾, that he said: He acts in the land. ﴿And destroy the crops﴾, he said: the vegetation of the earth. ﴿And the offspring﴾, the offspring of every living thing among animals, people and beasts.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from Mujahid that he was asked about His saying, ﴿and when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾, and he said: He takes charge in the land and works in it with aggression and oppression, so Allah withholds rain from the sky, and by the withholding of rain the crops and offspring perish, and Allah does not love corruption.

Then Mujahid recited: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum: 41].

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about His saying, ﴿and destroy the crops and offspring﴾, and he said: The harth is the crops, and the nasl is the offspring of every animal.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Among the greatest sins before Allah is that a man says to his brother, "Fear Allah," and he replies, "Keep to yourself; you are instructing me!"

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sufyan, who said: A man said to Malik ibn Mighwal, "Fear Allah," and he fell and placed his cheek on the earth in humility before Allah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying, ﴿and what an evil resting place﴾, that he said: an evil dwelling.

Both of them narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Evil is what they testified for themselves."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Suhayb, who said: When I wished to migrate from Makkah to the Prophet (ﷺ), Quraysh said to me: "O Suhayb, you came to us with no property, and you leave with your property? By Allah, that will never happen!" I said to them: "Tell me, if I hand over my property to you, will you let me go?" They said: "Yes." So I handed over my property to them, and they let me go. I left until I reached Madinah. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Suhayb has profited in the sale," twice.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated similarly from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated similarly from Suhayb.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Anas, who said: It was revealed concerning Suhayb's departure to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: They are the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

Both of them narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Evil is what they testified for themselves."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Suhayb, who said: When I wished to migrate from Makkah to the Prophet (ﷺ), Quraysh said to me: "O Suhayb, you came to us with no property, and you leave with your property? By Allah, that will never happen!" I said to them: "Tell me, if I hand over my property to you, will you let me go?" They said: "Yes." So I handed over my property to them, and they let me go. I left until I reached Madinah. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Suhayb has profited in the sale," twice.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated similarly from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated similarly from Suhayb.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Anas, who said: It was revealed concerning Suhayb's departure to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: They are the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

When Allah (glorified is He) mentioned the two groups of Muslims by His saying, ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾, He followed this with mention of the group of hypocrites, who display faith and conceal disbelief.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, as its explanation will come.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It was never established that al-Akhnas embraced Islam. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of the hypocrites. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, or falsehood and displays with his tongue the opposite of it.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and he pleases you﴾ is clear.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ is that he swears to that, saying: "Allah bears witness to what is in my heart of love for you," or "to what is in my heart of Islam," or he says: "Allah knows that I speak the truth and that I am sincere in what I say to you."

Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa-yashhadu Allah" with a fatha on the letter of the present tense and the noble Name in the nominative as the subject, and the meaning is: "and Allah knows from him the opposite of what he said." Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. The reading of the majority is more emphatic in censure.

Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa-Allahu yashhadu 'ala ma fi qalbihi." Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-yastashhidu Allaha 'ala ma fi qalbihi."

His saying ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is connected either to the speech or to "pleases you." On the first, the speech issues in the life of this world; on the second, the pleasing issues in it.

Al-alad means: the most intense in contention.

It is said: a man is alad, and a woman is laddaa. "Laddahu yaludduhu" means: when you argue with him and overcome him. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And a contentious one, with deviation against me, as though the enmity of his breast were boiling in a cauldron."

Al-khisam is the verbal noun of "khasama," as al-Khalil said. It has been said that it is a plural of khasm, as al-Zajjaj said, like kalb and kilab, sa'b and si'ab, dakhm and dikhám.

The meaning is: he is the most intense of the contenders in contention, due to the abundance of his disputing and the strength of his arguing. The annexing of alad to khisam is in the sense of "in": i.e., most contentious in the dispute; or khisam is made alad as an intensification.

His saying ﴿and when he turns away﴾ means: he turns his back and departs from you, O Muhammad. It has been said that it means: he goes astray and becomes angry. It has also been said that it means governance: i.e., if he is in authority, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the land.

The striving mentioned may be understood as striving with the feet toward what is corruption in the land, such as highway robbery and warring against the Muslims. It may also be understood as working at corruption, even if there is no striving with the feet, such as plotting against the Muslims to harm them, and employing tricks against them. Every action a person performs with his limbs or senses is called striving, and this is the apparent meaning of this verse.

His saying ﴿and destroy﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿to corrupt﴾. In Ubayy's reading it is "wa-li-yuhlika."

Qatadah read it in the nominative.

It was narrated from Ibn Kathir: "wa-yahlik" with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the kaf, and "al-harth wa-al-nasl" in the nominative. This is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin.

By al-harth is meant crops, and by al-nasl, offspring. It has been said: al-harth means women.

Al-Zajjaj said: That is because hypocrisy leads to the division of the word and the outbreak of fighting, and in it is the destruction of creation. It has been said: the meaning is that the wrongdoer corrupts the land, so Allah withholds the rain, and the crops and offspring perish.

The original meaning of harth in the language is: tilling/splitting, from which comes al-mihrath, the implement by which the earth is split. Harth also means earning and gathering wealth.

The original meaning of nasl in the language is: emergence and falling out, from which comes "the hair's nasl," and also His saying, ﴿they come forth from every mound﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96], and His saying, ﴿to their Lord they hasten﴾ [Ya-Sin: 51]. And whatever comes out of any female is called nasl because of its emergence from her.

His saying ﴿and Allah does not love corruption﴾ encompasses every kind of it, without distinction between what involves corruption of religion and what involves corruption of worldly affairs.

Al-'izzah means strength and dominance, from 'azzahu ya'uzzuhu, when he overcame him. From it is His saying, ﴿and he has overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. It has been said that al-'izzah here means zeal and pride. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Pride seized him from his ignorance, so he turned away angry, like one vexed."

It has also been said that al-'izzah here means protection and intensity of self.

The meaning of ﴿pride takes him to sin﴾ is: pride drives him to sin. From your saying, "akhadhtuhu bi-kadha," when you drive him to it and bind him to it. It has been said: pride took him by what makes him sinful, i.e., he committed disbelief out of pride. From it is His saying, ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in pride and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2]. It has been said that the ba' in "bi-al-ithm" has the sense of lam: i.e., pride and zeal seized him from accepting admonition because of the sin that was in his heart, which is hypocrisy. It has been said that the ba' has the sense of ma'a: i.e., pride seized him along with the sin.

His saying ﴿then Hell is sufficient for him﴾ means: it is enough as requital and punishment, as you say to a man, "Let what has befallen you suffice you," while you magnify for him what has befallen him.

Al-mihad is the plural of mahd, which is the place prepared for sleep, and from it comes the cradle of a child. Hell is called a mihad because it is the resting place of the disbelievers. It has been said that the meaning is that it is a replacement for them in place of a bed, like His saying, ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], and the saying of the poet:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Yashri means yabi': i.e., he sells his soul in seeking Allah's pleasure, such as by jihad and by enjoining good and forbidding evil. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. Its original meaning is exchange. And from it is the saying of another:

"He offers a price for it, yet he withholds it, and his companion says: Will you not buy?"

Al-mardah means al-rida: one says, "radiya yarda, ridan wa-mardatan."

The reason for mentioning kindness (ra'fah) here is that He obligated upon them what He obligated, so that He might reward and recompense them for it, and that was kindness toward them and gentleness to them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 208–210:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned that people divide into three groups: believers, disbelievers, and hypocrites (munafiqun), He then commanded them to be upon one religion (millah) (millah: religious community or creed).

The term "faith" (iman) was applied to the three groups because the People of the Book believe in their prophet and their book, and the hypocrite is a believer with his tongue, even if he is not a believer in his heart.

As-salm, with a fatha and with a kasra on the sin, Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is one and the same, and so it is according to the Basrans, and both of them apply to Islam and to peace (al-musalamah).

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: it is with a fatha for peace (al-musalamah), and with a kasra for Islam.

Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction.

Al-Jawhari said: as-salm with a fatha on the sin means reconciliation (al-sulh); it may be vocalized with a kasra, it may be masculine or feminine, and its origin is from submission (al-istislam) and yielding (al-inqiyad).

Al-Tabari preferred that here it means Islam, and from it is the saying of the Kindi poet:

"I called my tribe to peace when I saw them turning their backs in flight"

That is, to Islam.

Al-A'mash read "al-salami" with a fatha on the sin and the lam.

The Basrans have related that in silm, salam and salm the meaning is one and the same. Kaffatan (kaffah) is a circumstantial state (hal) either of as-salm or of the pronoun of the believers. So its meaning according to the first is: none of you should leave; and according to the second: nothing of the kinds of peace should be left out, but enter into it all together, that is, into the characteristics of Islam. It is derived from their saying "kafaftu", meaning "I prevented", that is, no one among you should refrain from entering Islam. Al-kaff means prevention, and what is intended by it here is the totality. "Enter into peace completely" means all together.

His saying: "And do not follow the footsteps of Satan" means do not take the path to which Satan calls you. The discussion of "khutuwat" has already preceded.

His saying: "zallatum" means you have deviated from the path of uprightness. The original sense of zalal is in the foot, then it was used for beliefs and other things. It is said: "zalla yazillu, zalalan, zuluhan", meaning his foot slipped.

It is also read "zalilتum" with a kasra on the lam, and both are dialects. The meaning: if you go astray and deviate from the truth "after the clear proofs have come to you", that is, the manifest evidences and sound demonstrations that entering Islam is the truth, "then know that Allah is Mighty", overpowering, whom retribution against you cannot overcome; "Wise", who does not take retribution except with right.

His saying: "Do they await" means do they wait. It is said: "nazartuhu" and "intazartuhu" with the same meaning. What is meant is: do those who refuse to enter into peace await...? Yazid also read "wal-malaikati" in the genitive, in coordination with "al-ghamam" or with "zulal".

Al-Akhfash said: "wal-malaikati" in the genitive means "and among the angels", and he said: the nominative is better.

Al-Zajjaj said: the estimate is "in shades of clouds and of angels".

The meaning: do they await nothing except that Allah should come to them with what He promised them of reckoning and punishment, "in shades of clouds and angels".

It was also said: the meaning is that the command and judgment of Allah will come to them. It was said that His saying "fi zulal" means "bi-zulal" (with shades). It was said the meaning is: He comes to them with His might in shades.

Al-Ghamam: the thin white cloud; it is named so because it "yaghummu", that is, covers.

The reason for the coming of punishment in the clouds, on the assumption that this is what is meant, is the horror and great effect of fear coming from a place of security, because clouds are the object of mercy, not the object of punishment.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 211–213 (part 1 of 2):

The one commanded to ask the Children of Israel is the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is permissible that it refers to every one of the askers. This is a question of reproach and rebuke.

*Kam* (كَمْ) is in the accusative position governed by the verb mentioned after it, as its object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *ataynā* (آتى, "We gave"). It is also permissible that it is accusative by a verb understood from the one mentioned, meaning: "How many signs did We give them, We gave them." It is considered to be placed later (in the sentence) because it has the front position of the sentence. It is either interrogative, for confirmation (*taqrir*), or declarative, for amplification (*takthir*).

*Min ayah* (مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is in the accusative position as a *tamyiz* (specification, a noun clarifying the quantity). The signs are the clear proofs that their prophets brought concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that what is meant by this is the signs that Moses brought, and they are the nine.

By "favour" (*ni'mah*) here is meant what came to them of the signs.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "The favour here is Islam." The apparent meaning includes every favour that God bestowed upon one of His servants, whoever he may be, so that he changes it and fails to give thanks for it. That the context concerns the Children of Israel, or that they were the cause of the revelation, does not negate this, because it is established that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. In His saying, *"Indeed, God is severe in punishment"* (﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾), there is an intimidation and warning beyond measure.

His saying *zuyyina* (زُيِّنَ, "was made attractive") is in the passive voice. The one who makes it attractive is Satan, or the souls inclined by nature to love of the immediate (world).

By "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) is meant the leaders of Quraysh, or every disbeliever.

Mujahid and Hamid ibn Qays read *zayyana* (زَيَّنَ) in the active voice. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an irregular reading (*shadhdh*), because no subject has been mentioned previously."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *zuyyinat* (زُيِّنَتْ). God singled out those who disbelieved for mention, although the world is made attractive to both the Muslim and the disbeliever, just as He described that He made what is on the earth an adornment for it, so that He might test the creation as to which of them is best in deed. This is because the disbeliever was seduced by this adornment and turned away from the Hereafter, whereas the Muslim was not seduced by it, but turned towards the Hereafter.

His saying: *"And those who disbelieved mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾). This sentence is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause, "while"): meaning, while those disbelievers mock those who believed, because they are poor and have no share of the world like the share of the chiefs of disbelief and the pillars of error. This is because the commodity of the world, in their view, is that whoever obtains it is fortunate and profitable, and whoever is deprived of it is wretched and a loser.

The majority of the believers at that time were poor, because they were occupied with worship and the matter of the Hereafter, and did not turn their attention to the world and its adornment.

Al-Akhfash related that one says: *sakhirtu minhu* (سَخِرْتُ مِنهُ) and *sakhirtu bihi* (سَخِرْتُ بِهِ), *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, and *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi*. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) and *al-sukhriyy* (السُّخْرِيُّ).

When the disbelievers committed what they committed of mockery against the believers, God responded to them with His saying: *"But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection"* (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾). By "above" (*fawqiyyah*) is meant here elevation in rank, because they are in Paradise and the disbelievers are in the Fire. It is also possible that "above" means place, because Paradise is in the heaven and the Fire is in the lowest of the low. Or (it means) that the believers are the dominant ones in this world, as happened in the spread of Islam, the fall of disbelief, the killing of its people, their capture and dispersal, and the imposition of the *jizyah* (poll tax) upon them. There is no obstacle to carrying the verse upon all of that, were it not for the restriction by its being on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: *"And God gives provision to whom He wills without account"* (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾). It is possible that this contains an indication that God, glorified is He, will provide for the weak among the believers and expand for them, and will make what He gives them of provision without account, meaning without measure. It is also possible that the meaning is: God expands provision for some of His servants as He expanded for those chiefs of the disbelievers, as a gradual lure (*istidraj*). There is no proof in the expansion that the one for whom it is expanded is pleased with him. It is also possible that what is meant by "without account" is regarding the ones provided for, as He, glorified is He, said: *"And He will provide for him from where he does not expect"* (﴿ويَرْزُقْهُ مِن حَيْثُ لا يَحْتَسِبُ﴾) [al-Talaq: 3].

His saying: *"Mankind was one community"* (﴿كانَ النّاسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾), meaning they were upon one religion, then they differed (﴿فاخْتَلَفُوا﴾), and God sent the prophets (﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ﴾). What indicates this omitted element, namely His saying "then they differed," is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets."

Concerning who the people mentioned in this verse are, there is disagreement. It was said: they are the children of Adam when God brought them forth as souls (*nasam*) from the back of Adam. It was said: Adam alone, and he was called "mankind" (*nas*) because he is the origin of the offspring. It was said: Adam and Eve. It was said: what is meant is the first generations that existed between Adam and Noah. It was said: what is meant is Noah and those in his ark. It was said: the meaning of the verse is "Mankind was one community," all of them disbelievers, "then God sent the prophets." It was said: what is meant is the report about mankind, who are the whole species, that they were one community in their lack of laws and their ignorance of realities, had God not favoured them by sending the messengers.

The word *ummah* (أُمَّةٌ) is derived from their saying *amamtu al-shay'* (أمَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning "I aimed at it," so that their aim was one, not differing.

His saying: *"Bringing good tidings and warning"* (﴿مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ﴾) is in the accusative as a *hal*.

His saying: *"And He sent down with them the Book"* (﴿وأنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الكِتابَ﴾), meaning the genus (of books).

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the *alif* and *lam* (ال) are for prior reference (*'ahd*), and what is meant is the Torah.

His saying: *"to judge"* (﴿لِيَحْكُمَ﴾) is attributed to the Book according to the majority's view, and this is a metaphor like His saying, exalted is He: *"This Book of Ours speaks against you with truth"* (﴿هَذا كِتابُنا يَنْطِقُ عَلَيْكم بِالحَقِّ﴾) [al-Jathiyah: 29]. It was said: the meaning is "so that each prophet might judge by his Book." It was said: "so that God might judge." The pronoun in His saying *"concerning it"* (﴿فِيهِ﴾) first refers to what is in His saying *"concerning what they differed"* (﴿فِيما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ﴾). The pronoun in His saying *"and none differed concerning it"* (﴿وما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ﴾) may refer to the Book, and it may refer to the one to whom it was sent down, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by al-Zajjaj, and it may refer to the truth.

His saying: *"except those who were given it"* (﴿إلّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾), meaning those who were given the Book, or were given the truth, or were given the Prophet, meaning they were given knowledge of him.

His saying: *"out of jealousy among themselves"* (﴿بَغْيًا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾) is in the accusative as an object (*maf'ul bihi*), meaning: they did not differ except out of envy (*baghy*), that is, jealousy and greed for the world. In this there is an alert to the foolishness of their action and the ugliness into which they fell, because they made the sending down of the Book the cause of intense disagreement.

His saying: *"Then God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed, by His permission"* (﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾) (p. 138): meaning God guided the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth, and that is by what He made clear to them in the Qur'an of the differing of those before them. It was said: its meaning is that God guided the community of Muhammad to affirm all the Books, unlike those before them, for some of them denied the Book of others. It was said: God guided them to the truth regarding the *qiblah* (direction of prayer). It was said: He guided them to the day of Friday. It was said: He guided them to the correct belief about Jesus, after the Jews denied him and the Christians made him a lord. It was said: what is meant by the truth is Islam.

Al-Farra' said: there is an inversion (*qalb*, reversal of word order) in the verse, and its intended sense is: "God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed." Ibn Jarir chose this, and Ibn 'Atiyyah considered it weak.

His saying: *"by His permission"* (﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "by His knowledge." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, and the meaning is "by His command."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, concerning His saying *"Ask the Children of Israel"* (﴿سَلْ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾): he said, "They are the Jews." *"How many a clear sign We gave them"* (﴿كَمْ آتَيْناهم مِن آيَةٍ بَيِّنَةٍ﴾): what God mentioned in the Qur'an and what He did not mention. *"And whoever replaces the favour of God"* (﴿ومَن يُبَدِّلْ نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ﴾): he said, "He disbelieves in it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: God gave them clear signs: the staff of Moses and his hand; He parted the sea for them and drowned their enemy while they watched; clouds of shade; and He sent down upon them the manna and the quails. *"And whoever replaces the favour of God"*: he says, "whoever disbelieves in the favour of God."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying *"The worldly life has been made attractive to those who disbelieve"* (﴿زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا الحَياةُ الدُّنْيا﴾): he said, "The disbelievers seek the worldly life and pursue it." *"And they mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): in their pursuit of the Hereafter.

Ibn Jurayj said: "I do not think it except from Ikrimah," who said: They said, "If Muhammad were a prophet, his leaders and nobles would have followed him. By God, no one followed him except the people in need, like Ibn Mas'ud and his companions."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying *"and they mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): they say, "These are not upon anything," as mockery and derision. *"But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection"* (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾): here is the *kam* of comparison (of superiority).

Abd al-Razzaq related from Qatadah, who said: "Above them" is in Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ata', who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about this verse: *"And God gives provision to whom He wills without account"* (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾). He said: its explanation is: "There is no watcher over God, nor anyone who calls Him to account."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Lord is not called to account."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani related with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Mankind was one community": he said, "upon Islam, all of them."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim related from him, who said: "Between Adam and Noah there were ten generations, all of them upon a law of truth, then they differed, so God sent the prophets."

He said: "And likewise in the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): 'Mankind was one community, then they differed.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "They were one community when they were presented to Adam, so God brought them forth upon Islam, and they acknowledged to Him servitude, and they were one community, Muslims. Then they differed after Adam." 

Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, concerning *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "Adam."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy that he used to recite it: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets," and that God only sent the messengers and revealed the Books after the differing. *"And none differed concerning it except those who were given it"* (﴿وما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾): he means the Children of Israel, who were given the Book and the knowledge, out of envy among themselves. He says: out of greed for the world, and the pursuit of its kingdom and its ornaments, as to which of them would have the kingdom and the awe among the people.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "disbelievers."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying *"Then God guided those who believed"* (﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in rank) on the Day of Resurrection, and the first of the people to enter (Paradise) will be those for whom it is begun. They were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. God guided us to what they differed concerning of the truth. This is the day about which they differed, and God guided us to it. So the people follow us in it: tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians." It is in the Sahih without mention of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning His words: ﴿Then Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾. He said: They differed concerning the day of Friday (al-Jumu'ah). The Jews took Saturday (al-Sabt), and the Christians took Sunday (al-Ahad), so Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to Friday.

They differed concerning the qiblah (direction of prayer). The Christians faced the east (al-mashriq), and the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and He guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the qiblah.

They differed concerning the prayer (al-salah). Among them was one who bowed but did not prostrate, and among them was one who prostrated but did not bow, and among them was one who prayed while speaking, and among them was one who prayed while walking. So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning fasting (al-siyam). Among them was one who fasted the day, and among them was one who fasted after eating (i.e., broke the fast after food, or fasted in part of the day). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Ibrahim (Abraham). The Jews said: He was a Jew. The Christians said: He was a Christian. And Allah made him a ḥanif (one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism) and a Muslim (one who submits). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Isa (Jesus). The Jews denied him and said against his mother a tremendous slander (buhtan). The Christians made him a god and a son. And Allah made him His spirit (ruh) and His word (kalimah). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 211–213 (part 1 of 2):

The one commanded to ask the Children of Israel is the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is permissible that it refers to every one of the askers. This is a question of reproach and rebuke.

*Kam* (كَمْ) is in the accusative position governed by the verb mentioned after it, as its object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *ataynā* (آتى, "We gave"). It is also permissible that it is accusative by a verb understood from the one mentioned, meaning: "How many signs did We give them, We gave them." It is considered to be placed later (in the sentence) because it has the front position of the sentence. It is either interrogative, for confirmation (*taqrir*), or declarative, for amplification (*takthir*).

*Min ayah* (مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is in the accusative position as a *tamyiz* (specification, a noun clarifying the quantity). The signs are the clear proofs that their prophets brought concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that what is meant by this is the signs that Moses brought, and they are the nine.

By "favour" (*ni'mah*) here is meant what came to them of the signs.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "The favour here is Islam." The apparent meaning includes every favour that God bestowed upon one of His servants, whoever he may be, so that he changes it and fails to give thanks for it. That the context concerns the Children of Israel, or that they were the cause of the revelation, does not negate this, because it is established that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. In His saying, *"Indeed, God is severe in punishment"* (﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾), there is an intimidation and warning beyond measure.

His saying *zuyyina* (زُيِّنَ, "was made attractive") is in the passive voice. The one who makes it attractive is Satan, or the souls inclined by nature to love of the immediate (world).

By "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) is meant the leaders of Quraysh, or every disbeliever.

Mujahid and Hamid ibn Qays read *zayyana* (زَيَّنَ) in the active voice. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an irregular reading (*shadhdh*), because no subject has been mentioned previously."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *zuyyinat* (زُيِّنَتْ). God singled out those who disbelieved for mention, although the world is made attractive to both the Muslim and the disbeliever, just as He described that He made what is on the earth an adornment for it, so that He might test the creation as to which of them is best in deed. This is because the disbeliever was seduced by this adornment and turned away from the Hereafter, whereas the Muslim was not seduced by it, but turned towards the Hereafter.

His saying: *"And those who disbelieved mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾). This sentence is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause, "while"): meaning, while those disbelievers mock those who believed, because they are poor and have no share of the world like the share of the chiefs of disbelief and the pillars of error. This is because the commodity of the world, in their view, is that whoever obtains it is fortunate and profitable, and whoever is deprived of it is wretched and a loser.

The majority of the believers at that time were poor, because they were occupied with worship and the matter of the Hereafter, and did not turn their attention to the world and its adornment.

Al-Akhfash related that one says: *sakhirtu minhu* (سَخِرْتُ مِنهُ) and *sakhirtu bihi* (سَخِرْتُ بِهِ), *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, and *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi*. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) and *al-sukhriyy* (السُّخْرِيُّ).

When the disbelievers committed what they committed of mockery against the believers, God responded to them with His saying: *"But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection"* (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾). By "above" (*fawqiyyah*) is meant here elevation in rank, because they are in Paradise and the disbelievers are in the Fire. It is also possible that "above" means place, because Paradise is in the heaven and the Fire is in the lowest of the low. Or (it means) that the believers are the dominant ones in this world, as happened in the spread of Islam, the fall of disbelief, the killing of its people, their capture and dispersal, and the imposition of the *jizyah* (poll tax) upon them. There is no obstacle to carrying the verse upon all of that, were it not for the restriction by its being on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: *"And God gives provision to whom He wills without account"* (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾). It is possible that this contains an indication that God, glorified is He, will provide for the weak among the believers and expand for them, and will make what He gives them of provision without account, meaning without measure. It is also possible that the meaning is: God expands provision for some of His servants as He expanded for those chiefs of the disbelievers, as a gradual lure (*istidraj*). There is no proof in the expansion that the one for whom it is expanded is pleased with him. It is also possible that what is meant by "without account" is regarding the ones provided for, as He, glorified is He, said: *"And He will provide for him from where he does not expect"* (﴿ويَرْزُقْهُ مِن حَيْثُ لا يَحْتَسِبُ﴾) [al-Talaq: 3].

He said: "And likewise in the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): 'Mankind was one community, then they differed.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "They were one community when they were presented to Adam, so God brought them forth upon Islam, and they acknowledged to Him servitude, and they were one community, Muslims. Then they differed after Adam." 

Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, concerning *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "Adam."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy that he used to recite it: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets," and that God only sent the messengers and revealed the Books after the differing. *"And none differed concerning it except those who were given it"* (﴿وما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾): he means the Children of Israel, who were given the Book and the knowledge, out of envy among themselves. He says: out of greed for the world, and the pursuit of its kingdom and its ornaments, as to which of them would have the kingdom and the awe among the people.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "disbelievers."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying *"Then God guided those who believed"* (﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in rank) on the Day of Resurrection, and the first of the people to enter (Paradise) will be those for whom it is begun. They were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. God guided us to what they differed concerning of the truth. This is the day about which they differed, and God guided us to it. So the people follow us in it: tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians." It is in the Sahih without mention of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning His words: ﴿Then Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾. He said: They differed concerning the day of Friday (al-Jumu'ah). The Jews took Saturday (al-Sabt), and the Christians took Sunday (al-Ahad), so Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to Friday.

They differed concerning the qiblah (direction of prayer). The Christians faced the east (al-mashriq), and the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and He guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the qiblah.

They differed concerning the prayer (al-salah). Among them was one who bowed but did not prostrate, and among them was one who prostrated but did not bow, and among them was one who prayed while speaking, and among them was one who prayed while walking. So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning fasting (al-siyam). Among them was one who fasted the day, and among them was one who fasted after eating (i.e., broke the fast after food, or fasted in part of the day). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Ibrahim (Abraham). The Jews said: He was a Jew. The Christians said: He was a Christian. And Allah made him a ḥanif (one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism) and a Muslim (one who submits). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Isa (Jesus). The Jews denied him and said against his mother a tremendous slander (buhtan). The Christians made him a god and a son. And Allah made him His spirit (ruh) and His word (kalimah). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 211–213 (part 1 of 2):

The one commanded to ask the Children of Israel is the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is permissible that it refers to every one of the askers. This is a question of reproach and rebuke.

*Kam* (كَمْ) is in the accusative position governed by the verb mentioned after it, as its object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *ataynā* (آتى, "We gave"). It is also permissible that it is accusative by a verb understood from the one mentioned, meaning: "How many signs did We give them, We gave them." It is considered to be placed later (in the sentence) because it has the front position of the sentence. It is either interrogative, for confirmation (*taqrir*), or declarative, for amplification (*takthir*).

*Min ayah* (مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is in the accusative position as a *tamyiz* (specification, a noun clarifying the quantity). The signs are the clear proofs that their prophets brought concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that what is meant by this is the signs that Moses brought, and they are the nine.

By "favour" (*ni'mah*) here is meant what came to them of the signs.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "The favour here is Islam." The apparent meaning includes every favour that God bestowed upon one of His servants, whoever he may be, so that he changes it and fails to give thanks for it. That the context concerns the Children of Israel, or that they were the cause of the revelation, does not negate this, because it is established that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. In His saying, *"Indeed, God is severe in punishment"* (﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾), there is an intimidation and warning beyond measure.

His saying *zuyyina* (زُيِّنَ, "was made attractive") is in the passive voice. The one who makes it attractive is Satan, or the souls inclined by nature to love of the immediate (world).

By "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) is meant the leaders of Quraysh, or every disbeliever.

Mujahid and Hamid ibn Qays read *zayyana* (زَيَّنَ) in the active voice. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an irregular reading (*shadhdh*), because no subject has been mentioned previously."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *zuyyinat* (زُيِّنَتْ). God singled out those who disbelieved for mention, although the world is made attractive to both the Muslim and the disbeliever, just as He described that He made what is on the earth an adornment for it, so that He might test the creation as to which of them is best in deed. This is because the disbeliever was seduced by this adornment and turned away from the Hereafter, whereas the Muslim was not seduced by it, but turned towards the Hereafter.

His saying: *"And those who disbelieved mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾). This sentence is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause, "while"): meaning, while those disbelievers mock those who believed, because they are poor and have no share of the world like the share of the chiefs of disbelief and the pillars of error. This is because the commodity of the world, in their view, is that whoever obtains it is fortunate and profitable, and whoever is deprived of it is wretched and a loser.

The majority of the believers at that time were poor, because they were occupied with worship and the matter of the Hereafter, and did not turn their attention to the world and its adornment.

Al-Akhfash related that one says: *sakhirtu minhu* (سَخِرْتُ مِنهُ) and *sakhirtu bihi* (سَخِرْتُ بِهِ), *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, and *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi*. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) and *al-sukhriyy* (السُّخْرِيُّ).

When the disbelievers committed what they committed of mockery against the believers, God responded to them with His saying: *"But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection"* (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾). By "above" (*fawqiyyah*) is meant here elevation in rank, because they are in Paradise and the disbelievers are in the Fire. It is also possible that "above" means place, because Paradise is in the heaven and the Fire is in the lowest of the low. Or (it means) that the believers are the dominant ones in this world, as happened in the spread of Islam, the fall of disbelief, the killing of its people, their capture and dispersal, and the imposition of the *jizyah* (poll tax) upon them. There is no obstacle to carrying the verse upon all of that, were it not for the restriction by its being on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: *"And God gives provision to whom He wills without account"* (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾). It is possible that this contains an indication that God, glorified is He, will provide for the weak among the believers and expand for them, and will make what He gives them of provision without account, meaning without measure. It is also possible that the meaning is: God expands provision for some of His servants as He expanded for those chiefs of the disbelievers, as a gradual lure (*istidraj*). There is no proof in the expansion that the one for whom it is expanded is pleased with him. It is also possible that what is meant by "without account" is regarding the ones provided for, as He, glorified is He, said: *"And He will provide for him from where he does not expect"* (﴿ويَرْزُقْهُ مِن حَيْثُ لا يَحْتَسِبُ﴾) [al-Talaq: 3].

His saying: *"Mankind was one community"* (﴿كانَ النّاسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾), meaning they were upon one religion, then they differed (﴿فاخْتَلَفُوا﴾), and God sent the prophets (﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ﴾). What indicates this omitted element, namely His saying "then they differed," is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets."

Concerning who the people mentioned in this verse are, there is disagreement. It was said: they are the children of Adam when God brought them forth as souls (*nasam*) from the back of Adam. It was said: Adam alone, and he was called "mankind" (*nas*) because he is the origin of the offspring. It was said: Adam and Eve. It was said: what is meant is the first generations that existed between Adam and Noah. It was said: what is meant is Noah and those in his ark. It was said: the meaning of the verse is "Mankind was one community," all of them disbelievers, "then God sent the prophets." It was said: what is meant is the report about mankind, who are the whole species, that they were one community in their lack of laws and their ignorance of realities, had God not favoured them by sending the messengers.

The word *ummah* (أُمَّةٌ) is derived from their saying *amamtu al-shay'* (أمَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning "I aimed at it," so that their aim was one, not differing.

His saying: *"Then God sent the prophets"* (﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ﴾). It was said: their total was one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and among them the messengers were three hundred and thirteen.

His saying: *"Bringing good tidings and warning"* (﴿مُبَشِّرِينَ ومُنْذِرِينَ﴾) is in the accusative as a *hal*.

His saying: *"And He sent down with them the Book"* (﴿وأنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الكِتابَ﴾), meaning the genus (of books).

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: the *alif* and *lam* (ال) are for prior reference (*'ahd*), and what is meant is the Torah.

His saying: *"to judge"* (﴿لِيَحْكُمَ﴾) is attributed to the Book according to the majority's view, and this is a metaphor like His saying, exalted is He: *"This Book of Ours speaks against you with truth"* (﴿هَذا كِتابُنا يَنْطِقُ عَلَيْكم بِالحَقِّ﴾) [al-Jathiyah: 29]. It was said: the meaning is "so that each prophet might judge by his Book." It was said: "so that God might judge." The pronoun in His saying *"concerning it"* (﴿فِيهِ﴾) first refers to what is in His saying *"concerning what they differed"* (﴿فِيما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ﴾). The pronoun in His saying *"and none differed concerning it"* (﴿وما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ﴾) may refer to the Book, and it may refer to the one to whom it was sent down, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by al-Zajjaj, and it may refer to the truth.

His saying: *"except those who were given it"* (﴿إلّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾), meaning those who were given the Book, or were given the truth, or were given the Prophet, meaning they were given knowledge of him.

His saying: *"out of jealousy among themselves"* (﴿بَغْيًا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾) is in the accusative as an object (*maf'ul bihi*), meaning: they did not differ except out of envy (*baghy*), that is, jealousy and greed for the world. In this there is an alert to the foolishness of their action and the ugliness into which they fell, because they made the sending down of the Book the cause of intense disagreement.

His saying: *"Then God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed, by His permission"* (﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِما اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾) (p. 138): meaning God guided the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth, and that is by what He made clear to them in the Qur'an of the differing of those before them. It was said: its meaning is that God guided the community of Muhammad to affirm all the Books, unlike those before them, for some of them denied the Book of others. It was said: God guided them to the truth regarding the *qiblah* (direction of prayer). It was said: He guided them to the day of Friday. It was said: He guided them to the correct belief about Jesus, after the Jews denied him and the Christians made him a lord. It was said: what is meant by the truth is Islam.

Al-Farra' said: there is an inversion (*qalb*, reversal of word order) in the verse, and its intended sense is: "God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed." Ibn Jarir chose this, and Ibn 'Atiyyah considered it weak.

His saying: *"by His permission"* (﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "by His knowledge." Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, and the meaning is "by His command."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, concerning His saying *"Ask the Children of Israel"* (﴿سَلْ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾): he said, "They are the Jews." *"How many a clear sign We gave them"* (﴿كَمْ آتَيْناهم مِن آيَةٍ بَيِّنَةٍ﴾): what God mentioned in the Qur'an and what He did not mention. *"And whoever replaces the favour of God"* (﴿ومَن يُبَدِّلْ نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ﴾): he said, "He disbelieves in it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: God gave them clear signs: the staff of Moses and his hand; He parted the sea for them and drowned their enemy while they watched; clouds of shade; and He sent down upon them the manna and the quails. *"And whoever replaces the favour of God"*: he says, "whoever disbelieves in the favour of God."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying *"The worldly life has been made attractive to those who disbelieve"* (﴿زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا الحَياةُ الدُّنْيا﴾): he said, "The disbelievers seek the worldly life and pursue it." *"And they mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): in their pursuit of the Hereafter.

Ibn Jurayj said: "I do not think it except from Ikrimah," who said: They said, "If Muhammad were a prophet, his leaders and nobles would have followed him. By God, no one followed him except the people in need, like Ibn Mas'ud and his companions."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying *"and they mock those who believed"* (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): they say, "These are not upon anything," as mockery and derision. *"But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection"* (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾): here is the *kam* of comparison (of superiority).

Abd al-Razzaq related from Qatadah, who said: "Above them" is in Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ata', who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about this verse: *"And God gives provision to whom He wills without account"* (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾). He said: its explanation is: "There is no watcher over God, nor anyone who calls Him to account."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Lord is not called to account."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani related with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Mankind was one community": he said, "upon Islam, all of them."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim related from him, who said: "Between Adam and Noah there were ten generations, all of them upon a law of truth, then they differed, so God sent the prophets."

He said: "And likewise in the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): 'Mankind was one community, then they differed.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "They were one community when they were presented to Adam, so God brought them forth upon Islam, and they acknowledged to Him servitude, and they were one community, Muslims. Then they differed after Adam." 

Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, concerning *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "Adam."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ubayy that he used to recite it: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets," and that God only sent the messengers and revealed the Books after the differing. *"And none differed concerning it except those who were given it"* (﴿وما اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾): he means the Children of Israel, who were given the Book and the knowledge, out of envy among themselves. He says: out of greed for the world, and the pursuit of its kingdom and its ornaments, as to which of them would have the kingdom and the awe among the people.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: *"Mankind was one community"*: he said, "disbelievers."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, concerning His saying *"Then God guided those who believed"* (﴿فَهَدى اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾): he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in rank) on the Day of Resurrection, and the first of the people to enter (Paradise) will be those for whom it is begun. They were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. God guided us to what they differed concerning of the truth. This is the day about which they differed, and God guided us to it. So the people follow us in it: tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians." It is in the Sahih without mention of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning His words: ﴿Then Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾. He said: They differed concerning the day of Friday (al-Jumu'ah). The Jews took Saturday (al-Sabt), and the Christians took Sunday (al-Ahad), so Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to Friday.

They differed concerning the qiblah (direction of prayer). The Christians faced the east (al-mashriq), and the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and He guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the qiblah.

They differed concerning the prayer (al-salah). Among them was one who bowed but did not prostrate, and among them was one who prostrated but did not bow, and among them was one who prayed while speaking, and among them was one who prayed while walking. So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning fasting (al-siyam). Among them was one who fasted the day, and among them was one who fasted after eating (i.e., broke the fast after food, or fasted in part of the day). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Ibrahim (Abraham). The Jews said: He was a Jew. The Christians said: He was a Christian. And Allah made him a ḥanif (one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism) and a Muslim (one who submits). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

They differed concerning Isa (Jesus). The Jews denied him and said against his mother a tremendous slander (buhtan). The Christians made him a god and a son. And Allah made him His spirit (ruh) and His word (kalimah). So Allah guided the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to the truth in that.

"Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather).

Some philologists have related that it may come in the function of the interrogative hamzah, with which speech is begun. In this case, the meaning of interrogation here is confirmation and rebuke: that is, "Do you suppose that your entry into Paradise is certain, while you have not been tested with the like of what those before you were tested with, so that you would endure as they endured?" Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned this consolation after He mentioned the disagreement of the nations over their prophets, to strengthen the believers and fortify their hearts. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strive[d]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1-2].

His saying, ﴿مَسَّتْهُمُ﴾ ("they were touched by"), is an explanation of His saying, ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا﴾ ("the example of those who passed on before you").

As for ﴿البَأْساءُ والضَّرّاءُ﴾ ("adversity and affliction"), their explanation has already passed. And al-zalzalah (violent shaking, trembling) is the intense agitation that occurs in persons and in conditions. It is said: Allah zalzala the earth, zalzalatan and zilzalan (with a kasrah), so it trembled (fa-tazalzalat) when it moved and was agitated. So the meaning of ﴿زُلْزِلُوا﴾ ("they were shaken") is: they were frightened and driven out with a severe driving-out.

al-Zajjaj said: The origin of al-zalzalah is moving a thing from its place. When you say "zalzaltuhu," its meaning is that you repeatedly caused it to slip from its place.

His saying, ﴿حَتّى يَقُولَ﴾ ("until [the Messenger] and those who believed with him say"), means: that state continued up to a limit, which is the saying of the Messenger and those with him, ﴿مَتى نَصْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ ("When is the help of Allah?"). The "Messenger" here is said to be Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace; it is also said to be Isaiah (Ash'iya'); and it is said to be every messenger sent to his nation.

Mujahid, al-A'raj, Nafi' and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿يَقُولُ﴾ in "hatta yaqula" with the dammah (raf'), while others read it with the fathah (nasb). The raf' reading is on the basis that it is a narration of a past state, and the nasb reading is by the implied "an," on the basis that it is a limit (ghayah) for what precedes it.

al-A'mash read: "wa-zulzilu wa-yaqulu al-Rasul" (and they were shaken, and the Messenger says) with the waw instead of "hatta." The meaning of this is that the Messenger and those with him reached such impatience that they uttered this statement, which demands the seeking of help and asks for its delay and deems its tardiness long. So Allah, glory be to Him, gave them good news with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾

Some said: there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the speech, and the sense is: "until those who believed say, 'When is the help of Allah?' and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, says, 'Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.'" But there is no need for this strained interpretation, because the saying of the Messenger and those with him, ﴿مَتى نَصْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, contains nothing but seeking the help of Allah, glory be to Him, quickly; and it contains nothing of the doubt and suspicion that they alleged, so as to require that far-fetched interpretation.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah that this verse was revealed on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and his companions were struck that day by trial and siege.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah informed the believers that the world is a abode of trial, and that He would test them in it, and He informed them that He had done thus with His prophets and His elect, so that their souls would be at ease. So He said: ﴿مَسَّتْهُمُ البَأْساءُ والضَّرّاءُ﴾ ("they were touched by adversity and affliction"). Thus al-ba'sa' is tribulations, and al-darra' is sickness, and "zulzilu" means they were shaken by tribulations and by the harm of people toward them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿ولَمّا يَأْتِكم مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا﴾ ("and there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you"), that he said: this befell them on the day of the Confederates, until one of them said: ﴿ما وعَدَنا اللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ إلّا غُرُورًا﴾ ("What Allah and His Messenger promised us was nothing but delusion") [al-Ahzab: 12].
