Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 215–216:

The askers (al-sa'iluna) here are the believers, who asked about the thing they spend: what is it? They were answered by explaining the recipients to whom they should give it, as a reminder that this is the more important matter to aim at, because a thing is not counted (as valuable) unless it is placed in its proper position and reaches its proper recipient. It has also been said that the words ﴿Whatever good you spend﴾ already include an explanation of what they spend, which is every kind of good. It has also been said that they only asked about the avenues of righteousness (birr) in which they should spend, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The discussion of the near relatives (al-aqrabun), orphans (al-yatama), the needy (al-masakin) and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) has already been given.

His saying "kutiba" means "it was prescribed" (furiḍa), and its meaning has already been explained.

Glorified is He, who explained that this, that is the prescription of fighting upon them, is among the trials with which they were tested.

By fighting (al-qital) is meant fighting the disbelievers.

Al-kurh with a ḍammah means hardship (al-mashaqqah), and with a fatḥah it means that to which one is compelled. A ḍammah may also be used with the meaning of the fatḥah, so the two are dialectal variants. It is said: "I disliked the thing (karihtu al-shay') karhan, karhan, karahiyatan and karahiyah, and I compelled him to it (akrahtuhu 'alayhi) ikrahan." Jihad was a hardship (kurh) because it involves spending wealth, leaving family and homeland, and exposing oneself to the loss of life. Expressing it with the verbal noun, which is his saying "kurh," is an intensification. It is possible that it means "the disliked thing" (al-makruh), as in their saying: "The dirham is the minting of the amir."

As for His saying ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing﴾, it has been said that "'asa" here means "qad" (indeed, perhaps), and this was reported from al-Asamm.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'Asa from Allah is an obligation." The meaning is: it may be that you dislike jihad because of the hardship in it, and it is good for you, for you may prevail, be victorious, take spoils, and be rewarded, and whoever dies, dies as a martyr (shahid). And it may be that you love ease (al-da'ah) and abandoning fighting, and it is evil for you, for the enemy may grow strong against you, overcome you, and march against the very heart of your homes, so that there befalls you something worse than what you feared from the jihad you disliked, together with what you miss of the immediate and deferred benefits. ﴿And Allah knows﴾ what in it is your righteousness and success, ﴿and you do not know﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, that he said: On the day this verse was revealed there was no zakah (obligatory alms). What was meant was the expenditure a man makes on his family and the charity he gives in alms, and then zakah abrogated (naskh) them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "The believers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Where should they place their wealth? So the verse ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾ was revealed," and that expenditure in voluntary charity and zakah is the same, all of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported that "'Amr ibn al-Jamuh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): What should we spend of our wealth, and where should we place it? So it was revealed."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾, that he said: Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers in Makkah to affirm the oneness of God, to establish prayer, to give zakah, and to restrain their hands from fighting. When he emigrated to Madinah, the rest of the obligations were revealed and they were permitted to fight, and so it was revealed: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾, meaning it was made obligatory upon you, and they were permitted it after it had been forbidden to them. ﴿And it is a hardship for you﴾, meaning fighting, which is a burden upon you. ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing﴾, meaning jihad, fighting the polytheists. ﴿And it is good for you﴾, and Allah makes its outcome a conquest, booty and martyrdom. ﴿And it may be that you love a thing﴾, meaning sitting back from jihad. ﴿And it is evil for you﴾, so Allah makes its outcome evil, and you will not attain victory or booty.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata: What do you say about His saying ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾? Was going out to fight made obligatory upon people on account of it? He said: No, it was prescribed upon those people at that time.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Shihab regarding the verse, that he said: Jihad is prescribed upon everyone, whether he fights or sits back. So the one who sits back, if he is sought for help, helps; if he is sought for aid, aids; if he is called to march forth, he marches; and if he is found to be not needed, he sits back. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿And it is a hardship for you﴾, that he said: It was abrogated (nasakhat) by this verse: ﴿And they say: We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285].

Ibn Jarir reported it connected (mawsulan) from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported through the chain of 'Ali, who said: "'Asa" from Allah is binding (wajib).

Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported similarly from al-Suddi.

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the merit of jihad and its obligation, but the scope of this place does not allow their full exposition.

**Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 217–218**

His saying: ﴿fighting in it﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion, i.e. a substitute that is connected to the thing it replaces by way of containment), as Sibawayh said.

Its basis is that the question about the month was only about what took place in it of fighting.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is, "They ask you about fighting in the sacred month." Sibawayh quoted the verse of the poet:

*So the death of Qays was not the death of one man, but it was the building of a people that collapsed.*

So his saying "his death" is a *badal ishtimal* from "Qays." Al-Farra' said: it is in the genitive case, meaning: his saying ﴿fighting in it﴾ is governed by an implied *'an* (from). Abu 'Ubayda said: it is in the genitive case by *jiwar* (attraction of the case of a neighbouring word).

Al-Nahhas said: It is not permissible for a thing to be given a case by *jiwar* in the Book of God or in any speech. It occurs only in something anomalous, namely their saying: "This is the lizard-hole of a ruined lizard" (*hadha juhru dabbin kharib*).

Al-Nahhas was followed by Ibn 'Atiyya in rejecting Abu 'Ubayda's view.

Al-Nahhas said: It is not permissible to posit an implied *'an*; the correct view is that it is a *badal*.

Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ikrima read: "They ask you about the sacred month and about fighting in it."

Al-A'raj read "fighting in it" with the nominative (*qitalun fihi*).

Al-Nahhas said: This is obscure in Arabic grammar. The meaning is: "They ask you about the sacred month: fighting in it is permissible."

His saying: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great matter﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning: fighting in it is a great and reprehensible matter. "The sacred month" is meant as a class noun.

The Arabs used not to shed blood in it, nor to raid an enemy. The sacred months are: Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, Muharram, and Rajab, three in succession and one alone.

His saying: ﴿and barring from the way of God﴾ is a subject.

His saying: ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ is coordinated with "barring."

His saying: ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾ is coordinated with "the way of God."

His saying: ﴿and the expulsion of its people from it﴾ is also coordinated with "barring."

His saying: ﴿is greater in the sight of God﴾ is the predicate of "barring" and what is coordinated with it, meaning: barring from the way of God, disbelief in Him, barring from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling the people of the Sanctuary from it, ﴿are greater in the sight of God﴾, that is, more sinful and more grievous in wrongdoing than fighting in the sacred month. So said al-Mubarrad and others.

The pronoun in his saying ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ refers to God. It was also said that it refers to the Pilgrimage (*hajj*).

Al-Farra' said: his saying "and barring" is coordinated with "great," and "the Mosque" is coordinated with the pronoun in his saying ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾, so the speech is connected and not disjointed.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: That is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that ﴿disbelief in Him﴾, that is in God, is also coordinated with "great," and it would follow that the expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief in God. The falsity of this is clear.

The meaning of the verse according to the first view, which the majority held, is: You, O disbelievers of Quraysh, consider our fighting in the sacred month a grave matter, while what you yourselves do, of barring from the way of God those who wish to embrace Islam, and of disbelief in God, and of barring from the Sacred Mosque, and of expelling the people of the Sanctuary from it, is greater in crime in the sight of God.

The occasion of revelation supports this meaning and shows that it is what is intended, as will be explained below. The question they asked in this verse was a question of denunciation regarding what the expedition sent by the Prophet (ﷺ) had done.

The "trial" (*fitna*) here means disbelief: that is, your disbelief is greater than the killing carried out by the expedition the Prophet (ﷺ) sent.

It was said: the "trial" means the expulsion of the people of the Sanctuary from it. It was also said: the "trial" here means their seducing the weak among the believers away from their religion until they perish, or the very trial with which the disbelievers were engaged.

This is more probable than the first two views, because disbelief and expulsion have already been mentioned, and they, together with barring, are greater in the sight of God than fighting in the sacred month.

His saying: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ begins a new statement containing God's, Mighty and Majestic, information to the believers that these disbelievers will not cease to persist in fighting you and in enmity toward you, until they turn you back from Islam to disbelief, if they are able to do so and it is made possible for them over you. The restriction by this condition implies that their ability to do so is remote. Then God, glorified is He, warned the believers against being deceived by the disbelievers and against entering into what they want of turning them away from their religion, which is the ultimate aim of what they seek by fighting the believers. So He said: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those—their deeds have become void﴾ to the end of the verse.

Apostasy (*ridda*) is turning back from Islam to disbelief. The restriction by His saying ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ indicates that the deeds of one who apostatizes are only nullified if he dies upon disbelief.

*Habita* (to become void) means: it became null and corrupt. From it comes *habt*, which is the corruption that afflicts livestock in their bellies from eating too much pasture, so that their bellies swell, and they sometimes die from it. In this verse there is a threat to Muslims so that they remain steadfast in the religion of Islam.

The meaning of His saying ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is that for him no status of a Muslim remains in this world, so he does not receive anything of what Muslims are entitled to, does not obtain any share of the shares of Islam, and does not attain any of the reward of the Hereafter that Islam requires and that its adherents deserve.

The scholars have differed over whether apostasy by itself nullifies the deed, or whether it nullifies it only with death upon disbelief. What is obligatory is to apply what the verses stated elsewhere in absolute terms to the restriction found in this verse.

The discussion of the meaning of "abiding" (*khulud*) has already been given earlier.

His saying: ﴿and emigrated﴾. *Hijra* (emigration) means moving from one place to another and leaving the first for the sake of the second. *Hajr* is the opposite of joining, and *tahajur* is mutual severance. Here it means emigration from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam.

*Mujahada* (striving) means exerting one's effort: *jahada*, *mujahada* and *jihad*. *Jihad* and *tajahud* mean expending one's utmost.

His saying: ﴿hope for﴾ means they expect. He said "they hope" after those praiseworthy attributes with which He described them, because no one in this world knows that he will surely enter Paradise, however far he goes in obedience to God.

*Raja'* means hope, as in: "I hoped for so-and-so, I hope for him, a hope and a hoping." Hope may also mean fear, as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning: you do not fear the greatness of God.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* recorded, with a sound chain of narration, from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "he sent a detachment and appointed over them Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, or 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith. When he set out to depart, he wept out of longing and yearning for the Prophet (ﷺ), so he sat down, and he sent 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh in his place and wrote him a letter, and commanded him not to read the letter until he reached such-and-such a place, and said: 'Do not compel any of your companions to march with you.' When he read the letter he said the words of return (*istirja'*) and said: 'Hearing and obedience to God and His Messenger.' He informed them of the matter and read the letter to them. Two men turned back, and the rest went on. They encountered Ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they did not know that this day was from Rajab or Jumada. The polytheists said to the Muslims: 'You have killed in the sacred month.' So God revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ to the end of the verse. Some of them said: 'If they did not incur a sin, then they have no reward.' So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated﴾ to the end of the verse."

Al-Bazzar recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was this.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him that he said: The polytheists barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and turned him back from the Sacred Mosque in a sacred month, so God granted His Prophet victory in a sacred month of the following year, and the polytheists reproached the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for fighting in a sacred month.

So God said: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great matter, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and the expulsion of its people from it, are greater in the sight of God﴾ than fighting in it. And Muhammad (ﷺ) had sent a detachment, and they encountered 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami as he was coming from al-Ta'if at the end of a night of Jumada and the beginning of a night of Rajab. The companions of Muhammad thought that this night was from Jumada, but it was the first of Rajab, and they did not realize it. A man among them killed him and they took what he had with him. The polytheists sent to reproach him for that, and so the verse was revealed.

Ibn Ishaq recorded from him that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the slaying of 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami.

The occasion of revelation has come through many routes in this same way as the foregoing.

Ibn Abi Dawud recorded from 'Ata' ibn Maysara, who said: Fighting in the sacred month was made permissible in *Bara'a* (Surah 9) in His saying: ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein, and fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 36].

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sufyan al-Thawri that he was asked about this verse and said: This is something abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e. superseded by a later ruling), and there is no harm in fighting in the sacred month.

Al-Nahhas, in his work on abrogation (*al-nasikh wa-l-mansukh*, i.e. the abrogating and the abrogated), recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword in *Bara'a*: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And trial is greater than killing﴾ that he said: It is polytheism.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ that he said: They are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Those hope for the mercy of God﴾ that he said: These are the best of this community; God made them people of hope. Whoever hopes, seeks; and whoever fears, flees.

'Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada something similar.
