The "trial" (*fitna*) here means disbelief: that is, your disbelief is greater than the killing carried out by the expedition the Prophet (ﷺ) sent.

It was said: the "trial" means the expulsion of the people of the Sanctuary from it. It was also said: the "trial" here means their seducing the weak among the believers away from their religion until they perish, or the very trial with which the disbelievers were engaged.

This is more probable than the first two views, because disbelief and expulsion have already been mentioned, and they, together with barring, are greater in the sight of God than fighting in the sacred month.

His saying: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ begins a new statement containing God's, Mighty and Majestic, information to the believers that these disbelievers will not cease to persist in fighting you and in enmity toward you, until they turn you back from Islam to disbelief, if they are able to do so and it is made possible for them over you. The restriction by this condition implies that their ability to do so is remote. Then God, glorified is He, warned the believers against being deceived by the disbelievers and against entering into what they want of turning them away from their religion, which is the ultimate aim of what they seek by fighting the believers. So He said: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those—their deeds have become void﴾ to the end of the verse.

Apostasy (*ridda*) is turning back from Islam to disbelief. The restriction by His saying ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ indicates that the deeds of one who apostatizes are only nullified if he dies upon disbelief.

*Habita* (to become void) means: it became null and corrupt. From it comes *habt*, which is the corruption that afflicts livestock in their bellies from eating too much pasture, so that their bellies swell, and they sometimes die from it. In this verse there is a threat to Muslims so that they remain steadfast in the religion of Islam.

The meaning of His saying ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is that for him no status of a Muslim remains in this world, so he does not receive anything of what Muslims are entitled to, does not obtain any share of the shares of Islam, and does not attain any of the reward of the Hereafter that Islam requires and that its adherents deserve.

The scholars have differed over whether apostasy by itself nullifies the deed, or whether it nullifies it only with death upon disbelief. What is obligatory is to apply what the verses stated elsewhere in absolute terms to the restriction found in this verse.

The discussion of the meaning of "abiding" (*khulud*) has already been given earlier.

His saying: ﴿and emigrated﴾. *Hijra* (emigration) means moving from one place to another and leaving the first for the sake of the second. *Hajr* is the opposite of joining, and *tahajur* is mutual severance. Here it means emigration from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam.

*Mujahada* (striving) means exerting one's effort: *jahada*, *mujahada* and *jihad*. *Jihad* and *tajahud* mean expending one's utmost.

His saying: ﴿hope for﴾ means they expect. He said "they hope" after those praiseworthy attributes with which He described them, because no one in this world knows that he will surely enter Paradise, however far he goes in obedience to God.

*Raja'* means hope, as in: "I hoped for so-and-so, I hope for him, a hope and a hoping." Hope may also mean fear, as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning: you do not fear the greatness of God.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* recorded, with a sound chain of narration, from Jundab ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "he sent a detachment and appointed over them Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, or 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith. When he set out to depart, he wept out of longing and yearning for the Prophet (ﷺ), so he sat down, and he sent 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh in his place and wrote him a letter, and commanded him not to read the letter until he reached such-and-such a place, and said: 'Do not compel any of your companions to march with you.' When he read the letter he said the words of return (*istirja'*) and said: 'Hearing and obedience to God and His Messenger.' He informed them of the matter and read the letter to them. Two men turned back, and the rest went on. They encountered Ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they did not know that this day was from Rajab or Jumada. The polytheists said to the Muslims: 'You have killed in the sacred month.' So God revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ to the end of the verse. Some of them said: 'If they did not incur a sin, then they have no reward.' So God revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated﴾ to the end of the verse."

Al-Bazzar recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that the occasion of revelation of the verse was this.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him that he said: The polytheists barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and turned him back from the Sacred Mosque in a sacred month, so God granted His Prophet victory in a sacred month of the following year, and the polytheists reproached the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for fighting in a sacred month.

So God said: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great matter, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and the expulsion of its people from it, are greater in the sight of God﴾ than fighting in it. And Muhammad (ﷺ) had sent a detachment, and they encountered 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami as he was coming from al-Ta'if at the end of a night of Jumada and the beginning of a night of Rajab. The companions of Muhammad thought that this night was from Jumada, but it was the first of Rajab, and they did not realize it. A man among them killed him and they took what he had with him. The polytheists sent to reproach him for that, and so the verse was revealed.

Ibn Ishaq recorded from him that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the slaying of 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami.

The occasion of revelation has come through many routes in this same way as the foregoing.

Ibn Abi Dawud recorded from 'Ata' ibn Maysara, who said: Fighting in the sacred month was made permissible in *Bara'a* (Surah 9) in His saying: ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein, and fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 36].

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Sufyan al-Thawri that he was asked about this verse and said: This is something abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e. superseded by a later ruling), and there is no harm in fighting in the sacred month.

Al-Nahhas, in his work on abrogation (*al-nasikh wa-l-mansukh*, i.e. the abrogating and the abrogated), recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword in *Bara'a*: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And trial is greater than killing﴾ that he said: It is polytheism.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ that he said: They are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His saying: ﴿Those hope for the mercy of God﴾ that he said: These are the best of this community; God made them people of hope. Whoever hopes, seeks; and whoever fears, flees.

'Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada something similar.

The askers in His words, ﴿They ask you about wine⁠﴾, are the believers, as will be explained when the occasion of revelation of the verse is mentioned. *Khamr* (wine) is derived from *khamara*, meaning "he covered." From it comes *khimar* (a woman's head covering), and everything that covers something is said to have *khamara* it. From it also comes the statement, "Cover your vessels" (*khammiru aniyatakum*). It was called *khamr* because it "covers" the intellect (*yakhmuru al-'aql*): that is, it veils and conceals it. From the same root comes the name of the dense, intertwined trees, *al-khamr* (with a fatha on the *mim*), because it covers and conceals what is beneath it. It is said of them: "The land became *akhmarat*," meaning its thick vegetation increased.

The poet said:

*Ala ya Zayd wa-l-Dahhak sira / fa-qad jawaztuma khamra al-tariq*

(Oh Zayd and al-Dahhak, go on, for you have passed the thickets of the road.)

That is, you have passed the low ground. It was also said that wine was called *khamr* because it was left until it matured, as one says, "The dough has *ikhtamara*," meaning it reached its fermentation, and "The opinion was *khummira*," meaning it was left until its direction became clear. And it was said that wine was called *khamr* because it mixes with the intellect, from *mukhamara*, which means "mixing."

These three meanings are close to one another and all are present in wine: it was left until it matured, then it mixed with the intellect and covered it (*fa-khammarathu*), that is, concealed it. *Khamr* is the juice of grapes that has boiled, become strong, and thrown off foam. Whatever else covers the intellect is given the same ruling, as the majority of scholars held.

Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Ikrima, and a group of the jurists of Kufa said: whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than the wine of grapes, is lawful, meaning that what is less than the intoxicating amount in it is lawful.

Abu Hanifa also held that what has lost two-thirds of its volume by cooking is lawful. The disagreement on this is well known.

I have discussed the matter of wine at length in my commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let one refer to it there.

*Al-maysir* (gambling) is derived from *al-yusr*, which means something being due to its owner. One says, "*yasara li kadha*," meaning it became due to me. So he "*yaysiru yusran wa-maysaran*." The *ya'sir* is the one who plays with arrows (*al-qidah*).

It is also said, "*yasara yaysuru*."

The poet said:

*Fa-a'inhum wa-ysir kama yasaru bihi / wa-idha hum nazalu bi-dankin fa-nzil*

(So help them and play with them as they play with it, and when they descend into hardship, then descend with them.)

Al-Azhari said: *al-maysir* is the camel that they used to gamble over. It was called *maysir* because it is divided into portions, as if it were the place of division. Whatever you divide, you have *yassartahu*. And the *ya'sir* is the butcher. He said: this is the original meaning of *ya'sir*. Then the ones who strike with arrows and the ones who gamble over the camel are called *ya'sirun*, because they are butchers, since they were the cause of that.

In *al-Sihah*, it says: "*Yasara al-qawm al-jazur*" means when they cut it up and divided its parts among themselves. Then it says: "It is said *yasara al-qawm*" when they gambled. A man who is *maysir* and *ya'sir* have the same meaning, and the plural is *aysar*.

Al-Nabigha said:

*Inni utammimu ayst̄ari wa-amnahum / mashya al-aydi wa-akswu al-hafnata al-udama*

(I complete my gambling shares, and I give them the stride of the hands, and I clothe the handful with the reddish hides.)

What is meant by *al-maysir* in the verse is the gambling of the Arabs with arrows. A group of the early generation, from among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them, said: everything in which there is gambling, whether dice, chess, or other things, is *al-maysir*, even the children's games with walnuts and knucklebones, except what is permitted, such as betting on horses and drawing lots for the separation of rights.

Malik said: *al-maysir* is of two kinds: the *maysir* of amusement and the *maysir* of gambling. From the *maysir* of amusement are backgammon, chess, and all instruments of entertainment. The *maysir* of gambling is what people wager upon, and everything that is gambled upon is *maysir*. The discussion of this will come at length in Surat al-Ma'ida, at His words: ﴿Wine and gambling are only⁠﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 90].

His words: ﴿Say: In them is great sin⁠﴾ refer to wine and gambling. The sin of wine, that is, the sin of consuming it, arises from the corruption of the intellect of the one who uses it, so there proceeds from him what proceeds from a corrupt intellect: quarreling, insulting, speaking obscenity and falsehood, neglecting the prayers, and all else that is obligatory for him.

As for the sin of gambling, that is, the sin of engaging in it, it arises from poverty, the loss of wealth for no gain, enmity, and the stirring of hearts.

As for the benefits of wine, there is the profit from trading in it. It was also said: what proceeds from it of joy, vigor, strength of heart, steadfastness of the inner self, improvement of the stomach, and strength of sexual potency. Arab poets alluded to some of this. He said:

*Wa-idha sharibtu fa-innani / rabbu al-Khawarnaqi wa-l-Sadiri*

(When I drink, I am lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir.)

*Wa-idha sahawtu fa-innani / rabbu al-Shuwayhati wa-l-Ba'iri*

(And when I am sober, I am lord of al-Shuwayha and the camel.)

Another said:

*Wa-nashraba-ha fa-tatrukuna muluka / wa-usdan ma yunhinhuna al-liqa'*

(We drink it, and it leaves us kings and lions, whom the encounter does not repel.)

And one who pointed out what it contains of harms and benefits said:

*Ra'aytu al-khamra salihatan wa-fiha / khisalun tufsidu al-rajula al-halima*

(I saw wine as good, but in it are qualities that corrupt a man of forbearance.)

*Fa-la wa-llahi ashraba-ha sahihan / wa-la ushfi biha abadan saqima*

(By God, I will not drink it while healthy, nor will I ever cure a sick man with it.)

*Wa-la u'tii biha thamanan hayati / wa-la ad'u laha abadan nadima*

(I will not give my life for its price, nor will I ever call it a boon companion.)

The benefits of gambling: an item comes to a person without toil or exertion, and the joy and generosity that arise when a good share of it comes to him.

The arrows of *al-maysir* are eleven. Seven of them have shares according to the number of portions they hold:

The first is *al-fadhdh* (with a fatha on the *fa*, followed by a dotted letter). It has one mark, and it has a share, and it has a share against it (it gains one and pays one).

The second is *al-tawam* (with a fatha on the *ta* and a sukun on the *waw*, and a fatha on the hamza). It has two marks, and it has two shares, for and against.

The third is *al-raqib*. It has three marks, and it has three shares, for and against.

The fourth is *al-hils* (with two unpointed letters, the first with a kasra and the *lam* sukun). It has four marks, and it has four shares, for and against.

The fifth is *al-nafir* (with the *nun*, *fa*, and an unpointed letter). It is also said *al-nafis* (with an unpointed *sin* in place of the *ra*). It has five marks, and it has five shares, for and against.

The sixth is *al-musbal* (with a damma on the *mim*, a sukun on the unpointed letter, and a fatha on the *ba*). It has six marks, and it has six shares, for and against.

The seventh is *al-mu'alla* (with a damma on the *mim*, a fatha on the unpointed letter, and a shadda on the *lam* with a fatha). It has seven marks, and it has seven shares, for and against. It is the arrow with the greatest share and the highest rank.

So the total of these is twenty-eight shares. The camel is divided into twenty-eight parts; so said al-Asma'i. The remaining four arrows, which have no shares, are: *al-manih* (with a fatha on the *mim*, a kasra on the *nun*, a sukun on the lower *ya'*, and an unpointed letter after it); *al-safih* (with a fatha on the unpointed letter, a kasra on the *fa*, a sukun on the lower *ya'*, and an unpointed letter after it); *al-wafd* (with a fatha on the *waw*, a sukun on the dotted letter, and an unpointed letter after it); and *al-du'f* (with a dotted letter, followed by an unpointed letter and then a *fa*). They placed these four, which have no shares, among the arrows that do, so that the arrows would be many for the one who spins them and strikes with them, and he would find no way to favor anyone.

The one who spins the arrows used to wrap himself in a garment, crouch on his knees, and put his head out of the garment. Then he would put his hand into the *rubaba* (with a kasra on the unpointed letter, followed by a dotted *ba'*, and after the *alif* another *ba'*), which is the bag in which the arrows were placed. He would draw out an arrow in the name of each man. Whoever drew an arrow that had a share took his share; whoever drew an arrow that had no share took nothing and was charged the price of the camel. They used to give those shares to the poor.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Asma'i erred in his statement that the camel is divided into twenty-eight parts. He said: it is divided only into ten parts.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit⁠﴾: He, glory be to Him, informed that wine and gambling, even though there is benefit in them, the sin that befalls those who engage in them is greater than this benefit. For there is no good that equals the corruption of the intellect caused by wine, since there arises from it evils that cannot be counted. Likewise, there is no good in gambling that equals the risk to wealth it involves, the exposure to poverty, and the provoking of enmities that lead to the shedding of blood and the violation of sacred things.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *kathir* with the *tha'* (with three dots).

The rest read it with the *ba'* (with one dot).

Ubayy read: ﴿And their sin is nearer than their benefit⁠﴾.

His words: ﴿Say: The surplus⁠﴾: Al-Jumhur read it in the accusative (*al-'afwa*).

Abu 'Amr alone read it in the nominative (*al-'afwu*).

It is differently reported from Ibn Kathir. The nominative was read by al-Hasan and Qatada.

Al-Nahhas said: If *dha* is taken to mean *alladhi* (which), then the preferred reading is the nominative, in the sense: "What they spend is the surplus." If *ma* and *dha* are taken as one thing, then the preferred reading is the accusative, in the sense: "Say: they spend the surplus." *Al-'afw* is what is easy and comes without difficulty to the heart. The meaning is: spend what exceeds your needs, without exerting yourselves beyond your capacity. It was also said that it is what remains beyond the provision of one's dependents.

The majority of scholars said: it refers to voluntary expenditure. It was also said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukha*, meaning superseded by *naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of the obligatory zakat. It was also said that it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and that there is a right in wealth beyond zakat.

His words: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs⁠﴾: that is, concerning the matter of expenditure.

His words: ﴿In this world and the Hereafter⁠﴾ are connected to His words: ﴿that you may reflect⁠﴾: that is, you may reflect upon their matter, so you withhold from your wealth what you use to sustain the livelihood of your worldly life, and you spend the rest on the means that bring you near to the Hereafter. It was also said that there is inversion in the sentence: thus God makes clear to you the signs in this world and the Hereafter, so that you may reflect on this world and its passing, and on the Hereafter and its permanence, and so you turn away from the hasty to the deferred. It was also said that it may refer to His words: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit⁠﴾, that you may reflect on the matter of this world and the Hereafter. But this is not a good interpretation.

His words: ﴿And they ask you about orphans⁠﴾: this verse was revealed after the revelation of His words: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 152; al-Isra': 34], and His words: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans⁠﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]. The matter had become difficult for the guardians, as its explanation will come, God willing. So this verse was revealed.

What is meant by *al-islah* (reform, setting right) here is mixing with them in a way that improves their property, for that is better than avoiding them.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of disposing of orphans' property by guardians and executors, through sale, partnership (*mudaraba*), hire, and the like.

His words: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers⁠﴾: Scholars differed about the interpretation of mixing with them. Abu 'Ubayda said: mixing with orphans means that one of them has property and the one who is responsible for him finds it difficult to keep his food apart from him, and has no choice but to mix it with his dependents. So he takes from the orphan's property what he sees as sufficient for him, by estimation, and combines it with his household's expenses. In this, there may be excess or shortfall. So this verse indicates a concession, and it abrogates what came before it. It was also said that mixing means living together with orphans. It was also said that it means intermarriage with them.

The better view is not to restrict mixing to one particular type, but to include every form of mixing, as is derived from the conditional sentence.

His words: ﴿they are your brothers⁠﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, they are your brothers in religion.

In His words: ﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer⁠﴾ is a warning to guardians: that is, nothing of that is hidden from God, and He will recompense each person according to his deeds. Whoever sets things right does so for his own self, and whoever corrupts does so against his own self.

His words: ﴿He could have put you in distress⁠﴾: that is, had He willed, He would have made that difficult for you, burdensome for you, and brought you into what involves hardship and difficulty. It was also said that *al-'anat* here means destruction. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, while the root of *al-'anat* is hardship. Ibn al-Anbari said: the root of *al-'anat* is severity, and then it was transferred to the meaning of destruction.

His words: ﴿Mighty⁠﴾: that is, nothing can be withheld from Him, for He is dominant and cannot be overcome. ﴿Wise⁠﴾: He disposes of His dominion according to what His will and wisdom require, and it is not for you to choose for yourselves.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 219–220 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who declared it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, on the authority of Umar, that he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine, for it takes away wealth and reason." Then there was revealed ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, meaning this verse. Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine." Then there was revealed in Surah al-Nisa' ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he stood for prayer, would call out: "Let no intoxicated person approach prayer." Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine." Then there was revealed the verse that is in al-Ma'idah, and Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and when it reached ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], Umar said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Anas, who said: "We used to drink wine. Then there was revealed ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, the verse, and we said: 'We drink from it what benefits us.' Then there was revealed in al-Ma'idah ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling﴾, the verse [al-Ma'idah: 90]." They said: "O Allah, we have desisted."

Abu Ubayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar, who said: "Al-maysir is gambling (al-qimar)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas the like of it, and he said: "A man in the Jahiliyyah would stake his family and his wealth, and whichever of the two won over his companion would take away his family and his wealth."

As for His saying ﴿In both of them is a great sin﴾, meaning: what is lost of the religion when they are drunk; ﴿and benefits for people﴾, He says: in what they obtain of its pleasure and joy when they drink; ﴿but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, He says: what is lost of the religion, the sin in it is greater than what they obtain of its pleasure and joy when they drink it. Then Allah revealed after that ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], the verse, so they would not drink it near the prayer; when they had prayed the night prayer (al-'Isha') they would drink it. Then some Muslims drank it, and some of them fought with others and spoke what Allah does not approve of in speech, so Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], the verse, and He prohibited wine and forbade it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: "Their benefits were before the prohibition, and their sin is after He prohibited them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority that "a group of the Companions, when they were commanded to spend in the way of Allah, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We do not know what this spending is that we have been commanded to give from our wealth, so what should we spend from it?' Then Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾. Before that, a man would spend his wealth until he had nothing left to give in charity, nor anything to eat until someone gave him charity."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: "Al-'afw is what is not evident in your wealth, and this was before zakat was made obligatory."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated on his authority regarding the verse: "Al-'afw is what exceeds your family's needs," and in another wording he said: "The surplus beyond dependents."

Ibn Jarir narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿Say: the surplus﴾ that he said: "No fixed obligation was prescribed in it." Then he said ﴿Take what is given freely, and enjoin what is right﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. Then obligations were revealed after that, specified.

It is established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that which is given out of self-sufficiency, and begin with those you support."

Something similar is established in the Sahih as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam.

There are many hadiths on this matter.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿upon this world and the Hereafter﴾, he said: meaning in the passing away and perishing of this world and the coming and enduring of the Hereafter.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated on his authority that he said: "When Allah revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra': 34] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], the verse, those who had an orphan in their care separated their food from his food and their drink from his drink, and would set aside some of his food, which would be kept for him until he ate it or it spoiled and was thrown away. This was difficult for them, so they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾, the verse."

So they mixed their food with his food and their drink with his drink.

Something similar has been narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And if you mix with them﴾ that he said: "Mixing is that he drinks from your milk and you drink from his milk, he eats from your bowl and you eat from his bowl, he eats from your fruit and you eat from his fruit." ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾: He knows who deliberately consumes the orphan's property, and who avoids it and does not spare effort in putting it right. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾: He says, if He had willed, He would not have permitted for you what would make you suffer, what you did not intend.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿would have burdened you﴾: He says, He would have made you feel distressed and constrained, but He made things easy and facilitated them.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾ that he said: "And if He had willed, He would have made what you took from the orphans' property a cause of ruin."

The askers in His words, ﴿They ask you about wine⁠﴾, are the believers, as will be explained when the occasion of revelation of the verse is mentioned. *Khamr* (wine) is derived from *khamara*, meaning "he covered." From it comes *khimar* (a woman's head covering), and everything that covers something is said to have *khamara* it. From it also comes the statement, "Cover your vessels" (*khammiru aniyatakum*). It was called *khamr* because it "covers" the intellect (*yakhmuru al-'aql*): that is, it veils and conceals it. From the same root comes the name of the dense, intertwined trees, *al-khamr* (with a fatha on the *mim*), because it covers and conceals what is beneath it. It is said of them: "The land became *akhmarat*," meaning its thick vegetation increased.

The poet said:

*Ala ya Zayd wa-l-Dahhak sira / fa-qad jawaztuma khamra al-tariq*

(Oh Zayd and al-Dahhak, go on, for you have passed the thickets of the road.)

That is, you have passed the low ground. It was also said that wine was called *khamr* because it was left until it matured, as one says, "The dough has *ikhtamara*," meaning it reached its fermentation, and "The opinion was *khummira*," meaning it was left until its direction became clear. And it was said that wine was called *khamr* because it mixes with the intellect, from *mukhamara*, which means "mixing."

These three meanings are close to one another and all are present in wine: it was left until it matured, then it mixed with the intellect and covered it (*fa-khammarathu*), that is, concealed it. *Khamr* is the juice of grapes that has boiled, become strong, and thrown off foam. Whatever else covers the intellect is given the same ruling, as the majority of scholars held.

Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Ikrima, and a group of the jurists of Kufa said: whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than the wine of grapes, is lawful, meaning that what is less than the intoxicating amount in it is lawful.

Abu Hanifa also held that what has lost two-thirds of its volume by cooking is lawful. The disagreement on this is well known.

I have discussed the matter of wine at length in my commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, so let one refer to it there.

*Al-maysir* (gambling) is derived from *al-yusr*, which means something being due to its owner. One says, "*yasara li kadha*," meaning it became due to me. So he "*yaysiru yusran wa-maysaran*." The *ya'sir* is the one who plays with arrows (*al-qidah*).

It is also said, "*yasara yaysuru*."

The poet said:

*Fa-a'inhum wa-ysir kama yasaru bihi / wa-idha hum nazalu bi-dankin fa-nzil*

(So help them and play with them as they play with it, and when they descend into hardship, then descend with them.)

Al-Azhari said: *al-maysir* is the camel that they used to gamble over. It was called *maysir* because it is divided into portions, as if it were the place of division. Whatever you divide, you have *yassartahu*. And the *ya'sir* is the butcher. He said: this is the original meaning of *ya'sir*. Then the ones who strike with arrows and the ones who gamble over the camel are called *ya'sirun*, because they are butchers, since they were the cause of that.

In *al-Sihah*, it says: "*Yasara al-qawm al-jazur*" means when they cut it up and divided its parts among themselves. Then it says: "It is said *yasara al-qawm*" when they gambled. A man who is *maysir* and *ya'sir* have the same meaning, and the plural is *aysar*.

Al-Nabigha said:

*Inni utammimu ayst̄ari wa-amnahum / mashya al-aydi wa-akswu al-hafnata al-udama*

(I complete my gambling shares, and I give them the stride of the hands, and I clothe the handful with the reddish hides.)

What is meant by *al-maysir* in the verse is the gambling of the Arabs with arrows. A group of the early generation, from among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them, said: everything in which there is gambling, whether dice, chess, or other things, is *al-maysir*, even the children's games with walnuts and knucklebones, except what is permitted, such as betting on horses and drawing lots for the separation of rights.

Malik said: *al-maysir* is of two kinds: the *maysir* of amusement and the *maysir* of gambling. From the *maysir* of amusement are backgammon, chess, and all instruments of entertainment. The *maysir* of gambling is what people wager upon, and everything that is gambled upon is *maysir*. The discussion of this will come at length in Surat al-Ma'ida, at His words: ﴿Wine and gambling are only⁠﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 90].

His words: ﴿Say: In them is great sin⁠﴾ refer to wine and gambling. The sin of wine, that is, the sin of consuming it, arises from the corruption of the intellect of the one who uses it, so there proceeds from him what proceeds from a corrupt intellect: quarreling, insulting, speaking obscenity and falsehood, neglecting the prayers, and all else that is obligatory for him.

As for the sin of gambling, that is, the sin of engaging in it, it arises from poverty, the loss of wealth for no gain, enmity, and the stirring of hearts.

As for the benefits of wine, there is the profit from trading in it. It was also said: what proceeds from it of joy, vigor, strength of heart, steadfastness of the inner self, improvement of the stomach, and strength of sexual potency. Arab poets alluded to some of this. He said:

*Wa-idha sharibtu fa-innani / rabbu al-Khawarnaqi wa-l-Sadiri*

(When I drink, I am lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir.)

*Wa-idha sahawtu fa-innani / rabbu al-Shuwayhati wa-l-Ba'iri*

(And when I am sober, I am lord of al-Shuwayha and the camel.)

Another said:

*Wa-nashraba-ha fa-tatrukuna muluka / wa-usdan ma yunhinhuna al-liqa'*

(We drink it, and it leaves us kings and lions, whom the encounter does not repel.)

And one who pointed out what it contains of harms and benefits said:

*Ra'aytu al-khamra salihatan wa-fiha / khisalun tufsidu al-rajula al-halima*

(I saw wine as good, but in it are qualities that corrupt a man of forbearance.)

*Fa-la wa-llahi ashraba-ha sahihan / wa-la ushfi biha abadan saqima*

(By God, I will not drink it while healthy, nor will I ever cure a sick man with it.)

*Wa-la u'tii biha thamanan hayati / wa-la ad'u laha abadan nadima*

(I will not give my life for its price, nor will I ever call it a boon companion.)

The benefits of gambling: an item comes to a person without toil or exertion, and the joy and generosity that arise when a good share of it comes to him.

The arrows of *al-maysir* are eleven. Seven of them have shares according to the number of portions they hold:

The first is *al-fadhdh* (with a fatha on the *fa*, followed by a dotted letter). It has one mark, and it has a share, and it has a share against it (it gains one and pays one).

The second is *al-tawam* (with a fatha on the *ta* and a sukun on the *waw*, and a fatha on the hamza). It has two marks, and it has two shares, for and against.

The third is *al-raqib*. It has three marks, and it has three shares, for and against.

The fourth is *al-hils* (with two unpointed letters, the first with a kasra and the *lam* sukun). It has four marks, and it has four shares, for and against.

The fifth is *al-nafir* (with the *nun*, *fa*, and an unpointed letter). It is also said *al-nafis* (with an unpointed *sin* in place of the *ra*). It has five marks, and it has five shares, for and against.

The sixth is *al-musbal* (with a damma on the *mim*, a sukun on the unpointed letter, and a fatha on the *ba*). It has six marks, and it has six shares, for and against.

The seventh is *al-mu'alla* (with a damma on the *mim*, a fatha on the unpointed letter, and a shadda on the *lam* with a fatha). It has seven marks, and it has seven shares, for and against. It is the arrow with the greatest share and the highest rank.

So the total of these is twenty-eight shares. The camel is divided into twenty-eight parts; so said al-Asma'i. The remaining four arrows, which have no shares, are: *al-manih* (with a fatha on the *mim*, a kasra on the *nun*, a sukun on the lower *ya'*, and an unpointed letter after it); *al-safih* (with a fatha on the unpointed letter, a kasra on the *fa*, a sukun on the lower *ya'*, and an unpointed letter after it); *al-wafd* (with a fatha on the *waw*, a sukun on the dotted letter, and an unpointed letter after it); and *al-du'f* (with a dotted letter, followed by an unpointed letter and then a *fa*). They placed these four, which have no shares, among the arrows that do, so that the arrows would be many for the one who spins them and strikes with them, and he would find no way to favor anyone.

The one who spins the arrows used to wrap himself in a garment, crouch on his knees, and put his head out of the garment. Then he would put his hand into the *rubaba* (with a kasra on the unpointed letter, followed by a dotted *ba'*, and after the *alif* another *ba'*), which is the bag in which the arrows were placed. He would draw out an arrow in the name of each man. Whoever drew an arrow that had a share took his share; whoever drew an arrow that had no share took nothing and was charged the price of the camel. They used to give those shares to the poor.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Asma'i erred in his statement that the camel is divided into twenty-eight parts. He said: it is divided only into ten parts.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit⁠﴾: He, glory be to Him, informed that wine and gambling, even though there is benefit in them, the sin that befalls those who engage in them is greater than this benefit. For there is no good that equals the corruption of the intellect caused by wine, since there arises from it evils that cannot be counted. Likewise, there is no good in gambling that equals the risk to wealth it involves, the exposure to poverty, and the provoking of enmities that lead to the shedding of blood and the violation of sacred things.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *kathir* with the *tha'* (with three dots).

The rest read it with the *ba'* (with one dot).

Ubayy read: ﴿And their sin is nearer than their benefit⁠﴾.

His words: ﴿Say: The surplus⁠﴾: Al-Jumhur read it in the accusative (*al-'afwa*).

Abu 'Amr alone read it in the nominative (*al-'afwu*).

It is differently reported from Ibn Kathir. The nominative was read by al-Hasan and Qatada.

Al-Nahhas said: If *dha* is taken to mean *alladhi* (which), then the preferred reading is the nominative, in the sense: "What they spend is the surplus." If *ma* and *dha* are taken as one thing, then the preferred reading is the accusative, in the sense: "Say: they spend the surplus." *Al-'afw* is what is easy and comes without difficulty to the heart. The meaning is: spend what exceeds your needs, without exerting yourselves beyond your capacity. It was also said that it is what remains beyond the provision of one's dependents.

The majority of scholars said: it refers to voluntary expenditure. It was also said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukha*, meaning superseded by *naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of the obligatory zakat. It was also said that it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and that there is a right in wealth beyond zakat.

His words: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs⁠﴾: that is, concerning the matter of expenditure.

His words: ﴿In this world and the Hereafter⁠﴾ are connected to His words: ﴿that you may reflect⁠﴾: that is, you may reflect upon their matter, so you withhold from your wealth what you use to sustain the livelihood of your worldly life, and you spend the rest on the means that bring you near to the Hereafter. It was also said that there is inversion in the sentence: thus God makes clear to you the signs in this world and the Hereafter, so that you may reflect on this world and its passing, and on the Hereafter and its permanence, and so you turn away from the hasty to the deferred. It was also said that it may refer to His words: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit⁠﴾, that you may reflect on the matter of this world and the Hereafter. But this is not a good interpretation.

His words: ﴿And they ask you about orphans⁠﴾: this verse was revealed after the revelation of His words: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 152; al-Isra': 34], and His words: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans⁠﴾ [al-Nisa': 10]. The matter had become difficult for the guardians, as its explanation will come, God willing. So this verse was revealed.

What is meant by *al-islah* (reform, setting right) here is mixing with them in a way that improves their property, for that is better than avoiding them.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of disposing of orphans' property by guardians and executors, through sale, partnership (*mudaraba*), hire, and the like.

His words: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers⁠﴾: Scholars differed about the interpretation of mixing with them. Abu 'Ubayda said: mixing with orphans means that one of them has property and the one who is responsible for him finds it difficult to keep his food apart from him, and has no choice but to mix it with his dependents. So he takes from the orphan's property what he sees as sufficient for him, by estimation, and combines it with his household's expenses. In this, there may be excess or shortfall. So this verse indicates a concession, and it abrogates what came before it. It was also said that mixing means living together with orphans. It was also said that it means intermarriage with them.

The better view is not to restrict mixing to one particular type, but to include every form of mixing, as is derived from the conditional sentence.

His words: ﴿they are your brothers⁠﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, they are your brothers in religion.

In His words: ﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer⁠﴾ is a warning to guardians: that is, nothing of that is hidden from God, and He will recompense each person according to his deeds. Whoever sets things right does so for his own self, and whoever corrupts does so against his own self.

His words: ﴿He could have put you in distress⁠﴾: that is, had He willed, He would have made that difficult for you, burdensome for you, and brought you into what involves hardship and difficulty. It was also said that *al-'anat* here means destruction. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, while the root of *al-'anat* is hardship. Ibn al-Anbari said: the root of *al-'anat* is severity, and then it was transferred to the meaning of destruction.

His words: ﴿Mighty⁠﴾: that is, nothing can be withheld from Him, for He is dominant and cannot be overcome. ﴿Wise⁠﴾: He disposes of His dominion according to what His will and wisdom require, and it is not for you to choose for yourselves.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 219–220 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who declared it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, on the authority of Umar, that he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine, for it takes away wealth and reason." Then there was revealed ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, meaning this verse. Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine." Then there was revealed in Surah al-Nisa' ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whenever he stood for prayer, would call out: "Let no intoxicated person approach prayer." Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient clarification regarding wine." Then there was revealed the verse that is in al-Ma'idah, and Umar was summoned and it was recited to him, and when it reached ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], Umar said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Anas, who said: "We used to drink wine. Then there was revealed ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, the verse, and we said: 'We drink from it what benefits us.' Then there was revealed in al-Ma'idah ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling﴾, the verse [al-Ma'idah: 90]." They said: "O Allah, we have desisted."

Abu Ubayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar, who said: "Al-maysir is gambling (al-qimar)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas the like of it, and he said: "A man in the Jahiliyyah would stake his family and his wealth, and whichever of the two won over his companion would take away his family and his wealth."

As for His saying ﴿In both of them is a great sin﴾, meaning: what is lost of the religion when they are drunk; ﴿and benefits for people﴾, He says: in what they obtain of its pleasure and joy when they drink; ﴿but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, He says: what is lost of the religion, the sin in it is greater than what they obtain of its pleasure and joy when they drink it. Then Allah revealed after that ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], the verse, so they would not drink it near the prayer; when they had prayed the night prayer (al-'Isha') they would drink it. Then some Muslims drank it, and some of them fought with others and spoke what Allah does not approve of in speech, so Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], the verse, and He prohibited wine and forbade it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: "Their benefits were before the prohibition, and their sin is after He prohibited them."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority that "a group of the Companions, when they were commanded to spend in the way of Allah, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We do not know what this spending is that we have been commanded to give from our wealth, so what should we spend from it?' Then Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾. Before that, a man would spend his wealth until he had nothing left to give in charity, nor anything to eat until someone gave him charity."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: "Al-'afw is what is not evident in your wealth, and this was before zakat was made obligatory."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated on his authority regarding the verse: "Al-'afw is what exceeds your family's needs," and in another wording he said: "The surplus beyond dependents."

Ibn Jarir narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿Say: the surplus﴾ that he said: "No fixed obligation was prescribed in it." Then he said ﴿Take what is given freely, and enjoin what is right﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. Then obligations were revealed after that, specified.

It is established in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that which is given out of self-sufficiency, and begin with those you support."

Something similar is established in the Sahih as a marfu' hadith from the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam.

There are many hadiths on this matter.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿upon this world and the Hereafter﴾, he said: meaning in the passing away and perishing of this world and the coming and enduring of the Hereafter.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated on his authority that he said: "When Allah revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra': 34] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], the verse, those who had an orphan in their care separated their food from his food and their drink from his drink, and would set aside some of his food, which would be kept for him until he ate it or it spoiled and was thrown away. This was difficult for them, so they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: ﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾, the verse."

So they mixed their food with his food and their drink with his drink.

Something similar has been narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And if you mix with them﴾ that he said: "Mixing is that he drinks from your milk and you drink from his milk, he eats from your bowl and you eat from his bowl, he eats from your fruit and you eat from his fruit." ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾: He knows who deliberately consumes the orphan's property, and who avoids it and does not spare effort in putting it right. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾: He says, if He had willed, He would not have permitted for you what would make you suffer, what you did not intend.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿would have burdened you﴾: He says, He would have made you feel distressed and constrained, but He made things easy and facilitated them.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority regarding His saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾ that he said: "And if He had willed, He would have made what you took from the orphans' property a cause of ruin."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 221–222:

His saying: "Wa la tankihu" (and do not marry). The majority of readers recite it with a fatha on the tā' (tankihū, "tankihū" with fatḥa), while it was read in the shādh (irregular) readings with a ḍamma on it. It has been said that the meaning is: the one who was marrying her used to marry her to himself (i.e., the woman was given in marriage by the man who wished to marry her, or the prohibition addresses the guardians who would give women in marriage to polytheists).

In this verse there is a prohibition against marrying polytheist women (mushrikāt). It has been said that what is meant by "mushrikāt" is the idolatresses (wathaniyyāt). It has also been said that it encompasses the women of the People of the Book (kitābiyyāt), because the People of the Book are polytheists: ﴿And the Jews say, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. The people of knowledge differed concerning this verse. One group said: Allah has forbidden the marriage of polytheist women in it, and the women of the People of the Book are included in the general category; then the verse of al-Mā'idah came and specified the women of the People of the Book out of this generality.

This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mālik, Sufyān ibn Saʿīd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUmar, and al-Awzāʿī.

Another group held that this verse abrogates (nāsikhah li-) the verse of al-Mā'idah, and that it is forbidden to marry the women of the People of the Book and the polytheist women. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shāfiʿī, and a group of people of knowledge said likewise.

The claim that this verse abrogates the verse of al-Mā'idah is answered by saying that Sūrat al-Baqarah was among the first to be revealed, and Sūrat al-Mā'idah was among the last to be revealed.

The first opinion is the preponderant one.

It was said by ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ṭalḥah, Jābir, Ḥudhayfah, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Ṭāwūs, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, along with those who preceded them, as reported by al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from those mentioned, and added ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and said: "Nothing is authentically reported from anyone among the early generations that they forbade that."

Some people of knowledge said: the term "mushrik" does not include the People of the Book, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish that any good be sent down upon you from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], and He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not [going to be] separated [from their disbelief]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. And even if we suppose that the word "mushrikīn" is general, this generality is specified by the verse of al-Mā'idah, as we have mentioned.

His saying: ﴿And a believing slave-woman﴾, i.e., and a believing female slave. It has been said that what is meant by "amah" is a free woman, because all people are the servants of Allah and His bondsmen. But the first is better, because of what will come, since it is the apparent meaning of the wording, and because it is more eloquent: preferring a believing female slave over a polytheist free woman implies, by a stronger inference, the preference of a believing free woman over a polytheist free woman.

His saying: ﴿Even though she pleases you﴾, i.e., even though the polytheist woman pleases you because of her beauty, wealth, or nobility. This clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah).

His saying: ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheist men﴾, i.e., do not marry them to believing women, ﴿until they believe﴾. Al-Qurṭubī said: The Community is in agreement that a polytheist may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, because of the disgrace this would bring upon Islam. And the readers agreed on the ḍamma on the tā' in "tunkiḥū" (in the sense of giving in marriage).

His saying: "wa la ʿabdun" (and a believing slave): the discussion of it is like the discussion of "wa la amah," and the preference is like that preference.

His saying: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾: "ulāʾika" refers to the polytheist men and women, ﴿they invite to the Fire﴾, i.e., to the deeds that necessitate the Fire. Thus in intermarriage with them, association with them, and companionship with them there is a great danger into which it is not permissible for believers to expose themselves or enter. ﴿But Allah invites to Paradise﴾, i.e., to the deeds that necessitate Paradise. It has been said that what is meant is that the friends of Allah are the believers, who invite to Paradise.

His saying: ﴿by His permission﴾, i.e., by His command, as said by al-Zajjāj. It has been said: by His facilitation and granting of success, as said by the author of al-Kashshāf.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Abū Marthad al-Ghanawī, who asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to marry ʿAnāq, who was of considerable beauty and was a polytheist, while Abū Marthad was at that time a Muslim. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she pleases me.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾, that he said: "Allah excepted from this the women of the People of the Book, when He said: ﴿And chaste women from those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 5]."

This meaning has been reported from him through several chains.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾, that he meant the people of idols.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and al-Bayhaqī reported from Mujāhid something similar, and likewise ʿAbd al-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Qatādah something similar as well.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from al-Nakhaʿī something similar.

Ibn Abī Shaybah and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿUmar that he disliked marrying the women of the People of the Book, and he interpreted: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾.

(p-145) Al-Bukhārī reported from him, who said: "Allah has forbidden the marriage of polytheist women to Muslims, and I know of no polytheism greater than a woman saying that her lord is ʿĪsā, or that he is one of the servants of Allah."

al-Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAsākir reported through the chain of al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman﴾, that he said: It was revealed concerning "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah, who had a black slave-woman, and he became angry with her and slapped her. Then he was overcome with remorse and went to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of her story. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'What is she, O ʿAbd Allāh?' He said: 'She fasts, prays, performs wuḍū' well, and testifies that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah.' The Prophet said: 'O ʿAbd Allāh, this is a believer.' ʿAbd Allāh said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, I will free her and marry her.' He did so, and some Muslims criticized him, saying: 'He married a slave-woman!' They wanted to marry into polytheists and give their women to them out of desire for their lineage. So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman.﴾"

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported the like of it from al-Suddī.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, concerning His saying: ﴿And a believing slave-woman﴾, that he said: "We have been informed that she was a black slave-woman of Ḥudhayfah, and Ḥudhayfah freed her and married her."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, who said: "Marriage requires a guardian (walī) in the Book of Allah," then he recited: ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheist men until they believe.﴾

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 221–222:

His saying: "Wa la tankihu" (and do not marry). The majority of readers recite it with a fatha on the tā' (tankihū, "tankihū" with fatḥa), while it was read in the shādh (irregular) readings with a ḍamma on it. It has been said that the meaning is: the one who was marrying her used to marry her to himself (i.e., the woman was given in marriage by the man who wished to marry her, or the prohibition addresses the guardians who would give women in marriage to polytheists).

In this verse there is a prohibition against marrying polytheist women (mushrikāt). It has been said that what is meant by "mushrikāt" is the idolatresses (wathaniyyāt). It has also been said that it encompasses the women of the People of the Book (kitābiyyāt), because the People of the Book are polytheists: ﴿And the Jews say, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. The people of knowledge differed concerning this verse. One group said: Allah has forbidden the marriage of polytheist women in it, and the women of the People of the Book are included in the general category; then the verse of al-Mā'idah came and specified the women of the People of the Book out of this generality.

This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mālik, Sufyān ibn Saʿīd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUmar, and al-Awzāʿī.

Another group held that this verse abrogates (nāsikhah li-) the verse of al-Mā'idah, and that it is forbidden to marry the women of the People of the Book and the polytheist women. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shāfiʿī, and a group of people of knowledge said likewise.

The claim that this verse abrogates the verse of al-Mā'idah is answered by saying that Sūrat al-Baqarah was among the first to be revealed, and Sūrat al-Mā'idah was among the last to be revealed.

The first opinion is the preponderant one.

It was said by ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ṭalḥah, Jābir, Ḥudhayfah, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Ṭāwūs, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, along with those who preceded them, as reported by al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from those mentioned, and added ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and said: "Nothing is authentically reported from anyone among the early generations that they forbade that."

Some people of knowledge said: the term "mushrik" does not include the People of the Book, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists do not wish that any good be sent down upon you from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], and He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not [going to be] separated [from their disbelief]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. And even if we suppose that the word "mushrikīn" is general, this generality is specified by the verse of al-Mā'idah, as we have mentioned.

His saying: ﴿And a believing slave-woman﴾, i.e., and a believing female slave. It has been said that what is meant by "amah" is a free woman, because all people are the servants of Allah and His bondsmen. But the first is better, because of what will come, since it is the apparent meaning of the wording, and because it is more eloquent: preferring a believing female slave over a polytheist free woman implies, by a stronger inference, the preference of a believing free woman over a polytheist free woman.

His saying: ﴿Even though she pleases you﴾, i.e., even though the polytheist woman pleases you because of her beauty, wealth, or nobility. This clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah).

His saying: ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheist men﴾, i.e., do not marry them to believing women, ﴿until they believe﴾. Al-Qurṭubī said: The Community is in agreement that a polytheist may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, because of the disgrace this would bring upon Islam. And the readers agreed on the ḍamma on the tā' in "tunkiḥū" (in the sense of giving in marriage).

His saying: "wa la ʿabdun" (and a believing slave): the discussion of it is like the discussion of "wa la amah," and the preference is like that preference.

His saying: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾: "ulāʾika" refers to the polytheist men and women, ﴿they invite to the Fire﴾, i.e., to the deeds that necessitate the Fire. Thus in intermarriage with them, association with them, and companionship with them there is a great danger into which it is not permissible for believers to expose themselves or enter. ﴿But Allah invites to Paradise﴾, i.e., to the deeds that necessitate Paradise. It has been said that what is meant is that the friends of Allah are the believers, who invite to Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 223–224 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: *al-maḥīḍ* is *al-ḥayḍ* (menstruation, a term for the monthly bleeding), and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is said: "The woman menstruated (*ḥāḍat*) a menstruation (*ḥayḍan*) and a *maḥīḍ*, so she is *ḥā'iḍ* and *ḥā'iḍah*." Thus al-Farrā' said, and he recited:

*Like a menstruating woman with whom one commits adultery while she is not pure.*

Women are described as *ḥuyyaḍ* and *ḥawā'iḍ*. *Al-ḥīḍah* with a kasra is the single occurrence. It was said that it is a noun. It was also said that *al-maḥīḍ* refers to the time and the place, and that this is a metaphorical usage for both.

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī said: *al-maḥīḍ* is the name of *al-ḥayḍ*. Similar to it is the saying of Ru'ba:

*To You I complain of the hardship of the livelihood*

meaning, of the *'aysh* (livelihood). The root of this word is from flowing and gushing forth. It is said: "The torrent (*al-sayl*) gushed and overflowed (*ḥāḍa wa fāḍa*)," and "the tree menstruated (*ḥāḍat al-shajarah*)," meaning its moisture flowed. From this is also *al-ḥayḍ*, meaning *al-ḥawḍ* (the pool), because water flows into it (*yaḥūḍu ilayhi*), that is, it flows.

His saying: ﴿Say: It is an injury﴾, meaning: say, it is a thing that causes harm (*yataʾadhdhā bihi*), that is, by its smell. *Al-adhā* is a metaphor for filth, and it is also applied to a hateful speech. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:264]. From it also is His saying: ﴿And disregard their harm﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:48].

His saying: ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾, meaning: avoid them during the time of menstruation if *al-maḥīḍ* is taken as a verbal noun, or in the place of menstruation if it is taken as a noun.

The intended meaning of this *i'tizāl* (keeping away) is abstaining from intercourse, not abstaining from sitting with them or from physical contact, for that is permissible. Rather, enjoyment of them is permitted in what lies beyond the genital area, or in what is below the waist-wrap (*izār*), according to a difference of opinion on this. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbās and 'Ubaydah al-Salmānī, that a man must keep away from his wife's bedding when she menstruates, this is not correct. There is no disagreement among the scholars on the prohibition of intercourse with a menstruating woman, and this is known from the necessity of the religion (*ḍarūrat al-dīn*).

His saying: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure﴾. Nāfi', Abū 'Amr, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, and 'Āṣim in the transmission of Abū Bakr read *yaṭṭahharna* with a doubled *ṭā'* and an open vowel, and with an open *hā'* and doubled as well.

In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd, it is *wa-yatatahharna*. *Al-Ṭuhr* is the cessation of menstruation, and *al-tatahhur* is washing (*al-ightisāl*).

Because of the difference among the readers (*qurrā'*), the scholars differed. The majority held that a menstruating woman is not lawful for her husband to have intercourse with until she purifies herself with water.

Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī and Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr said: if the menstruating woman becomes pure and performs *tayammum* (dry ablution) where there is no water, she becomes lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed.

Mujāhid and 'Ikrimah said: the cessation of the bleeding makes her lawful to her husband, but she should perform *wuḍū'* (ablution).

Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf, and Muḥammad said: if her bleeding stops after ten days have passed, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her before she bathes. If the cessation was before the ten days, it is not permitted until she bathes or the time of prayer enters upon her.

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī preferred the doubled reading.

The better view is that Allah the Glorious made two limits for the permissibility, as the two readings require: one is the cessation of the bleeding, and the other is purification from it. The second limit includes an addition beyond the first, so it is necessary to adopt it.

That the second limit is the one that counts is shown by His saying after that: ﴿Then when they have purified themselves﴾, for this indicates that what counts is purification, not merely the cessation of bleeding.

It is established that the two readings are like the two verses. Just as it is necessary to combine two verses of which one contains an addition by acting on that addition, so too it is necessary to combine the two readings.

His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾, meaning: have intercourse with them. He expressed this by the term "coming" (*al-ityān*).

The intended meaning is that they have intercourse with them in the place of approach that Allah has permitted, which is the front passage (*al-qubul*). It was said that *min ḥaythu* here means *fī ḥaythu* (in which), as in His saying: ﴿When it is called for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:9], meaning on the day of Friday, and His saying: ﴿What have they created from the earth?﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 46:4], meaning in the earth. It was also said that the meaning is "from the direction that Allah has allowed you," that is, without fasting, *iḥrām*, or *i'tikāf*. It was also said that the meaning is "from the side of purity, not from the side of menstruation," and it was said: "from the side of what is lawful, not from the side of adultery."

His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who turn often (in repentance) and loves those who purify themselves﴾. It was said: the intended meaning of "those who turn often" is those who turn from sins, and "those who purify themselves" are those who purify themselves from major impurity (*janābah*) and minor impurities (*aḥdāth*). It was said: "those who turn often" are those who turn from having intercourse with women in their anuses, and it was said: from having intercourse with them during menstruation. The first is more evident.

His saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish﴾. The word *ḥarth* (tilth) indicates that the permission was only for the vagina that is the front passage, specifically, since it is the place where offspring are sown, just as *al-ḥarth* is the place where plants are sown.

Thus He likened what is cast into their wombs of the drops (*nuṭaf*) from which offspring come to what is cast into the earth of seeds from which plants come, on the basis that each of them is the material for what results from it. This sentence explains the first sentence, namely His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾.

His saying: ﴿As you wish﴾, meaning: from whatever direction you wish, from behind or in front, sitting, crouching, or lying down, as long as it is in the place of tilling. Tha'lab recited:

*Indeed the wombs are lands for us, tilled ones; so on us is the sowing in them, and on God is the growth.*

He, the Glorious, expressed it with the word *anna* (how/where/whenever) because in the language it is more general than *kayf* (how), *ayna* (where), and *matā* (when).

As for Sībawayh, he explained it here as *kayf* (how).

The early generations (*al-salaf*) and the later generations (*al-khalaf*) among the Companions, the Successors, and the imams went to what we have mentioned as the interpretation of the verse, and that having intercourse with one's wife in her anus is forbidden.

It was reported from Sa'īd ibn al-Musayyib, Nāfi', Ibn 'Umar, Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī, and 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn that it is permitted. Al-Qurṭubī related this from them in his *Tafsīr*. He said: this was attributed to Mālik in a book of his called *Kitāb al-Sirr* (the Book of the Secret). But the leading students and shaykhs of Mālik's school reject that book, and Mālik is too exalted to have a "book of secrets." This view also appears in *al-'Utbiyyah*.

Ibn al-'Arabī mentioned that Ibn Sha'bān attributed the permissibility of this to a large group of Companions and Successors and to Mālik through many narrations in his book *Jimā' al-Niswān wa-Aḥkām al-Qur'ān*. Al-Ṭaḥāwī said: Aṣbagh ibn al-Faraj related from 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim who said: "I did not meet anyone whom I would follow in my religion who doubted that it is lawful," meaning intercourse with a woman in her anus. Then he recited: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾, and then said: "What could be clearer than this?"

Al-Ḥākim, al-Dāraquṭnī, and al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī have related from Mālik through various chains what implies the permissibility of this, but there is weakness in their chains.

Al-Ṭaḥāwī related from Muḥammad ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Abd al-Ḥakam that he heard al-Shāfi'ī say: "Nothing has been authenticated from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding its permissibility or its prohibition, and by analogy it is lawful." Al-Khaṭīb also related this.

Ibn al-Ṣabbāgh said: al-Rabī' used to swear by Allah, there is no god but Him, that Ibn 'Abd al-Ḥakam lied about al-Shāfi'ī in this, for al-Shāfi'ī explicitly stated its prohibition in six of his books.

His saying: ﴿And send forward for yourselves﴾, meaning: good, as in His saying: ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:110]. It was said: seeking offspring. It was said: marrying chaste women. And other things were said.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ contains a warning against falling into any of the prohibited things.

His saying: ﴿And know that you are to meet Him﴾ contains an exaggeration in warning.

His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ contains reassurance for whoever does good and avoids evil.

Muslim, the authors of the *Sunan*, and others have related from Anas that "the Jews, when a woman among them menstruated, would expel her from the house, not eat with her, not drink with her, and not have intercourse with her in the houses. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about that, so Allah revealed: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Have intercourse with them in the houses, and do everything except marital intercourse.'"

Al-Nasā'ī and al-Bazzār related from Jābir who said: "The Jews said: whoever has intercourse with a woman in her anus, his child will be squint-eyed. So they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about that and about having intercourse with a menstruating woman, and this (verse) was revealed."

Ibn Jarīr related from Mujāhid who said: "*al-adhā* is blood."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his *Sunan* related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So keep away from women﴾ that he said: "Keep away from marrying their private parts (*nikāḥ furūjihinna*)."

Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure﴾, he said: "from the blood."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujāhid who said: "until the blood stops."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿Then when they have purified themselves﴾ that he said: "with water."

'Abd al-Razzāq and 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Mujāhid.

Ibn Jarīr related the like of it also from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujāhid and 'Aṭā' that they both said: "If she sees purity, there is no harm in her cleansing herself with water, and he may have intercourse with her before she bathes."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ that he said: "That is, that he comes to her when she is pure and not menstruating."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Qatādah.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ that he said: "From where He commanded you to avoid them."

Ibn Abī Shaybah related the like of it from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn 'Abbās who said: "From where He forbade you to approach them while they are menstruating, that is, from the front passage."

Ibn Abī Shaybah related from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah who said: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ means "from the side of marriage."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from 'Aṭā' regarding His saying: ﴿Loves those who turn often﴾ that he said: "from sins," and ﴿and loves those who purify themselves﴾ he said: "with water."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-A'mash who said: "Repentance is from sins, and purification is from polytheism."

Al-Bukhārī, the authors of the *Sunan*, and others related from Jābir who said: "The Jews used to say: if a man comes to his wife from behind, in her front passage, the child will be squint-eyed. So this was revealed: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish﴾, whether she is in a position of crouching or not crouching, but that is within one passage."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn Jarīr related the like of it from Murrah al-Hamdānī.

This has been related from a group of the early generations, and they explicitly stated that this was the cause (of revelation). Among those who related this is 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar in Ibn 'Asākir, and Umm Salamah in 'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shu'ab*.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Dārimī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, also related from her: "Some women of the Anṣār asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about *al-taḥbiyah* (having intercourse in a crouched position), so he recited the verse to her and said: 'One passage.'" *Al-ṣimām* means the path.

Aḥmad, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, al-Nasā'ī, al-Ḍiyā' in *al-Mukhtārah*, and others related from Ibn 'Abbās who said: "'Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am ruined.' He said: 'What has ruined you?' He said: 'I turned my mount last night.' He did not answer him at all. So Allah revealed to His Messenger this verse: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾, meaning: approach from the front or from behind, but guard against the anus [p-147] and menstruation."

Aḥmad related from Ibn 'Abbās, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that this verse was revealed concerning some people of the Anṣār who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him. He said: "Have intercourse with her in any state, as long as it is in the front passage."

Al-Dārimī, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Ḥākim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, "sound"), and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, related from him. Ibn ʿUmar said (may Allah forgive him; did he make a mistake?): "This clan of the Anṣār, who were people of idolatry, were together with this clan of the Jews, who were People of the Book, and they used to consider them superior in knowledge, so they would imitate much of their conduct. Among the practices of the People of the Book was that they did not have intercourse with women except from one side (ʿalā ḥarf), and that is the most concealing position for a woman. This clan of the Anṣār had adopted their practice. This clan of Quraysh, however, would lie with women thoroughly and enjoy them from the front, from behind, and lying on their backs. When the Muhājirūn came to Madīnah, a man of them married a woman of the Anṣār, and he went to do that with her, but she rejected it from him and said: 'We were only approached from one side (ʿalā ḥarf), so do that, or else keep away from me.' Their matter spread until it reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed the verse: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾; meaning, facing forward or backward, after it is in the vagina, even if it is from behind her, into her front passage." Al-Ṭabarānī added: Ibn ʿAbbās said, Ibn ʿUmar said: "in her rear passage," and so he made a mistake; may Allah forgive him. This hadith was only on this basis.
