Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Dārimī, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "The private parts (maḥāsh) of women are forbidden to you."

Al-Shāfiʿī in al-Umm, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related through the route of Khuzaymah ibn Thābit: "A questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about approaching women in their rear passages, and he said: 'It is permissible' or 'there is no harm.' When he turned away, he called him back and said: 'How did you say it? Is it from behind her into her front passage? Then yes. Or is it from behind her into her behind? Then no. Indeed Allah does not shy away from the truth. Do not approach women in their rear passages.'"

Ibn ʿAdī and al-Dāraqutnī related from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh something similar.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan, "good"), al-Nasāʾī, and Ibn Ḥibbān related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not look at a man who approaches a woman in the rear passage."

Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAmr that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The one who approaches his wife in her rear passage is the lesser Lūṭiyyah (the lesser sodomite)."

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasāʾī related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Cursed is the one who approaches his wife in her rear passage."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Bayhaqī related from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that he said: "Approaching men and women in their rear passages is disbelief (kufr)."

Ibn ʿAdī related this from Abū Hurayrah as a marfūʿ report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)), but Ibn Kathīr said: "The mawqūf (stopping at a Companion) is more sound."

The prohibition has been reported through several routes. Among them: in al-Bazzār from ʿUmar as marfūʿ, and in al-Nasāʾī from him as mawqūf, which is more sound. In Ibn ʿAdī's al-Kāmil from Ibn Masʿūd as marfūʿ; also in Ibn ʿAdī from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir as marfūʿ; in Aḥmad from Ṭalq ibn Yazīd or Yazīd ibn Ṭalq as marfūʿ; and in Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, and al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan) from ʿAlī ibn Ṭalq as marfūʿ. Something similar has been established from a group of the Companions and the Successors (tābiʿūn), both marfūʿ and mawqūf.

Al-Bukhārī and others related from Nāfiʿ, who said: "One day I recited: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, and Ibn ʿUmar said: 'Do you know about what this verse was revealed?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'It was revealed concerning approaching women in their rear passages.'"

Al-Bukhārī related from Ibn ʿUmar that he said regarding: ﴿So come to your tilth however you wish﴾: "It means in the rear passage."

This has been reported from Ibn ʿUmar through many routes.

In a narration in al-Dāraqutnī, Nāfiʿ said to him: "From behind her into her front passage?" He said: "No, only into her rear passage."

Ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭaḥāwī, and Ibn Mardawayh related with a ḥasan chain from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that a man had intercourse with his wife in her rear passage, and the people denounced him for it, so the verse was revealed.

al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, who said: "I was with Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī when a man came to him and said: 'What do you say about approaching a woman in her rear passage?' He said: 'This is a shaykh of Quraysh, so ask him,' meaning ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Sāʾib. He said: 'It is filthy (qadhar), even if it were permissible.'"

The view of its permissibility has been reported from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir in Ibn Jarīr, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah in Ibn Jarīr also, from Mālik ibn Anas in Ibn Jarīr and al-Khaṭīb and others, and from al-Shāfiʿī in al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-Ḥākim, and al-Khaṭīb.

We have already mentioned something similar. There is absolutely no proof in the statements of these people, and it is not permissible for anyone to act upon their statements, for they did not bring any evidence indicating permissibility. Whoever among them claims that he understood this from the verse has erred in his understanding.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the senior Companions have explained it to us, contrary to what this mistaken person understood, whoever he may be. As for whoever among them claims that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that a man approached his wife in her rear passage, there is nothing in this that indicates the verse made that permissible. Whoever claims that has erred. Rather, what the verse indicates is that it is forbidden. The fact that this was the occasion does not necessitate that the verse was revealed to make it permissible, for verses revealed on occasions sometimes come with permission for this and sometimes with prohibition of it.

It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he interpreted this verse differently from what has preceded. He said: Its meaning is: "If you wish, practice withdrawal (ʿazl); and if you wish, do not practice withdrawal."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Ḍiyāʾ in al-Mukhtārah related this from him.

Something similar has been reported from Ibn ʿUmar, related by Ibn Abī Shaybah, and from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, related by Ibn Abī Shaybah and Ibn Jarīr.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 223–224 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: *al-maḥīḍ* is *al-ḥayḍ* (menstruation, a term for the monthly bleeding), and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is said: "The woman menstruated (*ḥāḍat*) a menstruation (*ḥayḍan*) and a *maḥīḍ*, so she is *ḥā'iḍ* and *ḥā'iḍah*." Thus al-Farrā' said, and he recited:

*Like a menstruating woman with whom one commits adultery while she is not pure.*

Women are described as *ḥuyyaḍ* and *ḥawā'iḍ*. *Al-ḥīḍah* with a kasra is the single occurrence. It was said that it is a noun. It was also said that *al-maḥīḍ* refers to the time and the place, and that this is a metaphorical usage for both.

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī said: *al-maḥīḍ* is the name of *al-ḥayḍ*. Similar to it is the saying of Ru'ba:

*To You I complain of the hardship of the livelihood*

meaning, of the *'aysh* (livelihood). The root of this word is from flowing and gushing forth. It is said: "The torrent (*al-sayl*) gushed and overflowed (*ḥāḍa wa fāḍa*)," and "the tree menstruated (*ḥāḍat al-shajarah*)," meaning its moisture flowed. From this is also *al-ḥayḍ*, meaning *al-ḥawḍ* (the pool), because water flows into it (*yaḥūḍu ilayhi*), that is, it flows.

His saying: ﴿Say: It is an injury﴾, meaning: say, it is a thing that causes harm (*yataʾadhdhā bihi*), that is, by its smell. *Al-adhā* is a metaphor for filth, and it is also applied to a hateful speech. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:264]. From it also is His saying: ﴿And disregard their harm﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:48].

His saying: ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾, meaning: avoid them during the time of menstruation if *al-maḥīḍ* is taken as a verbal noun, or in the place of menstruation if it is taken as a noun.

The intended meaning of this *i'tizāl* (keeping away) is abstaining from intercourse, not abstaining from sitting with them or from physical contact, for that is permissible. Rather, enjoyment of them is permitted in what lies beyond the genital area, or in what is below the waist-wrap (*izār*), according to a difference of opinion on this. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbās and 'Ubaydah al-Salmānī, that a man must keep away from his wife's bedding when she menstruates, this is not correct. There is no disagreement among the scholars on the prohibition of intercourse with a menstruating woman, and this is known from the necessity of the religion (*ḍarūrat al-dīn*).

His saying: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure﴾. Nāfi', Abū 'Amr, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, and 'Āṣim in the transmission of Abū Bakr read *yaṭṭahharna* with a doubled *ṭā'* and an open vowel, and with an open *hā'* and doubled as well.

In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd, it is *wa-yatatahharna*. *Al-Ṭuhr* is the cessation of menstruation, and *al-tatahhur* is washing (*al-ightisāl*).

Because of the difference among the readers (*qurrā'*), the scholars differed. The majority held that a menstruating woman is not lawful for her husband to have intercourse with until she purifies herself with water.

Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī and Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr said: if the menstruating woman becomes pure and performs *tayammum* (dry ablution) where there is no water, she becomes lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed.

Mujāhid and 'Ikrimah said: the cessation of the bleeding makes her lawful to her husband, but she should perform *wuḍū'* (ablution).

Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf, and Muḥammad said: if her bleeding stops after ten days have passed, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her before she bathes. If the cessation was before the ten days, it is not permitted until she bathes or the time of prayer enters upon her.

Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī preferred the doubled reading.

The better view is that Allah the Glorious made two limits for the permissibility, as the two readings require: one is the cessation of the bleeding, and the other is purification from it. The second limit includes an addition beyond the first, so it is necessary to adopt it.

That the second limit is the one that counts is shown by His saying after that: ﴿Then when they have purified themselves﴾, for this indicates that what counts is purification, not merely the cessation of bleeding.

It is established that the two readings are like the two verses. Just as it is necessary to combine two verses of which one contains an addition by acting on that addition, so too it is necessary to combine the two readings.

His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾, meaning: have intercourse with them. He expressed this by the term "coming" (*al-ityān*).

The intended meaning is that they have intercourse with them in the place of approach that Allah has permitted, which is the front passage (*al-qubul*). It was said that *min ḥaythu* here means *fī ḥaythu* (in which), as in His saying: ﴿When it is called for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:9], meaning on the day of Friday, and His saying: ﴿What have they created from the earth?﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 46:4], meaning in the earth. It was also said that the meaning is "from the direction that Allah has allowed you," that is, without fasting, *iḥrām*, or *i'tikāf*. It was also said that the meaning is "from the side of purity, not from the side of menstruation," and it was said: "from the side of what is lawful, not from the side of adultery."

His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who turn often (in repentance) and loves those who purify themselves﴾. It was said: the intended meaning of "those who turn often" is those who turn from sins, and "those who purify themselves" are those who purify themselves from major impurity (*janābah*) and minor impurities (*aḥdāth*). It was said: "those who turn often" are those who turn from having intercourse with women in their anuses, and it was said: from having intercourse with them during menstruation. The first is more evident.

His saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish﴾. The word *ḥarth* (tilth) indicates that the permission was only for the vagina that is the front passage, specifically, since it is the place where offspring are sown, just as *al-ḥarth* is the place where plants are sown.

Thus He likened what is cast into their wombs of the drops (*nuṭaf*) from which offspring come to what is cast into the earth of seeds from which plants come, on the basis that each of them is the material for what results from it. This sentence explains the first sentence, namely His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾.

His saying: ﴿As you wish﴾, meaning: from whatever direction you wish, from behind or in front, sitting, crouching, or lying down, as long as it is in the place of tilling. Tha'lab recited:

*Indeed the wombs are lands for us, tilled ones; so on us is the sowing in them, and on God is the growth.*

He, the Glorious, expressed it with the word *anna* (how/where/whenever) because in the language it is more general than *kayf* (how), *ayna* (where), and *matā* (when).

As for Sībawayh, he explained it here as *kayf* (how).

The early generations (*al-salaf*) and the later generations (*al-khalaf*) among the Companions, the Successors, and the imams went to what we have mentioned as the interpretation of the verse, and that having intercourse with one's wife in her anus is forbidden.

It was reported from Sa'īd ibn al-Musayyib, Nāfi', Ibn 'Umar, Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī, and 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Mājishūn that it is permitted. Al-Qurṭubī related this from them in his *Tafsīr*. He said: this was attributed to Mālik in a book of his called *Kitāb al-Sirr* (the Book of the Secret). But the leading students and shaykhs of Mālik's school reject that book, and Mālik is too exalted to have a "book of secrets." This view also appears in *al-'Utbiyyah*.

Ibn al-'Arabī mentioned that Ibn Sha'bān attributed the permissibility of this to a large group of Companions and Successors and to Mālik through many narrations in his book *Jimā' al-Niswān wa-Aḥkām al-Qur'ān*. Al-Ṭaḥāwī said: Aṣbagh ibn al-Faraj related from 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim who said: "I did not meet anyone whom I would follow in my religion who doubted that it is lawful," meaning intercourse with a woman in her anus. Then he recited: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾, and then said: "What could be clearer than this?"

Al-Ḥākim, al-Dāraquṭnī, and al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī have related from Mālik through various chains what implies the permissibility of this, but there is weakness in their chains.

Al-Ṭaḥāwī related from Muḥammad ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Abd al-Ḥakam that he heard al-Shāfi'ī say: "Nothing has been authenticated from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding its permissibility or its prohibition, and by analogy it is lawful." Al-Khaṭīb also related this.

Ibn al-Ṣabbāgh said: al-Rabī' used to swear by Allah, there is no god but Him, that Ibn 'Abd al-Ḥakam lied about al-Shāfi'ī in this, for al-Shāfi'ī explicitly stated its prohibition in six of his books.

His saying: ﴿And send forward for yourselves﴾, meaning: good, as in His saying: ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:110]. It was said: seeking offspring. It was said: marrying chaste women. And other things were said.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ contains a warning against falling into any of the prohibited things.

His saying: ﴿And know that you are to meet Him﴾ contains an exaggeration in warning.

His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ contains reassurance for whoever does good and avoids evil.

Muslim, the authors of the *Sunan*, and others have related from Anas that "the Jews, when a woman among them menstruated, would expel her from the house, not eat with her, not drink with her, and not have intercourse with her in the houses. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about that, so Allah revealed: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Have intercourse with them in the houses, and do everything except marital intercourse.'"

Al-Nasā'ī and al-Bazzār related from Jābir who said: "The Jews said: whoever has intercourse with a woman in her anus, his child will be squint-eyed. So they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about that and about having intercourse with a menstruating woman, and this (verse) was revealed."

Ibn Jarīr related from Mujāhid who said: "*al-adhā* is blood."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his *Sunan* related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So keep away from women﴾ that he said: "Keep away from marrying their private parts (*nikāḥ furūjihinna*)."

Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not approach them until they become pure﴾, he said: "from the blood."

'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujāhid who said: "until the blood stops."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿Then when they have purified themselves﴾ that he said: "with water."

'Abd al-Razzāq and 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Mujāhid.

Ibn Jarīr related the like of it also from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujāhid and 'Aṭā' that they both said: "If she sees purity, there is no harm in her cleansing herself with water, and he may have intercourse with her before she bathes."

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ that he said: "That is, that he comes to her when she is pure and not menstruating."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Qatādah.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ that he said: "From where He commanded you to avoid them."

Ibn Abī Shaybah related the like of it from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn 'Abbās who said: "From where He forbade you to approach them while they are menstruating, that is, from the front passage."

Ibn Abī Shaybah related from Ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah who said: ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ means "from the side of marriage."

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from 'Aṭā' regarding His saying: ﴿Loves those who turn often﴾ that he said: "from sins," and ﴿and loves those who purify themselves﴾ he said: "with water."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-A'mash who said: "Repentance is from sins, and purification is from polytheism."

Al-Bukhārī, the authors of the *Sunan*, and others related from Jābir who said: "The Jews used to say: if a man comes to his wife from behind, in her front passage, the child will be squint-eyed. So this was revealed: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish﴾, whether she is in a position of crouching or not crouching, but that is within one passage."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and Ibn Jarīr related the like of it from Murrah al-Hamdānī.

This has been related from a group of the early generations, and they explicitly stated that this was the cause (of revelation). Among those who related this is 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar in Ibn 'Asākir, and Umm Salamah in 'Abd al-Razzāq, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shu'ab*.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Dārimī, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, also related from her: "Some women of the Anṣār asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about *al-taḥbiyah* (having intercourse in a crouched position), so he recited the verse to her and said: 'One passage.'" *Al-ṣimām* means the path.

Aḥmad, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it as ḥasan, al-Nasā'ī, al-Ḍiyā' in *al-Mukhtārah*, and others related from Ibn 'Abbās who said: "'Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am ruined.' He said: 'What has ruined you?' He said: 'I turned my mount last night.' He did not answer him at all. So Allah revealed to His Messenger this verse: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾, meaning: approach from the front or from behind, but guard against the anus [p-147] and menstruation."

Aḥmad related from Ibn 'Abbās, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that this verse was revealed concerning some people of the Anṣār who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him. He said: "Have intercourse with her in any state, as long as it is in the front passage."

Al-Dārimī, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Ḥākim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, "sound"), and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan, related from him. Ibn ʿUmar said (may Allah forgive him; did he make a mistake?): "This clan of the Anṣār, who were people of idolatry, were together with this clan of the Jews, who were People of the Book, and they used to consider them superior in knowledge, so they would imitate much of their conduct. Among the practices of the People of the Book was that they did not have intercourse with women except from one side (ʿalā ḥarf), and that is the most concealing position for a woman. This clan of the Anṣār had adopted their practice. This clan of Quraysh, however, would lie with women thoroughly and enjoy them from the front, from behind, and lying on their backs. When the Muhājirūn came to Madīnah, a man of them married a woman of the Anṣār, and he went to do that with her, but she rejected it from him and said: 'We were only approached from one side (ʿalā ḥarf), so do that, or else keep away from me.' Their matter spread until it reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed the verse: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾; meaning, facing forward or backward, after it is in the vagina, even if it is from behind her, into her front passage." Al-Ṭabarānī added: Ibn ʿAbbās said, Ibn ʿUmar said: "in her rear passage," and so he made a mistake; may Allah forgive him. This hadith was only on this basis.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Dārimī, and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "The private parts (maḥāsh) of women are forbidden to you."

Al-Shāfiʿī in al-Umm, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related through the route of Khuzaymah ibn Thābit: "A questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about approaching women in their rear passages, and he said: 'It is permissible' or 'there is no harm.' When he turned away, he called him back and said: 'How did you say it? Is it from behind her into her front passage? Then yes. Or is it from behind her into her behind? Then no. Indeed Allah does not shy away from the truth. Do not approach women in their rear passages.'"

Ibn ʿAdī and al-Dāraqutnī related from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh something similar.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan, "good"), al-Nasāʾī, and Ibn Ḥibbān related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah does not look at a man who approaches a woman in the rear passage."

Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAmr that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The one who approaches his wife in her rear passage is the lesser Lūṭiyyah (the lesser sodomite)."

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasāʾī related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Cursed is the one who approaches his wife in her rear passage."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Bayhaqī related from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that he said: "Approaching men and women in their rear passages is disbelief (kufr)."

Ibn ʿAdī related this from Abū Hurayrah as a marfūʿ report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ)), but Ibn Kathīr said: "The mawqūf (stopping at a Companion) is more sound."

The prohibition has been reported through several routes. Among them: in al-Bazzār from ʿUmar as marfūʿ, and in al-Nasāʾī from him as mawqūf, which is more sound. In Ibn ʿAdī's al-Kāmil from Ibn Masʿūd as marfūʿ; also in Ibn ʿAdī from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir as marfūʿ; in Aḥmad from Ṭalq ibn Yazīd or Yazīd ibn Ṭalq as marfūʿ; and in Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, and al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan) from ʿAlī ibn Ṭalq as marfūʿ. Something similar has been established from a group of the Companions and the Successors (tābiʿūn), both marfūʿ and mawqūf.

Al-Bukhārī and others related from Nāfiʿ, who said: "One day I recited: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, and Ibn ʿUmar said: 'Do you know about what this verse was revealed?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'It was revealed concerning approaching women in their rear passages.'"

Al-Bukhārī related from Ibn ʿUmar that he said regarding: ﴿So come to your tilth however you wish﴾: "It means in the rear passage."

This has been reported from Ibn ʿUmar through many routes.

In a narration in al-Dāraqutnī, Nāfiʿ said to him: "From behind her into her front passage?" He said: "No, only into her rear passage."

Ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭaḥāwī, and Ibn Mardawayh related with a ḥasan chain from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that a man had intercourse with his wife in her rear passage, and the people denounced him for it, so the verse was revealed.

al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, who said: "I was with Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī when a man came to him and said: 'What do you say about approaching a woman in her rear passage?' He said: 'This is a shaykh of Quraysh, so ask him,' meaning ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Sāʾib. He said: 'It is filthy (qadhar), even if it were permissible.'"

The view of its permissibility has been reported from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir in Ibn Jarīr, from Ibn Abī Mulaykah in Ibn Jarīr also, from Mālik ibn Anas in Ibn Jarīr and al-Khaṭīb and others, and from al-Shāfiʿī in al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-Ḥākim, and al-Khaṭīb.

We have already mentioned something similar. There is absolutely no proof in the statements of these people, and it is not permissible for anyone to act upon their statements, for they did not bring any evidence indicating permissibility. Whoever among them claims that he understood this from the verse has erred in his understanding.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the senior Companions have explained it to us, contrary to what this mistaken person understood, whoever he may be. As for whoever among them claims that the occasion of revelation of the verse was that a man approached his wife in her rear passage, there is nothing in this that indicates the verse made that permissible. Whoever claims that has erred. Rather, what the verse indicates is that it is forbidden. The fact that this was the occasion does not necessitate that the verse was revealed to make it permissible, for verses revealed on occasions sometimes come with permission for this and sometimes with prohibition of it.

It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he interpreted this verse differently from what has preceded. He said: Its meaning is: "If you wish, practice withdrawal (ʿazl); and if you wish, do not practice withdrawal."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Ḍiyāʾ in al-Mukhtārah related this from him.

Something similar has been reported from Ibn ʿUmar, related by Ibn Abī Shaybah, and from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, related by Ibn Abī Shaybah and Ibn Jarīr.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 225:**

Al-'Urdah (عُرْضَة, an obstacle or target) means al-nusbah (نُصْبَة, something set up as a target), as al-Jawhari (the lexicographer) said.

It is said: "I made so-and-so an 'urdah for such-and-such," meaning a nusbah. It is also said that al-'urdah derives from intensity and strength. From this comes the saying about a woman: "She is 'urdah for marriage," when she is fit for it and strong enough for it. And "so-and-so has 'urdah," meaning strength. From this is the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*From every fast-moving she-camel of the Diqri breed, when her strength has sweated out, a faded, unknown landmark.*

Similar to it is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

*And a fawn-coloured she-camel like a calf, one day I brought her to my saddle, and in her is vigour and jolting.*

'Urdah is also used to mean resolve (himmah). From this is the verse of the poet:

*They are the Ansar, whose 'urdah is meeting (in battle).*

That is, their resolve is meeting. It is said: "So-and-so is an 'urdah for people," meaning they never stop falling upon him (with criticism).

According to the meaning mentioned by al-Jawhari, that 'urdah is a nusbah, like qubdah (a handful) and ghurfah (a scoop), this would be a noun for what you set up in front of a thing, i.e., you make it a barrier and a hindrance to it. The meaning would be: do not make Allah a barrier and hindrance to what you have sworn to. This is because a man would swear not to do some good, such as keeping ties of kinship, doing kindness to another, or reconciling between people, and then he would refrain from doing it, justifying that refraining by saying that he had sworn not to do it. This meaning is what the majority (al-Jumhur) mentioned in the interpretation of the verse: Allah forbids them from making Him an 'urdah for their oaths, that is, a barrier and hindrance to what they have sworn to. The thing sworn to is called an oath (yamin) because it is bound up with the oath. On this basis, His saying ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "your oaths," meaning: do not make Allah a hindrance to the oaths which are your righteousness, your piety, and your reconciliation between people. His saying "for your oaths" is connected to "do not make," meaning: do not make Allah a hindrance and barrier for your oaths. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "'urdah," meaning: do not make Him a thing standing in opposition between you and righteousness and what follows it.

According to the second meaning, that 'urdah is intensity and strength, the meaning of the verse would be: do not make the oath by Allah a strength for yourselves, and a pretext for refraining from good. Interpreting the verse according to the third meaning, that 'urdah is resolve, is not valid. As for the fourth meaning, from the saying "so-and-so is never a target for people," meaning they keep falling upon him, the meaning of the verse according to it would be: do not make Allah exposed to your oaths, so that you spend Him by swearing by Him frequently. From this comes ﴿and guard your oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. Allah has censured those who swear frequently, saying ﴿and do not obey every habitual swearer, contemptible﴾ [al-Qalam: 10].

The Arabs used to praise one another for swearing little, to the point that one of them said:

*He swears little and guards his oath; even if an oath slips from him, he is faithful to it.*

On this basis, His saying ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is the reason for the prohibition, meaning: do not make Allah exposed to your oaths, intending that you be righteous, pious, and reconcile, because whoever swears by Allah frequently becomes bold in breaking oaths and transgresses in his oath.

Statements have been made in the interpretation of the verse that return to these aspects we have mentioned. Among them is the statement of al-Zajjaj: the meaning of the verse is that a man, when asked to do an action that contains good, makes the excuse of Allah, saying: "An oath is binding on me," while he has not sworn. It has also been said: its meaning is, do not swear by Allah falsely when you intend righteousness, piety, and reconciliation. It has also been said: its meaning is, if you swear not to keep your ties of kinship, not to give charity, not to reconcile, and similar acts of righteousness, then make expiation for the oath.

It has been said that His saying ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: righteousness and piety and reconciliation. Al-Zajjaj said this, and it is more preferable.

It has been said that it is in the accusative (mansub): meaning, the oath by Allah should not prevent you from righteousness, piety, and reconciliation. This is also narrated from al-Zajjaj. It has been said that its meaning is "lest you be righteous," with "la" (not) omitted, like His saying ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], meaning "lest you go astray." This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

It has been said that it is in the genitive position according to al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i, the estimate being in ﴿that you be righteous﴾.

His saying "All-Hearing" means: He hears the statements of the servants, "All-Knowing" means: He knows what proceeds from them.

Al-laghw (لَغْو, idle talk) is the verbal noun of laghā yalghū laghwan, and laghā yalghī laghyan, when one utters what is not needed in speech, or what has no good in it, and it is what falls away and is not counted. So the laghw of oaths is what falls away and is not counted. From this comes "laghw" in blood money, which is the young camel that falls away and is not counted among the young of the camels. Jarir said:

*And between them the camel-calf goes off as laghw, just as you disregarded the young camel in the blood money.*

Another said:

*And many a flock of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and obscene speech.*

That is, they do not speak with what is trivial and with obscenity. The meaning of the verse is: Allah will not punish you for the trivial among your oaths, but He will punish you for what your hearts have earned, that is, what they have committed deliberately, which is the binding oath. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for what you have bound with oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*You will not be taken to account for idle talk one utters, if you have not intended the binding resolutions.*

The people of knowledge have differed in the interpretation of laghw. Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, and also the majority of scholars held that it is a man's saying "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah" in his speech and conversation, without intending the oath and without wanting it.

Al-Marwazi said: this is the meaning of the laghw of oaths on which the scholars generally agree.

Abu Hurayrah and a group of the early generations (al-Salaf) said: it is that a man swears about something, not thinking except that it is that thing, and then it is not what he thought. To this view went the Hanafiyyah and the Zaydiyyah, and Malik also said so in al-Muwatta'.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the laghw of oaths is that you swear while you are angry. Tawus and Makhul also said so, and it is narrated from Malik. It has also been said that laghw is the oath of disobedience, as said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, and his brother 'Urwah, such as one who swears that he will drink wine or will sever kinship. It has also been said that the laghw of oaths is a man's supplication against himself, such as saying: "May Allah blind his eye, may Allah take away his wealth, he is a Jew, he is a polytheist."

This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Mujahid said: the laghw of oaths is that two men conduct a sale, and one of them says: "By Allah, I will not sell it to you for such-and-such," and the other says: "By Allah, I will not buy it for such-and-such."

Al-Dahhak said: the laghw of oaths is that which is expiated; that is, when it is expiated, it falls away and becomes laghw.

The preponderant view is the first, for it corresponds to the linguistic meaning and is supported by the evidences, as will come.

His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Forgiving, Forbearing﴾ means: since He did not hold you accountable for what you say with your tongues without deliberate intention and purpose.

And He holds you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately intended and your tongues have spoken, and that is the binding oath, the intended one.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿and do not make Allah an 'urdah for your oaths﴾: he said: "Do not make me an 'urdah for your oath that you will not do good; rather, make expiation for your oath and do good."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from him: it is that a man swears that he will not speak to his relative or will not give charity, and there is an estrangement between two men, so he swears that he will not reconcile between them, and says: "I have sworn." He said: "He makes expiation for [p. 149] his oath."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ata' who said: a man came to 'A'ishah and said: "I have vowed that if I speak to so-and-so, then every slave I own is free, and all my property is a covering for the Ka'bah." She said: "Do not make your slaves free, nor make your property a covering for the house, for Allah says: ﴿and do not make Allah an 'urdah for your oaths﴾. So make expiation for your oath."

It has been reported that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr regarding the matter of Mistah. Ibn Jarir narrated it from Ibn Jurayj, and the story is well known.

It is established in the authentic hadiths in the two Sahihs and others that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something other than it to be better, let him do what is better and make expiation for his oath."

It is also established in the two Sahihs and others that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, if Allah wills, I will not swear an oath and then see something other than it to be better, except that I will do what is better and make expiation for my oath."

Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'A'ishah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath to sever kinship or to commit disobedience, then his righteousness is to break it and retract his oath."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no vow nor oath concerning what the son of Adam does not possess, nor in disobedience to Allah, nor in severing kinship."

Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from 'Umar, marfu' (traced back to the Prophet), the like of it.

Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Malik al-Jushami who said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, my cousin comes to me, and I swear that I will not give him anything or keep ties with him." He said: "Make expiation for your oath."

Malik in al-Muwatta', 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, and others narrated from 'A'ishah who said: this verse was revealed: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the laghw in your oaths﴾ concerning a man's saying: "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah," and "Certainly not, by Allah."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated through the route of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that he was asked about the laghw in oaths and said: 'A'ishah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is a man's speech in his house: 'Certainly not, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'A'ishah that she said in interpreting the verse: the laghw is a people who dispute a matter, one saying: "No, by Allah," and another saying: "Certainly not, by Allah," disputing a matter on which their hearts have not resolved.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'A'ishah that she said: it is the laghw in jest and jocularity, which is a man's saying "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah." There is no expiation for that. The expiation is only for what his heart has resolved to do, then he does not do it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by people who were shooting arrows, and with the Prophet (ﷺ) was a man from among his companions. A man from the people shot, and said: 'By Allah, you hit, and by Allah, you missed.' The one who was with the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The man has broken his oath, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Certainly not. The oaths of archers are laghw, with no expiation for them and no punishment.'"

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and Ibn 'Amr that the laghw is "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the laghw of oaths is that you swear while you are angry.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: the laghw of oaths is a person's swearing about something, thinking it is the thing he swore about, and then it is other than that.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated the like of it from 'A'ishah.

Ibn Jarir narrated the like of it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is that a man swears to prohibit what Allah has made lawful for him.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: it is the man who swears to commit disobedience.

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Nakha'i: it is that a man swears about something and then forgets.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: "And Allah is All-Forgiving," meaning, since He overlooked the oath he swore, "Forbearing," since He did not place expiation in it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 226:

His saying: "yu'lūn" means "yaḥlifūn" (they swear). The verbal noun is "īlan," "ilyah," and "ilwah." Ibn ʿAbbas read "alladhīna ālū." It is said: "ālā yu'līy" and "ya'talī" with the letter tāʾ, "i'tilāʾan," meaning he swore. From this is the verse: ﴿And let not those of virtue among you swear off﴾ [al-Nur: 22]. From this also is the line of poetry:

"Qalīl al-alāyā ḥāfiẓun li-yamīnihi" (one who swears little and guards his oath), and so on.

The scholars have differed concerning īlāʾ (the oath of abstention from intercourse). The majority said: īlāʾ is that a man swears not to have intercourse with his wife for more than four months. If he swears for four months or less, he is not a muwallī (one who makes an oath of abstention), and it was for them a pure oath. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Abū Thawr.

al-Thawrī and the Kufans said: īlāʾ is that he swears for four months or more. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he is not a muwallī until he swears that he will never touch her.

A group said: if he swears that he will not approach his wife for a day, or less, or more, and then does not have intercourse for four months, she is separated from him by the īlāʾ.

This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Layla, al-Ḥakam, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Qatādah, and Isḥāq.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: many people of knowledge rejected this view.

His saying: ﴿from their wives﴾ includes free women and slave women when they are wives. Likewise, under His saying ﴿those who swear off﴾ enters a slave who swears off from his wife. This was said by al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Abū Thawr, who said: his īlāʾ is like that of a free man.

Mālik, al-Zuhrī, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū Ḥanīfah, and Isḥāq said: its term is two months.

al-Shaʿbī said: the īlāʾ of a slave woman is half the īlāʾ of a free woman.

And al-tarabbuṣ (waiting): deliberation and delay. The poet said:

"Tarabbaṣ bihā rayb al-manūn laʿallahā / tuṭallaqu yawman aw yamūtu ḥalīluhā" (Wait with her for the calamity of fate; perhaps she will be divorced one day or her husband will die).

God, glory be to Him, set this period to repel harm from the wife.

The people of the Jahiliyyah used to swear off for a year, two years, or more, intending by that to harm women.

It has been said: the four months are the period beyond which a woman cannot endure patience away from her husband.

His saying: ﴿And if they return﴾ means they go back. From this is: ﴿until it returns to the command of God﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], meaning it returns. From this the shadow after noon is called fay' because it returns from the side of the east to the side of the west. It is said: fāʾa yafīʾu fayʾatan and fuyūʾan, and "innahu la-sarīʿu al-fayʾah," that is, quick to return. From this is the poet's saying:

"Fa-fāʾat wa-lam taqḍi alladhī aqbalat lahu / wa-min ḥājati al-insān mā laysa qāḍiyā"

Ibn al-Mundhir said: All who are known for knowledge agreed that fay' is intercourse for one who has no excuse. If he has an excuse, such as illness or imprisonment, then she remains his wife. When the excuse ends and he refuses intercourse, they are separated if the term has passed. This was said by Mālik. A group said: if he calls witnesses to his return in his heart during the excuse, it suffices him.

This was said by al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Awzāʿī, and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal. The majority obligated expiation (kaffārah) upon the muwallī when he returns by having intercourse with his wife.

al-Ḥasan and al-Nakhaʿī said: there is no expiation upon him.

His saying: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾. al-ʿazm (resolve): the firm intention to do something. It is said ʿazama yaʿzimu ʿazman, ʿazīmah, and ʿuzmānan; and iʿtazama iʿtizāman. So the meaning of ʿazamū al-ṭalāq: they fixed their hearts upon it.

Al-ṭalāq (divorce) is from ṭalaqat al-mar'ah taṭluqu, like naṣara yanṣuru, ṭalāqan; she is ṭāliq and ṭāliqah also. It is permissible to say ṭaluqat with a ḍammah on the lām, like ʿaẓuma yaʿẓumu; al-Akhfash rejected this.

Al-ṭalāq is the untying of the knot of marriage. In this is evidence that she is not divorced by the passing of four months, as Mālik said, unless a pronouncement of divorce occurs after the term. Also, He said "samīʿ" (hearing), and "samīʿ" requires something heard after the passing of the term.

Abū Ḥanīfah said: "samīʿ" for his oath of abstention, "ʿalīm" of his resolve, which the passing of four months indicates.

Know that the people of every school have interpreted this verse in a way that agrees with their school, and they have strained toward what the wording does not indicate, nor any other evidence. Its meaning is clear and evident: God made the term for one who makes īlāʾ, that is, who swears against his wife, four months.

Then He said, informing His servants of the ruling for this muwallī after this period: if they return, that is, return to the continuation of the marital bond and the perpetuation of the marriage, ﴿then God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, that is, He will not hold them accountable for that oath, but will forgive them and have mercy upon them. ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾, that is, the resolve from them upon it and the intention for it has occurred, ﴿then God is Hearing﴾ of that from them, ﴿Knowing﴾ of it. This is the meaning of the verse about which there is no doubt or ambiguity. Whoever swears that he will have intercourse with his wife without specifying a term, or specifies a term beyond four months, it is incumbent upon us to give him four months. When they pass, he has a choice: either he returns to the marriage with his wife, and she is his wife after the passing of the term as she was his wife before it, or he divorces her and has the ruling of one who divorces his wife initially. As for if he specifies a term less than four months: if he wishes to fulfill his oath, he withdraws from the wife whom he swore off until the term ends, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did when he swore off from his wives for a month, withdrawing from them until the month passed. And if he wishes to have intercourse with his wife before the passing of that term, which is less than four months, he breaks his oath and expiation becomes incumbent upon him, and he is complying with what is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever swears to something and sees something other than it to be better, let him do what is better and let him make expiation for his oath."

Al-Shāfiʿī, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: īlāʾ is that he swears he will never have intercourse with her.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from him regarding His saying: ﴿those who swear off from their wives﴾, he said: it is the man who swears by God to his wife that he will not marry her, so she waits four months. If he marries her, he makes expiation for his oath. If four months pass before he marries her, the ruler gives him a choice: either he returns, or he resolves and divorces, as God, glory be to Him, said.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Bayhaqī related from him that he said: the īlāʾ of the Jahiliyyah was a year, two years, or more. So God set for them four months. If his īlāʾ is less than four months, it is not īlāʾ.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from ʿAlī that he said: īlāʾ is of two kinds: īlāʾ in anger and īlāʾ in contentment. As for īlāʾ in anger: when four months pass, she is separated from him. As for what occurs in contentment, he is not held accountable for it.

Ibn Jarīr related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: there is no īlāʾ except in anger.

Abū ʿUbayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he recited: "fa-in fāʾū fīhinna fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from ʿAlī that he said: al-fayʾ is intercourse.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Masʿud the like of it.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAlī that he said: al-fayʾ is contentment.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn Masʿud the like of it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from al-Ḥasan, who said: al-fayʾ is calling witnesses. ʿAbd al-Razzāq related from him that he said: al-fayʾ is intercourse; but if he has an excuse, it suffices him to return by his tongue.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn Masʿud that he said: if illness, travel, imprisonment, or something that excuses him comes between him and her, then calling witnesses is a return.

The predecessors held differing views on al-fayʾ, so it is incumbent to return to the linguistic meaning of al-fayʾ, which we have explained.

Ibn Jarīr related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he said regarding īlāʾ: when four months pass, there is nothing upon him until he is made to stand, then he either divorces or retains.

al-Shāfiʿī, Ibn Jarīr, and al-Bayhaqī related from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān something similar.

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and al-Bayhaqī related from ʿAlī something similar.

al-Bukhārī and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related from Ibn ʿUmar something similar also.

Ibn Jarīr and al-Bayhaqī related from ʿĀʾishah something similar.

Ibn Jarīr, al-Dāraqutnī, and al-Bayhaqī related through the route of Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ from his father, who said: I asked twelve men from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the man who swears off from his wife, and all of them said: there is nothing upon him until the four months pass, then he is made to stand; if he returns, well, otherwise he divorces.

al-Bayhaqī related from Thābit ibn ʿUbayd, client of Zayd ibn Thābit, from twelve men of the Companions something similar.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī related from ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Zayd ibn Thābit, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿAbbas that they said: īlāʾ is an irrevocable single divorce when four months pass before he returns; then she is more entitled to herself. The Companions and the Successors have differing and contradictory views on this, and what is required is to return to what is in the noble verse, which is what we have made known to you, so hold fast to it with both hands.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq related from ʿUmar that he said: the īlāʾ of a slave is two months.

Mālik related from Ibn Shihāb that he said: the īlāʾ of a slave is (p-150) similar to the īlāʾ of a free man.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 227–228 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And the divorced women" (al-mutallaqat). Under its general scope enters the woman divorced before consummation, but it was specified by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. Therefore it is obligatory to build the general (al-'amm) upon the specific (al-khass), and the woman divorced before consummation has gone out from this generality. Likewise the pregnant woman went out by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those who carry children, their term is until they give birth﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. Likewise the woman past menopause went out by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Talaq: 4].

Al-tarabbus (waiting, "tarabbus") means al-intizar (waiting). It was said: it is a report in the sense of a command, i.e., "let them wait" (li-yatarabbasna). He intended by expressing it in the form of a report to emphasize its occurrence, and its occurrence as a report of the subject further reinforces this emphasis.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is false. Rather, it is a report about the ruling of the Sharia. If a divorced woman is found who does not wait, that is not from the Sharia, and it does not follow from this that the report of God, glorified is He, is contrary to its reporter.

Al-quru' (القُرُوءُ) is the plural of qar' (قُرْءٌ).

It is narrated from Nafi' that he read "quruww" with a shadda on the waw.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a hamza.

Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the qaf, a sukun on the ra', and tanwin.

Al-Asma'i said: the singular is qur' with a damma on the qaf.

Abu Zayd said with a fatha: both of them said "aqra'at al-mar'ah" means she menstruated, and "aqra'at" means she became pure.

Al-Akhfash said: "aqra'at al-mar'ah" means when she becomes one who has menstruation; when she menstruates you say "qara'at" without an alif.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: Among the Arabs there are those who call menstruation qar', and among them those who call purity qar', and among them those who combine both, calling menstruation together with purity qar'. It should be known that qar' originally means "time." It is said: "the winds blew at their qur'ihā and qari'ihā," i.e., at their time. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I disliked the slaughter of the Banu Shalil when the winds blow at its time (liqari'ihā)."

So menstruation is called qar', and purity is called qar', because each of them has a known time.

The Arabs have used it sometimes for the periods of purity, and sometimes for menstruation. From its use for the periods of purity is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Each year are you a bearer of a raid, whose resolve tightens its far end?
Inheriting wealth, and in the tribe there is elevation,
for what was lost in them of the qurū' of your women."

That is, their periods of purity. From its use for menstruation is the saying of the poet:

"O how many a one harboring rancor against me, a striker, who has qurū' like the qurū' of a menstruating woman."

He means that he stabbed him and there was blood like the blood of a menstruating woman.

Some said: it is derived from qurya al-ma' in al-hawd, which is its gathering, and from it comes al-Qur'an for the gathering of meanings in it. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"The two forelegs of a gazelle, a white-skinned virgin doe of pure color, did not gather a fetus (taqra janinan)."

That is, she did not gather it in her belly.

The conclusion is that al-quru' in the language of the Arabs is shared (mushtarak) between menstruation and purity. Because of this shared meaning, the people of knowledge differed over determining which is meant by the qurū' mentioned in the verse. The people of Kufa said: they are menstruation, and this is the view of 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

The people of the Hijaz said: they are the periods of purity, and this is the view of 'A'isha, Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Zuhri, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and al-Shafi'i. Know that there is agreement among them that al-qar' means the time, so the meaning of the verse according to all is: "And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three times." Thus it is specified in number but unspecified in what is counted, so it is necessary to seek clarification of what is counted from elsewhere. The people of the first view argued that the intended meaning in this verse is menstruation by the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Leave the prayer during the days of your qurū'," and by his saying (ﷺ): "The divorce of a slave-woman is two pronouncements and her waiting period is two menstruations," and because the purpose of the waiting period is the cleansing of the womb (istibra' al-rahm), which is achieved by menstruation and not by purity.

The people of the second view argued by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], and there is no dispute that one is commanded to divorce at the time of purity. And by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Umar: "Command him, so let him take her back, then let him keep her until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure, for that is the waiting period by which God commanded women to be divorced," because the time of purity is the time in which women are divorced.

Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: We have not encountered any of our jurists except that they say: the qurū' are the periods of purity. So if a man divorces in a purity in which he did not have intercourse, she counts what remains of it even if an hour or a moment, then she begins a second purity after a menstruation. When she sees blood from the third menstruation, she has exited the waiting period. End.

In my view, there is no proof in some of what both parties have argued.

As for the saying of the first group that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave the prayer during the days of your qurū'," the most that this indicates is that the Prophet (ﷺ) applied the term qurū' to menstruation, and there is no dispute over the permissibility of this, as is the nature of a shared word, for it is used at times for this and at times for that. The dispute is only about the qurū' mentioned in this verse. As for his saying (ﷺ) concerning the slave-woman: "and her waiting period is two menstruations," it is a hadith that Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, and al-Hakim recorded and authenticated from 'A'isha, raised (marfu'). Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi recorded it from Ibn 'Umar, also raised. Its indication of what the first group said is strong.

As for their saying that the purpose of the waiting period is the cleansing of the womb, which is achieved by menstruation and not by purity: it is answered that this would be complete only if there were no menstruation in this waiting period, on the assumption that the qurū' are explained as purities. But this is not so; rather it includes menstruation just as it includes purities. As for the second group's argument by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], it is answered that the dispute over the lam in His saying "li-'iddatihinna" makes this an possibility, and proof is not established by a possibility.

As for their argument by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Umar: "Command him, so let him take her back," the hadith is in the Sahih, and its indication is strong for what they held. It is possible to say: the waiting period ends with three purities or with three menstruations, and there is no obstacle to this, for a group of scholars permitted carrying the shared word upon both of its meanings, and by this the evidences are reconciled, the disagreement is removed, and the dispute is dispelled.

Al-Zamakhshari raised a difficulty regarding the specification of the three by the phrase "qurū'" which is a plural of abundance (jam' kathrah) and not "aqra'" which is among the plurals of paucity (jam' qillah).

He answered that they are liberal in this, using each of the two plurals in place of the other because they share the quality of plurality.

His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾. It was said: what is meant is menstruation; it was said: pregnancy; it was said: both. The reason for the prohibition of concealment is the harm it may cause in some cases to the husband and the loss of his right. If the woman says "I have menstruated" when she has not, she takes away his right of return (irtija'); and if she says "I have not menstruated" when she has, she obliges him to pay maintenance he is not obliged to pay, thereby harming him. Likewise with pregnancy: she may conceal it to cut off his right of return, or claim it to make maintenance obligatory upon him, and similar aims that entail harm to the husband.

Opinions have differed regarding the period during which a woman is believed when she claims the end of her waiting period.

His saying: ﴿If they believe in God and the Last Day﴾: in it is a severe threat to the women who conceal, and a clarification that whoever of them conceals this does not deserve the name of belief.

Al-bu'ulah is the plural of ba'l, which is the husband. He was called ba'l for his elevation (ulluw) over the wife, for they use it of the Lord. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l?﴾ [al-Saffat: 125], i.e., Lord. It is said: bu'ul and bu'ulah, just as in the plural of male one says dhukur and dhukurah. This ta' is for feminizing the plural, which is anomalous (shadhdh) and not analogized upon; rather, hearing (sama') is to be relied on. Al-bu'ulah can also be a verbal noun from ba'ala al-rajul, yab'alu, like mana'a yamna'u, i.e., he became a ba'l.

His saying: ﴿They have more right to take them back﴾, i.e., to their return (rujj'atihinna). That applies specifically to the one for whom it is permissible for the husband to take her back, so it is in the position of specification relative to the generality of His saying: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves﴾, since that encompasses divorced women and others.

His saying: "in that," i.e., in the period of waiting. If the period of waiting ends, she is more entitled to herself, and she is not lawful to him except by a new marriage contract with a guardian, witnesses, and a new bridal gift. There is no dispute about this. Return (raj'ah) occurs by utterance and occurs by intercourse, and the one taking her back incurs none of the rulings of marriage, without dispute.

His saying: ﴿If they desire reconciliation﴾, i.e., by the return: that is, the reform of his condition with her and her condition with him. If he intends harm to her, it is forbidden by His saying: ﴿And do not retain them for harm, to transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. It was said: if he intends harm by the return, it is valid, though he commits a prohibited act and wrongs himself. On this basis, the condition mentioned in the verse serves to urge husbands to intend righteousness and to restrain them from intending harm; it is not meant to make the intention of reconciliation a condition for the validity of the return.

His saying: ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable﴾, i.e., for them are rights of marriage upon men similar to what men have over them, so he treats her kindly with what is known as the custom of people, which they do for their wives; and she likewise treats her husband kindly with what is known as the custom of women, such as obedience, adornment, endearment, and the like.

His saying: ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾, i.e., a rank that they do not have, which is his being responsible for her in maintenance, his being among the people of jihad, intellect, and strength, his having a greater share of inheritance than hers, and her being obliged to comply with his command and to stop at his pleasure. Even if there were no excellence of men over women except that women were created from men, that would suffice, since it is established that Eve was created from the rib of Adam.

Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded from Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan al-Ansariyyah, who said: I was divorced in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and there was no waiting period for the divorced woman, so God revealed when I was divorced the waiting period for divorce, and He said: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait﴾, the verse.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three qurū'﴾, then He said: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], so it was abrogated, and He said: ﴿Then if you divorce them before you touch them, you have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi recorded through various chains from 'A'isha that she said: al-quru' are the purities.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit the like of this.

The aforementioned recorded from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: al-quru' are menstruations, from the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ).

al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: "three qurū'," that he said: "three menstruations."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Qatada regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾, that he said: a woman used to conceal her pregnancy until she attributed it to another man, so God forbade them from that.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Umar regarding the verse that he said: "The pregnancy and the menstruation."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Sa'id ibn Mansur recorded from Mujahid the like of it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 227–228 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾, that he said: "If a man divorces his wife with one or two pronouncements while she is pregnant, he has more right to take her back as long as she has not given birth to her child. This is His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that﴾, that he said: "In the 'iddah (waiting period)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah the like of this, and he added: "As long as he has not divorced her three times."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His saying, ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them﴾, that he said: "When they obey Allah and obey their husbands, it is incumbent upon him to treat them well, to refrain from harming them, and to spend on them from his means."

The compilers of the Sunan narrated from 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, you have rights over your wives, and your wives have rights over you. As for your right over your wives, it is that they should not allow onto your bedding anyone you dislike, nor permit into your homes anyone you dislike. And as for their right over you, it is that you treat them well in their clothing and their food." al-Tirmidhi authenticated it.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is the right of the wife over the husband?" He said: "That you feed her when you eat, clothe her when you clothe yourself, do not strike the face, and do not revile her except within the house."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying, ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾, that he said: "It is the excellence with which Allah has favoured him over her through jihad, and the excess of his inheritance over her inheritance, and everything else in which he has been favoured over her."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik regarding the verse, that he said: "He divorces her while she has no say in the matter at all."

They both narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "It is the leadership (imarah)."

But this is not so; rather it includes menstruation just as it includes purities. As for the second group's argument by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], it is answered that the dispute over the lam in His saying "li-'iddatihinna" makes this an possibility, and proof is not established by a possibility.

As for their argument by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Umar: "Command him, so let him take her back," the hadith is in the Sahih, and its indication is strong for what they held. It is possible to say: the waiting period ends with three purities or with three menstruations, and there is no obstacle to this, for a group of scholars permitted carrying the shared word upon both of its meanings, and by this the evidences are reconciled, the disagreement is removed, and the dispute is dispelled.

Al-Zamakhshari raised a difficulty regarding the specification of the three by the phrase "qurū'" which is a plural of abundance (jam' kathrah) and not "aqra'" which is among the plurals of paucity (jam' qillah).

He answered that they are liberal in this, using each of the two plurals in place of the other because they share the quality of plurality.

His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾. It was said: what is meant is menstruation; it was said: pregnancy; it was said: both. The reason for the prohibition of concealment is the harm it may cause in some cases to the husband and the loss of his right. If the woman says "I have menstruated" when she has not, she takes away his right of return (irtija'); and if she says "I have not menstruated" when she has, she obliges him to pay maintenance he is not obliged to pay, thereby harming him. Likewise with pregnancy: she may conceal it to cut off his right of return, or claim it to make maintenance obligatory upon him, and similar aims that entail harm to the husband.

Opinions have differed regarding the period during which a woman is believed when she claims the end of her waiting period.

His saying: ﴿If they believe in God and the Last Day﴾: in it is a severe threat to the women who conceal, and a clarification that whoever of them conceals this does not deserve the name of belief.

Al-bu'ulah is the plural of ba'l, which is the husband. He was called ba'l for his elevation (ulluw) over the wife, for they use it of the Lord. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l?﴾ [al-Saffat: 125], i.e., Lord. It is said: bu'ul and bu'ulah, just as in the plural of male one says dhukur and dhukurah. This ta' is for feminizing the plural, which is anomalous (shadhdh) and not analogized upon; rather, hearing (sama') is to be relied on. Al-bu'ulah can also be a verbal noun from ba'ala al-rajul, yab'alu, like mana'a yamna'u, i.e., he became a ba'l.

His saying: ﴿They have more right to take them back﴾, i.e., to their return (rujj'atihinna). That applies specifically to the one for whom it is permissible for the husband to take her back, so it is in the position of specification relative to the generality of His saying: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves﴾, since that encompasses divorced women and others.

His saying: "in that," i.e., in the period of waiting. If the period of waiting ends, she is more entitled to herself, and she is not lawful to him except by a new marriage contract with a guardian, witnesses, and a new bridal gift. There is no dispute about this. Return (raj'ah) occurs by utterance and occurs by intercourse, and the one taking her back incurs none of the rulings of marriage, without dispute.

His saying: ﴿If they desire reconciliation﴾, i.e., by the return: that is, the reform of his condition with her and her condition with him. If he intends harm to her, it is forbidden by His saying: ﴿And do not retain them for harm, to transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. It was said: if he intends harm by the return, it is valid, though he commits a prohibited act and wrongs himself. On this basis, the condition mentioned in the verse serves to urge husbands to intend righteousness and to restrain them from intending harm; it is not meant to make the intention of reconciliation a condition for the validity of the return.

His saying: ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable﴾, i.e., for them are rights of marriage upon men similar to what men have over them, so he treats her kindly with what is known as the custom of people, which they do for their wives; and she likewise treats her husband kindly with what is known as the custom of women, such as obedience, adornment, endearment, and the like.

His saying: ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾, i.e., a rank that they do not have, which is his being responsible for her in maintenance, his being among the people of jihad, intellect, and strength, his having a greater share of inheritance than hers, and her being obliged to comply with his command and to stop at his pleasure. Even if there were no excellence of men over women except that women were created from men, that would suffice, since it is established that Eve was created from the rib of Adam.

Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded from Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan al-Ansariyyah, who said: I was divorced in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and there was no waiting period for the divorced woman, so God revealed when I was divorced the waiting period for divorce, and He said: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait﴾, the verse.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three qurū'﴾, then He said: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], so it was abrogated, and He said: ﴿Then if you divorce them before you touch them, you have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi recorded through various chains from 'A'isha that she said: al-quru' are the purities.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit the like of this.

The aforementioned recorded from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: al-quru' are menstruations, from the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ).

al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: "three qurū'," that he said: "three menstruations."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Qatada regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs﴾, that he said: a woman used to conceal her pregnancy until she attributed it to another man, so God forbade them from that.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Umar regarding the verse that he said: "The pregnancy and the menstruation."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Sa'id ibn Mansur recorded from Mujahid the like of it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 227–228 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾, that he said: "If a man divorces his wife with one or two pronouncements while she is pregnant, he has more right to take her back as long as she has not given birth to her child. This is His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying, ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that﴾, that he said: "In the 'iddah (waiting period)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah the like of this, and he added: "As long as he has not divorced her three times."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His saying, ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them﴾, that he said: "When they obey Allah and obey their husbands, it is incumbent upon him to treat them well, to refrain from harming them, and to spend on them from his means."

The compilers of the Sunan narrated from 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, you have rights over your wives, and your wives have rights over you. As for your right over your wives, it is that they should not allow onto your bedding anyone you dislike, nor permit into your homes anyone you dislike. And as for their right over you, it is that you treat them well in their clothing and their food." al-Tirmidhi authenticated it.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is the right of the wife over the husband?" He said: "That you feed her when you eat, clothe her when you clothe yourself, do not strike the face, and do not revile her except within the house."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying, ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾, that he said: "It is the excellence with which Allah has favoured him over her through jihad, and the excess of his inheritance over her inheritance, and everything else in which he has been favoured over her."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik regarding the verse, that he said: "He divorces her while she has no say in the matter at all."

They both narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "It is the leadership (imarah)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 229–230 (part 1 of 2):

The divorce mentioned here is the revocable divorce, as is shown by what preceded in the first verse. That is, the divorce in which the husbands have the right of return (raj'ah) is "two times," meaning the first and second pronouncement, since there is no return after the third. Almighty Allah said "two times" and did not say "two pronouncements" to indicate that divorce should be one time after another, not two pronouncements at once; so said a group of the exegetes. Since after the second pronouncement there remain only one of two matters, either pronouncing the third, by which the wife becomes irrevocably separated (tabin), or retaining her and continuing the marriage, and not pronouncing the third upon her, Almighty Allah said: ﴿Then either retain them in an honourable manner or release them with kindness﴾. That is: then either retention after return for one who has been divorced by her husband twice, in an honourable manner, meaning in what is recognized as good by people in good companionship; ﴿or release with kindness﴾, meaning by pronouncing a third pronouncement upon her without harming her. It has been said that the meaning is: ﴿then retain in an honourable manner﴾, meaning by return after the second pronouncement; ﴿or release with kindness﴾, meaning by leaving off return after the second until her waiting period (iddah) ends.

The first is more apparent.

His saying ﴿The divorce﴾ is a subject with an omitted modifier: that is, the number of divorces in which return is established is two times.

The scholars have differed concerning the pronouncing of three at once in a single utterance: does it take effect as three or as one only? The majority went to the first, and those other than them went to the second, which is the truth.

I have established this in my writings with thorough proof, and devoted a separate treatise to it.

His saying ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾: the address is to the husbands. That is, it is not lawful for husbands to take anything of the dower that they gave to their wives, in a manner of harm to them. The indefinite "anything" (shay'an) is for belittling: that is, anything trivial, let alone much. He specified what they gave them with the prohibition of taking from it, although it is not lawful for husbands to take any of their wealth that they own apart from the dower, because that is what the husband's soul is attached to and longs to take, to the exclusion of others, of what is in her possession.
