It is related in the two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) the prohibition of fleeing from the plague, and of entering a land in which it is present, from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا﴾ was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari said: 'O Messenger of God, does God indeed want a loan from us?' He said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah.' He said: 'Show me your hand, O Messenger of God.' So he gave him his hand. He said: 'Indeed, I have lent my orchard to my Lord, and He has in it six hundred palm trees.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted this story through the route of Zayd ibn Aslam. Al-Tabarani added, from his father, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn Ishaq and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿أضْعافًا كَثِيرَةً﴾ ("manifold multiples"), that he said: No one knows what this multiplication is.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, who said: A hadith reached me from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Indeed God writes for His believing servant, for one good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds." So I performed the pilgrimage that year, and I had intended to make the pilgrimage only to meet him about this hadith. I met Abu Hurayrah and mentioned it to him. He said: "That is not what I said, and he did not memorize the hadith you were related. What I said was: 'Indeed God gives the believing servant, for one good deed, two thousand thousand good deeds.'" Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Do you not find this in the Book of God? ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا فَيُضاعِفَهُ لَهُ أضْعافًا كَثِيرَةً﴾. So the 'many' with God is more than two thousand thousand and two thousand thousand. By Him in whose hand is my soul, I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed God multiplies the good deed two thousand thousand good deeds.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "When ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] to the end was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'My Lord, increase my community.' Then ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا فَيُضاعِفَهُ لَهُ أضْعافًا كَثِيرَةً﴾ was revealed. He said: 'My Lord, increase my community.' Then ﴿إنَّما يُوَفّى الصّابِرُونَ أجْرَهم بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾ [al-Zumar: 10] was revealed."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sufyan, who said: "When ﴿مَن جاءَ بِالحَسَنَةِ فَلَهُ عَشْرُ أمْثالِها﴾ [al-An'am: 160] was revealed, he said: 'My Lord, increase my community.' Then ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ﴾ was revealed; he said: 'My Lord, increase my community.' Then ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261] was revealed; he said: 'My Lord, increase my community.' Then ﴿إنَّما يُوَفّى الصّابِرُونَ﴾ was revealed." There are other hadiths on this subject; these are the best of them, and they will come up at the commentary on His saying: ﴿كَمَثَلِ حَبَّةٍ أنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ﴾, so investigate them there.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿واللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ ويَبْسُطُ﴾ that he said: "He withholds charity, and extends"; he said: "He replaces it." ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾: he said: "From dust you came, and to dust you return."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse, that he said: God knew that among those who fight in the way of God there are some who find no strength, and among those who do not fight in the way of God there are some who find wealth. So He urged these to lend, saying: ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ﴾. He said: "He extends for you while you are heavy about going out and do not desire it, and He withholds from this one while he is glad in spirit to go out and is light about it. So strengthen him with what is in your hand, and you will have your share."

The interrogative here is for affirmation (taqrir), and the seeing mentioned is the seeing of the heart, not the seeing of the eye.

According to Sibawayh, the meaning is: "Pay attention to the matter of those who went out." It is said that this seeing does not need two objects.

The summary of this is that the seeing here, which means perception (idrak), is construed with the meaning of alerting (tanbih). It may also be construed with the meaning of reaching a limit (intiha'), that is: has your knowledge not reached them? Or with the meaning of arrival (wusul), that is: has your knowledge not arrived at them? It may also be the seeing of the eye, that is: have you not looked at those who went out?

God, glorified is He, made the story of these people, since it had such currency and fame, something that compels everyone to acknowledge it, as though it were known to every individual or visible to every observer. This is because the People of the Book had been informed of it, recorded it, and made its matter widely known. The address here is to everyone who is fit to receive it.

The speech runs in the manner of a proverb (mathal), in a context of wonder, claiming that it is so manifest and clear that the present and the absent alike perceive it equally.

His saying ﴿وهم أُلُوفٌ﴾ ("and they were thousands") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "went out." "Uluf" is one of the plurals of multiplicity, which indicates that they were many thousands.

His saying ﴿حَذَرَ المَوْتِ﴾ ("fearing death") is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

His saying ﴿فَقالَ لَهُمُ اللَّهُ مُوتُوا﴾ ("So God said to them: Die") is a command of creation (amr takwin), an expression of the attachment of His will to their death all at once. Or it is an image (tamthil) of His causing them to die a single death, as though they were commanded and obeyed.

His saying ﴿ثُمَّ أحْياهُمْ﴾ ("Then He gave them life") is conjoined to an implied element required by the context. That is: God said to them, "Die," so they died, then He gave them life. Or it is conjoined to "He said," since "He said" was an expression for causing death.

His saying ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لَذُو فَضْلٍ عَلى النّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed God is full of bounty toward mankind"): the indefiniteness in His saying "bounty" is for magnification, that is: He is possessed of great bounty toward all of mankind. As for those who went out, it is because He gave them life so that they might take heed. As for the addressees, it is because He guided them to take heed and gain insight through the story of these people.

His saying ﴿وقاتِلُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("And fight in the way of God") is conjoined to an implied element, as though it were said: "Give thanks for His bounty by taking heed of what He has related to you, and fight." This is so if the address in "and fight" refers back to the addressees in ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ إلى الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا﴾, as most of the exegetes (mufassirun) have said. On this view, the mention of this story serves to encourage the Muslims to strive (jihad). It has been said that the address is to those among the Children of Israel who were brought to life, in which case it is conjoined to His saying "Die," and there is an omission in the speech, its estimated sense being: "And He said to them: Fight."

Ibn Jarir said: There is no basis for the view of those who say that the command to fight was addressed to those who were brought back to life.

His saying ﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ﴾ ("Who is it that will lend to God"): when He, glorified is He, had commanded fighting and striving, He commanded spending for that purpose. "Man" is interrogative and in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), "dha" is its predicate, and "alladhi" with its relative clause is a description of it or a substitute (badal) for it. The lending to God is an image (mathal) for sending ahead a righteous deed for which its doer deserves reward. The original meaning of "qard" (loan) is a name for anything for which a recompense is sought. It is said: "Fulan lent Fulan," meaning he gave him something that would be repaid to him.

The poet said:

"And when you are repaid a loan, then repay it."

Al-Zajjaj said: In the language, "qard" means a good trial and an evil trial.

Umayya said:

"Every man will be repaid his loan, good or evil, and his debt in the measure that he paid."

Another said:

"He repaid the loans with their like: good with good, and evil with evil."

Al-Kisa'i said: "Qard" is what you have sent ahead of a righteous or evil deed. The root of the word is cutting, and from it comes "miqrad" (scissors). The calling for a loan in the verse is only for familiarization and bringing people near through what they can understand.

God is the Rich, the Praiseworthy. He likened the giving of the believer, whose reward in the Hereafter he seeks, to a loan, just as He likened the giving of souls and wealth in order to obtain Paradise to buying and selling.

His saying ﴿حَسَنًا﴾ ("good") means: one whose soul is content with it, without reproach or harm.

His saying ﴿فَيُضاعِفَهُ﴾ ("so that He may multiply it for him"): 'Asim and others read it with an alif and a fatha on the fa'.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the alif and a damma on the fa'. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read "fayudhA'ifahu" with the alif dropped, the 'ain doubled, and a fatha on the fa'. Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read it with the doubling and a damma on the fa'.

As for the one who reads with a fatha, it is on the basis that it is the answer to the interrogative. As for the one who reads with a damma, it is on the basis of an implied subject, that is: "He multiplies it."

There has been disagreement about the quantity of this multiplication, in several opinions.

It has been said: No one knows it except God alone.

His saying ﴿واللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ ويَبْسُطُ﴾ ("And God withholds and extends") is general over everything; He is the one who withholds and extends. "Qabd" is restriction, and "bast" is expansion. In it is a warning that whoever is stingy instead of extending will soon have it replaced by withholding. This is why He said: ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("and to Him you will be returned"), that is, He will recompense you for what you sent ahead when you return to Him. If you spend from what He has widened for you, He will do good to you; if you are stingy, He will punish you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ إلى الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا مِن دِيارِهِمْ﴾ ("Have you not seen those who went out of their homes"), that he said: They were four thousand who went out fleeing from the plague, and they said: "We will go to a land where there is no death." When they reached a certain place, God said to them: "Die," and they died. Then a prophet of the prophets passed by them and prayed to his Lord that He would give them life so that they might worship Him, and He gave them life.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that the town they went out from was Dawardan.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this story at length from Abu Malik, and in it they were thirty-some thousand.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that their homes were Adhri'at.

He also transmitted from Abu Salih that they were nine thousand.

A group of the transmitting exegetes (muhaddithun mufassirun) related this story in various forms, and multiplying its chains brings no benefit.

It is related in the two Sahihs and others from the Prophet (ﷺ) the prohibition of fleeing from the plague, and of entering a land in which it is present, from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.

So strengthen him with what is in your hand, and you will have your share."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 250–252 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-mala') of the Children of Israel?﴾ The discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes?﴾ and we have already presented it. Al-mala' means the nobles among the people, as if they were "filled" (mulli'a) with nobility.

Al-Zajjaj said: They were named that because they are "filled" (mali'un) with what is needed from them. It is a collective noun, like al-qawm (the people) and al-rahT (the company).

In exhorting to fighting, God, glorified is He, mentioned another story that took place among the Children of Israel after the previous story.

His saying: ﴿after Musa﴾: "min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), and its governing element is implied: i.e., they were existing after Musa, meaning after his death.

His saying: ﴿a prophet for them﴾: It was said that he is Shamwil ibn Yar ibn 'Alqamah, who is known as Ibn al-'Ajuz. It is also said Shum'un. He is from the descendants of Ya'qub. It was also said he is from the offspring of Harun. It was said he is Yusha' ibn Nun, but this is very weak, because Yusha' was the servant of Musa, and Dawud did not appear until a long time after that. It was also said his name is Isma'il.

His saying: ﴿Send for us a king﴾: i.e., a commander to whom we return and act according to his opinion.

His saying: "nuqatil" with the nun and the jazm (jussive), as a response to the imperative. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it this way.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and the verb in the raf' (nominative), considering it a description (sifah) of the king.

It was also read with the nun and the raf', as a circumstantial clause (hal) or a new independent sentence.

His saying: ﴿Would you perhaps not fight?﴾ "'asaytum" is read with fath on the sin and with kasr, both being dialects. Nafi' read the second, and the rest read the first.

Al-Kashshaf said: The reading with kasr is weak.

Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for the kasr.

Abu 'Ali said: The basis for the kasr is the Arabs' saying: "huwa 'assa bidhalika," like "harra" and "shajja," and forms fa'ala and fa'ila have come in words like naqama and naqima. Thus 'asayta and 'asiyta (are similar). Makki said the same.

Al-Hasan and Talhah also read with kasr, so there is no basis for weakening it. It is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah): i.e., have you come close to not fighting? The placing of the interrogative particle before a verb of approximation is to affirm what is expected from it and to indicate that it will happen. The conditional clause separates 'asa from its predicate to show the importance of it.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿That you do not fight﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative): i.e., "would you perhaps be fighting?"

Al-Akhfash said: The "an" in His saying ﴿What is for us that we should not fight?﴾ is extra (za'idah).

Al-Farra' said: It is interpreted according to meaning: i.e., "what prevented us," as you say: "What is for you that you do not pray?" It was also said the meaning is: "What is it for us regarding not fighting?"

Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of these views.

His saying: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾ is a causal clause, and the sentence is a circumstantial one. The singling out of the children for mention is because they were the ones who were taken captive, or because they hold a place above the rest of the relatives.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed﴾: i.e., was obligated. He, glorified is He, informed that they turned away because of the disorder of their intentions and the weakness of their resolve.

There is disagreement about the number of the few whom God excepted, who were those who were satisfied with the handful (of water).

His saying: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾ begins the detailed account of what happened between them and their prophet of statements and actions.

Talut (Saul): a non-Arabic name. He was a water-carrier. It was said he was a tanner, and it was said he was a muleteer. He was not from the tribe of prophethood, which is the Banu Lawi, nor from the tribe of kingship, which is the Banu Yahudha. Therefore ﴿they said: How can he have kingship over us?﴾, i.e., how is that, when he was not from the house of kingship, nor was he one to whom abundant wealth had been given, so that we would follow him for his nobility or his wealth? This clause, namely His saying ﴿while we are more deserving﴾, is circumstantial, and so is the clause conjoined to it.

His saying: ﴿God has chosen him over you﴾: i.e., He preferred him. God's choice is a decisive proof.

Then He explained to them, along with that, the basis of the choosing: that God increased him in breadth of knowledge, which is the foundation of a human being, the head of virtues, and the greatest aspect of preference. And He increased him in breadth of body, through which effect shows in wars and similar things. So he was strong in his religion and his body, and that is what is considered, not the nobility of lineage.

For the virtues of the soul take precedence over it.

﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾: The kingdom is His kingdom, and the servants are His servants. So what is it for you to object to something that is not yours, nor is its decision in your hands?

Some exegetes went to the view that His saying ﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾ is from the words of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said it is from the words of their prophet, and this is the apparent meaning.

His saying: ﴿Vast﴾: i.e., vast in bounty, He expands for whom He wills of His servants. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves kingship and is fit for it.

Al-tabut (the chest) is on the pattern fa'lut, from al-tawb, which is return, because they return to it. I.e., the sign of his kingship is the coming of the chest that was taken from them, i.e., its return to you. It is the chest of the Torah.

Al-sakinah (tranquility) is on the pattern fa'ilah, derived from al-sukun, dignity and calm. I.e., in it is the cause of the tranquility of your hearts regarding what you disputed about the matter of Talut.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The correct view is that the chest contained excellent things from the remnants of the prophets and their relics, so that souls would be at peace with that, find comfort in it, and be strengthened.

There are differing views about the sakinah, and some of them will come with an explanation. Similarly, there is disagreement about al-baqiyyah (remainder). It was said: it is the staff of Musa and the fragments of the tablets. Other things have been said.

It was said: What is meant by "the family of Musa and Harun" is the two of them themselves, i.e., of what Harun and Musa left behind, and the word "family" is inserted to magnify their status. It was also said: what is meant is the prophets from the sons of Ya'qub, because they both are from the offspring of Ya'qub, so the rest of his relatives and whoever descended from him are a family to them both.

Fasala means: he set out with them. One says "fasaltu al-shay' fa-infasala" (I cut the thing and it was cut), i.e., I severed it and it was severed. Its origin is transitive. One says "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself), then it was used in the intransitive sense like infasala. It was said that fasala is used both intransitively and transitively: one says "fasala 'an al-balad fusulan" (he departed from the city), and "fasala nafsahu fasalan."

Al-ibtila': testing.

Al-nahr (the river): it was said it is between Jordan and Palestine. The majority read it as nahrin with fath on the ha'.

Hamid, Mujahid and al-A'raj read it with sukun on the ha'.

What is meant by this testing is testing their obedience. Whoever obeyed in that matter of the water obeyed in what else. Whoever disobeyed in this and was overcome by his self is, in disobedience in all other hardships, more likely to fail. He granted them permission regarding the handful so that the harm of thirst would be removed from them for those who are patient with the hardship of life and who restrain themselves from luxury.

So what is meant by His saying ﴿whoever drinks from it﴾ is: whoever gulped it down and did not limit himself to a handful. "Man" here is for the starting point.

The meaning of His saying ﴿then he is not of me﴾: i.e., he is not of my companions. This is from their saying: "So-and-so is from so-and-so," as if he were a part of him, because of their intermixing and long companionship. This is common and well known in Arabic speech. From it is the saying of the poet:

When you seek to commit wickedness against a lion, I am not of you and you are not of me.

His saying ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾: one says "ta'imtu al-shay'" (I tasted the thing), i.e., I experienced it, and "at'amtuhu al-ma'" (I made him taste the water), i.e., I let him taste it. In this there is evidence that water is called ta'am (food).

Al-ightiraf is taking from a thing with the hand or with a tool. Al-gharf is like al-ightiraf, and al-ghurfah is a single occurrence.

It has been read with fath on the ghayn and with damm. The fath is for the single occurrence, and the damm is a name for the thing scooped. It was said: with fath, al-ghurfah means a single handful, and with damm it means two handfuls. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning. From it is the saying of the poet:

They do not approach water with vessels, except by scooping from the pools with the palm.

His saying: ﴿except a few﴾: the number of them will come with explanation. It was also read: "illa qalilun" (with nominative). There is no basis for it except what has been said, that it is from omitting the word in favor of the meaning: i.e., it was not given except to a few. This is far-fetched.

His saying ﴿When he had crossed it﴾: i.e., when Talut crossed the river, ﴿and those who believed with him﴾, and they are the few who obeyed him. However, they differed in the strength of certainty. Some of them said ﴿We have no power today﴾, and ﴿those who were certain﴾ i.e., who were sure ﴿that they would meet God﴾ said. Al-fi'ah is the group, and al-qit'ah (a portion) of them is from "fa'uta ra'sahu bil-sayf," i.e., I cut it.

His saying: ﴿they came forth﴾, i.e., they came out into al-baraz, which is the open, wide land.

Jalut was the commander of the Amalekites.

They said: i.e., all of those with him from the believers. Al-ifraghh indicates the meaning of abundance.

His saying ﴿and make our feet firm﴾ is an expression of strength and absence of weakness. One says: "thabata qadamu fulanin 'ala kadha" when he settled in it and did not depart from it, and "thabata qadamuhu fi al-harb" when victory was his and success was with him.

His saying: ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ refers to Jalut and his soldiers.

He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to make clear what was the cause prompting the victory over them, which is their disbelief. He mentioned the victory after asking for firm feet, because the second is the goal of the first.

His saying: ﴿So they routed them by God's permission﴾. Al-hizm, with kasr, is from it; a "minhazim" water-skin is one whose part has bent over another while dry. From it is what is said about Zamzam, that it is the "hizmat Jibril," i.e., he struck it with his foot and the water came out. Al-hizm is also what is broken from dry firewood. The sense of the sentence is: God sent down victory upon them, ﴿so they routed them by God's permission﴾, i.e., by His command and will.

His saying: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. He is Dawud ibn Iysha, with kasr on the hamzah, then a silent ya' after it, then a dotted letter. It is also said: Dawud ibn Zakariyya ibn Bishuy, from the tribe of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. God combined for him prophethood and kingship after he had been a shepherd, and he was the youngest of his brothers. Talut chose him to fight Jalut, and he killed him.

What is meant by al-hikmah (wisdom) here is prophethood. It was said: it is his teaching of the craft of coats of mail and the speech of birds. It was said: it is his being given the chain (al-silsilah) by which they used to judge disputes.

His saying: ﴿And He taught him from what He willed﴾. It was said: the present tense here is placed in the position of the past tense, and the doer of this verb is God, the Exalted. It was said: it is Dawud.

The apparent meaning of this construction is that God, glorified is He, taught him from what His will decreed and His will was attached to. It has been said that among that is what we mentioned earlier, his being taught the craft of coats of mail and what follows it.

His saying: ﴿And were it not that God repels some people by means of others﴾: The majority read ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾. Nafi' read "difa'". Both are verbal nouns of "daf'a". So said Sibawayh.

Abu Hatim said: "dafi'" and "daf'" are the same, like "tarraqtu na'li" and "taraqtuhu."

Abu 'Ubaydah chose the reading of the majority and rejected the reading "difa'," saying: because God, mighty and majestic, is not overcome by anyone.

Makki said: Abu 'Ubaydah gives the impression that this is of the form of mufa'alah, but it is not. On both readings the verbal noun is annexed to its agent: i.e., ﴿And were it not for God's repelling the people﴾. "Some of them" is a substitute for "the people," and they are the ones who engage in the causes of evil and corruption through others among them, and they are the ones who restrain them from that and turn them back from it. ﴿The earth would have been corrupted﴾ because of the domination of the people of corruption over it and their creating of evils that destroy the crops and the offspring. The indefinite "bounty" (fadl) is for magnification.

The verses of God are what this story contains of the matters mentioned.

What is meant here by "the truth" is the correct report that has no doubt among the People of the Book and those acquainted with the histories of the world.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ is an information from God, glorified is He, that he is among the messengers of God, glorified is He, to strengthen his heart, to firm up his inner self, and to reinforce his matter.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel?﴾ He said: This was when prophethood had been lifted and the people of faith had been driven out, and the tyrants had expelled them from their homes and their children. ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them﴾, and that was when the Ark (al-tabut) came to them. He said: Among the Children of Israel there were two tribes: the tribe of prophethood and the tribe of rulership (khilafa). Rulership would not be held except by the tribe of rulership, and prophethood would not be held except by the tribe of prophethood. ﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed Allah has sent Talut to you as king. They said: How can he have kingship over us when we are more entitled to kingship than he is?﴾ He was from neither of the two tribes, neither the tribe of prophethood nor the tribe of rulership. ﴿He said: Indeed Allah has chosen him over you﴾. They refused to hand leadership over to him, until he said to them: ﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in it is tranquility (sakina) from your Lord and a remnant﴾. Musa, when he threw down the Tablets, they broke; some of them were lifted up, and what remained was gathered and placed in the Ark. The Amalekites had captured that Ark. The Amalekites were a group from 'Ad, who were at Ariha. The angels brought the Ark, carrying it between the sky and the earth while they looked on, until they set it down before Talut. When they saw that, they said: Yes. So they submitted to him and made him king. And when the prophets attended a battle, they would put the Ark before them and say: Adam descended with that Ark, and with the corner-stone (al-rukn), and with the staff of Musa, from Paradise.

It has reached me that the Ark and the staff of Musa are in the lake of Tiberias, and that they will emerge before the Day of Resurrection.

This meaning has been transmitted, both in brief and in extended form, from a group of the early generation (al-salaf). Therefore, lengthening the discussion with the mention of such matters brings no benefit that is worth counting.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth of knowledge and physique﴾: he said: "Excellence (fadila)". ﴿In knowledge and physique﴾: he said: He was great and large in body, surpassing the Children of Israel by his neck.

He also reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth in knowledge﴾: he said: Knowledge of war.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him (Ibn 'Abbas) that he was asked: Was Talut a prophet? He said: No, no revelation came to him.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he was asked about the size of the Ark of Musa. He said: About three cubits by two cubits.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Sakina is mercy.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: Sakina is tranquility and calm.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: Sakina is a creature the size of a cat, having two eyes with rays of light. Whenever the two hosts met, it would stretch out its two paws and look at them, and the army would be routed from terror.

Al-Tabarani, with a weak chain, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina is a wind that is turbulent (khajuj), and it has two heads.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina has a face like the face of a human, and then after that it is a gentle, rustling wind.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Mujahid, who said: Sakina is from Allah, like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾: a basin of gold from Paradise, with which the hearts of the prophets were washed, into which he cast the Tablets.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: It is a spirit from Allah that does not speak. Whenever they differed about a matter, it would speak and inform them of the clarification of what they wanted.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan, who said: It is something by which their hearts find rest.

'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Qatada, who said: In it is sakina, that is, dignity (waqar).

I say: These contradictory interpretations may have reached these eminent scholars from the Jews, may Allah disgrace them. They brought these matters with the aim of toying with the Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them, and sowing doubt among them. Observe how they made it at one time an animal, at another time an inanimate object, and at another time something that cannot be reasoned about, such as the saying of Mujahid: "like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, and two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat."

Thus every report from the Children of Israel is contradictory, and in most cases includes what cannot be understood. It is not possible that such contradictory interpretations were transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor an opinion held by their speaker; they are too exalted in rank to be interpretation by personal opinion (tafsir bi'l-ra'y) or by matters in which there is no room for ijtihad.

When this has been established for you, you will know that what is obligatory in such a matter is to return to the meaning of sakina linguistically, which is well known, and there is no need to engage in these strained and contradictory matters, for Allah has granted sufficiency concerning them. If an interpretation of sakina had been established for us from the Prophet (ﷺ), it would have been obligatory for us to adopt it and affirm it. But it has not been established by a sound route. Rather, it is established that it descended upon (p-172) some of the Companions while reciting the Qur'an, as in Sahih Muslim, from al-Bara', who said: "A man was reciting Surat al-Kahf, and beside him was a horse tied up. A cloud covered him and began to circle and draw near, and his horse began to shy away from it. When he woke in the morning, he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: That was the sakina that descended for the Qur'an."

There is nothing in this except that what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named was a cloud that circled around that reciter. Allah knows best.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and a remnant of what the family of Musa left behind﴾: he said: his staff and the fragments of the Tablets.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Salih, who said: In the Ark were the staff of Musa and the staff of Harun, the garments of Musa and the garments of Harun, two tablets of the Torah, the manna, and the word of relief: "There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous; glory be to Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne; and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada regarding ﴿the angels will carry it﴾: he said: The angels came bearing it, carrying it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and in the morning it was in his home.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: he said: a sign.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed Allah will test you with a river﴾: he said: with thirst. When he reached the river, which is the river Jordan, most of the people drank from it, and whoever drank from it only became more thirsty, while whoever took a single handful with his hand was sufficed and his thirst was relieved.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿so they drank from it, except a few of them﴾: he said: The few were three hundred and some ten, the number of the people of Badr.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from al-Bara', who said: We, the Companions of Muhammad, used to say that the Companions of Badr were equal in number to the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him, and that none crossed with him except a believer: some ten and three hundred.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his Companions on the day of Badr: You are equal in number to the companions of Talut on the day he met Jalut."

Ibn 'Asakir, through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, reported: They were three hundred thousand and three thousand, three hundred and thirteen. They all drank from it except three hundred and thirteen men, equal in number to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. Talut sent back the rest and went on with three hundred and thirteen.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding ﴿those who think﴾: he said: those who are certain.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: Talut was commander over the army. Abu Dawud sent something with Dawud to his brothers. Dawud said to Talut: What is for me? Jalut came forward and said: For you is a third of my kingdom, and I will marry you to my daughter. Dawud took a pouch and put three stones in it. Then he named Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and then put his hand in, saying: "In the name of Allah, my God and the God of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." He brought out one stone, which he placed in his sling, and he threw it at Jalut, and it pierced thirty-three eggs on his head and killed thirty thousand who were behind him.

The exegetes have mentioned many stories of this kind. Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others﴾: he said: Allah repels by means of one who prays from one who does not pray, by means of one who performs Hajj from one who does not perform Hajj, and by means of one who pays zakat from one who does not pay zakat.

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Jarir, with a weak chain, reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah repels calamity from a hundred households of the neighbours of a righteous Muslim." Then Ibn 'Umar recited ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people...﴾ the verse. In its chain is Yahya ibn Sa'id al-'Attar al-Himsi, who is extremely weak.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 250–252 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-mala') of the Children of Israel?﴾ The discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes?﴾ and we have already presented it. Al-mala' means the nobles among the people, as if they were "filled" (mulli'a) with nobility.

Al-Zajjaj said: They were named that because they are "filled" (mali'un) with what is needed from them. It is a collective noun, like al-qawm (the people) and al-rahT (the company).

In exhorting to fighting, God, glorified is He, mentioned another story that took place among the Children of Israel after the previous story.

His saying: ﴿after Musa﴾: "min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), and its governing element is implied: i.e., they were existing after Musa, meaning after his death.

His saying: ﴿a prophet for them﴾: It was said that he is Shamwil ibn Yar ibn 'Alqamah, who is known as Ibn al-'Ajuz. It is also said Shum'un. He is from the descendants of Ya'qub. It was also said he is from the offspring of Harun. It was said he is Yusha' ibn Nun, but this is very weak, because Yusha' was the servant of Musa, and Dawud did not appear until a long time after that. It was also said his name is Isma'il.

His saying: ﴿Send for us a king﴾: i.e., a commander to whom we return and act according to his opinion.

His saying: "nuqatil" with the nun and the jazm (jussive), as a response to the imperative. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it this way.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and the verb in the raf' (nominative), considering it a description (sifah) of the king.

It was also read with the nun and the raf', as a circumstantial clause (hal) or a new independent sentence.

His saying: ﴿Would you perhaps not fight?﴾ "'asaytum" is read with fath on the sin and with kasr, both being dialects. Nafi' read the second, and the rest read the first.

Al-Kashshaf said: The reading with kasr is weak.

Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for the kasr.

Abu 'Ali said: The basis for the kasr is the Arabs' saying: "huwa 'assa bidhalika," like "harra" and "shajja," and forms fa'ala and fa'ila have come in words like naqama and naqima. Thus 'asayta and 'asiyta (are similar). Makki said the same.

Al-Hasan and Talhah also read with kasr, so there is no basis for weakening it. It is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah): i.e., have you come close to not fighting? The placing of the interrogative particle before a verb of approximation is to affirm what is expected from it and to indicate that it will happen. The conditional clause separates 'asa from its predicate to show the importance of it.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿That you do not fight﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative): i.e., "would you perhaps be fighting?"

Al-Akhfash said: The "an" in His saying ﴿What is for us that we should not fight?﴾ is extra (za'idah).

Al-Farra' said: It is interpreted according to meaning: i.e., "what prevented us," as you say: "What is for you that you do not pray?" It was also said the meaning is: "What is it for us regarding not fighting?"

Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of these views.

His saying: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾ is a causal clause, and the sentence is a circumstantial one. The singling out of the children for mention is because they were the ones who were taken captive, or because they hold a place above the rest of the relatives.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed﴾: i.e., was obligated. He, glorified is He, informed that they turned away because of the disorder of their intentions and the weakness of their resolve.

There is disagreement about the number of the few whom God excepted, who were those who were satisfied with the handful (of water).

His saying: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾ begins the detailed account of what happened between them and their prophet of statements and actions.

Talut (Saul): a non-Arabic name. He was a water-carrier. It was said he was a tanner, and it was said he was a muleteer. He was not from the tribe of prophethood, which is the Banu Lawi, nor from the tribe of kingship, which is the Banu Yahudha. Therefore ﴿they said: How can he have kingship over us?﴾, i.e., how is that, when he was not from the house of kingship, nor was he one to whom abundant wealth had been given, so that we would follow him for his nobility or his wealth? This clause, namely His saying ﴿while we are more deserving﴾, is circumstantial, and so is the clause conjoined to it.

His saying: ﴿God has chosen him over you﴾: i.e., He preferred him. God's choice is a decisive proof.

Then He explained to them, along with that, the basis of the choosing: that God increased him in breadth of knowledge, which is the foundation of a human being, the head of virtues, and the greatest aspect of preference. And He increased him in breadth of body, through which effect shows in wars and similar things. So he was strong in his religion and his body, and that is what is considered, not the nobility of lineage.

For the virtues of the soul take precedence over it.

﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾: The kingdom is His kingdom, and the servants are His servants. So what is it for you to object to something that is not yours, nor is its decision in your hands?

Some exegetes went to the view that His saying ﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾ is from the words of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said it is from the words of their prophet, and this is the apparent meaning.

His saying: ﴿Vast﴾: i.e., vast in bounty, He expands for whom He wills of His servants. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves kingship and is fit for it.

Al-tabut (the chest) is on the pattern fa'lut, from al-tawb, which is return, because they return to it. I.e., the sign of his kingship is the coming of the chest that was taken from them, i.e., its return to you. It is the chest of the Torah.

Al-sakinah (tranquility) is on the pattern fa'ilah, derived from al-sukun, dignity and calm. I.e., in it is the cause of the tranquility of your hearts regarding what you disputed about the matter of Talut.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The correct view is that the chest contained excellent things from the remnants of the prophets and their relics, so that souls would be at peace with that, find comfort in it, and be strengthened.

There are differing views about the sakinah, and some of them will come with an explanation. Similarly, there is disagreement about al-baqiyyah (remainder). It was said: it is the staff of Musa and the fragments of the tablets. Other things have been said.

It was said: What is meant by "the family of Musa and Harun" is the two of them themselves, i.e., of what Harun and Musa left behind, and the word "family" is inserted to magnify their status. It was also said: what is meant is the prophets from the sons of Ya'qub, because they both are from the offspring of Ya'qub, so the rest of his relatives and whoever descended from him are a family to them both.

Fasala means: he set out with them. One says "fasaltu al-shay' fa-infasala" (I cut the thing and it was cut), i.e., I severed it and it was severed. Its origin is transitive. One says "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself), then it was used in the intransitive sense like infasala. It was said that fasala is used both intransitively and transitively: one says "fasala 'an al-balad fusulan" (he departed from the city), and "fasala nafsahu fasalan."

Al-ibtila': testing.

Al-nahr (the river): it was said it is between Jordan and Palestine. The majority read it as nahrin with fath on the ha'.

Hamid, Mujahid and al-A'raj read it with sukun on the ha'.

What is meant by this testing is testing their obedience. Whoever obeyed in that matter of the water obeyed in what else. Whoever disobeyed in this and was overcome by his self is, in disobedience in all other hardships, more likely to fail. He granted them permission regarding the handful so that the harm of thirst would be removed from them for those who are patient with the hardship of life and who restrain themselves from luxury.

So what is meant by His saying ﴿whoever drinks from it﴾ is: whoever gulped it down and did not limit himself to a handful. "Man" here is for the starting point.

The meaning of His saying ﴿then he is not of me﴾: i.e., he is not of my companions. This is from their saying: "So-and-so is from so-and-so," as if he were a part of him, because of their intermixing and long companionship. This is common and well known in Arabic speech. From it is the saying of the poet:

When you seek to commit wickedness against a lion, I am not of you and you are not of me.

His saying ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾: one says "ta'imtu al-shay'" (I tasted the thing), i.e., I experienced it, and "at'amtuhu al-ma'" (I made him taste the water), i.e., I let him taste it. In this there is evidence that water is called ta'am (food).

Al-ightiraf is taking from a thing with the hand or with a tool. Al-gharf is like al-ightiraf, and al-ghurfah is a single occurrence.

It has been read with fath on the ghayn and with damm. The fath is for the single occurrence, and the damm is a name for the thing scooped. It was said: with fath, al-ghurfah means a single handful, and with damm it means two handfuls. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning. From it is the saying of the poet:

They do not approach water with vessels, except by scooping from the pools with the palm.

His saying: ﴿except a few﴾: the number of them will come with explanation. It was also read: "illa qalilun" (with nominative). There is no basis for it except what has been said, that it is from omitting the word in favor of the meaning: i.e., it was not given except to a few. This is far-fetched.

His saying ﴿When he had crossed it﴾: i.e., when Talut crossed the river, ﴿and those who believed with him﴾, and they are the few who obeyed him. However, they differed in the strength of certainty. Some of them said ﴿We have no power today﴾, and ﴿those who were certain﴾ i.e., who were sure ﴿that they would meet God﴾ said. Al-fi'ah is the group, and al-qit'ah (a portion) of them is from "fa'uta ra'sahu bil-sayf," i.e., I cut it.

His saying: ﴿they came forth﴾, i.e., they came out into al-baraz, which is the open, wide land.

Jalut was the commander of the Amalekites.

They said: i.e., all of those with him from the believers. Al-ifraghh indicates the meaning of abundance.

His saying ﴿and make our feet firm﴾ is an expression of strength and absence of weakness. One says: "thabata qadamu fulanin 'ala kadha" when he settled in it and did not depart from it, and "thabata qadamuhu fi al-harb" when victory was his and success was with him.

His saying: ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ refers to Jalut and his soldiers.

He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to make clear what was the cause prompting the victory over them, which is their disbelief. He mentioned the victory after asking for firm feet, because the second is the goal of the first.

His saying: ﴿So they routed them by God's permission﴾. Al-hizm, with kasr, is from it; a "minhazim" water-skin is one whose part has bent over another while dry. From it is what is said about Zamzam, that it is the "hizmat Jibril," i.e., he struck it with his foot and the water came out. Al-hizm is also what is broken from dry firewood. The sense of the sentence is: God sent down victory upon them, ﴿so they routed them by God's permission﴾, i.e., by His command and will.

His saying: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. He is Dawud ibn Iysha, with kasr on the hamzah, then a silent ya' after it, then a dotted letter. It is also said: Dawud ibn Zakariyya ibn Bishuy, from the tribe of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. God combined for him prophethood and kingship after he had been a shepherd, and he was the youngest of his brothers. Talut chose him to fight Jalut, and he killed him.

What is meant by al-hikmah (wisdom) here is prophethood. It was said: it is his teaching of the craft of coats of mail and the speech of birds. It was said: it is his being given the chain (al-silsilah) by which they used to judge disputes.

His saying: ﴿And He taught him from what He willed﴾. It was said: the present tense here is placed in the position of the past tense, and the doer of this verb is God, the Exalted. It was said: it is Dawud.

The apparent meaning of this construction is that God, glorified is He, taught him from what His will decreed and His will was attached to. It has been said that among that is what we mentioned earlier, his being taught the craft of coats of mail and what follows it.

His saying: ﴿And were it not that God repels some people by means of others﴾: The majority read ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾. Nafi' read "difa'". Both are verbal nouns of "daf'a". So said Sibawayh.

Abu Hatim said: "dafi'" and "daf'" are the same, like "tarraqtu na'li" and "taraqtuhu."

Abu 'Ubaydah chose the reading of the majority and rejected the reading "difa'," saying: because God, mighty and majestic, is not overcome by anyone.

Makki said: Abu 'Ubaydah gives the impression that this is of the form of mufa'alah, but it is not. On both readings the verbal noun is annexed to its agent: i.e., ﴿And were it not for God's repelling the people﴾. "Some of them" is a substitute for "the people," and they are the ones who engage in the causes of evil and corruption through others among them, and they are the ones who restrain them from that and turn them back from it. ﴿The earth would have been corrupted﴾ because of the domination of the people of corruption over it and their creating of evils that destroy the crops and the offspring. The indefinite "bounty" (fadl) is for magnification.

The verses of God are what this story contains of the matters mentioned.

What is meant here by "the truth" is the correct report that has no doubt among the People of the Book and those acquainted with the histories of the world.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ is an information from God, glorified is He, that he is among the messengers of God, glorified is He, to strengthen his heart, to firm up his inner self, and to reinforce his matter.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel?﴾ He said: This was when prophethood had been lifted and the people of faith had been driven out, and the tyrants had expelled them from their homes and their children. ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them﴾, and that was when the Ark (al-tabut) came to them. He said: Among the Children of Israel there were two tribes: the tribe of prophethood and the tribe of rulership (khilafa). Rulership would not be held except by the tribe of rulership, and prophethood would not be held except by the tribe of prophethood. ﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed Allah has sent Talut to you as king. They said: How can he have kingship over us when we are more entitled to kingship than he is?﴾ He was from neither of the two tribes, neither the tribe of prophethood nor the tribe of rulership. ﴿He said: Indeed Allah has chosen him over you﴾. They refused to hand leadership over to him, until he said to them: ﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in it is tranquility (sakina) from your Lord and a remnant﴾. Musa, when he threw down the Tablets, they broke; some of them were lifted up, and what remained was gathered and placed in the Ark. The Amalekites had captured that Ark. The Amalekites were a group from 'Ad, who were at Ariha. The angels brought the Ark, carrying it between the sky and the earth while they looked on, until they set it down before Talut. When they saw that, they said: Yes. So they submitted to him and made him king. And when the prophets attended a battle, they would put the Ark before them and say: Adam descended with that Ark, and with the corner-stone (al-rukn), and with the staff of Musa, from Paradise.

It has reached me that the Ark and the staff of Musa are in the lake of Tiberias, and that they will emerge before the Day of Resurrection.

This meaning has been transmitted, both in brief and in extended form, from a group of the early generation (al-salaf). Therefore, lengthening the discussion with the mention of such matters brings no benefit that is worth counting.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth of knowledge and physique﴾: he said: "Excellence (fadila)". ﴿In knowledge and physique﴾: he said: He was great and large in body, surpassing the Children of Israel by his neck.

He also reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth in knowledge﴾: he said: Knowledge of war.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him (Ibn 'Abbas) that he was asked: Was Talut a prophet? He said: No, no revelation came to him.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he was asked about the size of the Ark of Musa. He said: About three cubits by two cubits.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Sakina is mercy.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: Sakina is tranquility and calm.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: Sakina is a creature the size of a cat, having two eyes with rays of light. Whenever the two hosts met, it would stretch out its two paws and look at them, and the army would be routed from terror.

Al-Tabarani, with a weak chain, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina is a wind that is turbulent (khajuj), and it has two heads.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina has a face like the face of a human, and then after that it is a gentle, rustling wind.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Mujahid, who said: Sakina is from Allah, like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾: a basin of gold from Paradise, with which the hearts of the prophets were washed, into which he cast the Tablets.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: It is a spirit from Allah that does not speak. Whenever they differed about a matter, it would speak and inform them of the clarification of what they wanted.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan, who said: It is something by which their hearts find rest.

'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Qatada, who said: In it is sakina, that is, dignity (waqar).

I say: These contradictory interpretations may have reached these eminent scholars from the Jews, may Allah disgrace them. They brought these matters with the aim of toying with the Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them, and sowing doubt among them. Observe how they made it at one time an animal, at another time an inanimate object, and at another time something that cannot be reasoned about, such as the saying of Mujahid: "like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, and two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat."

Thus every report from the Children of Israel is contradictory, and in most cases includes what cannot be understood. It is not possible that such contradictory interpretations were transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor an opinion held by their speaker; they are too exalted in rank to be interpretation by personal opinion (tafsir bi'l-ra'y) or by matters in which there is no room for ijtihad.

When this has been established for you, you will know that what is obligatory in such a matter is to return to the meaning of sakina linguistically, which is well known, and there is no need to engage in these strained and contradictory matters, for Allah has granted sufficiency concerning them. If an interpretation of sakina had been established for us from the Prophet (ﷺ), it would have been obligatory for us to adopt it and affirm it. But it has not been established by a sound route. Rather, it is established that it descended upon (p-172) some of the Companions while reciting the Qur'an, as in Sahih Muslim, from al-Bara', who said: "A man was reciting Surat al-Kahf, and beside him was a horse tied up. A cloud covered him and began to circle and draw near, and his horse began to shy away from it. When he woke in the morning, he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: That was the sakina that descended for the Qur'an."

There is nothing in this except that what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named was a cloud that circled around that reciter. Allah knows best.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and a remnant of what the family of Musa left behind﴾: he said: his staff and the fragments of the Tablets.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Salih, who said: In the Ark were the staff of Musa and the staff of Harun, the garments of Musa and the garments of Harun, two tablets of the Torah, the manna, and the word of relief: "There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous; glory be to Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne; and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada regarding ﴿the angels will carry it﴾: he said: The angels came bearing it, carrying it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and in the morning it was in his home.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: he said: a sign.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed Allah will test you with a river﴾: he said: with thirst. When he reached the river, which is the river Jordan, most of the people drank from it, and whoever drank from it only became more thirsty, while whoever took a single handful with his hand was sufficed and his thirst was relieved.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿so they drank from it, except a few of them﴾: he said: The few were three hundred and some ten, the number of the people of Badr.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from al-Bara', who said: We, the Companions of Muhammad, used to say that the Companions of Badr were equal in number to the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him, and that none crossed with him except a believer: some ten and three hundred.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his Companions on the day of Badr: You are equal in number to the companions of Talut on the day he met Jalut."

Ibn 'Asakir, through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, reported: They were three hundred thousand and three thousand, three hundred and thirteen. They all drank from it except three hundred and thirteen men, equal in number to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. Talut sent back the rest and went on with three hundred and thirteen.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding ﴿those who think﴾: he said: those who are certain.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: Talut was commander over the army. Abu Dawud sent something with Dawud to his brothers. Dawud said to Talut: What is for me? Jalut came forward and said: For you is a third of my kingdom, and I will marry you to my daughter. Dawud took a pouch and put three stones in it. Then he named Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and then put his hand in, saying: "In the name of Allah, my God and the God of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." He brought out one stone, which he placed in his sling, and he threw it at Jalut, and it pierced thirty-three eggs on his head and killed thirty thousand who were behind him.

The exegetes have mentioned many stories of this kind. Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others﴾: he said: Allah repels by means of one who prays from one who does not pray, by means of one who performs Hajj from one who does not perform Hajj, and by means of one who pays zakat from one who does not pay zakat.

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Jarir, with a weak chain, reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah repels calamity from a hundred households of the neighbours of a righteous Muslim." Then Ibn 'Umar recited ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people...﴾ the verse. In its chain is Yahya ibn Sa'id al-'Attar al-Himsi, who is extremely weak.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 250–252 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-mala') of the Children of Israel?﴾ The discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes?﴾ and we have already presented it. Al-mala' means the nobles among the people, as if they were "filled" (mulli'a) with nobility.

Al-Zajjaj said: They were named that because they are "filled" (mali'un) with what is needed from them. It is a collective noun, like al-qawm (the people) and al-rahT (the company).

In exhorting to fighting, God, glorified is He, mentioned another story that took place among the Children of Israel after the previous story.

His saying: ﴿after Musa﴾: "min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), and its governing element is implied: i.e., they were existing after Musa, meaning after his death.

His saying: ﴿a prophet for them﴾: It was said that he is Shamwil ibn Yar ibn 'Alqamah, who is known as Ibn al-'Ajuz. It is also said Shum'un. He is from the descendants of Ya'qub. It was also said he is from the offspring of Harun. It was said he is Yusha' ibn Nun, but this is very weak, because Yusha' was the servant of Musa, and Dawud did not appear until a long time after that. It was also said his name is Isma'il.

His saying: ﴿Send for us a king﴾: i.e., a commander to whom we return and act according to his opinion.

His saying: "nuqatil" with the nun and the jazm (jussive), as a response to the imperative. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it this way.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and the verb in the raf' (nominative), considering it a description (sifah) of the king.

It was also read with the nun and the raf', as a circumstantial clause (hal) or a new independent sentence.

His saying: ﴿Would you perhaps not fight?﴾ "'asaytum" is read with fath on the sin and with kasr, both being dialects. Nafi' read the second, and the rest read the first.

Al-Kashshaf said: The reading with kasr is weak.

Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for the kasr.

Abu 'Ali said: The basis for the kasr is the Arabs' saying: "huwa 'assa bidhalika," like "harra" and "shajja," and forms fa'ala and fa'ila have come in words like naqama and naqima. Thus 'asayta and 'asiyta (are similar). Makki said the same.

Al-Hasan and Talhah also read with kasr, so there is no basis for weakening it. It is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah): i.e., have you come close to not fighting? The placing of the interrogative particle before a verb of approximation is to affirm what is expected from it and to indicate that it will happen. The conditional clause separates 'asa from its predicate to show the importance of it.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿That you do not fight﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative): i.e., "would you perhaps be fighting?"

Al-Akhfash said: The "an" in His saying ﴿What is for us that we should not fight?﴾ is extra (za'idah).

Al-Farra' said: It is interpreted according to meaning: i.e., "what prevented us," as you say: "What is for you that you do not pray?" It was also said the meaning is: "What is it for us regarding not fighting?"

Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of these views.

His saying: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾ is a causal clause, and the sentence is a circumstantial one. The singling out of the children for mention is because they were the ones who were taken captive, or because they hold a place above the rest of the relatives.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed﴾: i.e., was obligated. He, glorified is He, informed that they turned away because of the disorder of their intentions and the weakness of their resolve.

There is disagreement about the number of the few whom God excepted, who were those who were satisfied with the handful (of water).

His saying: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾ begins the detailed account of what happened between them and their prophet of statements and actions.

Talut (Saul): a non-Arabic name. He was a water-carrier. It was said he was a tanner, and it was said he was a muleteer. He was not from the tribe of prophethood, which is the Banu Lawi, nor from the tribe of kingship, which is the Banu Yahudha. Therefore ﴿they said: How can he have kingship over us?﴾, i.e., how is that, when he was not from the house of kingship, nor was he one to whom abundant wealth had been given, so that we would follow him for his nobility or his wealth? This clause, namely His saying ﴿while we are more deserving﴾, is circumstantial, and so is the clause conjoined to it.

His saying: ﴿God has chosen him over you﴾: i.e., He preferred him. God's choice is a decisive proof.

Then He explained to them, along with that, the basis of the choosing: that God increased him in breadth of knowledge, which is the foundation of a human being, the head of virtues, and the greatest aspect of preference. And He increased him in breadth of body, through which effect shows in wars and similar things. So he was strong in his religion and his body, and that is what is considered, not the nobility of lineage.

For the virtues of the soul take precedence over it.

﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾: The kingdom is His kingdom, and the servants are His servants. So what is it for you to object to something that is not yours, nor is its decision in your hands?

Some exegetes went to the view that His saying ﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾ is from the words of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said it is from the words of their prophet, and this is the apparent meaning.

His saying: ﴿Vast﴾: i.e., vast in bounty, He expands for whom He wills of His servants. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves kingship and is fit for it.

Al-tabut (the chest) is on the pattern fa'lut, from al-tawb, which is return, because they return to it. I.e., the sign of his kingship is the coming of the chest that was taken from them, i.e., its return to you. It is the chest of the Torah.

Al-sakinah (tranquility) is on the pattern fa'ilah, derived from al-sukun, dignity and calm. I.e., in it is the cause of the tranquility of your hearts regarding what you disputed about the matter of Talut.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The correct view is that the chest contained excellent things from the remnants of the prophets and their relics, so that souls would be at peace with that, find comfort in it, and be strengthened.

There are differing views about the sakinah, and some of them will come with an explanation. Similarly, there is disagreement about al-baqiyyah (remainder). It was said: it is the staff of Musa and the fragments of the tablets. Other things have been said.

It was said: What is meant by "the family of Musa and Harun" is the two of them themselves, i.e., of what Harun and Musa left behind, and the word "family" is inserted to magnify their status. It was also said: what is meant is the prophets from the sons of Ya'qub, because they both are from the offspring of Ya'qub, so the rest of his relatives and whoever descended from him are a family to them both.

Fasala means: he set out with them. One says "fasaltu al-shay' fa-infasala" (I cut the thing and it was cut), i.e., I severed it and it was severed. Its origin is transitive. One says "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself), then it was used in the intransitive sense like infasala. It was said that fasala is used both intransitively and transitively: one says "fasala 'an al-balad fusulan" (he departed from the city), and "fasala nafsahu fasalan."

Al-ibtila': testing.

Al-nahr (the river): it was said it is between Jordan and Palestine. The majority read it as nahrin with fath on the ha'.

Hamid, Mujahid and al-A'raj read it with sukun on the ha'.

What is meant by this testing is testing their obedience. Whoever obeyed in that matter of the water obeyed in what else. Whoever disobeyed in this and was overcome by his self is, in disobedience in all other hardships, more likely to fail. He granted them permission regarding the handful so that the harm of thirst would be removed from them for those who are patient with the hardship of life and who restrain themselves from luxury.

So what is meant by His saying ﴿whoever drinks from it﴾ is: whoever gulped it down and did not limit himself to a handful. "Man" here is for the starting point.

The meaning of His saying ﴿then he is not of me﴾: i.e., he is not of my companions. This is from their saying: "So-and-so is from so-and-so," as if he were a part of him, because of their intermixing and long companionship. This is common and well known in Arabic speech. From it is the saying of the poet:

When you seek to commit wickedness against a lion, I am not of you and you are not of me.

His saying ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾: one says "ta'imtu al-shay'" (I tasted the thing), i.e., I experienced it, and "at'amtuhu al-ma'" (I made him taste the water), i.e., I let him taste it. In this there is evidence that water is called ta'am (food).

Al-ightiraf is taking from a thing with the hand or with a tool. Al-gharf is like al-ightiraf, and al-ghurfah is a single occurrence.

It has been read with fath on the ghayn and with damm. The fath is for the single occurrence, and the damm is a name for the thing scooped. It was said: with fath, al-ghurfah means a single handful, and with damm it means two handfuls. It was also said: they are two dialects with one meaning. From it is the saying of the poet:

They do not approach water with vessels, except by scooping from the pools with the palm.

His saying: ﴿except a few﴾: the number of them will come with explanation. It was also read: "illa qalilun" (with nominative). There is no basis for it except what has been said, that it is from omitting the word in favor of the meaning: i.e., it was not given except to a few. This is far-fetched.

His saying ﴿When he had crossed it﴾: i.e., when Talut crossed the river, ﴿and those who believed with him﴾, and they are the few who obeyed him. However, they differed in the strength of certainty. Some of them said ﴿We have no power today﴾, and ﴿those who were certain﴾ i.e., who were sure ﴿that they would meet God﴾ said. Al-fi'ah is the group, and al-qit'ah (a portion) of them is from "fa'uta ra'sahu bil-sayf," i.e., I cut it.

His saying: ﴿they came forth﴾, i.e., they came out into al-baraz, which is the open, wide land.

Jalut was the commander of the Amalekites.

They said: i.e., all of those with him from the believers. Al-ifraghh indicates the meaning of abundance.

His saying ﴿and make our feet firm﴾ is an expression of strength and absence of weakness. One says: "thabata qadamu fulanin 'ala kadha" when he settled in it and did not depart from it, and "thabata qadamuhu fi al-harb" when victory was his and success was with him.

His saying: ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ refers to Jalut and his soldiers.

He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to make clear what was the cause prompting the victory over them, which is their disbelief. He mentioned the victory after asking for firm feet, because the second is the goal of the first.

His saying: ﴿So they routed them by God's permission﴾. Al-hizm, with kasr, is from it; a "minhazim" water-skin is one whose part has bent over another while dry. From it is what is said about Zamzam, that it is the "hizmat Jibril," i.e., he struck it with his foot and the water came out. Al-hizm is also what is broken from dry firewood. The sense of the sentence is: God sent down victory upon them, ﴿so they routed them by God's permission﴾, i.e., by His command and will.

His saying: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. He is Dawud ibn Iysha, with kasr on the hamzah, then a silent ya' after it, then a dotted letter. It is also said: Dawud ibn Zakariyya ibn Bishuy, from the tribe of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. God combined for him prophethood and kingship after he had been a shepherd, and he was the youngest of his brothers. Talut chose him to fight Jalut, and he killed him.

What is meant by al-hikmah (wisdom) here is prophethood. It was said: it is his teaching of the craft of coats of mail and the speech of birds. It was said: it is his being given the chain (al-silsilah) by which they used to judge disputes.

His saying: ﴿And He taught him from what He willed﴾. It was said: the present tense here is placed in the position of the past tense, and the doer of this verb is God, the Exalted. It was said: it is Dawud.

The apparent meaning of this construction is that God, glorified is He, taught him from what His will decreed and His will was attached to. It has been said that among that is what we mentioned earlier, his being taught the craft of coats of mail and what follows it.

His saying: ﴿And were it not that God repels some people by means of others﴾: The majority read ﴿wa-lawla daf'u Allah﴾. Nafi' read "difa'". Both are verbal nouns of "daf'a". So said Sibawayh.

Abu Hatim said: "dafi'" and "daf'" are the same, like "tarraqtu na'li" and "taraqtuhu."

Abu 'Ubaydah chose the reading of the majority and rejected the reading "difa'," saying: because God, mighty and majestic, is not overcome by anyone.

Makki said: Abu 'Ubaydah gives the impression that this is of the form of mufa'alah, but it is not. On both readings the verbal noun is annexed to its agent: i.e., ﴿And were it not for God's repelling the people﴾. "Some of them" is a substitute for "the people," and they are the ones who engage in the causes of evil and corruption through others among them, and they are the ones who restrain them from that and turn them back from it. ﴿The earth would have been corrupted﴾ because of the domination of the people of corruption over it and their creating of evils that destroy the crops and the offspring. The indefinite "bounty" (fadl) is for magnification.

The verses of God are what this story contains of the matters mentioned.

What is meant here by "the truth" is the correct report that has no doubt among the People of the Book and those acquainted with the histories of the world.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ is an information from God, glorified is He, that he is among the messengers of God, glorified is He, to strengthen his heart, to firm up his inner self, and to reinforce his matter.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel?﴾ He said: This was when prophethood had been lifted and the people of faith had been driven out, and the tyrants had expelled them from their homes and their children. ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them﴾, and that was when the Ark (al-tabut) came to them. He said: Among the Children of Israel there were two tribes: the tribe of prophethood and the tribe of rulership (khilafa). Rulership would not be held except by the tribe of rulership, and prophethood would not be held except by the tribe of prophethood. ﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed Allah has sent Talut to you as king. They said: How can he have kingship over us when we are more entitled to kingship than he is?﴾ He was from neither of the two tribes, neither the tribe of prophethood nor the tribe of rulership. ﴿He said: Indeed Allah has chosen him over you﴾. They refused to hand leadership over to him, until he said to them: ﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you, in it is tranquility (sakina) from your Lord and a remnant﴾. Musa, when he threw down the Tablets, they broke; some of them were lifted up, and what remained was gathered and placed in the Ark. The Amalekites had captured that Ark. The Amalekites were a group from 'Ad, who were at Ariha. The angels brought the Ark, carrying it between the sky and the earth while they looked on, until they set it down before Talut. When they saw that, they said: Yes. So they submitted to him and made him king. And when the prophets attended a battle, they would put the Ark before them and say: Adam descended with that Ark, and with the corner-stone (al-rukn), and with the staff of Musa, from Paradise.

It has reached me that the Ark and the staff of Musa are in the lake of Tiberias, and that they will emerge before the Day of Resurrection.

This meaning has been transmitted, both in brief and in extended form, from a group of the early generation (al-salaf). Therefore, lengthening the discussion with the mention of such matters brings no benefit that is worth counting.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth of knowledge and physique﴾: he said: "Excellence (fadila)". ﴿In knowledge and physique﴾: he said: He was great and large in body, surpassing the Children of Israel by his neck.

He also reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih regarding ﴿and increased him in breadth in knowledge﴾: he said: Knowledge of war.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him (Ibn 'Abbas) that he was asked: Was Talut a prophet? He said: No, no revelation came to him.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he was asked about the size of the Ark of Musa. He said: About three cubits by two cubits.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Sakina is mercy.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: Sakina is tranquility and calm.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: Sakina is a creature the size of a cat, having two eyes with rays of light. Whenever the two hosts met, it would stretch out its two paws and look at them, and the army would be routed from terror.

Al-Tabarani, with a weak chain, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina is a wind that is turbulent (khajuj), and it has two heads.
