'Abd al-Razzaq, Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from 'Ali, who said: Sakina has a face like the face of a human, and then after that it is a gentle, rustling wind.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Mujahid, who said: Sakina is from Allah, like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding ﴿in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾: a basin of gold from Paradise, with which the hearts of the prophets were washed, into which he cast the Tablets.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: It is a spirit from Allah that does not speak. Whenever they differed about a matter, it would speak and inform them of the clarification of what they wanted.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan, who said: It is something by which their hearts find rest.

'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Qatada, who said: In it is sakina, that is, dignity (waqar).

I say: These contradictory interpretations may have reached these eminent scholars from the Jews, may Allah disgrace them. They brought these matters with the aim of toying with the Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them, and sowing doubt among them. Observe how they made it at one time an animal, at another time an inanimate object, and at another time something that cannot be reasoned about, such as the saying of Mujahid: "like the form of a wind; it has a face like the face of a cat, and two wings, and a tail like the tail of a cat."

Thus every report from the Children of Israel is contradictory, and in most cases includes what cannot be understood. It is not possible that such contradictory interpretations were transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor an opinion held by their speaker; they are too exalted in rank to be interpretation by personal opinion (tafsir bi'l-ra'y) or by matters in which there is no room for ijtihad.

When this has been established for you, you will know that what is obligatory in such a matter is to return to the meaning of sakina linguistically, which is well known, and there is no need to engage in these strained and contradictory matters, for Allah has granted sufficiency concerning them. If an interpretation of sakina had been established for us from the Prophet (ﷺ), it would have been obligatory for us to adopt it and affirm it. But it has not been established by a sound route. Rather, it is established that it descended upon (p-172) some of the Companions while reciting the Qur'an, as in Sahih Muslim, from al-Bara', who said: "A man was reciting Surat al-Kahf, and beside him was a horse tied up. A cloud covered him and began to circle and draw near, and his horse began to shy away from it. When he woke in the morning, he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: That was the sakina that descended for the Qur'an."

There is nothing in this except that what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named was a cloud that circled around that reciter. Allah knows best.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and a remnant of what the family of Musa left behind﴾: he said: his staff and the fragments of the Tablets.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Salih, who said: In the Ark were the staff of Musa and the staff of Harun, the garments of Musa and the garments of Harun, two tablets of the Torah, the manna, and the word of relief: "There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous; glory be to Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne; and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada regarding ﴿the angels will carry it﴾: he said: The angels came bearing it, carrying it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and in the morning it was in his home.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: he said: a sign.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Indeed Allah will test you with a river﴾: he said: with thirst. When he reached the river, which is the river Jordan, most of the people drank from it, and whoever drank from it only became more thirsty, while whoever took a single handful with his hand was sufficed and his thirst was relieved.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿so they drank from it, except a few of them﴾: he said: The few were three hundred and some ten, the number of the people of Badr.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from al-Bara', who said: We, the Companions of Muhammad, used to say that the Companions of Badr were equal in number to the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him, and that none crossed with him except a believer: some ten and three hundred.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his Companions on the day of Badr: You are equal in number to the companions of Talut on the day he met Jalut."

Ibn 'Asakir, through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, reported: They were three hundred thousand and three thousand, three hundred and thirteen. They all drank from it except three hundred and thirteen men, equal in number to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. Talut sent back the rest and went on with three hundred and thirteen.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding ﴿those who think﴾: he said: those who are certain.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: Talut was commander over the army. Abu Dawud sent something with Dawud to his brothers. Dawud said to Talut: What is for me? Jalut came forward and said: For you is a third of my kingdom, and I will marry you to my daughter. Dawud took a pouch and put three stones in it. Then he named Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, and then put his hand in, saying: "In the name of Allah, my God and the God of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." He brought out one stone, which he placed in his sling, and he threw it at Jalut, and it pierced thirty-three eggs on his head and killed thirty thousand who were behind him.

The exegetes have mentioned many stories of this kind. Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others﴾: he said: Allah repels by means of one who prays from one who does not pray, by means of one who performs Hajj from one who does not perform Hajj, and by means of one who pays zakat from one who does not pay zakat.

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Jarir, with a weak chain, reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah repels calamity from a hundred households of the neighbours of a righteous Muslim." Then Ibn 'Umar recited ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people...﴾ the verse. In its chain is Yahya ibn Sa'id al-'Attar al-Himsi, who is extremely weak.

His statement, ﴿Those are the messengers﴾. It is said that this refers to all the messengers, so the *alif* and *lam* are for *istighraq* (the comprehensive sense, meaning "all"). It is also said that it refers to the prophets mentioned in this surah, and it is said that it refers to the prophets whose knowledge reached the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning of "some of them over others" is that Allah, glory be to Him, gave some of them more of the qualities of perfection than He gave the others. So the one with more of these qualities is superior, and the other is inferior.

Just as this verse shows that some prophets are better than others, another verse does the same, namely His saying, ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Isra: 55].

A group of scholars have found it difficult to reconcile this verse with what is established in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet, with the wording "Do not prefer me over the prophets," and in another wording, "Do not prefer some of the prophets over others," and in another wording, "Do not choose between the prophets." Some people said that this statement of his (ﷺ) was made before he was revealed the preference, and that the Qur'an abrogated the prohibition of preference (*naskh*, abrogation). It was also said that he (ﷺ) said this as a matter of humility, as he said, "None of you should say, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta,'" out of humility, while knowing that he was the best of the prophets, as his saying "I am the master of the children of Adam" indicates. It was also said that he only forbade this to cut off argument and dispute about the prophets, so it applies only to such cases, and not when such a statement is safe from causing harm. It was also said that the prohibition is only with respect to prophethood alone, because it is one characteristic in which there is no superiority, and there is no prohibition on preference by means of additional special qualities and honors. It was also said that what is meant is the prohibition of preference merely based on desires and partisanship.

All of these opinions are weak.

In my view, there is no contradiction between the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The Qur'an indicates that Allah preferred some of His prophets over others, but this does not imply that we are permitted to prefer some of them over others. The qualities that are the basis of preference are known to Allah, nothing of them is hidden from Him, but they are not known to human beings. The followers of a prophet may be ignorant of some of his qualities and special characteristics, let alone the qualities of others. Preference is not permitted except after knowing all the causes by which one is superior and the other inferior, not before knowing some of them, or most of them, or the least of them. Preferring without that knowledge is preference based on ignorance, and an act undertaken without knowledge by the one who does it, which is forbidden. So even if the Qur'an alone had been revealed, informing us that Allah preferred some of His prophets over others, there would have been no evidence that human beings may prefer among the prophets. How much more so when authentic Sunnah has come with a prohibition against this! When you understand this, you know that there is no contradiction between the Qur'an and the Sunnah in any respect. The Qur'an contains Allah's report that He preferred some of His prophets over others, and the Sunnah contains a prohibition on His servants preferring among His prophets. Whoever takes up the matter of reconciling them, claiming that they contradict each other, has clearly erred.

His statement, ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾: this refers to Musa and to our Prophet, may the peace of Allah be upon them both.

It has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said about Adam, "He is a prophet who was spoken to."

Something that supports this is established in the *Sahih* of Ibn Hibban from the hadith of Abu Dharr.

His statement, ﴿and raised some of them in degrees﴾: this "some" may be understood to mean whoever among the prophets had the highest rank with Allah, glory be to Him. It may also be understood to mean our Prophet (ﷺ), because of the abundance of his qualities that call for his preference. It may also be understood to mean Idris, because Allah, glory be to Him, informed us that He raised him to a lofty place. It was also said that they are the *Ulu al-'Azm* (the prophets of firm resolve). It was also said that it means Ibrahim. You are not unaware that Allah, glory be to Him, left this "some" who were raised undefined. So it is not permitted for us to specify it except with proof from Allah, glory be to Him, or from His prophets, peace be upon them, and no indication leading to that has come. So specifying it is interpreting the Noble Qur'an by mere opinion. You already know the severe warning concerning that, together with the fact that it is a pathway to preference among the prophets, which we have been forbidden. Many leading scholars of *tafsir* have firmly stated that it is our Prophet (ﷺ), and they have extended their discussion on this, citing what Allah specially granted him of miracles, qualities of perfection, and characteristics of excellence. Yet by this firm assertion, based on evidence that does not indicate the intended meaning, they have fallen into two dangers and committed two prohibited acts: interpreting the Qur'an by opinion, and entering into the pathways of preference among the prophets. Even if that is not an explicit preference, it is undoubtedly a pathway to it. For whoever firmly asserts that this "some" raised in degrees is such-and-such a prophet has moved from that to the forbidden preference. Allah has already sufficed His chosen Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with what needs nothing else of virtues and favors. So beware of seeking nearness to him (ﷺ) by entering doors that he has forbidden you to enter, so that you disobey him while you think you are obedient and doing good.

His statement, ﴿And We gave Isa son of Maryam clear proofs﴾: that is, the manifest signs and the evident miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the sick, and other things.

His statement, ﴿and We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾: this is Jibril. The discussion of this has already passed.

His statement, ﴿Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾: that is, after the messengers. It was also said that it means after Musa, Isa, and Muhammad, because the last is mentioned explicitly, while the first and third are indicated by His saying, ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke.﴾ The meaning is: had Allah willed that they not fight one another, they would not have fought. The object of the will is omitted according to the rule. The phrase ﴿but they differed﴾ is an exception from the conditional clause. That is, the fighting arose from their extreme disagreement, to the point that they became different religions: some believed and some disbelieved. Had Allah willed that they not fight after this disagreement, ﴿they would not have fought, but Allah does what He wills﴾. No one can repel His judgment, and none can change His decree. He does what He wills and decides what He desires.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His saying, ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾, that he said: Allah took Ibrahim as a friend (*khalil*), spoke to Musa directly, and made Isa like Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was. He is the servant of Allah, His word, and His spirit. He gave Dawud the Psalms, and gave Sulayman a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, and forgave Muhammad his earlier and later sins.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying, ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾, that he said: Allah spoke to Musa, and He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to all people.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Amir al-Sha'bi concerning His saying, ﴿and raised some of them in degrees﴾, that he said: Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾, that he said: "after Musa and Isa."

Ibn Asakir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him were Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Mu'awiyah, when Ali came. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Mu'awiyah, 'Do you love Ali?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Among you there will be a trial, a brief one.' Mu'awiyah said, 'And what comes after that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said, 'The pardon and good pleasure of Allah.' He said, 'We are content with the decree of Allah.' Then at that moment this verse was revealed: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought, but Allah does what He wills.﴾" Al-Suyuti said: "Its chain is weak."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 2, verse 254:

The apparent meaning of the command in His words, ﴿Spend﴾, is obligation (*wujub*). A group of scholars understood it as referring to obligatory charity (*sadaqat al-fard*) for this reason, and because of the severe warning at the end of the verse. It has also been said that this verse includes both obligatory almsgiving (*zakat al-fard*) and voluntary giving (*tatawwu'*).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is correct. However, the preceding verses, which mention fighting and that God repels [the harm of disbelievers] through the believers and [that He] cools the breasts of the disbelievers, indicate that this recommendation (*nadb*) is specifically in the way of God.

Al-Qurtubi said: According to this interpretation, spending wealth is sometimes obligatory and sometimes recommended, depending on whether jihad is obligatory for a person or not.

His words, ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trading in it﴾, mean: spend while you are still able, ﴿before there comes﴾ that in which spending will no longer be possible for you, namely ﴿a Day in which there is no trading in it﴾, that is, a day on which people do not trade with one another.

*Khullah* (close friendship) is pure affection, derived from the penetration of secrets between two friends.

He, glory be to Him, informs us that on the Day of Resurrection there is no friendship that benefits, and no intercession that is effective, except for one whom God has permitted.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿no trading﴾ and ﴿no friendship nor intercession﴾ with the accusative (*naṣb*) and without nunation (*tanwin*). The rest of the readers read them with the nominative (*raf'*) and with nunation. Both are well-known dialects of the Arabs and two recognized options among the grammarians. An example of the first is the verse of Hassan:

Is there no spear-thrust? Is there no charging of horsemen? Will your bellies not belch around the ovens?

An example of the second is the verse of al-Ra'i:

I did not cut you off until you said openly: there is no she-camel of mine in this, nor a male camel.

It is permissible outside the Qur'an to have variation in case, with some words in the nominative and others in the accusative, as is established in the science of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*).

His words, ﴿And the disbelievers – they are the wrongdoers﴾, indicate that every disbeliever is a wrongdoer against himself. Among those included in this general statement is the one who withholds zakat in a way that makes his disbelief necessary, since this occurs within the context of the command to spend.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Juraij, regarding His words, ﴿O you who believe, spend of what We have provided you﴾, that he said: [This refers] to zakat and voluntary giving.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sufyan, who said: It is said that zakat abrogated (*nasakha*) every charity in the Qur'an, and that the month of Ramadan abrogated every fast.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding the verse, that he said: God knows that people befriend one another in this world and intercede for one another, but on the Day of Resurrection there is no friendship except the friendship of the God-fearing.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata', who said: Praise belongs to God, who said ﴿And the disbelievers – they are the wrongdoers﴾ and did not say ﴿And the wrongdoers – they are the disbelievers﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾, meaning there is no one worthy of worship except Him. This sentence is the predicate of the subject.

Al-Hayy: the Ever-Living, the one who remains. It was said: the one who does not cease or change. It was said: the one who directs affairs and decrees things.

Al-Tabari said, concerning a group of people, that it is said "Hayy" just as He described Himself, and that this is accepted without examining it. It is a second predicate, or a subject whose predicate is omitted.

Al-Qayyum: the one who stands over every soul for what it has earned. It was said: the one who subsists by His own essence and sustains others. It was said: the one who manages the creation and preserves it. It was said: the one who does not sleep. It was said: the one for whom there is no substitute.

The origin of qayyum is qayyawm. The yaʼ and the waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the first was assimilated into the second after the waw was changed to yaʼ.

Ibn Masʼud, ʿAlqama, al-Nakhaʼi and al-Aʻmash read "al-Hayyu al-Qayyam" with an alif, and this is narrated from ʿUmar. There is no disagreement among the people of the language that qayyum is better known among the Arabs, more sound in its form, and more established in its derivation.

Al-Sina (drowsiness) is, according to the majority, slumber (nuʻas). Nuʻas is the lethargy and closing of the eyes that precedes sleep; when it reaches the heart, it becomes sleep.

Al-Mufassal distinguished between sina, nuʻas and nawm, saying: sina is in the head, nuʻas is in the eye, and nawm is in the heart. End.

What should be relied upon in distinguishing sina from nawm is that with sina the intellect is not lost, unlike with nawm, which is the relaxation of the members of the brain from the moisture of vapours, to the point that the intellect is lost with it, and indeed all perceptions through the senses. The meaning is that none of these befalls Him, glory be to Him. He mentioned sina before nawm because it precedes it in existence.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: If sina is what precedes sleep, then when it is said "sina does not seize Him," it indicates that sleep does not seize Him a fortiori. So mentioning nawm would be a repetition. We say: the sense of the verse is "sina does not seize Him, let alone nawm." And God knows His intent. End.

I say: this priority that he mentioned is not accepted, for sleep may come on suddenly without the drowsiness mentioned. When it comes upon the heart and the eye at once, it is called nawm and not sina, so negating sina does not necessarily negate nawm.

It has been transmitted from the Arabs that both are negated together, such as the saying of Zuhayr:
"Neither drowsiness seizes Him through all time, nor does He sleep, and in His affair there is no weakness."

He did not suffice with negating sina. Also, a person can ward off sina from himself but cannot ward off nawm; nawm may seize him while sina does not. So if the Qur'anic wording were limited to negating sina, it would not imply the negation of nawm, and likewise if it were limited to negating nawm, it would not imply the negation of sina, for many a person in drowsiness is not sleeping. He repeated the negative particle to specify that the negation covers each of them.

His words: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ In this interrogative there is a rebuke of the one who claims that any of His servants can benefit anyone with intercession or otherwise, and a censure and reproach of him that cannot be exceeded. In it there is a repelling in the breasts of the worshippers of graves, a turning away from their faces, and a weakening of their supports, to a degree that cannot be measured nor reached. What is derived from it is beyond what is derived from His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing except after God gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm: 26], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿They do not speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ [al-Naba'], with many degrees.

The sound hadiths established in the collections of Islam have clarified the description of intercession, for whom it is, and who performs it.

His words: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. The two pronouns refer to what is in the heavens and the earth, with the rational beings given precedence over the others. "What is before them and what is behind them" is an expression for what precedes them and what follows them, or for this world and the Hereafter and what is in them.

His words: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾. The meaning of encompassing has already been mentioned. Knowledge here is in the sense of the known: that is, they do not encompass anything of His known things.

His words: "His Kursi encompasses." The apparent meaning of al-Kursi is that it is the body described in the narrations, as will come explained.

A group of the Mu'tazila denied its existence, and they erred in this with a clear error and committed a gross blunder.

Some of the early scholars said: the Kursi here is an expression for knowledge. They said: from this, scholars are called kara'is, and from this comes the kurrasa in which knowledge is gathered, and from this is the saying of the poet:
"Around them are white faces and a band of kara'is with reports when calamities befall."

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this view. It was also said: His Kursi is His power by which He holds the heavens and the earth, as one says: "Make a kursi for this wall," meaning what supports it. It was said: the Kursi is the Throne. It was said: it is a depiction of His greatness with no reality. It was said: it is an expression for dominion.

The truth is the first view. There is no reason to turn away from the real meaning except mere imaginings arising from ignorance and misguidance. The meaning of His Kursi encompassing the heavens and the earth is that they are within it, and that it encompasses them without being constricted by them, being vast and expansive.

His words: ﴿And its preservation does not burden Him﴾. Its meaning is that it does not weigh on Him with the weight of the least thing, from the expression "it burdened me and I bore from it hardship."

Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in His words "yauduhu" may refer to Allah, glory be to Him, and it may refer to the Kursi, since it is among the affairs of the Exalted God, meaning the loftiness of power and rank.

al-Tabari reported from a group that they said: He is the Exalted above His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: these are the sayings of ignorant anthropomorphists, and what was obligatory was that they not be recounted. End.

The disagreement over affirming direction is well known among the early and later scholars, and the dispute over it exists among them, and the evidences from the Book and the Sunna are well known. But the one raised upon a school that regards others as outside the Shariʻa does not examine their evidences nor pay attention to them. The Book and the Sunna are the criterion by which truth is known from falsehood, and by which the sound is distinguished from the corrupt: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Muminun: 71]. There is no doubt that this word is applied to the dominant apparent sense, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], and the poet said:
"So when we rose above them and prevailed over them, we left them fallen as prey for the vulture and the hawk."

Al-ʿAzim means that His rank and station are great.

In the Kashshaf it is said: the first sentence explains His standing over the creation in managing it and His being watchful over it, not heedless of it. The second explains His being the owner of what He manages. The third explains the grandeur of His majesty. The fourth explains His encompassing of the states of the creation and His knowledge of those He approves of, who deserve intercession, and of those He does not approve. The fifth explains the vastness of His knowledge and its connection to all the known things, or His majesty and the greatness of His station.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, regarding His words "al-Hayy," that it means the Living who does not die; "al-Qayyum" means the Standing who has no substitute.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Mujahid regarding "al-Qayyum," that he said: the one standing over everything.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan who said: al-Qayyum is the one for whom there is no cessation.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Drowsiness does not seize Him, nor sleep﴾, that he said: sina is nuʻas, and nawm is nawm.

They transmitted, except al-Bayhaqi, from al-Suddi who said: sina is the breeze of sleep that seizes a person in the face so that he becomes drowsy.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾, that he said: what has passed of the world and what is behind them of the Hereafter.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "what is before them" is what they sent forward of their deeds, and "what is behind them" is what they neglected of their deeds.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿His Kursi encompasses﴾, that he said: "His knowledge. Do you not see His words: ﴿and its preservation does not burden Him﴾?"

al-Daraqutni in al-Sifat and al-Khatib in his History transmitted from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the words of God: ﴿His Kursi encompasses﴾, and he said: His Kursi is the place of His feet, and the Throne none can measure its measure except God, Mighty and Majestic."

al-Hakim transmitted it and declared it sound.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari a similar report, as a mawquf narration.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "If the seven heavens and the seven earths were spread out and then joined one to another, they would not be in its vastness, meaning the Kursi, except like a ring in a desert."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzama, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari: "that he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the Kursi, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, the seven heavens compared to the Kursi are only like a ring thrown in a barren desert, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over that ring."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Abu Yaʻla, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani and al-Diya al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtara transmitted from ʿUmar who said: "A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Pray to God that He admit me to Paradise. He magnified the Lord, glory be to Him, and said: His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth, and it has a creaking like the creaking of a new saddle from its weight." In its chain is ʿAbd Allah ibn Khalifa, who is not well known. Regarding his hearing from ʿUmar there is doubt, and some narrate it from ʿUmar as a mawquf report.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra as a marfuʻ report: that it is the place of the two feet. In its chain is al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr al-Fazari al-Kufi, who is matruk (abandoned).

Reports describing the Kursi have come down from a number of the early Companions and others, which need not be expanded upon.

Abu Dawud in the Book of Sunna in his Sunan narrated a hadith about its description from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im, and Ibn Mardawayh similarly cited it from Buraydah, Jabir and others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿and its preservation does not burden Him﴾ that he said: it does not weigh on Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, regarding "wa la yaʼuduhu," that he said: "nor does it overwhelm Him."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: al-ʿAzim is the one whose greatness is complete.

Know that there have come in the excellence of this verse hadiths.

Ahmad and Muslim, and the wording is his, transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʻb that "the Prophet ﷺ asked him: Which verse in the Book of God is greatest? He said: The Verse of the Kursi. He said: May knowledge be pleasant for you, Abu al-Mundhir."

Al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "He had a granary containing dates, and he would keep an eye on it, but he found it diminishing. So he stood guard over it one night, and behold, there was a creature resembling a grown youth. He said: I greeted it, and it returned the greeting. I said: What are you, a jinn or a human? It said: A jinn. I said: Give me your hand. It gave me its hand, and behold, its hand was the hand of a dog and its hair was the hair of a dog. I said: Is this how the jinn are created? It said: The jinn know well that among them there is none stronger than me. I said: What led you to do what you did? It said: I heard that you are a man who loves giving charity, so we wished to partake of your food. Ubayy said to it: Then what protects us from you? (p-176) It said: This verse, the Verse of the Throne in Surah al-Baqarah. Whoever recites it when he enters the evening will be protected from us until morning, and whoever recites it when he enters the morning will be protected from us until evening. When morning came, he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: The wicked one has spoken the truth."

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, related from Ibn al-Asqa' al-Bakri: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to them in the attire of the emigrants, and a man asked him: Which verse in the Qur'an is greatest? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿Allah! There is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep.﴾ until the verse was finished."

Ahmad related a similar report from the hadith of Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Khatib al-Baghdadi in his Tarikh related a similar report from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), as well.

al-Darimi related a similar report from Anfa' ibn 'Abd Allah al-Kala'i.

Al-Bukhari in his Sahih related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan. A visitor came and began scooping up (food), and he mentioned a story. At its end, he said to him: Let me teach you some words by which Allah will benefit you. I said: What are they? He said: When you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne, for there will always be a guardian from Allah over you, and no devil will come near you until morning. Abu Hurayrah informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of this, and he said: As for him, he spoke the truth though he is a liar. Do you know whom you are addressing, Abu Hurayrah? He said: No. He said: That was a devil."

Ahmad related something similar from Abu Ayyub.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The greatest verse in the Book of Allah is ﴿Allah! There is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.﴾"

Ahmad, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related something similar from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ahmad and al-Tabarani also related something similar from the hadith of Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "In Surah al-Baqarah there is a verse, the chief of the verses of the Qur'an. It is not recited in a house in which there is a devil except that it leaves it: the Verse of the Throne."

Al-Hakim said: Its chain is sound, but they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not include it.

Al-Hakim related from the hadith of Za'idah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surah al-Baqarah, and in it is a verse that is the chief of the verses of the Qur'an, the Verse of the Throne." He said: It is gharib, and we do not know it except from the hadith of Hakim ibn Jubayr.

Shu'bah spoke against it and declared it weak; likewise Ahmad, Yahya ibn Ma'in and others declared it weak, Ibn Mahdi abandoned it, and al-Sa'di accused its narrator of lying.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who declared it sound, related from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say concerning these two verses: ﴿Allah! There is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.﴾ and ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah! There is no deity except Him.﴾: Indeed in them is the Greatest Name of Allah."

Hadiths about its virtue have been transmitted other than these, and it has also been transmitted concerning the virtue of reciting it after the prescribed prayers and other matters; it has also been transmitted concerning its virtue together with the sharing of other verses with it, and a great deal has been reported from the early generations (al-salaf) concerning this.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 256–257:

The scholars have differed regarding His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and they have given several opinions.

The first: it is abrogated (mansukhah), because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) compelled the Arabs to adopt the religion of Islam, fought them, and accepted from them nothing but Islam. The verse that abrogates it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you, and let them find harshness in you, and know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123], and His saying: ﴿You will be called to a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit﴾ [al-Fath: 16]. Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) have held this view.

The second opinion: it is not abrogated. It was revealed only concerning the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and they are not compelled to accept Islam if they pay the jizyah (poll tax). Rather, those who are compelled are the idolaters: from them nothing is accepted except Islam or the sword. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The third opinion: this verse was revealed specifically concerning the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah), and the account of what was transmitted about that will come.

The fourth opinion: its meaning is: Do not say to one who embraced Islam under the sword that he is coerced; so there is no compulsion in religion.

The fifth opinion: it was revealed concerning captives (sabi), whenever they were from the People of the Book; they are not to be forced to accept Islam.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: That is, do not compel anyone to enter the religion of Islam, for it is clear, evident and manifest; its proofs and evidences do not need anyone to be forced to enter it. Rather, whoever Allah guides to Islam, opens his breast for it and illuminates his insight, enters it with clear evidence. And whoever Allah blinds in heart and sets a seal upon his hearing and sight, entering the religion while compelled and constrained does not benefit him. This may serve as a sixth opinion.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf in his tafsir of this verse: That is, Allah has not ordained faith by coercion and force, but by empowerment (tamkin) and choice. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed together. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]; that is, had He willed, He would have forced them into faith, but He did not do so, and the matter was founded upon choice. This may serve as a seventh opinion.

What should be relied upon, and what must be adhered to, is this: concerning the occasion of its revelation, the verse is decisive (muhkamah) and not abrogated. That occasion is that a woman among the Ansar would be one whose children do not survive; so she would vow, if a child lived for her, that she would make him a Jew. When the Jews of Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them sons of the Ansar, and they said: "We will not leave our sons," so this verse was revealed. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah reported it from Ibn 'Abbas.

This story has been transmitted through several channels; its substance is what Ibn 'Abbas mentioned, with additions which include that the Ansar said: "We only made them adhere to their religion" — that is, the religion of the Jews — "and we see that their religion is better than our religion, and Allah has sent Islam, so we shall compel them." When the verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the sons the choice and did not compel them to accept Islam.

This implies that the People of the Book are not compelled to accept Islam if they choose to remain upon their religion and pay the jizyah.

As for the people of war (ahl al-harb), the verse, although it encompasses them — because the indefinite noun (al-nakirah) in the context of negation and the definite article on "religion" both convey this — the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion. Nevertheless, this generality has been specified by the verses that came concerning compelling the disbelieving people of war to accept Islam.

His saying: ﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾. "The right course" (al-rushd) here is faith, and "error" (al-ghayy) is disbelief; that is, each has become distinguished from the other.

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) which contains the reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it.

And "al-taghut" is on the pattern fa'lut, derived from taghā yatghī and yatghū: when one exceeds the limit.

Sibawayh said: it is a singular masculine noun, that is, a generic noun (ism jins) which includes the few and the many. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) like rahabut and jabarut, which is used as a description for the singular and the plural. Its lam was moved to the place of the 'ayn, and its 'ayn to the place of the lam, as in jabadha and jadhaba; then the waw is changed to alif because it is vowelled and what precedes it is vowelled, so it became "taghut". Al-Nahhas chose this view. It was also said: the origin of "taghut" in the language is derived from tughyan, conveying its meaning without derivation, as it is said: "la'ali (pearls) from al-lu'lu'".

Al-Mubarrad said: it is a plural. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is rejected.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-taghut" is the soothsayer, the devil, and every head of misguidance, and it may be singular.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They desire to seek judgement from the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. And it may be plural.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their protectors are the taghut﴾, and its plural is tawaghit. That is: whoever disbelieves in the devil, or in idols, or in the people of soothsaying and the heads of misguidance, or in all of them, and believes in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after the right course has become distinct to him from error, has indeed succeeded and has grasped the firm handhold, that is, the firm, sound one.

Al-Wuthqa is on the pattern fu'la from al-wathaqah (firmness), and its plural is wuthuq, like al-fudla and al-fudul.

The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of "al-'urwah al-wuthqa" (the firm handhold), although they agreed that this is a figure of speech and an analogy, in which something known through proof is likened to something perceived by the senses. It was said: what is meant by the handhold is faith; it was said: Islam; it was said: "There is no god but Allah." There is no barrier to taking all of these together.

"Al-infisam" is breaking without separation.

Al-Jawhari said: fasama al-shay'a means "he broke it without separating it."

As for "al-qasm" with a qaf, it is breaking with separation. The author of al-Kashshaf interpreted "al-infisam" as "cutting off."

His saying: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe﴾. Al-Walī is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and it means the Helper.

His saying: "He brings them out" is an explanation of the wilayah (protection), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in walī. This indicates that what is meant by His saying "those who believe" is those who intended faith, because one who has in fact believed has already come out of the darknesses into the light, unless what is meant by "bringing out" is bringing them out of the doubts which confront believers, in which case there is no need to posit an implied intention.

What is meant by the light in His saying: ﴿They bring them out of the light into darknesses﴾ is what the prophets of Allah brought of the call to religion, for that is light for the disbelievers; their protectors removed them from it into the darkness of disbelief; that is, their protectors kept them upon the disbelief they were in, by diverting them from answering the caller to Allah from among the prophets.

It was also said: what is meant by "those who disbelieve" here are those whose disbelief was established in His knowledge, Exalted is He; their protectors from the devils and the heads of misguidance bring them out from the light, which is the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind, into the darknesses of disbelief into which they fell because of that removal.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to what preceded from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the occasion of revelation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and he added: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the sons the choice."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi something similar as well, and he said: "Then those who had not embraced Islam joined them," that is, joined the Banu al-Nadir, and those who had embraced Islam remained.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid who said: "The people among the Ansar used to be nursed among Banu Qurayzah, and they remained steadfast upon their religion. When Islam came, their families wished to compel them to accept Islam, so this verse was revealed."

Ibn Jarir reported something similar from al-Hasan.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾": He said: It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf called al-Husayn, who had two Christian sons, while he himself was a Muslim man. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not compel them, for they have refused anything but Christianity?" So this verse was revealed.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported something similar from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubaydah.

Likewise Abu Dawud in his Nasikh (work on abrogation) and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Suddi something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah who said: "The Arabs had no religion, so they were compelled to adopt a religion by the sword."

He said: "But do not compel the Jews, the Christians and the Magians if they pay the jizyah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur reported something similar from al-Hasan.

Al-Bukhari reported from Aslam: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say to an old Christian woman: "Embrace Islam and you will be safe." She refused, so he said: "O Allah, bear witness," then he recited: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him that he said to Zanbaq the Roman, his slave: "If you embraced Islam, I would seek your help in the trust of the Muslims," but he refused, so he said: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sulayman ibn Musa concerning His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, that he said: "It was abrogated by: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾" [al-Tawbah: 73].

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab who said: "The taghut is the devil."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrimah who said: "The taghut is the soothsayer."

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah who said: "The taghut is the sorcerer."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Malik ibn Anas who said: "The taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The firm handhold is: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas ibn Malik: that it is the Qur'an.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid: that it is faith.

And from Sufyan: that it is the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlas).

It is established in the two Sahihs that the interpretation of "al-'urwah al-wuthqa" in another verse is Islam, as a hadith raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in his interpretation of the dream of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

Ibn 'Asakir reported from Abu al-Darda' who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and 'Umar, for they are the extended rope of Allah. Whoever holds fast to them has held fast to the firm handhold of Allah which has no severance."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "When one affirms the oneness of Allah and believes in divine decree (qadar), that is the firm handhold."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mu'adh that he was asked about His saying: ﴿It has no severance﴾, and he said: "It has no cutting off short of entering Paradise."

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe﴾, the verse, that he said: "They are a people who had disbelieved in Jesus, then believed in Muhammad (ﷺ)." And concerning ﴿those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾, the verse, he said: "They are a people who believed in Jesus, then when Muhammad was sent, they disbelieved in him."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak who said: "The darknesses are disbelief, and the light is faith."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi something similar.

Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]; that is, had He willed, He would have forced them into faith, but He did not do so, and the matter was founded upon choice. This may serve as a seventh opinion.

What should be relied upon, and what must be adhered to, is this: concerning the occasion of its revelation, the verse is decisive (muhkamah) and not abrogated. That occasion is that a woman among the Ansar would be one whose children do not survive; so she would vow, if a child lived for her, that she would make him a Jew. When the Jews of Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them sons of the Ansar, and they said: "We will not leave our sons," so this verse was revealed. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah reported it from Ibn 'Abbas.

This story has been transmitted through several channels; its substance is what Ibn 'Abbas mentioned, with additions which include that the Ansar said: "We only made them adhere to their religion" — that is, the religion of the Jews — "and we see that their religion is better than our religion, and Allah has sent Islam, so we shall compel them." When the verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the sons the choice and did not compel them to accept Islam.

This implies that the People of the Book are not compelled to accept Islam if they choose to remain upon their religion and pay the jizyah.

As for the people of war (ahl al-harb), the verse, although it encompasses them — because the indefinite noun (al-nakirah) in the context of negation and the definite article on "religion" both convey this — the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion. Nevertheless, this generality has been specified by the verses that came concerning compelling the disbelieving people of war to accept Islam.

His saying: ﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾. "The right course" (al-rushd) here is faith, and "error" (al-ghayy) is disbelief; that is, each has become distinguished from the other.

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) which contains the reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it.

And "al-taghut" is on the pattern fa'lut, derived from taghā yatghī and yatghū: when one exceeds the limit.

Sibawayh said: it is a singular masculine noun, that is, a generic noun (ism jins) which includes the few and the many. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) like rahabut and jabarut, which is used as a description for the singular and the plural. Its lam was moved to the place of the 'ayn, and its 'ayn to the place of the lam, as in jabadha and jadhaba; then the waw is changed to alif because it is vowelled and what precedes it is vowelled, so it became "taghut". Al-Nahhas chose this view. It was also said: the origin of "taghut" in the language is derived from tughyan, conveying its meaning without derivation, as it is said: "la'ali (pearls) from al-lu'lu'".

Al-Mubarrad said: it is a plural. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is rejected.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-taghut" is the soothsayer, the devil, and every head of misguidance, and it may be singular.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They desire to seek judgement from the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ [al-Nisa': 60]. And it may be plural.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their protectors are the taghut﴾, and its plural is tawaghit. That is: whoever disbelieves in the devil, or in idols, or in the people of soothsaying and the heads of misguidance, or in all of them, and believes in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after the right course has become distinct to him from error, has indeed succeeded and has grasped the firm handhold, that is, the firm, sound one.

Al-Wuthqa is on the pattern fu'la from al-wathaqah (firmness), and its plural is wuthuq, like al-fudla and al-fudul.

The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of "al-'urwah al-wuthqa" (the firm handhold), although they agreed that this is a figure of speech and an analogy, in which something known through proof is likened to something perceived by the senses. It was said: what is meant by the handhold is faith; it was said: Islam; it was said: "There is no god but Allah." There is no barrier to taking all of these together.

"Al-infisam" is breaking without separation.

Al-Jawhari said: fasama al-shay'a means "he broke it without separating it."

As for "al-qasm" with a qaf, it is breaking with separation. The author of al-Kashshaf interpreted "al-infisam" as "cutting off."

His saying: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe﴾. Al-Walī is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), and it means the Helper.

His saying: "He brings them out" is an explanation of the wilayah (protection), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in walī. This indicates that what is meant by His saying "those who believe" is those who intended faith, because one who has in fact believed has already come out of the darknesses into the light, unless what is meant by "bringing out" is bringing them out of the doubts which confront believers, in which case there is no need to posit an implied intention.

What is meant by the light in His saying: ﴿They bring them out of the light into darknesses﴾ is what the prophets of Allah brought of the call to religion, for that is light for the disbelievers; their protectors removed them from it into the darkness of disbelief; that is, their protectors kept them upon the disbelief they were in, by diverting them from answering the caller to Allah from among the prophets.

It was also said: what is meant by "those who disbelieve" here are those whose disbelief was established in His knowledge, Exalted is He; their protectors from the devils and the heads of misguidance bring them out from the light, which is the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind, into the darknesses of disbelief into which they fell because of that removal.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar to what preceded from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the occasion of revelation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and he added: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the sons the choice."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi something similar as well, and he said: "Then those who had not embraced Islam joined them," that is, joined the Banu al-Nadir, and those who had embraced Islam remained.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid who said: "The people among the Ansar used to be nursed among Banu Qurayzah, and they remained steadfast upon their religion. When Islam came, their families wished to compel them to accept Islam, so this verse was revealed."

Ibn Jarir reported something similar from al-Hasan.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾": He said: It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf called al-Husayn, who had two Christian sons, while he himself was a Muslim man. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not compel them, for they have refused anything but Christianity?" So this verse was revealed.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported something similar from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubaydah.

Likewise Abu Dawud in his Nasikh (work on abrogation) and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Suddi something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah who said: "The Arabs had no religion, so they were compelled to adopt a religion by the sword."

He said: "But do not compel the Jews, the Christians and the Magians if they pay the jizyah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur reported something similar from al-Hasan.

Al-Bukhari reported from Aslam: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say to an old Christian woman: "Embrace Islam and you will be safe." She refused, so he said: "O Allah, bear witness," then he recited: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him that he said to Zanbaq the Roman, his slave: "If you embraced Islam, I would seek your help in the trust of the Muslims," but he refused, so he said: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sulayman ibn Musa concerning His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, that he said: "It was abrogated by: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾" [al-Tawbah: 73].

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab who said: "The taghut is the devil."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrimah who said: "The taghut is the soothsayer."

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliyah who said: "The taghut is the sorcerer."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Malik ibn Anas who said: "The taghut is whatever is worshipped besides Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The firm handhold is: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas ibn Malik: that it is the Qur'an.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid: that it is faith.

And from Sufyan: that it is the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlas).

It is established in the two Sahihs that the interpretation of "al-'urwah al-wuthqa" in another verse is Islam, as a hadith raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in his interpretation of the dream of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.

Ibn 'Asakir reported from Abu al-Darda' who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and 'Umar, for they are the extended rope of Allah. Whoever holds fast to them has held fast to the firm handhold of Allah which has no severance."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "When one affirms the oneness of Allah and believes in divine decree (qadar), that is the firm handhold."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mu'adh that he was asked about His saying: ﴿It has no severance﴾, and he said: "It has no cutting off short of entering Paradise."

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe﴾, the verse, that he said: "They are a people who had disbelieved in Jesus, then believed in Muhammad (ﷺ)." And concerning ﴿those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾, the verse, he said: "They are a people who believed in Jesus, then when Muhammad was sent, they disbelieved in him."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak who said: "The darknesses are disbelief, and the light is faith."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi something similar.

In this verse there is evidence for what was mentioned earlier, that the disbelievers have the Taghut (false deities/transgressors) as their protectors. The interrogative hamzah (alif of interrogation) is for denying a negation, and the implied sense is: "Has your knowledge or your reflection not reached this man who produced this argument?"

Al-Farra' said: "Alam tara" (have you not seen) carries the meaning of "hal ra'ayta" (have you seen): i.e., have you seen the one who argued with Ibrahim, who was Nimrud ibn Kus ibn Kan'an ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It was also said that he was Nimrud ibn Falakh ibn Amir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam.

His words, ﴿because Allah had given him the kingdom﴾, mean: because Allah had given him (the kingdom), or on account of Allah having given him the kingdom, in the sense that the giving of kingship made him arrogant and inherited for him pride and tyranny, so he argued on that account. Or it means that he placed the argument, which is the ugliest form of disbelief, in place of the gratitude that was incumbent upon him, as one says, "You have shown enmity to me because I have done good to you." Or it means "at the time when Allah gave him the kingdom."

His words, ﴿when Ibrahim said﴾, are a temporal clause (zarf) governing "hajja" (argued). It was said that it is a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿that Allah had given him the kingdom﴾ according to the last interpretation, and this is far-fetched.

His words, ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾: the ya' of "rabbiya" is read with fath (rabbiya), and it was also read with its deletion.

His words, "Ana uhyi" (I give life): the majority of reciters read "ana uhyi" with the alif after the nun of "ana" omitted in continuous recitation, while Nafi' and Ibn Abi Uways kept it, as in the verse of the poet:

*Ana shaykhu al-'ashira fa'rifuni / hamidan qad tadharrabtu al-sanama*
(I am the elder of the clan, so recognise me, / praised, for I have sharpened my teeth.)

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meant that Allah is the One who creates life and death in bodies, while the disbeliever meant that he is able to pardon from killing, which would be giving life, and to kill, which would be causing death. So this was a foolish answer, not fit to be set against the proof of Ibrahim, because he meant something other than what Ibrahim meant. Had Ibrahim said to him, "His Lord is the One who creates life and death in bodies; can you do that?", the one who disbelieved would have been confounded at the very first moment. But he moved with him to another argument, to ease his strangulation and to let loose the reins of the debate, and so he said: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾. This argument is one in which sophistry does not enter, and the disbeliever cannot easily escape it by way of obstinacy and contention.

His words, ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾: "buhita al-rajulu", "bahata" and "bahita" mean: when he was cut off and fell silent, bewildered.

Ibn Jarir said: It is reported from some Arabs that in this meaning the form "bahata" with fath on the ba' and the ha' is used.

Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywa read "fa-bahuta" with fath on the ba' and damm on the ha', which is a dialect of "buhita" with kasr on the ha'. He said: Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "fa-bahata" with fath on both the ba' and the ha', meaning: then Ibrahim confounded the one who disbelieved, so "alladhi" is in the accusative position. He said: It may also be that "bahata" with fath on both is a dialect of "buhita."

Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash reported the reading "fa-buhita" with kasr on the ha', and said: the more common is with fath on the ha'.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Some people have interpreted, regarding the reading of those who read "fa-bahata" with fath on both, that it means he reviled and slandered, and that Nimrud was the one who reviled when he was cut off and had no stratagem left. End of quotation.

And He, glory be to Him, said ﴿so the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ and did not say "so the one who argued was confounded," to indicate that this argument was itself disbelief.

His words, ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, are a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the content of the sentence before it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ali ibn Abi Talib that the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord was Nimrud ibn Kan'an.

Ibn Jarir related it from Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah related from Zayd ibn Aslam that the first tyrant on earth was Nimrud. People used to go out to obtain food from him, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, went out to obtain food along with those who went. Whenever a group of people passed by him, he would say, "Who is your lord?" They would say, "You." Until Ibrahim passed by him, and he said, "Who is your lord?" He said, "The One who gives life and causes death." He said, "I give life and cause death." He said, "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was confounded, and he sent him away without food.

Ibrahim returned to his family and passed by a mound of yellow sand, and said, "Shall I not take some of this and bring it to my family, so that their hearts will be pleased when I enter upon them?" He took some of it and came to his family, placed his provisions down, then slept. His wife got up to his provisions, opened them, and found in them the finest food one could ever see. She prepared some of it for him and brought it to him. Now his custom with his family was that there was no food with them. He said, "Where did this come from?" She said, "From the food you brought." He knew that Allah had provided for him, and he praised Allah.

Then Allah sent an angel to the tyrant, saying: "Believe, and I will leave you in your kingdom."

He said: "Is there any lord other than me?" The angel came to him a second time and said this to him, and he refused. Then he came to him a third time and he refused. The angel said to him: "Gather your hosts for three days." The tyrant gathered his hosts, and Allah commanded the angel, who opened against him a gate of gnats, and the sun rose but they did not see it because of their multitude. Allah sent them against them, and they ate their fat and drank their blood until nothing remained but the bones, while the king himself, as he was, was not touched by any of that. Then Allah sent against him a gnat, which entered his nostril, and he remained for four hundred years with his head being struck with hammers. The people most merciful to him were those who joined their hands and struck his head with them. He had been a tyrant for four hundred years, so Allah punished him for four hundred years, corresponding to his kingdom. Then Allah caused him to die. He is the one who had built a tower toward the sky, and Allah brought its building from the foundations.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: It is Nimrud ibn Kan'an. They claim that he was the first to rule on earth. He brought two men, killed one of them and left the other, and said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, he said: "To faith."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 259:**

His saying: *aw ka-alladhī* ("or like the one who"). *Aw* is used for conjunction (*li-l-ʿaṭf*), by taking it as a coordination according to the sense (*ḥamlan ʿalā al-maʿnā*). The implied meaning is: "Have you not seen (the like of) the one who disputed, or the like of the one who passed by a town?"

This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is: "Have you not seen the one who disputed with Ibrahim concerning his Lord? Have you not seen who is like the one who passed by a town?" So his saying *man huwa* ("who is") was omitted.

A group has chosen that the *kāf* (*ka-*, "like") is superfluous (*zāʾida*), and others have chosen that it is a noun (*ismiyya*).

The well-known view is that the town is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) after Bukhtunasr (Nebuchadnezzar) had destroyed it. It has also been said that what is meant by "the town" is its people.

His saying: ﴿fallen down upon its roofs﴾, that is, fallen upon its roofs (*ʿurūsh*), meaning the roof collapsed and then the walls fell upon it. This was said by al-Suddi, and Ibn Jarir chose it. It has also been said: its meaning is "empty of people while the houses still stand." The root of *khawāʾ* is emptiness (*khulūw*). One says: *khawat al-dār* and *khawiyat takhwī khawāʾan* (a verbal noun, *mamdūd*), *khuwiyyan* and *khawyan*, meaning the house became desolate. *Khawāʾ* also means hunger, because the stomach is empty of food.

The apparent meaning is the first view, based on the indication of his saying *ʿalā ʿurūshihā* ("upon its roofs"), from *khawā al-bayt* when it falls, or from *khawat al-arḍ* when it is destroyed. This clause is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*, a *ḥāl* clause), meaning: "in the state of being so."

His saying: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life﴾, that is, "when" (*matā*) will He give it life, or "how" (*kayfa*) will He give it life. It is an expression of astonishment at its revival while it is in that state, which resembles the state of the dead, and which is the opposite of the state of the living. The object is placed before the verb (*taqdīm al-mafʿūl*) because the astonishment arises from the object, not from the agent.

When the passer-by said this statement, astonished at the revival of the mentioned town through rebuilding it and inhabiting it, Allah struck for him a parable in himself, with something greater than what he asked about: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up﴾. Al-Tabari related from some of them that he said: this statement was a doubt concerning Allah's power, glorified is He, to revive a town by bringing population to it. Doubt is conceivable only if his question concerned the revival of its dead.

His saying: "*miʾata ʿāmin*" ("a hundred years") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarfiyya*).

*Al-ʿām* means "the year." Its origin is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like *al-ʿawm* (swimming), and this period of time was named by it.

His saying: *baʿathahu* means "he gave him life."

His saying: ﴿He said, "How long have you remained?"﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*), as if a questioner asked: "What did He say to him after raising him?"

The subject of *qāla* ("he said") is disputed. It has been said it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that a angel of the heavens called him with this, and it has been said it was Jibril, and it has been said it was other than him. It has also been said that he was a prophet among the prophets, and it has been said a man of the believers from his people who witnessed him when Allah caused him to die and he was kept alive until his resurrection.

The first view is preferable because of His saying afterwards: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾.

Ibn ʿĀmir and the people of Kufa, except ʿĀṣim, recited *kam labithtum* with *idghām* (assimilation) of the *thāʾ* into the *tāʾ*, because they are close in articulation (*takārub fī al-makhraj*). Others recited with *iẓhār* (clear pronunciation), which is better because the point of articulation of the *thāʾ* is distant from that of the *tāʾ*.

*Kam* is in the position of the accusative as an adverb of time. He said: ﴿a day or part of a day﴾ according to what he had in his understanding and in his opinion, so he was not lying. Similar to this is the statement of the People of the Cave: ﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day"﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Similar also is the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: "I was not shortened, and I did not forget." This supports the view of those who say that truthfulness is the agreement of a statement with belief, and lying is its disagreement with it.

His saying: ﴿He said, "Rather you have remained a hundred years"﴾ is also a resumptive sentence, as has preceded. That is: you did not remain a day or part of a day; rather, he remained a hundred years.

His saying: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled﴾. He, glorified is He, commanded him to look at this great sign of His power: the food and drink did not change despite the length of that period.

Ibn Masʿud recited *wa-hādhā ṭaʿāmuka wa-sharābuka lam yatasannah* ("and this is your food and drink, it has not spoiled"). Talha ibn Musarrif recited *wa-nẓur li-ṭaʿāmika wa-sharābika li-miʾati sanatin* ("and look at your food and drink for a hundred years").

It is also related from Talha that he recited *lam yassann* with the assimilation of the *tāʾ* into the *sīn* and the deletion of the *hāʾ*.

The majority recited it with the *hāʾ* retained in pausal pronunciation (*fī al-waṣl*). *Al-tasannuh* is derived from *al-sana* (year): that is, the years did not change it. Its origin is *sanhah* or *sanwah*, from *sanahat al-nakhla* and *tasannahat* when the years passed over the date palm. A date palm that is *sanā* bears fruit in one year and not in another. *Asnahtu ʿinda Banī Fulān* means "I stayed with them." Its origin is *yatasannā*: the *alif* was dropped for the jussive (*li-l-jazm*) and the *hāʾ* for the pause (*li-l-sakt*).

It has also been said: it comes from *asina al-māʾ*, when water changes. According to this, it should have been said *yata'assan*, from His saying: ﴿of black mud, moulded﴾ [al-Hijr: 26–28]. This was said by Abu ʿAmr al-Shaybani.

Al-Zajjaj said this is not so, because His saying *masnūn* does not mean "changed"; rather it means "poured upon the clay (*sanah*) of the earth."

His saying: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾: the commentators differed about its meaning. The majority held that it means: look at it, how its parts were scattered and its bones decayed, then Allah gave it life and it returned as it was.

Al-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: look at your donkey standing in its stable, nothing having touched it after a hundred years had passed over it. The first view is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. The second view is supported by its suitability to His saying: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled﴾. He, glorified is He, mentioned that the food and drink did not change after informing him that he had remained a hundred years. Yet the non-change of that food and drink cannot be evidence for that long period; rather it is evidence for what he said about remaining a day or part of a day, in order to increase the magnitude of that which Allah caused him to die for that period. When he saw that his food and drink had not changed, while he had thought he had remained only a day or part of a day, his bewilderment increased and the doubt strengthened over him. Then when he looked at his donkey as decayed bones, it became firmly established for him that this was the work of One whose power produces what minds cannot encompass, since food and drink change quickly.

Yet that food and drink had remained this long period unchanged, and the donkey living such a long period, and it had become so: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 14].

His saying: ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. Al-Farra' said: He placed the *wāw* (*wa-li-najʿalaka*, "and that We may make you") to indicate that it is a condition for a verb following it. Its meaning: "And that We may make you a sign for the people and a proof of resurrection after death, We did that."

If you wish, you may consider the *wāw* superfluous and added.

Al-Aʿmash said: the aspect of his being a sign is that he came as a young man in his state on the day he died, and found the sons and grandchildren old men.

His saying: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. The Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir recited it with *zāy* (*nunshizuhā*), and the rest with *rāʾ* (*nunshiruhā*).

Abban related from ʿĀṣim: *nanshuruhā*, with a fatha on the first *nūn*, sukun on the second, and a damma on the *shīn* and the *rāʾ*.

Al-Hakim related and authenticated from Zayd ibn Thabit that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited *kayfa nunshizuhā* with the *zāy*.

The meaning of the recitation with *zāy* is "We raise them," from which comes *al-nashaz*, which is the high ground of the earth: that is, He raises some of them to others.

As for the meaning of the recitation with the unpointed *rāʾ*, it is clear from *anshara Allāh al-mawtā*: that is, He gives life to the dead.

His saying: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾: that is, We cover them with it, just as we cover the body with clothing. So he borrowed clothing for that, as al-Nabigha borrowed it for Islam when he said:

His saying: ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾, that is, of the signs mentioned earlier that Allah, glorified is He, showed him, and commanded him to look at them and reflect upon them: ﴿he said, "I know that Allah is over all things competent"﴾, nothing among things is beyond Him.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of His saying ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾ is that when it became manifest to him by direct sight what had been strange in Allah's power in his estimation before seeing it.

He said: "*aʿlamu*" ("I know"). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said its meaning is: "I know that this kind of knowledge is one which I had not known."

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *qāla iʿlam* in the imperative form, addressing himself, in the manner of *tajrīd* (self-address).
