Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verse 263–265 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "like a grain" — it is not valid to make this the predicate (khabar) of His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth﴾, because the two differ. Therefore a omitted element must be supplied, either in the first: i.e., "the likeness of the spending of those who spend," or in the second: i.e., "like the likeness of one who sows a grain." By "the seven spikes" is meant those that come out on a single stalk from which seven branches divide, with a spike on each branch. "Grain" (ḥabba) is the name for everything that the son of Adam sows, and from it is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"I have sworn never to eat the grain of Iraq as long as I live, while the weevil eats the grain in the village."

It has been said: the "spikes" here means the spikes of millet (dukhn), for it is in their spike that there is this number.

Al-Qurtubi said: the spike of millet comes with more than this number, by two-fold or more, according to what we have witnessed.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: In a wheat spike there may be found one that has a hundred grains, and as for the rest of the grains, [there may be found] more; but the example was given with this quantity.

al-Tabari said: His saying, ﴿in every spike a hundred grains﴾, its meaning is: if that is found; otherwise, [it is] on the basis that you assume it.

His saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies [it] for whom He wills﴾ — it is possible that the meaning is: He multiplies this multiplication for whom He wills, or He multiplies this number, so He adds to it multiples of it for whom He wills; and this is the preferred view because of what comes later.

The Qur'an has stated that a good deed carries ten times its like, and this verse indicates that the reward of spending in jihad is seven hundredfold; so the general is built upon the specific. This is based on the view that the path of Allah is jihad alone. But if what is meant by it is all forms of good, then this multiplication to seven hundred applies specifically to the reward of expenditures, and the tenfold multiplication applies to what is other than that.

His saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾ — this sentence contains an explanation of the manner of the spending mentioned earlier, i.e., it is the spending of those who spend and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders (mann) or injury (adha). Mann is mentioning the favor in order to enumerate it and reproach with it. It has been said: mann is speaking of what one has given to the point that the recipient is harmed by it. Mann is among the major sins, as established in Sahih Muslim and others, that it is one of the three whom Allah will not look at, nor purify, and for whom there is a painful punishment.

And adha: abuse, arrogance, and complaining.

In al-Kashshaf it says: The meaning of "thumma" (then) is to show the difference between spending and abandoning mann and adha, and that abandoning them is better than the spending itself, just as He made steadfastness upon faith better than entering into it, with His saying: "then they remained steadfast." End of quote.

Mann is mentioned before adha because of its frequency of occurrence, and the word "la" (not) is placed in the middle to indicate the comprehensiveness of the negation.

His saying: "with their Lord" contains emphasis and honor.

His saying: ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ — its apparent meaning is the negation of fear from them in both abodes, because of the comprehensiveness conveyed by an indefinite noun in the context of negation; and likewise ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ indicates the continuous absence of sorrow from them.

His saying: ﴿A kind word and forgiveness﴾ — it has been said: the predicate is omitted, i.e., "better and more fitting." This was mentioned by al-Nahhas.

He said: It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "what you have been commanded is a kind word."

And His saying: "and forgiveness" is also a subject, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿better than a charity﴾. It has also been said: His saying "better" is a predicate of His saying "a kind word" and of His saying "and forgiveness," and beginning with two indefinite nouns is permitted because the first is specified by the attribute and the second by the conjunction. The meaning: the kind word from the one asked to the one asking, which is reassurance and hope in what is with Allah, and a gracious refusal, is better than a charity followed by injury.

It is established in Sahih Muslim from him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "A good word is a charity, and among good deeds is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face." How fine is what Ibn Duraid said:

"Let not weariness at a beggar overcome you; the best of your lifetime is that you be seen as one who is asked."
"Do not confront with rejection the face of one who hopes; the endurance of your honor is that you be seen as one who is hoped in."

By "forgiveness" is meant concealing the poverty and the wretched state of the needy, (p-183) and pardoning the beggar if he has shown an insistence that troubles the heart of the one asked. It has been said: the pardon is from the side of the asker, because if he refuses him graciously, he excuses him. It has been said: the meaning is that an act which leads to forgiveness is better than charity, i.e., Allah's forgiveness is better than your charity.

This sentence is a resumed clause confirming the abandonment of following charity with mann and adha.

His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ — nullifying charities is removing their effect and corrupting their benefit, i.e., do not nullify them by mann and adha, or by one of the two.

His saying: "like the one who" — i.e., nullification like the nullification of the one who. It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and it may be a circumstantial clause: i.e., do not nullify, being like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, and "to be seen" is put in the accusative as a cause for his saying "spends," i.e., for the sake of showing off; or it is a circumstantial clause, i.e., he spends showing off, not intending thereby the face of Allah and the reward of the Hereafter, but doing that to be seen by people, seeking their praise and commendation. It has been said: what is meant by him is the hypocrite, based on His saying: ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

His saying: ﴿So his example is like the example of a smooth rock﴾ — al-Safwan is a large, smooth stone.

al-Akhfash said: Safwan is the plural of safwana.

al-Kisa'i said: Safwan is singular, and its plural is ṣufiyy and aṣfā, but al-Mubarrad rejected this.

al-Nahhas said: it may be a plural and it may be singular, and the singular is preferable because of His saying: ﴿upon it is dust, then a heavy rain struck it﴾. Al-Wabil is heavy rain. Allah, glory be to Him, has likened this spender to a smooth rock upon which is dust, which the observer thinks is good, fertile land; then when a heavy rain strikes it, it removes the dust from it and leaves it bare: i.e., stripped and clean of the dust that was on it. Likewise this showy person, for his spending does not benefit him, just as rain falling on the smooth rock that has dust upon it does not benefit it. His saying: ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ — i.e., they gain no benefit from what they did for show, and find no reward for it. The sentence is a resumed clause, as if it were said: what will their state be then? So it was said: "they have no power" etc. The two pronouns refer to the relative pronoun, i.e., "like the one who," according to meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you plunged as those who plunged﴾ [al-Tawba: 69], i.e., the category, or the group, or the party.

His saying: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and for strengthening [their] souls﴾ — it has been said that His saying: ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and "strengthening" is conjoined to it, and it is also an object of purpose: i.e., the spending is for the sake of seeking.

Strengthening (tathbit): so said Makki in al-Mushkil.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is rejected; it is not valid that "strengthening" be an object of purpose, because spending is not for the sake of strengthening.

He said: "seeking" is put in the accusative as a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial clause, and it could have been treated as an object of purpose, but the accusative as a verbal noun is the correct one, from the aspect that the verbal noun "strengthening" is conjoined to it. "Seeking" means desire, and "pleasure" is the verbal noun of "he was pleased, he is pleased." "Strengthening" means: they strengthen themselves by giving their wealth for faith and the rest of the acts of worship, training and disciplining themselves; or strengthening may mean confirmation: i.e., affirmation of Islam arising from their own selves.

The early scholars differed about the meaning of this term. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: its meaning is that they are careful in choosing where to place their charities. It was said: its meaning is confirmation and certainty; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: its meaning is reckoning from their own selves; this was said by Qatada. It was said: its meaning is that their souls have insight, so they strengthen them in spending in obedience to Allah; this was said by al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Salih, and this is preferred over what came before.

It is said: "I strengthened so-and-so in this matter, I strengthen him, strengthening," i.e., I corrected his resolve.

His saying: ﴿like a garden on a height, struck by a heavy rain﴾ — the garden (jannah) is an orchard, a land in which trees grow until they cover it, derived from the word "jinn" and "janin" (embryo) because of its concealment.

Rabwa is an elevated place with slight elevation; it is triptote in its ra' vowels, and it was read thus. He specified the rabwa because its vegetation is better than others, while it is generally not struck by frost, due to the lightness of its air from the blowing of gentle winds.

al-Tabari said: It is the gardens of al-Hazn, which the Arabs frequently mention. Ibn 'Atiyya objected to him, saying: the gardens of al-Hazn are attributed to Najd, because they are better than the gardens of Tihama, and Najd's vegetation is more fragrant, and its breeze cooler and finer.

Najd is also called Hazn, and this one mentioned here is not from that. The word rabwa is derived from raba, yarbu, when it increases.

al-Khalil said: rabwa is high, good land.

Wabil is heavy rain as previously mentioned; it is said: the sky poured (wabalat al-sama' tabil), and the land is wabila (drenched).

al-Akhfash said: from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a severe seizing﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16], i.e., severe; and a severe blow, and a severe punishment.

﴿Its fruit (ukul)﴾ with a dammah on the hamza: the produce that is eaten, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿giving its produce every season﴾ [Ibrahim: 25]. Its attribution to the garden is an attribution of association, like the saddle of the horse and the door of the house.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "ukla" with a dammah on the hamza and sukun on the kaf, for lightness.

'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the kaf vowelled with a dammah.

His saying: "two-fold" means twice what it used to bear because of the heavy rain.

So by "ḍi'f" is meant "mithl" (equal amount). It has been said: four times. Its accusative is as a circumstantial clause from "ukuluha," i.e., multiplied.

His saying: ﴿But if a heavy rain does not reach it, then a light rain﴾ — i.e., the light rain suffices for it, and it is the rain of weak, fine drops.

al-Mubarrad and others said: its estimate is "then a light rain suffices for it."

al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is "then what reaches it is a light rain," and the meaning is that the light rain takes the place of the heavy rain in bringing forth its fruit twofold.

Some said: al-tall is dew.

In al-Sihah: al-tall is the weakest rain, and its plural is atlal.

al-Mawardi said: The crop of light rain is weaker than the crop of heavy rain.

The meaning is: the expenditures of these people are pure in the sight of Allah, never wasted in any state, although they vary; and it is possible that the example be taken as comparing their condition, in regard to the great and small amounts they spend, with the known garden, in regard to the heavy and light rain it receives. Just as each of the two rains doubles its produce, so their expenditure, whether great or small, after it is intended for the face of Allah, is pure and increased in their rewards.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ — al-Zuhri read it with a yā' (third person), and the majority read it with a tā' (second person). In this there is encouragement toward what they gain through sincerity, along with warning against showing off and the like; so it is both promise and threat.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, regarding His saying: ﴿like a grain that grows seven spikes﴾ (p-184), from al-Rabi': "Whoever pledged allegiance to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, for emigration and stationed with him in Madinah, and did not go anywhere except with his permission, had for his good deed seven hundredfold; and whoever pledged allegiance for Islam, his good deed had ten times its like."

Muslim, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that "a man gave a charity of a bridled she-camel in the way of Allah, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: For you, on the Day of Resurrection, for it, seven hundred she-camels, all of them bridled."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Khuzaym ibn Fatik who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Whoever spends an expenditure in the way of Allah, there is written for him seven hundredfold."

al-Bukhari narrated it in his Tarikh from the hadith of Anas.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 263–265 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad narrated it from the hadith of Abu 'Ubaydah, and he added: "Whoever spends on himself and on his family, or visits a sick person, then the good deed is (rewarded) tenfold."

al-Nasa'i narrated something similar in (the book of) Fasting.

Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, 'Ali, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Abu Umamah, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and Jabir, all of whom narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever sends forth expenditure in the way of Allah and remains in his house, for him there is, for every dirham, on the Day of Resurrection, seven hundred dirhams. And whoever fights himself in the way of Allah and spends for that purpose, for him there is, for every dirham, on the Day of Resurrection, seven hundred thousand dirhams." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And Allah multiplies (it) for whom He wills﴾.

Ibn Majah also narrated it from the hadith of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali.

Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied: the good deed by ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to whatever Allah wills. Allah says: Except fasting, for it is for Me, and I shall reward it."

Muslim also narrated it.

al-Tabarani narrated from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Blessed is the one who mentions Allah much in jihad in the way of Allah, for he has for every word seventy thousand good deeds, each good deed of which is ten times."

The mention of a portion of the hadiths on the multiplication of good deeds has already passed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245].

Authentic hadiths have indeed come concerning the reward of one who equips a fighter.

Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Sahl ibn Mu'adh, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, prayer, fasting and remembrance are multiplied, compared with expenditure in the way of Allah, seven hundredfold."

Ahmad, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Expenditure on the Hajj is like expenditure in the way of Allah, by seven hundredfold."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said, in explaining His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent with reminder (of favour) or injury﴾: Indeed, there are people who send a man from among them in the way of Allah, or who spend on a man, or give him expenditure, then they remind him of it and hurt him; meaning that this is the occasion of revelation.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Authentic hadiths have indeed come concerning the prohibition of reminder (of favour) and injury, and concerning the excellence of spending in the way of Allah, on relatives, and in good causes. There is no need to lengthen by mentioning them, for they are well known in their places.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "It has reached us that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'There is no charity more beloved to Allah than the word of truth. Did you not hear the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury﴾?'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying: "a kind word," he said: a gracious response; you say: "May Allah have mercy on you, may Allah provide for you," and you do not scold him or speak harshly to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "No reminder-giver enters Paradise, and this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminder and injury﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "ṣafwān," he said: the rock; "fa-tarakahu ṣaldan," he said: there is nothing on it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "al-wābil" is the rain.

They both narrated from Qatadah, who said: "al-wābil" is the heavy, intense rain. He said: This is a parable which Allah struck for the deeds of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿They have no power over anything of what they earned﴾ on that day, just as this rain left this rock with nothing on it, cleaner than it was.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿fa-tarakahu ṣaldan﴾, he said: dry, barren, bringing forth nothing.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, he said: This is a parable which Allah struck for the deed of the believer.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Sha'bi concerning His saying: ﴿and firm assurance from themselves﴾, he said: affirmation and certainty.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Salih something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated: they make sure where they place their wealth.

They both narrated from al-Hasan, who said: When a man intended to give charity, he made sure; if it was for Allah, he carried it out, and if some show-off (riya') mixed with it, he withheld.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: "tathbītan," he said: intention.

al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Rabwah" is the elevated part of the land.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "al-Rabwah" is level land that is elevated.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It is the high place where rivers do not flow.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning His saying, Exalted is He: "fa-ṭallun," he said: dew.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "al-ṭall" is the fine drizzle of rain, meaning its gentle part.

They both narrated from Qatadah, who said: This is a parable which Allah struck for the deed of the believer; he says: its good has no lack, just as this garden has no lack in any condition, whether a heavy rain reaches it or a light drizzle.

The meaning of *al-wudd* is love for a thing together with wishing for it. The hamza (interrogative particle) that enters the verb is for denying that the event occurs. *Al-jannah* (garden) is applied both to a dense cluster of trees and to the land in which trees stand.

The first meaning is preferable here because of His saying: ﴿Rivers flow beneath it﴾ (p-185), since the pronoun then refers back to the trees without needing an omitted genitive noun (*mudaf mahdhuf*, a noun understood but not stated). On the second meaning, that noun must be supplied, i.e. "beneath its trees." Likewise His saying ﴿it was burned﴾ needs no omitted noun on the first meaning, whereas on the second it requires one: "its trees were burned." The palm trees and grapevines are singled out for mention, together with His saying ﴿for him therein is every kind of fruit﴾, because they are the most noble of trees. These clauses are descriptions of the garden.

As for the *waw* in His saying ﴿and old age has overtaken him﴾, it has been said that it is a conjunction linking it to His saying ﴿should be﴾, a past verb linked to a future one. It has also been said that it links to His saying ﴿wishes﴾. It has further been said that it is conditioned by meaning, since ﴿should be﴾ carries the sense of ﴿was﴾. And it has been said that it is the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*, introducing a circumstantial clause), meaning "and old age had already overtaken him." This last view is the more preferred.

Old age is the condition most likely to bring acute need, because the one who reaches it becomes unable to pursue the means of livelihood.

His saying ﴿and he has weak offspring﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿overtaken him﴾. That is: "while the circumstance is that he has weak offspring." Whoever combines advanced age with weak dependants will have the greatest grief over that garden.

*Al-i'sar* (whirlwind) is a violent wind that blows from the earth up to the sky like a column. It is what is called *al-zawba'ah*, as al-Zajjaj said.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-zawba'ah* is a chief of the jinn, and from it the whirlwind was named *zawba'ah*. It is also said "the mother of Zawba'ah." It is a wind that stirs dust and rises to the sky as if it were a pillar. It has also been said that it is a wind that raises a cloud containing thunder and lightning.

His saying ﴿so it was burned﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿so it struck it﴾. This verse is a parable (*tamthil*) of one who does good deeds but mixes with them what nullifies them. On the Day of Resurrection he finds them when he most needs them, yet they neither nourish nor relieve hunger, like the situation of one who owns that described garden while himself bearing that very attribute.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "ʿUmar said one day to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'About what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any one of you like to have a garden...﴾?' They said: 'God knows best.' He said: 'Say: we know, or we do not know.' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'I have something in my mind about it, O Commander of the Faithful.' ʿUmar said: 'O son of my brother, speak and do not belittle yourself.' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'It was struck as a parable for a deed.' ʿUmar said: 'What deed?' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'For a wealthy man who works in obedience to God, then God sends Satan to him, and he engages in sins until his deed is drowned.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿUmar that he said: "This is a parable struck for a person who performs a righteous deed, until, when he reaches the end of his life and is most in need of it, he does evil deeds."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, narrated through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying ﴿a whirlwind in which is fire﴾: "It is a wind in which there are severe scorching blasts."

Likewise His saying ﴿it was burned﴾ needs no omitted noun on the first meaning, whereas on the second it requires one: "its trees were burned." The palm trees and grapevines are singled out for mention, together with His saying ﴿for him therein is every kind of fruit﴾, because they are the most noble of trees. These clauses are descriptions of the garden.

As for the *waw* in His saying ﴿and old age has overtaken him﴾, it has been said that it is a conjunction linking it to His saying ﴿should be﴾, a past verb linked to a future one. It has also been said that it links to His saying ﴿wishes﴾. It has further been said that it is conditioned by meaning, since ﴿should be﴾ carries the sense of ﴿was﴾. And it has been said that it is the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*, introducing a circumstantial clause), meaning "and old age had already overtaken him." This last view is the more preferred.

Old age is the condition most likely to bring acute need, because the one who reaches it becomes unable to pursue the means of livelihood.

His saying ﴿and he has weak offspring﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿overtaken him﴾. That is: "while the circumstance is that he has weak offspring." Whoever combines advanced age with weak dependants will have the greatest grief over that garden.

*Al-i'sar* (whirlwind) is a violent wind that blows from the earth up to the sky like a column. It is what is called *al-zawba'ah*, as al-Zajjaj said.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-zawba'ah* is a chief of the jinn, and from it the whirlwind was named *zawba'ah*. It is also said "the mother of Zawba'ah." It is a wind that stirs dust and rises to the sky as if it were a pillar. It has also been said that it is a wind that raises a cloud containing thunder and lightning.

His saying ﴿so it was burned﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿so it struck it﴾. This verse is a parable (*tamthil*) of one who does good deeds but mixes with them what nullifies them. On the Day of Resurrection he finds them when he most needs them, yet they neither nourish nor relieve hunger, like the situation of one who owns that described garden while himself bearing that very attribute.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "ʿUmar said one day to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'About what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any one of you like to have a garden...﴾?' They said: 'God knows best.' He said: 'Say: we know, or we do not know.' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'I have something in my mind about it, O Commander of the Faithful.' ʿUmar said: 'O son of my brother, speak and do not belittle yourself.' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'It was struck as a parable for a deed.' ʿUmar said: 'What deed?' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'For a wealthy man who works in obedience to God, then God sends Satan to him, and he engages in sins until his deed is drowned.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿUmar that he said: "This is a parable struck for a person who performs a righteous deed, until, when he reaches the end of his life and is most in need of it, he does evil deeds."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, narrated through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying ﴿a whirlwind in which is fire﴾: "It is a wind in which there are severe scorching blasts."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 269–271 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿from the good things you have earned﴾: that is, from the best and choicest of what you have earned. This is what the majority (al-Jumhur) said.

A group said that the meaning of "the good things" here is the lawful (al-halal).

There is no obstacle to considering both meanings together, because the best and choicest earnings are called lawful only according to the people of the Sharia (religious law). The lexicographers (ahl al-lugha) apply the word to whatever is good in itself, whether lawful or unlawful. The technical legal usage (al-haqiqa al-shar'iyya) takes precedence over the linguistic usage (al-lughawiyya).

His saying: ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾: that is, and from the good things of what We have brought forth for you from the earth. The qualifier was omitted because what precedes it indicates it. What is meant is plants, minerals and buried treasure (al-rikaz).

His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad﴾: that is, do not intend the inferior wealth. The majority read the imperfect verb-prefix with a fatha and the yaʾ lightened. Ibn Kathir read it with the yaʾ doubled (tashdid).

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-la ta'ammamu﴾, and this is a dialect form (lugha).

Abu Muslim ibn Khabbab read it with a damma on the initial letter and a kasra on the mim.

Abu Amr reported that Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ta'ammamu﴾ with a hamza after the damma.

The verse contains a command to spend of what is good and a prohibition against spending what is bad.

A group of the early generations (al-salaf) held that the verse concerns obligatory charity (al-sadaqa al-mafrusa), while others held that it covers both obligatory and voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'). The latter is the apparent meaning, and evidence that supports this will come later. The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿from it you spend﴾ conveys restriction: that is, do not restrict spending to the bad. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, do not intend the bad wealth, restricting your spending to it and confining yourselves to it.

His saying: ﴿while you would not take it yourselves﴾: that is, while you would not accept it in your dealings at any time. This is how the majority explained its meaning. It was also said that the meaning is: you would not take it even if you found it being sold in the market.

His saying: ﴿except that you overlook in it﴾ is from the verb aghmada al-rajul fi amr kadhā (a man "overlooked" a matter), meaning that he was lenient, accepted part of his right, let it pass, and turned a blind eye to it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"How often, and how often, are there things from you that disturb me;
I overlook them, and I am not blind to them."

al-Zuhri read ﴿tughmiḍū﴾ with a fatha on the initial letter, a kasra on the mim, and lightened. It is also reported from him that he read it with a damma on the initial letter, a fatha on the ghayn, and a kasra on the mim doubled, and Qatada read it the same way. The meaning according to the first of these two readings is: unless you press down its price upon the seller from you. According to the second: unless you take it at a reduction.

Ibn Atiyya said: the reading of the majority can be understood as "passing over" or "closing the eye," because aghmada is equivalent to ghammada, and it can also be taken to mean "until" (hatta): that is, until you arrive at what is obscure of interpretation and consideration in taking that.

His saying: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty﴾: the meaning of Satan and its derivation has already been explained.

Ya'idukum means yukhawwifukum (frightens you) the poverty: that is, with poverty, so that you do not spend. This verse is connected to what came before it.

It was read as ﴿al-fuqr﴾ with a damma on the initial letter, and this is a dialect form. al-Jawhari said: al-fuqr is a dialect form of al-faqr, like al-ḍu'f and al-ḍu'f (weakness).

al-Fahsha' is the disgraceful trait: it is sins, spending in them, and withholding from spending in acts of obedience. In al-Kashshaf it is said: "The fahish (the disgraceful one) among the Arabs is the miser." From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-Abd:

"I see death selecting the noble and choosing
the precious wealth of the stingy, the strict one."

But although the Arabs applied it to the miser, that does not preclude their applying it to other sins, and it occurs frequently in their speech.

His saying: ﴿and Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾: when the word waʿd (promise) is used without qualification in the speech of the Arabs, it refers to good. When it is qualified, it is sometimes qualified with good and sometimes with evil. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire Allah has promised to those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. Also from this is what is in this verse: the restriction of Satan's promise to poverty and the restriction of Allah's promise, glory be to Him, to forgiveness and bounty.

Forgiveness (al-maghfira) is covering over for His servants in this world and the Hereafter for their sins and their expiation. Bounty (al-fadl) is that He replaces for them something better than what they spent, widening their provision for them and bestowing favour upon them in the Hereafter with what is better, greater, more majestic and more beautiful.

His saying: ﴿He gives wisdom﴾: it is knowledge. It was also said: understanding; it was also said: correctness in speech. There is no obstacle to taking it as all of these, either inclusively or as alternatives. It was said: it is prophethood; it was said: intellect; it was said: fear (of Allah); it was said: scrupulousness (wara'). The root of wisdom (al-hikma) is what prevents foolishness, which is every ugly thing.

The meaning is: whoever Allah gives wisdom has indeed been given much good: that is, great in value, of lofty worth.

al-Zuhri and Ya'qub read ﴿wa-man yu'ti﴾ with the verb built for the active subject. The majority read it with the verb built for the passive. al-Albab means the intellects; its singular is lubb, and the discussion of it has already been given.

His saying: ﴿and whatever you spend of expenditure﴾: "ma" here is conditional, and it may also be relative (mawsula), with an omitted returning pronoun: that is, "what you spent." This is a statement of a general ruling covering every accepted and unaccepted charity and every accepted or unaccepted vow.

His saying: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ contains the meaning of a promise for those who spend and vow in the accepted manner, and a warning for those who do the opposite.

He made the pronoun singular although its referents are two things, the expenditure and the vow, because the implied sense is: "whatever expenditure you spend, indeed Allah knows it, or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it," and then one of them was omitted, being sufficed by the other. This is what al-Nahhas said. It was also said that when the conjunction is "aw" (or), as in your saying "Zayd or ʿAmr," one says "I honoured him" and does not say "I honoured both of them." The better view is that conjunction with "aw" permits both: singularising the pronoun, as in this verse and in His saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or amusement, they disperse to it﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 11], and His saying: ﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin, then throws it upon an innocent one﴾ [al-Nisa': 112]; and dualising it, as in His saying: ﴿If he is rich or poor, then Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. From the first type, with conjunction by "wa" (and), is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Tawdih and al-Miqrat, whose traces have not been effaced
by what the south and north winds have woven."

From it is the saying of the poet:

"We are content with what we have, and you are content
with what you have, and opinions differ."

From it also is: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾ [al-Tawba: 34]. It was said: when a pronoun is found after mention of two things or many things, it is taken to refer to what was mentioned, that is, "indeed Allah knows what was mentioned." Ibn Atiyya affirmed this and preferred it, al-Qurtubi favoured it, and many grammarians mentioned its meaning in their works.

His saying: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾: that is, for the wrongdoers, who have fallen into sin by opposing what Allah commanded of spending in the ways of good, there are no helpers who support them or protect them from Allah's punishment because of the wrong they did to themselves. The better view is to take it in generality without specification, as the context indicates: that is, the wrongdoers, whatever injustice they committed, have no helpers.

His saying: ﴿If you disclose the charities, then excellent is what they are﴾ was read with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ʿayn; with a kasra on both; with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the ʿayn; and with a kasra on the nun and the vowel of the ʿayn suppressed (ikhfa').

The grammarians have recorded four dialect forms for "niʿimma," and these are the ones by which it was read. In this there is a kind of detail explaining what was left general in the preceding conditional: that is, if you make the charities apparent, then excellent is making them apparent; and if you conceal them and they reach their proper recipients among the poor, then concealment is better for you.

The majority of the exegetes held that this verse concerns voluntary charity, not obligatory charity, so there is no merit in concealment for it. Indeed, it has been said that disclosure is better in it. A group said that concealment is better in both obligatory and voluntary charity.

His saying: ﴿and He will remove from you of your misdeeds﴾: Abu Amr and ʿAsim, in the transmission of Hafs, read it with the yaʾ and a nominative (raf').

al-Aʿmash, Nafiʿ, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the nun and a jazm (jussive). Ibn ʿAbbas read it with the taʾ and a fatha on the fa' and a jazm. al-Husayn ibn ʿAli al-Ju'fi read it with the nun and a nasb (accusative) on the ra'.

Whoever read it with the nominative takes it as conjoined to the position (mahall) of the clause that is the response after the fa', or as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Whoever read it with the jazm takes it as conjoined to the fa' and what follows it.

Whoever read it with the nasb takes it as governed by an implied "an" (that).

Sibawayh said: the nominative here is the good form, and he permitted the jazm by interpreting it as: "and if you conceal them, the concealment will be better for you, and He will remove..." Al-Khalil also said something like Sibawayh's view.

The "min" in His saying: ﴿of your misdeeds﴾ is partitive: that is, some of your misdeeds.

al-Tabari reported from a group that it is superfluous (za'ida), and this is according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: that is an error on their part.

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾, that he said: "from gold and silver"; ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾, meaning: "from grain and fruit, and everything upon which there is zakat."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned﴾, that he said: "from trade"; ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾, he said: "from fruits."

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib regarding His saying: ﴿And do not aim at the bad to spend from it﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning us, the group of the Ansar. We were owners of palm trees, and a man would bring from his palm according to its abundance or scarcity. A man would bring a cluster or two clusters and hang it in the mosque. The People of the Suffa (ahl al-Suffa, the poor companions who lodged in the mosque) had no food, so whenever one of them was hungry he would come to the cluster, strike it with his stick, and the unripe dates and ripe dates would fall, and he would eat. Some people who did not care for good would bring a man a cluster in which there was shis (inferior dates) and hashaf (dry, worthless dates), or a cluster that had broken, and hang it. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad to spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves except that you overlook in it﴾." He said: "If one of you were given a gift like what he gave, he would not take it except with overlooking and shame." He said: "After that, each of us would bring the best of what he had."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that a man would own two orchards, and he would look at the worse of them in dates, give it in charity, and mix in the hashaf. So the verse was revealed, and Allah reproached them for that and forbade them from it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad ibn Abihi, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the charity of breaking the fast (sadaqat al-fitr), a man came with bad dates, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the one who estimates the palm-trees' yield not to accept it."

Then Allah revealed this verse.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Sahl ibn Hunayf, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave an order and said: 'Who brought this?' Every person who brought something was attributed to it, so the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not aim at the bad﴾ to the end of the verse."

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade two types of dates from being found in the charity: al-Ju'rur and lawn al-Hubayq."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to buy cheap food and give it in charity, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿUbaydah al-Salmani, who said: I asked ʿAli ibn Abi Talib about the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, spend﴾ [the verse]. He said: This verse was revealed concerning the obligatory zakat (almsgiving). A man would go to the dates, cut them, and set aside the good ones in one place. Then when the collector of the charity came, he would give him from the inferior ones.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. He said: It is knowledge of the Qur'an: its abrogating (nasikh) and abrogated (mansukh) parts, its clear (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) parts, its earlier and later parts, its lawful and unlawful, and its parables.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that it is the Qur'an, meaning its exegesis (tafsir).

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that it is prophethood.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: It is the understanding (fiqh) of the Qur'an.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-Darda', concerning ﴿He gives wisdom﴾, that he said: It is the recitation of the Qur'an and reflection upon it.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: It is the Book and understanding of it.

He also reported the same from al-Nakhaʿi.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid, who said: It is the Book, whose correctness (ischabah) He gives to whom He wills.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him that he said: It is correctness in speech.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah, who said: It is the fear of God.

He also reported the same from Mattar al-Warraq.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr the same.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, God knows it﴾. He said: He counts it.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the Sahih and other collections, regarding vows of obedience and disobedience, what is well known, such as his saying (ﷺ): "There is no vow in disobedience to God," and his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever vows to obey God, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Him, let him not disobey Him," and his saying (ﷺ): "A vow is only that by which the face of God is sought." It has also been established from him regarding the expiation (kaffarah) of a vow what is well known.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent﴾ [the verse]. He said: He made secret voluntary (tatawwuʿ) charity exceed its public form by seventy times, and made public obligatory (fard) charity better than its secret form by twenty-five times.

And likewise all obligatory and voluntary acts in all matters.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [the verse], that he said: This was practiced before Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) was revealed. When Bara'ah was revealed with the obligatory charities and their details, charities came to an end in that form.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [the verse], that he said: This is abrogated (mansukh).

And concerning His words: ﴿And in their wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾, he said: It is abrogated; it abrogated every charity in the Qur'an, namely the verse in Surat al-Tawbah: ﴿Charities are only for the poor﴾.

Authentic elevated (marfuʿ) hadiths have been transmitted concerning the excellence of secret charity.

He said: "If one of you were given a gift like what he gave, he would not take it except with overlooking and shame." He said: "After that, each of us would bring the best of what he had."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that a man would own two orchards, and he would look at the worse of them in dates, give it in charity, and mix in the hashaf. So the verse was revealed, and Allah reproached them for that and forbade them from it."

Then Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that it is prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-Darda', concerning ﴿He gives wisdom﴾, that he said: It is the recitation of the Qur'an and reflection upon it.

He also reported the same from al-Nakhaʿi.

He also reported the same from Mattar al-Warraq.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr the same.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the Sahih and other collections, regarding vows of obedience and disobedience, what is well known, such as his saying (ﷺ): "There is no vow in disobedience to God," and his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever vows to obey God, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Him, let him not disobey Him," and his saying (ﷺ): "A vow is only that by which the face of God is sought." It has also been established from him regarding the expiation (kaffarah) of a vow what is well known.

He said: He made secret voluntary (tatawwuʿ) charity exceed its public form by seventy times, and made public obligatory (fard) charity better than its secret form by twenty-five times.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [the verse], that he said: This was practiced before Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) was revealed. Authentic elevated (marfuʿ) hadiths have been transmitted concerning the excellence of secret charity.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 269–271 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿from the good things you have earned﴾: that is, from the best and choicest of what you have earned. This is what the majority (al-Jumhur) said.

A group said that the meaning of "the good things" here is the lawful (al-halal).

There is no obstacle to considering both meanings together, because the best and choicest earnings are called lawful only according to the people of the Sharia (religious law). The lexicographers (ahl al-lugha) apply the word to whatever is good in itself, whether lawful or unlawful. The technical legal usage (al-haqiqa al-shar'iyya) takes precedence over the linguistic usage (al-lughawiyya).

His saying: ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾: that is, and from the good things of what We have brought forth for you from the earth. The qualifier was omitted because what precedes it indicates it. What is meant is plants, minerals and buried treasure (al-rikaz).

His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad﴾: that is, do not intend the inferior wealth. The majority read the imperfect verb-prefix with a fatha and the yaʾ lightened. Ibn Kathir read it with the yaʾ doubled (tashdid).

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-la ta'ammamu﴾, and this is a dialect form (lugha).

Abu Muslim ibn Khabbab read it with a damma on the initial letter and a kasra on the mim.

Abu Amr reported that Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ta'ammamu﴾ with a hamza after the damma.

The verse contains a command to spend of what is good and a prohibition against spending what is bad.

A group of the early generations (al-salaf) held that the verse concerns obligatory charity (al-sadaqa al-mafrusa), while others held that it covers both obligatory and voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'). The latter is the apparent meaning, and evidence that supports this will come later. The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿from it you spend﴾ conveys restriction: that is, do not restrict spending to the bad. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, do not intend the bad wealth, restricting your spending to it and confining yourselves to it.

His saying: ﴿while you would not take it yourselves﴾: that is, while you would not accept it in your dealings at any time. This is how the majority explained its meaning. It was also said that the meaning is: you would not take it even if you found it being sold in the market.

His saying: ﴿except that you overlook in it﴾ is from the verb aghmada al-rajul fi amr kadhā (a man "overlooked" a matter), meaning that he was lenient, accepted part of his right, let it pass, and turned a blind eye to it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"How often, and how often, are there things from you that disturb me;
I overlook them, and I am not blind to them."

al-Zuhri read ﴿tughmiḍū﴾ with a fatha on the initial letter, a kasra on the mim, and lightened. It is also reported from him that he read it with a damma on the initial letter, a fatha on the ghayn, and a kasra on the mim doubled, and Qatada read it the same way. The meaning according to the first of these two readings is: unless you press down its price upon the seller from you. According to the second: unless you take it at a reduction.

Ibn Atiyya said: the reading of the majority can be understood as "passing over" or "closing the eye," because aghmada is equivalent to ghammada, and it can also be taken to mean "until" (hatta): that is, until you arrive at what is obscure of interpretation and consideration in taking that.

His saying: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty﴾: the meaning of Satan and its derivation has already been explained.

Ya'idukum means yukhawwifukum (frightens you) the poverty: that is, with poverty, so that you do not spend. This verse is connected to what came before it.

It was read as ﴿al-fuqr﴾ with a damma on the initial letter, and this is a dialect form. al-Jawhari said: al-fuqr is a dialect form of al-faqr, like al-ḍu'f and al-ḍu'f (weakness).

al-Fahsha' is the disgraceful trait: it is sins, spending in them, and withholding from spending in acts of obedience. In al-Kashshaf it is said: "The fahish (the disgraceful one) among the Arabs is the miser." From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-Abd:

"I see death selecting the noble and choosing
the precious wealth of the stingy, the strict one."

But although the Arabs applied it to the miser, that does not preclude their applying it to other sins, and it occurs frequently in their speech.

His saying: ﴿and Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾: when the word waʿd (promise) is used without qualification in the speech of the Arabs, it refers to good. When it is qualified, it is sometimes qualified with good and sometimes with evil. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire Allah has promised to those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. Also from this is what is in this verse: the restriction of Satan's promise to poverty and the restriction of Allah's promise, glory be to Him, to forgiveness and bounty.

Forgiveness (al-maghfira) is covering over for His servants in this world and the Hereafter for their sins and their expiation. Bounty (al-fadl) is that He replaces for them something better than what they spent, widening their provision for them and bestowing favour upon them in the Hereafter with what is better, greater, more majestic and more beautiful.

His saying: ﴿He gives wisdom﴾: it is knowledge. It was also said: understanding; it was also said: correctness in speech. There is no obstacle to taking it as all of these, either inclusively or as alternatives. It was said: it is prophethood; it was said: intellect; it was said: fear (of Allah); it was said: scrupulousness (wara'). The root of wisdom (al-hikma) is what prevents foolishness, which is every ugly thing.

The meaning is: whoever Allah gives wisdom has indeed been given much good: that is, great in value, of lofty worth.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 2, verses 272–274:**

His words, ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: meaning, it is not obligatory upon you to make them guided, accepting what they were commanded and forbidden. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾: a guidance that brings him to the sought goal. This sentence is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), and in it there is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). The occasion of its revelation will come later. By His words, ﴿from good﴾, is meant everything that truly qualifies as "good," whatever it may be. It is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "Whatever thing you spend, being of good." Then He explained that the expenditure that is counted and accepted is only that which is sought for the Face of Allah, glorified is He; that is, for seeking the Face of Allah.

His words, ﴿will be repaid to you﴾: that is, its reward and recompense, in the manner mentioned earlier of multiplication.

His words, ﴿for the poor﴾: it is connected to His words, ﴿and whatever you spend of good﴾, or to an omitted element, meaning: "Make that for the poor." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "Your spending is for the poor who (p-188) have been confined in the way of Allah by fighting or striving (jihad)." It was also said: they were prevented from earning a livelihood because of the weakness they were in. ﴿They cannot go about in the land﴾: to earn a living by trade, farming, and the like, due to their weakness. It was said: they are the people of the Suffah (Ahl al-Suffah, the companions who lived in a shaded area of the Prophet's mosque). It was also said: they are everyone who is characterized by poverty and what is mentioned with it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned of the states of those poor people what requires tenderness toward them and compassion for them, which is that they are restrained from asking and from displaying need, to the extent that the ignorant one about them thinks them to be rich.

Al-ta'affuf is on the pattern of tafa''ul, and it is a form of intensification from ''affa 'an al-shay', when one refrains from something and keeps himself free from seeking it. In His words, ﴿yahsabuhum﴾, there are two readings: opening the sin (fath al-sin) and kasrah (kasr) of it.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "The fath is more analogical (aqyas), because the 'ayn of the past tense is kasrah, so its pattern is to come in the present tense with fath."

So the reading with kasr is, on this basis, good, even if it is shadhdh (irregular/non-canonical).

The "min" in His words, ﴿from restraint﴾, is for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghayah), and it was said: it is for the explanation of the kind (bayan al-jins).

His words, ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾: that is, by the shabbiness of their clothes, the weakness of their bodies, and everything that indicates poverty and need.

The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. Al-simā, with a short vowel, means the sign, and it may be lengthened.

Al-ilhaf is persistence in asking, and it is derived from al-lihaf (the covering/blanket). It was named so because it encompasses all the ways of demanding in asking, just as a blanket encompasses covering.

The meaning of His words, ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾, is that they do not ask them at all, neither asking with persistence nor asking without persistence.

This was the view of al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj, and most of the exegetes went to it. Its basis is that restraint is a permanent attribute of theirs that does not leave them, and mere asking contradicts it. It was also said: what is meant is that when they ask, they ask gently and do not press in their asking. Although this is the apparent meaning from directing the negation toward the condition and not toward the conditioned, the attribute of restraint contradicts it. Also, the ignorant one about them thinking them rich occurs only if they do not ask at all.

His words, ﴿by night and by day﴾, indicate the increase of their eagerness to spend and the intensity of their zeal for it, to the extent that they do not leave that by night or by day, and they do it secretly and openly, whenever the need of the needy befalls them and the poverty of the destitute becomes evident to them, at all times and in all conditions.

The entry of the fa' into the predicate of the relative clause, namely His words, ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, is to indicate the causality of what precedes it for what follows. It was also said: it is for coordination, and the predicate of the relative clause is omitted, meaning: "And among them are those who spend."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, all transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They used to dislike giving (yarda'a) to their kin among the polytheists, so this verse was revealed: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ to His words, ﴿and you will not be wronged﴾, and He permitted them."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' transmitted from him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to command us not to give charity except to the people of Islam, until this verse was revealed, and then he commanded charity after it to everyone who asks you from every religion."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted the like of it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted the like of it from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Some people of the Ansar had lineage and kinship with Quraydhah and al-Nadir, and they were careful not to give charity to them, and they wanted them to embrace Islam. So ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ was revealed, the verse."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Amr al-Hilali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: 'Shall we give charity to the poor among the People of the Book?' So Allah revealed ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ata al-Khurasani, who said concerning His words, ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah﴾: "If you give for the Face of Allah, then there is no fault upon you regarding what his deed was."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas concerning His words, ﴿for the poor who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾, who said: "They are the people of the Suffah."

Ibn Sa'd transmitted the like of it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "They are the Emigrants of Quraysh in Medina with the Prophet (ﷺ); they were commanded to be given charity."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' concerning His words, ﴿who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾, who said: "They confined themselves in the way of Allah for fighting, so they cannot engage in trade."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They are a people whom wounds befell in the way of Allah, so they became disabled, and He made for them a right in the wealth of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Raja' ibn Haywah concerning His words, ﴿They cannot go about in the land﴾, who said: "They cannot engage in trade."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words, ﴿the ignorant one thinks them rich﴾, who said: "Allah guided the believers to them and made their expenditures for them, and commanded them to place their expenditures upon them, and He was pleased with them."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words, ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾, who said: "It is at-tajashshu (excessive, pressing demand)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' that its meaning is: "You recognize in their faces the effort from need."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, "﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾," who said: "It is the shabbiness of their clothes."

It is established in the two Sahihs and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The poor man (miskin) is not the one who is turned away by a date or two dates, or a morsel or two morsels. Rather, the poor man is the one who refrains (yata'affaf). Recite if you wish: ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾." Numerous hadiths have also come prohibiting asking, except to one who holds authority or in a matter from which one has no alternative.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi, al-Tabarani, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Gharib al-Mulaykii, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "This verse was revealed, ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day﴾, concerning the people of horses."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Asakir transmitted the like of it from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "It concerns the one who does not tie it (the horse) out of arrogance, nor for show, nor for reputation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted the like of it from Abu al-Darda'.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hanash al-San'ani that he heard Ibn Abbas say concerning this verse: "They are those who feed horses in the way of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Asakir transmitted through the route of Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid from his father from Ibn Abbas concerning this verse, who said: "It was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). He had four dirhams, and he spent one dirham by night, one dirham by day, one dirham secretly, and one dirham openly."

Abd al-Wahhab is weak, but Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through another route from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah concerning this verse, who said: "These are a people who spent in the way of Allah, which He had made obligatory upon them, without extravagance, without destitution, without squandering, and without corruption."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "It was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with them) regarding their spending in the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usrah)."
