Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted the like of it from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Some people of the Ansar had lineage and kinship with Quraydhah and al-Nadir, and they were careful not to give charity to them, and they wanted them to embrace Islam. So ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ was revealed, the verse."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Amr al-Hilali, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: 'Shall we give charity to the poor among the People of the Book?' So Allah revealed ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ata al-Khurasani, who said concerning His words, ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah﴾: "If you give for the Face of Allah, then there is no fault upon you regarding what his deed was."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas concerning His words, ﴿for the poor who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾, who said: "They are the people of the Suffah."

Ibn Sa'd transmitted the like of it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "They are the Emigrants of Quraysh in Medina with the Prophet (ﷺ); they were commanded to be given charity."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' concerning His words, ﴿who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾, who said: "They confined themselves in the way of Allah for fighting, so they cannot engage in trade."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They are a people whom wounds befell in the way of Allah, so they became disabled, and He made for them a right in the wealth of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Raja' ibn Haywah concerning His words, ﴿They cannot go about in the land﴾, who said: "They cannot engage in trade."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the like of it from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words, ﴿the ignorant one thinks them rich﴾, who said: "Allah guided the believers to them and made their expenditures for them, and commanded them to place their expenditures upon them, and He was pleased with them."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words, ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾, who said: "It is at-tajashshu (excessive, pressing demand)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Rabi' that its meaning is: "You recognize in their faces the effort from need."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, "﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾," who said: "It is the shabbiness of their clothes."

It is established in the two Sahihs and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The poor man (miskin) is not the one who is turned away by a date or two dates, or a morsel or two morsels. Rather, the poor man is the one who refrains (yata'affaf). Recite if you wish: ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾." Numerous hadiths have also come prohibiting asking, except to one who holds authority or in a matter from which one has no alternative.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi, al-Tabarani, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Gharib al-Mulaykii, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "This verse was revealed, ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day﴾, concerning the people of horses."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Asakir transmitted the like of it from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "It concerns the one who does not tie it (the horse) out of arrogance, nor for show, nor for reputation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted the like of it from Abu al-Darda'.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hanash al-San'ani that he heard Ibn Abbas say concerning this verse: "They are those who feed horses in the way of Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Asakir transmitted through the route of Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid from his father from Ibn Abbas concerning this verse, who said: "It was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). He had four dirhams, and he spent one dirham by night, one dirham by day, one dirham secretly, and one dirham openly."

Abd al-Wahhab is weak, but Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through another route from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah concerning this verse, who said: "These are a people who spent in the way of Allah, which He had made obligatory upon them, without extravagance, without destitution, without squandering, and without corruption."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "It was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with them) regarding their spending in the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usrah)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 275–277 (part 1 of 2):

Ribā (ربا) in the language means increase in general; one says "rabā al-shay'u yarbū" when the thing increases. In the Sharia (sacred law) the term applies to two things: ribā al-faḍl (ribā of excess) and ribā al-nasī'ah (ribā of deferral), as is detailed in the books of substantive law (kutub al-furū'). Most of what the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to do was that when the term of a debt came due, the creditor would say to the debtor: "Will you pay or will you increase (the debt)?" If he did not pay, he would add an amount to the money he owed and postpone the term for a period.

This is prohibited by consensus (bi-l-ittifāq). The orthographic analogy for writing ribā is with yā' because of the kasrah at its beginning.

However, they wrote it in the muṣḥaf with a wāw. Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: "It is according to the dialect of those who pronounce it with emphasis (tafkhīm), just as the words ṣalāh and zakāh were written, and an alif was added after them, likening it to the wāw of the plural," end of quote.

I say: This is merely a convention that need not be followed, for these written forms are conventional matters over which one should not dispute, except regarding what the letter indicates from the root letter of the word and the like, as is established in the discussions of orthography (khaṭṭ) within the science of morphology (ṣarf). In any case, writing the word and shaping its written form according to how it is pronounced is preferable. So whatever is pronounced as an alif, such as ṣalāh and zakāh and the like, it is preferable that it be written in that manner. As for whether the origin of this alif is a wāw or a yā', this is not hidden from one who knows the science of morphology. These written forms serve only to convey the pronunciation of the word they signify, as it is spoken by those who speak it, and not to indicate what the root of the word is, which is not part of actual pronunciation. So understand this, and do not occupy yourself with what many scholars consider regarding these written forms, and which they impose upon themselves and criticize whoever opposes it, for that is among the disputes over conventional matters that do not bind anyone to adhere to them. Rather, you should write these forms according to how the reader pronounces them when reciting, for this is the required purpose of their establishment and of the agreement upon them. The required purpose of them is not that they indicate the root of the word as the speaker pronounces it, which does not come into his present pronunciation. So do not be deceived by what is reported from Sibawayh and the grammarians of Basra, that ribā is written with a wāw because he says in its dual form "ribawān."

The Kufans said: It is written with a yā', and its dual is "riban."

Al-Zajjāj said: "I have not seen a mistake more ugly or more shameful than this. They are not content with the error in writing until they err in the dual, while they recite: ﴿And what you give in usury that it may increase within the wealth of people—it does not increase with Allah﴾ [al-Rūm: 39]."

The address here with His words ﴿Those who consume ribā﴾ does not mean that this threat is restricted to the one who consumes it; rather, it is general for everyone who deals in ribā, taking it and giving it. The word "consume" is singled out only to intensify the reproach upon its doer, and because it is the most important aim, for the taker of ribā takes it only for consumption.

His words: "They will not stand" means on the Day of Resurrection, as indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: "They will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has struck with madness on the Day of Resurrection."

This was reported by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and most of the exegetes interpreted it this way. They said: He will be raised like a madman as a punishment for him and as a disgrace before the people of the gathering. It was also said that the intended meaning is to liken one who is greedy in his trade and gathers his wealth from ribā to the standing of a madman, because greed, covetousness and desire for accumulation have so provoked him that he becomes like a madman in his movements, just as one says of someone who hurries in his walking and is erratic in his movements: "He has gone mad." From this is the saying of al-A'shā about his she-camel:

"And she arrives in the morning after the fatigue of the journey as if a jinn-spirit's madness has seized her."

So he made her, in the swiftness of her walk and her vigor, like a madman.

His words: ﴿except as one stands whom Satan has struck by touch﴾ mean: except with a standing like the standing of one whom Satan has struck. Al-khabṭ is striking without balance, like the stumbling of one in the dark, and it refers to one who is seized (al-maṣrū').

Al-mass is madness, al-amass is the madman, and likewise al-awlaq. It is connected to His words "they stand," meaning: they do not stand, due to the touch that is upon them, ﴿except as one stands whom Satan has struck﴾, or it is connected to "yaqūm" (stands).

In the verse there is evidence against the view of one who says that seizure (ṣara') does not come from the jinn, claiming it is from the natural causes, and says that the verse is an exception to what the Arabs used to believe, namely that Satan strikes a human. This is not correct: Satan does not enter into a human and there is no touch from him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge from Satan striking him, as reported by al-Nasā'ī and others.

His words: "That" refers to what has been mentioned of their condition and their punishment, because of their saying: ﴿Trade is only like ribā﴾, meaning they made trade and ribā one and the same. They likened trade to ribā only as an exaggeration, by making ribā the principle and trade the branch. That is: "Trade is only like" a sale without increase when the term comes due, just like a sale with increase when it comes due. The Arabs did not recognize ribā except as that. So Allah, glorified is He, refuted them with His words: ﴿But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden ribā﴾, meaning: Allah permitted trade and forbade a type of it, namely the sale that involves ribā.

Trade (al-bay') is the verbal noun of bā'a yabī': one gives a consideration and takes a counter-value. The clause is explanatory and has no place in the grammatical structure (lā maḥalla lahā mina al-i'rāb).

His words: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾ mean: whoever has received an admonition from Allah among the admonitions that the commands and prohibitions contain, and among them is what occurred here of the prohibition of ribā, and he desisted, meaning he complied with the prohibition that came to him and with the restraint from what was forbidden. The verb "desisted" (fa-intahā) is coordinated with "came to him" (jā'ahu).

His words "from his Lord" are connected to "came to him," or to an implied element functioning as an attribute of "admonition": that is, one that originates from ﴿from his Lord﴾. "So he desisted; for him is what has passed" means what he had previously taken of ribā is not held against him, because he did it before the prohibition of ribā reached him, or before the verse prohibiting ribā was revealed.

His words: ﴿And his affair is up to Allah﴾: it has been said the pronoun refers to "what has passed": that is, his affair is up to Allah regarding pardoning him and dropping the consequence. It has also been said the pronoun refers to the one who takes ribā: that is, the affair of whoever deals in ribā is up to Allah regarding his being firm in desisting, or returning to disobedience. "But whoever returns (to it), those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally." The reference is to whoever returns, and "companions" is plural in consideration of the meaning of "whoever." It has been said that the meaning of "whoever returns" is that he returns to saying ﴿Trade is only like ribā﴾, and that he thereby disbelieves and so deserves eternal abiding. According to the first interpretation, "eternal abiding" is used figuratively in the sense of exaggeration, as the Arabs say "a eternal kingdom," meaning one of long duration. Resorting to this interpretation is necessary because of the mutawātir (widely transmitted) hadiths stating that monotheists will be brought out of the Fire.

His words: ﴿Allah deprives ribā of blessing﴾: meaning He removes its blessing in this world, even if it is abundant, so it does not remain in the hand of its owner. It has also been said: He removes its blessing in the Hereafter.

His words: ﴿and gives increase for charities﴾: meaning He increases the wealth whose charity has been given. It has also been said: He blesses the reward of charity, multiplies it and increases the reward of the one who gives charity. There is no objection to carrying this on both meanings together.

His words: ﴿And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾: meaning He does not approve, because love is specific to those who repent much. In this there is strong emphasis and severe harshness toward the one who deals in ribā, since He has judged him to be a disbeliever and described him as a sinner for emphasis. It has been said it is to remove ambiguity, since the word may apply to farmers. It is possible that the intended meaning of "every ungrateful one" is one from whom a trait that entails disbelief proceeds, and the connection to the context is that those who said "Trade is only like ribā" are disbelievers.

The explanation of His words ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ to the end of the verse has already been given.

Abū Ya'lā reported through al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: ﴿Those who consume ribā will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has struck by touch﴾, he said: They will be recognized on the Day of Resurrection by that; they will not be able to stand except as the one who is struck and strangled stands. ﴿That is because they said, "Trade is only like ribā"﴾ and they lied against Allah. ﴿But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden ribā﴾, and whoever returns and consumes ribā ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him regarding the verse, he said: The consumer of ribā will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a madman who is choked.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him through another route, also regarding His words "will not stand": he said: That is at the time he is raised from his grave.

al-Iṣbahānī in his al-Targhīb reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The consumer of ribā will come on the Day of Resurrection bewildered, dragging his lips," then he recited: ﴿They will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has struck by touch﴾. Many hadiths have been transmitted magnifying the sin of ribā, among them the hadith of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd in al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Ribā has seventy-three gates; the least of them is like a man marrying his mother, and the worst of ribā is the honor of a Muslim man." And from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah raised (to the Prophet) in Ibn Mājah and al-Bayhaqī with the wording "seventy gates." This meaning has also been transmitted, with a difference in the number, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas.

Ibn Jarīr reported from al-Rabīʿ regarding the verse, he said: They will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with an insanity from Satan upon them. In some readings it is: "They will not stand on the Day of Resurrection."

Meaning the reading of Ibn Masʿūd mentioned earlier.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, from the hadith of ʿĀ'ishah who said: "When the verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah concerning ribā were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to the mosque and recited them to the people, then he prohibited trade in wine."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he gave a sermon and said: "Among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed is the verse on ribā, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died without explaining it to us, so leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful."

al-Bukhārī and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "The last verse that Allah revealed to His Messenger was the verse on ribā."

al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalā'il reported the same from ʿUmar.

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid regarding the ribā that Allah forbade, he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to have a debt owed to them by a man, and he would say: "For you such-and-such, and you postpone (the payment) from me," and he would postpone it.

He also reported similarly from Qatādah.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported similarly from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and added in regard to His words: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾: he said: that is, the clarification in the Qur'an concerning the prohibition of ribā, "and desisted from it." ﴿For him is what has passed﴾: that is, for him is what he had consumed of ribā before the prohibition. ﴿And his affair is up to Allah﴾: that is, after the prohibition and after leaving it; if He wills He protects him from it, and if He wills he does not do so. ﴿And whoever returns﴾: that is, to ribā after the prohibition, making it lawful by their saying ﴿Trade is only like ribā﴾, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾: that is, they will not die.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Allah deprives ribā﴾, he said: He diminishes ribā, ﴿and gives increase for charities﴾, he said: He increases them.

It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet): "Whoever gives in charity the equivalent of a date from good earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, Allah receives it with His right hand, then He nurtures it for its owner just as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain."

(p-191) Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Hibban and al-Tabarani also narrated something similar to it from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, in Nawadir al-Usul, narrated something similar to it as well, from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the hadith of ʿĀʾishah and Ibn ʿUmar, after relating the hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Allah deprives usury of blessing, and makes charities grow.﴾

Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a servant gives charity with a morsel, and it grows with Allah until it becomes like Uhud." These hadiths clarify the meaning of the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 275–277 (part 1 of 2):

Ribā (ربا) in the language means increase in general; one says "rabā al-shay'u yarbū" when the thing increases. In the Sharia (sacred law) the term applies to two things: ribā al-faḍl (ribā of excess) and ribā al-nasī'ah (ribā of deferral), as is detailed in the books of substantive law (kutub al-furū'). Most of what the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to do was that when the term of a debt came due, the creditor would say to the debtor: "Will you pay or will you increase (the debt)?" If he did not pay, he would add an amount to the money he owed and postpone the term for a period.

This is prohibited by consensus (bi-l-ittifāq). The orthographic analogy for writing ribā is with yā' because of the kasrah at its beginning.

However, they wrote it in the muṣḥaf with a wāw. Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: "It is according to the dialect of those who pronounce it with emphasis (tafkhīm), just as the words ṣalāh and zakāh were written, and an alif was added after them, likening it to the wāw of the plural," end of quote.

I say: This is merely a convention that need not be followed, for these written forms are conventional matters over which one should not dispute, except regarding what the letter indicates from the root letter of the word and the like, as is established in the discussions of orthography (khaṭṭ) within the science of morphology (ṣarf). In any case, writing the word and shaping its written form according to how it is pronounced is preferable. So whatever is pronounced as an alif, such as ṣalāh and zakāh and the like, it is preferable that it be written in that manner. As for whether the origin of this alif is a wāw or a yā', this is not hidden from one who knows the science of morphology. These written forms serve only to convey the pronunciation of the word they signify, as it is spoken by those who speak it, and not to indicate what the root of the word is, which is not part of actual pronunciation. So understand this, and do not occupy yourself with what many scholars consider regarding these written forms, and which they impose upon themselves and criticize whoever opposes it, for that is among the disputes over conventional matters that do not bind anyone to adhere to them. Rather, you should write these forms according to how the reader pronounces them when reciting, for this is the required purpose of their establishment and of the agreement upon them. The required purpose of them is not that they indicate the root of the word as the speaker pronounces it, which does not come into his present pronunciation. So do not be deceived by what is reported from Sibawayh and the grammarians of Basra, that ribā is written with a wāw because he says in its dual form "ribawān."

The Kufans said: It is written with a yā', and its dual is "riban."

Al-Zajjāj said: "I have not seen a mistake more ugly or more shameful than this. They are not content with the error in writing until they err in the dual, while they recite: ﴿And what you give in usury that it may increase within the wealth of people—it does not increase with Allah﴾ [al-Rūm: 39]."

The address here with His words ﴿Those who consume ribā﴾ does not mean that this threat is restricted to the one who consumes it; rather, it is general for everyone who deals in ribā, taking it and giving it. The word "consume" is singled out only to intensify the reproach upon its doer, and because it is the most important aim, for the taker of ribā takes it only for consumption.

His words: "They will not stand" means on the Day of Resurrection, as indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: "They will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has struck with madness on the Day of Resurrection."

This was reported by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and most of the exegetes interpreted it this way. They said: He will be raised like a madman as a punishment for him and as a disgrace before the people of the gathering. It was also said that the intended meaning is to liken one who is greedy in his trade and gathers his wealth from ribā to the standing of a madman, because greed, covetousness and desire for accumulation have so provoked him that he becomes like a madman in his movements, just as one says of someone who hurries in his walking and is erratic in his movements: "He has gone mad." From this is the saying of al-A'shā about his she-camel:

"And she arrives in the morning after the fatigue of the journey as if a jinn-spirit's madness has seized her."

So he made her, in the swiftness of her walk and her vigor, like a madman.

His words: ﴿except as one stands whom Satan has struck by touch﴾ mean: except with a standing like the standing of one whom Satan has struck. Al-khabṭ is striking without balance, like the stumbling of one in the dark, and it refers to one who is seized (al-maṣrū').

Al-mass is madness, al-amass is the madman, and likewise al-awlaq. It is connected to His words "they stand," meaning: they do not stand, due to the touch that is upon them, ﴿except as one stands whom Satan has struck﴾, or it is connected to "yaqūm" (stands).

In the verse there is evidence against the view of one who says that seizure (ṣara') does not come from the jinn, claiming it is from the natural causes, and says that the verse is an exception to what the Arabs used to believe, namely that Satan strikes a human. This is not correct: Satan does not enter into a human and there is no touch from him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge from Satan striking him, as reported by al-Nasā'ī and others.

His words: "That" refers to what has been mentioned of their condition and their punishment, because of their saying: ﴿Trade is only like ribā﴾, meaning they made trade and ribā one and the same. They likened trade to ribā only as an exaggeration, by making ribā the principle and trade the branch. That is: "Trade is only like" a sale without increase when the term comes due, just like a sale with increase when it comes due. The Arabs did not recognize ribā except as that. So Allah, glorified is He, refuted them with His words: ﴿But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden ribā﴾, meaning: Allah permitted trade and forbade a type of it, namely the sale that involves ribā.

Trade (al-bay') is the verbal noun of bā'a yabī': one gives a consideration and takes a counter-value. The clause is explanatory and has no place in the grammatical structure (lā maḥalla lahā mina al-i'rāb).

His words: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾ mean: whoever has received an admonition from Allah among the admonitions that the commands and prohibitions contain, and among them is what occurred here of the prohibition of ribā, and he desisted, meaning he complied with the prohibition that came to him and with the restraint from what was forbidden. The verb "desisted" (fa-intahā) is coordinated with "came to him" (jā'ahu).

His words "from his Lord" are connected to "came to him," or to an implied element functioning as an attribute of "admonition": that is, one that originates from ﴿from his Lord﴾. "So he desisted; for him is what has passed" means what he had previously taken of ribā is not held against him, because he did it before the prohibition of ribā reached him, or before the verse prohibiting ribā was revealed.

His words: ﴿And his affair is up to Allah﴾: it has been said the pronoun refers to "what has passed": that is, his affair is up to Allah regarding pardoning him and dropping the consequence. It has also been said the pronoun refers to the one who takes ribā: that is, the affair of whoever deals in ribā is up to Allah regarding his being firm in desisting, or returning to disobedience. The reference is to whoever returns, and "companions" is plural in consideration of the meaning of "whoever." Resorting to this interpretation is necessary because of the mutawātir (widely transmitted) hadiths stating that monotheists will be brought out of the Fire.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 278–281:**

His saying: ﴿Fear Allah﴾ means: protect yourselves from His punishment, and leave the remainders of interest (*riba*) that are still owed to you. Its apparent meaning is that He nullified from interest whatever had not been received.

His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾ It has been said that this is a figurative conditional (*shart majazi*) for the sake of emphasis. It has also been said that *in* (إنْ) in this verse carries the meaning of *idh* (إذْ, "since").

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This is rejected; it is not known in the language. The apparent meaning is: "if you are believers in truth," for that entails obeying the commands and prohibitions of Allah.

His saying: ﴿But if you do not do it﴾ means: if you do not do what you were commanded, namely, to be mindful (of Allah) and to leave what remains of interest, ﴿then be warned of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. That is, know of it, from *udhina bi-l-shay'* (أُذِنَ بِالشَّيْءِ), meaning "he came to know of the thing." It has been said that it derives from *al-idhn bi-l-shay'* (الإذْنِ بِالشَّيْءِ), meaning listening, since that is one of the means of knowledge.

Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, and Hamzah read *fa-ādhinū* (فَآذِنُوا), with the meaning: "inform others that you are at war with them."

This verse indicates that consuming interest and practising it are among the major sins (*kabāʾir*), and there is no disagreement on this. The indefinite form of *ḥarb* (war) is for magnification. Its magnitude is further increased by attributing it to the greatest name of Allah and to His Messenger, who is the noblest of His creation.

His saying: ﴿But if you repent﴾ that is, from interest, ﴿then you shall have your principal (*ru'ūs amwālikum*)﴾ which you will take, ﴿you will not wrong [others] nor be wronged﴾: you will not wrong your debtors by taking the surplus, and you will not be wronged by them through procrastination and deficiency. The clause is either circumstantial (*ḥāliyyah*) or resumptive (*isti'nāfiyyah*).

In this is evidence that their wealth, while they have not repented, is lawful for one who takes it from the rulers and those like them who act on their behalf.

His saying: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾ When He, glory be to Him, decreed for the people of interest their principal when the debtors were in a state of having wealth, He decreed for those in hardship that they be given time until they are in ease. *Al-ʿusrah* means hardship of circumstances due to lack of wealth; from it comes *jaysh al-ʿusrah* (the army of hardship).

*Al-nazirah* means postponement, and *al-maysarah* is a verbal noun meaning ease. The word *dhū* (ذُو) is in the nominative because it is the complete verb *kāna* (كانَ) meaning "there was/existed." This is the view of Sibawayh, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others.

Sibawayh cited the verse:

*Ransom be to the Banu Dhuhl ibn Shaybān, O youth, when there is a day with stars, grey-white.*

In the Codex of Ubayy (*Muṣḥaf Ubayy*) it reads: *wa-in kāna dhā ʿusrah* (وإنْ كانَ ذا عُسْرَةٍ), with the meaning: "if the one owed (*al-maṭlūb*) is in hardship."

Al-Aʿmash read *wa-in kāna muʿsiran* (وإنْ كانَ مُعْسِرًا). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani said, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Musa: "Likewise it is in the Codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb."

Al-Muʿtamir narrated from Hajjaj al-Warraq, who said: "In the Codex of ʿUthman it reads: ﴿And if there is one in hardship﴾." Al-Nahhas, Makki and al-Naqqash said: "On this reading the wording of the verse is specific to the people of interest. On the reading *dhū* (ذُو), it is general to everyone who has a debt upon him." The majority adopted this view.

The majority of readers read *fa-naẓiratun* (فَنَظِرَةٌ) with a kasrah on the *ẓāʾ*. Mujahid, Abu Rajaʾ and al-Hasan read it with a sukun, and this is the dialect of Tamim.

Nafiʿ alone read *maysurah* (مَيْسُرَةٍ) with a ḍammah on the *sīn*, while the majority read it with a fatḥah, meaning ease (*al-yasār*).

His saying: ﴿And that you give charity﴾ with one of the two *tāʾs* omitted. It was also read with a shaddah on the *ṣād*. That is: "And that you give charity to the debtors who are in hardship by remitting the debt is better for you." In this is encouragement for them to give their principal as charity to one who has fallen into hardship, and to consider that better than granting him time. This was said by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak.

Al-Tabari said: Others said the meaning of the verse is: "And that you give charity to the wealthy and the poor is better for you."

The first view is correct, and there is no place in the verse for the wealthy.

His saying: ﴿if you know﴾ its answer is omitted: that is, "if you know that it is better for you, act upon it."

His saying: ﴿And fear a Day﴾ It is the Day of Resurrection, and its indefiniteness is for inspiring awe. It is in the accusative as a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*), not as a time adverb (*ẓarf*).

His saying: ﴿on which you will be returned to Allah﴾ is a description of it.

Abu ʿAmr read *tur-jaʿūna* (تُرْجَعُونَ) with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, while the rest read it with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *jīm*. A group held that this Day is the Day of Death, while the majority held that it is the Day of Resurrection, as previously mentioned.

His saying: ﴿to Allah﴾ contains an omitted genitive construction; its estimated form is "to the judgement of Allah." ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full﴾ from among the accountable souls ﴿for what it earned﴾, that is, the recompense for what it did of good or evil. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is circumstantial. The pronoun is in the plural because it is more fitting to the state of recompense, just as the singular is more fitting to the state of earning. This verse contains a fine admonition for all people.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest﴾ that he said: It was revealed concerning al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and a man from Bani al-Mughirah, who were partners in the Jahiliyyah lending interest to some people of Thaqif. Then Islam came, and they had great wealth in interest, so Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Thaqif had made a treaty with the Prophet (ﷺ) that whatever interest they were owed by the people would stand, and whatever interest the people were owed by them would be void. Its magnitude is further increased by attributing it to the greatest name of Allah and to His Messenger, who is the noblest of His creation.

The clause is either circumstantial (*ḥāliyyah*) or resumptive (*isti'nāfiyyah*).

His saying: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾ When He, glory be to Him, decreed for the people of interest their principal when the debtors were in a state of having wealth, He decreed for those in hardship that they be given time until they are in ease. *Al-ʿusrah* means hardship of circumstances due to lack of wealth; from it comes *jaysh al-ʿusrah* (the army of hardship).

*Al-nazirah* means postponement, and *al-maysarah* is a verbal noun meaning ease. The word *dhū* (ذُو) is in the nominative because it is the complete verb *kāna* (كانَ) meaning "there was/existed." This is the view of Sibawayh, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others.

Sibawayh cited the verse:

*Ransom be to the Banu Dhuhl ibn Shaybān, O youth, when there is a day with stars, grey-white.*

In the Codex of Ubayy (*Muṣḥaf Ubayy*) it reads: *wa-in kāna dhā ʿusrah* (وإنْ كانَ ذا عُسْرَةٍ), with the meaning: "if the one owed (*al-maṭlūb*) is in hardship."

Al-Aʿmash read *wa-in kāna muʿsiran* (وإنْ كانَ مُعْسِرًا). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani said, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Musa: "Likewise it is in the Codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb."

Al-Muʿtamir narrated from Hajjaj al-Warraq, who said: "In the Codex of ʿUthman it reads: ﴿And if there is one in hardship﴾." Al-Nahhas, Makki and al-Naqqash said: "On this reading the wording of the verse is specific to the people of interest. On the reading *dhū* (ذُو), it is general to everyone who has a debt upon him." The majority adopted this view.

The majority of readers read *fa-naẓiratun* (فَنَظِرَةٌ) with a kasrah on the *ẓāʾ*. Mujahid, Abu Rajaʾ and al-Hasan read it with a sukun, and this is the dialect of Tamim.

Nafiʿ alone read *maysurah* (مَيْسُرَةٍ) with a ḍammah on the *sīn*, while the majority read it with a fatḥah, meaning ease (*al-yasār*).

His saying: ﴿And that you give charity﴾ with one of the two *tāʾs* omitted. It was also read with a shaddah on the *ṣād*. That is: "And that you give charity to the debtors who are in hardship by remitting the debt is better for you." In this is encouragement for them to give their principal as charity to one who has fallen into hardship, and to consider that better than granting him time. This was said by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak.

Al-Tabari said: Others said the meaning of the verse is: "And that you give charity to the wealthy and the poor is better for you."

The first view is correct, and there is no place in the verse for the wealthy.

His saying: ﴿if you know﴾ its answer is omitted: that is, "if you know that it is better for you, act upon it."

His saying: ﴿And fear a Day﴾ It is the Day of Resurrection, and its indefiniteness is for inspiring awe. It is in the accusative as a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*), not as a time adverb (*ẓarf*).

His saying: ﴿on which you will be returned to Allah﴾ is a description of it.

Abu ʿAmr read *tur-jaʿūna* (تُرْجَعُونَ) with a fatḥah on the *tāʾ* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, while the rest read it with a ḍammah on the *tāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *jīm*. A group held that this Day is the Day of Death, while the majority held that it is the Day of Resurrection, as previously mentioned.

His saying: ﴿to Allah﴾ contains an omitted genitive construction; its estimated form is "to the judgement of Allah." ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full﴾ from among the accountable souls ﴿for what it earned﴾, that is, the recompense for what it did of good or evil. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is circumstantial. The pronoun is in the plural because it is more fitting to the state of recompense, just as the singular is more fitting to the state of earning. This verse contains a fine admonition for all people.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest﴾ that he said: It was revealed concerning al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and a man from Bani al-Mughirah, who were partners in the Jahiliyyah lending interest to some people of Thaqif. Then Islam came, and they had great wealth in interest, so Allah revealed this verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: "Thaqif had made a treaty with the Prophet (ﷺ) that whatever interest they were owed by the people would stand, and whatever interest the people were owed by them would be void. When the Conquest came, he appointed ʿAttab ibn Asid over Makkah. The Banu ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf used to take interest from the Banu al-Mughirah, and the Banu al-Mughirah used to pay them interest in the Jahiliyyah. Then Islam came and they still owed them a great deal of wealth. The Banu ʿAmr came seeking their interest, but the Banu al-Mughirah refused to pay them in Islam, and they raised the matter to ʿAttab ibn Asid. ʿAttab wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote with it to ʿAttab and said: 'If they agree, well; otherwise, announce war against them.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "then announce war," he said: "Whoever persists in interest and does not give it up, it is incumbent upon the leader of the Muslims to ask him to repent. If he gives it up, well; otherwise, he strikes his neck."

They also narrated from him regarding His saying: "then announce war" that he said: "Be certain of war."

The compilers of the Sunan and others narrated from ʿAmr ibn al-Ahwas that he witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Behold, every interest of the Jahiliyyah is void. For you is your principal: you do not wrong, nor are you wronged. The first interest to be made void is the interest of al-ʿAbbas."

Ibn Mandah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: This verse was revealed concerning Rabiʿah ibn ʿAmr and his companions: ﴿But if you repent, then you shall have your principal﴾.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And if there is one in hardship﴾ that he said: It was revealed concerning interest.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Shurayh something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "Likewise, every debt owed by a Muslim."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar.

Authentic hadiths have come in the two Sahihs and other collections encouraging the one who is owed a debt by a debtor in hardship to grant him time.

Abu ʿUbayd, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The last verse of the Qur'an to be revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) was: ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to Allah﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated something similar from al-Suddi and ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated something similar also from Abu Salih and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that it was the last verse revealed, and that between its revelation and the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) there were eighty-one days.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the Prophet (ﷺ) lived after its revelation for nine nights, and then he died.

This is the opening of the discussion of the debt transaction (al-mudayana) between people, following the discussion of usury (riba). That is: if some of you contract a debt with one another and deal with each other on that basis. He mentioned "debt" (al-dayn) after mentioning what the act of contracting a debt already implies, for the sake of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ (6:38). It was also said that it was mentioned so that the pronoun in His saying "then write it" would have something to refer back to. Had He said "then write the debt," it would not have had the same beauty as His saying ﴿when you contract a debt (idha tadayantum bi-dayn)﴾.

Al-dayn (debt) is a term for any transaction in which one of the two exchanged items is cash and the other is deferred as a liability (fi al-dhimma, nasi'a). For the Arabs, "ayn" (cash) was what was present, and "dayn" was what was absent. The poet said:

"She promised us, for two dirhams, wine and roast meat, prompt and not on credit (ghayra dayn)."

And another said:

"When they kindle a fire and firewood, that is death in cash, not on credit."

Allah, glorified is He, clarified this meaning with His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾. It has been cited as evidence that an unknown term is not permissible, especially the term in a salam (advance-payment sale) contract.

It is established in the Sahih, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever pays in advance for dates, let him pay in advance for a known measure, for a known term." The majority of scholars held this view and stipulated that the term be fixed in days, months or years. They said it is not permissible to fix it to the harvest, the threshing, or the return of a caravan, or the like.

Malik permitted it.

His saying "then write it" means the debt with its term, because that is more effective in preventing dispute and more decisive in ending disagreement.

His saying ﴿and let a scribe write between you﴾ explains how the writing commanded is to be done. The apparent meaning of the command is obligation, and this is the view of 'Ata', al-Sha'bi and others, who made it obligatory on the scribe to write when asked, if no other scribe is available. It was also said that the command is recommendation (nadb).

His saying ﴿with justice (bil-'adl)﴾ is connected to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "scribe": that is, a scribe who is with justice, i.e., who writes evenhandedly, neither adding nor subtracting, and not leaning toward either side. It is also a command to the two contracting parties to choose a scribe characterized by this quality, in whose heart and pen there is no partiality (hawada) for one of them over the other, but who seeks out the truth between them and fairness toward them.

His saying ﴿and let no scribe refuse﴾: the indefinite noun in a negative context implies generality. That is, no scribe should refuse to write the debt document ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾, that is, in the manner Allah taught him to write, or as Allah taught him by His saying "with justice."

His saying ﴿and let the one who owes the debt dictate (wal-yumlil alladhi 'alayhi al-haqq)﴾: "imlal" and "imla'" are two dialects: the first is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad, and the second is the dialect of Banu Tamim. This verse came in the first dialect, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ (25:5) came in the second. "The one upon whom the truth lies" is the debtor. Allah commanded him to dictate, because testimony is given on his acknowledgment of the debt's existence in his liability. Allah commanded him to fear Allah in what he dictates to the scribe, and He emphasized this by combining the name and the attribute in His saying ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, and forbade him from defrauding (bakhs), which is diminishing. It was also said that this is a prohibition addressed to the scribe.

The first view is preferable, because the one upon whom the truth lies is the one from whom diminishing is expected. Had it been a prohibition to the scribe, it would not have been restricted to diminishing, since increasing is also expected from him, just as diminishing is.

The safih (the foolish or wasteful person) is one who has no judgment in good management, so he does not know how to take or give well. He is likened to a thin, loosely woven garment (thawb safih), which is one that is light in its weave. The Arabs use "safah" sometimes for weakness of intellect and sometimes for weakness of body. Of the first kind is the poet's saying:

"We fear that our wisdom becomes foolish, and that we become ignorant of the age alongside the ignorant."

Of the second kind is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"They walked as spears sway, their tips made weak (tasaffahat) by the motion of the gentle, wafting winds."

That is, the wind made them weak and gentle through its movement. In sum, the safih is the squanderer, either out of ignorance of disposal or because he plays with money uselessly, while not being ignorant of what is right.

The da'if (weak) is either the old, decrepit man or the child.

The people of language said: "al-dhu'f" with a dammah on the dad refers to bodily weakness, and with a fatha refers to weakness of judgment.

The one who cannot dictate is the mute or the one with a speech impediment who cannot express himself as he should. It was also said that the weak one is the one whose mind is confused, lacking intelligence, unable to dictate, and the one who cannot dictate is the child.

His saying ﴿then let his guardian dictate with justice﴾: the pronoun refers to "the one upon whom the truth lies." So for the foolish person, his guardian (waliyyuhu), appointed for him after he is restricted (hajr) from disposing of his property, dictates on his behalf. For the child, his guardian (wasiyyuhu) or his protector dictates. Likewise, for one who cannot dictate because his guardian is weak, the dictation is made on his behalf, since he is in the position of a child, or of one appointed on his behalf by the imam or judge. And for one who cannot dictate, his agent dictates if he is sound of mind and has an affliction in his tongue or not, but he is ignorant and cannot express himself as he should.

Al-Tabari said that the pronoun in "waliyyuhu" refers to "al-haqq" (the truth), but this is very weak.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: The disposition of a restricted foolish person without his guardian is void by consensus, it is annulled forever, does not produce a ruling and has no effect. If a foolish person disposes of his property while no restriction is placed on him, there is disagreement.

His saying ﴿and call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾: al-istishhad is seeking testimony. He called them "two witnesses" before they testified, which is a metaphor of the first kind, i.e., by consideration of what their matter will become, namely testimony. "From among your men" is connected to "call upon," or to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "two witnesses": that is, being from among your men, i.e., from among the Muslims, which excludes the disbelievers. There is no basis for excluding slaves from this verse, since if they are Muslims, they are among the men of the Muslims. This is the view of Shurayh, 'Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Abu Thawr.

Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars said: the testimony of a slave is not permissible, because of the deficiency that slavery entails.

Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: it is valid in minor matters but not in major ones.

The majority argued against the permissibility of a slave's testimony by saying that the address in this verse is to those who deal in debts, and slaves do not own anything in which transactions can take place.

This is answered by saying that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. Also, a slave can validly engage in debts and all other transactions if his owner permits him to do so.

People differed on whether calling witnesses is obligatory or recommended. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Umar, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Jabir ibn Zayd, Mujahid, and Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Zahiri and his son said it is obligatory, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this view. Al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions held that it is recommended. This disagreement among them concerns whether calling witnesses to a sale is obligatory.

Those who hold it obligatory argued with His saying: ﴿and call witnesses when you trade﴾ (2:282 in another reading). There is no difference between this command and His saying "and call upon witnesses," so those who hold that calling witnesses in sale is obligatory must hold that it is obligatory in debts too.

His saying ﴿but if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾: i.e., the witnesses. That is, let a man and two women testify, or "a man and two women" will suffice.

His saying ﴿of those you accept as witnesses﴾ is connected to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "a man and two women": that is, being among those you accept, while being among the witnesses.

What is meant by "those you accept" is their religion and uprightness (adala). It implies that two women are equivalent to a man in testimony, and that women's testimony is not permissible except together with a man, not alone, except in matters that no one other than women would witness, out of necessity.

Scholars differed on whether a ruling may be made on the testimony of two women together with the oath of the claimant, just as a ruling may be made on a man together with the oath of the claimant. Malik and al-Shafi'i held that this is permissible, because Allah, glorified is He, made two women like a man in this verse.

Abu Hanifa and his companions held that this is not permissible. This goes back to the disagreement over ruling on a single witness together with the oath of the claimant. The truth is that it is permissible, because evidence has come for it, and it is an addition that does not contradict what is in the Noble Book, so its acceptance is required.

We have clarified this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa and our other works. It is well known to everyone who understands that there is nothing in this verse by which the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgment with a witness and oath could be rejected. They could only dismiss it by a principle built on the edge of a crumbling precipice, namely their saying: adding to the text is naskh (abrogation). This is a false claim. Rather, adding to the text is an established legal ruling that was brought to us by the one who brought the earlier text. Furthermore, they would have been obliged not to rule by the refusal of the defendant (nukul al-matlub) nor by the oath of return (yamin al-radd) on the plaintiff. Yet they ruled by both. The answer is what it is.

His saying ﴿that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾: Abu 'Ubayd said that the meaning of "tadilla" is "forget." Erring about testimony is only forgetting part of it and remembering part of it.

Hamza read ﴿in tadilla﴾ with a kasra on the hamza.

His saying ﴿fa-tudhakkira (then she reminds)﴾ is its answer (jawab) in this reading. In the reading of the majority, it is in the subjunctive by coordination with "tadilla." Whoever reads it in the indicative does so as a new clause.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿fa-tudhkira﴾ with the dhal and kaf lightened, meaning: she makes her remember more.

The reading of the group is with the shadda (intensive), meaning: as a reminder when she is heedless and forgets.

This verse gives the reason for taking the number of women into account: that is, let a man testify, and two women testify in place of the other man, so that one of them can remind the other if she errs. In this case, there is an omission in the speech, namely a questioner asking why two women are taken in place of one man. It was said: the reason is that if one of them errs, the other reminds her. The real cause is the reminding, but since erring was the cause of it, it took its place. The agent in "tadilla" and "tudhakkira" is left unspecified, because each of them can have either attribute. So the meaning is: if this one errs, that one reminds her; and if that one errs, this one reminds her, not specifically. That is: if one of the two women errs, the other woman reminds her. This reminding was considered because of the weakness that befalls women, unlike men.

The purpose of leaving it unspecified may be that this erring and reminding happen between them in turn, so that perhaps one of them errs about one point and the other about another, and each reminds the other.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-tudhakkira iḥdahuma al-ukhra﴾ is "makes her a male," meaning that the combined testimony of the two women is like the testimony of one man.

Something similar is narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. There is no doubt that this is false, and no legal text, language, or reason supports it.

His saying ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾: that is, to give the testimony they have already undertaken before. It was also said: when they are called to undertake the testimony. Calling them witnesses is metaphorical, as already mentioned. Al-Hasan took it to mean both.

The apparent meaning of this prohibition is that refusing to give testimony is forbidden.

His saying ﴿and do not be weary of writing it﴾: "tas'amu" means "become bored."

Al-Akhfash said: one says "sa'imtu as'amu sa'amatan wa si'aman." Of this is the poet's saying:

"I have grown weary of the burdens of life, and whoever lives eighty years, without a father to you, will grow weary."

That is: do not grow weary of writing it down, that is, the debt that you have contracted with one another. It was also said that it refers to the right (of the creditor), or to the witness, or to the document. Allah, glory be to Him, forbade them from this because they might grow weary of writing, owing to the frequency of their dealings in debt. Then He emphasized this, saying: ﴿small or large﴾, that is, whether that which is written is small or large. In other words, do not grow weary in any circumstance, whether the debt is great or little. It was also said that He used "weariness" as a metaphor for "laziness."

The first view is preferable.

He placed "small" before "large" here for the sake of emphasis, to repel what might be said: that this is a small amount, that is, a little, so there is no need to write it down. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to the document mentioned in the pronoun of His saying: "that you write it." ﴿More just﴾ (aqsat) means "more equitable," that is, more correct and more secure. ﴿And more upright for testimony﴾ means more helpful in establishing testimony and more firm for it. It is derived from aqama, and likewise aqsat is derived from its verb, namely aqsata.

Sibawayh has explicitly stated that this is analogical, that is, that the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is formed in this way.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿so that you will not doubt﴾ is that it is closer to removing doubt (rayb) in your transactions, that is, suspicion. This is because the writing that they produce repels whatever doubt may arise for them, whatever it may be.

His saying: ﴿except that it be a present trade that you conduct among yourselves﴾. "An" (that) is in the place of the accusative by way of exception, as al-Akhfash said. And "kana" (be) is complete (taammah), meaning: except that a trade should occur or come into existence. The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: but at the time of your exchange, and your trade is present by the presence of both exchanged items. ﴿That you conduct among yourselves﴾ means that you hand them over to one another hand to hand; so idarah (conducting) means handling and exchanging, and what is meant is the immediate sale, hand to hand. Therefore there is no blame upon you if you do not write it down.

It was also read with the accusative in ﴿trade﴾ (tijaratan), on the basis that "kana" is defective (naqisah), meaning: except that the trade should be a present trade.

His saying: ﴿And take witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾. It was said that its meaning is: take witnesses when you conclude this sale mentioned here, which is the present trade, on the basis that calling witnesses in it is sufficient. It was also said that its meaning is: whenever you conclude any sale, whether present or deferred, because that is more effective in removing the source of dispute and more decisive in cutting off the cause of quarrel.

The disagreement concerning whether this calling of witnesses is obligatory or recommended has already been mentioned shortly before.

His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾. It may be either active or passive. On the first reading its meaning is: no scribe or witness should be harmed by being sought for this by them, either by non-compliance, or by altering, substituting, adding to, or omitting from his writing. This is supported by the reading of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq: "wa la yudarrir" with a kasra on the first ra. On the second reading: no scribe or witness should be made to suffer harm by being summoned to that while occupied with an important matter of his own, and be constricted in responding, and be harmed if any delay occurs from them, or be required to attend from a distant place. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la yudarrar" with a fatha on the first ra. The form of mufa'alah indicates that both matters are taken into account together.

This has already been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No mother should be harmed through her child﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. If you consult it, it will increase your insight, God willing.

His saying: ﴿And if you do, indeed it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾. That is, if you do what you were forbidden from, namely harm, then that action of yours is fusuq, meaning departure from obedience into disobedience, attached to you. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in doing what He has commanded you and in abandoning what He has forbidden you. ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ what you need of knowledge. In this is the promise to whoever fears Him that He will teach him. Among the similar statements is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 29].

His saying: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the legislation of writing and calling witnesses for the preservation of wealth and the removal of doubt, He followed this with mention of the situation of excuse regarding the absence of a scribe, and He specified the situation of travel, for it is among the states of excuse. Every excuse that stands in place of travel is included in this. He made the pledges taken in hand (al-rihan al-maqbudah) stand in place of writing. That is: if you are travelling ﴿and do not find a scribe﴾ on your journey, then ﴿a pledge taken in hand﴾. The people of knowledge said: pledging (al-rahn) during travel is established by the explicit text of the revelation, and in residence it is established by the act of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as it is established in the two Sahihs that "he ﷺ pawned his coat of mail to a Jew."

al-Jumhur (the majority) read "katiban," that is, a man who writes for you.

Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah read "kitaban." Ibn al-Anbari said: Mujahid explained it, saying: its meaning is: if you do not find ink (midad), meaning during journeys.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "fa-rుhun" with a damma on the ra and the ha.

It is also narrated from them that the ha is lightened, as the plural of rihan. This was said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud read "fa-rahn" with a fatha on the ra and a sukun on the ha.

The reading of the majority is "rihan." al-Zajjaj said: it is said for the pledge, "rahantu" or "arhantu," and likewise said Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Akhfash.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is said "arhantu" in transactions, but in loans and sales it is "rahantu." Tha'lab said: all the transmitters, in the verse of the poet:

"When I feared their claws,
I escaped and pawned Malik to them."

read "arhantuhum" (I pawned them), on the basis that it is permissible to say "rahantuhu" and "arhantuhu." Except al-Asma'i, who narrated it as "wa arhanuhum" (and I pawn them), as a conjunction of a future verb to a past verb, comparing it with his saying: "qumtu wa asukku wajhahu" (I stood and I strike his face).

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "arhantu" in both cases means "aslaftu" (I lent). The one who takes the pledge is al-murtahin; the thing pledged is marhun and rahin. And "rahantu fulanan 'ala kadha muraharatan" means I wagered with him.

The majority have taken the taking of possession (al-qabd) into account, as the Qur'an explicitly states. Malik held that pawning is valid by offer and acceptance without taking possession.

His saying: ﴿And if one of you entrusts another, then let the one who has been entrusted fulfill his trust﴾. That is: if the one who owes the right is trustworthy in the sight of the rightful owner, because of the rightful owner's good opinion of him and the trustworthiness he has in his eyes, and he is thereby exempted from pawning, ﴿then let him who has been entrusted﴾, who is the debtor, ﴿fulfill his trust﴾, that is, the debt that is upon him. The word amanah (trust) is a verbal noun used for that which is in the liability, and He attributed it to the one upon whom the debt lies because it has a relation to him. It was read "ayta-mana" with the hamza changed to ya'. It was also read with the ya' assimilated into the ta', but that is an error, because what has been changed from a hamza is not assimilated, since it has the same ruling. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ in not concealing anything of the right.

His saying: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾. This is a prohibition to witnesses against concealing what they have undertaken of testimony. It has the force of an explanation of His saying: ﴿And no scribe should be harmed﴾, that is, "la yudarrir" with a kasra on the first ra, according to one of the two explanations mentioned earlier.

His saying: ﴿And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾. He singled out the heart for mention because concealment is one of its acts, and because it is the head of the organs; it is the lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. The heart is in the nominative, either as the subject, or as the topic with "sinful" as its predicate, as is established in the science of grammar. It is permissible that "his heart" be a substitute for "sinful," a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). It is also permissible that it be a substitute for the pronoun in "sinful" which refers back to "whoever." It was also read "qalbahu" in the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130].

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning salam (advance sale) for a known measure up to a known term.

al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari and others narrated from him, saying: I testify that the advance payment for a guaranteed item up to a specified term, Allah has made it a term, and he recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: He commanded testimony at the time of contracting debt, so that neither denial nor forgetting may enter into it. Whoever does not call witnesses for that has disobeyed. ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, meaning: whoever among the Muslims is needed to bear witness, or has testimony in his possession, then it is not lawful for him to refuse when he is called. Then he said after this: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾. Harm (dirar) is that a man says to a man, while he is independent of him: "Indeed Allah has commanded you not to refuse when you are called," thereby harming him, while the other has sufficiency elsewhere. So Allah forbade that.

He said: ﴿And if you do, then indeed it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾, meaning disobedience.

He said: Among the grave sins is concealing testimony, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning His saying: ﴿And let no scribe refuse﴾, that he said: It is obligatory upon the scribe to write.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: Writing was a binding obligation, then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: ﴿If the one upon whom the right lies is feeble-minded﴾: he is the ignorant, or weak, he said: he is the foolish.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak and al-Suddi concerning His saying "feeble-minded," they both said: he is the young child.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of 'Ata' al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas: ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾, he said: the creditor.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: the guardian of the orphan.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: the guardian of the feeble-minded or the weak.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿from among your men﴾, he said: from among the free.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: ﴿of those whom you accept as witnesses﴾, he said: upright ('udul).

al-Shafi'i and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid, who said: two just, free, Muslim men.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾, he says: that one of the two women forgets the testimony, ﴿so one of them may remind the other﴾, meaning, she reminds her whose testimony was nullified.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, he said: when they possess testimony.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi', who said: A man would go around among a large group inviting them to bear witness, and none of them would follow him, so Allah revealed: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'A'ishah concerning His saying: ﴿more just in the sight of Allah﴾, she said: more equitable.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾, he said: A man comes to two men and invites them to write or to testify, and they say: "We have a need." He says: "Indeed you have been commanded to respond," so he has no right to harm them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Tawus: ﴿And no scribe should be harmed﴾, so that he writes what has not been dictated to him, and no witness should be harmed so that he testifies to what he was not asked to testify to.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾, the verse, he said: Whoever is on a journey and sells on credit to a term, and does not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand is permitted for him. If he finds a scribe, he is not permitted to take a pledge.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: Pledging is only during travel.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Pledging is only by taking possession.

al-Bukhari in his History, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Majah, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he recited this verse: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾ until he reached ﴿And if one of you entrusts another﴾, and said: This abrogated what came before it.

I say: may Allah be pleased with this noble Companion. This is not a case of abrogation (naskh), for this (ruling) is restricted to the case of trust (amanah), while what precedes it is established and definitive (muhkam), not abrogated, and it applies where there is no trust.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿آثِمٌ قَلْبُهُ﴾ ("its heart is sinful"), that he said: "its heart is wicked."

Ibn Jarir also reported with a sound chain of narration (isnad) from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that it reached him that the most recent of the Qur'an to come down from the Throne is the verse of debt.

Abu 'Ubayd reported in his Fada'il from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The last of the Qur'an to be given (to the Prophet) from the Throne is the verse of usury (riba) and the verse of debt."

This is the opening of the discussion of the debt transaction (al-mudayana) between people, following the discussion of usury (riba). That is: if some of you contract a debt with one another and deal with each other on that basis. He mentioned "debt" (al-dayn) after mentioning what the act of contracting a debt already implies, for the sake of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ (6:38). It was also said that it was mentioned so that the pronoun in His saying "then write it" would have something to refer back to. Had He said "then write the debt," it would not have had the same beauty as His saying ﴿when you contract a debt (idha tadayantum bi-dayn)﴾.

Al-dayn (debt) is a term for any transaction in which one of the two exchanged items is cash and the other is deferred as a liability (fi al-dhimma, nasi'a). For the Arabs, "ayn" (cash) was what was present, and "dayn" was what was absent. The poet said:

"She promised us, for two dirhams, wine and roast meat, prompt and not on credit (ghayra dayn)."

And another said:

"When they kindle a fire and firewood, that is death in cash, not on credit."

Allah, glorified is He, clarified this meaning with His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾. It has been cited as evidence that an unknown term is not permissible, especially the term in a salam (advance-payment sale) contract.

It is established in the Sahih, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever pays in advance for dates, let him pay in advance for a known measure, for a known term." The majority of scholars held this view and stipulated that the term be fixed in days, months or years. They said it is not permissible to fix it to the harvest, the threshing, or the return of a caravan, or the like.

Malik permitted it.

His saying "then write it" means the debt with its term, because that is more effective in preventing dispute and more decisive in ending disagreement.

His saying ﴿and let a scribe write between you﴾ explains how the writing commanded is to be done. The apparent meaning of the command is obligation, and this is the view of 'Ata', al-Sha'bi and others, who made it obligatory on the scribe to write when asked, if no other scribe is available. It was also said that the command is recommendation (nadb).

His saying ﴿with justice (bil-'adl)﴾ is connected to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "scribe": that is, a scribe who is with justice, i.e., who writes evenhandedly, neither adding nor subtracting, and not leaning toward either side. It is also a command to the two contracting parties to choose a scribe characterized by this quality, in whose heart and pen there is no partiality (hawada) for one of them over the other, but who seeks out the truth between them and fairness toward them.

His saying ﴿and let no scribe refuse﴾: the indefinite noun in a negative context implies generality. That is, no scribe should refuse to write the debt document ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾, that is, in the manner Allah taught him to write, or as Allah taught him by His saying "with justice."

His saying ﴿and let the one who owes the debt dictate (wal-yumlil alladhi 'alayhi al-haqq)﴾: "imlal" and "imla'" are two dialects: the first is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad, and the second is the dialect of Banu Tamim. This verse came in the first dialect, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ (25:5) came in the second. "The one upon whom the truth lies" is the debtor. Allah commanded him to dictate, because testimony is given on his acknowledgment of the debt's existence in his liability. Allah commanded him to fear Allah in what he dictates to the scribe, and He emphasized this by combining the name and the attribute in His saying ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, and forbade him from defrauding (bakhs), which is diminishing. It was also said that this is a prohibition addressed to the scribe.

The first view is preferable, because the one upon whom the truth lies is the one from whom diminishing is expected. Had it been a prohibition to the scribe, it would not have been restricted to diminishing, since increasing is also expected from him, just as diminishing is.

The safih (the foolish or wasteful person) is one who has no judgment in good management, so he does not know how to take or give well. He is likened to a thin, loosely woven garment (thawb safih), which is one that is light in its weave. The Arabs use "safah" sometimes for weakness of intellect and sometimes for weakness of body. Of the first kind is the poet's saying:

"We fear that our wisdom becomes foolish, and that we become ignorant of the age alongside the ignorant."

Of the second kind is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"They walked as spears sway, their tips made weak (tasaffahat) by the motion of the gentle, wafting winds."

That is, the wind made them weak and gentle through its movement. In sum, the safih is the squanderer, either out of ignorance of disposal or because he plays with money uselessly, while not being ignorant of what is right.

The da'if (weak) is either the old, decrepit man or the child.

The people of language said: "al-dhu'f" with a dammah on the dad refers to bodily weakness, and with a fatha refers to weakness of judgment.

The one who cannot dictate is the mute or the one with a speech impediment who cannot express himself as he should. It was also said that the weak one is the one whose mind is confused, lacking intelligence, unable to dictate, and the one who cannot dictate is the child.

His saying ﴿then let his guardian dictate with justice﴾: the pronoun refers to "the one upon whom the truth lies." So for the foolish person, his guardian (waliyyuhu), appointed for him after he is restricted (hajr) from disposing of his property, dictates on his behalf. For the child, his guardian (wasiyyuhu) or his protector dictates. Likewise, for one who cannot dictate because his guardian is weak, the dictation is made on his behalf, since he is in the position of a child, or of one appointed on his behalf by the imam or judge. And for one who cannot dictate, his agent dictates if he is sound of mind and has an affliction in his tongue or not, but he is ignorant and cannot express himself as he should.

Al-Tabari said that the pronoun in "waliyyuhu" refers to "al-haqq" (the truth), but this is very weak.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: The disposition of a restricted foolish person without his guardian is void by consensus, it is annulled forever, does not produce a ruling and has no effect. If a foolish person disposes of his property while no restriction is placed on him, there is disagreement.

His saying ﴿and call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾: al-istishhad is seeking testimony. He called them "two witnesses" before they testified, which is a metaphor of the first kind, i.e., by consideration of what their matter will become, namely testimony. "From among your men" is connected to "call upon," or to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "two witnesses": that is, being from among your men, i.e., from among the Muslims, which excludes the disbelievers. There is no basis for excluding slaves from this verse, since if they are Muslims, they are among the men of the Muslims. This is the view of Shurayh, 'Uthman al-Batti, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Abu Thawr.

Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of scholars said: the testimony of a slave is not permissible, because of the deficiency that slavery entails.

Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: it is valid in minor matters but not in major ones.

The majority argued against the permissibility of a slave's testimony by saying that the address in this verse is to those who deal in debts, and slaves do not own anything in which transactions can take place.

This is answered by saying that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. Also, a slave can validly engage in debts and all other transactions if his owner permits him to do so.

People differed on whether calling witnesses is obligatory or recommended. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Umar, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Jabir ibn Zayd, Mujahid, and Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Zahiri and his son said it is obligatory, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred this view. Al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions held that it is recommended. This disagreement among them concerns whether calling witnesses to a sale is obligatory.

Those who hold it obligatory argued with His saying: ﴿and call witnesses when you trade﴾ (2:282 in another reading).
