There is no difference between this command and His saying "and call upon witnesses," so those who hold that calling witnesses in sale is obligatory must hold that it is obligatory in debts too.

His saying ﴿but if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾: i.e., the witnesses. That is, let a man and two women testify, or "a man and two women" will suffice.

His saying ﴿of those you accept as witnesses﴾ is connected to a deleted element functioning as a qualifier of "a man and two women": that is, being among those you accept, while being among the witnesses.

What is meant by "those you accept" is their religion and uprightness (adala). It implies that two women are equivalent to a man in testimony, and that women's testimony is not permissible except together with a man, not alone, except in matters that no one other than women would witness, out of necessity.

Scholars differed on whether a ruling may be made on the testimony of two women together with the oath of the claimant, just as a ruling may be made on a man together with the oath of the claimant. Malik and al-Shafi'i held that this is permissible, because Allah, glorified is He, made two women like a man in this verse.

Abu Hanifa and his companions held that this is not permissible. This goes back to the disagreement over ruling on a single witness together with the oath of the claimant. The truth is that it is permissible, because evidence has come for it, and it is an addition that does not contradict what is in the Noble Book, so its acceptance is required.

We have clarified this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa and our other works. It is well known to everyone who understands that there is nothing in this verse by which the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgment with a witness and oath could be rejected. They could only dismiss it by a principle built on the edge of a crumbling precipice, namely their saying: adding to the text is naskh (abrogation). This is a false claim. Rather, adding to the text is an established legal ruling that was brought to us by the one who brought the earlier text. Furthermore, they would have been obliged not to rule by the refusal of the defendant (nukul al-matlub) nor by the oath of return (yamin al-radd) on the plaintiff. Yet they ruled by both. The answer is what it is.

His saying ﴿that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾: Abu 'Ubayd said that the meaning of "tadilla" is "forget." Erring about testimony is only forgetting part of it and remembering part of it.

Hamza read ﴿in tadilla﴾ with a kasra on the hamza.

His saying ﴿fa-tudhakkira (then she reminds)﴾ is its answer (jawab) in this reading. In the reading of the majority, it is in the subjunctive by coordination with "tadilla." Whoever reads it in the indicative does so as a new clause.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿fa-tudhkira﴾ with the dhal and kaf lightened, meaning: she makes her remember more.

The reading of the group is with the shadda (intensive), meaning: as a reminder when she is heedless and forgets.

This verse gives the reason for taking the number of women into account: that is, let a man testify, and two women testify in place of the other man, so that one of them can remind the other if she errs. In this case, there is an omission in the speech, namely a questioner asking why two women are taken in place of one man. It was said: the reason is that if one of them errs, the other reminds her. The real cause is the reminding, but since erring was the cause of it, it took its place. The agent in "tadilla" and "tudhakkira" is left unspecified, because each of them can have either attribute. So the meaning is: if this one errs, that one reminds her; and if that one errs, this one reminds her, not specifically. That is: if one of the two women errs, the other woman reminds her. This reminding was considered because of the weakness that befalls women, unlike men.

The purpose of leaving it unspecified may be that this erring and reminding happen between them in turn, so that perhaps one of them errs about one point and the other about another, and each reminds the other.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-tudhakkira iḥdahuma al-ukhra﴾ is "makes her a male," meaning that the combined testimony of the two women is like the testimony of one man.

Something similar is narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. There is no doubt that this is false, and no legal text, language, or reason supports it.

His saying ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾: that is, to give the testimony they have already undertaken before. It was also said: when they are called to undertake the testimony. Calling them witnesses is metaphorical, as already mentioned. Al-Hasan took it to mean both.

The apparent meaning of this prohibition is that refusing to give testimony is forbidden.

His saying ﴿and do not be weary of writing it﴾: "tas'amu" means "become bored."

Al-Akhfash said: one says "sa'imtu as'amu sa'amatan wa si'aman." Of this is the poet's saying:

"I have grown weary of the burdens of life, and whoever lives eighty years, without a father to you, will grow weary."

That is: do not grow weary of writing it down, that is, the debt that you have contracted with one another. It was also said that it refers to the right (of the creditor), or to the witness, or to the document. Allah, glory be to Him, forbade them from this because they might grow weary of writing, owing to the frequency of their dealings in debt. Then He emphasized this, saying: ﴿small or large﴾, that is, whether that which is written is small or large. In other words, do not grow weary in any circumstance, whether the debt is great or little. It was also said that He used "weariness" as a metaphor for "laziness."

The first view is preferable.

He placed "small" before "large" here for the sake of emphasis, to repel what might be said: that this is a small amount, that is, a little, so there is no need to write it down. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to the document mentioned in the pronoun of His saying: "that you write it." ﴿More just﴾ (aqsat) means "more equitable," that is, more correct and more secure. ﴿And more upright for testimony﴾ means more helpful in establishing testimony and more firm for it. It is derived from aqama, and likewise aqsat is derived from its verb, namely aqsata.

Sibawayh has explicitly stated that this is analogical, that is, that the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is formed in this way.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿so that you will not doubt﴾ is that it is closer to removing doubt (rayb) in your transactions, that is, suspicion. This is because the writing that they produce repels whatever doubt may arise for them, whatever it may be.

His saying: ﴿except that it be a present trade that you conduct among yourselves﴾. "An" (that) is in the place of the accusative by way of exception, as al-Akhfash said. And "kana" (be) is complete (taammah), meaning: except that a trade should occur or come into existence. The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: but at the time of your exchange, and your trade is present by the presence of both exchanged items. ﴿That you conduct among yourselves﴾ means that you hand them over to one another hand to hand; so idarah (conducting) means handling and exchanging, and what is meant is the immediate sale, hand to hand. Therefore there is no blame upon you if you do not write it down.

It was also read with the accusative in ﴿trade﴾ (tijaratan), on the basis that "kana" is defective (naqisah), meaning: except that the trade should be a present trade.

His saying: ﴿And take witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾. It was said that its meaning is: take witnesses when you conclude this sale mentioned here, which is the present trade, on the basis that calling witnesses in it is sufficient. It was also said that its meaning is: whenever you conclude any sale, whether present or deferred, because that is more effective in removing the source of dispute and more decisive in cutting off the cause of quarrel.

The disagreement concerning whether this calling of witnesses is obligatory or recommended has already been mentioned shortly before.

His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾. It may be either active or passive. On the first reading its meaning is: no scribe or witness should be harmed by being sought for this by them, either by non-compliance, or by altering, substituting, adding to, or omitting from his writing. This is supported by the reading of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq: "wa la yudarrir" with a kasra on the first ra. On the second reading: no scribe or witness should be made to suffer harm by being summoned to that while occupied with an important matter of his own, and be constricted in responding, and be harmed if any delay occurs from them, or be required to attend from a distant place. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la yudarrar" with a fatha on the first ra. The form of mufa'alah indicates that both matters are taken into account together.

This has already been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No mother should be harmed through her child﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. If you consult it, it will increase your insight, God willing.

His saying: ﴿And if you do, indeed it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾. That is, if you do what you were forbidden from, namely harm, then that action of yours is fusuq, meaning departure from obedience into disobedience, attached to you. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in doing what He has commanded you and in abandoning what He has forbidden you. ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ what you need of knowledge. In this is the promise to whoever fears Him that He will teach him. Among the similar statements is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 29].

His saying: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the legislation of writing and calling witnesses for the preservation of wealth and the removal of doubt, He followed this with mention of the situation of excuse regarding the absence of a scribe, and He specified the situation of travel, for it is among the states of excuse. Every excuse that stands in place of travel is included in this. He made the pledges taken in hand (al-rihan al-maqbudah) stand in place of writing. That is: if you are travelling ﴿and do not find a scribe﴾ on your journey, then ﴿a pledge taken in hand﴾. The people of knowledge said: pledging (al-rahn) during travel is established by the explicit text of the revelation, and in residence it is established by the act of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as it is established in the two Sahihs that "he ﷺ pawned his coat of mail to a Jew."

al-Jumhur (the majority) read "katiban," that is, a man who writes for you.

Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah read "kitaban." Ibn al-Anbari said: Mujahid explained it, saying: its meaning is: if you do not find ink (midad), meaning during journeys.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "fa-rుhun" with a damma on the ra and the ha.

It is also narrated from them that the ha is lightened, as the plural of rihan. This was said by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud read "fa-rahn" with a fatha on the ra and a sukun on the ha.

The reading of the majority is "rihan." al-Zajjaj said: it is said for the pledge, "rahantu" or "arhantu," and likewise said Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Akhfash.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is said "arhantu" in transactions, but in loans and sales it is "rahantu." Tha'lab said: all the transmitters, in the verse of the poet:

"When I feared their claws,
I escaped and pawned Malik to them."

read "arhantuhum" (I pawned them), on the basis that it is permissible to say "rahantuhu" and "arhantuhu." Except al-Asma'i, who narrated it as "wa arhanuhum" (and I pawn them), as a conjunction of a future verb to a past verb, comparing it with his saying: "qumtu wa asukku wajhahu" (I stood and I strike his face).

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "arhantu" in both cases means "aslaftu" (I lent). The one who takes the pledge is al-murtahin; the thing pledged is marhun and rahin. And "rahantu fulanan 'ala kadha muraharatan" means I wagered with him.

The majority have taken the taking of possession (al-qabd) into account, as the Qur'an explicitly states. Malik held that pawning is valid by offer and acceptance without taking possession.

His saying: ﴿And if one of you entrusts another, then let the one who has been entrusted fulfill his trust﴾. That is: if the one who owes the right is trustworthy in the sight of the rightful owner, because of the rightful owner's good opinion of him and the trustworthiness he has in his eyes, and he is thereby exempted from pawning, ﴿then let him who has been entrusted﴾, who is the debtor, ﴿fulfill his trust﴾, that is, the debt that is upon him. The word amanah (trust) is a verbal noun used for that which is in the liability, and He attributed it to the one upon whom the debt lies because it has a relation to him. It was read "ayta-mana" with the hamza changed to ya'. It was also read with the ya' assimilated into the ta', but that is an error, because what has been changed from a hamza is not assimilated, since it has the same ruling. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ in not concealing anything of the right.

His saying: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾. This is a prohibition to witnesses against concealing what they have undertaken of testimony. It has the force of an explanation of His saying: ﴿And no scribe should be harmed﴾, that is, "la yudarrir" with a kasra on the first ra, according to one of the two explanations mentioned earlier.

His saying: ﴿And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾. He singled out the heart for mention because concealment is one of its acts, and because it is the head of the organs; it is the lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. The heart is in the nominative, either as the subject, or as the topic with "sinful" as its predicate, as is established in the science of grammar. It is permissible that "his heart" be a substitute for "sinful," a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). It is also permissible that it be a substitute for the pronoun in "sinful" which refers back to "whoever." It was also read "qalbahu" in the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130].

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning salam (advance sale) for a known measure up to a known term.

al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari and others narrated from him, saying: I testify that the advance payment for a guaranteed item up to a specified term, Allah has made it a term, and he recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: He commanded testimony at the time of contracting debt, so that neither denial nor forgetting may enter into it. Whoever does not call witnesses for that has disobeyed. ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, meaning: whoever among the Muslims is needed to bear witness, or has testimony in his possession, then it is not lawful for him to refuse when he is called. Then he said after this: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾. Harm (dirar) is that a man says to a man, while he is independent of him: "Indeed Allah has commanded you not to refuse when you are called," thereby harming him, while the other has sufficiency elsewhere. So Allah forbade that.

He said: ﴿And if you do, then indeed it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾, meaning disobedience.

He said: Among the grave sins is concealing testimony, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning His saying: ﴿And let no scribe refuse﴾, that he said: It is obligatory upon the scribe to write.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: Writing was a binding obligation, then it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: ﴿If the one upon whom the right lies is feeble-minded﴾: he is the ignorant, or weak, he said: he is the foolish.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak and al-Suddi concerning His saying "feeble-minded," they both said: he is the young child.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of 'Ata' al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas: ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾, he said: the creditor.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: the guardian of the orphan.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: the guardian of the feeble-minded or the weak.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿from among your men﴾, he said: from among the free.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: ﴿of those whom you accept as witnesses﴾, he said: upright ('udul).

al-Shafi'i and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mujahid, who said: two just, free, Muslim men.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾, he says: that one of the two women forgets the testimony, ﴿so one of them may remind the other﴾, meaning, she reminds her whose testimony was nullified.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, he said: when they possess testimony.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi', who said: A man would go around among a large group inviting them to bear witness, and none of them would follow him, so Allah revealed: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'A'ishah concerning His saying: ﴿more just in the sight of Allah﴾, she said: more equitable.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And no scribe or witness should be harmed﴾, he said: A man comes to two men and invites them to write or to testify, and they say: "We have a need." He says: "Indeed you have been commanded to respond," so he has no right to harm them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Tawus: ﴿And no scribe should be harmed﴾, so that he writes what has not been dictated to him, and no witness should be harmed so that he testifies to what he was not asked to testify to.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾, the verse, he said: Whoever is on a journey and sells on credit to a term, and does not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand is permitted for him. If he finds a scribe, he is not permitted to take a pledge.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: Pledging is only during travel.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Pledging is only by taking possession.

al-Bukhari in his History, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Majah, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he recited this verse: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾ until he reached ﴿And if one of you entrusts another﴾, and said: This abrogated what came before it.

I say: may Allah be pleased with this noble Companion. This is not a case of abrogation (naskh), for this (ruling) is restricted to the case of trust (amanah), while what precedes it is established and definitive (muhkam), not abrogated, and it applies where there is no trust.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿آثِمٌ قَلْبُهُ﴾ ("its heart is sinful"), that he said: "its heart is wicked."

Ibn Jarir also reported with a sound chain of narration (isnad) from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that it reached him that the most recent of the Qur'an to come down from the Throne is the verse of debt.

Abu 'Ubayd reported in his Fada'il from Ibn Shihab, who said: "The last of the Qur'an to be given (to the Prophet) from the Throne is the verse of usury (riba) and the verse of debt."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 2, verse 284:

His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Its tafsir (exegesis) has already been given.

His saying: ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it...﴾ to the end of the verse. Its apparent meaning is that Allah calls the servants to account for what their selves harbour or reveal of the matters for which they are held accountable. So He forgives whom He wills among them what He forgives of them, and punishes whom He wills among them for what they have concealed or revealed. This is the meaning of the verse according to the requirements of the Arabic language.

The scholars differed concerning this verse, giving several opinions.

The first: although it is general, it is restricted to the concealment of testimony, and that whoever conceals testimony is held accountable for his concealment, whether or not he shows people that he is concealing testimony.

This has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbi and Mujahid. But it is rejected, because the wording of the verse is general, and what precedes this verse, the prohibition against concealing testimony, cannot make it specific to that.

The second opinion: what is in the verse is specific to the matters that arise in the souls that lie between doubt and certainty. This was said by Mujahid, but it is also a restriction without a restricting proof.

The third opinion: the verse is muhkam (clear, not abrogated) and general, but punishment for what is in the soul is specific to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Al-Tabari related this from a group of people. This too is a restriction without a restricting proof, since His saying ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ is not specific to a particular person unless there is evidence.

The fourth opinion: this verse is mansukh (abrogated). This was said by Ibn Masʿud, ʿAʾishah, Abu Hurayrah, al-Shaʿbi, ʿAtaʾ, Muhammad ibn Sirin, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Musa ibn ʿUbaydah. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group of the Companions and the Successors. This is the correct view, because of the explicit statement of its abrogation that will come, and because of what is established from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has forgiven this Ummah what its souls whisper to it."

His saying: ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾. He placed the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-l-majrur) before the subject to show concern for it. He placed showing (al-ibda') before concealing (al-ikhfa'), because the basic matters for which one is held accountable are visible deeds. As for placing concealing first in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: whether you conceal what is in your breasts or show it, Allah knows it﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:29), this is because knowledge relates equally to hidden and visible deeds. He placed forgiveness before punishment because His mercy precedes His wrath. The clause ﴿So He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah), meaning: so He forgives. It contains a detailed explanation of what was stated in summary in ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾. This is according to the reading of Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim.

As for the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisai, with the jazm (apocopate) on the rāʾ and the bāʾ, the fāʾ is conjunctive, linking what follows to the jussive form before it, which is the answer of the conditional, namely His saying ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿraj, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read with the naṣb (accusative) on the rāʾ and the bāʾ in His saying "فَيَغْفِرَ" and "ويُعَذِّبَ", with the particle "أنْ" implied, in coordination with the meaning.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "يَغْفِرُ" without the fāʾ, as a substitution (badal), and al-Juʿfi and Khallad read it this way too.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "When this was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you show what is in your selves...﴾ to the end of the verse, it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and then knelt on their knees and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we were charged with deeds we can bear: prayer, fasting, jihad and charity. Now Allah has revealed this verse to you, and we cannot bear it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do you want to say as the People of the Two Books before you said: "We hear and we disobey"? Rather say: ﴿We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the destination﴾' (al-Baqarah 2:285). When the people recited it and their tongues were made to submit to it, Allah revealed after it: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:285) to the end of the verse. When they did this, Allah abrogated it and revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286) to its end."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, with a marfuʿ (attributed to the Prophet) report similar to this, and added: Allah revealed ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make errors﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286). He said: "I have done so." ﴿Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed on those before us﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286). He said: "I have done so." ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286). He said: "I have done so." ﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy upon us﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286) to the end of the verse. He said: "I have done so."

This story has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas through several chains (turuq).

Al-Bukhari and al-Bayhaqi related from Marwan al-Asfar, from a man of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), I think it was Ibn ʿUmar, concerning ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it﴾, that he said: "It was abrogated by the verse that follows it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and al-Tirmidhi related from ʿAli something similar.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani related from Ibn Masʿud something similar.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAʾishah something similar too.

By the totality of what has preceded, the weakness becomes clear of what Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning this verse, that he said: "It was revealed concerning the concealment of testimony," for if it were so, the matter would not have weighed upon the Companions.

In any case, after these hadiths that explicitly state the abrogation and the abrogating verse, there is no room left for opposing them. What supports this is what is established in the two Sahihs and the four Sunan from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has overlooked for me, concerning my Ummah, what their souls whisper, so long as they do not speak it or act upon it."

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAʾishah that she said: "Every servant who intends evil or disobedience and whispers it to his soul, Allah will call him to account for it in this world; he will fear and grieve, and his concern will intensify, and nothing of that will reach him, just as he intended evil but did not act upon any of it."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related something similar from her, and the hadiths mentioned earlier that explicitly state the abrogation repel it.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: 'My scribes did not record of your deeds except what appeared of them. As for what you kept secret in your selves, I will call you to account for it today, so I forgive whom I will and punish whom I will.'" This is rejected by what has preceded.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 285–286 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿in what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾, meaning, in all that Allah sent down. "And the believers" is in apposition (*'atf*, coordination) to "the Messenger." His saying "each" means each of the Messenger and the believers. "Believed in Allah" may also be read as follows: "and the believers" is the *mubtada'* (subject), and "each" (*kullun*) is the second *mubtada'*, and "believed in Allah" is the *khabar* (predicate) of the second *mubtada'*. That whole clause is the *khabar* of the first *mubtada'*.

He used the singular pronoun in "believed in Allah," although it refers to all the believers, because the purpose is to state the faith of each individual among them, without considering them as a group, as is considered in His saying: ﴿and all come to Him humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87].

Al-Zajjaj said: When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in this surah the obligation of prayer and zakat, explained the rulings of the Hajj, the ruling on menstruation, divorce and *ila'* (oath of abstention from marital relations), the stories of the prophets, and the ruling on usury, He then glorified Himself by saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Then He mentioned the confirmation of His Prophet (ﷺ), and then the confirmation of the believers of all of that, saying: ﴿The Messenger has believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾, meaning the Messenger affirmed all these matters that have been mentioned. Likewise, all the believers affirmed Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers. It was also said: the cause of its revelation is the verse that precedes it. This has already been explained.

His saying "and His angels" means insofar as they are His honoured servants who mediate between Him and His prophets in the sending down of His books. His saying "and His books" is because they include the laws by which His servants worship Him. His saying "and His messengers" is because they are the ones who convey to His servants what was sent down to them.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir, read *wa-kutubihi* ("and His books") in the plural. In the chapter of *al-Tahrim* they read *wa-kitabihi* ("and His Book") in the singular. Ibn 'Abbas read *wa-kitabihi* here, and so did Hamza and al-Kisa'i. It is narrated from him that he said: "*al-Kitab* (the Book) is more comprehensive than *al-kutub* (the books)."

The author of *al-Kashshaf* explained this, saying: Because when the singular is intended as a genus (*jins*), and the quality of genus (*jinsiyyah*) is present in every individual of the genus, nothing is excluded from it. As for the plural, it does not include except those plural forms in which the quality of genus is present. End of quote.

Whoever wishes to verify this point should refer to the detailed commentary on *Talkhis al-Miftah* (*al-Mutawwal*), at the statement of the author of *Talkhis*: "and the inclusiveness of the singular noun is more comprehensive."

The majority read *wa-rusulihi* with a *damma* on the *sin* (*rusulihi*). Abu 'Amr read it with the *sin* lightened (*rusulihi*).

The majority read *la nufarriqu* with *nun* ("we do not differentiate"). The meaning is: they say, "We do not differentiate." Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Abu Zur'ah, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Jarir, and Ya'qub read *la yufarriqu* with *ya'* ("he does not differentiate").

His saying "between any one" and not "between any of them" (*bayna aahad* rather than *bayna ahad*-plural) is because *ahad* (any one) covers both the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿none of you could withhold Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]. He described it with "withholding" (*hajizin*), because it has the meaning of a plural. This clause may be in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause), or it may be another *khabar* to His saying "each."

His saying "among His messengers" uses the explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to guard against the assumption that the angels are included in the ruling, or to indicate the reason for not differentiating among them.

His saying: ﴿and they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ is coordinated with His saying "has believed." Although the verb "has believed" is singular and this one is plural, it is permissible, considering the sense. That is, we perceived it with our hearing and understood it, and we obey what is in it. It was also said: the meaning of "we hear" is "we answer your call."

His saying "Your forgiveness" (*ghufranaka*) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning: "grant us Your forgiveness." This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. They placed hearing and obedience before the request for forgiveness, because the means (*wasilah*) precedes what one seeks through it.

His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾. *Taklif* (burden) is the command to do what involves hardship and difficulty. *Wus'* (capacity) is ability. *Wus'* is that which contains a person and does not constrict him. This is an independent sentence that came after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], to relieve the distress of the Muslims and remove the hardship upon them regarding the obligation concerning what is within the self. It is like His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾. This contains encouragement and warning. That is: it has the reward of the good it earned, and upon it is the burden of the evil it earned. "It has" (*laha*) and "against it" (*alayha*) were placed before the two verbs to indicate that this belongs to it and not to another, and that it is upon it and not upon another. This is based on the view that *kasaba* is used only for good, and *iktasaba* only for evil, as stated by the author of *al-Kashshaf* and others. It was also said: each of the two verbs applies to both matters. The verb was repeated and the two conjugations were varied only to embellish the composition, as in His saying: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them respite, a little while﴾ [al-Tariq: 17].

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes﴾. That is: do not hold us accountable for the sin of what proceeds from us from these two matters.

Several exegetes and others found this supplication problematic, saying: error and forgetfulness are forgiven, and one is not held accountable for them, so what is the meaning of asking for that? It is then seeking what is already attained.

It was answered that what is intended is a request not to be held accountable for the causes that lead to forgetfulness and error, such as negligence and indifference, not for forgetfulness and error themselves, since there is no accountability for these, as His (ﷺ) saying indicates: "My nation has been relieved of error and forgetfulness," and its source will come. It was also said: it is permissible for a person to ask for something that he already has before the supplication, in order to seek its continuation. It was also said: even though it is established by the Law that one is not held accountable for these two, there is no impossibility, by reason, in being held accountable for them. It was also said: because they were on a great level of piety, such that sin would not proceed from them deliberately, but only by error or forgetfulness. So it is as if He described them by supplicating in this manner, as a declaration of the purity of their conduct from what they might be held accountable for. As if it were said: if forgetfulness and error were among the things for which one is held accountable, then there is no cause for accountability among them except error and forgetfulness.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement that sin is lifted. Disagreement concerns what follows from that regarding the rulings: is it lifted, with nothing necessitated by it, or are all the rulings of that necessitated? There is disagreement about this. The correct view is that it differs according to the cases. One category does not drop by agreement, such as financial penalties (*gharamat*), blood-money obligations (*diyat*), and the obligatory prayers. Another category drops by agreement, such as retaliation (*qisas*) and uttering a word of disbelief. A third category is disputed, such as one who eats while forgetful during Ramadan, or who breaks an oath inadvertently, and what is similar to that which happens by error or forgetfulness. This is known in the branches of jurisprudence. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (*isran*) like that which You laid upon those before us﴾ is coordinated with the sentence before it. Repeating the call (*nida'*) indicates greater humility and seeking refuge in Allah, glorified is He.

*Isr* (burden) is the heavy load that binds its bearer (*ya'sir sahibahu*), that is, holds him in place so that he cannot move because of its weight. What is meant here is the arduous obligation and the difficult, severe matter. It was also said: *isr* is the severity of the work and what was harsh upon the Children of Israel, such as killing oneself and cutting off the place of impurity. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*"O you who prevent oppression from reaching their nobles,
and who lift the burden from them after they had drowned."*

It was also said: *isr* is transformation into apes and swine. It was also said: *isr* is a covenant, and from this is His saying: ﴿and you accepted My covenant upon that﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]. This disagreement goes back to explaining what the *isr* was that was upon those before us, not to the meaning of *isr* in the Arabic language, for its meaning has already been mentioned without dispute. *Al-isar* is the rope with which loads and the like are tied. It is said: *asara ya'siru isran*, meaning he detained. *Al-isr* with a *kasra* on the *hamza* is derived from this.

Al-Jawhari said: The place is *ma'sir*, and the plural is *ma'sir*; the common people say *ma'sir* (with different vowels).

The meaning of the verse is that they asked Allah, glorified is He, not to place upon them from the weight of obligations what He placed upon the nations before them.

His saying "as You laid it" is an adjective (*sifah*) of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a laying like Your laying it upon those before us; or it is an adjective of *isran*, meaning: a burden like the burden that You laid upon those before us.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾ is likewise coordinated with what precedes it, and repeating the call is for the reason mentioned before this.

The meaning is: do not burden us with deeds that we cannot bear. It was also said: it is an expression for sending down punishments, as if He said: do not send down punishments upon us for our neglect in observing those arduous obligations with which You charged those before us. It was also said: what is meant is the difficult matter from the obligations that can hardly be borne.

In *al-Kashshaf* he said: This is a restatement of His saying: ﴿and do not lay upon us a burden﴾.

His saying: ﴿and pardon us﴾, that is, pardon our sins. It is said: *afa 'an dhanbihi* when you leave it and do not punish him for it. ﴿and forgive us﴾, that is, cover our sins; *al-ghafr* is covering. ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾, that is, bestow upon us Your mercy. ﴿You are our Protector (*mawlana*)﴾, that is, our Guardian and our Helper. This is presented as a lesson on how to supplicate. It was also said: its meaning is: You are our Master and we are Your servants. ﴿So give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾, for it is the right of a master to give victory to his servants. What is meant is all the disbelievers, and it contains an indication toward raising the word of Allah through jihad in His cause.

We have already mentioned, in explaining the verse before this one, namely His saying: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], etc., that it is established in the authentic collections from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah, the Exalted, said after each of these supplications: "I have done it." That was evidence that He, glorified is He, did not hold them accountable for anything of error or forgetfulness, did not lay upon them any of the burden He laid upon those before them, did not burden them with what they had no ability to bear, pardoned them, forgave them, had mercy upon them, and gave them victory over the disbelieving people. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan regarding ﴿We do not differentiate between any of His messengers﴾: we do not disbelieve in what the messengers brought, and we do not differentiate between any of them, and we do not deny Him. ﴿And they say, "We hear"﴾, meaning the Qur'an which came from Allah, ﴿and we obey﴾, they acknowledged to Allah that they would obey Him in His command and His prohibition.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾: He said: "I have forgiven you." ﴿And to You is the final destination﴾: He said: "To You is the return and the place of return on the Day when the Reckoning takes place."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hakim ibn Jabir, who said: "When the verse ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾ was revealed, Jibril said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Allah has praised you and your nation excellently, so ask and you will be given.' So he said: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, until he finished the surah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾: He said: "They are the believers. Allah made the matter of their religion easy for them, so He said: ﴿and He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and He said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and He said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾: He said: "From the deed."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿except its capacity﴾: He said: "except its ability." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih*, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my nation error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do."

Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Thawban, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it from his hadith.

Ibn 'Adi narrated it in *al-Kamil*, and Abu Nu'aym narrated it from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of Umm al-Darda'.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from the hadith of al-Hasan as a *mursal* (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain). 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from the hadith of al-Sha'bi as a *mursal*.

There is criticism of the chains of these hadiths, but some of them strengthen others, so they do not fall short of the rank of *hasan li-ghayrihi* (a hadith that is fair because of supporting narrations).

The hadith "Indeed God said: I have done it" has already been mentioned, and it is in the *Sahih*, and it bears witness to these hadiths. [p. 199]

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his statement, "*iṣran*" (a burden), that he said: "a covenant."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated the same from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Ibn Jurayj.

He also narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, regarding the verse ﴿and do not burden us with what we cannot bear﴾, that he said: "Do not transform us into apes and swine."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse that *al-isr* is the sin for which there is no repentance and no expiation.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Fudayl regarding the verse that he said: "A man from the Children of Israel, if he sinned, was told: 'Your repentance is that you kill yourself,' and he would kill himself. So these burdens were removed from this Community."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Ata' who said: "When these verses were revealed, ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task﴾ and so on, whenever Jibril recited them to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Prophet would say: 'Amin, Lord of the worlds.'"

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Maysarah that "Jibril taught the Prophet (ﷺ) the conclusion of *al-Baqarah*, and [the Prophet said] 'Amin.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that whenever he finished reciting this surah, he would say: "Amin."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr that he used to say: "Amin, amin."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Dharr who said: "They are specific to the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding this verse that he said: "The Prophet of God asked his Lord for them, and He gave them to him, so they were specific to the Prophet (ﷺ)."

It is established in the two *Shaykhs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim), the authors of the Sunan, and others, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* in a night, they will suffice him."

Abu 'Ubayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God wrote a Book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded *Surat al-Baqarah*. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil will not approach it."

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated with a sound chain from Hudhayfah that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I have been given these verses from the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* from a treasure beneath the Throne, which no prophet before me was given."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ahmad and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Recite these two verses from the end of *Surat al-Baqarah*, "The Messenger believes," to its end, for God chose Muhammad through them.'" Its chain is *hasan*.

Muslim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of *al-Baqarah*, and it was forgiven for whoever among his Community does not associate anything with God, the grave sins."

al-Hakim narrated, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* graded it sound, from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God concluded *Surat al-Baqarah* with two verses which He gave me from His treasure beneath the Throne. So learn them, and teach them to your women and your children, for they are prayer, Qur'an and supplication."

al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two things that are Qur'an and that heal, and that God loves: the two verses at the end of *al-Baqarah*."

al-Tabarani narrated with a good chain from Shaddad ibn Aws who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God wrote a Book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded *Surat al-Baqarah*. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil will not approach it."

Ibn 'Adi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud al-Ansari that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Merciful wrote with His hand two thousand years before He created creation. Whoever recites them after the late night prayer, they will suffice him for the night prayer."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* or the Verse of the Throne, he would smile and say: 'They are from a treasure beneath the Throne.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been given the Opening of the Book and the conclusions of *Surat al-Baqarah* from beneath the Throne."

Muslim and al-Nasa'i narrated, and the wording is his, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was with Jibril, he heard a sound, so Jibril raised his eyes and said: 'This is a gate that has been opened from heaven, which has never been opened before.' Then an angel descended from it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that you have been given, which no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book and the conclusions of *Surat al-Baqarah*. You will not recite a letter from them except that you will be given it.'"

So these are thirteen hadiths concerning the virtue of these two verses, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It has also been narrated concerning their virtue, from non-traced (non-prophetic) reports, from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, al-Hasan and Abu Qilabah. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) is sufficient without the others.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 2, verses 285–286 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿in what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾, meaning, in all that Allah sent down. "And the believers" is in apposition (*'atf*, coordination) to "the Messenger." His saying "each" means each of the Messenger and the believers. "Believed in Allah" may also be read as follows: "and the believers" is the *mubtada'* (subject), and "each" (*kullun*) is the second *mubtada'*, and "believed in Allah" is the *khabar* (predicate) of the second *mubtada'*. That whole clause is the *khabar* of the first *mubtada'*.

He used the singular pronoun in "believed in Allah," although it refers to all the believers, because the purpose is to state the faith of each individual among them, without considering them as a group, as is considered in His saying: ﴿and all come to Him humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87].

Al-Zajjaj said: When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in this surah the obligation of prayer and zakat, explained the rulings of the Hajj, the ruling on menstruation, divorce and *ila'* (oath of abstention from marital relations), the stories of the prophets, and the ruling on usury, He then glorified Himself by saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Then He mentioned the confirmation of His Prophet (ﷺ), and then the confirmation of the believers of all of that, saying: ﴿The Messenger has believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾, meaning the Messenger affirmed all these matters that have been mentioned. Likewise, all the believers affirmed Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers. It was also said: the cause of its revelation is the verse that precedes it. This has already been explained.

His saying "and His angels" means insofar as they are His honoured servants who mediate between Him and His prophets in the sending down of His books. His saying "and His books" is because they include the laws by which His servants worship Him. His saying "and His messengers" is because they are the ones who convey to His servants what was sent down to them.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir, read *wa-kutubihi* ("and His books") in the plural. In the chapter of *al-Tahrim* they read *wa-kitabihi* ("and His Book") in the singular. Ibn 'Abbas read *wa-kitabihi* here, and so did Hamza and al-Kisa'i. It is narrated from him that he said: "*al-Kitab* (the Book) is more comprehensive than *al-kutub* (the books)."

The author of *al-Kashshaf* explained this, saying: Because when the singular is intended as a genus (*jins*), and the quality of genus (*jinsiyyah*) is present in every individual of the genus, nothing is excluded from it. As for the plural, it does not include except those plural forms in which the quality of genus is present. End of quote.

Whoever wishes to verify this point should refer to the detailed commentary on *Talkhis al-Miftah* (*al-Mutawwal*), at the statement of the author of *Talkhis*: "and the inclusiveness of the singular noun is more comprehensive."

The majority read *wa-rusulihi* with a *damma* on the *sin* (*rusulihi*). Abu 'Amr read it with the *sin* lightened (*rusulihi*).

The majority read *la nufarriqu* with *nun* ("we do not differentiate"). The meaning is: they say, "We do not differentiate." Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Abu Zur'ah, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Jarir, and Ya'qub read *la yufarriqu* with *ya'* ("he does not differentiate").

His saying "between any one" and not "between any of them" (*bayna aahad* rather than *bayna ahad*-plural) is because *ahad* (any one) covers both the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿none of you could withhold Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]. He described it with "withholding" (*hajizin*), because it has the meaning of a plural. This clause may be in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause), or it may be another *khabar* to His saying "each."

His saying "among His messengers" uses the explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to guard against the assumption that the angels are included in the ruling, or to indicate the reason for not differentiating among them.

His saying: ﴿and they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ is coordinated with His saying "has believed." Although the verb "has believed" is singular and this one is plural, it is permissible, considering the sense. That is, we perceived it with our hearing and understood it, and we obey what is in it. It was also said: the meaning of "we hear" is "we answer your call."

His saying "Your forgiveness" (*ghufranaka*) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning: "grant us Your forgiveness." This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. They placed hearing and obedience before the request for forgiveness, because the means (*wasilah*) precedes what one seeks through it.

His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾. *Taklif* (burden) is the command to do what involves hardship and difficulty. *Wus'* (capacity) is ability. *Wus'* is that which contains a person and does not constrict him. This is an independent sentence that came after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], to relieve the distress of the Muslims and remove the hardship upon them regarding the obligation concerning what is within the self. It is like His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾. This contains encouragement and warning. That is: it has the reward of the good it earned, and upon it is the burden of the evil it earned. "It has" (*laha*) and "against it" (*alayha*) were placed before the two verbs to indicate that this belongs to it and not to another, and that it is upon it and not upon another. This is based on the view that *kasaba* is used only for good, and *iktasaba* only for evil, as stated by the author of *al-Kashshaf* and others. It was also said: each of the two verbs applies to both matters. The verb was repeated and the two conjugations were varied only to embellish the composition, as in His saying: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them respite, a little while﴾ [al-Tariq: 17].

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes﴾. That is: do not hold us accountable for the sin of what proceeds from us from these two matters.

Several exegetes and others found this supplication problematic, saying: error and forgetfulness are forgiven, and one is not held accountable for them, so what is the meaning of asking for that? It is then seeking what is already attained.

It was answered that what is intended is a request not to be held accountable for the causes that lead to forgetfulness and error, such as negligence and indifference, not for forgetfulness and error themselves, since there is no accountability for these, as His (ﷺ) saying indicates: "My nation has been relieved of error and forgetfulness," and its source will come. It was also said: it is permissible for a person to ask for something that he already has before the supplication, in order to seek its continuation. It was also said: even though it is established by the Law that one is not held accountable for these two, there is no impossibility, by reason, in being held accountable for them. It was also said: because they were on a great level of piety, such that sin would not proceed from them deliberately, but only by error or forgetfulness. So it is as if He described them by supplicating in this manner, as a declaration of the purity of their conduct from what they might be held accountable for. As if it were said: if forgetfulness and error were among the things for which one is held accountable, then there is no cause for accountability among them except error and forgetfulness.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement that sin is lifted. Disagreement concerns what follows from that regarding the rulings: is it lifted, with nothing necessitated by it, or are all the rulings of that necessitated? There is disagreement about this. The correct view is that it differs according to the cases. One category does not drop by agreement, such as financial penalties (*gharamat*), blood-money obligations (*diyat*), and the obligatory prayers. Another category drops by agreement, such as retaliation (*qisas*) and uttering a word of disbelief. A third category is disputed, such as one who eats while forgetful during Ramadan, or who breaks an oath inadvertently, and what is similar to that which happens by error or forgetfulness. This is known in the branches of jurisprudence. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (*isran*) like that which You laid upon those before us﴾ is coordinated with the sentence before it. Repeating the call (*nida'*) indicates greater humility and seeking refuge in Allah, glorified is He.

*Isr* (burden) is the heavy load that binds its bearer (*ya'sir sahibahu*), that is, holds him in place so that he cannot move because of its weight. What is meant here is the arduous obligation and the difficult, severe matter. It was also said: *isr* is the severity of the work and what was harsh upon the Children of Israel, such as killing oneself and cutting off the place of impurity. From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

*"O you who prevent oppression from reaching their nobles,
and who lift the burden from them after they had drowned."*

It was also said: *isr* is transformation into apes and swine. It was also said: *isr* is a covenant, and from this is His saying: ﴿and you accepted My covenant upon that﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]. This disagreement goes back to explaining what the *isr* was that was upon those before us, not to the meaning of *isr* in the Arabic language, for its meaning has already been mentioned without dispute. *Al-isar* is the rope with which loads and the like are tied. It is said: *asara ya'siru isran*, meaning he detained. *Al-isr* with a *kasra* on the *hamza* is derived from this.

Al-Jawhari said: The place is *ma'sir*, and the plural is *ma'sir*; the common people say *ma'sir* (with different vowels).

The meaning of the verse is that they asked Allah, glorified is He, not to place upon them from the weight of obligations what He placed upon the nations before them.

His saying "as You laid it" is an adjective (*sifah*) of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a laying like Your laying it upon those before us; or it is an adjective of *isran*, meaning: a burden like the burden that You laid upon those before us.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾ is likewise coordinated with what precedes it, and repeating the call is for the reason mentioned before this.

The meaning is: do not burden us with deeds that we cannot bear. It was also said: it is an expression for sending down punishments, as if He said: do not send down punishments upon us for our neglect in observing those arduous obligations with which You charged those before us. It was also said: what is meant is the difficult matter from the obligations that can hardly be borne.

In *al-Kashshaf* he said: This is a restatement of His saying: ﴿and do not lay upon us a burden﴾.

His saying: ﴿and pardon us﴾, that is, pardon our sins. It is said: *afa 'an dhanbihi* when you leave it and do not punish him for it. ﴿and forgive us﴾, that is, cover our sins; *al-ghafr* is covering. ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾, that is, bestow upon us Your mercy. ﴿You are our Protector (*mawlana*)﴾, that is, our Guardian and our Helper. This is presented as a lesson on how to supplicate. It was also said: its meaning is: You are our Master and we are Your servants. ﴿So give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾, for it is the right of a master to give victory to his servants. What is meant is all the disbelievers, and it contains an indication toward raising the word of Allah through jihad in His cause.

We have already mentioned, in explaining the verse before this one, namely His saying: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], etc., that it is established in the authentic collections from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah, the Exalted, said after each of these supplications: "I have done it." That was evidence that He, glorified is He, did not hold them accountable for anything of error or forgetfulness, did not lay upon them any of the burden He laid upon those before them, did not burden them with what they had no ability to bear, pardoned them, forgave them, had mercy upon them, and gave them victory over the disbelieving people. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan regarding ﴿We do not differentiate between any of His messengers﴾: we do not disbelieve in what the messengers brought, and we do not differentiate between any of them, and we do not deny Him. ﴿And they say, "We hear"﴾, meaning the Qur'an which came from Allah, ﴿and we obey﴾, they acknowledged to Allah that they would obey Him in His command and His prohibition.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾: He said: "I have forgiven you." ﴿And to You is the final destination﴾: He said: "To You is the return and the place of return on the Day when the Reckoning takes place."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hakim ibn Jabir, who said: "When the verse ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾ was revealed, Jibril said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Allah has praised you and your nation excellently, so ask and you will be given.' So he said: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, until he finished the surah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾: He said: "They are the believers. Allah made the matter of their religion easy for them, so He said: ﴿and He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and He said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and He said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾: He said: "From the deed."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿except its capacity﴾: He said: "except its ability." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih*, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my nation error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do."

Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Thawban, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it from his hadith.

Ibn 'Adi narrated it in *al-Kamil*, and Abu Nu'aym narrated it from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of Umm al-Darda'.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from the hadith of al-Hasan as a *mursal* (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain). 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from the hadith of al-Sha'bi as a *mursal*.

There is criticism of the chains of these hadiths, but some of them strengthen others, so they do not fall short of the rank of *hasan li-ghayrihi* (a hadith that is fair because of supporting narrations).

The hadith "Indeed God said: I have done it" has already been mentioned, and it is in the *Sahih*, and it bears witness to these hadiths. [p. 199]

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his statement, "*iṣran*" (a burden), that he said: "a covenant."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated the same from Mujahid.

Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Ibn Jurayj.

He also narrated from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, regarding the verse ﴿and do not burden us with what we cannot bear﴾, that he said: "Do not transform us into apes and swine."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse that *al-isr* is the sin for which there is no repentance and no expiation.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Fudayl regarding the verse that he said: "A man from the Children of Israel, if he sinned, was told: 'Your repentance is that you kill yourself,' and he would kill himself. So these burdens were removed from this Community."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Ata' who said: "When these verses were revealed, ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task﴾ and so on, whenever Jibril recited them to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Prophet would say: 'Amin, Lord of the worlds.'"

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Maysarah that "Jibril taught the Prophet (ﷺ) the conclusion of *al-Baqarah*, and [the Prophet said] 'Amin.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that whenever he finished reciting this surah, he would say: "Amin."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr that he used to say: "Amin, amin."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Dharr who said: "They are specific to the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding this verse that he said: "The Prophet of God asked his Lord for them, and He gave them to him, so they were specific to the Prophet (ﷺ)."

It is established in the two *Shaykhs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim), the authors of the Sunan, and others, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* in a night, they will suffice him."

Abu 'Ubayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God wrote a Book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded *Surat al-Baqarah*. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil will not approach it."

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated with a sound chain from Hudhayfah that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I have been given these verses from the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* from a treasure beneath the Throne, which no prophet before me was given."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ahmad and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Recite these two verses from the end of *Surat al-Baqarah*, "The Messenger believes," to its end, for God chose Muhammad through them.'" Its chain is *hasan*.

Muslim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of *al-Baqarah*, and it was forgiven for whoever among his Community does not associate anything with God, the grave sins."

al-Hakim narrated, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* graded it sound, from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God concluded *Surat al-Baqarah* with two verses which He gave me from His treasure beneath the Throne. So learn them, and teach them to your women and your children, for they are prayer, Qur'an and supplication."

al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two things that are Qur'an and that heal, and that God loves: the two verses at the end of *al-Baqarah*."

al-Tabarani narrated with a good chain from Shaddad ibn Aws who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God wrote a Book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded *Surat al-Baqarah*. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil will not approach it."

Ibn 'Adi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud al-Ansari that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Merciful wrote with His hand two thousand years before He created creation. Whoever recites them after the late night prayer, they will suffice him for the night prayer."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited the end of *Surat al-Baqarah* or the Verse of the Throne, he would smile and say: 'They are from a treasure beneath the Throne.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been given the Opening of the Book and the conclusions of *Surat al-Baqarah* from beneath the Throne."

Muslim and al-Nasa'i narrated, and the wording is his, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was with Jibril, he heard a sound, so Jibril raised his eyes and said: 'This is a gate that has been opened from heaven, which has never been opened before.' Then an angel descended from it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that you have been given, which no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book and the conclusions of *Surat al-Baqarah*. You will not recite a letter from them except that you will be given it.'"

So these are thirteen hadiths concerning the virtue of these two verses, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It has also been narrated concerning their virtue, from non-traced (non-prophetic) reports, from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Mas'ud, Ka'b al-Ahbar, al-Hasan and Abu Qilabah. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) is sufficient without the others.
